## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## (Volume I)
## Prologue

1. The Blessed One who has transcended the entire world of beings and the world of formations, who is endowed with all perfections and all sublime qualities. He is liberated from all defilements along with their latent tendencies (vāsana). He also bestows the supreme fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna.

2. He whose mind is always cooled by the sandalwood water of compassion. He whose objects of knowledge (neyyadhamma) are illuminated by the sun of wisdom. Having bowed my head to that Blessed One, the foremost among all beings, known as the Protector (Nātha) in the true sense.

3. The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), who, apart from the Buddha, is the most supreme among all beings. Among the infinite number of the Buddha's sons (disciples), he followed the Buddha's example in working for the welfare of all beings through the virtues of compassion and wisdom.

4. The son of the Brahmin lady Sārī, the heart-son of the King of Dhamma (the Buddha), who is beautiful with many firm virtues such as morality (sīla). His fame and reputation spread through the power of his wisdom, and he possessed well-calmed conduct. I also pay homage to that Great Elder Sāriputta.

5. He who caused the Wheel of Dhamma—consisting of the excellent scriptures (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha)—to turn in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; who is the leader of the army of the Good Dhamma; who attained the realization of the true meaning in the Sutta texts taught by the Buddha...
2:
He who caused the Wheel of the Good Dhamma to continue, the disciple of the General of the Good Dhamma, who reached the knowledge of the true meaning in the Sutta discourses.

The excellent Pali text, which was spoken by that Elder who was skilled in speaking and was a leader who lit the lamp of Dhamma, and which is specifically named "Paṭisambhidāmagga" because it is the path to attaining the discriminations (paṭisambhidā).

It is filled with various and wonderful methods, always delved into by those of profound wisdom, and constantly resorted to by good people who desire their own benefit and the benefit of the world.

While explaining the unprecedented meaning of that Pali text, which brings about various types of knowledge and is practiced by many yogis, following the sequence of the Suttas and logic.

Without departing from my own tradition and without disparaging the traditions of others, and combining the methods of the ancient teachers' instructions and commentaries as appropriate.

I shall respectfully write this commentary named "Saddhammappakāsinī" for the benefit of the people and for the long-lasting endurance of the Good Dhamma. May the virtuous listen to and remember this commentary well.

In those verses, because it is said, "It is specifically designated by that name because it is the path to attaining the discriminations," the nature of the Paṭisambhidāmagga as the "Path of Discriminations" should first be explained. There are four discriminations: the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the discrimination of ideas (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the discrimination of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the discrimination of perspicacity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā). It is called "Paṭisambhidāmagga" because it is the path to attainment (adhigamūpāya) or the cause for the acquisition of those discriminations. How is this teaching the path to them? Because it is a teaching taught in detail, it brings about the knowledge of the discriminations.
3:
Indeed, the teaching that is divided into various parts produces the various types of knowledge of discrimination in the noble persons (ariya) who listen to it. For worldlings (puthujjana), it serves as a condition for the future arising of the various types of knowledge of discrimination. It is also stated in the commentaries: "A teaching given in detail brings about the knowledge of discrimination that analyzes the compact (ghana)." Since this teaching is divided into various parts, its status as the cause (path) for the knowledges of discrimination is established.

In that context, "four" is a numerical delimitation. "Paṭisambhidā" means divisions (of knowledge). Because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Knowledge regarding the meaning is the discrimination of meaning; knowledge regarding the ideas is the discrimination of ideas; knowledge regarding the linguistic expression of those ideas is the discrimination of language; knowledge regarding the knowledges is the discrimination of perspicacity," it is not a division of anything else, but a division of knowledge itself. Therefore, "four discriminations" means four divisions of knowledge.

The knowledge that has reached the division into the five meanings (results), which is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the divisions of meaning, is called the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā). The knowledge that has reached the division into the five ideas (causes), which is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the divisions of ideas, is called the discrimination of ideas (dhammapaṭisambhidā). The knowledge that has reached the division into the sounds that express the meaning and the ideas, which is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the divisions of language, is called the discrimination of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā). The knowledge that has reached the division into the previous three knowledges, which is capable of noting, clarifying, and defining the divisions of perspicacity, is called the discrimination of perspicacity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).

Among those four, "Attha" (meaning/result) is, in brief, the fruit of a cause. Because that fruit is reached, understood, and attained in accordance with the cause, it is called "Attha". In detail, however, these five things should be understood as "Attha": whatever is produced by conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant consciousness (vipāka), and functional consciousness (kiriya). For one who contemplates those five meanings, the knowledge that has reached the division within those meanings is called the discrimination of meaning.

"Dhamma" (idea/cause) is, in brief, the condition. Because it arranges, sets in motion, and leads to various results, it is called "Dhamma". In detail, however, these five things should be understood as "Dhamma": any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path, the spoken Pali text, wholesome consciousness (kusala), and unwholesome consciousness (akusala). For one who contemplates those five causes, the knowledge that has reached the division within those causes is called the discrimination of ideas. This same meaning is stated in the Abhidhamma: "Knowledge regarding suffering is the discrimination of meaning; knowledge regarding the origin of suffering is the discrimination of ideas; knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering is the discrimination of meaning; knowledge regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering..."
4:
Knowledge is called Dhammapaṭisambhidā. Knowledge of causes is Dhammapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the effects of causes is Atthapaṭisambhidā. Whatever states have arisen, come to be, been produced, been generated, been manifested—knowledge of these effects is Atthapaṭisambhidā. The causes from which those states have arisen, come to be, been produced, been generated, been manifested—knowledge of those causes is Dhammapaṭisambhidā.

Knowledge of aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) is Atthapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of birth (jāti), which is the cause of aging and death, is Dhammapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death, is Atthapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the Path (magga), which is the practice leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death, is Dhammapaṭisambhidā. Knowledge of birth... (similarly) ...knowledge of existence... knowledge of clinging... knowledge of craving... knowledge of feeling... knowledge of contact... knowledge of the six bases... knowledge of name-and-form... knowledge of consciousness... knowledge of volitional formations (saṅkhāra) is Atthapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of ignorance (avijjā), which is the cause of formations, is Dhammapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of Nibbāna, which is the cessation of formations, is Atthapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the Path, which is the practice leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of formations, is Dhammapaṭisambhidā.

In this Dispensation, a monk knows the Dhamma—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. This knowledge is called Dhammapaṭisambhidā. He knows the meaning of those various spoken Pali texts: 'This is the meaning of this Pali text; this is the meaning of that Pali text.' This knowledge is called Atthapaṭisambhidā.

Which states are wholesome (kusala)? At a time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) has arisen, accompanied by joy (somanassa), associated with knowledge, having a form as object... or a mental state as object, or whatever object it may be—at that time there is contact (phassa)... there is non-distraction (avikkhepa/samādhi). These states are wholesome. Knowledge of these wholesome states is Dhammapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of their result (vipāka) is Atthapaṭisambhidā. Thus it is shown by analyzing repeatedly.

Among those [four analytical knowledges], regarding the knowledge of the expression of the language of the Dhamma (dhammaniruttābhilāpa): there is a natural language (sabhāvanirutti), an unerring usage, regarding those effects and causes. In the expression and speaking of that usage...
5:
...uttered by mouth, recited by others, spoken, or expressed—for one who contemplates by taking that natural linguistic sound (sabhāvaniruttisadda) ending in a case-ending as an object, the knowledge that differentiates within that natural language (sabhāvanirutti), which is the Māgadhī language, the root language of all beings, and is marked as dhammanirutti, thinking 'This sound is natural language, this sound is not natural language'—this is called Niruttipaṭisambhidā. Thus, this Niruttipaṭisambhidā arises with sound as its object, not concepts (paññatti). Why? Because upon hearing the linguistic sound, one knows: 'This sound is natural language, this sound is not natural language.'

Indeed, one who has attained the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), when 'Phasso' is uttered, knows: 'This sound is natural language.' But when 'Phassā' or 'Phassaṃ' is uttered, he knows: 'This sound is not natural language.' The same method applies to terms like feeling (vedanā) and so on. Furthermore, does this person know or not know the sounds of nouns, verbs, prefixes, particles, and consonants other than those of the Māgadhī language? Since he knows 'This sound is natural language, this sound is not natural language' upon hearing the sound, he will also know those other languages [by learning them]. However, such knowledge is rejected as not being the function of paṭisambhidā knowledge, and it is said: 'Beings learn languages.' This is explained as follows:

Truly, when parents are young, they lay their small sons on a couch or a bench and perform various tasks while speaking various words. The children note those various languages of the parents, thinking: 'By this word, this meaning is expressed; by that word, that meaning is expressed.' As time passes, they know the entire language. If the mother is a Damiḷa and the father is an Andhaka, the child born to them will speak the Damiḷa language if he hears the mother's speech first. If he hears the father's speech first, he will speak the Andhaka language. But if he does not hear the speech of either parent, he will speak the Māgadhī language.

Even a child born in a great forest where there is no village, and there is no one else to speak there, will speak only the Māgadhī language when he produces speech by his own nature. In all worlds—hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, the human world, and the deva world—the Māgadhī language alone is prevalent. There, the remaining languages such as Oṭṭa, Kirāta, Andhaka, Yonaka, and Damiḷa change and deviate. Only this one Māgadhī language, known as the true Brahmavohāra (Brahma usage) and Ariyavohāra (Noble usage), does not change. Even the Fully Enlightened One, when setting down the Buddha's word of the Tipitaka into Pali, did so only in the Māgadhī language. Why? Because setting it down in this way makes it easy to convey the meaning. For the Buddha's word set down in Pali through the Māgadhī language, its mere arrival at the ear-door of those who have attained the paṭisambhidā...
6:
Proliferation (papañca) means merely reaching the state of being an object of ear-consciousness. Just by the impact (of sound) at the ear-door, the meaning appears in hundreds and thousands of ways. In other languages, however, the Pāli text must be studied by repeatedly striking (laboriously learning). Even if one learns much, there is no such thing as a worldling (puthujjana) reaching the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); yet, there is no noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who has not reached the analytical knowledges.

'Knowledge of knowledges' refers to the knowledge that reaches differentiation within that knowledge for one who reflects by making the knowledge occurring in all objects the object. Alternatively, the knowledge that reaches expansion by way of object, function, etc., in those three aforementioned knowledges is called the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).

These four analytical knowledges reach differentiation in two stages and should be known to become clear through five causes. In which two stages do they reach differentiation? In the stage of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi) and the stage of the non-trainee (asekkhabhūmi). Therein, the analytical knowledges of the eighty great elders, such as the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Mahākaccāyana, and the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita, reach differentiation in the stage of the non-trainee. The analytical knowledges of such persons as the Elder Ānanda, Citta the householder, Dhammika the lay follower, Upāli the householder, and Khujjuttarā the lay follower reach differentiation in the stage of the trainee. Thus, they reach differentiation in these two stages.

Through which five causes do they become clear? Through attainment (adhigama), learning (pariyatti), hearing (savana), inquiry (paripucchā), and previous effort (pubbayoga). Therein, attainment means the reaching of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala). For one who has reached Arahantship, the analytical knowledges become clear. Learning means the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana). For one who learns that word of the Buddha, the analytical knowledges become clear. Hearing means hearing the true Dhamma (saddhammasavana). For one who listens to the Dhamma respectfully and attentively, the analytical knowledges become clear. Inquiry means the discussion for deciding the meaning of difficult words and passages in the Pāli, commentaries, and so forth. For one who inquires about the meaning in the learned Pāli and so forth, the analytical knowledges become clear. Previous effort means the practice of insight (vipassanā) reaching as far as the vicinity of conformity (anuloma) and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) knowledge, while carrying the meditation subject back and forth (gatapaccāgatika) through being a practitioner in the dispensation of previous Buddhas. For one who has made previous effort, the analytical knowledges become clear. They become clear through these five causes.

Among these causes, these three—learning, hearing, and inquiry—are the powerful causes for differentiation (pabheda) alone. Previous effort is the powerful condition for attainment (adhigama).
7:
Does the cause for the analytical knowledge of differentiation occur or not? It does occur, but not in that way (as a partial cause). Whether learning the scriptures, hearing the Dhamma, and inquiring into the decisions occurred in the past or not, there is no such thing as attaining analytical knowledge without the comprehension of formations (saṅkhārasammasana) in the past and in the present through previous effort. These two (previous effort and attainment), being combined, support the analytical knowledges and make them clear. Other teachers say:

“Previous effort, great learning, knowledge of local dialects, scriptural tradition,
Inquiry, attainment, reliance on a teacher,
And success in friendship—these are the conditions for analytical knowledge.”

Among those eight, previous effort is just as previously described. Great learning (bāhusacca) means proficiency in various sciences and arts. Knowledge of local dialects (desabhāsā) means proficiency in the expressions of the hundred and one races, especially skill in the Magadhan language (māgadhabhāsā). Scriptural tradition (āgama) means learning the word of the Buddha, even as little as the Opammavagga. Inquiry (paripucchā) means inquiring into the decision of the meaning even in a single verse. Attainment (adhigama) means the state of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an Arahant. Reliance on a teacher (garusannissaya) means living in the presence of teachers who are rich in learning and perspicuity. Success in friendship (mittasampatti) means obtaining such good friends.

Among those causes, the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas reach analytical knowledge by relying only on previous effort and attainment. Disciples, however, reach it by relying on all these causes. There is no separate practice of meditation for the sake of reaching analytical knowledge. For trainees, the reaching of analytical knowledge occurs at the end of the trainee-fruition (sekkhaphala); for non-trainees, it occurs at the end of the non-trainee-fruition (asekkhaphala). Just as the ten powers of the Tathāgatas are perfected by the noble fruits, so too for the noble ones, the analytical knowledges are perfected by the noble fruits alone. Because it is the path to these four analytical knowledges, it is called the 'Path of Analytical Knowledge' (Paṭisambhidāmagga). The Paṭisambhidāmagga itself, being a treatise, is called the 'Paṭisambhidāmagga-ppakaraṇa'. It is called a treatise (pakaraṇa) because profound meanings of various kinds are explained therein in detail.

This very Paṭisambhidāmagga treatise is perfect in meaning, perfect in phrasing, profound, has profound meaning, illuminates the supramundane, is connected with emptiness (suññatā), achieves the distinction of the fruit of practice, prevents states contrary to practice, is the standing place for the noble jewel of the yogis' knowledge, is the cause for the distinguished quality of being able to flourish in the preaching of the Dhamma by preachers, has the benefit of producing relief in Nibbāna—the escape from suffering—by showing the path that is the cause of that Nibbāna for those who fear the danger of saṃsāra, has the benefit of destroying states contrary to that Nibbāna, and has the benefit of greatly pleasing the hearts of the virtuous by explaining the meaning of many sutta passages that have profound meanings. The Buddha, with the great light of the lamp of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) which is unobstructed in all things, [dispelled] the states such as ignorance...
8:
This treatise, the Paṭisambhidāmagga, is perfect in meaning and perfect in phrasing. (Alternatively, it is endowed with the six aspects of meaning such as saṅkāsana and pakāsana, and the six aspects of phrasing such as akkhara and pada.) It possesses depth of meaning through the depth of the Dhamma and the depth of the teaching, and it has profound meaning by virtue of the depth of penetration (paṭivedha-gambhīra). It points to the supramundane Dhamma and is associated with the Path of Emptiness (suññata-magga) and the Nibbāna of Emptiness (suññata-nibbāna). It makes known the special fruits of practice and prohibits opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). It is the mine of the precious jewel of knowledge for practitioners (yogāvacara). It is the cause for the special excellence in the eloquence of Dhamma preachers (or commentators).

For those who fear the danger of Saṃsāra, it provides relief by showing the Path that leads to Nibbāna, the escape from suffering. It serves the purpose of destroying the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) and the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), which are the opposites of Nibbāna and the Path. It also delights the hearts of the virtuous by explaining the meaning of many Suttas with profound significance.

The Blessed One—the Well-Gone (Sugata), the Worthy One (Arahat), who possesses the great lamp-light of unimpeded omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) regarding all knowable things, whose heart is softened by the moisture of great compassion (mahākaruṇā) pervading all beings—in order to dispel the darkness of defilements (kilesa) in the hearts of those to be tamed (veneyya), He poured the oil of various meanings of the Pariyatti Saddhamma into the great lamp of the Pariyatti Saddhamma, wishing it to burn continuously for five thousand years. Out of compassion for the world, the Venerable Sāriputta, who is like the Teacher (the Buddha) and is the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) to the King of Dhamma, spoke this Paṭisambhidāmagga. Having heard it, the Venerable Ānanda recited it at the time of the First Great Council exactly as he had heard it.

Among the three baskets—the Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka—this treatise is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Among the five great Nikāyas—Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the Teacher’s Dispensation—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—it is categorized under Geyya and Veyyākaraṇa as appropriate.

"I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; these eighty-four thousand teachings are current in me" (Theragāthā 1027). Among the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups (dhammakkhandha) acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda—who was designated as the foremost (etadagga) in five positions—this treatise is counted among the many hundreds of Dhamma-groups within the two thousand Dhamma-groups learned from the monks. In this treatise, there are three divisions (vagga): the Mahāvagga, Majjhimavagga, and Cūḷavagga. In each division, there are ten discourses, making a total of thirty discourses starting from the Ñāṇakathā and ending with the Mātikākathā. Thus, we shall explain the meanings of the new terms in this Paṭisambhidāmagga, which is defined in various ways, in their proper order. Indeed, those who present this treatise in brief or in detail, whether by text or by meaning, should do so respectfully. The student who learns it should also learn and retain it respectfully. Why? Because this treatise is profound. It should be presented in brief and in detail, learned, and retained so that it may endure for a long time in the world for the welfare of all beings.
9:
(This treatise) should be respectfully learned and retained. Why is that? Because this treatise is profound and for the purpose of its long endurance in the world for the welfare of all beings.

Among the thirty discourses in this Paṭisambhidāmagga, if it is asked why the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā) is taught at the beginning: it is taught at the beginning because knowledge purifies the stains of practice and because it is the starting point of practice. The Blessed One also said this:

"Therefore, bhikkhu, you should purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is well-purified virtue (sīla) and straight view (diṭṭhi)" (stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

"Straight view" refers to the knowledge known as Right View (sammādiṭṭhi). For this reason also, the Discourse on Knowledge is taught at the beginning.

In another teaching, He also said:
"Therein, bhikkhus, Right View is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is Right View the forerunner? One understands right view as 'right view' and wrong view as 'wrong view.' This is one's Right View. One understands right intention as 'right intention' and wrong intention as 'wrong intention.' One understands right speech as 'right speech' and wrong speech as 'wrong speech.' One understands right action as 'right action' and wrong action as 'wrong action.' One understands right livelihood as 'right livelihood' and wrong livelihood as 'wrong livelihood.' One understands right effort as 'right effort' and wrong effort as 'wrong effort.' One understands right mindfulness as 'right mindfulness' and wrong mindfulness as 'wrong mindfulness.' One understands right concentration as 'right concentration' and wrong concentration as 'wrong concentration.' This is one's Right View" (stated in the Majjhima Nikāya).

When Right View, which is the forerunner, is established, one will also be able to know the nature of wrong views as wrong views. Therefore, the Discourse on Knowledge is taught at the beginning in order to first purify the knowledge known as Right View.
10:
"Udāyi, let the past (the former end) be, let the future (the latter end) be. I will teach you the Dhamma: 'When this (ignorance) exists, this (volitional formation) comes to be; with the arising of this (ignorance), this (volitional formation) arises. When this (ignorance) does not exist, this (volitional formation) does not come to be; with the cessation of this (ignorance), this (volitional formation) ceases.'" (M. Ni. 2.271)

Setting aside the views that run after the past and the future, because only knowledge is spoken of, the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā) is taught from the beginning.

"Subhadda, let this question be: 'Have all those (sectarians such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, etc.), according to their own claim, realized (the truth), or have they all not realized it, or have some realized it and some not?' Subhadda, I will teach you the Dhamma. Listen well to that Dhamma and pay close attention; I will speak." (Dī. Ni. 2.213)

Setting aside the doctrines of many recluses and brahmins of other views, because the Noble Eightfold Path is taught, and because in the Noble Eightfold Path, the knowledge known as Right View is predominant, the Discourse on Knowledge is taught from the beginning.

"Monks, these four are the factors of stream-entry: association with superior persons, hearing the True Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1046, Dī. Ni. 3.311)

"One who has gained faith approaches (a teacher); approaching, he attends; attending, he lends an ear; lending an ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he remembers it; he examines the meaning of the remembered teachings with wisdom; while examining the meaning, the teachings are accepted through reflection; with acceptance through reflection, desire (to practice) arises; when desire has arisen, he exerts effort; having exerted effort, he scrutinizes (through impermanence, etc.); having scrutinized, he strives; being resolute, he realizes the ultimate truth (Nibbāna) with the body (nāmakāya) and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom." (M. Ni. 2.183, 432)

"A Tathāgata arises in this world... He teaches the Dhamma, beautiful in the beginning..." (Dī. Ni. 1.190)

In accordance with many such sutta passages, starting with the knowledge consisting in what is heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa), the Discourse on Knowledge is taught in due order from the beginning.
11:
This Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā) is established in two ways: by way of brief exposition (uddesa-vāra) and detailed exposition (niddesa-vāra). In the brief exposition, those seventy-three kinds of knowledge are briefly presented by way of a matrix (mātikā) in the manner beginning with: "Wisdom in attending to what is heard is the knowledge consisting in what is heard."

In the detailed exposition, those same seventy-three kinds of knowledge are presented in detail in the manner beginning with: "How is wisdom in attending to what is heard the knowledge consisting in what is heard? 'These things are to be known with direct knowledge'—this is attending to what is heard (sotāvadhāna); the wisdom that knows that thing in various ways is the knowledge consisting in what is heard." Thus it should be understood.

## The Introduction to the Text is finished.
12:
## (1) Mahāvagga
## 1. Commentary on the Matrix of the Discourse on Knowledge
In the brief exposition of that Discourse on Knowledge, first, in the sentence "Wisdom in attending to what is heard is the knowledge consisting in what is heard," the word 'sota' (ear/stream) has many different meanings. This is true; because it has many meanings, that word 'sota' is seen:

In the physical ear, ear-consciousness, and the ear of knowledge;
In craving and so forth;
In a current (of water), in the Noble Path, and also in the mental continuum.

In passages such as "the ear-base, the ear-element, the ear-faculty," this word 'sota' is seen in the sense of the physical ear (ear-sensitivity). In passages such as "having heard a sound with the ear," it is in the sense of ear-consciousness. In passages such as "with the divine ear-element," it is in the sense of the ear of knowledge (wisdom). In passages such as "Whatever streams (sota) there are in the world, I have taught, shown, analyzed, and made them clear; they are the stream of craving, the stream of views, the stream of defilements, the stream of misconduct, and the stream of ignorance," it is seen in the five things beginning with craving. In passages such as "The Blessed One saw a large log being carried along by the current (sota) of the river Ganges," it is in the sense of a current of water. In passages such as "Friend, 'the stream' is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path," it is in the sense of the Noble Path. In passages such as "He knows the stream of consciousness of a person, established in this world and established in the next world, un-cut on both sides," it is in the sense of the mental continuum.

Here, however, this word 'sota' should be understood as the physical ear (ear-sensitivity). Attending (avadhāna), placing, or establishing (the Dhamma) in the mind by means of that ear as the cause or instrument is called "attending to what is heard" (sotāvadhāna). What is that? It is the heard text (suta). "Suta" refers to the collection of teachings (Pali) known and remembered through the ear-door, as in passages like "He is very learned (bahussuta), a bearer of what is heard, a hoarder of what is heard"; this is called "attending to what is heard" (sotāvadhāna) here. Wisdom occurring in that "heard text" called "attending to what is heard" is "wisdom in attending to what is heard." "Wisdom" (paññā) is so called because of its sense of making known (paññāpana) by clarifying various meanings, or it is called wisdom because it knows things through various modes such as impermanence.
13:
In the phrase "sutamaye ñāṇaṃ," the word "suta," whether with or without a prefix, exists in the following meanings:

It is found in the sense of going, fame (renown), wetness, exertion, accumulation, sound (the object of hearing), and states known through the ear-door.

Indeed, in sentences such as "senāya pasuto," it means "going." In sentences such as "sutadhammassa passato," it means "one who has a well-known (famous) Dhamma." In sentences such as "avassutā avassutassa purisapuggalassa," it means "one who is wet with defilements." In sentences such as "ye jhānapasutā dhīrā," it means "those who are devoted (exerting)." In sentences such as "tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ," it means "accumulated." In sentences such as "diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ," it means "sound." In sentences such as "bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo," it means "one who remembers the Dhamma known through the ear-door."

In this context, however, the word "suta" signifies that which is known and noted through the ear-door. "Sutamaye ñāṇaṃ" refers to the wisdom that arises first and subsequently by taking as its object the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) which has been heard, known, and noted. It means "knowledge consisting in what is heard" (sutamaya-ñāṇa). The term "sutamaye" stands in the nominative case (paccattavacana), just as in the phrases "na hevaṃ vattabbe," "vanappagumbe yathā phussitagge," and "natthi attakāre natthi parakāre natthi purisakāre." Therefore, it is said to mean "sutamaya-ñāṇa."

Alternatively, the collection of states such as contact (phassa) produced by the Dhamma that has been heard is called "sutamaya." The knowledge arising within that sutamaya collection of states and associated with them is "sutamaye ñāṇaṃ." It is called "knowledge" (ñāṇa) because it knows states by way of their individual essence (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa). It should be understood that this same knowledge is first referred to indefinitely as "wisdom" (paññā) to clarify the intended meaning through a synonym, and is later specified as "knowledge" (ñāṇa).

Knowledge has the characteristic of penetrating the nature of things (sabhāva-paṭivedha), or the characteristic of unerring penetration (akkhalita-paṭivedha), like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer. Its function (rasa) is to illuminate the object (visayobhāsana), like a lamp. Its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is non-delusion (asammoha), like a good guide in a forest. Its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is concentration (samādhi), according to the teaching: "Bhikkhus, one who is concentrated knows things as they really are."

In the context of characteristics and so forth, either the individual essence or the general nature is called "characteristic" (lakkhaṇa). Either the function or achievement (sampatti) is called "function" (rasa). Either the mode of appearance or the result (phala) is called "manifestation" (paccupaṭṭhāna). The proximate cause is called "padaṭṭhāna."
14:
It should be understood that lakkhaṇa is the (natural) characteristic; rasa is the function or achievement (sampatti); paccupaṭṭhāna is the mode of appearance before knowledge or the result (phala); and padaṭṭhāna is the proximate cause.

Regarding "wisdom consisting in restraint through hearing":
Restraint of the Pātimokkha, mindfulness, knowledge, patience, and energy—these five states are declared as "restraint" (saṃvara).

"He is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, provided with, complete in, and characterized by this restraint of the Pātimokkha"—this is the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara) as mentioned in the Vibhaṅga. "Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he were to dwell leaving the eye-faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might flow in after him, he practices for its restraint, he guards the eye-faculty, he achieves restraint over the eye-faculty"—the restraint mentioned in this manner is restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara).

"Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita (said the Blessed One), mindfulness is their dam. I call it the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut off"—the restraint mentioned in this verse is restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara). "And what, bhikkhus, are the taints (āsavas) to be abandoned by reflecting and using? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, uses the robe..."—the restraint of reflecting and using the four requisites mentioned in this manner is also included within restraint by knowledge. "He is one who endures cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents; he is one who endures ill-spoken, unwelcome words and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, displeasing, and life-threatening"—the restraint mentioned thus is restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara). "He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence"—the restraint mentioned in this manner is restraint by energy (vīriya-saṃvara). "Here, a noble disciple [abandons] wrong livelihood..."
15:
"Having abandoned wrong livelihood, one makes one's living by right livelihood" (as stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya), the restraint of livelihood purification (ājīvapārisuddhi-saṃvara) is also included within the restraint of energy (vīriya-saṃvara). Among those seven types of restraint, the four restraints known as the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara), the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara), the restraint of livelihood purification (ājīvapārisuddhi-saṃvara), and the restraint regarding the use of requisites (paccaya-paṭisevana-saṃvara) are intended here in [the context of] wisdom based on hearing (sutamayapaññā). Among these four, the restraint of the Pātimokkha is especially intended. All these restraints are called 'saṃvara' because they block and prevent bodily misconduct and so forth, which ought to be restrained according to their respective natures. For a person who, having heard the Dhamma explained in the wisdom based on hearing, practices restraint and performs restraint, the wisdom that arises in that restraint and is associated with it is called "wisdom based on hearing that occurs in restraint." Alternatively, since the word 'sutvā' (having heard) can imply a causal sense, it also means wisdom in restraint that arises because of the cause of hearing.

In the phrase "wisdom based on virtue" (sīlamayañāṇa), "virtue" (sīla) is so called in the sense of composing (sīlana). What is this composing? It is the sense of well-composing (samādhāna), meaning the state of non-scatteredness of bodily actions and so forth by virtue of good conduct. Or it is the sense of upholding (upadhāraṇa), meaning the state of being a support by way of being a foundation for wholesome states. Indeed, those who know the characteristics of grammar accept only these two meanings: samādhāna and upadhāraṇa. Other wise scholars, however, explain that it is called 'sīla' because it is to be frequented (adhisevana), because of the sense of conduct (ācāra), because of the sense of nature (tassīla), because of the sense of being like a head (sira), because of the sense of being cool (sītala), and because of the sense of being safe (siva).

Just as the characteristic of a visual object (rūpāyatana), though diverse in many ways such as blue, yellow, etc., is its visibility (sanidassana),
likewise, the characteristic of that virtue, though diverse in many ways such as volition (cetanā), abstinence (virati), etc., is its sense of composing (sīlana).

Just as a visual object, though diverse in many ways such as blue, yellow, etc., does not transcend the nature of visibility, and thus visibility is its characteristic; likewise, virtue, though diverse in many ways such as volition and so forth, does not transcend the nature of well-composing (samādhāna) bodily actions and so forth, and the nature of being a foundation (patiṭṭhāna) for wholesome states. Therefore, that sense of composing (sīlana) itself is the characteristic. For virtue having such a characteristic—

The destruction of immorality (dussīlya) is called its function (rasa) in the sense of duty (kicca);
likewise, the achievement of the quality of blamelessness is called its function (rasa) in the sense of achievement (sampatti).

Therefore, this virtue should be understood as having the function of destroying immorality by way of its function as a duty, and as being endowed with the quality of blamelessness by way of its function as an achievement.
16:
That virtue has purity as its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna). Its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is described by the wise as shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa).

That virtue has purity as its manifestation, as taught in the Itivuttaka: "purity of body, purity of speech, purity of mind." It manifests to the knowledge as a state of purity; it reaches the state of being perceived. Shame and fear of wrongdoing are described by the wise as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), meaning the most immediate cause. For when shame and fear of wrongdoing exist, virtue both arises and persists. When they are absent, it neither arises nor persists. The wisdom associated with and occurring together with virtue of such a kind is called "wisdom based on virtue" (sīlamayañāṇa). Alternatively, virtue itself is called 'sīlamaya' because it is accomplished [by causes]; the wisdom associated with that 'sīlamaya' is wisdom based on virtue. The contemplation of the danger in non-restraint (asaṃvara), the contemplation of the benefit in restraint (saṃvara), the contemplation of the purification of restraint, and the contemplation of the defilement and cleansing of restraint are all included within wisdom based on virtue.

"Wisdom in well-composing (concentration) through restraint" means the wisdom associated with and arising in that well-composing (concentration) for one who, having restrained with the restraint of virtue mentioned in the wisdom based on virtue, having practiced restraint and established oneself in virtue, brings about one-pointedness of mind by way of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā). Composing and establishing evenly and rightly is called 'samādahana'; this is a synonymous term for concentration (samādhi).

In the phrase "wisdom based on the development of concentration" (samādhibhāvanāmayañāṇa), one-pointedness of wholesome mind (ekaggatā) is called concentration (samādhi). In what sense is it concentration? It is concentration in the sense of well-composing (samādhāna). What is this well-composing? It means the even and right placing and establishing of the mind and mental factors on a single object. Therefore, it should be understood that well-composing (samādhāna) is that state by the power of which the mind and mental factors remain on a single object, being evenly and rightly non-distracted and non-scattered. Of that concentration—

Non-distraction (avikkhepa) is the characteristic; the destruction of distraction (vikkhepa-viddhaṃsana) is the function (rasa);
steadiness (akampana) is the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna); and happiness (sukha) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

It is called 'bhāvanā' (development) because it is developed and increased. Concentration itself is the development, thus 'samādhibhāvanā'; or the developing and increasing of concentration is 'samādhibhāvanā'. By the term 'samādhibhāvanā', other [types of] development are excluded. As mentioned before, wisdom based on the development of concentration occurs by way of access and absorption concentration.
17:
In the phrase "knowledge in grasping conditions," an effect is called a "condition" (paccaya) because it arises depending on a cause. "Depending" (paṭicca) means arising without being separate from that cause and without discarding it. "Arises" (eti) means both newly arising and persisting after having arisen. Alternatively, the meaning of condition is the sense of being helpful (upakāraka). Because these conditions are manifold, the wisdom involved in grasping and defining those conditions is called "knowledge in grasping conditions" (paccayapariggaha-paññā).

In the phrase "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa), the word "dhamma" is found in the senses of nature, wisdom, merit, designation, offense, learning, non-self, change, quality, condition (paccaya), and result (paccayuppanna), and so on. This word "dhamma" is found in the sense of nature (sabhāva) in such passages as "wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena."

It is found in the sense of wisdom (paññā) in such passages as: "In whom these four dhammas exist—truth, wisdom, persistence, and generosity—that faithful house-seeker does not sorrow after passing away."

It is found in the sense of merit (puñña) in such passages as: "For merit and demerit do not both have equal results; demerit leads to hell, while merit brings one to a happy destination."

It is found in the sense of designation (paññatti) in such passages as: "Designation-phenomena, terminology-phenomena, derivative-phenomena."

It is found in the sense of offense (āpatti) in such passages as: "Pārājika phenomena, Saṅghādisesa phenomena."

It is found in the sense of learning (pariyatti) in such passages as: "Here, a monk knows the Dhamma: the Sutta, Geyya, and Veyyākaraṇa."

It is found in the sense of non-self (nissattatā) in such passages as: "At that time, phenomena (dhammā) exist; he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena."

It is found in the sense of change (vikāra) in such passages as: "Phenomena subject to birth, phenomena subject to aging, phenomena subject to death."

It is found in the sense of quality (guṇa) in such passages as: "Of the six Buddha-qualities."

It is found in the sense of condition (paccaya) in such passages as: "Knowledge of the cause is the discrimination of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā)."

It is found in the sense of result (paccayuppanna) in such passages as: "That element stands, the stability of phenomena, the fixed course of phenomena." Here also, the word "dhamma" should be understood as the result. In terms of meaning, they are called "phenomena" (dhamma) as appropriate because they bear their own nature, or because they are borne by conditions, or because they bear their own fruit, or because they bear the one who fulfills them so that he does not fall into woeful states, or because they bear their respective characteristics, or because they are grasped by the mind. In this context, however, their own...
18:
...borne by causes, they are called "dhamma." The cause that makes the phenomena produced by causes arise, exist, and proceed is called "dhammaṭṭhiti" (stability of phenomena). This is a designation for the causal phenomena. The knowledge of that stability of phenomena is "dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa" (knowledge of the stability of phenomena).

Indeed, this knowledge of the stability of phenomena arises for a person who, having discerned mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), strives for the sake of knowledge and vision of things as they really are with a mind concentrated by the concentration mentioned in the knowledge consisting of the development of concentration, through the method of discerning the causes of those mentality-materiality.

Why is it called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" instead of directly saying "knowledge of discerning mentality-materiality"? Because by discerning the cause itself, the discernment of the mentality-materiality produced by the cause is accomplished. Indeed, without discerning the mentality-materiality produced by the cause, it is not possible to discern the cause. Therefore, it should be understood that by taking the "knowledge of the stability of phenomena," the "knowledge of discerning mentality-materiality" which was previously accomplished as its cause is also stated.

Why is it not said "Having concentrated, wisdom in discerning causes," like the second and third knowledges? Because calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are yoked together (yuganaddha).

"Having concentrated, in whatever way one sees with insight;
while seeing with insight, in that same way one should concentrate.
Then insight and calm are of equal share,
proceeding yoked together."

So it is said. Therefore, it should be understood that it is stated only as "Wisdom in discerning causes is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena" to make it known that one should strive until the Noble Path, making concentration and knowledge a pair without abandoning concentration.

In the phrase "wisdom in discerning past, future, and present phenomena by summarizing them": "Past" (atīta) means those that have passed away, having reached their own nature or the moment of arising, etc. "Future" (anāgata) means those that have not yet reached either of those two. "Present" (paccuppanna) means those that have arisen and proceeded above the moment of arising, etc., depending on various causes. Among the present of duration (addhā), continuity (santati), and moment (khaṇa), the present of continuity (santati-paccuppanna) is intended here. It is the wisdom in discerning, deciding, and well-completing the phenomena of the five aggregates of the past, future, and present by summarizing them into the characteristics of each aggregate and making them into groups (kalāpa).

"Knowledge of comprehension" (sammasana-ñāṇa) means the knowledge in well-comprehending, reflecting, and observing; it means "knowledge of comprehension by groups" (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa). This knowledge [arises] immediately after the knowledge of discerning mentality-materiality...
19:
For one established in the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa), which discerns the causes of mentality-materiality, the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa) arises. This occurs as they practice insight by applying the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—to each of the aggregates previously defined. This is done through the method of comprehension taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'Whatever materiality there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one defines all that materiality as impermanent; this is one comprehension. One defines it as suffering; this is one comprehension. One defines it as non-self; this is one comprehension,' and so forth.

'Wisdom in the repeated contemplation of the change and destruction of present phenomena' refers to the wisdom in seeing the change and dissolution (bhaṅga) of the five aggregates within the internal continuity (santati) of the present. Since the mind is fixed on destruction (bheda) even after apprehending arising (udaya) with the thought, 'These phenomena arise and then perish,' it should be understood that although 'arising' (udaya) is not explicitly mentioned, it is indeed included. Alternatively, by seeing present phenomena, the seeing of arising is established; thus, arising is already spoken of. Indeed, the state of phenomena having arisen cannot be established without arising. Therefore, even if it is not stated as 'wisdom in the repeated contemplation of the arising and change-destruction of present phenomena,' it should be understood as being stated. Furthermore, because it is defined as 'knowledge in the contemplation of arising and falling away,' the seeing of arising is already established. Thus, for one who reaches the end of the previously mentioned knowledge of comprehension and, discerning the arising and falling away that becomes clear within that very comprehension, strives in the repeated contemplation of arising and falling away to define formations (saṅkhāra), the knowledge of contemplation of arising and falling away (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa) arises. It is called 'contemplation of arising and falling away' because it repeatedly contemplates arising and falling away.

'Reflecting on the object' means knowing and seeing by reflecting on objects such as the aggregate of materiality in terms of dissolution (bhaṅga). 'Wisdom in the repeated contemplation of dissolution is the knowledge in insight' means that the wisdom involved in repeatedly contemplating the dissolution of the knowledge that arose by reflecting on that object in terms of dissolution is called 'knowledge in insight.' Insight (vipassanā) means seeing in various ways. There is also a reading 'ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā.' Its meaning is reflecting on, knowing, and seeing the object. In the same manner as described, it is stated that 'wisdom in the repeated contemplation of dissolution through reflecting on the object is the knowledge in insight.' Because insight reaches its peak only through the repeated contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā), this knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution alone is specifically called 'knowledge in insight.'

Because insight reaches its peak only through the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution, this knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution alone is called 'knowledge in insight.' For one established in the knowledge of contemplation of arising and falling away, the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi) arises. Therefore, when that knowledge of contemplation of arising and falling away is completed, that knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path is also completed. Thus, it should be understood that the knowledge which is the peak of insight is described through the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution alone, without separately mentioning the knowledge of what is the path and what is not. When the formations, well-defined by one who has clearly seen arising and falling away through the knowledge of contemplation of arising and falling away, become rapidly apparent, the knowledge of arising and falling away becomes sharp. When it leads to higher knowledge, one abandons the contemplation of arising, and mindfulness becomes well-established only in dissolution. Thus, for that person who contemplates that dissolution, thinking, 'These formations arise and then perish'...
20:
It is said: "Knowledge occurring in insight (Vipassanā)." Because for one established in the contemplation of arising and falling (udayabbayānupassanā), the knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana) arises; therefore, when that contemplation of arising and falling is completed, that knowledge and vision of path and not-path is also completed. For this reason, without mentioning the knowledge and vision of path and not-path separately, it should be understood that the knowledge which is the peak of insight is described through the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) alone. For one who has clearly seen arising and falling through the contemplation of arising and falling, when the well-defined formations (saṅkhāra) appear rapidly, and when the knowledge is sharp and leads upwards, one abandons the observation of arising and mindfulness becomes well-established only in dissolution. To such a person who sees, "Having arisen in this way, these formations dissolve in this way," the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa) arises at this stage of observing dissolution.

Wisdom in the appearance as terror (bhayatupaṭṭhāna) means the wisdom in the knowledge that reaches the taking of the object as fearful, due to its association with oppression, when the arising, occurrence, sign, accumulation, and rebirth-linking of formations appear as terror. It means [wisdom] in the object called "appearance as terror" because it appears as terror. Alternatively, the wisdom that stands as terror is called "appearance as terror."

The term "knowledge in danger (ādīnava)" is simply in the locative case. Since it is said, "The wisdom in the appearance as terror, the knowledge in danger, and disenchantment (nibbidā)—these states are one in meaning and differ only in phrasing" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.227), although spoken of as one, it actually has three aspects according to the difference in stages, like the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa) and so on. Therefore, it should be understood that when the knowledge of appearance as terror and the contemplation of danger are completed, the contemplation of disenchantment is also completed; thus, even if not explicitly mentioned, it is as if it were mentioned.

For one who pursues, develops, and cultivates the contemplation of dissolution which takes the dissolution of all formations as its object, the breaking formations in the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings appear as a great terror, like lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, ogres, demons, fierce bulls, fierce dogs, rutting wild elephants, fierce snakes, thunderbolts, cemeteries, battlefields, and burning charcoal pits appear to a fearful man who desires to live in comfort. To such a person who sees, "Past formations have ceased, present formations are ceasing, and future formations will likewise cease," the knowledge of appearance as terror arises at this stage. For one who pursues, develops, and cultivates that knowledge of appearance as terror, no protection (tāṇa), shelter (leṇa), refuge (gati), or support (paṭisaraṇa) is found in any realm of existence, mode of birth, destination, station, or abode. Among the formations occurring in all realms, births, destinations, stations, and abodes, there is no longer any longing (patthanā) or misapprehension (parāmāsa) even for a single formation. The three realms of existence appear like charcoal pits filled with flameless embers. The four great elements appear like fierce poisonous snakes. The five aggregates appear like executioners with raised swords. The six internal bases appear like an empty village. The six external bases appear like dacoits attacking a village. The seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of beings appear as if burning, blazing, and glowing with the eleven fires. All formations appear like boils, like diseases.
21:
Neither misapprehension (parāmāsa) nor delight (through craving and views) occurs any longer. The three realms of existence—the sense realm, the fine-material realm, and the immaterial realm—appear like charcoal pits filled with flameless embers. The four great elements appear like fierce poisonous snakes. The five aggregates appear like executioners with raised swords who are about to kill. The six internal bases appear like an empty village. The six external bases appear like dacoits who attack and destroy a village. The seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of beings appear as if burning, blazing, and glowing with the eleven fires. All formations appear like a boil (an ulcer), like a disease, like a dart, like a calamity, like an affliction; they appear as joyless, tasteless, and as a great mass of danger.

Just as a forest full of wild beasts, a cave with a tiger, water with crocodiles and ogres, enemies with raised swords, poisoned food, a road with thieves, a burning house, or a battlefield where troops are advancing appear to a fearful man who desires to live in comfort (even if they seem attractive in form), so too, when all formations appear as terror by the power of the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, the meditator (yogāvacara) sees only the tasteless, joyless danger on all sides. To one who sees thus, the knowledge of contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa) arises.

Seeing all formations as danger in this way, that person becomes disenchanted with, weary of, and finds no delight in the breaking formations included within all realms of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. Just as the Golden Swan King who delights at the foot of Mount Cittakūṭa finds no delight in a dirty pit at the gate of a Caṇḍāla village, but delights only in the seven great lakes; even so, this Swan King of a meditator finds no delight in the breaking formations whose danger has been well seen, but because of being endowed with delight in development and delight in meditation, he delights only in the seven contemplations. And just as a Lion King placed in a golden cage finds no delight there, but delights only in the Himālaya forest which is three thousand leagues wide; even so, this Lion of a meditator finds no delight even in the three happy realms of existence, but delights only in the three contemplations. And just as the Chaddanta Elephant King, who is all-white, established in seven points, possessed of psychic power, and able to travel through the air, finds no delight in the middle of a city, but delights only in the Chaddanta Lake in the Himālaya; even so, this noble Elephant of a meditator finds no delight in any formations.
22:
One delights only in Nibbāna, the state of peace described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga by such methods as "Non-arising is safety" (anuppādo khemaṃ). One's mind inclines, slopes, and leans towards that Nibbāna. By this much, the Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa) has arisen in him.

Regarding "The wisdom of the desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, and steadfastness is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations": One is called "desirous of deliverance" (muñcitukāma) because one wishes to be delivered from, or to abandon, formations. The state of being desirous of deliverance is "desire for deliverance" (muñcitukamyatā). It is called "reflective contemplation" (paṭisaṅkhā) because one investigates repeatedly, or the act of investigating is reflective contemplation. It is called "steadfastness" (santiṭṭhanā) because one stands evenly and observes, or the act of standing evenly is steadfastness. The wisdom that is the desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, and steadfastness is called "knowledge of the desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, and steadfastness."

Thus, for one who is disenchanted through the earlier Knowledge of Disenchantment, the desire to abandon formations such as arising (uppāda), occurrence (pavatta), and signs (nimitta) is the desire for deliverance. The repeated investigation in the middle to find a means of deliverance is reflective contemplation. The indifferent observation at the end after being delivered is steadfastness. Thus, wisdom which is threefold according to its stages is the knowledge in the indifferent observation of formations. For one who wishes to show the state of equanimity towards formations of these three wisdoms, which are distinct by stage—namely, desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, and steadfastness—the plural forms "wisdoms" (paññā) and "equanimity towards formations" (saṅkhārupekkhāsu) are used. However, because it is one in essence despite being distinct by stage, the singular form "knowledge" (ñāṇaṃ) is used. As it is said: "That which is the desire for deliverance, that which is reflective contemplation, and that which is equanimity towards formations—these states are one in meaning and differ only in phrasing."

Some teachers say that the plural "saṅkhārupekkhāsu" is used because equanimity towards formations is manifold by way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). It should be understood that the term "saṅkhārupekkhāsu" is used in relation to the action. By stage, however, the mind of one who is disenchanted and weary through that Knowledge of Disenchantment does not stick, does not adhere, and is not bound to the perishable formations in all types of existence, birth, destination, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings; it only desires to be delivered from and to discard all formations.

Alternatively, just as a fish in a net, a frog in a snake's mouth, a jungle fowl in a cage, a deer caught in a strong snare, a snake in the hands of a snake charmer, an elephant fallen into a great swamp, a naga king in a garuda's mouth, the moon entered into Rahu's mouth, or a man surrounded by enemies—all these desire only to be delivered and to escape from those respective dangers—likewise, the mind of that yogi desires only to be delivered and to escape from all formations. When stated thus, the reading "the desire for deliverance of one who desires to be delivered" (muñcitukāmasa muñcitukamyatā) is appropriate. This being so...
23:
In phrases such as "uppādaṃ muñcitukamyatā" (desire for deliverance from arising), it should be stated as "uppādā muñcitukamyatā" (desire for deliverance from arising [ablative]), therefore the previously mentioned meaning is better. Then, for that person who is free from attachment to all formations and desires to be delivered from all formations, the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa) arises.

That yogi, desiring to be delivered from formations accompanied by the nature of destruction within all existences, modes of generation, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, again contemplates those very formations by applying the three characteristics through the knowledge of reflective contemplation (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa) in order to accomplish the means of deliverance. To that yogi contemplating thus, the reflective contemplation knowledge that knows the sign of formations (nimitta) by way of the characteristic of impermanence (anicca) arises; the reflective contemplation knowledge that knows the occurrence (pavatta) by way of the characteristic of suffering (dukkha) arises; and the reflective contemplation knowledge that knows both the sign and the occurrence by way of the characteristic of non-self (anatta) arises.

Seeing with the knowledge of reflective contemplation that "all formations are empty," and applying the three characteristics while grasping formations, he abandons both fear and delight. Just as a man who has seen the faults of his wife and has divorced her becomes indifferent and neutral towards that wife, so too he becomes indifferent and neutral towards formations, not grasping them as "I" or "mine." For him who thus knows and sees, the mind recoils, draws back, and retreats from the three planes of existence; it does not stretch out. Just as water drops on a lotus leaf that is slightly slanted recoil, draw back, and retreat, and do not spread out; or just as a chicken feather or a piece of sinew thrown into a fire recoils, draws back, and retreats, and does not spread out; even so, his mind recoils, draws back, and retreats from the three planes of existence and does not spread out; equanimity becomes established. Thus, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) arises in him.

It should be understood that along with this knowledge of equanimity towards formations, the conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) which accomplishes the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) above it, though not explicitly mentioned by name among the preceding and succeeding knowledges, is indeed already mentioned. For the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu who sees any formation as permanent should be possessed of conformity-tolerance (anulomika-khanti)—this is impossible. That one who is not possessed of conformity-tolerance should enter the certainty of rightness (sammatta-niyāma)—this is impossible. That one who does not enter the certainty of rightness should realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of Arahantship—this is impossible," etc.

And the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) also said: "In how many ways does one obtain conformity-tolerance? In how many ways does one enter the certainty of rightness? In forty ways one obtains conformity-tolerance; in forty ways one enters the certainty of rightness."
24:
“He obtains conformity-tolerance (insight wisdom that conforms to preceding and succeeding knowledges); he enters the rightness-determination (the Path) through forty modes,” and so forth (as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

In the Paṭṭhāna also, the Blessed One stated: “Conformity is a condition for change-of-lineage by way of proximity condition; conformity is a condition for purification (vodāna) by way of proximity condition,” and so forth.

For that meditator who frequents, develops, and cultivates that knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa), faith characterized by resolution (adhimokkha) becomes stronger, energy is well-exerted, mindfulness is well-established, the mind is well-concentrated, and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations proceeds more keenly. At the moment when it is said, “Now the Path will arise,” having contemplated formations as “impermanent,” “suffering,” or “non-self” through the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, the mind sinks into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Immediately after the life-continuum, mind-door adverting arises, taking formations as its object in the same manner as was done in the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, as “impermanent,” “suffering,” or “non-self.” Immediately after that mind-door adverting, two, three, or four impulsion (javana) moments arise, taking formations as their object in that same way. The knowledge associated with those impulsion moments is called conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa). This is because that conformity-knowledge conforms to the true function of the preceding eight insight knowledges and also conforms to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) to be attained above.

For example, just as a righteous king, seated in the place of judgment, listens to the decision of eight judicial ministers, and having abandoned bias, remains impartial and joyfully grants permission, saying, “Let it be so,” thus conforming both to the decision of those ministers and to the ancient royal law. In this analogy, the conformity-knowledge is like the king; the eight insight knowledges are like the eight judicial ministers; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are like the ancient royal law. Just as the king, rejoicing and saying “Let it be so,” conforms to the ministers’ decision and the royal law, so too this conformity-knowledge, arising by taking formations as its object in the mode of impermanence and so on, conforms to the true function of the eight insight knowledges and to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to be attained above. Therefore, it is called conformity-knowledge.

“Wisdom in emerging and turning away from the external is change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa).” In this phrase, “external (bahiddhā)” refers to the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta). This is because that sign of formations is called “external” in comparison to the unwholesome aggregates within one’s own mental continuity. Therefore, it emerges from the external sign of formations (becoming detached)...
25:
It is called vuṭṭhāna (emergence) because it stands above. It is called vivaṭṭana (turning away) because it turns back or turns away. Since it is both emergence and turning away, it is called vuṭṭhāna-vivaṭṭana. Therefore, it is said (in the Visuddhimagga): “Because change-of-lineage knowledge does not emerge from the process [of aggregates] since it does not [yet] completely cut off the origin (samudaya), but it does emerge from the sign by taking Nibbāna as its object, it is emergence in one respect (ekato vuṭṭhāna).”

It is called gotrabhū (change-of-lineage) because it overcomes the lineage of worldlings (puthujjana) and because it develops the lineage of Noble Ones (ariya). This change-of-lineage knowledge arises at the end of the repetition (āsevana) of conformity-knowledge, with a mind that recedes from all formations just as a drop of water recedes from a lotus leaf. Taking the signless Nibbāna as its object, it transcends the worldling’s lineage, the worldling’s designation, and the worldling’s plane, and enters the Noble One’s lineage, the Noble One’s designation, and the Noble One’s plane. Being the first turning, the first attention, and the first bringing to mind towards the object of Nibbāna, it fulfills the state of being a condition for the Path in six ways: by way of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), repetition (āsevana), decisive support (upanissaya), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata). It reaches the peak of insight, becomes its summit, and arises in a manner that does not turn back.

“Wisdom in emerging and turning away from both is the knowledge in the Path.” Here, ‘from both’ (dubhato) means from two things or in two ways. Because it completely cuts off the defilements, it emerges and turns away from the defilements and from the aggregates that follow them; and because it takes Nibbāna as its object, it emerges and turns away from all external signs of formations. Thus, it is called ‘wisdom in emerging and turning away from both.’ Therefore, it is said: “All four Path-knowledges emerge from the sign because they have the signless [Nibbāna] as their object, and they emerge from the process because they completely cut off the origin. Thus, they are emergences from both (dubhato vuṭṭhāna).”

In the phrase “knowledge in the Path (magge ñāṇa),” it is called magga (Path) because it seeks or sees Nibbāna; or because it is sought or searched for by those desiring Nibbāna; or because it goes along killing the defilements. The knowledge in that Path is Path-knowledge. Here, the singular form is used to represent the class (jāti). That Path-knowledge arises immediately after change-of-lineage knowledge, taking Nibbāna as its object, completely cutting off the defilements that are to be killed by itself, drying up the ocean of suffering in the beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra), closing all doors to the woeful planes (apāya), making present the seven noble treasures, and abandoning the eightfold wrong path...
26:
It is called 'Magga' (Path) because it is the means of seeing, because it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna, and because it arises while killing the defilements. The knowledge that arises in that Path is Path Knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa). Taking the four Path Knowledges by their faultless and pure nature, they are expressed in the singular.

To speak in detail, for those individuals endowed with the Path, that Knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) arises immediately after the Change-of-lineage Knowledge (Gotrabhū-ñāṇa), taking Nibbāna as its object, completely cutting off the defilements to be abandoned by it, drying up the ocean of suffering in the beginningless round of rebirths (Saṃsāra), closing all doors to the woeful states (Apāya), making manifest the seven types of Noble Wealth (Ariya-dhana), abandoning the eightfold wrong path (Micchā-magga), calming all dangers and fears, leading to the state of being a breast-born son of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, and bringing about hundreds of other various benefits.

Just as a man wishing to stand on the other bank of a ditch might run with great speed, and grabbing a rope or a stick tied to a tree on this bank, he leaps across, with his body leaning toward the other side, and upon reaching the other side, he lets go of the rope or stick, and though shaking, stands firmly on the far bank.

In the same way, the practitioner (Yogāvacara), seeing danger on this bank of identity (Sakkāya) and wishing to stand on the other bank of the Deathless (Amata) which is free from danger, comes with the speed of the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbaya-ñāṇa) and so forth, and firmly grasps the rope of the form-aggregate (Rūpakkhandha) or the stick of the other four mental aggregates (Nāmakkhandha) through the adverting mind of conformity (Anuloma) as previously described. Then, leaping across by means of the Conformity Knowledges (Anuloma-ñāṇa), he leans toward Nibbāna and approaches its vicinity. Letting go of that object, shaking with the Change-of-lineage Knowledge (Gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which has not yet attained repetition (Āsevana), he falls to the far side of the conditioned (Sankhata) and thereafter stands firmly by means of Path Knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa).

Just as a man wishing to see the moon when it is covered by masses of clouds might see the moon when the coarse, subtle, and very subtle clouds are cleared away in succession by the wind; in the same way, when the delusion (Moha) that covers the Truth is destroyed in succession by the Conformity Knowledges, the Change-of-lineage Knowledge sees the Deathless Nibbāna.

Just as the winds do not see the moon, the Conformity Knowledges do not see Nibbāna. Just as the man does not dispel the clouds, the Change-of-lineage Knowledge cannot dispel the darkness of delusion.

Just as a man standing on a revolving mechanical wheel might shoot and hit a target of a hundred boards at the fall of an arrow, without seeing it, but by following a mark given by another; in this case, the Path Knowledge, while occurring in Nibbāna without abandoning the mark given by the Change-of-lineage Knowledge, destroys the mass of greed and so forth.

It should be understood that this Path Knowledge dries up the ocean of suffering in Saṃsāra. It closes the door to the woeful states. It makes one a possessor of Noble Wealth. It abandons the wrong path. It calms all dangers and fears. It makes one a breast-born son of the Buddha. It also grants many other benefits.

12. In the sentence 'Knowledge of the Fruit is the wisdom of the stilling of effort' (Payogappaṭippassaddhipaññā phale ñāṇam), 'effort' (Payoga) means great exertion. It is the exertion to emerge from both the sign (Nimitta) and the occurrence (Pavatta) by developing the Path for the realization of the Fruit. The calming or completion of that exertion is called 'Payogappaṭippassaddhi'. What is that calming? It is the completion of the tasks of the four Paths.
27:
This knowledge dries up the ocean of the suffering of Saṃsāra; it closes the door to woeful states.
It makes one a possessor of the wealth of the Noble Ones; it abandons the wrong path.
It calms all dangers and fears; it makes one a breast-born son of the Lord.
It also grants hundreds of other various benefits.

12. In this phrase 'Payogappaṭippassaddhipaññā phale ñāṇam', 'effort' (Payoga) means great exertion. It is the great exertion to emerge from both [the sign and the occurrence] by means of Path-development, which is the realization of the Fruit. The calming or completion of that exertion is called 'Payogappaṭippassaddhi'. What is that? It is the completion of the tasks of the four Paths. The wisdom associated with the Fruit that arises due to that Payogappaṭippassaddhi as its cause is called 'Payogappaṭippassaddhipaññā'. It is called 'Fruit' (Phala) because it matures or ripens; the knowledge associated with that Fruit is the knowledge in the Fruit. Immediately after each Path Knowledge, three, two, or one moments of Fruit-consciousness (Phala-citta) arise, having Nibbāna as their object, as the result of that very Path. Because supramundane wholesome states (Lokuttara-kusala) give results immediately, it is said: 'They call concentration immediate (Ānantarika)' and 'He slowly reaches the immediate [Path] for the destruction of the taints (Āsava)', and so forth. For one who has two moments of Conformity (Anuloma), the third is Change-of-lineage (Gotrabhū), the fourth is Path-consciousness (Magga-citta), and there are three moments of Fruit-consciousness. For one who has three moments of Conformity, the fourth is Change-of-lineage, the fifth is Path-consciousness, and there are two moments of Fruit-consciousness. For one who has four moments of Conformity, the fifth is Change-of-lineage, the sixth is Path-consciousness, and there is one moment of Fruit-consciousness. This is the Fruit in the Path-process (Magga-vīthi). Furthermore, the Fruit arising at a different time by the power of attainment (Samāpatti), and the Fruit arising for one emerging from the attainment of cessation (Nirodha-samāpatti), are also included by this Fruit that arises immediately after the Path.

13.
