'Wisdom in reviewing the cut path' (Chinnavaṭumānupassane paññā) is the wisdom that subsequently reviews those respective defilements (Upakkilesa) that have been utterly cut off by those respective Noble Paths. 'Vimutti-ñāṇa' is the knowledge in liberation. 'Liberation' (Vimutti) refers to the mind that is pure and liberated from defilements, or the state of being liberated. The knowledge that knows that liberation is 'Vimutti-ñāṇa'. When a person reviews the mental continuum liberated from defilements or the state of being liberated from defilements, they do not review it apart from the abandoned defilements; therefore, by this statement, the reviewing of abandoned defilements (Pahīnakilesa-paccavekkhaṇā) is expressed. The statement 'When liberated, there is the knowledge: "It is liberated"' is said with reference to this reviewing knowledge of abandoned defilements. Although the reviewing of remaining defilements is not directly mentioned, it should be understood as being expressed by this very statement. It has also been said— 'By one taught Dhamma, all Dhammas of similar characteristics are already taught; such teaching is called the Method of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra),' as taught by the Elder Mahākaccāyana. Alternatively, since there is no reviewing of remaining defilements for one who has reached the Path of Arahantship, it should be understood that only the reviewing of abandoned defilements, which is attained by all four Noble Ones, is taught by the words beginning with 'Chinnavaṭumānupassane'.
28:
“When one phenomenon is taught, all phenomena having the same characteristic as that are also said to be taught. Thus, this is called the Method of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra)” (as stated in the Nettippakaraṇa). Alternatively, it should be understood that since an Arahant has no reflection on remaining defilements, it refers only to the reflection on abandoned defilements that occurs for the four types of Noble Ones (ariya).

“Wisdom in seeing the phenomena that have arisen at that time” refers to the wisdom of seeing, reflecting upon, and specifically knowing the Path and Fruition states, as well as the Four Noble Truths, which have arrived, been attained, and are fully possessed by way of achievement and penetration at the moments of the Path and Fruition.

“Knowledge in reflection” refers to the knowledge that turns back and sees or knows repeatedly and intensely. By these two types of knowledge, the Reviewing Knowledges (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) are meant.

In detail, in the Path-process (magga-vīthi) of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), at the conclusion of the Fruition of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), the mind descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjana) arises for the purpose of reviewing the Path. When that mind ceases, seven impulsion (javana) moments of reviewing the Path arise in succession. Again, having descended into the life-continuum, advertence and other mind-moments arise in the same manner for the purpose of reviewing the Fruition and so forth. Through the arising of these minds, the Stream-enterer reviews the Path, reviews the Fruition, reviews the abandoned defilements, reviews the remaining defilements, and reviews Nibbāna.

Indeed, he reviews the Path, thinking: “By this Path, I have certainly come.” Then he reviews the Fruition, thinking: “This is the benefit I have gained.” Then he reviews the abandoned defilements, thinking: “These defilements have been abandoned by me.” Then he reviews the defilements to be abandoned by the higher Paths, thinking: “These defilements still remain in me.” Finally, he reviews the Deathless Nibbāna, thinking: “I have attained this Dhamma as an object.”

Thus, for the Noble Disciple who is a Stream-enterer, there are five reflections. As for the Stream-enterer, so it is for the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) and the Non-returner (anāgāmī). For the Arahant, however, there is no such thing as reflection on remaining defilements; thus, there are only four reflections. In this way, there are nineteen Reviewing Knowledges in total. This is the maximum limit. The reflection on abandoned and remaining defilements may or may not occur for Trainees (sekha). It was precisely because of the absence of such reflection that Mahānāma the Sakyan asked the Blessed One: “What Dhamma is there still unabandoned within me, because of which states of greed at times possess my mind and remain?” and so forth.
29:
In this context, to clarify the eleven knowledges beginning with the Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena (dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa), this simile should be understood: Suppose a man, thinking “I will catch some fish,” takes a fish-trap, places it in suitable water, and thrusts his hand into the mouth of the trap. He firmly grasps a cobra by the neck in the water, perceiving it to be a fish. Delighted, thinking “I have caught a great fish,” he pulls it out and looks at it. Seeing the three stripes (on its hood), he realizes “It is a snake!” He becomes terrified, sees the danger, and feeling revulsion toward his catch, desires to release it. Seeking a means to release it, he unwinds his hand starting from the tip of the tail, lifts his arm, and swings the snake around his head two or three times to weaken it. Then, saying “Go, you wicked snake!” he throws it away, quickly climbs up onto dry land, and while standing there, rejoices, thinking: “Oh, I have been delivered from the mouth of a great snake!” and looks back at the path by which he came.

In this simile, the man’s firm grasping of the cobra with the perception of it being a fish and his subsequent delight is like the worldling (bālaputhujjana) who, from the beginning, firmly clings to the five aggregates—which are actually terrifying due to their impermanence and so forth—with the perception of permanence and so forth, through the influence of wrong view and craving, thinking “I” and “mine,” and takes delight in them. The man’s pulling the snake out of the trap, seeing the three stripes, and realizing “It is a snake” is like the yogi’s discerning of mind and matter along with their causes, breaking down the compact mass (ghana-vinibbhoga), seeing the three characteristics of impermanence and so forth of the five aggregates through knowledges such as Comprehension by Groups (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa), and defining them as “impermanent, suffering, and non-self.”

The man’s fear is like this yogi’s Knowledge of the Appearance as Terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa). Seeing the danger in the snake is like the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger (ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa). Revulsion in catching the snake is like the Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa). The desire to release the snake is like the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa). Seeking a means to release it is like the Knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa). Swinging the snake to weaken it so that it cannot turn back and bite is like weakening the formations (saṅkhāra) by applying the three characteristics through the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) and Conformity Knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa), so that they are no longer able to appear as permanent, pleasant, or self. Releasing the snake is like Change-of-lineage Knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Releasing the snake and standing on dry land is like the Path and Fruition Knowledges (magga-phala-ñāṇa) which have ascended to and stand upon the dry land of Nibbāna. Looking back at the path he came from with joy is like the Reviewing Knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that reviews the Path and so forth.

Because the order of the teaching (desanā-kakkama) is given according to the order of arising and the order of practice of these fourteen knowledges beginning with Knowledge Based on Learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa), it should be understood that among the reflections (paccavekkhaṇa), the reflection on defilements occurs first, and after that, the reflections on the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.
30:
“One develops supramundane jhāna for the purpose of liberation from the round of suffering, for the diminution of defilements, for the abandoning of wrong views, for the attenuation of sensual lust and ill-will, for the total abandoning of sensual lust and ill-will, and for the total abandoning of lust for fine-material existence, lust for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.” Since the practice of the path is taught by giving prominence to the abandoning of defilements, it is appropriate that the contemplation of defilements occurs first in accordance with the practice. The order mentioned in the Commentary has already been shown. That order is fivefold: the order of arising (uppattikkama), the order of abandoning (pahanakkama), the order of practice (paṭipattikkama), the order of planes (bhūmikkama), and the order of teaching (desanakkama).

“First there is the kalala (embryo in the first week), from the kalala comes the abbuda (second week), from the abbuda is born the pesi (third week), from the pesi the ghana (fourth week) arises.” This and so forth is the order of arising (uppattikkama). “States to be abandoned by vision, states to be abandoned by development.” This and so forth is the order of abandoning (pahanakkama). “Purification of virtue, purification of mind, purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, purification by knowledge and vision.” This and so forth is the order of practice (paṭipattikkama). “States of the sense sphere, states of the fine-material sphere, states of the immaterial sphere.” This and so forth is the order of planes (bhūmikkama). “The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,” or, “He gave a progressive discourse; that is to say, talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven, and he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.” This and so forth is the order of teaching (desanakkama). In this context, however, because the order of arising and the order of practice of the fourteen knowledges are taught sequentially by way of both, it should be understood as the order of teaching, thus comprising three types of order.

Now, since the knowledge of the delimitation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpavavatthāna-ñāṇa) was not taught by its specific nature below, the five knowledges such as “Wisdom in the delimitation of the internal is the knowledge of the diversity of bases” are briefly presented in order to show the fivefold division of mentality-materiality. When the entirety of mentality-materiality is taught, one will grasp what can be grasped and what should be grasped. Supramundane mentality, however, cannot be grasped because it has not yet been attained, and it is not to be grasped because it is not the object of insight (vipassanā). Therein, regarding “ajjhattavavatthāne” (in the delimitation of the internal): it is called “internal” (ajjhatta) because it occurs by making oneself the priority, as if with the intention, “May we, who are thus proceeding, come to the grasping of a self.” This word “ajjhatta” is found in four meanings: internal as object (gocarajjhatta), internal as one's own (niyakajjhatta), internal as internal bases (ajjhattajjhatta), and internal as domain (visayajjhatta). In such passages as, “Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should well-establish the mind internally in that very same previous sign of concentration; he is delighted internally and concentrated,” this word ajjhatta is seen in the sense of internal as object (gocarajjhatta). In passages such as, “Internal tranquility,” and “He dwells contemplating the dhamma in dhammas internally,” it is seen in the sense of internal as one's own (niyakajjhatta).
31:
It is called “internal” (ajjhatta) because it occurs by making oneself the priority, with the intention as if to say, “Let us come to the grasping of a self.” The word ajjhatta is found in four meanings: internal as object (gocarajjhatta), internal as one's own (niyakajjhatta), internal as internal bases (ajjhattajjhatta), and internal as domain (visayajjhatta). In such passages as, “Ānanda, that bhikkhu should well-establish the mind internally in that very same previous sign of concentration; he is delighted internally and concentrated,” this word ajjhatta appears in the sense of internal as object (gocarajjhatta). In “Internal tranquility,” and “He dwells contemplating the dhamma in dhammas internally,” it appears in the sense of internal as one's own (niyakajjhatta). In “The six internal bases, internal states,” it appears in the sense of internal as internal bases (ajjhattajjhatta). In “Ānanda, this dwelling is fully realized by the Tathāgata, that is, by not attending to any signs, he enters and dwells in the internal fruition attainment of emptiness,” it appears in the sense of internal as domain (visayajjhatta), meaning the place of mastery (issariyatthana). Indeed, the fruition attainment (phalasamapatti) is the place of mastery for the Buddhas. In this context, however, it should be understood as internal as internal bases (ajjhattajjhatta). The delimitation of those internal states is “delimitation of the internal” (ajjhattavavatthāna). It is called “diversity of bases” (vatthunānatta) because of the diverse nature of the bases, meaning in diverse bases. Here, the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga), which is the condition for the impulsion mind-consciousness (javana-manoviññāṇa), is also called a “base” (vatthu) because it is a place of arising, just like the five bases such as the eye. Adverting (āvajjana) also occurs only by depending on that life-continuum.

“External” (bahiddha) refers to the states occurring in the objects that are outside of the six internal bases. It is called “diversity of objects” (gocaranānatta) because of the diverse variety of objects, meaning in the diversity of objects.

Delimiting the behaviors by way of behavior of consciousness (viññāṇacariya), behavior of non-knowledge (aññāṇacariya), and behavior of knowledge (ñāṇacariya) is called “delimitation of behavior” (cariyāvavatthāna). Some also read it as “cariyavavatthāna,” making the vowel short.

Delimiting the fourfold states by way of the fourteen tetrads (catukka) such as the plane of the sense sphere is called “delimitation of the fourfold states” (catudhammavavatthāna). The word “plane” (bhūmi) occurs in the sense of “earth” in passages such as, “Whether on the earth or situated in the sky.” It occurs in the sense of “domain” (visaya) in passages such as, “Dear, do not resort to what is not your domain.” It occurs in the sense of “place of arising” in passages such as, “In the sense sphere, which is a plane of happiness.” In this context, however, it occurs in the sense of “portion” (koṭṭhāsa). Some also say it means “delimitation” (pariccheda).
32:
"Defining nine things" (nava-dhamma-vavatthāna) refers to the definition of nine groups of nine things by way of the nine states starting with wholesome states of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala), the nine states rooted in joy (pāmojja-mūlaka), and the nine states rooted in wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra-mūlaka). Among these five knowledges, the knowledge of the diversity of bases (vatthu-nānatta-ñāṇa) is taught first because internal states (ajjhatta-dhamma/ajjhattikāyatana) must be defined first. Next, the knowledge of the diversity of domains (gocara-nānatta-ñāṇa) is taught immediately after because their objects (visaya) must then be defined. Thereafter, the remaining three knowledges are taught in numerical order by way of three, four, and nine.

Now, the knowledge that defines by way of the distinctions of mind and matter is called full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). Immediately following that is full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and then full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā); thus there are three full understandings. In connection with these three full understandings, development (bhāvanā) and realization (sacchikiriyā) occur. Therefore, immediately after the knowledges of the diversity of states (dhamma-nānatta-ñāṇa), the five knowledges beginning with knowledge in the sense of the known (ñātaṭṭhe ñāṇa) are pointed out. The three full understandings are: full understanding of the known, full understanding by investigation, and full understanding by abandoning. Among them, the wisdom that proceeds by way of well-noting the individual characteristics (paccatta-lakkhaṇa) of various states, such as "matter has the characteristic of being molested (ruppana-lakkhaṇa), feeling has the characteristic of being felt (vedayita-lakkhaṇa)," is called full understanding of the known. The insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) that takes the characteristics as its object, proceeding by attributing the general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) to those various states in such ways as "matter is impermanent, suffering, non-self; feeling is impermanent, suffering, non-self," is called full understanding by investigation. That same insight wisdom taking the characteristics as its object, which proceeds by way of abandoning the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) and so on regarding those very states, is called full understanding by abandoning.

Among those three, the stage (bhūmi) of full understanding of the known begins from the delimitation of formations (saṅkhāra-pariccheda/nāmarūpa-pariccheda-ñāṇa) up to the discernment of conditions (paccaya-pariggaha-ñāṇa). Indeed, within this interval, the penetration of the individual characteristics of states is predominant. The stage of full understanding by investigation begins from the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa) up to the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa). Indeed, within this interval, the penetration of the general characteristics is predominant. The stage of full understanding by abandoning begins from the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa) and upwards. From then on, there is the predominance of the seven contemplations (anupassanā) that effect the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so on, as follows: "One contemplating as impermanent abandons the perception of permanence; one contemplating as suffering abandons the perception of pleasure; one contemplating as non-self abandons the perception of self; one becoming disenchanted abandons delight; one becoming dispassionate abandons lust; one causing cessation abandons origination; one relinquishing abandons grasping."
33:
Among those (five knowledges), "wisdom of direct knowledge" (abhiññā-paññā) is the wisdom that knows states by their nature, such as being molested (ruppana). This wisdom is called 'abhiññā' because the prefix 'abhi' has the sense of 'excellent' (sobhana), meaning "excellent knowing by way of knowing the nature of various states." Knowledge in the sense of the known (ñātaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is knowledge that has the nature of knowing.

"Wisdom of full understanding" (pariññā-paññā) is the wisdom that knows thoroughly. This wisdom is called 'pariññā' because the prefix 'pari' has the sense of 'pervading' (byāpana), meaning "pervasive knowing by way of the general characteristics such as impermanence, or by way of completing one's own task." Knowledge in the sense of investigation (tīraṇaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is knowledge that has the nature of investigating or comprehending by way of the general characteristics such as impermanence.

"Wisdom in abandoning" (pahāne paññā) is the wisdom that abandons the perception of permanence and so on. It is called 'pahāna' (abandoning) because it abandons, or because one abandons by means of this knowledge. Knowledge in the sense of relinquishment (pariccāgaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is knowledge that has the nature of relinquishing.

"Wisdom of development" (bhāvanā-paññā) is the wisdom that increases. Knowledge in the sense of a single taste (ekarasaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is knowledge that has the nature of a single function, or knowledge that has the nature of a single taste by way of the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa).

"Wisdom of realization" (sacchikiriyā-paññā) is the wisdom that makes manifest by way of penetration (paṭivedha) or by way of attainment (paṭilābha). Knowledge in the sense of touching (phassanaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is knowledge that has the nature of experiencing by way of both of those.

25-28. Now, because the wisdom of abandoning, the wisdom of development, and the wisdom of realization are associated with the Noble Path and the Noble Fruit, immediately after those (five knowledges), the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), which are attained only by Noble Persons (ariya-puggala), are briefly shown. Among those four analytical knowledges, the knowledge of the analysis of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) is shown first because the effect (attha) produced by a cause is evident and easy to understand like the truth of suffering. Immediately after that, the knowledge of the analysis of states (dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) is shown because it takes the cause (dhamma) of that effect as its object. Immediately after those two, the knowledge of the analysis of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) is shown because it takes the language (nirutti) that falls upon both meaning and state as its object. Immediately after those three, the knowledge of the analysis of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) is shown because it occurs within those three knowledges. They also recite it as 'pāṭisambhidā' by making the letter 'pa' long.

29-31. Following these analytical knowledges, the three knowledges beginning with knowledge in the sense of abiding (vihāraṭṭha-ñāṇa) are briefly shown immediately after the analytical knowledges because they occur only to Noble Persons and because they are distinctions of the analytical knowledges. Knowledge in the sense of abiding is indeed the knowledge of the analysis of states. In the sense of attainment...
34:
Knowledge regarding the result (effect) is called the Discrimination of Meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā). In the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali (Paṭi. M. 2.30), knowledge regarding the nature of things (dhammasabhāva) is called the 'Discrimination of Phenomena' (dhammapaṭisambhidā). Knowledge regarding Nibbāna, however, is only the Discrimination of Meaning.

In the term 'diversity of abidings' (vihāranānatta), it refers to the various abidings of insight (vipassanā-vihāra) by way of contemplation on impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and so forth. The 'nature of abiding' (vihāraṭṭha) refers to the nature of the abiding of insight. 'Abiding' (vihāra) itself is insight (vipassanā) together with its associated states. 'Diversity of attainments' (samāpattinānatta) refers to the various attainments of fruition (phalasamāpatti) by way of the signless (animitta) and so forth. 'Attainment' (samāpatti) refers to the mental states—consciousness and mental factors—that constitute the supramundane fruition. The term 'diversity of abidings and attainments' (vihārasamāpattinānatta) is spoken by way of both.

Thereafter, for the purpose of explaining in another way the Path-knowledge—which was previously mentioned as 'wisdom in the turning away from both and in the turning away from the conditioned' (dubhato vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā) and which accomplishes the knowledge of abiding and attainment—by specifying its cause, namely its ability to utterly eradicate the taints (āsava) and its quality of yielding its fruit immediately, that same Path-knowledge is briefly presented as 'knowledge in the concentration of immediacy' (ānantarikasamādhi).

In that Pali, 'due to the purity of non-distraction' (avikkhepaparisuddhattā) means: the mind is distracted by that state, therefore it is called 'distraction' (vikkhepa); this is a name for restlessness (uddhacca). The absence of distraction is 'non-distraction' (avikkhepa); this is a name for concentration (samādhi), which is the opposite of restlessness. The state of being pure is 'purity' (parisuddhatta). The purity of non-distraction is 'avikkhepaparisuddhatta'. Therefore, 'avikkhepaparisuddhattā' means because of the pure state of concentration. This is a statement of the cause for the utter eradication of taints and for the yielding of the fruit immediately.

In the term 'eradication of taints' (āsavasamuccheda), they are called 'taints' (āsava) because they flow out. It means they flow or occur from the eye-door... and from the mind-door. Alternatively, they are called taints because they flow, in terms of phenomena, up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and in terms of location, up to the peak of existence (bhavagga). It means they occur by including these phenomena and this location within them. For this prefix 'ā' has the sense of 'including within'. They are also called taints because they are like fermented spirits (madira) and such, in the sense of being long-matured. In the world, long-matured spirits and such are called 'āsava'. If they are taints in the sense of being long-matured, then only these phenomena (such as ignorance, etc.) deserve to be called taints. Thus it is said: 'Bhikkhus, the preceding point of ignorance is not manifest, such that one could say: Before this, ignorance did not exist, but then it arose later,' and so forth. Alternatively, they are called taints because they flow or produce the long suffering of saṃsāra. 'Samuccheda' means that which is utterly eradicated by this [Path]. 'Wisdom' (paññā) is the wisdom in the utter eradication of the four taints, such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava).
35:
Knowledge in the concentration of immediacy (ānantarikasamādhi) refers to the Path-concentration (maggasamādhi), which has received the name 'immediacy' (ānantarika) because it yields its fruit (phala) invariably and immediately after its own occurrence. Indeed, when Path-concentration has arisen, there is no obstacle whatsoever that can prevent the arising of its fruit. As it was said: 'If this person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), and it were the time for the world-cycle to burn up, the world-cycle would not burn up as long as this person has not realized the fruit of stream-entry; this person is called one who stays for an aeon (ṭhitakappī). All individuals possessed of the Path are ṭhitakappī.' This knowledge is the knowledge associated with that concentration of immediacy.

Since this Path-knowledge occurs only for noble ones (ariyas) who have reached the fruit, the four knowledges starting with the knowledge of the conflict-free abiding (araṇavihārañāṇa) are briefly presented immediately after this knowledge. Among those four, the knowledge of the conflict-free abiding is presented first because it occurs constantly only for Arahants. Thereafter, the knowledge of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpattiñāṇa) is presented because, although the attainment of cessation can occur for Non-returners (anāgāmis) and Arahants, it has many requirements (sambhāra) and especially because cessation is considered Nibbāna. Thereafter, the knowledge of final Nibbāna (parinibbānañāṇa) is presented as 'long-duration' (dīghakālika) because final Nibbāna occurs after a long time, reaching the time of final passing away. Thereafter, the knowledge of one who is equal-headed (samasīsaṭṭhañāṇa) is presented as 'short-duration' (rassakālika) because it reaches the time of final Nibbāna immediately after the destruction of all defilements.

In that Pali, the word 'ca' (and) in 'santo ca' should be connected with all three terms: predominance of vision (dassanādhipateyya), the attainment of the peaceful abiding (santo vihārādhigamo), and the resolution on the sublime (paṇītādhimuttatā). 'Vision' (dassana) is insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa). It is called 'predominance' (ādhipateyya) either because it is predominant or because it comes from the predominant factor of investigation (vīmaṃsādhipati). Because it is both a vision and a predominant factor, it is called 'predominance of vision' (dassanādhipateyya). It is called 'abiding' (vihāra) because one abides or because they abide by means of that state. It is called 'attainment' (adhigama) because it is reached or attained through insight. Since the abiding itself is the attainment, it is called 'attainment of abiding' (vihārādhigama). That attainment of abiding is called 'peaceful' (santa) because it is free from the fever of defilements. It is the wisdom of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpattipaññā). It is called 'sublime' (paṇīta) because of its excellent sense or because of its insatiable sense (atatpakaṭṭhena). Or it is called sublime because it leads to an excellent state. It is called 'resolved on the sublime' (paṇītādhimutta) because the mind is inclined toward the sublime attainment of fruition. The state of being resolved on the sublime is 'resolution on the sublime' (paṇītādhimuttatā). This is the insight-wisdom occurring in the preliminary stage that is inclined toward the attainment of fruition.
36:
Araṇavihāra means a dwelling free from defilements. Defilements such as lust (rāga) cause suffering to beings, they crush them, and they oppress them; therefore, they are called 'raṇa' (conflict/defilement). Alternatively, because of these defilements such as lust, beings weep and lament; for this reason also, they are called 'raṇa'. Among the three types of dwellings mentioned above, it is called 'araṇa' because it is free from the 'raṇa' of defilements. It is called 'vihāra' (dwelling) because, through this knowledge, various opposing states are removed. In that araṇavihāra, the first jhāna and so forth, which are taught in the Niddesavāra, are also included by way of 'inclination towards the sublime' (paṇītādhimuttatā), specifically towards the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Indeed, desiring to enter the attainment of fruition, one enters the first jhāna and so forth, and after emerging from the jhāna, one contemplates with insight (vipassanā) the states associated with that jhāna. It should also be understood that the 'practice of non-conflict' (araṇapaṭipadā) taught by the Blessed One in the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta is also included within this araṇavihāra. In that Sutta, the Blessed One taught as follows:

"Monks, I will teach you the Araṇavibhaṅga (The Exposition of Non-conflict). ... One should not pursue sensual pleasure, which is low, vulgar, the way of worldlings, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Nor should one pursue the practice of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Monks, without veering towards either of these two extremes, there is the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. One should know what it is to extol and one should know what it is to disparage. Having known both, one should neither extol nor disparage anyone, but should teach only the Dhamma. One should know how to define happiness; having known how to define happiness, one should pursue internal happiness. One should not speak words of blame behind someone's back, nor should one speak offensive words in their presence. One should speak unhurriedly, not hurriedly. One should not cling to local dialects, nor should one override common usage." This is the brief summary of the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta. ... Monks, among those states, the non-pursuit of the joy and pleasure associated with sensual desires is a state that is low ... unbeneficial. This practice of non-pursuit is a practice that is without suffering, without distress, without despair, and without fever; it is the Right Practice (sammāpaṭipadā). Therefore, this state is called 'araṇa' (non-conflict). ... Monks, among those states, the non-pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial, is also a state without suffering...
37:
... Therefore, this state is called 'araṇa' (non-conflict). Monks, among those states, there is that Middle Way fully awakened to by the Tathāgata ... this state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. ... Monks, among those states, there is that teaching of the Dhamma which neither extols nor disparages. This state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. ... Monks, among those states, there are the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha), the happiness of seclusion (paviveka-sukha), the happiness of peace (upasama-sukha), and the happiness of enlightenment (sambodhi-sukha). This state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. ... Monks, among those states, there is that speech spoken behind the back which is factual, true, and beneficial. This state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. ... Monks, among those states, there is that speech spoken in one's presence which is factual, true, and beneficial, even if it is sharp (khīṇavāda). This state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. ... Monks, among those states, there is the speech of one who is unhurried. This state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. ... Monks, among those states, there is the non-clinging to local dialects and the non-overriding of common usage. This state is without suffering, therefore this state is called 'araṇa'. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall know the state with conflict (saraṇa) and we shall know the state without conflict (araṇa). Having known both, we shall practice the way of non-conflict (araṇa-paṭipadā).' Monks, the clansman Subhūti is one who practices the way of non-conflict."

Among those states, the Middle Way is included by way of the predominance of vision (dassanādhipateyya) and the attainment of the peaceful dwelling (santeana vihārādhigama). The non-pursuit of sensual pleasure and self-mortification is itself the Middle Way. For an Arahant, the Middle Way exists in the preliminary stage of insight, and the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti) is also the Middle Way by virtue of the Eightfold Path. The remaining states should be understood as being included by way of inclination towards the sublime (paṇītādhimuttatā). Although all Arahants are dwellers in non-conflict (araṇavihārī), other Arahants, when teaching the Dhamma, may extol or disparage based on the person, saying, "The one who practices rightly is practicing rightly," or "The one who practices wrongly is practicing wrongly." However, the Elder Subhūti taught the Dhamma based solely on the Dhamma itself, saying, "This is the wrong practice, this is the right practice." For this reason, the Blessed One praised him as one who "practices the way of non-conflict" and appointed him to the foremost position (aggaṭṭhāna) among those who dwell in non-conflict, saying, "Monks, among my monk disciples who dwell in non-conflict, Subhūti is the foremost."

"By two powers" (dvīhi balehi) refers to the power of serenity (samatha-bala) and the power of insight (vipassanā-bala). "By the fact of being possessed of" (samannāgatattā) means because of being associated with or because of being complete in. The term "tayo ca" (and three) is a case variation (vibhatti-vipallāsa) and means "of the three" (tiṇṇañca). "Of formations" (saṅkhārānaṃ) refers to verbal formations, bodily formations, and mental formations. "For the subsiding" (paṭippassaddhiyā) means for the purpose of peace, cessation, or non-arising. "By sixteen" (soḷasahi) refers to the eight types of insight such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and the eight stages of the Path and Fruition, totaling sixteen. "By the activities of knowledge" (ñāṇacariyāhi) means by the occurrences of knowledge. "By nine" (navahi) refers to the meditative absorptions (samādhi) of the fine-material and immaterial spheres and their access concentration (upacāra).
38:
The meaning is: "Saṅkhārānaṃ" refers to the meaning of verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra), bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra), and mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra). "Paṭippassaddhiyā" means for the sake of the benefit of tranquility, the benefit of cessation, and the benefit of non-arising. "Soḷasahi" (by the sixteen) means by the sixteen, consisting of the eight such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and the eight paths and fruits (magga-phala). "Ñāṇacariyāhi" means by the occurrences of knowledge. "Navahi" (by the nine) means by the nine, consisting of the four fine-material sphere concentrations (rūpāvacara-samādhi), the four immaterial sphere concentrations (arūpāvacara-samādhi), and their access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).

"Vasībhāvatā paññā" refers to speed, occurrence as desired, sovereignty, and desire. Because that person possesses that power, they are called "vasī" (a master). The state of a master is "vasībhāva." "Vasībhāva" itself is "vasībhāvatā," just as "pāṭikulya" (loathsomeness) is "pāṭikulyatā." Alternatively, it means wisdom of such a nature is the wisdom of mastery. They also recite by lengthening the syllable "si" to "sī." In the sentences "samannāgatattā ca, paṭippassaddhiyā ca, ñāṇacariyāhi ca, samādhicariyāhi ca," the word "ca" (and) should be understood as connecting them.

"Nirodhasamāpattiyā ñāṇaṃ" is the knowledge that arises due to the cause of the attainment of cessation of Non-returners (anāgāmī) and Arahants. It is like killing a leopard because one desires its skin. The attainment of cessation is merely the absence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). It is not any ultimate reality (paramattha). Because it is merely an absence, it is also called cessation (nirodha), which is a mere designation (paññatti). It is called an attainment (samāpatti) because it is attained by one who wishes to enter it.

"Sampajānassa" means "sampajāna" because one knows well in various ways. It refers to that clearly comprehending person. "Pavattapariyādāne": "pavatta" refers to the occurrence. The exhaustion and non-occurrence of the occurrence of defilements and the occurrence of the aggregates is called "pavatta-pariyādāna." It means in that exhaustion of occurrence. "Parinibbāne ñāṇaṃ" is the knowledge that occurs in the Parinibbāna of defilements and the Parinibbāna of the aggregates of an Arahant who reviews the non-occurrence of sensual desire, etc., and the Parinibbāna without remaining substrate (anupādisesa-parinibbāna).

"Sabbadhammānaṃ" means of all things belonging to the three planes of existence. "Sammā samucchede" means in the thorough cessation by way of the cutting off of continuity. "Nirodhe ca anupaṭṭhānatā" means the state of not appearing again after reaching cessation, meaning non-arising again. In the sentences "sammāsamucchede ca" and "nirodhe ca anupaṭṭhānatā ca," the word "ca" should be connected.

"Samasīsaṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ" refers to the thirty-seven "sama" (equal/calmed) states such as renunciation (nekkhamma) and the thirteen "sīsa" (head/chief) states such as craving (taṇhā). They are called "sama" because they calm the opposing states. They are called "sīsa" because they are predominant as appropriate and are the peaks. Whether in a single posture...
39:
...or in a single disease, or in a single life-faculty (jīvitindriya) by way of a similar continuity, the "sama" states such as renunciation and the "sīsa" (chief) states such as faith (saddhā) exist for that person; therefore, they are called "samasīsī" (equal-headed). The meaning of "samasīsī" is "samasīsaṭṭha." It means in that state of "samasīsaṭṭha" or in the state of being "samasīsī." Having undertaken insight (vipassanā) in a single posture, or in a disease, or in the life-faculty by way of a similar continuity, and having reached the four paths and fruits in that very posture, disease, or similar life-faculty, the state of "samasīsī" occurs for the Arahant who attains Parinibbāna right there. The knowledge in that state of "samasīsī" is called "samasīsaṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ." It is also stated in the Puggalapaññatti text and its commentary: "Who is the person who is equal-headed (samasīsī)? For which person the exhaustion of the taints (āsava) and the exhaustion of the life-faculty occur neither before nor after (simultaneously). This person is called an equal-headed person."

In the description of "samasīsī," "apubbaṃ acarimaṃ" (neither before nor after) means occurring only once, at the same moment, by way of the continuity of the present. "Pariyādānaṃ" means complete exhaustion. This person is called "samasīsī." That "samasīsī" person is of three types: posture equal-headed (iriyāpatha-samasīsī), disease equal-headed (roga-samasīsī), and life equal-headed (jīvita-samasīsī). Among those three, one who undertakes insight while walking, reaches Arahantship, and attains Parinibbāna while walking; one who undertakes insight while standing, reaches Arahantship, and attains Parinibbāna while standing; one who undertakes insight while sitting, reaches Arahantship, and attains Parinibbāna while sitting; one who undertakes insight while lying down, reaches Arahantship, and attains Parinibbāna while lying down—this person is called "posture equal-headed" (iriyāpatha-samasīsī). One who, while experiencing a certain disease, undertakes insight within that disease, reaches Arahantship, and attains Parinibbāna through that very disease—this person is called "disease equal-headed" (roga-samasīsī).

What is "life equal-headed" (jīvita-samasīsī)? There are thirteen "sīsa" (chief) states. Among them, the path of Arahantship exhausts ignorance (avijjā), which is the chief of defilements. The death-consciousness (cuti-citta) exhausts the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), which is the chief of the occurrence (of life). The consciousness that exhausts ignorance cannot exhaust the life-faculty. The consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty cannot exhaust ignorance. The consciousness that exhausts ignorance is one, and the consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty is another. For the person for whom these two chief states reach exhaustion simultaneously, they are called "life equal-headed" (jīvita-samasīsī). How does this simultaneous exhaustion occur? It is through the equality of the turn (vāra). When...
40:
When the emergence from the path (magga-vuṭṭhāna) occurs, one stands in the nineteenth reviewing knowledge—comprising five in the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), five in the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga), five in the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga), and four in the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga)—and then, descending into the life-continuum (the death-consciousness), one attains final Nibbāna (parinibbāna). Because of this equality between the stage of reviewing and the stage of death, the exhaustion of both the 'heads' of ignorance and the life-faculty is said to be equal. Therefore, such a person is called 'one who is equal-headed in life' (jīvitasamasīsī). And in this context, it is precisely this jīvitasamasīsī person who is intended.

Now, because the knowledges consisting of learning (sutamaya), virtue (sīlamaya), and mental development (bhāvanāmaya) are merely foundations for the round of rebirth, they are not called 'effacement' (sallekha), which cuts off opposing states. Only these knowledges that are foundations for the supramundane, along with other such knowledges, are called 'effacement'. Therefore, to show the knowledges that proceed by way of effacing opposing states, the knowledge in the sense of effacement (sallekhaṭṭha-ñāṇa) is briefly pointed out immediately after the knowledge in the sense of being equal-headed.

In that sallekhaṭṭha-ñāṇa, 'wisdom in the exhaustion of various and diverse powers (teja)' refers to the wisdom in the exhaustion (relinquishing) of various states such as lust (rāga), which are distinct because they do not mix with supramundane states; and diverse states such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda); and those termed 'powers' (teja) such as immorality (dusīlya) because of their nature to burn. It refers to the wisdom associated with the thirty-seven factors such as renunciation (nekkhamma). Alternatively, it means the wisdom that is the exhaustion of the five 'powers' such as immorality, which are distinct and diverse in nature. We shall explain the inclusion of various and diverse states through these 'powers' in the detailed exposition (niddesa-vāra).

'Knowledge in the sense of effacement' (sallekhaṭṭha-ñāṇa) is called 'effacement' because it scrapes away or cuts off opposing states. It is the knowledge concerning the thirty-seven types of effacing states such as renunciation. It should be understood that the forty-four types of effacement taught by the Blessed One in the Sallekha Sutta, beginning with: "Others may be harmful, but here we shall be harmless; thus effacement should be practiced," are also included within this knowledge of effacement.

Now, to show the right effort (sammasappadhāna-vīriya) that should be performed by one established in the knowledge of effacement, the knowledge of the inception of energy (vīriyārambha-ñāṇa) is briefly pointed out immediately after it. In that vīriyārambha-ñāṇa, 'the state of having an unsluggish mind, the state of having a resolute mind, and the sense of exertion' are explained as follows: 'Asallīnattā' (unsluggishness of mind) means having a mind that is not shrunken or withdrawn due to laziness. 'Attā' refers to the mind. As it was said:

"Irrigators lead the water,
Fletchers straighten the arrow,
Carpenters shape the wood,
The wise master themselves (their minds)." (Dhammapada 80-82)
41:
One is called 'pahitattā' (one with a resolute mind) because one's mind is relinquished, sent forth, and released without regard for either body or life. Here, 'attā' refers to the individual existence (the group of five aggregates). As it was said: "If a nun should weep, striking herself (attānaṃ)..." (Pācittiya 880). One who has a mind that is not sluggish due to laziness and whose mind is sent forth by energy is called 'asallīnattā-pahitattā'. 'Paggaha' (exertion) means that which uplifts and supports the co-nascent states. Since exertion is its very nature, it is called 'paggahaṭṭha' (the sense of exertion). The sense of exertion of one who has an unsluggish and resolute mind is called 'asallīnattā-pahitattā-paggahaṭṭha'.

Regarding this asallīnattā-pahitattā-paggahaṭṭha: "Therefore, monks, you should strive with unfaltering effort. Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up. As long as that which is attainable by manly strength, manly energy, and manly effort has not been attained, there shall be no stopping of energy." Because of this teaching, the term 'asallīnattā-pahitattā' expresses non-faltering and non-retreating in striving. The term 'paggahaṭṭha' expresses energy that is free from laziness and restlessness, and which proceeds evenly.

In the phrase 'knowledge of the inception of energy' (vīriyārambha-ñāṇa), 'vīriya' (energy) means the state of being brave, or the work of the energetic, or that which should be stirred up and set in motion by proper method and means. It has the characteristic of striving, the function of supporting and strengthening co-nascent states, and the manifestation of non-collapse. Because it is said, "One who is stirred (saṃviggo) strives wisely," its proximate cause is spiritual urgency (saṃvega), or its proximate cause is the eight grounds for the inception of energy (vīriyārambha-vatthu). Energy that is well-initiated should be seen as the root of all attainments. The inception characterized by energy is 'vīriyārambha'. By this, other types of 'ārambha' (inception/undertaking) are excluded.

Indeed, this word 'ārambha' appears in many senses, such as action (kamma), offense (āpatti), activity (kiriyā), energy (vīriya), harm (hiṃsā), and destruction (vikopana).

"Whatever suffering arises, it all arises because of undertakings (ārambha/kamma); with the cessation of undertakings, there is no arising of suffering." (Sutta Nipāta 749). In this context, 'ārambha' means kamma.

"He commits an offense (ārambhati) and becomes remorseful." In this context, it means an offense (āpatti).

"Great sacrifices involve great undertakings (mahārambhā); they are not of great fruit." In this context, it means activities (kiriyā) such as setting up the sacrificial post.

"Strive (ārambhatha), go forth, exert yourselves in the Buddha's teaching." In this context, it means energy (vīriya).

"They harm (ārambhanti) living beings on account of the ascetic Gotama." In this context, it means harm (hiṃsā).

"He is one who abstains from damaging (samārambhā) seeds and plants..."
42:
In the Pali text "Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hoti" (found in the Dīgha Nikāya and Majjhima Nikāya), "ārambha" refers to destruction such as cutting or breaking. However, in this context, only effort (vīriya) is intended. Therefore, it is said, "Effort known as exertion is vīriyārambha." It is called "ārambha" by virtue of initiating effort. It refers to the knowledge occurring in that initiation of effort. Some also read it as "asallīnattā pahitattā," meaning due to the state of being unsluggish and having a mind directed towards Nibbāna. The former reading is better. Some teachers explain: "The balance of mindfulness, investigation of states, effort, and joy enlightenment factors is called asallīnattatā; the balance of mindfulness, concentration, tranquility, and equanimity enlightenment factors is called pahitattatā; and the balance of all seven enlightenment factors is called paggahaṭṭha (the sense of uplifting)."

39. Now, to show that the noble person (ariya) who has reached the Path and Fruit accomplished through Right Effort should teach the Dhamma for the benefit of the world, the "Knowledge of Demonstrating the Meaning" (atthasandassana-ñāṇa) is briefly shown immediately after that initiation of effort. In that knowledge, "nānādhammap-pakāsanatā" means the exposition, illustration, and teaching of various phenomena by way of all conditioned and unconditioned states. "Pakāsanatā" simply means exposition. "Atthasandassane" refers to the knowledge in demonstrating various meanings to others. Both the phenomena (dhammas) and the meanings (atthas) are those very conditioned and unconditioned states.

40. Now, to show the "Purity of Vision" (dassanavisuddhi), which is the cause for that noble person who demonstrates and teaches with Dhamma-talk to others to teach according to the true nature of things, the "Knowledge of Purity of Vision" (dassanavisuddhi-ñāṇa) is briefly shown immediately after that knowledge of demonstrating the meaning. In that knowledge, "sabbadhammānaṃ ekasaṅgahatā nānattekatta-paṭivedhe" means the penetration (abhisamaya) of the fact that all conditioned and unconditioned states are counted as a single group, as well as the penetration of the diversity (nānatta) of states like sensual desire and the unity (ekatta) of states like renunciation. That penetrative wisdom consists of Path-knowledge and Fruit-knowledge. Path-knowledge is called penetration because it penetrates by way of realizing the truths at the moment of realizing the Four Noble Truths. Fruit-knowledge is called penetration because the truths have been penetrated.

In this context of "ekasaṅgahatā" (state of being grouped as one), there are four types of grouping: grouping by class (jāti-saṅgaha), grouping by origin (sañjāti-saṅgaha), grouping by action (kiriya-saṅgaha), and grouping by count (gaṇana-saṅgaha). Among these four, the grouping expressed as "Let all kings come, let all brahmins, all merchants, and all workers come," or "Friend Visākha, these states—Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood—are grouped within the aggregate of virtue" (M. i. 462), is called grouping by class (jāti-saṅgaha). Just as in the phrase "Let those of the same class come," here all are taken as a single group by way of their class. "Let all those from Kosala come, ...
43:
...let all those from Magadha come, let all those from Bhārukaccha come," or "Friend Visākha, whatever Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration there are, these states are grouped within the aggregate of concentration" (M. i. 462)—this grouping is called grouping by origin (sañjāti-saṅgaha). Just as in the phrase "Let those born and raised in the same place come," here in this sañjāti-saṅgaha, all are taken as a single group by way of their place of birth or residence.

"Let all elephant riders come, let all horse riders come, let all chariot riders come," or "Friend Visākha, whatever Right View and Right Intention there are, these states are grouped within the aggregate of wisdom" (M. i. 462)—this grouping is called grouping by action (kiriya-saṅgaha). Indeed, all those persons (or states) are taken as a single group by the performance of their respective actions.

"To which aggregate count does the eye-base belong? The eye-base belongs to the count of the form aggregate. O challenger, if the eye-base belongs to the count of the form aggregate, then indeed it should be said that the eye-base is grouped with the form aggregate" (Kv. 471)—this grouping is called grouping by count (gaṇana-saṅgaha). In this context, this grouping by count is intended. Since there is a grouping by numerical delimitation of those conditioned and unconditioned states through any one of the twelve modes such as "the state of being thus" (tathaṭṭha), they are called "single groupings" (ekasaṅgaha). The state of these single groupings is "ekasaṅgahatā."

Regarding "Knowledge of Purity of Vision" (dassanavisuddhi-ñāṇa): Path-knowledge and Fruit-knowledge are called vision (dassana). Vision itself is purity, hence "purity of vision" (dassanavisuddhi). Purity of vision itself is knowledge, hence "knowledge of purity of vision" (dassanavisuddhi-ñāṇa). Path-knowledge is purity of vision because it is being purified; Fruit-knowledge is purity of vision because it has been purified.

41. Now, to show the insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that accomplish the knowledge of purity of vision in two ways, the "Knowledge of Acceptance" (khanti-ñāṇa) and the "Knowledge of Immersion" (pariyogāhaṇa-ñāṇa) are briefly shown immediately after that knowledge of purity of vision. Between these two knowledges, "wisdom due to being known" (viditattā paññā) is the wisdom that arises because the form aggregate and so on are manifest through their common characteristics such as impermanence. "Knowledge of Acceptance" (khanti-ñāṇa) is called "khanti" because it approves only of the manifest five aggregates; that very approving wisdom, being knowledge, is "khanti-ñāṇa." By this term "khanti-ñāṇa," the Buddha excludes "patience as endurance" (adhivāsana-khanti). This khanti-ñāṇa is tender insight knowledge (taruṇa-vipassanā-ñāṇa) occurring by way of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana) and so forth.

42. "Wisdom due to being touched" (phuṭṭhattā paññā) is the wisdom that arises because the form aggregate and so on are touched by "knowledge-contact" (ñāṇa-phassa) by way of impermanence and so forth. "Knowledge of Immersion" (pariyogāhaṇa-ñāṇa) is so called because it immerses into only those five aggregates touched by knowledge-contact. Some also read it as "pariyogahaṇa," shortening the "gā" syllable. This pariyogāhaṇa-ñāṇa is sharp insight knowledge (tikkha-vipassanā-ñāṇa) occurring by way of the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) and so forth. Some teachers, however, say: "Insight knowledge itself is called khanti-ñāṇa for a person led by faith (saddhā-vāhī), and pariyogāhaṇa-ñāṇa for a person led by wisdom (paññā-vāhī)." If this were so, these two knowledges would not [occur] to a single person...
44:
(These two knowledges) are possible. If these two knowledges were not possible in a single disciple, then the sixty-seven knowledges common to disciples would not be possible (simultaneously). Therefore, that statement (of some teachers) is not appropriate.

Now, worldlings and learners alike must contemplate all states such as the aggregates, etc., which are suitable for insight; they cannot contemplate only a portion of the aggregates, sense bases, and so on. Therefore, for those worldlings and learners, the "abiding in a part" (padesavihāra), which is dwelling by observing a portion, is not attained. Only for an Arahant is the "abiding in a part"—dwelling by observing a portion of the aggregates, sense bases, etc., as desired—attained. Having spoken of the knowledges that accomplish the purification of vision (dassana-visuddhi), immediately following that, the "knowledge of abiding in a part" (padesavihāra-ñāṇa), which is accomplished through the Arahant's purification of vision, is briefly indicated. In that knowledge of abiding in a part, "wisdom in combining" (samodahane paññā) refers to the wisdom that combines the group of feelings, which is a portion of the aggregates and so on; it is the wisdom of collecting into a mass. There is also a reading "samodhāne paññā"; the meaning is the same.

"Knowledge of abiding in a part" (padesavihāre ñāṇaṃ) means abiding by way of a portion (by grasping the aggregate of feeling, etc.) of the aggregates and so on; this is called padesavihāra. It is the knowledge occurring in that abiding in a part. In this context, "part" (padesa) is diverse, such as a part of the aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, faculties, the mode of conditions (dependent origination), foundations of mindfulness, jhānas, mentality-materiality, and dhammas. This diverse "part" is indeed only feeling (vedanā). How? Among the five aggregates, it is a part of the aggregates by way of the feeling aggregate (vedanā-kkhandha). Among the twelve sense bases, it is a part of the mind-object base (dhammāyatana) by way of feeling. Among the eighteen elements, it is a part of the mind-object element (dhammadhātu) by way of feeling. Among the four truths, it is a part of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) by way of feeling. Among the twenty-two faculties, it is a part of the faculties by way of the five feeling faculties (vedanindriya). Among the twelve factors of dependent origination, it is a part of the mode of conditions by way of "with contact as condition, feeling" (phassa-paccayā vedanā). Among the four foundations of mindfulness, it is a part of the foundations of mindfulness by way of the contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā). Among the four jhānas, it is a part of the jhānas by way of pleasant feeling and equanimous feeling. Among mentality-materiality, it is a part of mentality-materiality by way of feeling. Among all states such as the wholesome, etc., it is a part of the dhammas by way of feeling. Thus, feeling alone is the "part" (padesa) of the aggregates and so on. Abiding in a part is the name for the power of reviewing that very feeling.

Now, worldlings and learners who develop knowledges such as the knowledge consisting in the development of concentration (samādhibhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa), etc., make those respective states of development primary and supreme. By means of those states of development, they contemplate the various states of an opposing nature that are to be abandoned, seeing them as disadvantages because of their many faults. Having established the mind by way of those respective states of development, they abandon those respective opposing states. While abandoning...
45:
...at the time of insight, they see all formations as empty of self and what belongs to self, and subsequently, at the moment of the path, they abandon them by way of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Even while abandoning in this way, they abandon while penetrating the four truths by the power of a single realization (abhisamaya), which is the truth of the path. All noble ones (ariya) practice accordingly by these six modes mentioned above. Therefore, immediately following the knowledge of abiding in a part, the six knowledges beginning with the knowledge of the turning away of perception (saññā-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa) are briefly indicated in order.

Among those six knowledges, "wisdom as predominance" (adhipatattā paññā) means making states such as renunciation (jhāna), etc., primary and supreme, and refers to the wisdom that occurs in the mode of turning away from sensual desire, etc., because of that predominance. "Knowledge of the turning away of perception" (saññā-vivaṭṭe ñāṇaṃ) means the turning back or turning away from perception; this is called the turning away of perception (saññā-vivaṭṭa). It means the knowledge that occurs in the turning away from sensual desire, etc., through that perception—whether as a cause (hetu) or as an instrument (karaṇa)—by which one makes those respective states of development such as renunciation, non-ill will, and the perception of light primary. Although the words "from this" (etto) are not mentioned here, it should be understood as "turning away from that very state" (sensual desire, etc.) from which it turns away, just as it is understood in the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā).

That perception (saññā) has the characteristic of perceiving. It has the function (rasa) of making a mark which is the cause for perceiving again, "This object is that very same one," just as carpenters make marks on wood, etc. It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of the act of interpreting by the power of a mark as it was previously grasped, like blind men who have "seen" an elephant. Or, it has the manifestation of not lasting long because it does not occur by deeply penetrating the object, like a flash of lightning. It has the object that appears as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), like the perception "It is a man" that arises in young deer regarding scarecrows made of grass.

45. "Wisdom in diversity" (nānatte paññā) is the wisdom that occurs by seeing the faults in states such as sensual desire, etc., which have a nature different from the various states of development. The word "nānatte" is a term in the locative case used in the sense of cause (nimitta). Alternatively, the abandoning of various states like sensual desire, etc., is called "nānatta"; it means the wisdom that occurs by the power of association in states such as renunciation, etc., because of that cause which is the abandoning of diversity; or it means the reviewing wisdom (paccavekkhaṇa-paññā) that occurs by taking renunciation, etc., as an object. "Knowledge of the turning away of the mind" (cetovivaṭṭe ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge occurring in states such as renunciation, etc., when volition (cetanā) turns away from sensual desire and so on. Here, by the word "ceto", volition (cetanā) is intended. That volition has the characteristic of coordinating or the characteristic of striving. It has the characteristic of arranging associated states. It has the function (rasa) of striving. It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of arranging. It is like a senior pupil or a master carpenter who accomplishes their own work and the work of others. Furthermore, in such things as the recollection of urgent tasks, this volition is evident by way of its state of inciting the associated states.

46. "Wisdom in establishing" (adhiṭṭhāne paññā) is the wisdom occurring in the establishing of the mind upon its own object by the power of renunciation and so on. "Knowledge of the turning away of the mind" (cittavivaṭṭe ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge occurring in making the mind turn away from sensual desire, etc., by the power of abandoning sensual desire and so on.

47. "Wisdom in emptiness" (suññate paññā) is the wisdom of the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā-paññā) occurring in the state of non-self because of being empty of self and what belongs to self. "Knowledge of the turning away of knowledge" (ñāṇavivaṭṭe ñāṇaṃ)...
46:
Knowledge. Here, consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing, the function of being a precursor, the manifestation of connecting, and the proximate cause of mind-and-matter.

Wisdom in emptiness means the insight of non-self (anattānupassanā) occurring in non-self and what belongs to non-self, because of being empty of self and what belongs to self. Knowledge in the turning away of knowledge (ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa) means that knowledge itself is called 'turning away' (vivaṭṭa) because it turns away from clinging (through view and conceit); knowledge that has reached such turning away is knowledge in the turning away of knowledge.

Wisdom in relinquishment (vossagga) means it is called relinquishment because it relinquishes (defilements) in this Dhamma; it is the wisdom in renunciation (nekkhamma) etc., which is the relinquishing of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) etc. Knowledge in the turning away of liberation (vimokkha-vivaṭṭa) means it is called liberation because it is liberated from sensual desire etc.; liberation itself is called turning away (vivaṭṭa), thus it is the turning away of liberation, and that turning away of liberation is itself knowledge.

Wisdom in the sense of reality (tathattha) means the wisdom that arises without confusion by the power of function in the fourfold unerring nature of each truth. Knowledge in the turning away of the truths (sacca-vivaṭṭa) means it is called the turning away of the truths because it turns away by the power of emerging from both (defilements and objects) in the four truths; that turning away of the truths is itself knowledge. The single knowledge is taught in four ways: as "turning away of perception" (saññā-vivaṭṭa) by the power of the predominant state; as "turning away of the mind" (ceto-vivaṭṭa) by the power of the state to be abandoned; as "turning away of consciousness" (citta-vivaṭṭa) by the power of establishing the mind; and as "turning away of liberation" (vimokkha-vivaṭṭa) by the power of abandoning the opposite states. Insight into non-self itself is taught as "knowledge in the turning away of knowledge" by the power of the mode of emptiness. Path-knowledge itself is taught below in two ways: as "knowledge in the path" and as "knowledge in the concentration of immediate succession" (ānantarika-samādhi); it is also taught as "knowledge in the turning away of the truths" by the power of the mode of turning away.

Now, the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) that arise by the power of the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), which in turn arises by the power of that knowledge of the turning away of the truths, are briefly shown in order. Among those six knowledges, the knowledge of the various psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) is shown first because it has power well-known in the world and is extremely wonderful. The knowledge of the divine ear (dibba-sota-ñāṇa) is shown second because it has a grosser object than the object of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa). The knowledge of penetrating others' minds is shown third because it has a subtle object. Among the three true knowledges (vijjā), the knowledge of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) is shown first because it dispels the darkness of delusion that covers the past. The knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) is shown second because it dispels the darkness of delusion that covers the present and the future. The knowledge of the destruction of taints is shown third because it completely cuts off all darkness of delusion. In these knowledges, "kāyampi" refers to the material body (rūpa-kāya), and "cittampi" refers to the mind of the preliminary jhāna (pādaka-jhāna).
47:
Single-determination (ekavavatthānatā) means placing (the mental body and the material body) together by the preliminary mind, and also the mixing of the body and mind as appropriate when wishing to go with the visible body or the invisible body. Here, kāya refers to the physical body. The body is called kāya because it is a collection of loathsome things such as hair, and because it is the place of origin for hundreds of diseases such as eye diseases. In the phrase "perception of happiness (sukha-saññā) and perception of lightness (lahu-saññā)", the single perception associated with the fourth jhāna is divided into two due to the difference in mode, and the word 'ca' (and) is used in the sense of combination. In the fourth jhāna, equanimity is called happiness (sukha) because it is peaceful, and the perception associated with that equanimity is the perception of happiness. That same perception is called the perception of lightness because it is liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and from opposing states such as applied thought (vitakka). "By the power of resolve" (adhiṭṭhānavasena) means by the power of standing after making it primary, or it means by the power of entering (into the jhāna process). In the phrase "adhiṭṭhānavasena ca", the word 'ca' should also be connected. Thus far, the appropriate cause for all kinds of psychic powers (iddhividha) has been stated.

Wisdom in the sense of succeeding means wisdom in the nature of succeeding. Knowledge in the various psychic powers (iddhividha) means it is called iddhi because of the sense of succeeding, and because of the sense of accomplishment and attainment. Whatever is accomplished and attained is said to "succeed" (ijjhati). As the Blessed One said:

"If for one desiring sensual pleasures, those sensual pleasures succeed."

Likewise:

"Renunciation (nekkhamma) is iddhi because it succeeds; it is a miracle (pāṭihāriya) because it wards off (the opposite). The path of arahantship is iddhi because it succeeds; it is a miracle because it wards off (defilements)." Another way: It is called iddhi because of the sense of succeeding; this is a designation for the perfection of means (upāya-sampadā). The perfection of means is said to succeed because it produces the desired fruit. As the Blessed One said:

"This Citta the Householder is virtuous and of good character. If he should aspire, 'May I become a Wheel-turning Monarch in the future,' the mental aspiration of a virtuous person will succeed because of its purity." Another way: It is called iddhi because beings prosper by this iddhi. "They succeed" means they become noble, they prosper, and they reach the pinnacle. Iddhividha means iddhi itself as a category; it means a portion of iddhi or the various classifications of iddhi. Knowledge occurring in that iddhividha is called the knowledge of the various psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa).

"By the power of the expansion of applied thought" (vitakkavipphāravasena) means by the power of the expansion of one's own applied thought or by the power of the force of applied thought upon the signs of sound at the time of performing the preliminary work for the sake of producing the divine ear element. Here, vitakka is called so because it thinks, or the act of thinking is vitakka; it means hitting upon (ūhana). That applied thought has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object.
48:
(Applied thought) has the function of striking and threshing the object. Therefore, it is said that by means of that applied thought, the practitioner (yogāvacara) strikes the object and threshes the object with applied thought. It has the manifestation of leading the mind to the object. Because it arises without hindrance in an object that is perceived through the six faculties and through appropriate attention (manasikāra) to that applied thought, it is said to have the object that has come into range as its proximate cause.

'Nānattekatta-sadda-nimittānaṃ' refers to the signs known as sounds, which have either diverse natures or a single nature. In this context, sounds themselves are called 'signs' (nimitta) because they are the cause for the arising of applied thought and because they are signs of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta). Many sounds that have become a single mass by way of the sound of a large drum and so on, or sounds in various directions, or the sounds of various beings, are called 'diverse sounds' (nānatta-sadda). Sounds occurring in a single direction, or the sound of a single being, or individual sounds by way of the sound of a large drum and so on, are called 'unified sounds' (ekatta-sadda). In this term 'sadda' (sound), it is called 'sadda' because it is uttered, or because it becomes an object of the ear-consciousness. 'Uttered' means the sense. 'Pariyogāhaṇe paññā' means the wisdom that penetrates the object, the wisdom of discerning. 'Sota-dhātu-visuddhi-ñāṇa' (knowledge of the purification of the ear-element): it is called 'ear-element' (sota-dhātu) because of its nature of hearing and its nature of non-self (nijjīva). It is also called 'ear-element' because it is like the ear-element by way of performing the function of the ear-element. It is called 'purification' (visuddhi) because it is pure and free from defilements. The ear-element itself is the purification, thus 'sota-dhātu-visuddhi'. The purification of the ear-element itself is the knowledge, thus it is called 'sota-dhātu-visuddhi-ñāṇa'.

'Tiṇṇannaṃ cittānaṃ' refers to the three types of mind by way of those associated with joy (somanassa), those associated with grief (domanassa), and those associated with equanimity (upekkhā). 'Vipphārattā' means because of the state of diffusion, or because of the impulse. Here, the ablative case (nissakka-vacana) is used in the sense of cause (hetu). It means: by cause of the diffusion of the three types of minds of others at the time of performing the preliminary work (parikamma) for the purpose of producing the knowledge of discerning the minds of others (ceto-pariya-ñāṇa). 'Indriyānaṃ pasāda-vasena' means by way of the clarity of the six faculties such as the eye-faculty. Here, the locations where the faculties are established are called 'faculties' (indriya) by way of metonymy of the effect for the cause (phalu-pacāra). This is like the saying: "Friend, your faculties are very clear, your skin color is pure and bright." Among the locations where the faculties are established, in this context, only the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is intended. 'Pasāda-vasena' means by way of the state of being undisturbed. It should be understood that although it should be said 'pasāda-appasāda-vasena' (by way of clarity and lack of clarity), the word 'appasāda' (lack of clarity) has been omitted. Alternatively, since the perception that 'this object is not clear' can only occur in relation to clarity, it should be understood that by the word 'pasāda-vasena' alone, lack of clarity (appasāda) is also expressed.

'Nānattekatta-viññāṇa-cariyā pariyogāhaṇe paññā' is the wisdom that knows the occurrence of the eighty-nine types of consciousness, which have diverse natures or a single nature as the case may be. In this context, the conduct of consciousness (viññāṇa-cariyā) of an unconcentrated person is 'diversity' (nānatta), and the conduct of consciousness of a concentrated person is 'unity' (ekatta).
49:
A mind with lust and so forth is called diversity (nānatta); a mind without lust and so forth is called unity (ekatta). In the term 'knowledge of encompassing the minds' (cetopariyañāṇa), 'pariya' means encompassing from all around; it has the meaning of knowing by delimiting. Because it delimits the minds of others from various aspects, it is called 'cetopariya'. Since it is both the delimiting of others' minds and that knowledge itself, it is called 'cetopariyañāṇa'. There is also a reading 'vipphāratā', which means 'in the state of pervasiveness'.

'Phenomena proceeding from conditions' (paccayappavattānaṃ dhammānaṃ) refers to the present phenomena—consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—which arise due to past causes, namely ignorance, formations, craving, clinging, and becoming, by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). In the phrase 'by way of the pervasiveness of diverse and unified karma' (nānattekatta-kamma-vipphāra-vasena), unwholesome karma is called diversity, and wholesome karma is called unity. Alternatively, sense-sphere karma is diversity, while fine-material and immaterial sphere karma is unity. The wisdom that occurs in penetrating and grasping the resultant phenomena that proceed from causes by way of the pervasiveness of karma of various natures is the connection here.

'Knowledge of the recollection of past dwellings' (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa): 'past dwellings' (pubbenivāsa) refers to the aggregates that lived in past births. 'Lived' means those that occurred and ceased within one's own continuity, having been inhabited and experienced. Alternatively, 'past dwellings' refers to the phenomena that were dwelt upon by way of being objects in past births. These are the aggregates known and delimited by one's own consciousness, or those known by the consciousness of others. Those known by the consciousness of others are attained only by the Buddhas. The mindfulness by which one recollects the aggregates lived in previous lives is called 'recollection of past dwellings' (pubbenivāsānussati); the knowledge associated with that mindfulness is 'knowledge of the recollection of past dwellings' (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa).

'By way of radiance' (obhāsa-vasena) means by way of the radiance of a kasiṇa—one of the fire kasiṇa, white kasiṇa, or light kasiṇa—which is the object of the fourth jhāna, extended for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye. 'Of the signs of diverse and unified forms' (nānattekatta-rūpa-nimittānaṃ): the forms of various beings, or the forms of beings born in the realm of diverse bodies (nānattakāya), or forms in various directions, or unmixed forms, are called 'diverse forms' (nānatta-rūpa). The forms of a single being, or the forms of a being born in the realm of unified bodies (ekattakāya), or forms in a single direction, or forms that are mixed with those of various directions and so forth, are called 'unified forms' (ekatta-rūpa). Here, 'form' (rūpa) refers specifically to the base of visible form (rūpāyatana). It is called 'rūpa' because it shows itself; it means it reveals the state of the heart while undergoing changes in color. Visible form itself is the 'sign of form' (rūpa-nimitta). It is the wisdom in the nature of seeing those signs of forms of diverse and unified natures.

'Knowledge of the divine eye' (dibbacakkhuñāṇa): it is called 'divine' (dibba) because it is similar to the eyes of the devas. The divine sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) of the devas is born of well-performed karma, is not obstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and being free from defilements, is capable of receiving objects even at a distance. This eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu), born of the power of energetic development (vīriya-bhāvanā), is also called 'divine' because it is similar to that. It is called 'divine' because it is attained by way of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra) of the fourth jhāna, or because it relies on the divine abiding. It is called 'divine' because it has a great radiance through the grasping of the light kasiṇa, and because it has a vast range capable of seeing forms outside of walls. It is called 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing. It is also called 'eye' because it performs the function of the eye—seeing visible forms—and thus resembles the sensitive eye (cakkhu-pasāda). Since it is both divine and an eye, it is called 'divine eye' (dibbacakkhu). Since it is both the divine eye and knowledge, it is called 'divine eye knowledge' (dibbacakkhuñāṇa).
