'By sixty-four modes' means by way of the eight faculties in any one of the eight paths and fruits, totaling sixty-four modes. 'Of those with sharp faculties' (tikkhindriyānaṃ) refers to the faculty of one who has known (aññindriya) or the wisdom of the path of Arahatship, which arises from the practice of these three faculties: the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), the faculty of higher knowledge (aññindriya), and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya).
50:
It is called 'divine' (dibba) because it is obtained (through the power of jhāna), and because the divine eye higher knowledge itself depends on the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra) known as the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. It is also called 'divine' because it possesses great radiance through the grasping of the light kasiṇa (āloka-kasiṇa). Furthermore, it is called 'divine' because it has a vast range, being able to see forms situated on the other side of a wall and so forth, and because it is highly wonderful. All this should be understood according to the method of the science of grammar. It is called an 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing. It is also called an 'eye' because it performs the function of an eye, namely seeing forms, and is thus like the (physical) eye (the eye-sensitivity). Since it is both divine and an eye, it is called the 'divine eye' (dibba-cakkhu). Since it is both the divine eye and knowledge, it is called 'divine-eye knowledge' (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa).

'By sixty-four modes' (catusaṭṭhiyā ākārehi) means that it occurs by way of the eight faculties in each of the eight paths and eight fruits, thus making sixty-four modes. 'Of the three faculties' (tiṇṇannaṃ indriyānaṃ) refers to these three faculties: the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). 'Wisdom through mastery' (vasībhāvatā paññā) is wisdom that arises by way of mastery. It should be understood that although the mastery of the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) by way of the eight modes of the eight faculties in the fruit of arahantship does not exist at the moment of the path of arahantship, it is spoken of as such because it accomplishes that purpose through the fulfillment of the cause, which is the path of arahantship. 'Knowledge of the destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge of the path of arahantship which brings about the destruction of the taints that are to be abandoned by itself (the path).

56–59. Now, in connection with the knowledge of the path of arahantship, also known as the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, the four knowledges beginning with 'Wisdom in the sense of full understanding' (pariññaṭṭhe paññā) are briefly set forth to show the simultaneous penetration (of the four truths) by each of the four path knowledges. Among those four knowledges, the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) is mentioned first because it is coarse, common to all beings, and thus easy to understand. The truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) is mentioned immediately after it to show the cause of that truth of suffering. The truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) is mentioned next to make known that with the cessation of the cause, the effect ceases. The truth of the path (magga-sacca) is mentioned at the end to show the means for attaining that truth of cessation.

Alternatively, the truth of suffering is mentioned first to produce spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in beings who are attached to the enjoyment of worldly happiness. The truth of the origin is mentioned next to make known that this suffering does not arise without a cause, nor does it arise from a creator god and so forth, but it arises precisely from this craving. Then, the truth of cessation is mentioned to provide relief by showing the escape to beings who, being oppressed by suffering along with its cause, have minds filled with spiritual urgency and are seeking an escape from suffering. Thereafter, the truth of the path is mentioned as the way leading to cessation for the purpose of attaining the truth of cessation. Now, the knowledges that have these four truths as their objects are set forth in that same order. Therein, 'in the sense of full understanding' (pariññaṭṭhe) refers to the knowledge of the nature of the truth of suffering which is to be fully understood in four ways, such as in the sense of oppressing (pīḷanaṭṭha), etc. 'In the sense of abandoning' (pahānaṭṭhe) refers to the knowledge of the nature of the truth of the origin which is to be abandoned in four ways, such as in the sense of accumulating (āyūhanaṭṭha), etc. 'In the sense of realization' (sacchikiriyaṭṭhe) refers to the knowledge of the nature of the truth of cessation which is to be realized in four ways, such as in the sense of escape (nissaraṇaṭṭha), etc. 'In the sense of development' (bhāvanaṭṭhe) refers to the knowledge of the nature of the truth of the path which is to be developed in four ways, such as in the sense of leading out (niyyānaṭṭha), etc.
51:
60-63. Now, to show the knowledges of the truths individually, either by way of reflection (paccavekkhaṇā) for one who has developed the path, or by way of hearing (anussava) for one who has not yet developed the path, the four knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering are briefly stated. Therein, in the word "dukkha", the syllable "du" is evident in the sense of vile (kucchita). Indeed, a vile son is called "duputta". The syllable "kha", however, is in the sense of empty (tuccha). Empty space is called "kha". This first truth is also vile because it is the site of many dangers, and it is empty because it is devoid of the states of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self as imagined by the foolish. Therefore, because of being vile and empty, it is called "dukkha".

In the word "dukkhasamudaya", the syllable "saṃ" indicates conjunction (saṃyoga), as in "samāgamo, sametaṃ", etc. The syllable "u" indicates arising (uppatti), as in "uppannaṃ, uditaṃ", etc. The word "aya" indicates cause (kāraṇa). This second truth is the cause of the arising of suffering when there is the conjunction of the remaining conditions. Thus, because it is the cause of the arising of suffering through the conjunction of causes, it is called "dukkhasamudaya".

In the word "dukkhanirodha", the syllable "ni" indicates absence (abhāva), and the word "rodha" indicates a prison (cāraka). Therefore, in this Nibbāna, there is the absence of the obstruction of suffering called the prison of saṃsāra, because it is void of all destinations (gati). Or, when that Nibbāna is attained, because it is the opposite of that suffering, there is the absence of the obstruction of suffering which is the prison of saṃsāra; thus also it is called "dukkhanirodha". Or, because it is the condition for the cessation of suffering without further arising, it is called "dukkhanirodha".

In the phrase "dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā", because this truth of the path goes towards Nibbāna by making Nibbāna its object and being directed towards it, and because it is the practice leading to the attainment of the cessation of suffering, it is called "dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā". The four path-knowledges themselves are called "knowledge of the path" (magge ñāṇa) by way of showing the manner of emerging from the round of rebirths. They are called "knowledge in the concentration of immediate result" (ānantarikasamādhimhi ñāṇa) by way of showing the cause that gives fruit immediately. They are called "knowledge in the turning away from the truths" (saccavivaṭṭe ñāṇa) by way of showing the manner of turning away. To show the arising of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship only through the sequence of the paths, and to show the nature of higher knowledge of that knowledge, the knowledge of the path of Arahatship itself is called "knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇa). Again, to show the single penetration of all four path-knowledges, the four knowledges beginning with "knowledge of suffering in the sense of being fully understood" (pariññaṭṭhe paññā dukkhe ñāṇa) are stated. Again, by way of showing the individual arising in each truth, the four knowledges beginning with "knowledge of suffering" are briefly stated; thus the distinction between the preceding and the following should be understood.
52:
64-67. Now, to show that the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are accomplished for all noble persons (ariya-puggala) only through the power of the noble path, the four analytical knowledges beginning with "knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meanings" (atthapaṭisambhide ñāṇa) are briefly stated again. For these, although not differentiated by way of analytical divisions (or not being differentiated analytical knowledges), are pure analytical knowledges (suddhika-paṭisambhidā) common to all noble persons. However, the analytical knowledges stated below should be understood as differentiated analytical knowledges (pabhinna-paṭisambhidā) that have reached differentiation. This is the distinction in the statement of these analytical knowledges in two places.

Alternatively, the knowledge that takes the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation as its object is called the analytical knowledge of meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā). The knowledge that takes the truth of the origin and the truth of the path as its object is called the analytical knowledge of dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). The knowledge that knows the language (sounds) expressing those truths is called the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). The knowledge that knows those three knowledges is called the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). Therefore, to show such a specific meaning, the pure analytical knowledges are briefly stated. For this very reason, they were stated below with the word "diversity" (nānatta) as a distinction, but here they are stated without such distinction.

Thus, having briefly stated the sixty-seven knowledges common to disciples (sāvaka) in sequence, now to show the six unique knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) that are not common to disciples but belong only to the Tathāgatas (āveṇika), the knowledges beginning with the knowledge of the maturity of faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) are briefly stated. Among those six knowledges, the Tathāgatas, when looking at whether beings are suitable or unsuitable for the teaching of the Dhamma, look with the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakkhu). What is called the Buddha-eye is just the two knowledges: the knowledge of the maturity of faculties and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. As it is said: "The Blessed One, looking at the world with the Buddha-eye, saw beings with little dust in their eyes and much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and dull faculties," etc.

When looking at the mental continuity of beings, they first look at the maturity or immaturity of the faculties. Having known the maturity of the faculties, they then look at the inclinations, latent tendencies, and temperaments in order to teach the Dhamma accordingly. Therefore, the knowledge of the maturity of faculties is stated first, and immediately after that, the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. And when teaching the Dhamma, because they perform miracles for those who should be disciplined by miracles, the knowledge of the twin miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) is stated immediately after the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. To show the root cause of these three knowledges, the knowledge of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-ñāṇa) is stated immediately after them. To show the purity of the knowledge of great compassion, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is stated immediately after it. To show how the knowledge of omniscience is connected with the reflection (āvajjana) on all dhammas and the unobstructed nature of the knowledge of omniscience, the unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) is briefly stated immediately after it.

The meaning in the term "indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa" should be understood. The term "sattānaṃ" (of beings) mentioned above should be brought here and connected as "the knowledge that knows the low state and the high state of the faculties of beings."
53:
To demonstrate the unobstructed nature of the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and immediately following that, the Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) is pointed out.

In the term "indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇaṃ," the word "sattānaṃ" from above should be brought here and connected as "sattānaṃ indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇaṃ" (the knowledge that knows the higher and lower states of the faculties of beings). In the phrase where things are described as both superior (para) and inferior (apara) as "parāparāni," it is called "paroparāni" by changing the letter to "ro" through the rule of euphonic combination (sandhi). The state of being superior and inferior is called "paropariya," and "paropariya" itself is "paropariyatta." The superior and inferior states of the five faculties, such as faith (saddhā), of beings to be guided (veneyya-satta) is called "indriyaparopariyatta." The knowledge that knows that indriyaparopariyatta is called "indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa." It means the knowledge of the superior and inferior states of the faculties. There is also a reading as "indriyavarovariyatta-ñāṇaṃ." Things that are both excellent (vara) and not excellent (avara) are called "varovariyāni." The state of being varovariyāni is connected as "varovariyatta." "Avariyāni" means things that are not excellent. Alternatively, things that are superior (para) and inferior (opara) are called "paroparāni." Their state is connected as "paropariyatta." "Oparāni" means inferior things (orāni), as in the verses beginning with "paroparā yassa samecca dhammā." There is also a reading with the locative case as "indriyaparopariyatte ñāṇaṃ."

In the phrase "sattānaṃ āsayānusaye ñāṇaṃ," they are called "sattā" (beings) because they are particularly attached (visatta) with strong lust (chandarāga) to the five aggregates, such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). Regarding this, the Blessed One taught:
"Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for the aggregate of form; there one is attached, there one is particularly attached; therefore, one is called a 'being' (satto). Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; there one is attached, there one is particularly attached; therefore, one is called a 'being'."

Grammarians (akkharacintaka), however, without considering the meaning of the root, maintain that this name "satta" is merely a name. Those teachers who do investigate the meaning maintain that they are "sattā" due to their connection with substances such as jewels. (Knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies) of those beings. It is called "āsaya" (inclination) because wrong view or right view, or sense-desire etc., or renunciation etc., resort to (nissayanti) this mental continuum. It is a designation for the mental continuum permeated by those qualities. They are called "anusaya" (latent tendencies) because they lie dormant (anusenti) or follow along in the continuum of beings. This is a designation for the powerful (thāmagata) sensual lust and so on. Because it is both inclination and latent tendency, it is called "āsayānusaya." It should be understood as a singular number (ekavacana) by way of class inclusion or by way of a dvanda compound.
54:
Since temperament (carita) and resolve (adhimutti) are included within inclinations (āsaya) and latent tendencies (anusaya), in the brief exposition (uddesa), the knowledges regarding temperament and resolve are subsumed under the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies and stated as "knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusaye ñāṇaṃ)." It should be understood that the detailed exposition (niddesa) is made with the same intention as the brief exposition was made.

In the phrase "knowledge of the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihīre ñāṇaṃ)," it is called "yamaka" (twin/pair) because of the simultaneous production of masses of fire and streams of water, etc., without one preceding or following the other. It is called "pāṭihīra" (miracle) because it removes (haraṇa) opposing states such as lack of faith. Being both a twin and a miracle, it is called the "Twin Miracle" (yamakapāṭihīra).

In the phrase "knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇāsamāpattiyā ñāṇaṃ)," it is called "karuṇā" (compassion) because it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble (kampana) when there is suffering in others. Or, it is called "karuṇā" because it destroys (kiṇāti) or eliminates the suffering of others. Or, it is called "karuṇā" because it pervades (kirīyati) or extends by way of diffusion among those who are suffering. It is "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā) because it is great by way of the act of diffusion and by way of the power of the attributes of that action. It is called "samāpatti" (attainment) because the Great Compassionate Ones (the Buddhas) enter into (samāpajjanti) it. Being both Great Compassion and an attainment, it is called the "attainment of Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇāsamāpatti). The knowledge associated with that attainment of Great Compassion is the knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion.

72-73. In the phrase "Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa)," He is called "Sabbaññū" (Omniscient) because He has known everything divided into the five paths of the knowable (neyyapatha). The state of being Omniscient is "sabbaññutā." Since that sabbaññutā itself is knowledge, it is called "sabbaññuta-ñāṇa" where it should be said as "sabbaññutā-ñāṇa." Indeed, all phenomena (dhamma) divided into conditioned and unconditioned, etc., are only the five paths of the knowable: formations (saṅkhāra), alterations (vikāra), characteristics (lakkhaṇa), Nibbāna, and concepts (paññatti). Regarding "Sabbaññū," there could be five kinds of Omniscient Ones: sequential (kama-sabbaññū), simultaneous (sakiṃ-sabbaññū), constant (satata-sabbaññū), potential (satti-sabbaññū), and known (ñāta-sabbaññū). Sequential omniscience is not possible because there is no time when everything is known in sequence. Simultaneous omniscience is not possible because there is no grasping of all objects at once. Constant omniscience is not possible because eye-consciousness etc. arise according to their respective objects, because of the conflict with the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta), and because it lacks logical consistency. By elimination, it could be potential omniscience (satti-sabbaññuta) because of the capacity to know everything, or it could be known omniscience (ñāta-sabbaññuta) because all phenomena have been known. However, since a potential omniscient one does not [actually] know everything [at all times], taking that potential omniscience is also not appropriate.
55:
“In this world, there is nothing whatsoever that is not seen by the Blessed One; furthermore, there is no known dhamma that is not manifest to Him. The Blessed One has known the entirety of all that should be known; therefore, the Tathāgata is called the ‘All-Seer’ (Samantacakkhu).” Because this was stated (in the Mahāniddesa Pāḷi, etc.), it is appropriate that in this context, it refers only to the Omniscient Knowledge that has already known (ñāta-sabbaññuta).

When it is thus appropriate to refer only to the ñāta-sabbaññuta, it should be understood that it is indeed Omniscience (sabbaññuta) by way of its function, by way of the absence of delusion that covers the object, by way of the accomplishment of the cause which is the Path, and by way of its connection with reflection (āvajjana). Precisely because it is connected with reflection, there is no obstruction (āvaraṇa) for this Omniscient Knowledge; therefore, it is called ‘unobstructed’ (anāvaraṇa), and that very quality is called ‘Unobstructed Knowledge’ (anāvaraṇaññāṇa).

“These seventy-three knowledges” refers to these seventy-three knowledges summarized by way of those shared and those not shared with disciples (sāvakas). “Among these seventy-three knowledges” means among these seventy-three knowledges stated from the beginning. Here, the genitive case (chaṭṭhī vibhatti) is used in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa). There is also a variant reading “tesattatīnaṃ.” Where it is stated as “tesattatiyā,” it should be understood that the plural inflection is used for a single group. “Sixty-seven knowledges” refers to the sixty-seven knowledges described from the beginning. “Knowledges shared with disciples” means they are called disciples (sāvakas) because they are born into the noble birth at the end of hearing the Dhamma. Because there is a common bearing (knowledge) of these knowledges (by both the Buddha and disciples), they are called shared (sādhāraṇa). The knowledges of the Tathāgatas that are shared with noble disciples are called sāvaka-sādhāraṇa-ñāṇas. “Six knowledges” refers to the six knowledges summarized at the end. These are knowledges unique to the Tathāgatas, not shared with disciples.

## From the Saddhammappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga
## The Explanation of the Summary of the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā-mātikuddesa-vāra-vaṇṇanā) is Finished.
## 1. Explanation of the Exposition of Knowledge Based on Learning (Sutamayaññāṇa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Summary of the Answers (Vissajjanuddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Now, in order to show in detail the dhammas included in the summary as they were laid down, the section of exposition (niddesavāra) beginning with “How is the wisdom arising from listening a knowledge based on learning?” is commenced. In that summary (mātikā uddesa), regarding the statement “The wisdom arising from listening is knowledge based on learning,” the meaning should be understood as: in what manner does this occur? This question “How (kathaṃ)?” is a “question from a desire to speak” (kathetukamyatāpucchā), asked with the intention to explain.

Indeed, there are five kinds of questions (pucchā): the question to illuminate the unseen (adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā), the question to compare the seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā), the question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanāpucchā), the question for consent (anumatipucchā), and the question from a desire to speak (kathetukamyatāpucchā). The differences between these five questions are as follows: What is the question to illuminate the unseen? It is when a characteristic is naturally unknown, unseen, unweighed, uninvestigated, unmanifested, and not made clear. One asks a question for the purpose of knowing, seeing, weighing, investigating, manifesting, and making clear that characteristic. This is called adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā. What is the question to compare the seen? It is when a characteristic is naturally known, seen, weighed, investigated, manifested, and made clear. That person asks a question for the purpose of comparing and discussing what they know with other wise people. This is called diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā. What is the question to cut off doubt? It is when one naturally falls into doubt and uncertainty, being of two minds, thinking, “Is it thus, or is it not thus? How is it? In what way is it?” That person asks a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt. This is called vimaticchedanāpucchā. What is the question for consent? It is when the Blessed One asks a question to obtain the agreement (consent) of the monks.
56:
Regarding “knowledge,” how does that knowledge occur? This question is a “question from a desire to speak” (kathetukamyatāpucchā). Indeed, there are five kinds of questions: the question to illuminate the unseen (adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā), the question to compare the seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā), the question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanāpucchā), the question for consent (anumatipucchā), and the question from a desire to speak (kathetukamyatāpucchā). The distinction between them is as follows:

What is the question to illuminate the unseen? When the characteristic of a phenomenon is naturally unknown, unseen, unweighed, uninvestigated, unmanifested, and not yet made clear, asking a question for the purpose of knowing, seeing, weighing, investigating, and manifesting that characteristic is called adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā.

What is the question to compare the seen? When the characteristic of a phenomenon is naturally known, seen, weighed, investigated, manifested, and already made clear, but that person asks a question for the purpose of comparing and discussing it with other wise people, it is called diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā.

What is the question to cut off doubt? When one falls into doubt regarding a phenomenon, thinking “Is it thus? Is it not thus? How is it? In what way is it?” and being of two minds, asking a question for the purpose of cutting off that doubt is called vimaticchedanāpucchā.

What is the question for consent? The Blessed One asks a question to obtain the consent of the monks: “What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, Bhante.” “Is that which is impermanent painful or pleasant?” “Painful, Bhante.” “Is it fit to regard that which is impermanent, painful, and subject to change as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, Bhante.” This is called anumatipucchā.

What is the question from a desire to speak? The Blessed One asks a question to the monks with the desire to speak (a discourse): “Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?” This is called kathetukamyatāpucchā. Among these questions, this question of the Venerable Sāriputta should be understood as a kathetukamyatāpucchā.

Now, following the question from a desire to speak which summarizes the mātikā, there are sixteen detailed explanations (vissajjanā) such as: “Listening means these dhammas are to be known with higher knowledge; the wisdom that fully understands that (listening) is knowledge based on learning.” Among those sixteen, in the phrase “these dhammas are to be known with higher knowledge,” the remaining Pāḷi words “of the one who is teaching” should be supplied and understood. When the Blessed One or another respected fellow practitioner in the holy life is teaching the Dhamma, saying “these dhammas are to be known with higher knowledge,” the act of listening as previously described is the listening called “suta.” The wisdom that fully understands that which has been listened to...
57:
The wisdom that distinguishes the Dhamma heard is the wisdom that distinguishes through various methods, known as the knowledge consisting of what is heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa). 'Tassa pajānanā' means the distinguishing knowledge of that heard Dhamma, formed as a genitive compound. Alternatively, it can be expressed with the accusative case as 'taṃ pajānanā' through case mutation. 'Abhiññeyya' refers to things to be known through the power of penetrating their individual characteristics in an excellent manner. 'Pariññeyya' refers to things to be known comprehensively through the power of penetrating common characteristics and through the completion of the task. 'Bhāvetabba' refers to things to be developed. 'Sacchikātabba' refers to things to be realized. Indeed, realization (sacchikiriyā) is of two kinds: realization through attainment (paṭilābha-sacchikiriyā) and realization through objectification (ārammaṇa-sacchikiriyā). Things that lead to decline due to the occurrence of opposing states are called 'partaking of diminution' (hānabhāgiya). Things that lead to stability through the establishment of mindfulness appropriate to that concentration are called 'partaking of stability' (ṭhitibhāgiya). Things that lead to distinction through the attainment of higher special qualities are called 'partaking of distinction' (visesabhāgiya). The Noble Path is called 'penetration' (nibbedha) because it pierces the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion which have never been pierced or broken before. Things that lead to that penetration through the occurrence of perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment are called 'partaking of penetration' (nibbedhabhāgiya).

'Sabbe saṅkhārā' refers to all things that arise with causes. These are called 'conditioned formations' (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra). They are called 'formations' (saṅkhāra) because they are produced by the meeting of causes, and specifically called 'conditioned' (saṅkhata) because they have been made by the meeting of causes. In the Commentaries, the material and immaterial phenomena of the three planes produced by kamma are called 'kamma-produced formations' (abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra). These are also included under 'conditioned formations' in passages such as 'Formations are indeed impermanent.' The wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes found in passages such as 'Formations [conditioned] by ignorance' are called 'volitional formations' (abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra). The physical and mental energy found in passages such as 'As far as the range of the formation...' is called 'formation of effort' (payogābhisaṅkhāra). Initial and sustained application (vitakka-vicāra) found in passages such as 'For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling...' are called 'verbal formations' (vacīsaṅkhāra) because they fashion speech. In-breaths and out-breaths are called 'bodily formations' (kāyasaṅkhāra) because they are fashioned by the body. Perception and feeling are called 'mental formations' (cittasaṅkhāra) because they are fashioned by the mind. Here, 'conditioned formations' (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra) are intended. 'Anicca' means impermanent things in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. 'Dukkha' means suffering things in the sense of being oppressive. 'Sabbe dhammā' refers to all things, including Nibbāna. 'Anatta' means non-self things in the sense of not following one's will. In passages such as 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering,' although it should be said 'dukkha-samudayo' and 'dukkha-nirodho,' they are used with a change of gender as 'dukkha-samudayaṃ' and 'dukkha-nirodhaṃ.' They are called 'Noble Truths' (Ariyasacca) because Noble Ones such as the Buddha penetrate them.
58:
They are called 'bodily formations' (kāyasaṅkhāra) because they fashion [the body]. Perception and feeling are called 'mental formations' (cittasaṅkhāra) because they are fashioned by the mind. In this context, 'conditioned formations' (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra) are intended.

They are 'impermanent' (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. They are 'suffering' (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressive. 'All things' (sabbe dhammā) is said including Nibbāna within it. They are 'non-self' (anatta) in the sense of not being subject to one's will. In passages such as 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering,' where it should be said 'dukkha-samudayo' and 'dukkha-nirodho,' a change of gender is made to 'dukkha-samudayaṃ' and 'dukkha-nirodhaṃ.' Because Noble Ones such as the Buddha penetrate them, they are called 'Noble Truths' (Ariyasacca). As the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, these Noble Truths are four... Bhikkhus, these are indeed the four Noble Truths. Noble Ones penetrate these truths; therefore, they are called Noble Truths.' They are also called 'Noble Truths' because they are the truths of the Noble One. As he said: 'In the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is the Noble One; therefore, they are called Noble Truths.' They are also called 'Noble Truths' because one achieves the state of a Noble One by penetrating these truths. As he said: 'Bhikkhus, because of penetrating these four Noble Truths as they really are, the Tathāgata, the Arahat, the Perfectly Enlightened One is called a Noble One.' They are also called 'Noble Truths' because they are noble (unerring) truths. 'Noble' here means unerring and non-deceptive. As he said: 'Bhikkhus, these four Noble Truths are real, unerring, and not otherwise; therefore, they are called Noble Truths.'

If it is asked, 'In the term "truths," what is the meaning of truth?' It is not something that is distorted like a magician's trick to those who investigate with the eye of wisdom, nor is it misleading like a mirage, nor is it of a non-existent nature like the 'self' imagined by sectarians. Rather, it is truly the domain of Noble Knowledge in its real and non-distorted nature through the modes of oppression, origin, peace, and escape. This real and non-distorted nature should be understood as the meaning of truth, just like the characteristic of heat in fire or the nature of the world. As he said in detail: 'Bhikkhus, "this is suffering"—this is real, this is unerring, this is not otherwise.' Furthermore:

Since there is no suffering that does not oppress, and there is no other thing that oppresses besides suffering,
By the certainty of its oppressive nature, this is known as a Truth.
Since suffering does not arise from anything else except that craving, and suffering does not fail to arise from it,
By the certainty of being the cause of suffering, craving (vissatikā) is known as a Truth.
59:
It is not a nature to be obtained like the "self" (attabhāva) imagined by the heretics. In truth, it is the object of the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), and reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that correctly perceives the truth according to its unerring nature—as the power of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) which oppresses beings, as the cessation of the rounds of rebirth, and as the various means of escape from the rounds of rebirth. This nature, which is the object of this unerring knowledge, should be understood as having the meaning of "Truth" (sacca), being evident as a true and unchanging nature, just like the characteristic of fire is heat or the nature of the world. It should be understood in detail as the Buddha taught: "Monks, this is suffering; this is true, unerring, and not otherwise."

The Truth of Suffering is not non-oppressive, and there is no other oppressive thing besides the Truth of Suffering. Because of the delimitation of this oppressive nature, this suffering is known as "Truth." Apart from that craving (taṇhā), the Truth of Suffering does not arise from any other cause; nor is it that this Truth of Suffering does not arise because of that craving—it arises only because of craving. Because of the delimitation of this status as the cause of suffering, craving is known as "Truth."

There is no phenomenon that is peaceful other than Nibbāna, and that Nibbāna is not non-peaceful; it is only peaceful. Because of the delimitation of this peaceful nature, this Nibbāna is known as "Truth."

There is no phenomenon that is the means of escape other than the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), and that Truth of the Path is not a non-escape. Because it is the true means of escape, these eight factors of the Path are designated as "Truth."

Thus, regarding the Four Truths such as suffering, etc., the wise say that the meaning of "Truth" is the existence of a true and unerring nature.

That word "Truth" (sacca) is evident in various meanings. For example: in passages such as "Saccaṃ bhaṇe na kujjheyya" (One should speak the truth and not get angry), it is evident in the sense of verbal truth (vācā-sacca). In passages such as "Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca" (Recluses and brahmins stand in truth), it is evident in the sense of truth as abstinence (virati-sacca). In passages such as "Kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānā" (Why do they speak of various truths?), it is evident in the sense of truth as views (diṭṭhi-sacca). In passages such as "Ekañhi saccaṃ na dutīyamatthi" (Truth is indeed one, there is no second), it is evident in the sense of ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), namely Nibbāna and the Path. In passages such as "Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ kati kusalā" (Of the four truths, how many are wholesome?), it is evident in the sense of the Noble Truths (ariya-sacca). Here also, it occurs in the sense of the Noble Truths.

## The explanation of the Exposition of Answers
## included in the Section of Expositions is finished.
## Explanation of the Exposition of Things to be Known by Higher Knowledge

Now, in order to show the phenomena included in the Exposition of Answers by way of their classification, the Section of Expositions beginning with "How are these phenomena to be known by higher knowledge?" is commenced. There, in the five expositions such as the Exposition of Things to be Known by Higher Knowledge, ten answers each are presented from the beginning by way of the groups of one, etc., correlating them with the sequence of the Dasuttara Sutta.

Among those five expositions, in the Exposition of Things to be Known by Higher Knowledge, first, "all beings" (sabbe sattā) refers to all beings in all planes of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence, the existence with perception, and the existence with one constituent. "Sustained by nutriment" (āhāratthitikā) means they have a standing due to nutriment. Here, "standing" (ṭhiti) means the state of existing in one's own moment. Thus, the single phenomenon called nutriment, which is the cause of the standing of all beings, should be known with higher knowledge. When the cause is known, the phenomena produced by the cause are also known. Since both cause and effect are mutually dependent, this statement intends to speak of full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā).

If it is said that all beings have a standing due to nutriment, one might ask: "Does this not contradict the statement that 'the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) have no nutriment and no contact'?" It does not contradict. Why? Because for those non-percipient beings, the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere wholesome karma is the cause (nutriment). If there is such a cause as jhāna, one might ask: "Does this not contradict the Pali text: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth'?"
60:
The single phenomenon called nutriment should be known with higher knowledge. When the cause is known, the effects produced by the cause are also known, because both cause and effect have a nature of mutual dependence. In this way, full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) is taught. If it is said that all beings exist because of nutriment, one might ask: "Does this not contradict the words in the Vibhaṅga: 'The non-percipient deities (asaññasattā devā) are without cause, without nutriment, and without contact'?" It does not contradict. The reason is that for those non-percipient deities, jhāna itself is the nutriment. Even if jhāna is called nutriment, one might say: "Does this not contradict the Saṃyutta Pali: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth. What are the four? Nutritive essence (kabaḷīkāro āhāro) whether gross or subtle, contact (phassa) is the second, mental volition (manosañcetanā) is the third, and consciousness (viññāṇa) is the fourth'?" This also does not contradict. In that Sutta, only those phenomena that have the literal characteristic of nutriment are taught as nutriment. Here, however, the cause (paccaya) is intended as nutriment in a figurative sense (pariyāya). It is appropriate for all conditioned phenomena to have a cause, and because that cause brings (āharati) whatever fruit it produces, it is called nutriment (āhāra). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I say that ignorance (avijjā) also has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what, monks, is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: 'The five hindrances.' Monks, I say that the five hindrances also have a nutriment, not that they are without nutriment. And what, monks, is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: 'Unwise attention' (ayoniso manasikāra)," and so forth. This is the meaning intended here. When nutriment is taken as "cause" (paccaya-āhāra), both figurative nutriment and literal nutriment are all included.

Among those nutriments, nutriment as a cause is obtained in the non-percipient realm. Before the arising of the Buddha, some would go forth in the systems of heretics, perform preparatory work on the air-kasiṇa, and produce the fourth jhāna. Emerging from that jhāna, they would reflect: "Disgusting is the mind, disgusting is the mind; the very absence of the mind is excellent. Depending on the mind, suffering such as killing and binding arises; if there is no mind, that suffering does not exist." Having produced such acceptance and preference, those with non-declining jhāna, when they pass away, are reborn in the non-percipient realm. In whatever posture a person remained in the human world, they are reborn in that same posture in the non-percipient realm and remain for five hundred aeons. For this duration, they are as if lying down, as if sitting, or as if standing. For beings of such nature, nutriment as a cause is obtained. The reason is that they are reborn having developed that jhāna...
61:
That jhāna itself is the cause for them. For example, just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels as long as the force of the bowstring exists, similarly, they remain as long as the cause, which is jhāna, exists. When the momentum of that jhāna is exhausted, they fall like an arrow whose momentum is spent.

What is the nutriment (āhāra) of the hell-beings who are said to be "not living on the fruit of exertion, nor living on the fruit of merit"? Their kamma itself is the nutriment. Are there five nutriments? One should not say "five" or "not five." Is it not said that "cause is nutriment"? Therefore, the very kamma by which they are reborn in hell is called nutriment because it is the cause for their persistence. With reference to this, it was said: "He does not die as long as that evil kamma is not exhausted" (A. i. 36; M. iii. 250). Therefore, "subsisting by nutriment" means "subsisting by cause." One should not argue here based on edible food (kabaḷīkāra āhāra). For even the saliva produced in their mouths performs the function of nutriment for them. Saliva is a cause for painful feeling in hell and a cause for pleasant feeling in heaven. Thus, in the sense-sphere (kāmabhava), there are strictly four nutriments. In the fine-material sphere (rūpabhava) and immaterial sphere (arūpabhava), excluding the non-percipient realm (asaññasatta), the remaining Brahmas have three nutriments. Since the non-percipient beings and others have condition-nutriment (paccayāhāra), all beings subsist by nutriment.

"All beings" is a teaching of Dhamma in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna dhammadesanā), meaning "all conditioned things" (saṅkhāra). The Buddha's teaching is of four kinds by way of Dhamma and persons: teaching of Dhamma in terms of Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna dhammadesanā), teaching of Dhamma in terms of persons (dhammādhiṭṭhāna puggaladesanā), teaching of persons in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna puggaladesanā), and teaching of persons in terms of Dhamma (puggalādhiṭṭhāna dhammadesanā). "Monks, I do not see even one other thing that, when developed, is so wieldy as this mind. Monks, the mind, when developed, is wieldy" (A. i. 22)—such a teaching is a teaching of Dhamma in terms of Dhamma. "Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person attained to right view should regard any conditioned thing as permanent; such a case does not exist" (A. i. 268)—such a teaching is a teaching of Dhamma in terms of persons. "Monks, there is one person who, when arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans" (A. i. 170, 309)—such a teaching is a teaching of persons in terms of persons. "Monks, with the manifestation of one person, there is the manifestation of the great eye of wisdom" (A. i. 175-186)—such a teaching is a teaching of persons in terms of Dhamma. Among those four, here it is the teaching of persons in terms of...
62:
Dhamma. This teaching is a teaching of Dhamma that explains conditioned things (saṅkhāra) based on persons. Since only dhammas are taken up to the tenth [item] above, it should be understood that by the term "beings," "dhammas" are taken. Or specifically, because the dhammas included in the continuity of beings are to be investigated according to their nature by superior knowledge, the term "beings" is used. Or because the designation "being" arises only based on conditioned things (saṅkhāra), by metonymy of effect for cause, conditioned things are called "beings." There is no being subsisting by cause other than conditioned things, but it is said so by way of conventional usage. Thus, in this Pali, full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā) is stated.

Two elements (dhātu) are the conditioned element (saṅkhatadhātu) and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu). Therein, the five aggregates produced by the combination of many conditions are the conditioned element. Nibbāna, not produced by any conditions, is the unconditioned element.

Three elements are the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu), the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu). Therein, what is the sense-sphere element? Starting from the Avīci hell below and including the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas above, the aggregates, elements, bases, matter, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that range within this interval and are included therein—this is called the sense-sphere element. Therein, what is the fine-material element? Starting from the Brahma-world below and including the Akaniṭṭha devas above, the mental and mental factors of one who has attained [jhāna], or one who has been reborn [there], or one who dwells happily in the present life within this interval, ranging and included therein—this is called the fine-material element. Therein, what is the immaterial element? Starting from the devas who have reached the base of infinite space below and including the devas who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception above, the mental and mental factors of one who has attained [jhāna], or one who has been reborn [there], or one who dwells happily in the present life within this interval, ranging and included therein—this is called the immaterial element. In the Commentary, however, it is said: "The sense-sphere element is the five aggregates obtained in the sense-sphere existence; the fine-material element is the five aggregates obtained in the fine-material existence; the immaterial element is the four aggregates obtained in the immaterial existence." This is the application according to the method of the Dasuttara Sutta.

According to the method of the Saṅgīti Sutta: "Three wholesome elements are the element of renunciation (nekkhammadhātu), the element of non-ill will (abyāpādadhātu), and the element of non-harming (avihiṃsādhātu). Another three elements are the fine-material element, the immaterial element, and the element of cessation (nirodhadhātu). Another three elements are the low element, the middle element..."
63:
The elements spoken of in the Dīgha Nikāya as 'dhātu paṇītā dhātu' are also appropriate here. The thought (vitakka) associated with renunciation (nekkhamma) ... (pe) ... right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) is called the element of renunciation (nekkhamma-dhātu). All wholesome states (kusala dhamma) are also called the element of renunciation. The thought associated with non-ill-will (abyāpāda) ... (pe) ... right intention is called the element of non-ill-will (abyāpāda-dhātu). There is loving-kindness (mettā) towards beings, the mode of loving, the state of being one who loves, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti). This state is called the element of non-ill-will. The thought associated with non-cruelty (avihiṃsā) ... (pe) ... right intention is called the element of non-cruelty (avihiṃsā-dhātu). There is compassion (karuṇā) towards beings, the mode of compassion, the state of being one who is compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion (karuṇā-cetovimutti). This state is called the element of non-cruelty. The fine-material element (rūpa-dhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpa-dhātu) have already been mentioned. Nibbāna is called the element of cessation (nirodha-dhātu). The twelve types of unwholesome consciousness (akusala cittuppāda) are called the low element (hīna-dhātu). The states belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka dhamma) remaining after the unwholesome consciousness are called the middle element (majjhima-dhātu). The nine supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) are called the exalted element (paṇīta-dhātu). All states are called elements (dhātu) in the sense of being non-living (nijjīva).

The Four Noble Truths are: the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha), the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (samudaya), the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (nirodha), and the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering (magga). The explanation of these four truths will be presented only in the section on the exposition of the truths.

The five bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) are: hearing the teaching of the Dhamma delivered by others for one's own benefit; teaching the Dhamma to others as one has heard it for their benefit; reciting the Dhamma as one has heard it; reflecting on the Dhamma as one has heard it with the mind; and taking up an object suitable to one's temperament among the kasiṇas, foulness (asubha), etc. These are the five causes of liberation. As it was said:

'Here, bhikkhus, the Teacher or a certain fellow practitioner in a respected position teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu. Bhikkhus, in whatever way the Teacher or a certain fellow practitioner in a respected position teaches the Dhamma, in that very way, that bhikkhu gains a sense of the meaning (attha) and a sense of the text (dhamma) in that teaching. For him who has a sense of the meaning and a sense of the text, gladness (pāmojja) arises. For one who is glad, rapture (pīti) arises. For one whose mind is rapturous, the mental body (nāmakāya) becomes tranquil. One whose mental body is tranquil feels happiness (sukha). For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated (samādhi). This is the first base of liberation.'
64:
'Furthermore, bhikkhus, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a certain fellow practitioner in a respected position teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, but he teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and learned it. Bhikkhus, in whatever way the bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, in that very way, that bhikkhu gains a sense of the meaning and a sense of the text in that teaching. For him who has a sense of the meaning and a sense of the text, gladness arises. For one who is glad, rapture arises. For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the second base of liberation.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a certain fellow practitioner in a respected position teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does he teach the Dhamma to others in detail, but he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it and learned it. Bhikkhus, in whatever way the bhikkhu recites the Dhamma ... for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the third base of liberation.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a certain fellow practitioner in a respected position teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does he teach the Dhamma to others in detail, nor does he recite it, but he reflects on the Dhamma with his mind, examines it, and contemplates it as he has heard it and learned it. Bhikkhus, in whatever way the bhikkhu reflects on the Dhamma with his mind, examines it, and contemplates it ... for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the fourth base of liberation.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a certain fellow practitioner in a respected position teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does he teach the Dhamma to others in detail, nor does he recite it, nor does he reflect on it and examine it with his mind, but a certain meditation sign (samādhi-nimitta) is well grasped by him, well attended to, well sustained, and well penetrated by wisdom. Bhikkhus, in whatever way a certain meditation sign is well grasped, well attended to, well sustained, and well penetrated by wisdom by a bhikkhu, in that very way, that bhikkhu gains a sense of the meaning and a sense of the text in that teaching. For him who has a sense of the meaning and a sense of the text, gladness arises. For one who is glad, rapture arises.'
65:
For one who is full of joy, rapture arises. For one whose mind is rapturous, the body (mental body) becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated (with the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship). This is the fifth basis of liberation (vimuttāyatana).

In this term 'Six Supreme Things' (cha anuttariyāni), they are called 'anuttarāni' because there is nothing superior to that seeing, hearing, and so forth. 'Anuttarāni' is the same as 'anuttariyāni'. It means things that are most noble. This was spoken by the Blessed One as follows:

"Monks, these six are the supreme things. What are the six? The supreme seeing (dassanānuttariya), the supreme hearing (savanānuttariya), the supreme gain (lābhānuttariya), the supreme training (sikkhānuttariya), the supreme service (pāricariyānuttariya), and the supreme recollection (anussatānuttariya)."

"Monks, what is the supreme seeing? Monks, here in this world, some go to see the elephant-treasure, some go to see the horse-treasure, some go to see the jewel-treasure, or they go to see various high and low objects, or they go to see an ascetic or a brahmin of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, such seeing exists; I do not say it does not. However, monks, that kind of seeing is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna."

"Monks, when someone, having established faith, established love, and having a mind of unwavering confidence, goes to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. Monks, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true path, and for the realization of Nibbāna—this going to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata with established faith, established love, and unwavering confidence—this is the supreme among seeings. Monks, this is called the supreme seeing (dassanānuttariya). Thus is the supreme seeing."

"What is the supreme hearing? Monks, here in this world, some go to hear the sound of drums, some go to hear the sound of the lute, some go to hear the sound of singing, or they go to hear various high and low sounds, or they go to hear the teaching of an ascetic or a brahmin of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, such hearing exists; I do not say it does not. ..."
66:
Monks, such hearing exists; I do not say it does not. However, monks, that kind of hearing is very low. ... [Pe] ... it does not lead to the realization of Nibbāna. Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love, being unwavering and greatly confident, goes to hear the Dhamma of the Tathāgata or the Dhamma of a disciple of the Tathāgata. Monks, for the purification of beings ... [Pe] ... for the realization of Nibbāna, this going to hear the Dhamma of the Tathāgata or the Dhamma of a disciple of the Tathāgata is called the supreme hearing (savanānuttariya). Thus there are the supreme seeing (dassanānuttariya) and the supreme hearing (savanānuttariya).

What is the supreme gain (lābhānuttariya)? Monks, here in this world, some obtain the gain of a son, the gain of a wife, the gain of wealth, or various other gains. Or they obtain faith in ascetics and brahmins of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, such gain exists; I do not say it does not. However, monks, that kind of gain is very low. ... [Pe] ... it does not lead to the realization of Nibbāna. Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love in the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, being unwavering and greatly confident, obtains faith. Monks, for the purification of beings ... [Pe] ... for the realization of Nibbāna, obtaining faith in the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is called the supreme gain (lābhānuttariya). Thus there are dassanānuttariya, savanānuttariya, and lābhānuttariya.

What is the supreme training (sikkhānuttariya)? Monks, here in this world, some learn the art of elephants, the art of horses, the art of chariots, the art of archery, the art of swordsmanship, and so forth. Or they learn various other arts. Or they learn from ascetics and brahmins of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, such training exists; I do not say it does not. However, monks, that kind of training is very low. ... [Pe] ... it does not lead to the realization of Nibbāna. Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love, being unwavering and greatly confident, learns and practices the higher virtue (adhisīla), the higher mind (adhicitta), and the higher wisdom (adhipaññā) in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Such training is...
67:
Monks, what is the supreme training (sikkhānuttariya) for the purification of beings... for the realization of Nibbāna? In this Dhamma-Vinaya—consisting of the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya—taught by the Tathāgata, a person who has established faith, established love, and is entirely and supremely devoted, trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), trains in higher mind (adhicitta), and trains in higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Monks, this training is called the supreme training. Thus, there are the supreme seeing (dassanānuttariya), the supreme hearing (savanānuttariya), the supreme gain (lābhānuttariya), and the supreme training (sikkhānuttariya).

And how is there the supreme service (pāricariyānuttariya)? Monks, in this world, some person serves a king, serves a brahmin, serves a householder, or serves someone high or low; or serves a recluse or brahmin of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, I do not say that such service does not exist. However, monks, that service is low... it does not lead to Nibbāna. Monks, when a person who has established faith, established love, and is entirely and supremely devoted, serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. Monks, for the purification of beings... for the realization of Nibbāna, this service to the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is called the supreme service. Thus, there are the supreme seeing, the supreme hearing, the supreme gain, the supreme training, and the supreme service.

And how is there the supreme recollection (anussatānuttariya)? Monks, in this world, some person recollects the gain of a son, recollects the gain of a wife, recollects the gain of wealth, or recollects a gain high or low; or recollects a recluse or brahmin of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, I do not say that such recollection does not exist. However, monks, that recollection is low... it does not lead to Nibbāna. Monks, when a person who has established faith, established love, and is entirely and supremely devoted, recollects the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. Monks, for the purification of beings... for the realization of Nibbāna, this recollection of the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is called the supreme recollection.
68: Monks, this recollection is called the supreme recollection (anussatānuttariya). Monks, these are the six supreme things (anuttariya). (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Book of Sixes, 30).## In the phrase "satta niddasavatthūni," one is called "niddasa" because for that person, there are no more ten years (of future life). The causes for being a niddasa (being an Arahant) are called "grounds for the niddasa" (niddasavatthu). Indeed, an Arahant (khīṇāsava) who attains Parinibbāna at the ten-year mark is called "niddasa" because, due to the absence of future rebirth, he does not become a ten-year-old again. Not only does he not become a ten-year-old, but he also does not become a nine-year-old... or even one who exists for a single moment in a new life. It is not only the one who attains Parinibbāna at the ten-year mark who is called niddasa; even one who attains Parinibbāna at the seven-year mark is "nissatta" (no longer seven), "niddasa" (no longer ten), and "nimuhutta" (no longer even for a moment). The Blessed One, wishing to show the absence of such an Arahant (or qualities) among the sectarians and their presence in this Dispensation by applying a term used in sectarian doctrines to the Arahant in the Dispensation, spoke of the causes for such a nature of Arahantship as the "seven grounds for the niddasa." As he said:## "Monks, there are these seven grounds for the niddasa. What seven? Here, monks, a monk has intense desire for undertaking the three trainings, and in the future, he has undiminished love for undertaking the trainings. He has intense desire for the investigation of the Dhamma (insight wisdom), and in the future, he has undiminished love for the investigation of the Dhamma. He has intense desire for the removal of desire, and in the future, he has undiminished love for the removal of desire. He has intense desire for seclusion (paṭisallāna), and in the future, he has undiminished love for seclusion. He has intense desire for the arousal of energy, and in the future, he has undiminished love for the arousal of energy. He has intense desire for mindfulness and prudence (satinepakka), and in the future, he has undiminished love for mindfulness and prudence. He has intense desire for the penetration of views through the Path-knowledge (diṭṭhipaṭivedha), and in the future, he has undiminished love for the penetration of views. Monks, these are the seven grounds for the niddasa." (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Book of Sevens, 20).## The Elder also, extracting the teaching in the same way, spoke of the "seven grounds for the niddasa."## In the phrase "aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni," these are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhāyatana) because they are meditative absorptions (jhānas) that have objects which are mastered. "Bases" (āyatanāni) refers to the objects of the kasiṇa counterparts (kasiṇa-paṭibhāga-nimitta), which are called bases in the sense of being the foundation for access concentration and fixed concentration. A person of superior wisdom...
69:
A person of pure knowledge, reflecting, "Where should I enter into this counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) object? For me, there is no burden in achieving one-pointedness of mind (samādhi)," overcomes those objects and enters [the attainment]. This means that as soon as the counterpart sign arises, they produce absorption (appanā) in that object. The jhanas produced in this way are called "Abhibhāyatana" (Spheres of Mastery).

What are the eight Spheres of Mastery?

One, perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the first Sphere of Mastery.

One, perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the second Sphere of Mastery.

One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the third Sphere of Mastery.

One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the fourth Sphere of Mastery.

One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster. Just as the flax flower (umāpuppha) is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster; or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster; in the same way, one, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the fifth Sphere of Mastery.

One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster. Just as the kaṇikāra flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster; or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides...
70:
...is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster; in the same way, one, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the sixth Sphere of Mastery.

One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luster. For example, just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luster; or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luster; in the same way, one, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, red in luster. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the seventh Sphere of Mastery.

One, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luster. For example, just as the star Osadhī (osadhītārakā) is white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luster; or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luster; in the same way, one, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in luster. Being of such perception that "Having mastered those forms, I know, I see," this is the eighth Sphere of Mastery. These are the eight Spheres of Mastery.

The nine successive dwellings (anupubbavihāra) are so called because "anupubba" means following each preceding [jhana]. They are called "vihāra" (dwellings/attainments) because they are to be dwelt in or entered into successively. This means attainments that are to be entered into in order.
71:
What are the nine? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.’ With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of space. With the complete surmounting of the base of the infinity of space, [perceiving] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of consciousness. With the complete surmounting of the base of the infinity of consciousness, [perceiving] ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. With the complete surmounting of the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. With the complete surmounting of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Thus, these are the nine successive attainments (anupubbavihāra) that have been taught.

The ten bases of wearing away (nijjara-vatthu): they are called 'nijjara' because they effectively wear away or destroy wrong view and so forth. 'Vatthu' means causes. Because they are causes that destroy, they are called 'nijjara-vatthu'. This is another name for the path factors such as Right View.

What are the ten? Bhikkhus, for one of right view, wrong view is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as condition are also worn away. And the many wholesome states that have right view as condition go to fulfillment by development.

Bhikkhus, for one of right intention, wrong intention is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong intention as condition...
72:
...arise, those unwholesome states are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right intention as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the path-factor of right speech, wrong speech is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong speech as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right speech as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the path-factor of right action, wrong action is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong action as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right action as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the path-factor of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong livelihood as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right livelihood as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the path-factor of right effort, wrong effort is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong effort as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right effort as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the path-factor of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong mindfulness as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right mindfulness as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the path-factor of right concentration, wrong concentration is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong concentration as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right concentration as condition go to fulfillment by development.

“Bhikkhus, for one established in the knowledge of the path and fruit, wrong knowledge (knowing in a distorted way) is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong knowledge as condition are worn away for that person; and the many wholesome states that have right knowledge as condition go to fulfillment by development.”
73:
“Monks, for one who has right liberation (sammāvimutti), wrong liberation (micchāvimutti) is exhausted. Many evil unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation are also exhausted for that person. Many wholesome states conditioned by right liberation reach fulfillment through mental development (bhāvanā).” Thus, the ten grounds for wearing away [defilements] (nijjaravatthu) were taught.

It should be understood that the teaching taught by the Blessed One, beginning with “Monks, all things should be known with direct knowledge (abhiññeyya),” is brought forth and shown here [in the Paṭisambhidāmagga]. In the phrase “kiñca-iti,” the syllable “ca” is merely a particle used for completing the verse. The thirty answers, such as the eye and so forth, are presented according to the sequence of the occurrence of doors and objects, by taking five for each of the six doors. In that context, the eye (cakkhu) is of two kinds: the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) and the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu). Among these, the wisdom eye is of five kinds: the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu), the universal eye (samantacakkhu), the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu), the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), and the Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu). This eye described as “Monks, when I looked at the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw,” is called the Buddha-eye. This eye described as “The universal eye is called omniscience,” is called the universal eye. This eye described as “The eye of wisdom arose, knowledge arose,” is called the eye of knowledge. This eye described as “Monks, I saw with the pure divine eye (dibbacakkhu),” is called the divine eye. This eye described as “The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu) arose,” which is the knowledge consisting of the three lower paths, is called the Dhamma-eye.

The fleshly eye is also of two kinds: the composite eye (sasambhāracakkhu) and the eye-sensitivity (pasādacakkhu). The lump of flesh situated in the eye-socket, bounded below by the cheekbone, above by the eyebrow bone, on both sides by the corners of the eye, and outside by the eyelashes; connected to the brain by a nerve-thread emerging from the center of the eye-socket; and variegated with white, black, and very black circles—this is called the composite eye. The sensitivity that is dependent on that composite eye, connected to it, and derived from the four great essentials (mahābhūta)—this is called the eye-sensitivity. Here, this eye-sensitivity is intended. That eye-sensitivity is located in the center of the black circle surrounded by the white circle of the composite eye, in the pupil which is the place where the reflection of the bodies of those standing in front appears. It pervades the seven layers of the eye, just as oil poured on seven layers of cotton pervades them. In size, it is about the size of a split pea, [serving] as the physical basis and door for eye-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate...
74:
That eye-sensitivity remains, accomplishing the state of being the physical basis (vatthu) and the door (dvāra) for eye-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate. It is called “cakkhu” because it relishes [objects]. The meaning is that it relishes the visual object and makes it manifest. They are called “rūpa” because they manifest. The meaning is that they reach a change in color and reveal the nature of the mind (or the nature of the mental process dependent on the heart-base). The consciousness that occurs from the eye-sensitivity, or the consciousness of the eye, is called eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa). It is called “phassa” because it touches. It is called “samphassa” by adorning the word with the prefix “saṃ.” The contact that occurs from the eye-door is called eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa). “Conditioned by eye-contact” (cakkhusamphassapaccayā) means conditioned by the contact associated with eye-consciousness. “Vedayita” is the act of experiencing, meaning feeling (vedanā). That same feeling is called “sukha” (pleasant) because it causes ease. The meaning is that it makes the person in whom it arises happy. Alternatively, it is called “sukha” because it thoroughly consumes or digs out the affliction of body and mind. It is called “dukkha” (painful) because it causes suffering. The meaning is that it makes the person in whom it arises miserable. It is called “adukkhamasukha” because it is neither painful nor pleasant. The letter “m” is included for the sake of euphonic junction (padasandhi). That eye-contact is a condition for the feeling associated with itself in eight ways: by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), resultant (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). It is a condition for the feeling associated with receiving [consciousness] (sampaṭicchana) in five ways: by way of contiguity (anantara), immediate contiguity (samanantara), decisive support of contiguity (anantarūpanissaya), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata). It is a condition for the feelings associated with investigating [consciousness] (santīraṇa) and so forth only by way of decisive support (upanissaya).

It is called “sota” (ear) because it hears. It remains within the physical ear-hole, in a place shaped like a finger-ring and covered with fine reddish hairs, accomplishing the state of being the physical basis and door for ear-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate. They are called “sadda” (sounds) because they are sounded. The meaning is that they are uttered. It is called “ghāna” (nose) because it smells. It remains within the physical nose-hole, in a place shaped like a goat's hoof, accomplishing the state of being the physical basis and door for nose-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate. They are called “gandha” (smells) because they indicate (or betray). The meaning is that they indicate their own physical basis. It is called “jivhā” (tongue) because it calls for life (or nutriment). Alternatively, it is called “jivhā” because of the sense of licking. That tongue-sensitivity, excluding the very tip, the root, and the sides of the physical tongue, remains in the middle of the upper surface in a place shaped like the tip of a split lotus leaf, accomplishing the state of being the physical basis and door for tongue-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate. They are called “rasa” (tastes) because beings relish them. The meaning is that they are relished. It is called “kāya” (body) because it is the place of origin for despicable taints (āsava). “Āya” means the place of origin (uppattidesa). That body-sensitivity remains, for the most part, wherever there is the occurrence of kamma-born matter in this body, accomplishing the state of being the physical basis and door for body-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate. They are called “phoṭṭhabba” (tangibles) because they are touched. It is called “mana” (mind) because it knows. The meaning is that it cognizes. (They are called “dhamma”) because they bear their own characteristics.
75:
What are the dhammas? Mind (mano) is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) together with the adverting (āvajjana) consciousness. Dhammas are the twelvefold varieties of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa). Mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) is the impulsion (javana) mind-consciousness. Mind-contact (manosamphassa) is the contact associated with that mind-consciousness.
