That mind-contact assists the feeling (vedanā) associated with it through seven conditions, excluding the result (vipāka) condition: conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), nutriment (āhāra), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). It assists the second impulsion (javana) which follows immediately through the conditions of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), decisive support of proximity (anantarūpanissaya), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata). It assists the remaining third impulsion and so forth only by the power of the decisive support (upanissaya) condition.

The five answers beginning with form (rūpa) are shown by way of the aggregates (khandha). It is called form (rūpa) because it is deformed and oppressed by cold, heat, and so forth. It is called feeling (vedanā) because it feels. It is called perception (saññā) because it perceives and notes well. They are called mental formations (saṅkhāra) because they process and construct. It is called consciousness (viññāṇa) because it knows specifically. The sixty answers, consisting of the ten sixfold groups (chakka) beginning with the eye (cakkhu) and ending with the investigation of dhammas (dhamma-vicāra), are shown by way of the pleasing and agreeable (piyarūpa sātarūpa). Feelings born of eye-contact (cakkhusamphassajā) and so forth are only those feelings associated with their respective eye-contact and so forth. Perception occurring in forms is called form-perception (rūpasaññā). It is called volition (sañcetanā) because it incites and coordinates; it has the meaning of urging. It is called craving (taṇhā) because it thirsts and trembles; it has the meaning of thirsting. It is called initial application (vitakka) because it thinks; it means thinking or the lifting of the mind onto the object (ūhana). It is called sustained application (vicāra) because the mind wanders upon the object by means of that vicāra; it means wandering or wandering repeatedly (anusañcaraṇa).

The six answers beginning with the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) are shown briefly by way of the determination of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-vavatthāna). It is called pathavī because of its spreading. It is called āpo because it flows, increases, or is increased. It is called tejo because it heats and glows. It is called vāyo because it blows. It is called ākāsa because it cannot be scratched, cut, or broken. It is called element (dhātu) because of its nature of non-being (nissatta).

The ten answers beginning with the earth kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa) are shown by way of kasiṇa meditation (kasiṇa-bhāvanā). Kasiṇa refers to the kasiṇa circle by way of total pervasion, the sign (nimitta) that appears in that circle, and the absorption (jhāna) that takes that sign as its object. Here, however, jhāna is intended. In the beginning, there are four jhānas having the four great elements as their kasiṇa objects, followed by four jhānas having the four color kasiṇas as their objects. Space kasiṇa (ākāsa-kasiṇa) refers to the delimited space (paricchedākāsa) and the jhāna having that space as its object, as well as the space from the removal of the kasiṇa (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa) and the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) jhāna having that space as its object. Consciousness kasiṇa (viññāṇa-kasiṇa) refers to the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) jhāna having that consciousness as its object.

The thirty-two answers beginning with the hair of the head are shown by way of the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra-kammaṭṭhāna). Among those, when hair and so forth appear as repulsive, it is the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). When they appear by way of color, it is the kasiṇa meditation. When they appear by way of the nature of elements, it is the meditation on the determination of the four elements (catu-dhātu-vavatthāna). For those to whom hair and so forth appear as repulsive or by way of color, the jhānas having those as objects should be understood. For those to whom they appear by way of the nature of elements, those thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) and the element meditation having those as objects should be understood. The hairs of the head are delimited by the two ear-slopes, the forehead-fringe in front, and the nape of the neck behind; they are fixed, having entered about the tip of a grain of paddy into the skin covering the skull, and they number more than one hundred thousand. The hairs of the body, excluding the places where the hairs of the head and so forth are fixed and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, are mostly fixed, having entered to the extent of a louse-egg (likkhā) into the ninety-nine thousand pores in the skin of the body. The nails are fixed on the back of the tips of the fingers and toes; they are twenty in number. The teeth are fixed in the jawbones; they are thirty-two in number.
76:
When those parts such as the hair of the head appear as repulsive, it becomes the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). When they appear by way of color, it becomes the kasiṇa meditation (kasiṇa-kammaṭṭhāna). When they appear by way of the nature of elements, it becomes the meditation on the determination of the four elements (catu-dhātu-vavatthāna). For those to whom hair and so forth appear as repulsive or by way of color, the jhānas having that repulsiveness or color-kasiṇa as their object should be understood. For those to whom they appear by way of the nature of elements, those thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) and the element meditation (dhātu-bhāvanā) having those parts as its object should be understood.

The hairs of the head (kesā) are delimited by the two ear-slopes, the forehead-fringe in front, and the nape of the neck behind; they are fixed, having entered about the tip of a grain of paddy into the skin covering the skull. They number more than one hundred thousand.

The hairs of the body (lomā), excluding the places where the hairs of the head and so forth are fixed and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, are mostly fixed, having entered to the extent of a louse-egg (likkhā) into the ninety-nine thousand pores in the skin of the body.

The nails (nakhā) are fixed on the back of the tips of the fingers and toes. They are twenty in number.

The teeth (dantā) are fixed in the two jawbones. They are mostly thirty-two in number.

The skin (taco) covers the whole body; it is the inner skin situated above the visible membrane and below the outer epidermis.

The flesh (maṃsaṃ) consists of the nine hundred pieces of flesh that are fixed, plastering the more than three hundred bones.

The sinews (nhārū) are the nine hundred sinews that are fixed, binding the bones together throughout the whole body.

The bones (aṭṭhī) are the more than three hundred bones situated above the lower bones throughout the whole body.

The bone marrow (aṭṭhimiñjā) is the marrow situated inside the various bones.

The kidneys (vakkaṃ) are two lumps of flesh that are bound by a thick sinew which, starting from a single root coming from the throat, goes a little way and divides into two, and they stand surrounding the heart.

The heart (hadayaṃ) is situated in the middle of the two breasts inside the body. It is the support for the mind within, filled with about half a handful of blood, and is a piece of heart-flesh with a hollow about the size of the place where a punnāga seed is kept.

The liver (yakanaṃ) is a pair of flesh-layers situated inside the two breasts, depending on the right side.

The pleura (kilomakaṃ) is of two kinds: the concealed pleura (paṭicchanna-kilomaka) which stands covering the heart and kidneys, and the unconcealed pleura (appaṭicchanna-kilomaka) which stands covering the flesh under the skin throughout the whole body; it is the flesh that wraps around.

The spleen (pihakaṃ) is the flesh of the 'belly-tongue' situated on the left side of the heart, depending on the upper part of the belly-layer.

The lungs (papphāsaṃ) are the lung-flesh consisting of thirty-two pieces of flesh, which stand hanging down, covering the heart and liver in the middle of the two breasts inside the body.
77:
The large intestine (anta) is firmly attached above at the gullet and below at the rectum; it is situated within the body between the gullet and the rectum. It is thirty-two cubits long in a man and twenty-eight cubits long in a woman, and it is the intestinal coil that lies folded in twenty-one places.

The mesentery (antaguṇa) is the binding that holds the intestinal coils together so that they do not slip to one side, situated between the twenty-one coils of the large intestine.

Undigested food (udariya) is what has been ground into fine pieces by the pestle of the teeth, turned over by the hand of the tongue, and moistened by saliva and digestive juices. It is that which, at the moment of being chewed, is devoid of its original color, smell, and taste; it resembles the rice-paste used by weavers or a dog's vomit. Having fallen into the stomach, it is enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind, boiled by the heat of the stomach fire, infested with swarms of worms, and emitting foam and bubbles from above. It reaches a state of extreme filth, foul odor, and loathsomeness, and is the various kinds of eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted matter situated in the stomach (āmāsaya) in the layer above the navel.

Feces (karīsa) is the excrement situated at the end of the intestine in the receptacle for digested food (pakkāsaya), between the navel and the base of the spine, measuring about eight finger-breadths in depth.

Bile (pitta) is of two kinds. That which is situated between the heart and the lungs, relying on the liver and contained in the gallbladder which resembles a large bitter luffa gourd, is called 'bound bile' (baddha-pitta). That which spreads throughout the entire body—excluding the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, the flesh-free areas, and the hard dry skin—is called 'unbound bile' (abaddha-pitta).

Phlegm (semha) is situated in the stomach lining and is about a bowlful in quantity.

Pus (pubba) is the morbid transformation of blood that has ripened, occurring either in parts of the body struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames, etc., or in boils and abscesses arising from the disturbance of internal elements.

Blood (lohita) is of two kinds. That which fills the lower part of the liver and drips drop by drop onto the heart, kidneys, and lungs, keeping the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs moist, and is about a bowlful in quantity, is called 'stored blood' (sannicita-lohita). That which spreads throughout the entire organic body (upādiṇṇa-sarīra) following the network of veins—excluding the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, the flesh-free areas, and the hard dry skin—is called 'circulating blood' (saṃsaraṇa-lohita).

Sweat (seda) is the liquid element (āpo-dhātu) that flows out from all the pores of the hair and body hair when the body is heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, or seasonal changes.

Fat (meda) is the solid grease which, in a stout person, is situated between the skin and the flesh throughout the whole body, and in a thin person, is situated relying on the flesh of the calves and other such parts.

Tears (assu) are the liquid element (āpo-dhātu) that arises due to joy, grief, or unsuitable food and climate, and remains filling the eye sockets or flows out from them.
78:
Grease (vasā) is the melted oil that is situated mostly on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the points of the shoulders when heat is generated by the heat of fire, the sun, or unsuitable climate.

Saliva (kheḷa) is the liquid element (āpo-dhātu) mixed with foam that arises excessively when seeing, remembering, or placing such food in the mouth, or when the heart is agitated, or when disgust arises for something; it descends from both sides of the cheeks and remains on the tongue.

Snot (siṅghāṇikā) is the foul, impure, and slimy matter that drips from the brain inside the head, descends through the opening above the palate, and remains filling the nostrils or flows out when there is a disturbance of elements caused by unsuitable food or climate, or when crying.

Synovial fluid (lasikā) is the slimy, putrid matter situated within the one hundred and eighty joints, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints.

Urine (mutta) is the liquid element (āpo-dhātu) situated within the bladder through the power of food and climate.

Brain (matthalunga) is the mass of marrow situated within the skull, consisting of a collection of four lumps relying on the four sutures.

The twelve bases (āyatana) such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) are shown by way of the twelve bases. It is called 'āyatana' because it is the place of origin (āya) for the mind and mental factors, because it extends (tanana) the range of the mind, and because it leads (nayana) to the long suffering of saṃsāra. This means that in the eye, visible forms, etc., the mental states (citta-cetasika) arising at the respective doors and objects arise, strive, and exert effort through their respective functions such as experiencing. Furthermore, these bases extend and expand those mental states which are the 'āya'. Moreover, as long as this extremely long suffering of saṃsāra, which has occurred in the beginningless cycle, does not cease, they lead it on and keep it going.

Furthermore, it is called 'āyatana' in the sense of a dwelling place, a mine (source), a meeting place, a place of birth, and a cause. This is true. In the world, in terms such as 'issarāyatana' (dwelling of the lords) or 'vāsudevāyatana' (dwelling of the Vāsudevas), a dwelling place is called an 'āyatana'. In terms such as 'suvaṇṇāyatana' (gold mine) or 'rajatāyatana' (silver mine), a mine is called an 'āyatana'. In the Dispensation (Sāsana), however, in such passages as 'In a delightful meeting place (āyatana), birds (monks) resort to it,' a meeting place is called an 'āyatana'. In such passages as 'The Southern Region (Dakkhiṇāpatha) is the birthplace (āyatana) of cattle,' a place of birth is called an 'āyatana'. In such passages as 'When there is a cause (āyatana) for being a witness,' a cause is called an 'āyatana'. In the case of the eye and so on, those various mental states dwell in the eye, etc., because they occur in dependence on them; therefore, the eye and so on are their dwelling places.
79:
The various states arising in the eye and so forth are as if dwelling there because they occur in connection with the eye and so forth. Therefore, the eye and so forth are the 'dwelling place' (nivāsaṭṭhāna) of those consciousnesses and mental factors. Also, because they depend on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and take the visible form (rūpārammaṇa) as an object, they are spread and established there; thus, the eye and so forth are the 'source' (ākara) of those mental states. Because they are the place of convergence through the power of the respective base, door, and object, the eye and so forth are the 'meeting place' (samosaraṇaṭṭhāna). Because they arise in that very place by depending on the eye-sensitivity and taking the visible form as an object, the eye and so forth are the 'place of birth' (sañjātidesa). Because consciousness and mental factors cannot exist in the absence of the eye and so forth, the eye and so forth are the 'cause' (kāraṇa). For these stated reasons, it is called 'eye-base' (cakkhāyatana) because it is both the eye and a base. The remaining bases should be understood in the same way.

The eighteen explanations (vissajjanā) beginning with the eye-element are presented by way of the eighteen elements. Among the eye and so forth, each state 'arranges' (vidahati) or 'produces' as appropriate; therefore, it is an 'element' (dhātu). It 'is borne' (dhīyate); therefore, it is an element. It is an 'arrangement' (vidhāna); it is arranged by this state; therefore, it is an element. Or, it is 'placed' (dhīyate) in this; therefore, it is an element. Indeed, the mundane elements, being established as causes, arrange (produce) the manifold suffering of Saṃsāra, just as mineral elements like gold and silver produce gold and silver. And they 'are borne' (dhīyate) by beings like a burden by burden-bearers; 'are borne' (dhārīyanti) is the meaning. These states are merely the arrangement of suffering because they are not subject to one's will. By these states, which act as causes, the suffering of Saṃsāra is repeatedly arranged by beings. And that suffering so arranged is 'placed' (dhīyate) in these very states; 'is placed' (ṭhapīyati) is the meaning.

Furthermore, unlike the 'Self' (attā) imagined by the sectarians which does not exist in reality, these states are not non-existent. Rather, they are called 'elements' (dhātu) because they bear (dhārenti) their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva). Just as in the world, various parts of stone such as orpiment (haritāla) and realgar (manosilā) are called elements, these states are also called elements because they are like those elements. This is because they are diverse parts that are to be known by knowledge. Or, just as the name 'element' is applied to blood, flesh, and so forth, which are parts of the collection called the 'body' and are delimited by mutually dissimilar characteristics, so too the name 'element' should be understood in these parts of the person (attabhāva) called the collection of the five aggregates, such as the eye and so forth. This is because these, the eye and so forth, are delimited by mutually dissimilar characteristics.

Furthermore, 'element' (dhātu) is a designation for that which is merely soulless (nijjīva). For this reason, the Blessed One taught the discourse on elements in such passages as, 'Bhikkhu, this person consists of six elements,' in order to uproot the notion of a soul (jīva-saññā). For the reasons stated, it is called 'eye-element' (cakkhudhātu) because it is both the eye and an element. The remaining elements are the same. The 'mind-element' (manodhātu) refers to the three mind-elements. The 'dhamma-element' (dhammadhātu) refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, the sixteen types of subtle matter, and Nibbāna. The 'mind-consciousness-element' (manoviññāṇadhātu) refers to the seventy-six mind-consciousness elements.
80:
The twenty-two answers, beginning with the eye-faculty, are explained by way of the twenty-two faculties. The eye-sensitivity itself is called the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of seeing. The ear itself is called the ear-faculty (sotindriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of hearing. The nose itself is called the nose-faculty (ghānindriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of smelling. The tongue itself is called the tongue-faculty (jivhindriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of tasting. The body itself is called the body-faculty (kāyindriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of touching. It is called mind (mano) because it cognizes; the meaning is 'vijānāti' (it cognizes distinctly). But the Commentators say: "It is called mind (mano) because it cognizes the object as if measuring with a measuring cup or weighing with a large scale; that mind itself is called the mind-faculty (manindriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of cognizing."

It is called life (jīvita) because by that life, the states conascent with it live; that life itself is called the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of maintaining (conascent states). That life-faculty is of two kinds: the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) and the mental life-faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya). The state that arises together with all kamma-born matter and maintains the matter conascent with itself is called the physical life-faculty. The state that arises together with all consciousness and maintains the mental states conascent with itself is called the mental life-faculty.

In that woman, the fetus is established and reaches cohesion; therefore, she is called a woman (itthi). It is called a faculty (indriya) because it exercises predominance in the female sex-mark and so forth. Because it is a faculty belonging invariably to a woman, it is called the female faculty (itthindriya). Hell is called 'puṃ'; because he is tormented in the hell called 'puṃ', he is called a man (purisa). It is called a faculty (indriya) because it exercises predominance in the male sex-mark and so forth. Because it is a faculty belonging invariably to a man, it is called the male faculty (purisindriya). Of these two faculties, each arises together with kamma-born matter for each individual man or woman who possesses the sex-nature (bhāva-rūpa).

The pleasant feeling associated with wholesome-resultant body-consciousness is called a faculty because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of bodily pleasure. Pleasure itself being a faculty is called the pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya). The painful feeling associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness is called a faculty because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of bodily pain. Pain itself being a faculty is called the pain-faculty (dukkhindriya).

Because of association with joy (pīti), one has a good mind, thus one is 'sumana' (well-minded). The state of being well-minded is 'somanassa' (joy). It is called a faculty because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of mental pleasure. Joy itself being a faculty is called the joy-faculty (somanassindriya). Because of association with grief (domanassa), one has a bad mind, or because of having a low feeling, one has a loathsome mind, thus one is 'dummana' (ill-minded). The state of being ill-minded is 'domanassa' (grief). It is called a faculty because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of mental pain. Grief itself being a faculty is called the grief-faculty (domanassindriya). It looks on with indifference at the feeling occurring by way of pleasure or pain; because it stands in a neutral mode and occurs in that mode, it is called equanimity (upekkhā). It is called a faculty because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of neutrality (indifference). Equanimity itself being a faculty is called the equanimity-faculty (upekkhindriya).
81:
By means of that [nature], they believe; or it believes by itself; or it is merely the act of believing—thus it is called faith (saddhā). Because it overcomes lack of faith (assaddhiya), it is called a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance. Alternatively, it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of resolution (adhimokkha). Faith itself being a faculty, it is called the faculty of faith (saddhindriya).

The state of being heroic is called energy (viriya). Alternatively, the work of the energetic is called energy. Alternatively, it is called energy because it is to be instigated or carried out by appropriate means. Because it overcomes laziness (kosajja), it is called a faculty in the sense of predominance. Alternatively, it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of upholding (paggahaṇa). Energy itself being a faculty, it is called the faculty of energy (viriyindriya).

By means of that [nature], they remember; or it remembers by itself; or it is merely the act of remembering—thus it is called mindfulness (sati). Because it overcomes forgetfulness (muṭṭhasacca), it is called a faculty in the sense of predominance. Alternatively, it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of presence (upaṭṭhāna). Mindfulness itself being a faculty, it is called the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya).

Because it places the mind well upon the object, it is called concentration (samādhi). Because it overcomes distraction (vikkhepa), it is called a faculty in the sense of predominance. Alternatively, it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of non-distraction (avikkhepa). Concentration itself being a faculty, it is called the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya).

Because it knows the Noble Truths by such methods as 'This is suffering', it is called wisdom (paññā). In the Commentary, however, it is stated: 'It is called wisdom by virtue of being able to designate [things] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anattā).' Because it overcomes ignorance (avijjā), it is called a faculty in the sense of predominance. Alternatively, it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing (dassana). Wisdom itself being a faculty, it is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya).

The faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is so called because it arises in one who practices with the thought, 'I shall know the deathless state of Nibbāna, or the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which has never been known before in the beginningless round of rebirth (saṃsāra)'; and because the nature of a faculty is present in it. This is the name for the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga-ñāṇa).

The faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) is so called because it is the faculty of thorough knowing, which knows only those Four Noble Truths already known by the first path, without overstepping the limit known by that path; and because the nature of a faculty is present in it. This is the name for the knowledge in the six stages beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

The faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) is so called because it arises in an Arahant who has completed the task of knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths; and because the nature of a faculty is present in it. Alternatively, it is called the faculty of one who has known because it accomplishes the nature of lordship within the mental continuum of Arahants who have completed their task regarding the Four Noble Truths and remain having penetrated the Four Noble Truths. This is the name for the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala-ñāṇa).

All these are called faculties (indriya) according to the appropriate sense: as a mark of Inda (Kamma), as taught by Inda (the Buddha), as seen by Inda (the Buddha), as created by Inda (Kamma), and as cultivated by Inda (the Buddha). Indeed, the Blessed One is called 'Inda' because of His supreme lordship; and wholesome and unwholesome kamma is also called 'Inda' because there is no lordship of others over kammas. Therefore, in this context, the faculties produced by kamma [refer to] wholesome and unwholesome kamma...
82:
These faculties, which arise due to kamma, indicate wholesome and unwholesome kamma; they are also produced by that wholesome and unwholesome kamma. Thus, they are called 'faculties' (indriya) in the sense of indicating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, which is called 'Indra', and in the sense of being prepared, conditioned, and brought into existence by that wholesome and unwholesome kamma called 'Indra'. Furthermore, all these faculties were expounded as they truly are by the Blessed One, the Lord of Munis, and were realized by Him through higher knowledge. Thus, they are called 'faculties' in the sense of being taught by the Blessed One (Indra) and in the sense of being seen by the Blessed One. Moreover, the Blessed One, the Lord of Munis Himself, resorted to some faculties through gocarāsevana (resorting to objects) and cultivated some through bhāvanāsevana (cultivation). Thus, they are called 'faculties' in the sense of being used by the Blessed One. Alternatively, these, such as the eye, are called 'faculties' in the sense of lordship, known as predominance (adhipacca). Indeed, in the arising of eye-consciousness and so forth, the lordship of the eye-sensitivity and so forth is established. It should be understood that if the eye-faculty is sharp, the eye-consciousness is sharp, and if the eye-sensitivity is weak, the eye-consciousness is weak.

The twelve answers beginning with the sensual element (kāmadhātu) are explained by way of the divisions of existence (bhava). The element associated with the defilement of sensuality called sensual lust (kāmarāga) is the sensual element (kāmadhātu); or, the element known as sensual existence (kāmabhava) is the sensual element.

The element associated with the fine-material sphere Jhana, having abandoned sensual defilement, is the fine-material element (rūpadhātu); or, the element known as fine-material existence (rūpabhava) is the fine-material element.

The element associated with the immaterial sphere Jhana, having abandoned both sensuality and fine-materiality, is the immaterial element (arūpadhātu); or, the element known as immaterial existence (arūpabhava) is the immaterial element.

These three elements themselves are again taught by the figurative term 'existence' (bhava). It is called 'existence' because it 'becomes' (bhavati). Existence associated with perception is perceptive existence (saññābhava); or, existence that arises together with perception is perceptive existence; or, because there is perception in this rebirth-existence (upapattibhava), it is called perceptive existence. That perceptive existence is the sensual existence (kāmabhava), the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) excluding non-perceptive existence (asaññabhava), and the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) excluding the existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññābhava).

That which is not perceptive existence is non-perceptive existence (asaññābhava); that non-perceptive existence is a part of fine-material existence.

Because of the absence of gross perception, it is called 'neither-perception' (nevasaññā); because of the presence of subtle perception, it is called 'not-non-perception' (nāsaññā); therefore, it is 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'. Existence associated with that neither-perception-nor-non-perception is neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence. Alternatively, because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception in this existence, it is called neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence. That neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence is a part of immaterial existence.

Existence mixed with one aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), or because this existence has the characteristic of being mixed with one aggregate of matter, it is called one-constituent existence (ekavokārabhava). That one-constituent existence is indeed non-perceptive existence (asaññabhava).

Existence mixed with the four mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha), or because this existence has the characteristic of being mixed with the four mental aggregates, it is called four-constituent existence (catuvokārabhava). That four-constituent existence is indeed immaterial existence (arūpabhava).

Existence mixed with the five aggregates, or because this existence has the characteristic of being mixed with the five aggregates, it is called five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava). That five-constituent existence is both sensual existence and a part of fine-material existence.

The twelve answers beginning with the first Jhana are explained by way of Jhana attainments (samāpatti). In this context, 'Jhana' is intended as merely the Jhanas of the Divine Abidings (brahmavihāra). The Jhana associated with initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is the first Jhana. The Jhana associated with zest, happiness, and one-pointedness is the second Jhana.
83:
The Jhana associated with bliss (sukha) and one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is the third Jhana. The Jhana associated with equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is the fourth Jhana.

It is called mettā because it loves; 'to love' is the meaning. Alternatively, it is called mettā because it arises in a friend (mitta). Or, this state is called mettā because it is the occurrence (of body, speech, and mind) of a friend. It is called deliverance (vimutti) because it is liberated from the opposing states of ill-will, and because it is inclined towards the object. Because it is the deliverance or inclination of the mind, it is called deliverance of mind (cetovimutti). Since mettā itself is a deliverance of mind, it is called mettā-cetovimutti.

Compassion (karuṇā) also has its meaning according to the method already mentioned.

It is called muditā because those endowed with it rejoice by means of that state. Or, it rejoices by itself. Or, it is called muditā because it is merely the act of rejoicing. It is called equanimity (upekkhā) because it views things appropriately by abandoning efforts such as 'May they be free from enmity' and by arriving at a state of neutrality. The three divine abodes (brahmavihāra) beginning with mettā are associated with the three Jhanas beginning with the first. The equanimity divine abode is associated with the fourth Jhana.

It is called infinite (ananta) because there is no limit by way of mental expansion towards that concept of space. The concept of space obtained by removing the counterpart sign of the kasiṇa (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa) is called ākāsānanta because it is infinite. This is indeed the space from which the kasiṇa is removed. Ākāsānanta itself is called ākāsānañca. That ākāsānañca is called the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) because it is the base (āyatana) for that Jhana along with its associated states, in the sense of being a dwelling place, just as the dwelling place of the gods is called devāyatana. Ākāsānañcāyatana itself is called the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-samāpatti) because it is an attainment. That consciousness which pervades the first immaterial state is called infinite (ananta) because it is infinite. This refers to the consciousness that has that space from which the kasiṇa is removed as its object. The word ananta itself is ānañca. Because the consciousness is infinite, it is called viññāṇañca instead of viññāṇānañca. Here, the word viññāṇa is a conventional term (ruḷhi-sadda). That infinite consciousness is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) because it is the base for that Jhana along with its associated states, in the sense of being a dwelling place, just as the dwelling place of the gods is called devāyatana. It is called nothingness (akiñcana) because there is not even a slight remainder of that first immaterial consciousness. It means there is not even a remainder of its dissolution (bhaṅga). The state of nothingness is ākiñcañña. This name ākiñcañña is the designation for the non-existence (natthibhāva-paññatti) of the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space. That ākiñcañña is called the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) because it is the base for that Jhana along with its associated states, in the sense of being a dwelling place, just as the dwelling place of the gods is called devāyatana. Because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, that Jhana along with its associated states is called neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsañña) because it neither has gross perception nor is it without subtle perception. That nevasaññānāsañña is also a base (āyatana) because it is included within the mind-base (manāyatana) and mental-object base (dhammāyatana); therefore, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). Alternatively, the perception in this fourth immaterial Jhana is called nevasaññā because it is unable to perform the function of distinct perception. It is called nāsaññā because it exists as a subtle perception, being a remainder of formations (saṅkhāra). That nevasaññānāsañña is also a base because it is the base for the remaining states; therefore, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). This is the name of the fourth immaterial attainment which has the sphere of nothingness as its object. In this fourth immaterial Jhana, purely...
84:
Just as perception is of this nature (subtle perception), feeling is also neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling (neva-vedanā-nāvedanā). Consciousness is also neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness. Contact is also neither-contact-nor-non-contact. This method applies to the remaining associated states as well. However, this teaching is given with perception as the heading.

The twelve answers beginning with ignorance (avijjā) are explained by way of the factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Because they are improper to fulfill, bodily misconduct and the like are called 'avindiya' (not to be found/attained). Because it finds that which is not to be found, it is called 'avijjā' (ignorance). Conversely, bodily good conduct and the like are called 'vindiya' (to be found/attained). Because it does not find that which is to be found, it is called 'avijjā'. Because it makes unknown the meaning of the aggregates as a heap, the meaning of the bases as an origin, the meaning of the elements as empty, the meaning of the faculties as predominance, and the meaning of the truths as reality, it is called 'avijjā'. Because it makes unknown the fourfold meanings of suffering and the other truths by way of oppression (pīḷana) and so forth, it is also called 'avijjā'. Because it causes beings to run through the endless cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) in all types of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), planes of existence (bhava), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), it is called 'avijjā'. Because it runs towards women, men, and so forth, which do not exist in the ultimate sense, and does not run towards the aggregates and so forth, which do exist, it is called 'avijjā'. Furthermore, because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and so forth, as well as the laws of dependent origination and the dependently arisen states, it is also called 'avijjā'. Because they process the conditioned, they are called 'saṅkhāra' (formations). Because it cognizes, it is called 'viññāṇa' (consciousness). Because it bends towards an object, or causes to bend, it is called 'nāma' (name). Because it is deformed (or afflicted), it is called 'rūpa' (form). Because it extends the mind and mental factors, or because it leads to the long suffering of saṃsāra, it is called 'āyatana' (base). Because it touches, it is called 'phassa' (contact). Because it feels, it is called 'vedanā' (feeling). Because it trembles or because it thirsts, it is called 'taṇhā' (craving). Because it clings firmly, it is called 'upādāna' (clinging). Because it becomes, or causes to become, it is called 'bhava' (becoming). Arising is 'jāti' (birth). Decaying is 'jarā' (aging). Because one dies by it (at the moment of dissolution), it is 'maraṇa' (death).

The eight hundred and eight answers beginning with suffering are explained by way of the connection with the Four Noble Truths. In the passages such as "Suffering is to be fully known by direct knowledge," twenty-four answers are given by way of six tetrads. In the elision (peyyāla) of "eye, aging and death," starting from "The eye is to be fully known by direct knowledge, the ear is to be fully known by direct knowledge" and ending with "Birth is to be fully known by direct knowledge," it is taught by connecting with one hundred and ninety-five answers. There are one hundred and ninety-five tetrads; by way of these tetrads, there are seven hundred and eighty answers. In the tetrad beginning with "Aging and death are to be fully known by direct knowledge," there are four answers, thus totaling eight hundred and eight answers. Here, the principal cause of each respective state should be understood as 'samudaya' (origin). Nibbāna, which is empty of all formations, should be understood as 'nirodha' (cessation). Regarding the three supramundane faculties such as the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), the teaching of "the cessation of the faculty 'I shall know the unknown'" and so forth is appropriate, referring to their absence here. "The practice leading to cessation" (nirodhagāminīpaṭipadā) refers only to the Noble Path in all instances. In speaking of the Noble Path thus, because the term 'Path' can also be applied to the Fruit, it is also appropriate for the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) and the faculty of one who has final knowledge (aññātāvindriya) to be the practice leading to cessation. Again, by way of the meaning of full understanding (pariññā) and so forth of suffering...
85:
is appropriate. "The practice leading to cessation" (nirodhagāminīpaṭipadā) refers only to the Noble Path in all instances. When the Noble Path is spoken of in this way, because the designation 'Path' can also occur for the Fruit, it is also appropriate for the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) and the faculty of one who has final knowledge (aññātāvindriya) to be the practice leading to cessation. Again, eight hundred and eight answers are explained by way of the meaning of full understanding (pariññā) and so forth of suffering and the rest. Again, eight hundred and eight answers are explained by way of the meaning of full understanding and penetration (pariññā-paṭivedha) and so forth of suffering and the rest. That very nature of full understanding (pariññā) is also called penetration (paṭivedha) because it is to be penetrated; therefore, it is called 'pariññā-paṭivedha'. The nature of pariññā-paṭivedha itself is the meaning, thus it is called 'pariññā-paṭivedhaṭṭha'.

Again, those two hundred and two terms starting from suffering and ending with aging and death are connected with seven terms each, such as origin (samudaya), and by way of two hundred and two octads (aṭṭhaka), one thousand six hundred and sixteen answers are explained. Among those answers, the principal cause is called 'samudaya' (origin). The cessation of that origin is 'samudaya-nirodha'. Desire itself is lust, thus it is 'chanda-rāga' (desire-lust). The desire-lust that occurs by perceiving pleasure in suffering is the desire-lust for suffering; the cessation of that desire-lust is 'chanda-rāga-nirodha'. The pleasure and joy that arise depending on suffering are the gratification (assāda) of suffering. The impermanence and the nature of changeability of suffering are the danger (ādīnava) of suffering. The removal of desire-lust and the abandoning of desire-lust for suffering are the escape (nissaraṇa) from suffering. According to the statement, "Whatever is become, conditioned, and dependently arisen, its cessation is the escape from it," Nibbāna alone is the escape from suffering. It should be understood that in these four places—namely, cessation of suffering, cessation of origin, cessation of desire-lust, and escape from suffering—Nibbāna alone is spoken of by various synonymous terms by way of opposition to various conditioned states.

However, some teachers say: "The arising of suffering due to the arising of nutriment is 'dukkha-samudaya'; the cessation of suffering due to the cessation of nutriment is 'dukkha-nirodha'; the cessation of origin by way of its own function is 'samudaya-nirodha'; or else, the cessation of origin by seeing the arising and passing away is 'samudaya-nirodha'; the Path together with insight is 'chanda-rāga-nirodha'." If it were said thus, because the supramundane faculties do not fall under insight, it would not be common to all terms; therefore, only the first-mentioned method should be accepted. Indeed, in the supramundane faculties, because of the very absence of desire-lust, the name 'cessation of desire-lust' (chanda-rāga-nirodha) is appropriate. By having desire-lust for the body, desire-lust is already established in the parts of the body such as the hair; by having desire-lust for things that have aging and death, desire-lust is already established in aging and death themselves. In this same way, gratification (assāda) and danger (ādīnava) should also be connected. Again, the two hundred and two terms starting from suffering and ending with aging and death are connected with the six terms starting from origin...
86:
By combining with the six terms and by way of the seven hundred and two heptads, one thousand four hundred and fourteen (1414) answers have been explained in detail.

Now, in order to explain the two hundred and one terms beginning with materiality (rūpa) and ending with aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) by combining them with the seven contemplations, first, the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) are stated. All those two hundred and one terms, together with the seven answers of pure contemplation, result in one thousand four hundred and fourteen answers. Repeatedly viewing as impermanent is called the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). That contemplation of impermanence is the opposite of the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā). Repeatedly viewing as suffering is called the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). That contemplation of suffering is the opposite of the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā). Repeatedly viewing as non-self is called the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). That contemplation of non-self is the opposite of the perception of self (atta-saññā). Because of the fulfillment of the three contemplations, one becomes disenchanted, thus it is called disenchantment (nibbidā); because it is both disenchanting and repeatedly viewing, it is called the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā). That contemplation of disenchantment is the opposite of delight (nandi). Because of the fulfillment of the four contemplations, one becomes dispassionate, thus it is called dispassion (virāga); because it is both dispassionate and repeatedly viewing, it is called the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā). That contemplation of dispassion is the opposite of lust (rāga). Because of the fulfillment of the five contemplations, it causes the cessation of lust, thus it is called cessation (nirodha); because it causes cessation and is repeatedly viewing, it is called the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā). That contemplation of cessation is the opposite of the origin (samudaya). Because of the fulfillment of the six contemplations, one relinquishes, thus it is called relinquishment (paṭinissagga); because it is relinquishing and repeatedly viewing, it is called the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā). That contemplation of relinquishment is the opposite of grasping (ādāna). Even though the supramundane faculties (lokuttara indriya) do not approach insight (vipassanā), according to the words "All conditioned things are impermanent, all conditioned things are suffering, all phenomena are non-self," those supramundane faculties should be understood as being combined with the seven contemplations because they also have the nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self; because of the absence of the perceptions of permanence, pleasure, and self, and of delight and lust in those faculties, they are viewed as having cessation; and because of the possibility of relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) and relinquishment as leaping forward (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga). When the aggregates that possess aging and death are seen by way of impermanence and so on, aging and death are also said to be seen by way of impermanence and so on. When one is disenchanted and dispassionate regarding the aggregates that possess aging and death, one is disenchanted and dispassionate regarding aging and death. When the aggregates that possess aging and death are seen by way of cessation (nirodha), aging and death are also said to be seen by way of cessation. When one relinquishes the aggregates that possess aging and death, it is simply called relinquishing aging and death. In this way, it should be understood that the seven contemplations are combined with aging and death.

Now, by way of the five objects such as arising (uppāda) which are the basis for the knowledge of danger (ādīnavañāṇa), fifteen answers consisting of arising and its synonyms are stated.
87:
By way of the objects such as non-arising (anuppāda), which are the opposites of arising and so on, for the knowledge of the state of peace (santipadañāṇa), fifteen answers are stated. Again, by combining those very terms such as arising and non-arising by way of pairs, thirty answers are stated. Thus, in this method, there are sixty answers. Among those answers, arising (uppāda) is the appearance in this life (rebirth) due to past kamma. Occurrence (pavatta) is the proceeding of what has thus arisen. Sign (nimitta) is the sign of all conditioned things. For the practitioner (yogāvacara), conditioned things appear as if they have a shape; therefore, they are called signs. Accumulation (āyūhana) is kamma that is the cause of rebirth in the future. That kamma is called accumulation in the sense of constructing.

Rebirth (paṭisandhi) is the arising in the future. It is called rebirth because it connects one existence with another. Destination (gati) is the destination where that rebirth occurs. It is called destination because it is where one must go. Manifestation (nibbattī) is the manifestation of the aggregates. Rebirth-process (upapatti) is the occurrence of the result (vipāka) as stated in the words "of one who has attained or of one who has been reborn". Birth (jāti) is the act of being born. It is the first manifestation of whichever aggregates appear for beings being born in various existences. Aging (jarā) is the process of growing old. That aging is of two kinds: the conditioned characteristic known as the characteristic of change while standing (ṭhitanyathatta), and the state of being old of the aggregates included within a single existence in the sequence conventionally called broken teeth and so on; here, the latter is intended. Sickness (byādhi) is the eightfold ailment caused by the disturbance of the elements, through bile, phlegm, wind, their combination, seasonal change, improper posture, effort, or the result of kamma. It is called sickness because it brings or produces various sufferings, or because it causes pain, heat, or trembling. Death (maraṇa) is dying. That death is of two kinds: the conditioned characteristic known as the characteristic of fall (vaya-lakkhaṇa), and the cutting off of the continuity of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) included within a single existence; here, the latter is intended.

Sorrow (soka) is grieving. It is the burning of the mind in one affected by the loss of relatives, wealth, health, virtue, or right view. Lamentation (parideva) is wailing. It is the verbal outcry in one affected by the loss of relatives and so on. Despair (upāyāsa) is intense exhaustion. It is the very anger produced from extreme mental suffering in one affected by the loss of relatives and so on. And here, only the five terms such as arising (uppāda) are stated as the basis for the knowledge of danger (ādīnavañāṇa); the remaining terms are by way of their synonyms. For manifestation (nibbattī) is a synonym for arising (uppāda); birth (jāti) is a synonym for rebirth (paṭisandhi); this pair, destination (gati) and rebirth-process (upapatti), are synonyms for occurrence (pavatta); and aging and so on are synonyms for the sign (nimitta). By the words such as non-arising (anuppāda), only Nibbāna is stated.

Again, by combining those sixty terms such as arising and non-arising with the terms suffering and happiness, sixty answers are stated; and by combining them with the terms fear and safety, sixty answers are stated.
88:
Sixty answers have been presented in connection with the terms 'carnal' (sāmisa) and 'spiritual' (nirāmisa), and sixty answers in connection with the terms 'formations' (saṅkhāra) and 'Nibbāna'. Among those answers, suffering (dukkha) is called 'suffering' because of its impermanent nature (anicca). Because it is the opposite of suffering, it is called 'happiness' (sukha). Whatever is suffering is 'fear' (bhaya). Because it is the opposite of fear, it is called 'security' (khema). Whatever is fear is called 'carnal' (sāmisa) because it is not yet free from the bait (āmisa) of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the bait of worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Because it is the opposite of the carnal, it is called 'spiritual' (nirāmisa). Whatever is carnal is merely a formation (saṅkhāra). Because it is the opposite of formations and is peaceful (from the fires of defilements), it is called 'Nibbāna'. Indeed, formations are consumed (by the eleven fires), while Nibbāna is peaceful. It should be understood that these were taught in various ways with reference to the occurrence of formations in the aspect of suffering, the aspect of fear, the aspect of the carnal, and the aspect of formations.

Thirty-one answers, beginning with the sense of embracing (pariggahaṭṭha), are presented by way of the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga). The states associated with the Noble Path are called 'embracing' (pariggaha) because they are embraced for the sake of arising from the beginning (virtue) onwards; their nature is the 'sense of embracing' (pariggahaṭṭha). They are the 'sense of retinue' (parivāraṭṭha) because they serve as each other's retinue. They are the 'sense of fulfillment' (paripūraṭṭha) by way of the perfection of development (bhāvanā). They are the 'sense of one-pointedness' (ekaggaṭṭha) by way of concentration (samādhi), regarding the embracing of a single object. They are the 'sense of non-distraction' (avikkhepaṭṭha), regarding the absence of distraction toward various objects. They are the 'sense of exertion' (paggahaṭṭha) by way of energy (vīriya). They are the 'sense of non-diffusion' (avisāraṭṭha) by way of concentration, because of the absence of scattering, like bathing powder mixed with water. They are the 'sense of non-turbidity' (anāvilaṭṭha) because of being undisturbed through the application of concentration. They are the 'sense of immovability' (aniñjanaṭṭha) because of being unshaken. 'By way of the appearance of oneness' (ekattupaṭṭhānavasena) means both through the application of concentration and through the firm establishment in a single object (Nibbāna). The 'sense of steadiness' (thitaṭṭha) is the nature of being established and motionless in the object. It is the 'sense of the object' (ārammaṇaṭṭha) because of the state of firmly grasping that object of Nibbāna. It is the 'sense of the range' (gocaraṭṭha) because of the state of being able to move at will within that Nibbāna. The 'sense of abandoning' (pahānaṭṭha) of Nibbāna should be understood by way of the abandonment through deliverance (nissaraṇapahāna). The 'sense of relinquishment' (pariccāgaṭṭha) of the Noble Path should be understood by way of the relinquishment of defilements. It is the 'sense of emergence' (vuṭṭhānaṭṭha) by way of emerging from both (the sign of formations and the sign of occurrence). It is the 'sense of turning away' (nivattanaṭṭha) by way of retreating from the sign (nimitta) and occurrence (pavatti). It is the 'sense of peace' (santaṭṭha) because of being quenched (from defilements). It is the 'sense of the sublime' (paṇītaṭṭha) because of the absence of burning and because of its excellence. It is the 'sense of liberation' (vimuttaṭṭha) because of being liberated from defilements and because of being inclined toward the object. It is the 'sense of being taintless' (anāsavaṭṭha) because of being pure, not being the range of the taints (āsava). It is the 'sense of crossing over' (taraṇaṭṭha) because of crossing over the wilderness of defilements and the wilderness of saṃsāra. It is the 'sense of the signless' (animittaṭṭha) because of the absence of the sign of formations. It is the 'sense of the desireless' (appaṇihitaṭṭha) because of the absence of longing through craving. It is the 'sense of emptiness' (suññataṭṭha) because of the absence of a core of self. It is the 'sense of single taste' (ekarasaṭṭha) either because of having a single function through the taste of liberation or because of the equal function of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). The 'sense of non-overrunning' (anativattanaṭṭha) where tranquility and insight do not exceed each other should be understood. The 'sense of yoking' (yuganaddhaṭṭha) of that same tranquility and insight should be understood. From the formations of the Noble Path...
89: It is the 'sense of deliverance' (niyyānaṭṭha) because it leads out from the formations of the three planes. It is the 'sense of cause' (hetuṭṭha) because it is the cause for reaching Nibbāna. It is the 'sense of seeing' (dassanaṭṭha) because of the realization of Nibbāna. It is the 'sense of predominance' (ādhipateyyaṭṭha) because of its state of being the chief. Four types of answers beginning with tranquility (samatha) are presented by way of tranquility and insight. It is the 'sense of contemplation' (anupassanāṭṭha) because of repeatedly seeing by way of impermanence and so on. The state of not overrunning each other through the single-taste nature of the yoked pair of tranquility and insight is the 'sense of non-overrunning' (anativattanaṭṭha). Nine types of answers beginning with training (sikkhā) are presented by way of the beginning, middle, and end of the Noble Path. It is called 'training' (sikkhā) because it is to be practiced. It is the 'sense of undertaking' (samādānaṭṭha) because that training is to be undertaken. It is the 'sense of the range' (gocaraṭṭha) because it is the place for the development of the object taken by way of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) while established in virtue, and because it is the place of its activity. The 'sense of exertion' (paggahaṭṭha) is the act of energizing the mind that has shrunk through laziness during the time of tranquility or insight, by way of developing the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (vīriya), and joy (pīti). The 'sense of restraint' (niggahaṭṭha) is the act of calming the distracted mind by way of developing the enlightenment factors of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā). 'Of those purified in both' (ubho visuddhānaṃ) means the minds that are purified by being restrained from the two sides of sluggishness and distraction. It should be understood that the plural form is used by way of the minds that occur in succession while established in the middle state. The 'sense of looking on with equanimity' (ajjhupekkhaṇaṭṭha) is the absence of one's own activity in energizing or calming. The 'sense of attaining distinction' (visesādhigamaṭṭha) is the development by way of the mind that occurs evenly. The 'sense of further penetration' (uttaripaṭivedhaṭṭha) is the penetration into higher stages by way of the manifestation of the Noble Path. The 'sense of the realization of the truths' (saccābhisamayaṭṭha) is the penetration of the Four Noble Truths accomplished by the Noble Path. The 'sense of establishing' (patiṭṭhāpakaṭṭha) is the sense of establishing one in cessation (nirodha) by way of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Indeed, that attainment of fruition establishes the person possessed of it in Nibbāna, which is called cessation. Five types of answers beginning with the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) are presented by way of the sense of faculty (indriya). The 'sense of resolution' (adhimokkhaṭṭha) is the sense of firm conviction. The 'sense of establishment' (upaṭṭhānaṭṭha) is the sense of being established by approaching the object. The 'sense of seeing' (dassanaṭṭha) is the sense of observing the nature of things. Five types of answers beginning with the power of faith (saddhābala) are presented by way of the sense of power (bala). Faith itself is a power because of its sense of being unshakable; thus it is the 'power of faith' (saddhābala). 'In lack of faith' (assaddhiye) means by way of lack of faith. Lack of faith is the arising of consciousness that is the opposite of faith. The 'sense of being unshakable' (akampiyaṭṭha) is the sense of that which should not be shaken; it means it cannot be shaken. 'In laziness' (kosajje) means because of sloth and torpor (thina-middha), which is called laziness. 'In negligence' (pamāde) means because of the arising of consciousness that is the opposite of mindfulness (sati). 'In agitation' (uddhacce) means because of agitation, which is called lack of peace. 'In ignorance' (avijjāyā) means because of delusion (moha). Seven types of answers beginning with the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga) are presented by way of the sense of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). Of the person who will realize the Four Noble Truths...
90:
It is called bojjhaṅga because it is a constituent factor of one who will realize the Four Noble Truths. It is called sambojjhaṅga because it is a praised and excellent factor of enlightenment. Mindfulness itself being a factor of enlightenment, it is called satisambojjhaṅga. It is called dhammavicaya because it investigates phenomena; this is a name for wisdom (paññā). The meaning of pavicaya is the sense of investigation. It is called pīti because it causes delight. The meaning of pharaṇa is the sense of pervading (or spreading). Tranquillity is called passaddhi. The meaning of upasama is the sense of being free from distress. It is called upekkhā because it looks on appropriately; it means looking on with balance without falling into either extreme. Here, it is tatramajjhattūpekkhā (equanimity as neutrality) and is also named bojjhaṅgupekkhā. Because it has the characteristic of maintaining balance, it has the sense of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna).

The eight answers beginning with right view (sammādiṭṭhi) are explained by way of the path (magga). It is called sammādiṭṭhi because it sees rightly, or because they see rightly by means of that wisdom, or because it is a praised and excellent view. (This is the meaning) of that right view. It is called sammāsaṅkappa because it intends rightly, or because they intend rightly by means of that thought (vitakka), or because it is a praised and excellent intention. It has the sense of applying (abhiropana), the sense of applying the mind to the object. There is also a reading: the sense of firmly applying [the mind] to the object. It is called sammāvācā because it speaks rightly, or because they speak rightly by means of that right speech, or because it is a praised and excellent speech. This is the name for the abstinence from wrong speech. It has the sense of encompassing (pariggaha), encompassing the fourfold restraint of speech. It is called sammākamma because it acts rightly, or because they act rightly by means of that right action, or because it is a praised and excellent action. Sammākamma itself is called sammākammanta. This is the name for the abstinence from wrong action. It has the sense of origination (samuṭṭhāna) occurring in the threefold restraint of the body. It is called sammā-ājīva because it lives rightly, or because they live rightly by means of that right livelihood, or because it is a praised and excellent livelihood. This is the name for the abstinence from wrong livelihood. It has the sense of purification (vodāna). It is called sammāvāyāma because it strives rightly, or because they strive rightly by means of that right effort, or because it is a praised and excellent effort. It is called sammāsati because it remembers rightly, or because they remember rightly by means of that right mindfulness, or because it is a praised and excellent mindfulness. It is called sammāsamādhi because it concentrates rightly, or because they concentrate rightly by means of that right concentration, or because it is a praised and excellent concentration.

The ten answers beginning with the faculties (indriya) are explained in successive order as a group. It is called the sense of predominance (ādhipateyya) because it performs the function of lordship. It is the sense of being unshakable (akampiya) because it cannot be shaken by opposing states. It is the sense of leading out (niyyāna) because it emerges from the opposing states of both mundane and supramundane factors of enlightenment. It is called the sense of cause (hetu) because it is the cause for abandoning wrong view and so forth, or because all [factors] such as right view and so forth are the causes for reaching Nibbāna. In the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)...
91:
It is called 'upaṭṭhāna' because it descends into, rushes into, and is firmly established in objects such as the body and feelings, which are the foundations of mindfulness. Mindfulness itself is called 'satipaṭṭhāna' because it is firmly established. This satipaṭṭhāna is fourfold based on the mode of perceiving the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self in the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects, and based on the accomplishment of the function of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. These foundations of mindfulness are obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage of the Path; however, at the moment of the Path, the single mindfulness itself receives four names.

In the 'sammappadhāna' (right efforts), one strives well by means of this energy; therefore, it is called 'padhāna'. It is called 'sammappadhāna' because it is a noble (beautiful) striving. Alternatively, it is called 'sammappadhāna' because one strives rightly by means of this energy. Or, it is called 'sammappadhāna' because it is noble (beautiful) due to being free from the deformity of defilements, and it is 'padhāna' (foremost) because it brings about the state of excellence by accomplishing welfare and happiness, or because it performs the state of striving. This is a designation for energy (vīriya). Its fourfold division occurs because it functions to accomplish the tasks of abandoning and not arising of unarisen and arisen unwholesome states, and the arising and maintenance of unarisen and arisen wholesome states. These right efforts are also obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage of the Path; however, at the moment of the Path, the single energy itself receives four names. The term 'padahanaṭṭha' means the sense of striving. There is also a reading 'padhānaṭṭha', which has the same meaning.

In the 'iddhipāda' (bases of power), among desire (chanda), energy (vīriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā), each one succeeds; therefore, it is called 'iddhi', meaning it succeeds or is accomplished. Alternatively, beings prosper and reach excellence by means of these factors such as desire; therefore, it is called 'iddhi'. According to the first sense, 'iddhi' itself is the base (pāda) because it is the means of reaching, thus it is 'iddhipāda', meaning a constituent of success. According to the second sense, it is 'iddhipāda' because it is the base for success. 'Pāda' means the foundation or the means of attainment. Indeed, because one reaches or attains the 'iddhi' known as the higher and higher distinctions by means of these factors such as desire, it is called 'pāda'. These factors such as desire are obtained in various consciousnesses by way of predominance (adhipati) in the preliminary stage of the Path; however, at the moment of the Path, they are obtained simultaneously. The term 'ijjhanaṭṭha' means the sense of accomplishment or the sense of foundation.

'Saccānaṃ' refers to the sense of the four Noble Truths. 'Tathaṭṭha' means the sense of having the nature of reality. These eight explanations are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. 'Payogānaṃ' refers to the sense of the four endeavors (activities) of the Noble Path. 'Paṭippassaddhaṭṭha' means the sense of tranquillity of the four Noble Fruits. Indeed, the endeavor of the Path becomes tranquil at the moment of the Fruit because its task is completed. Alternatively, it is the state of being tranquil by the arising of the Fruit of the Path's endeavors. 'Sacchikiriyaṭṭha' of the Fruits means the sense of making manifest by way of reflection on the Noble Fruits. It means making manifest by way of taking as an object, or making manifest by way of attainment at the moment of the Fruit. The five explanations starting with 'vitakka' (initial thought) are shown by way of the factors of jhāna. Thinking is called 'vitakka'.
92:
It is said to be 'ūhana' (lifting/directing). Sustained thinking is called 'vicāra', meaning repeated exploration. The sense of 'upavicāra' is the sense of repeated investigation. The sense of 'abhisandana' is the sense of moistening, or the sense of one-pointedness of mind by way of concentration.

The fifteen explanations starting with 'āvajjana' (adverting) are shown by way of miscellaneous categories. 'Āvajjana' is the sense of adverting or turning of the two consciousnesses that incline the mental continuum toward an object other than the bhavaṅga objects (kamma, kamma-nimitta, gati-nimitta) in the five doors and the mind door. 'Vijānanatṭha' is the sense of cognizing of consciousness (viññāṇa). 'Pajānanaṭṭha' is the sense of clearly knowing of wisdom (paññā). 'Sañjānanaṭṭha' is the sense of perceiving by marking of perception (saññā). 'Ekodaṭṭha' is the sense of unification of concentration (samādhi). Indeed, in the second jhāna, concentration is called 'ekodi' because it arises as 'one' (singular/noble). It means it arises as 'agga' (foremost/noble) because it is not overwhelmed by initial and sustained thought. In the world, the noble is also called 'eka' (one). Alternatively, it is appropriate to call it 'ekodi' because it arises as 'one' without a companion, being devoid of initial and sustained thought. Or, it is appropriate to call it 'ekodi' because all wholesome concentration arises as 'agga' (foremost) since it cannot be overwhelmed by the hindrances (especially restlessness/uddhacca) as it is their opposite, or because it arises as 'one' without a companion as it is devoid of them. The 'ñāta' sense of direct knowledge (abhiññā) is the sense of knowing the nature by way of 'ñāta-pariññā' (full understanding of the known). The 'tīraṇa' sense of full understanding (pariññā) is the sense of investigating by way of impermanence, etc., through 'tīraṇa-pariññā' (full understanding by investigation). The 'pariccāga' sense of abandoning (pahāna) is the sense of abandoning the opposite defilements through 'pahāna-pariññā' (full understanding by abandoning). 'Ekarasaṭṭha' (the sense of single flavor/function) is the sense of the development (bhāvanā) that occurs uniformly. 'Phassanaṭṭha' is the sense of touching or experiencing. 'Khandhaṭṭha' (the sense of aggregate) is by way of bearing the burden of suffering, etc. 'Dhātuṭṭha' (the sense of element) is by way of being void of a living soul (satta-jīva), etc. 'Āyatanaṭṭha' (the sense of base) is by way of expanding in their respective limits, etc. 'Saṅkhataṭṭha' (the sense of the conditioned) is by way of being produced by the meeting of causes. 'Asaṅkhataṭṭha' (the sense of the unconditioned) is by way of being the opposite of that.

The fifteen explanations starting with 'cittaṭṭha' are shown in connection with the word 'citta' (mind). In the sense of 'cittaṭṭha', it is called 'citta' because it thinks of an object, meaning it cognizes. Here, the 'javana' (impulsion) is called 'citta' because it arranges (increases) its own continuum by way of the javana-process. The 'vipāka' (resultant) is called 'citta' because it is arranged (increased) by kamma and defilements. All mind is called 'citta' because it is variegated (diverse) in an appropriate manner, or because it causes variegation. The mind that is the cause of the round of rebirths is also called 'citta' because it accumulates (increases) the suffering of saṃsāra. Thus, the sense of 'cittaṭṭha' should be understood by way of variegation in the object, etc. It is called 'anantara' because there is no interval in the production of consciousness or in the production of the Fruit. The state of being 'anantara' is 'ānantariya'. The state of being without interval of the mind is 'cittānantariya', which is the sense of 'cittānantariya'. The meaning is that, excluding the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) of Arahants, any consciousness that has just ceased has the power to produce the subsequent consciousness without interval, and the Path-consciousness has the power to produce the Fruit without interval. The sense of 'vuṭṭhāna' (emergence) of the mind is...
93:
The change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū-citta) is called the sense of emergence (vuṭṭhānaṭṭha) because it emerges from the signs of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta); the path consciousness (magga-citta) is also called so because it emerges from the signs of formations and the resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāmakkhandha or pavatta-dhamma). The sense of turning away (vivaṭṭanaṭṭha) of the mind refers to the sense of turning (shifting) towards Nibbāna of those two types of consciousness—the change-of-lineage and the path—which have emerged from the aforementioned signs of formations and resultant mental aggregates. The sense of root cause (hetuṭṭha) of the mind is the sense of being the cause for the nine roots that assist the mind as root-conditions (hetu-paccaya). The sense of condition (paccayaṭṭha) of the mind is the sense of various conditions such as the physical base (vatthu), the object (ārammaṇa), and so on. The sense of physical base (vatthuṭṭha) of the mind is the sense of being the location of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and heart-base, which are the physical bases of the mind. The sense of plane (bhūmaṭṭha) of the mind is the sense of the plane, such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), according to the place where the mind arises. The sense of object (ārammaṇaṭṭha) of the mind is the sense of apprehending objects such as visible forms and so on. It is called the sense of resort (gocaraṭṭha) because it is the place of constant occurrence (frequenting) in a practiced object. It is called the sense of conduct (cariyaṭṭha) by way of the conduct of consciousness (viññāṇa-cariya) to be mentioned hereafter. Alternatively, the sense of producing associated states is called the sense of conduct. Although the mind does not travel to another place, it is called the sense of having gone (gataṭṭha) by way of its ability to apprehend distant or near objects. The sense of directing (abhinīhāraṭṭha) is the sense of directing the mind from an apprehended object for the purpose of attending to another object. The sense of deliverance (niyyānaṭṭha) of the mind is the sense of the path consciousness delivering one from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). The sense of escape (nissaraṇaṭṭha) of the mind is according to the method: "The mind of one who has attained renunciation (nekkhamma/jhana) is escaped from sensual desire (kāmacchanda)," and so forth.

The forty-two answers beginning with singleness (ekatta) are explained in connection with the word 'singleness'. Singleness (ekatta) means being established in a single object (ekārammaṇa). It is the sense of plunging into (the object) (pakkhandanaṭṭha) by the power of the first jhana; the sense of clarifying (pasīdanaṭṭha) by the power of the second jhana; the sense of steadying well (santiṭṭhanaṭṭha) by the power of the third jhana; and the sense of being liberated (from hindrances) (muccanaṭṭha) by the power of the fourth jhana. It is the sense of seeing (passanaṭṭha) by the power of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), "This state is peaceful."

The five beginning with the sense of having been made into a vehicle (yānikataṭṭha) are specific masteries (vasībhāva) of concentration (samādhi). The sense of having been made into a vehicle (yānikataṭṭha) is the sense of having been made like a well-prepared vehicle. The sense of having been made into a foundation (vatthukataṭṭha) is the sense of having been made like a foundation (vatthu) in the sense of being a support. The sense of being well-established (anuṭṭhitaṭṭha) is the sense of being present. The sense of being consolidated (paricitaṭṭha) is the sense of being cultivated all around. The sense of being well-undertaken (susamāraddhaṭṭha) is the sense of being well-undertaken, meaning well-performed. Alternatively, these five terms should be applied respectively to the five masteries: adverting (āvajjana), attaining (samāpajjana), resolving (adhiṭṭhāna), emerging (vuṭṭhāna), and reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa).

When meditation (bhāvanā) on an object such as a kasiṇa reaches its peak, there are the senses of encompassing, surrounding, and fulfilling of the mind and mental factors. Because those very mind and mental factors are well-concentrated, it is called the sense of combination (samodhānaṭṭha) by way of converging on a single object. Because those very mind and mental factors have reached power, it is called the sense of determination (adhiṭṭhānaṭṭha) by way of standing firm, having overcome the object. It is called the sense of cultivation (āsevanaṭṭha) by way of practicing with respect from the beginning of either serenity (samatha) or insight (vipassanā). By way of increasing (vaḍḍhanavasena)...
94:
The meaning of development (bhāvanāṭṭha) is by way of developing. The meaning of frequent practice (bahulīkammaṭṭha) is by way of doing repeatedly. The meaning of being well-arisen (susamuggataṭṭha) is by way of the excellent arising of that which has been practiced repeatedly. The meaning of being well-liberated (suvimuttaṭṭha) is by way of being well-freed from the opposing defilements and by way of being well-fixed upon the object (Nibbāna).

The four terms beginning with the meaning of awakening (bujjhano) are stated by way of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). These are: the meaning of awakening (bujjhano) of the factors of enlightenment of the Path of Stream-entry; the meaning of subsequent awakening (anubujjhano) of the factors of enlightenment of the Path of Once-returning; the meaning of piercing awakening (paṭibujjhano) of the factors of enlightenment of the Path of Non-returning; and the meaning of full awakening (sambujjhano) of the factors of enlightenment of the Path of Arahantship. Alternatively, it is said: the meaning of awakening of the factors of enlightenment of insight (vipassanā); the meaning of subsequent awakening of the factors of enlightenment of the Path of Seeing (dassana-magga); the meaning of piercing awakening of the factors of enlightenment of the Path of Development (bhāvanā-magga); and the meaning of full awakening of the factors of enlightenment of Fruition (phala). In the same manner as mentioned, the four meanings such as the meaning of causing to awaken (bodhanā) should be understood because of causing those persons, such as Stream-enterers, to awaken. Because they exist as a benefit for the person named 'Bodha' (the Awakened One) due to the sense of awakening of the aforementioned factors of enlightenment, they are called 'belonging to enlightenment' (bodhipakkhiya). The four meanings such as the meaning of belonging to enlightenment of those factors of enlightenment should also be understood.
