The meaning of illuminating (jotanaṭṭha) is by way of insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). By way of the four Path-wisdoms in succession, there are the meanings of ujjotana (lighting up), anujjotana (subsequent lighting up), paṭijjotana (lighting against), and sañjotana (thorough lighting up). Or, the meanings such as jotana are by way of the four Path-wisdoms in succession, and the meaning of sañjotana should be understood by way of Fruition-wisdom.

The eighteen answers (vissajjanā) beginning with patāpana (scorching/shining) are shown by way of the Noble Path (ariya magga). Indeed, for whichever person the Noble Path arises, it makes that person radiant, brilliant, and lustrous; thus it is called patāpana, and its meaning is the meaning of scorching/shining (patāpanaṭṭha). Due to the state of extreme brilliance of that Path, it is the meaning of self-shining (virocanaṭṭha). Because it dries up the defilements, it is the meaning of burning (santāpanaṭṭha). Because it takes the stainless Nibbāna as its object, it is the meaning of being stainless (amalaṭṭha). Because of the absence of associated defilements, it is the meaning of being pure (vimalaṭṭha). Because of the absence of defilements arising from taking an object, it is the meaning of being without stain (nimmalaṭṭha). Alternatively, it should be understood as: the meaning of amala of the Path of Stream-entry; the meaning of vimala of the Paths of Once-returning and Non-returning; and the meaning of nimmala of the Path of Arahantship. Or: the meaning of amala of the Disciple's Path (sāvaka-magga); the meaning of vimala of the Paccekabuddha's Path; and the meaning of nimmala of the Path of the Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha-magga). Because of the absence of the unevenness of defilements, it is the meaning of evenness (samaṭṭha). Because of the sense of abandoning defilements, as in the passage 'by the right penetration of conceit' (sammā mānābhisamayā), it is the meaning of abandoning (samayaṭṭha). Among the five kinds of seclusion (viveka)—namely, seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana), by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), by destruction (samuccheda), by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi), and by escape (nissaraṇa)—it is the meaning of seclusion (vivekaṭṭha) or the meaning of separation (vinābhāvaṭṭha) because it is seclusion by destruction. Because it occurs in Nibbāna, which is seclusion by escape, it is the meaning of faring in seclusion (vivekacariyaṭṭha). Among the five kinds of fading away (virāga), it is the meaning of fading away (virāgaṭṭha) or the meaning of dispassion (virajjanaṭṭha) because it is fading away by destruction. Because it occurs in Nibbāna, which is fading away by escape, it is the meaning of faring in fading away (virāgacariyaṭṭha). Among the five kinds of cessation (nirodha), it is the meaning of cessation (nirodhaṭṭha) because it is cessation by destruction. Because it occurs in Nibbāna, which is the cessation of suffering, it is the meaning of faring in cessation (nirodhacariyaṭṭha). Because it is pariccāga (giving up), pakkhandana (entering into), and vossagga (relinquishment), it is the meaning of relinquishment (vossaggaṭṭha). Indeed, the Noble Path is called relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-vossagga) because it abandons defilements by way of abandonment by destruction (samuccheda-pahāna). It is also called relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga) because it enters into Nibbāna by way of taking Nibbāna as its object. Insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is called relinquishment as giving up because it abandons defilements by way of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), and it is called relinquishment as entering into because it inclines towards Nibbāna. However, that insight is not intended here. Because it is only the Noble Path that acts by abandoning defilements and entering into Nibbāna, it is called the meaning of faring in relinquishment (vossaggacariyaṭṭha). Among the five kinds of liberation (vimutti), it is the meaning of liberation (vimuttaṭṭha) because it is liberation by destruction. Because it occurs in liberation by escape, it is the meaning of faring in liberation (vimutticariyaṭṭha).

Among the four bases of power (iddhipāda) called desire (chanda), energy (vīriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā), the forty answers beginning with desire are shown by way of the four bases of power, making ten for each base of power. The meaning of merely wishing to act is called desire (chanda).
95:
It is the meaning of dispassion (*virāga*) and the meaning of cutting off because it is dispassion by eradication (*samuccheda-virāga*). It is the meaning of the practice of dispassion (*virāgacariya*) because it occurs in Nibbāna, which is dispassion by escape (*nissaraṇa-virāga*). Among the five types of cessation, it is the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*) because it is cessation by eradication (*samuccheda-nirodha*). It is the meaning of the practice of cessation (*nirodhacariya*) because it occurs in Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. It is the meaning of relinquishment (*vossagga*) because of giving up, entering into, and abandoning. Indeed, the Noble Path is 'relinquishment by giving up' (*pariccāga-vossagga*) because it abandons defilements by way of eradication, and it is also 'relinquishment by entering into' (*pakkhandana-vossagga*) because it enters into Nibbāna by making it the object. Insight (*vipassanā*), however, is 'relinquishment by giving up' because it abandons defilements by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), and it is 'relinquishment by entering into' because it enters into Nibbāna by being inclined towards it. That insight is not intended here. It is the meaning of the practice of relinquishment (*vossaggacariya*) because it occurs by way of relinquishment. Among the five types of liberation, it is the meaning of liberation (*vimutta*) because it is liberation by eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*). It is the meaning of the practice of liberation (*vimutticariya*) because it occurs in liberation by escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).

Among the four bases of power (*iddhipāda*)—namely, desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation—forty answers, such as the meaning of desire, are shown by taking ten for each basis of power. The meaning of the desire to act is the meaning of desire (*chanda*). It is the meaning of root (*mūla*) at the time of beginning meditation, with desire as the head. It is the meaning of base (*pāda*) because it is the support for co-nascent states. There is also a variant reading as 'the meaning of step' (*pada*). Because it is a base of power, it is the meaning of predominant (*padhāna*) by way of being the leader. It is the meaning of succeeding (*ijjan*) at the time of exertion. It is the meaning of resolution (*adhimokkha*) because it is associated with faith (*saddhā*). It is the meaning of upholding (*paggaha*) because it is associated with energy (*vīriya*). It is the meaning of establishing (*upaṭṭhāna*) because it is associated with mindfulness (*sati*). It is the meaning of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) because it is associated with concentration (*samādhi*). It is the meaning of seeing (*dassana*) because it is associated with wisdom (*paññā*). The meaning of upholding is the meaning of energy (*vīriya*). It is the meaning of root at the time of beginning meditation, with energy as the head. It is the meaning of upholding because it is energy itself. The meaning of thinking, etc., is the meaning of consciousness (*citta*). It is the meaning of root at the time of beginning meditation, with consciousness as the head. The meaning of examining is the meaning of investigation (*vīmaṃsā*). It is the meaning of root at the time of beginning meditation, with investigation as the head. It is the meaning of seeing because it is investigation itself.

The sixteen answers, such as the meaning of oppression of suffering, are shown by way of the true characteristics of the Four Noble Truths. By the very seeing of the Truth of Suffering, it is the meaning of oppression (*pīḷana*). By seeing the Truth of Origin (*samudaya*) which causes suffering, it is the meaning of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*). By seeing the Truth of the Path (*magga*) which is extremely cool and removes the heat of all defilements, it is the meaning of burning (*santāpa*). By seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha*) which is unchanging, it is the meaning of change (*vipariṇāma*). By the very seeing of the Truth of Origin, it is the meaning of striving (*āyūhana*). By seeing the Truth of Suffering produced by the striving of the Truth of Origin, it is the meaning of cause (*nidāna*). By seeing the Truth of Cessation which is disconnected from defilements, it is the meaning of yoke (*saññoga*). By seeing the Truth of the Path which is the way out, it is the meaning of obstacle (*palibodha*). By the very seeing of the Truth of Cessation, it is the meaning of escape (*nissaraṇa*). By seeing the Truth of Origin which is non-secluded, it is the meaning of seclusion (*viveka*). By seeing the Truth of the Path which is conditioned, it is the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*). By seeing the Truth of Suffering which is like poison, it is the meaning of the deathless (*amata*).
96: By seeing the Truth of the Path itself, the meaning of release (niyyānaṭṭha) of the Truth of the Path becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of the Origin, which is not the cause of Nibbāna, the meaning of cause (hetaṭṭha) of the Truth of the Path becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of Cessation, which is very difficult to see, the meaning of seeing (dassanaṭṭha) of the Truth of the Path becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of Suffering, which is like a destitute person, the meaning of predominance (ādhipateyyaṭṭha), which is like a noble family, becomes manifest. Thus, by seeing each respective truth and by seeing the other truths, the four characteristics or meanings for each single truth have been taught. Twelve answers, beginning with tathaṭṭha, are presented by way of the twelve terms that encompass all phenomena. Therein, tathaṭṭha means the sense of being according to reality. Anattaṭṭha means the sense of being devoid of a self. Saccaṭṭha means the sense of being non-deceptive. Paṭivedhaṭṭha means the sense of being that which should be penetrated. Abhijānanaṭṭha means the sense of being that which should be directly known. Parijānanaṭṭha means the sense of being that which should be fully understood through the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) and the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). Dhammaṭṭha means the sense of bearing its own nature and so forth. Dhatuṭṭha means the sense of being empty of a soul or being and so forth. Ñātaṭṭha means the sense of being capable of being known. Sacchikiriyāṭṭha means the sense of being that which should be realized. Phassanaṭṭha means the sense of being that which should be touched by knowledge. Abhisamayaṭṭha means the sense of being that which should be properly attained through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), or the sense of being that which should be obtained by knowledge. For even 'obtaining' (paṭilābha) is called 'attainment' (abhisamaya), as in the passage 'the wise one through the attainment of the goal' (atthābhisamayā dhīro) and so forth. Seven answers, beginning with nekkhamma, are presented by way of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). Nekkhamma is non-greed, which is the opposite of sensual desire (kāmacchanda). Āloka-saññā is the perception of the sign of light, which is the opposite of sloth and torpor (thina-middha). Avikkhepa is concentration (samādhi), which is the opposite of restlessness (uddhacca). Dhamma-vavatthāna is knowledge (ñāṇa), which is the opposite of doubt (vicikiccā). Ñāṇa is knowledge, which is the opposite of ignorance (avijjā). Pāmojja is joy (pīti), which is the opposite of discontent (arati). Eight answers, beginning with the first jhāna, are presented by way of the fine-material and immaterial attainments. Below, however, immediately after the fine-material attainments, the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) were presented because of their connection with the fine-material jhānas. Insights beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) are presented by way of the eighteen great insights (mahā-vipassanā) in the preliminary stage of the supramundane path. Below, however, only seven contemplations suitable for application to the aggregate of form and so forth were taught. But here, all of them are taught. If it is asked, 'Why were the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa) and the contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa) not taught?'—it is because through the power of those two knowledges, the eighteen insights such as the contemplation of impermanence are accomplished; thus, when these eighteen are taught, those two are also already taught. Or, because those two cannot occur without the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, when these eighteen are taught, those two are also already taught. Khayānupassanā (contemplation of destruction) is the knowledge that contemplates the destruction of the present aggregate of form and so forth, and the knowledge that contemplates the destruction of the mind and mental factors that have that destruction as their object immediately after the knowledge contemplating that destruction. Vayānupassanā (contemplation of fall) is the knowledge that contemplates the destruction of past and future aggregates, following the sequence of the knowledge contemplating the destruction of present aggregates. Vipariṇāmānupassanā (contemplation of change) is the knowledge that contemplates the change of all aggregates, thinking that all past, future, and present aggregates are of a nature to change, because of the completion of the reflection on the cessation of the five aggregates called dissolution (bhaṅga).
97:
The knowledge that sees the dissolution of the present aggregates such as the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha), and immediately following that, the knowledge that sees the dissolution of the consciousness and mental factors that take that dissolution as their object (is called the contemplation of destruction - khayānupassanā). Contemplation of vanishing (vayānupassanā) is the knowledge that sees the dissolution of past and future aggregates by following the sequence of the knowledge that sees the dissolution of present aggregates. Contemplation of change (vipariṇāmānupassanā) is the knowledge that sees the change of all aggregates—past, future, and present—because of the completion of attention to the cessation known as dissolution (bhaṅga), realizing that all aggregates are subject to change.

Signless contemplation (animittānupassanā) is so called because, for one who sees the change of all formations (saṅkhāra) and practices insight through impermanence (anicca), that very contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) removes the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta) that one used to cling to; thus, it is signless. Desireless contemplation (appaṇihitānupassanā) is so called because the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) that occurs immediately after the contemplation of impermanence removes the craving that longs for pleasure (sukha); thus, there is no longing (paṇidhi).

Emptiness contemplation (suññatānupassanā) is so called because the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) that occurs immediately after the contemplation of suffering removes the perception of self (atta) by seeing the emptiness of self. Insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā) is the insight that arises by repeatedly seeing the dissolution (bhaṅga) of formations and practicing insight through impermanence, etc., taking the collection of formations as empty of self, realizing: "Only formations dissolve; there is only the death of formations; there is no other person or being besides formations." This insight is both higher wisdom (adhipaññā) and insight into the characteristics of phenomena (dhamma); therefore, it is called "insight into phenomena through higher wisdom."

Knowledge and vision according to reality (yathābhūtañāṇadassana) is the knowledge of the appearance as terror (bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇa) that arises by repeatedly seeing dissolution and realizing: "Formations are accompanied by fear." Contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) is the knowledge that sees the faults in all states of existence, etc., arising through the power of the knowledge of the appearance as terror. According to the teaching: "The wisdom in the appearance as terror, the knowledge of danger, and the knowledge of disenchantment—these states are one in meaning, only the phrasing is different," when the knowledge of the appearance as terror and the contemplation of danger are taught, the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā) is also taught. However, because it was taught as the fourth in the earlier section, it is not repeated here.

Contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā) is the insight knowledge of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, known as the contemplation of reflection, which arises through the power of the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa) and acts as a means for liberation. According to the teaching: "The knowledge of desire for deliverance, the knowledge of the contemplation of reflection, and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations—these states are one in meaning, only the phrasing is different," when the contemplation of reflection is taught, the knowledge of desire for deliverance and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa) are also taught. Contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā) is the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa) that arises through the power of conformity knowledge (anulomañāṇa). Since change-of-lineage knowledge is perfected by conformity knowledge, when change-of-lineage knowledge is taught, conformity knowledge is also taught. In this way (if the eighteen great insights are stated in order, it is consistent with the Indriya-kathā Pali which will come later).
98:
The explanation of the sequence of the eighteen great insights (mahā-vipassanā) is consistent with the Pali texts. As stated in the Indriya-kathā:

"In the preliminary stage, by means of the five faculties, through the power of the first jhāna, the five faculties are liberated; in the first jhāna, by means of the five faculties, through the power of the second jhāna, the five faculties are liberated"—in this manner, the faculties are taught in successive order up to the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, the eighteen great insights in the stated order are consistent with the Pali texts.

In the Visuddhimagga, however, it is stated:

"Khayānupassanā is the knowledge of one who sees destruction as impermanent in the sense of being destroyed, having dissected the compactness (ghana). Vipariṇāmānupassanā is the seeing of the occurrence in another way, having transcended each respective limitation by way of the heptads of materiality (rūpa-sattaka), the heptads of immateriality (nāma-sattaka), and so forth. Or, it is the seeing of the change of what has arisen in two ways: by aging (jarā) and by death (maraṇa). Yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana is the discerning of mind and matter (nāmarūpa) along with their causes." This statement seems to contradict that Pali text.

It is said that Vivaṭṭanānupassanā consists of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) and conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa). This statement also seems to contradict the Pali text. In the Cariyā-kathā, however:

"For the purpose of the contemplation of impermanence, the functional (kiriya) indeterminate (abyākata) adverting (āvajjana) is called consciousness-behavior (viññāṇa-cariyā). The contemplation of impermanence is called knowledge-behavior (ñāṇa-cariyā). ... For the purpose of the contemplation of reflection, the functional indeterminate adverting is called consciousness-behavior. The contemplation of reflection is called knowledge-behavior." Thus, for whichever knowledge a separate adverting is obtained, the separate adverting for that respective knowledge is taught.

In the case of Vivaṭṭanānupassanā, however, it is taught as "Vivaṭṭanānupassanā is knowledge-behavior" without mentioning an adverting. If the knowledge of equanimity towards formations and conformity knowledge were called Vivaṭṭanānupassanā, then adverting should have been mentioned for them, as adverting can arise in those knowledges; however, adverting was not mentioned for those knowledges. But for the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), separately...
99:
Because the occurrence of gotrabhū (change-of-lineage) is only in the thought-process containing the anuloma-āvajjana (conformity-adverting), there is no separate adverting for gotrabhū-ñāṇa. Therefore, since adverting is not mentioned for the purpose of vivaṭṭanānupassanā (contemplation of turning away), it is appropriate to call gotrabhū-ñāṇa itself "vivaṭṭanānupassanā".

The eight answers beginning with the Path of Stream-entry are explained by way of the supramundane paths and fruits. Entering the stream, which is the Noble Path, is called sotāpatti. Since that sotāpatti itself is a path, it is called the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). The benefit of the Path of Stream-entry is called the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Because it is attained, it is called an attainment (samāpatti). Since the Fruit of Stream-entry itself is an attainment, it is called the Attainment of the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala-samāpatti). Because one returns to this sense-sphere world only once by way of rebirth, one is called a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī). His path is the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga). The benefit of the Once-returner is the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala). Because one does not return to the sense-sphere world by way of rebirth, one is called a Non-returner (anāgāmī). His path is the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). The benefit of the Non-returner is the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). He is called Arahaṃ because he is far from defilements, because the enemies (defilements) have been slain, because the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed, because he has no secrecy in doing evil, and because he is worthy of receiving requisites and so on. The state of an Arahant is arahatta. What is that state of an Arahant? It is the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). The cause of the Fruit of Arahantship is the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Since Arahantship itself is the fruit, it is called the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala).

The thirty-three answers beginning with "saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhaṭṭhena" (the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution) and ending with "saccaṃ tathaṭṭhena" (truth in the sense of reality) are explained. These are identical to the thirty-three answers explained below, such as "saddhindriyassa adhimokkhaṭṭho". The difference is that in the former method, the meanings were explained by way of the dhammas, whereas in this latter method, the dhammas are explained by way of the meanings. The difference between the four answers beginning with "samatho avikkhepaṭṭhena" (calm in the sense of non-distraction) and the four answers explained below such as "samathassa avikkhepaṭṭho" should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

The eight answers beginning with "saṃvaraṭṭhena" (in the sense of restraint) are explained by way of the dhammas starting from virtue (sīla) and ending with powers (bala). Sīlavisuddhi (purification of virtue) refers to the fourfold virtue such as the very pure pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint according to the Patimokkha), because it cleanses the stain of immorality. Cittavisuddhi (purification of mind) refers to the eight attainments along with access concentration (upacāra). Here, concentration (samādhi) is referred to by the head-term "mind" (citta). It is called purification of mind because it cleanses the stains of the mind. Diṭṭhivisuddhi (purification of view) is the wisdom that sees mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa) according to their true nature, because it cleanses the seven types of stains of view. Muttaṭṭhena (in the sense of being released) means being released from defilements by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) and in the sense of being resolved upon the object. Vimokkha (liberation) refers to tadaṅga-vimokkha (liberation by substitution of opposites). Vijjā paṭivedhaṭṭhena (knowledge in the sense of penetration) means the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) is called vijjā in the sense of penetrating and knowing past existences.
100:
Divine-eye knowledge (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) is called vijjā in the sense of penetrating and knowing the passing away and rebirth of beings. The knowledge occurring at the destruction of the taints (āsava) is called vijjā in the sense of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. Paṭivedhaṭṭha (the sense of penetration) simply means the sense of knowing. Regarding "liberation (vimutti) in the sense of relinquishment", it is called Fruit-liberation (phala-vimutti) because of being liberated from those defilements that have been completely relinquished by the respective paths. "Knowledge in the destruction [of defilements] in the sense of eradication" refers to the knowledge in the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of defilements in the sense of completely eradicating them. "Knowledge in non-arising in the sense of tranquillization" refers to the knowledge in the Noble Fruit which arises at the end of the non-arising of those defilements abandoned by the respective paths, having reached the state of non-arising by way of rebirth because the effort (vyāpāra) known as the function of the path has been tranquillized.

The nine answers beginning with "zeal (chanda) has the sense of root" are explained by way of the beginning, middle, and end of the Noble Path. "Zeal has the sense of root" means that the desire-to-act (kattukamyatā-chanda) for wholesome states is the sense of root because it is the root cause for the practice of the path and the completion of the path and fruit. "Attention (manasikāra) has the sense of originating" means that wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra) is the sense of originating (samuṭṭhānaṭṭha) because it originates all wholesome states. "Contact (phassa) has the sense of collation" is said because feeling (vedanā) is the primary cause for the arising of craving (taṇhā), and when craving is abandoned, it is abandoned specifically through the full understanding of feeling. Furthermore, contact is the primary cause of that feeling; when that contact is fully understood, feeling is also fully understood. Therefore, among the seven objects to be directly known (abhiññeyya-vatthu), contact is mentioned first. That contact is to be directly known in the sense of collation (samodhānaṭṭha) because it is known by way of its own cause, which is the meeting of the triad [base, object, consciousness], and because it is said that "the meeting of the triad is its manifestation". Some teachers, however, say that "knowledge-contact is [what is meant by] contact".

Feeling (vedanā) is said to be directly known in the sense of convergence (samosaraṇaṭṭha) because it makes the mind and mental factors follow its own will and converges into those mental factors, or because it converges only into the mental continuum. Some teachers say: "All things to be fully understood converge in feelings; when feelings are fully understood, all causes of craving are fully understood. Why is that? Because all craving arises due to the cause of feeling. Therefore, feeling is to be directly known in the sense of convergence." Just as the pinnacle of a peaked house (kūṭāgāra-kaṇṇikā) which holds all the rafters together is the chief, so concentration (samādhi) is the chief and leader of wholesome states because it binds together the mind and mental factors. Therefore, it is said that concentration has the sense of being the chief (pamukhaṭṭha). There is also a variant reading "pāmukhaṭṭha". For one who develops calm and insight, mindfulness (sati) is the chief in terms of establishing the object...
101:
When an object is established through mindfulness, all wholesome states accomplish their respective functions; therefore, it is said that mindfulness should be known in the sense of predominance (ādhipateyyaṭṭha). Wisdom should be known in the sense of being superior to that (taduttaraṭṭha) means that the wisdom associated with the Noble Path should be known in the sense of being superior to and more excellent than those wholesome states. Alternatively, it is called 'taduttara' because it transcends or overcomes the defilements or the round of rebirth (saṃsāravaṭṭa) because of those wholesome states; the meaning of that transcending is 'taduttaraṭṭha'. It should be known by that sense. There is also a variant reading 'tatuttaraṭṭha', which means the sense of being superior to that.

Liberation (vimutti) should be known in the sense of essence (sāraṭṭha) means that liberation, which is the fruition of arahantship (arahattaphala), is called essence (sāra) because it is firm and stable by way of non-decline. It is also called essence because there is no other fruition to be sought beyond that fruition of arahantship. That liberation should be known by that sense of essence. Nibbāna, which is plunged into the deathless (amatogadha), is called 'amata' (deathless) because there is no 'mata' (death) in that Nibbāna. It is also called 'amata' (medicine/ambrosia) because it is the opposite of the poison of defilements. It is called 'ogadha' (foundation/plunged into) because it is the standing place for beings through its realization. It is called 'nibbāna' because it is 'nibbuta' (extinguished) as it is the cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirth. It is also called 'nibbāna' because there is no 'vāna' (weaving/craving) known as craving in that Nibbāna. Since that Nibbāna is the end of the Dispensation (Sāsana), it should be known in the sense of the end (pariyosānaṭṭha). Thus, in this Exposition on What Should Be Known by Higher Knowledge (Abhiññeyyaniddesa), there are seven thousand seven hundred and forty answers (vissajjanā).

Now, regarding these states thus pointed out, the conclusion is made: "Whatever states are known by higher knowledge, those states are known (fully)." It means they are known by making that conclusion evident. It is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing those states in the manner described. It is called 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of knowing specifically (pajānana). By the words "By that it is said..." and so on, the questions asked at the beginning are shown as concluded. For that reason, it means: "The inclining of the mind to listen, saying 'these states should be known by higher knowledge,' and the wisdom of knowing those states specifically, is called knowledge based on learning (suta-maya-ñāṇa)."

## In the Saddhammappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga,
## the Explanation of the Exposition on What Should Be Known by Higher Knowledge is finished.
## Explanation of the Exposition on What Should Be Fully Understood

In the Exposition on What Should Be Fully Understood (Pariññeyyaniddesa), although the three types of full understanding—full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariñā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariñā), and full understanding as abandonment (pahāna-pariñā)—are included by the word 'pariññā', here only full understanding by investigation is intended. This is because 'ñāta-pariñā' was already mentioned below by the word 'abhiññeyyā' (to be known by higher knowledge), and 'pahāna-pariñā' will be mentioned above by the word 'pahātabbā' (to be abandoned). Contact (phassa) pertaining to the three planes of existence, which is the cause of the taints (āsava) and the cause of clinging (upādāna)...
102:
"Yo" (which) refers to contact (phassa) pertaining to the three planes of existence, which is the cause of both the taints (āsava) and the objects of clinging (upādāna). That contact in the three planes is called 'sāsava' (subject to taints) because it occurs together with the taints that take itself as an object. It is called 'upādāniya' (subject to clinging) because it approaches the state of being an object and is beneficial to the objects of clinging through the bond of clinging. Because when contact is fully understood through the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), the remaining mental states (arūpa-dhamma) are fully understood starting with contact, and the physical states (rūpa-dhamma) are also fully understood following those mental states; therefore, only contact is mentioned. In this same way, it should be applied to the remaining states as appropriate.

"Mentality" (nāma) refers to the four mental aggregates and Nibbāna. "Form" (rūpa) refers to the four great elements and the twenty-four types of derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) based on the four great elements. The four mental aggregates are called 'nāma' in the sense of bending towards an object. Indeed, they bend towards the object. All mental states are also called 'nāma' in the sense of causing to bend. The four aggregates cause each other to bend towards the object. Nibbāna, by way of being the object-predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya), causes faultless states to bend towards itself. Matter is called 'rūpa' in the sense of being deformed by cold, heat, etc., by way of the continuity (of matter). The sense of being deformed means the sense of being disturbed. Indeed, the collection of phenomena that can be impacted by cold, heat, etc., by way of the transformation of the continuity, is called 'rūpa'. Here, however, by 'nāma', only mundane mentality is intended. Matter, on the other hand, is invariably mundane.

"The three feelings" (vedanā) are pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These feelings are only mundane. "Nutriments" (āhāra) means causes. Causes are called nutriments because they bring (āharanti) their own results. There are four nutriments: physical food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), contact (phassāhāra), mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇāhāra). It is called 'kabaḷīkāra' because it is made into mouthfuls by way of its physical substance. It is called 'āhāra' because it is swallowed. This is a name for the nutritive essence (ojā) based on substances such as cooked rice and gruel. That nutritive essence is called 'āhāra' because it brings the octad of matter with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamaka-rūpa). The sixfold contact, such as eye-contact, is called 'āhāra' because it brings the three feelings. It is called 'manosañcetanā' because it is the volition of the mind and not of a being. It is like the term 'one-pointedness of mind' (cittekaggatā). Alternatively, it is called 'manosañcetanā' because it is volition associated with the mind, like a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses (ājaññaratha). It refers to wholesome and unwholesome volition in the three planes. That mundane wholesome and unwholesome volition is called 'āhāra' because it brings the three types of existence. "Consciousness" (viññāṇa) refers to the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness. That rebirth-linking consciousness is called 'āhāra' because it brings mentality and matter at the time of rebirth-linking. "Aggregates of clinging" (upādānakkhandhā) means the aggregates that are the objects of clinging; the middle term (gocara) should be understood as elided. Or, the aggregates produced by the four types of clinging are called 'upādānakkhandhā'. For example...
103:
Just as a fire is named after grass or chaff (the aggregates are called clinging-aggregates because they arise from clinging). Or, like a man associated with a king, the aggregates associated with clinging are called clinging-aggregates (upādānakkhandhā). Or, like a tree that is the source of flowers or fruits, the aggregates that arise from clinging are called clinging-aggregates. There are four types of clinging (upādāna): clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna), and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). In terms of meaning, clinging refers to firm grasping. There are five clinging-aggregates: the clinging-aggregate of form (rūpupādānakkhandha), the clinging-aggregate of feeling (vedanupādānakkhandha), the clinging-aggregate of perception (saññupādānakkhandha), the clinging-aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārupādānakkhandha), and the clinging-aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇupādānakkhandha).

The six internal sense bases (ajjhattikāni āyatanāni) are: the eye base (cakkhāyatana), the ear base (sotāyatana), the nose base (ghānāyatana), the tongue base (jivhāyatana), the body base (kāyāyatana), and the mind base (manāyatana).

What are the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo)? Regarding these seven stations of consciousness, the Blessed One taught as follows:

"Monks, there are beings with diversity of body and diversity of perception, such as human beings, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation (vinipātikā). This is the first station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings with diversity of body and unity of perception, such as the devas of the Brahma-group (brahmakāyikā) who are first reborn [through the first absorption]. This is the second station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings with unity of body and diversity of perception, such as the Ābhassara devas. This is the third station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings with unity of body and unity of perception, such as the Subhakiṇhā devas. This is the fourth station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' have reached the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). This is the fifth station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' have reached the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). This is the sixth station of consciousness."
104:
"Monks, there are beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing,' have reached the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This is the seventh station of consciousness. These, monks, are the seven stations of consciousness."

'Stations of consciousness' (viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo) refers to the four mental aggregates associated with rebirth-consciousness, which serve as the stations for rebirth-consciousness. In that text, the word 'seyyathāpi' is a particle used in the sense of an illustration. 'Humans' (manussā) means that among the infinite number of humans in infinite world systems, no two people are exactly alike in terms of complexion, shape, and so forth. Even those who are similar in complexion or shape are still dissimilar in their manner of looking, glancing, and so on; therefore, they are called 'diverse in body' (nānattakāya). Their rebirth-perception (paṭisandhisaññā) can be triple-rooted (tihetuka), double-rooted (duhetuka), or rootless (ahetuka); therefore, they are called 'diverse in perception' (nānattasaññī). 'Some devas' refers to the inhabitants of the six sense-sphere deva realms. Among those devas, the bodies of some are blue in color, while others are yellow and so forth. Their rebirth-perception is either triple-rooted or double-rooted, but never rootless. 'Some beings in the states of deprivation' (vinipātikā) refers to those such as the yakkhinī mother of Punabbasu, the mother of Piyaṅkara, Phussamittā, and Dhammaguttā, who are freed from rebirth in the four lower realms, as well as other mansion-dwelling ghosts (vemānika peta). For these beings, their bodies are diverse due to colors such as white, black, or the color of a bedbug's back, and due to being thin, fat, short, or tall. Like humans, their rebirth-perception is also diverse, being triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless. However, unlike devas, they do not possess great power; they live with little power like lonely poor people, suffering from the difficulty of obtaining food and clothing. Some suffer during the dark fortnight and are happy during the bright fortnight. Thus, because they have fallen away from a mass of happiness, they are called 'vinipātika'. Among those beings, for those with triple-rooted rebirth, the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) is possible, as in the case of Piyaṅkara's mother and others.

'Brahmakāyikā' refers to the Brahma-pārisajja, Brahma-purohita, and Mahābrahmā. 'First reborn' means all of them are reborn through the first absorption (jhāna). The Brahma-pārisajja are born from a limited degree of the first absorption. The Brahma-purohita are born from a middling degree, and their bodies are more expansive. The Mahābrahmā are born from a superior degree, and their bodies are extremely expansive. Thus, they are called 'diverse in body and uniform in perception' (nānattakāya ekattasaññī) because of the difference in the size of their bodies and the uniformity of their perception through the power of the first absorption. Just as these Brahmas are described, so too are the beings in the four woeful states 'diverse in body and uniform in perception'. Indeed, in the hell realms, some beings have bodies as large as a gāvuta (approx. 2 miles), while others...
105:
Some beings have a physical form (attabhāva) of half a yojana; some have three gāvutas; but Devadatta came to have a physical form of a hundred yojanas. Among animals, some are small and some are large. In the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), some are sixty cubits tall, some are eighty cubits tall; some are beautiful and some are ugly. The Asuras named Kālakañcikā are also like those petas. Indeed, in this realm of petas, those named Dīghapiṭṭhika are even sixty yojanas in size. However, the rebirth-perception (paṭisandhi-saññā) for all beings in the woeful states is only the unwholesome resultant rootless (akusala-vipāka ahetuka) consciousness. Therefore, beings in the woeful states are also designated as "those with diverse bodies but uniform perception."

Ābhassara means that just as a flame emerges from a torch, the radiance from the bodies of these Brahmās breaks off and falls away repeatedly as if flowing out; thus they are called Ābhassara (Radiant). Among those second jhāna Brahmās, those who developed the two jhānas—the second and third in the fivefold method—to a minor (paritta) degree are born as Parittābhā. Those who developed them to a medium (majjhima) degree are born as Appamāṇābhā. Those who developed them to a superior (paṇīta) degree are born as Ābhassara. In this context, however, all those second jhāna Brahmās are included under the highest classification. Indeed, the bodies of all those second jhāna Brahmās have a uniform diffusion (ekavipphāra). Their rebirth-perception, however, is diverse, being either with only sustained thought (vicāra-matta) without initial thought (vitakka), or without both initial and sustained thought.

Subhakiṇha means pervaded or strewn with beauty. The meaning is that they are a solid mass of beautiful bodily radiance. For these Subhakiṇha Brahmās, radiance does not break off and emerge as it does for the Ābhassara Brahmās. By virtue of the minor, medium, and superior levels of the third jhāna in the fourfold method, or the fourth jhāna in the fivefold method, they are born as Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha Brahmās. Thus, all those third jhāna Brahmās should be understood as having uniform bodies and uniform perception through the perception associated with the fourth jhāna. The Vehapphala Brahmās also belong to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). The non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), due to the absence of consciousness, are not included here in the seven stations of consciousness, but they are included in the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

The Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Brahmās stand on the side of the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa); they do not exist at all times. They do not appear in the world during a void (suñña) interval of a hundred thousand aeons or even an incalculable aeon without a Buddha. They appear only when Buddhas arise within a period of sixteen thousand aeons. They are like the temporary encampment (khandhāvāra) of the Blessed One who has turned the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, they do not belong to the seven stations of consciousness, nor to the nine abodes of beings. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said, "Sāriputta, that abode of beings is not easily found which I have not previously inhabited in this long journey, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas" (M. Ni. 1.160). Based on this sutta, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās also...
106:
The Elder Mahāsīva says that [the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās] resort to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings. That statement is accepted because it is not contradicted by the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.

In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), just as perception is extremely subtle, consciousness is also extremely subtle, and is thus called neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the seven stations of consciousness.

## Eight Worldly Conditions (Aṭṭha Lokadhamma)
Gain (lābha), loss (alābha), fame (yasa), obscurity (ayasa), blame (nindā), praise (pasaṃsā), happiness (sukha), and pain (dukkha). These eight are called worldly conditions (lokadhamma) because they are the nature of the world that does not cease as long as the world's process exists. There is no being who is free from these worldly conditions; they occur even to the Buddhas. As it was said:

"Monks, these eight worldly conditions follow the world, and the world follows these eight worldly conditions. Which eight? Gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, happiness and pain. Monks, indeed these eight worldly conditions follow the world, and the world follows these eight worldly conditions."

In that passage, 'follow' (anuparivattanti) means they follow and bind continuously; they do not let go, and they do not recede from the world. 'Gain' (lābha) refers to the acquisition of the four requisites like robes for a monk, and wealth, grain, etc., for a householder. The non-acquisition of those same things is 'loss' (alābha). When it is said 'non-gain is loss,' it should be understood as a thing to be fully known (pariññeyya) lest the meaning be unclear. 'Fame' (yasa) means having a retinue. The non-acquisition of that is 'obscurity' (ayasa). 'Blame' (nindā) means speaking of faults. 'Praise' (pasaṃsā) means speaking of virtues. 'Happiness' (sukha) refers to the bodily and mental pleasure of those in the sense-sphere. 'Pain' (dukkha) refers to the bodily and mental pain of worldlings, Stream-enters, and Once-returners; for Non-returners and Arahants, it is only bodily pain (kāyika-dukkha).

## Nine Abodes of Beings (Nava Sattāvāsa)
This means the dwelling places or habitats of beings. Those places are simply the aggregates (khandha) as manifested. What are the nine? This was stated by the Blessed One:

"Monks, there are these nine abodes of beings. Which nine? Monks, there are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some fallen hungry ghosts (vinipātika peta). This is the first abode of beings. Monks, there are beings with diverse bodies but uniform perception, such as the Brahmakāyika devas born in the first jhāna realm. This is the second abode of beings. Monks, there are beings with uniform bodies but diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhassara Brahmās. This is the third abode of beings. Monks, there are beings with uniform bodies and uniform perceptions, such as the Subhakiṇha Brahmās. This is the fourth abode of beings. Monks, there are beings without perception and without feeling, such as the non-percipient (asaññasatta) Brahmās. This is the fifth abode of beings. Monks, in every respect..."
107:
Some are devas, and some are vinipātika spirits (petas). This is the first abode of beings (sattāvāsa). Bhikkhus, there are beings diverse in body and unified in perception, such as the brahmakāyika devas who are first reborn [in that plane]. This is the second abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings unified in body and diverse in perception, such as the ābhassara devas. This is the third abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings unified in body and unified in perception, such as the subhakiṇha devas. This is the fourth abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings who are perceptionless and non-experiencing, such as the asaññasatta devas. This is the fifth abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [attain] 'space is infinite' and reach the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). This is the sixth abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, [attain] 'consciousness is infinite' and reach the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). This is the seventh abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [attain] 'there is nothing' and reach the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This is the eighth abode of beings. Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, reach the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). This is the ninth abode of beings. Bhikkhus, these are the nine abodes of beings. 

The ten bases (āyatanas) are: the eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the flavor-base, the body-base, and the tangible-base. The mind-base and the mental-object-base are not included here because they are mixed with supramundane states. In these ten explanations, by the power of insight (vipassanā)...
108:
Full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā) is stated. However, in discourses such as 'Bhikkhus, all should be fully understood,' tīraṇapariññā is stated by virtue of the attainment of these states: the three faculties starting with the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya); the sense of realization and the sense of development of the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path; the sense of penetration of those very truths; the fifteen senses such as the sense of escape from suffering and the sense of non-arising (anuppāda); the thirty-one senses such as the sense of grasping (pariggahaṭṭha); the three senses such as the sense of further penetration; the eight path factors; the two senses such as 'the sense of the subsiding of efforts' (payogānaṃ paṭippassaddhaṭṭha); the sense of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata); the two senses such as the sense of emergence (vuṭṭhānaṭṭha); the sense of leading out (niyyānaṭṭha); the three senses such as the sense of subsequent awakening (anubujjhanaṭṭha); the three senses such as the sense of subsequent enlightenment (anubodhanaṭṭha); the three senses such as the sense of the factors of subsequent enlightenment; the four senses such as the sense of illumination (ujjotanaṭṭha); the eighteen senses such as the sense of burning away (patapanaṭṭha); the nine senses such as the insight of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā); and the attainment of these states: the knowledge of destruction (khayeñāṇa), the knowledge of non-arising (anuppādeñāṇa), wisdom, liberation, and Nibbāna. For the remaining states, it should be understood that tīraṇapariññā is stated by virtue of insight and by virtue of attainment as appropriate.

For one who strives for the sake of attaining whichever states, those states are attained. Thus, because of the sense of completing the task, tīraṇapariññā is stated, meaning those states are both 'fully known' (pariññāta) and 'investigated' (tīrita). This is because when the task of effort is completed, those states are attained. Some teachers, however, say: 'Full understanding as the known (ñātapariññā) refers to states that do not reach insight.' That statement is not good because ñātapariññā has already been mentioned in the Exposition of Things to be Directly Known (abhiññeyyaniddesa). The phrase 'they are both fully known and investigated' means that those very states which have been attained are called 'fully known' and 'investigated.' Thus, the meaning of 'fully known' is stated by virtue of the sense of completing the task.

Now, in order to show that same meaning by applying it to each state by virtue of attainment and concluding at the end, he said 'Renunciation' (nekkhammaṃ), etc. All that should be understood according to the method previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Things to be Fully Understood is finished.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Things to be Abandoned

In the Exposition of Things to be Abandoned, 'the conceit I am' (asmimāna) is the conceit 'I am' that occurs in the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), such as the aggregate of form. When that conceit is abandoned, one is said to have reached Arahantship (or to have attained the fruit of Arahantship).
109:
## 
Even though lust for form (rūpa-rāga) and so forth exist, the mention of only the conceit 'I am' (asmi-māna) without mentioning the remaining states should be understood as being due to its resemblance to wrong view (diṭṭhi) and its grossness. Ignorance (avijjā), according to the Suttanta method, is non-knowledge regarding the four bases such as suffering (dukkha); according to the Abhidhamma method, it is non-knowledge regarding the eight bases including the prior end (pubbanta) and so forth. Regarding this, it is said: "Therein, what is ignorance? It is non-knowledge regarding suffering, non-knowledge regarding the origin of suffering (samudaya), non-knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering (nirodha), non-knowledge regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering (magga), non-knowledge regarding the prior end, non-knowledge regarding the posterior end (aparanta), non-knowledge regarding both the prior and posterior ends, and non-knowledge regarding the phenomena of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), namely, specific conditionality (idappaccayatā)."

Craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) is the longing for existences such as the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava). As it is taught: "Therein, what is craving for existence? It is the desire for existence, lust for existence, delight in existence, craving for existence, affection for existence, fever for existence, infatuation with existence, and obsession with existence in regard to existences."

The three cravings are craving for sense pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). Their detailed explanation is given in the Abhidhamma as follows: "Therein, what is craving for existence? Lust accompanied by the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) ... the intense lust of the mind is called craving for existence. Therein, what is craving for non-existence? Lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) ... the intense lust of the mind is called craving for non-existence. The remaining craving is called craving for sense pleasures. Therein, what is craving for sense pleasures? Lust associated with the sense-sphere element (kāma-dhātu) ... the intense lust of the mind is called craving for sense pleasures. Therein, what is craving for existence? Lust associated with the fine-material element (rūpa-dhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpa-dhātu) ... Therein, what is craving for non-existence? Lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism ..." so it is stated.

In the Commentary, however, it is said: "Lust for the five cords of sense pleasure is called craving for sense pleasures. Lust for fine-material and immaterial existences, delight in meditative absorption (jhāna), lust accompanied by the view of eternalism, and longing by the power of existence are called craving for existence. Lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism is called craving for non-existence." This is the application according to the Dasuttara Sutta method. According to the Saṅgīti Sutta method and the Abhidhamma method: "Another three cravings are craving for sense pleasures, craving for fine-material existence (rūpa-taṇhā), and craving for immaterial existence (arūpa-taṇhā). Yet another three cravings are craving for fine-material existence, craving for immaterial existence ..."
110:
## 
"... and craving for cessation (nirodha-taṇhā)"—the cravings thus taught are also appropriate here (among the three cravings). Among those (six) cravings, five cravings are associated with the sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element. The final one (craving for cessation) is accompanied by the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

The four floods (ogha) are the flood of sense pleasure (kāmogha), the flood of existence (bhavogha), the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), and the flood of ignorance (avijjogha). They are called floods because they cause the person in whom they exist to sink and drown in the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). These are powerful defilements. The flood in regard to sense pleasures, known as the cords of sense pleasure, is the flood of sense pleasure. This is another name for craving for sense pleasures (kāma-taṇhā). The flood in regard to the two types of existence, known as fine-material (rūpa) and immaterial (arūpa), both by way of kamma and by way of rebirth (upapatti), is the flood of existence. This is another name for craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). Wrong view (diṭṭhi) itself is a flood, hence the flood of views. This is the name for views such as "The world is eternal." Ignorance (avijjā) itself is a flood, hence the flood of ignorance. This is the name for non-knowledge (moha) regarding the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) and so forth.

The five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of ill will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca-nīvaraṇa), and the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa). They are called hindrances because they obstruct and envelop the mind. They are called 'kāma' because they are desired; these are the five cords of sense pleasure. Desire for the cords of sense pleasure is sensual desire (kāmacchanda). Alternatively, it is called 'kāma' because it desires; defilement-kāma itself is the desire. It is called sensual desire because it is neither the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) nor the desire for the Dhamma (dhamma-chanda). This is a name for craving for sense pleasures. By that (anger), the mind reaches a state of putrefaction, or because it destroys the practice of discipline (vinaya), the perfection of form, and welfare and happiness, it is called ill will (byāpāda). This is a name for anger (dosa). Stiffness of the mind is sloth (thina); stiffness of the mental factors is torpor (middha). It means weariness due to lack of energy and lack of capability. Sloth is the mind's lack of energy, and torpor is the unworkability of the mental factors; the combination of these two is called sloth and torpor. The state of a restless mind is restlessness (uddhacca), meaning lack of tranquility. This is a name for mental distraction (vikkhepa). A bad deed is called 'kukata'; the state of a consciousness possessing that bad deed is remorse (kukkucca), meaning the state of performing a censurable act. This is a name for subsequent regret (pacchānutāpa). It is called doubt (vicikicchā) because it is devoid of the wisdom that can remedy it, meaning lack of wisdom. Alternatively, it is called doubt because one becomes weary when investigating the nature of things. This is a name for uncertainty (saṃsaya) regarding the Buddha and so forth. Sensual desire itself is a hindrance, hence the hindrance of sensual desire. The same applies to the remaining hindrances.

There is also a variant reading "cha dhammā" or "chaddhammā". The six groups of craving (taṇhā-kāya) are craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā), craving for sounds (sadda-taṇhā), craving for smells (gandha-taṇhā), craving for tastes (rasa-taṇhā), craving for tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-taṇhā), and craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā). Craving for forms is craving for forms. That same craving for forms is called a 'group' (kāya) in the sense of a collection because it is divided into many types such as craving for sense pleasures and so forth. The same applies to the remaining cravings for sounds and so forth.
111:
The seven latent tendencies (anusaya) are the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of aversion, the latent tendency of conceit, the latent tendency of wrong view, the latent tendency of doubt, the latent tendency of lust for existence, and the latent tendency of ignorance. They are called latent tendencies because they lie dormant repeatedly in the sense of not being abandoned by the Path. Lust for the objects of sensuality is called sensual lust (kāmarāga). Alternatively, because defilement-sensuality itself is lust, it is called sensual lust. It is called aversion (paṭigha) because it strikes against the object. It is called wrong view (diṭṭhi) in the sense of seeing incorrectly. It is called conceit (māna) because one conceives in terms of "I am superior," and so on. Lust for existences is called lust for existence (bhavarāga). Sensual lust that has reached strength is called the latent tendency of sensual lust. The same should be understood for the remaining terms.

The eight wrongnesses (micchatta) are wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. Although one aspires, "This practice will bring me welfare and happiness," they are called wrongnesses because they do not turn out that way, and because they occur pervertedly, such as seeing the beautiful in the unattractive, and because they are of a wrong nature. It is called wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) because one sees wrongly. Or, it is called wrong view because one sees pervertedly through this nature. Alternatively, it is called wrong view because it is a view that has deviated from right view. Or, it is called wrong view because it is an incorrect view. Or, it is called wrong view because it is a distorted view due to grasping erroneously. Or, it is called wrong view because it is a view loathed by the wise for bringing about harm. The same method applies to wrong intention and the others. Wrong view is the adherence to the views of eternalism and annihilationism. Wrong intention is the threefold thought, such as the thought of sensuality. Wrong speech is the fourfold volition, such as false speech. Wrong action is the threefold volition, such as taking life. Wrong livelihood is the volition that originates the practice of wrong livelihood. Wrong effort is the energy associated with unwholesome consciousness. Wrong mindfulness is the unwholesome state of mind that is the opposite of mindfulness. Wrong concentration is the concentration associated with the unwholesome.

The nine things rooted in craving (taṇhāmūlaka) are: dependent on craving, there is pursuit; dependent on pursuit, there is gain; dependent on gain, there is decision-making; dependent on decision-making, there is desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust, there is attachment; dependent on attachment, there is possession; dependent on possession, there is stinginess; dependent on stinginess, there is safeguarding; and because of safeguarding, there arise various evil unwholesome states such as the taking up of sticks and weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, insulting speech, slander, and lying. These are the nine things rooted in craving. They are called "rooted in craving" because craving is their root. Pursuit and the others are indeed unwholesome. "Dependent on craving" (taṇhaṃ paṭicca) means relying on craving. Pursuit means the seeking of objects such as visible forms.
112:
That pursuit occurs when there is craving. Gain is the acquisition of objects such as visible forms; that acquisition of visible forms and so on occurs when there is pursuit.

Specifically, decision-making (vinicchaya) is of four types by way of: knowledge, craving, wrong view, and thought. Among those four, "One should know the decision regarding happiness; having known the decision regarding happiness, one should pursue internal happiness"—this decision is the decision of knowledge (ñāṇa-vinicchaya). As it is stated, "Decision-making is of two kinds: the decision of craving and the decision of wrong view," the one hundred and eight modes of craving are called the decision of craving. The sixty-two types of wrong views are called the decision of wrong view. In this sutta, "Sakka, desire has thought as its source," the "decision-making" mentioned refers only to thought. Indeed, having obtained a gain, one decides by way of thought whether it is desirable or undesirable, good or bad: "This much will be for the sake of visible objects, this much for the sake of sounds and other objects, this much will be for me, this much for others, this much I will enjoy, this much I will store away." Therefore, it is said, "Dependent on gain, there is decision-making."

Desire and lust (chandarāga) refers to the arising of weak lust and strong lust regarding the object thought about with such unwholesome thoughts. Here, "desire" (chanda) is a designation for weak lust, and "lust" (rāga) is for strong lust. Attachment (ajjhosāna) is the strong determination as "I" and "mine." Possession (pariggaha) is the act of grasping by the power of craving and wrong view. Stinginess (macchariya) is the inability to tolerate sharing with others. For that very reason, the ancient teachers say regarding the definition of stinginess: "It is called stinginess because it arises as 'Let this wonderful thing be mine alone, let it not be a wonderful thing for another.'"

Safeguarding (ārakkha) is the act of guarding well by way of closing doors, securing with boxes, and so on. It is called "adhikaraṇa" because it excessively produces [the result]; this name is a name for the cause. "Ārakkhādhikaraṇa" is an adverbial phrase meaning "having safeguarding as its cause." In "taking up of sticks" (daṇḍādāna) and so on, the taking up of a stick or staff to ward off others is called "taking up of sticks." The taking up of a weapon such as a single-edged sword is called "taking up of weapons" (satthādāna). Quarrel (kalaha) is both physical quarrel and verbal quarrel. Strife (viggaha) is the initial opposition. Dispute (vivāda) is the subsequent contention. "Tuvaṃtuvaṃ" means saying "you, you" in a disrespectful manner.

The ten wrongnesses (micchatta) are wrong view... up to... wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation. Among those ten, wrong knowledge (micchā-ñāṇa) is the delusion that arises by way of planning means for committing evil deeds, and by way of reflecting after having done evil, "It was well done by me." Wrong liberation (micchā-vimutti) is the perception of being liberated while one is not yet liberated from the defilements.
113:
Now, to show the dhammas to be abandoned through various types of abandonment (pahāna), the section beginning with "Dve pahānāni" (Two types of abandonment) is commenced. Indeed, when the types of abandonment (pahāna) are understood, the dhammas to be abandoned by each respective abandonment become easily understood. Among the five types of abandonment, setting aside the two mundane abandonments (tadaṅga-pahāna and vikkhambhana-pahāna) and the abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna), which is Nibbāna where defilements are absent, the two supramundane abandonments, which are also characterized by the absence of defilements, are mentioned first. Because defilements are thoroughly eradicated by these four paths, it is called eradication (samuccheda). Because defilements are abandoned by these four paths, it is called abandonment (pahāna). Since it is the abandonment known as eradication and not the remaining four types of abandonment, it is called abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Because it brings about the tranquillization of defilements, it is called tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi). Because defilements have been abandoned, it is called abandonment. Since it is the abandonment known as tranquillization, it is called abandonment by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna). Because it transcends the world, it is called supramundane (lokuttara). Because it reaches the state of destruction (khaya) known as Nibbāna, it is called khayagāmī. Since the dhamma that reaches that Nibbāna is the path, it is called the path leading to destruction (khayagāmimagga). For one who develops that path leading to destruction, that path is the abandonment by eradication; this is the meaning. Similarly, at the moment of the fruit, the supramundane fruit itself is the abandonment by tranquillization.

In the Pali passages beginning with "Kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ," it is called escape (nissaraṇa) because one escapes from sense-desires (kāma), from form (rūpa), and from the conditioned (saṅkhata) by means of this dhamma. Alternatively, it is called escape because of being freed from those sense-desires, forms, and conditioned things. The meditation on foulness (asubha-jhāna) is called renunciation (nekkhamma) because it escapes from sense-desires. Alternatively, the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) is called renunciation. The meditation on foulness is the escape from sense-desires by way of suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). However, the path of non-returning, which is produced based on that meditation on foulness, is the permanent escape from sense-desires by way of absolute eradication (samuccheda). It is called form (rūpa) because it is subject to change (ruppati). It is called formless (arūpa) because it is the opposite of form. Just as the opposite of a friend is called an enemy (amitta), and the opposites of greed and so on are called non-greed and so on, it means the opposite of form. Alternatively, it is called formless because form does not exist in these formless absorptions by virtue of the result. The term arūpa itself is called āruppa. It refers to the formless absorptions (arūpa-jhāna). These are called the escape from form. The path of arahantship (arahatta-magga), which is higher than the formless absorptions, is also called the total escape from form because it prevents the re-arising of form. Bhūta means arisen. Saṅkhata means conditioned or produced by a combination of causes. Paṭiccasamuppanna means dependently originated, arising together in harmony depending on various causes. By the first term "bhūta," the nature of impermanence (anicca) is shown by demonstrating the arising. By the second term "saṅkhata," even though it is an impermanent dhamma, the nature of dependence on other causes (parāyatta) is shown by demonstrating the power of causes. By the third term "paṭiccasamuppanna," even though it depends on other causes, the nature of natural law (dhammatā) is shown by demonstrating the absence of a conscious effort (avyāpāra) in the causes. Cessation (nirodha) is Nibbāna. It is called cessation because suffering ceases depending on Nibbāna. That Nibbāna itself is called the escape (nissaraṇa) from conditioned things because it is freed from all conditioned things. However, in the Commentary—
114:
"Cessation is the escape from that conditioned thing"—in this context, the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala) is intended by the word "cessation" (nirodha). The reason is that when Nibbāna is seen through the fruit of arahantship, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) no longer arise in the future. Therefore, because it is the object-decisive support condition (ārammaṇūpanissaya-paccaya) for cessation known as the fruit of arahantship, (Nibbāna) is called "cessation." In the words beginning with "For one who has attained renunciation (nekkhamma)," sense-desires (kāma) are both abandoned and relinquished by the meditation on foulness as an escape through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), and by the path of non-returning as an escape through abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). In the same way, forms (rūpa) should be applied to the formless absorptions as an escape and to the path of arahantship as an escape. For, by abandoning desire and lust (chandarāga) for forms, the absolute eradication (samuccheda) of forms occurs. Here, in the word "rūpā," a gender transformation (changing neuter to masculine) is made. Conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are both abandoned and relinquished by Nibbāna as an escape through abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna), and by the fruit of arahantship as an escape through abandonment by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna). And because Nibbāna is the escape, its attainment should be understood by way of making it an object.

In the words beginning with "The truth of suffering" (dukkha-sacca), terms like "penetration by full understanding" (pariññā-paṭivedha) are used as adverbial expressions. Penetration through full understanding is called penetration by full understanding. One should understand that penetration by full understanding. The same method applies to the remaining: penetration by abandonment, penetration by realization, and penetration by development. "Abandons" means that one who penetrates the truths in various ways abandons the defilements that are to be abandoned. Alternatively, it means that one abandons those truths by abandoning desire and lust for the mundane and supramundane truths. There is also a variant reading "pajahati." Just as a boat, in a single moment without before or after, performs four tasks: abandoning the near shore, cutting the current, carrying the cargo, and reaching the far shore; even so, the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), in a single moment without before or after, penetrates the Four Truths. It understands the truth of suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā); it understands the truth of the origin through the penetration of abandonment (pahāna); it understands the truth of the path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā); and it understands the truth of cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā). What is meant by this? Since it is said, "By making cessation (Nibbāna) the object, one reaches, sees, and penetrates the Four Truths," it should be understood that the types of abandonment are spoken of as if they occur separately, even within a single moment. Among the five types of abandonment, just as moss is removed by a pot dipped into water covered with moss, the pushing aside and distancing of opposing dhammas such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by means of various mundane concentrations is called abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). Because the abandonment of the hindrances is prominent, it is called abandonment by suppression.
115:
For one developing the first jhāna, it should be understood that the abandoning of only the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is mentioned because it is prominent. Indeed, the hindrances do not suddenly overwhelm the mind in the preceding or following stages of jhāna. If those hindrances do overwhelm it, the jhāna declines. However, states such as initial application (vitakka) and so forth occur before and after the second jhāna and others without being in opposition to them. Therefore, the suppression of the hindrances (vikkhambhana-pahāna) is prominent.

Just as darkness is dispelled by a bright lamp at night, the abandoning of those respective states to be abandoned by means of the respective jhāna factors, which are parts of insight, through the way of opposition, is called abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna). In the statement, "For one developing the concentration leading to penetration (nibbhedabhāgiya-samādhi) to abandon wrong views (diṭṭhigata)," it should be understood that the abandoning of only wrong views is mentioned in terms of their grossness. Wrong views are gross; perceptions of permanence (nicca-saññā) and so forth are subtle. In that text, "diṭṭhigatānaṃ" means wrong view itself is "diṭṭhigata," similar to terms like "gūthagata" (excrement) and "muttagata" (urine). It is called "diṭṭhigata" because there is no destination to go to, being merely the occurrence of wrong view, or because it is included within the sixty-two types of wrong views. It is mentioned in the plural as "those wrong views." Concentration leading to penetration refers to concentration associated with insight (vipassanā).

Like a tree struck by a thunderbolt, the abandoning of the fetters (saṃyojana) by the Path Knowledge of the Noble One (ariya-magga-ñāṇa) so that they never arise again is called abandoning by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna). Cessation (nirodha) refers to Nibbāna.

Having thus shown the states to be abandoned by way of abandoning, the Teacher now says, "Monks, everything should be abandoned," and so forth, to show the states to be abandoned by their own nature. In that text, the eye and so forth are to be abandoned by abandoning desire and lust (chanda-rāga). In passages such as "One who sees form abandons it," one who sees form as impermanent (anicca) and so forth abandons the defilements that should be abandoned. In the two elisions (peyyāla) starting with "The eye... etc... aging and death... etc... Nibbāna which is merged in the Deathless," in passages like "One who sees the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) abandons it," it should be understood accordingly that a person who sees, looks for, regards, or desires that faculty "I shall know the unknown" among those supramundane faculties (as impermanent, suffering, non-self, etc.) abandons the defilements to be abandoned at the moments of insight.

## The Explanation of the Description of What Should Be Abandoned is Finished.
116:
## Explanation of the Description of What Should Be Developed

In the description of what should be developed, "mindfulness directed to the body" (kāyagatāsati) refers to the mindfulness associated with the attention to breathing (ānāpāna), the four major postures (iriyāpatha), minor activities (khuddaka-iriyāpatha), the thirty-two parts of the body (dva-ttiṃsākāra), the four elements (catudhātu), the nine cemetery contemplations (sivathika), repulsiveness (paṭikūla), and the definition of the four elements, as taught in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, and associated with fine-material jhāna (rūpajjāna) as appropriate. Because that mindfulness has gone to (gatā) or occurs in those bodies such as the breath and postures, it is called "kāyagatā" (directed to the body).

"Accompanied by pleasure" (sātasahagatā) means reaching the state of co-arising and so forth with "sāta," which is the feeling of joy (somanassa-vedanā) known as the experience of sweet happiness.
