In the Buddha's words, the word "sahagata" (accompanied by) is seen in five meanings: (1) being that state (tabbhāva), (2) intermingled (vokiṇṇa), (3) object (ārammaṇa), (4) support (nissaya), and (5) conjoined (saṃsaṭṭha).

In the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta passage, "This craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust (nandirāga-sahagatā)," it has the meaning of "being that state," meaning it has become delight and lust. In the passage, "Monks, whatever investigation is accompanied by sloth (kosajja-sahagatā), conjoined with sloth," it has the meaning of "intermingled," meaning intermingled with sloth arising at intervals. In the Puggalapaññatti passage, "He is a gainer of attainments accompanied by form (rūpa-sahagatā) or attainments accompanied by the formless (arūpa-sahagatā)," it has the meaning of "object," meaning having form or formless objects. In the passage, "He develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton (aṭṭhikasaññā-sahagata)," it has the meaning of "support," meaning the enlightenment factor of mindfulness obtained by basing it on (relying on) the perception of a skeleton. In the Vibhaṅga passage, "This happiness is accompanied by this rapture (pītiyā sahagata), co-arisen, conjoined," it has the meaning of "conjoined," meaning mixed.

In this term "sātasahagatā" as well, the meaning of "conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭha) is intended. Mindfulness conjoined with the feeling of joy is called "sātasahagatā." That mindfulness, excluding the fourth jhāna, is conjoined with the feeling of joy in the remaining three jhānas. Although it is accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā) in the fourth jhāna, it is called "sātasahagatā" for the most part. Or, because the fourth jhāna is based on the previous three jhānas, it can also be called "sātasahagatā." Or, because the Blessed One has described equanimity as peaceful happiness, the mindfulness associated with the fourth jhāna is also certainly called "sātasahagatā."

"Serenity and insight" (samatha ca vipassanā): It is called "serenity" (samatha) because it calms or destroys opposing states such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda). This is a name for concentration (samādhi). It is called "insight" (vipassanā) because it sees states in various ways by way of impermanence and so forth. This is a name for wisdom (paññā). These two are called states preceding the Path in the Dasuttara Sutta, and in the Saṅgīti Sutta, they are described as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

"Three kinds of concentration" (tayo samādhi) refers to concentration with initial and sustained application, concentration without initial but with sustained application, and concentration without initial and without sustained application. Concentration with initial and sustained application includes momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), insight concentration (vipassanā-samādhi), access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and first jhāna concentration. Concentration without initial but with sustained application is concentration that takes only sustained application as its measure without initial application and does not reach association with initial application; according to the fivefold method (pañcaka-naya), it is the second jhāna concentration. Concentration free from both initial and sustained application refers to fine-material concentration starting from the second jhāna according to the fourfold method (catukka-naya), and fine-material concentration starting from the third jhāna according to the fivefold method. All three of these concentrations are mundane only. In the Suttanta method, the void (suññata)...
117:
Concentration (concentration with initial thought and sustained thought), concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, and concentration without both initial thought and sustained thought (these are the three types). It is called 'with initial thought' (savitakka) because it occurs with initial thought through the power of association, and 'with sustained thought' (savicāra) because it occurs with sustained thought. This (concentration with initial and sustained thought) includes momentary concentration (khaṇikasamādhi), insight concentration (vipassanāsamādhi), access concentration (upacārasamādhi), and the first absorption concentration (paṭhamajjhānasamādhi). It is called 'without initial thought' (avitakka) because it lacks initial thought. Among initial and sustained thought, it is called 'sustained thought only' (vicāramatta) because sustained thought is its limit or maximum extent; the meaning is that it does not reach association with initial thought beyond sustained thought. This (concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only) is the second absorption concentration in the fivefold method. Concentration that is devoid of both initial and sustained thought is called 'concentration without initial thought and without sustained thought' (avitakka-avicāra-samādhi). This concentration refers to the fine-material sphere concentration (rūpāvacarasamādhi) starting from the second absorption in the fourfold method, and starting from the third absorption in the fivefold method. All these three are mundane (lokiya) only. In the Saṅgīti Sutta, three other types of concentration are also taught: 'void concentration (suññata-samādhi), signless concentration (animitta-samādhi), and undirected concentration (appanihita-samādhi).' These are not intended here.

The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are: mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna), mindfulness of feeling (vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna), mindfulness of the mind (cittānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna), and mindfulness of mental objects (dhammānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna). It should be understood that for one who grasps the body in fourteen ways in the preliminary stage, it is mindfulness of the body; for one who grasps feeling in nine ways, it is mindfulness of feeling; for one who grasps the mind in sixteen ways, it is mindfulness of the mind; and for one who grasps mental objects in five ways, it is mindfulness of mental objects. Supramundane (lokuttara) foundations of mindfulness are not intended here. 

It is called 'five-factored concentration' (pañcaṅgika-samādhi) because it possesses five factors; it is the fourth absorption concentration. The five factors are: pervading with rapture (pītipharaṇatā), pervading with happiness (sukhapharaṇatā), pervading with the mind (cetopharaṇatā), pervading with light (ālokapharaṇatā), and the sign of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇanimitta). The wisdom occurring in two absorptions by pervading with rapture is called 'pervading with rapture.' The wisdom occurring in three absorptions by pervading with happiness is called 'pervading with happiness.' The wisdom of knowing others' minds (cetopariya-paññā) by pervading their minds is called 'pervading with the mind.' The wisdom of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-paññā) by pervading with light is called 'pervading with light.' The reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) is called the 'sign of reviewing.' Thus it is also stated:

'Wisdom in two absorptions is pervading with rapture; wisdom in three absorptions is pervading with happiness; wisdom of others' minds is pervading with the mind; wisdom of the divine eye is pervading with light; and the reviewing knowledge of one who has emerged from various concentrations is the sign of reviewing' (as taught in the Vibhaṅga).
118:
That reviewing knowledge is called a 'sign' (nimitta) because it grasps the mode of occurrence of one who has emerged from concentration. In that Vibhaṅga passage, pervading with rapture and pervading with happiness are like two feet; pervading with the mind and pervading with light are like two hands; the fourth absorption, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), is like the torso; and the sign of reviewing is like the head. Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, illustrated the five-factored right concentration as being like a man complete with all limbs and parts.

Regarding the six bases of recollection (anussatiṭṭhāna): they are called 'recollections' (anussati) because they arise repeatedly. They are also called 'recollections' because they are types of mindfulness suitable for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, occurring only in the proper objects where they should occur. These recollections themselves are called 'bases of recollection' (anussatiṭṭhāna) because they are the bases for rapture and so forth. What are the six? They are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of devas.

The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are the factors of enlightenment (bodhi), or the factors of the enlightened person (bodhi). This is what is meant: the harmony of states (dhamma-sāmaggī) which arises at the moment of the supramundane path and acts as the opposite to many dangers such as sloth and torpor, restlessness, craving, wrong view, devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, the view of annihilation, and the view of eternalism—this harmony of states consisting of mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—is called 'enlightenment' (bodhi) because by it the noble disciple awakens. 'He awakens' (bujjhati) means he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or he realizes Nibbāna itself. Because they are parts of that enlightenment consisting of the harmony of states, they are called 'factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅga), like the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) or factors of the path (maggaṅga). Furthermore, the noble disciple who awakens by means of this harmony of states of the kind described is called 'enlightenment' (bodhi); because they are the factors of that enlightenment (the person), they are called 'factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅga), like the factors of an army (senaṅga) or the factors of a chariot (rathaṅga). Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries said: 'They are bojjhaṅga because they are the factors of the person who awakens.' Moreover, the meaning of bojjhaṅga should be understood according to the method in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'In what sense are they bojjhaṅga? They are bojjhaṅga because they lead to enlightenment (bodhāya saṃvattanti).'

The Noble Eightfold Path is called 'Noble' (ariya) because it is far from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it makes one noble, and because it causes the attainment of the noble fruit. It is called 'eightfold' (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it has eight factors. This path is merely a collection of factors, like an army with four factors or an orchestra with five factors; there is no path apart from its factors. The factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path are supramundane; however, according to the method of the Dasuttara Sutta, those occurring in the preliminary stage are also found.
119:
The nine factors of the effort for purification are: the factor of effort for purification of virtue, the factor of effort for purification of mind, the factor of effort for purification of view, the factor of effort for purification by overcoming doubt, the factor of effort for purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path, the factor of effort for purification by knowledge and vision of the way, the factor of effort for purification by knowledge and vision, the factor of effort for purification of wisdom, and the factor of effort for purification of liberation (Dīgha Nikāya, Pāthikavagga Pāḷi, 359).

Purification of virtue refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) which is capable of leading to Nibbāna, the state of purity. Indeed, this virtue cleanses the impurity of immorality. The factor of effort for purification (pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga) means the noble factor that is the cause of purity.

Purification of mind refers to the eight well-practiced attainments (samāpatti) which are the proximate cause of insight (vipassanā). Indeed, these attainments cleanse the impurities of the mind such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and other hindrances.

Purification of view is the knowledge that sees mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa) along with their causes. Indeed, this knowledge cleanses the impurity of the view of a being (satta-diṭṭhi).

Purification by overcoming doubt is the knowledge that understands dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Indeed, one who sees with this knowledge that phenomena (dhammā) arise by way of causes in the three periods of time, overcomes the impurity of doubt regarding beings (satta-kankhā) in the three periods and becomes pure.

Purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path is the knowledge that distinguishes between what is the path and what is not the path, such as: the ten corruptions of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa)—namely, radiance (obhāsa), knowledge (ñāṇa), rapture (pīti), tranquillity (passaddhi), happiness (sukha), resolution (adhimokkha), exertion (paggaha), establishment (upaṭṭhāna), equanimity (upekkhā), and attachment (nikanti)—which arise during the insight into arising and passing away (udayabbayānupassanāñāṇa) are not the path; only the knowledge of arising and passing away that has entered the course of insight is the path. Indeed, this knowledge cleanses the impurity of mistaking what is not the path for the path.

Purification by knowledge and vision of the way refers to these nine insight knowledges that have entered the course of insight: knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, knowledge of contemplation of appearance as terror, knowledge of contemplation of danger, knowledge of contemplation of dispassion, knowledge of desire for deliverance, knowledge of contemplation of reflection, knowledge of equanimity towards formations, and conformity knowledge. Indeed, these knowledges cleanse impurities such as the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) and so forth.

Purification by knowledge and vision is the wisdom of the four noble paths. Indeed, this path-wisdom cleanses the impurities of defilements to be abandoned by each respective path through total eradication (samuccheda).

Wisdom refers to the wisdom of the fruition of Arahantship. Liberation refers to the liberation of the fruition of Arahantship.

Ten kasiṇa bases (dasa kasiṇāyatanāni): "One perceives the earth-kasiṇa—above, below, across, undivided, and immeasurable. One perceives the water-kasiṇa... [as before]... the fire-kasiṇa... the air-kasiṇa... the blue-kasiṇa... the yellow-kasiṇa... the red-kasiṇa... the white-kasiṇa... the space-kasiṇa... One perceives the consciousness-kasiṇa—above, below, across, undivided, and immeasurable" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Dasakanipāta, 25; Dīgha Nikāya, Pāthikavagga Pāḷi, 360). These are the ten as taught.
120:
These kasinas are called 'kasiṇa' because of the sense of pervading the whole. They are called 'āyatana' because they are the field of activity (khetta) or the foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) for the states that take them as objects. 'Uddhaṃ' (above) means facing towards the upper sky. 'Adho' (below) means facing towards the ground below. 'Tiriyaṃ' (across) means delimited all around like the circumference of a field. Some people develop the kasina only upwards, some downwards, and some all around. Even a single person, for various reasons, spreads it like light, desiring to see forms. Therefore, it is said: "One perceives the earth-kasina—above, below, and across." This term 'adwayaṃ' (undivided) is stated so that one state does not change into another. Just as for one who has entered into water, there is only water in all directions and nothing else, so too, the earth-kasina remains only as the earth-kasina; there is no mixing with other kasinas. This method applies to all. This term 'appamāṇaṃ' (immeasurable) is stated by way of the boundlessness of the pervading of each kasina. When pervading it with the mind, one pervades the whole; one does not take a limit, thinking, "This is its beginning, this is its middle." 'Space-kasina' (ākāsakasiṇa) refers to the space obtained by removing the kasina and the delimited space-kasina. 'Consciousness-kasina' (viññāṇakasiṇa) is the consciousness occurring in the space where the kasina was removed. Therein, the state of being above, below, and across should be understood in the space where the kasina was removed by way of the kasina, and in the consciousness occurring there by way of the space where the kasina was removed. Since the delimited space-kasina is also to be developed, it should also be understood by way of that.

Now, wishing to show the different types of development (bhāvanā), he said 'dve bhāvanā' (two developments) and so on. Therein, regarding the terms 'lokiya' (mundane) and so on, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is called 'loka' (world) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. Because of being included in that world, the development associated with the world is called 'lokiya'. Although it is expressed as 'the development of states' (dhammānaṃ bhāvanā), there is no development separate from those states. Those states themselves, when being developed, are called 'development'. 'Uttara' means transcending. Because of not being included in the world, that which transcends the world is called 'lokuttara' (supramundane).

They are called 'rūpāvacara' (belonging to the fine-material sphere) because they frequent the fine-material existence known as the rūpa-bhava. Here, the word 'kusala' (wholesome) is found in the senses of health (ārogya), blamelessness (anavajja), skillfulness (cheka), and having a happy result (sukhavipāka). In passages such as "Is the venerable one healthy? Is the venerable one free from illness?", it is used in the sense of health. In passages such as "Venerable sir, what kind of bodily conduct is wholesome? Great King, that bodily conduct which is blameless" and "Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states", it is used in the sense of blamelessness.
121:
In the passages such as "Prince, are you skilled in the various parts of a chariot?" (M.ii.87) and "Women who are skilled and trained in dancing and singing" (Ja.ii.22.94), [the word kusala] is used in the sense of being clever or skillful (cheka). In the passages such as "Due to the undertaking of wholesome states, this merit (puñña) increases" (D.iii.80) and "Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma" (Dhs.431), it is used in the sense of a happy result (sukhavipāka). In this context, however, the word kusala is appropriate in the senses of health (ārogya), faultlessness (anavajja), and happy result (sukhavipāka).

The word-definition (vacanattha) is as follows: They are called 'kusala' because they shake, disturb, or destroy despicable, evil, unwholesome states. Alternatively, unwholesome states existing in a despicable manner are called 'kusa'; they are called 'kusala' because they cut (lunanti) those unwholesome states known as kusa. Or, wisdom (ñāṇa) is called 'kusa' because it makes despicable unwholesome states thin; they are called 'kusala' because they are to be taken, attained, or developed by that kusa (wisdom). Or, just as kusa grass cuts both parts of the hand that grasps it, these states cut both groups of defilements—those that have arisen and those that have not yet arisen; thus, they are called 'kusala' in the sense that they cut like kusa grass.

The development of those fine-material sphere wholesome states is bhāvanā. They are called 'immaterial sphere' (arūpāvacara) because they frequent the immaterial realms known as the immaterial existence. They are called 'included' (pariyāpanna) because they are contained within the round of rebirths of the three planes. Supramundane states, which are not contained within that round, are called 'unincluded' (apariyāpanna).

If it is asked why the development (bhāvanā) of sense-sphere wholesome states is not mentioned, it is because in the Abhidhamma, 'development' (bhāvanā) is intended only as the development that has reached absorption (appanā). Regarding this, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga:

"Whether in works managed by wisdom, or in crafts managed by wisdom, or in branches of science managed by wisdom, if one—without hearing from another—attains such conformable patience (anulomika-khanti), view, preference, inclination, desire, or patience in reflecting on the Dhamma, through the knowledge of ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) or the knowledge in conformity with the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa), thinking 'Materiality is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, mental formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent,' this is called 'wisdom resulting from reflection' (cintāmayā paññā). If one attains such wisdom in works managed by wisdom... etc., after hearing from another, this is called 'wisdom resulting from hearing' (sutamayā paññā). All wisdom of a person who has attained meditative attainment is 'wisdom resulting from development' (bhāvanāmayā paññā)."
122:
It should be understood that sense-sphere development (kāmāvacara-bhāvanā) is not called 'bhāvanā' [in this specific context] because it is interrupted by advertence (āvajjanā) and the falling into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). However, because it is included within all three bases of meritorious action—namely, giving, virtue, and development—the status of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and insight concentration (vipassanā-samādhi) as 'merit consisting in development' (bhāvanāmaya-puñña) is established. In this context, it is categorized only under mundane development (lokiya-bhāvanā).

Regarding the three-fold distinction of fine-material and immaterial sphere developments as inferior, medium, and superior: 'hīna' means a low development. 'majjhima' is so called because it occurs in the middle of the inferior and the superior; there is also a reading 'majjhimā'. 'paṇīta' means superior, having reached the state of excellence. This state of being inferior, medium, or superior should be understood by the power of exertion (āyūhana). For if, at the moment of exertion, the desire (chanda), energy (vīriya), consciousness (citta), or investigation (vīmaṃsā) is inferior, then that development is called inferior (hīna). If those states are medium, it is called medium (majjhima). If those states are superior, it is called superior (paṇīta). Alternatively, development associated with weak faculties (indriya) is called inferior; that associated with medium faculties is medium; and that associated with intense faculties is called superior. Since there is no state of being inferior or medium in supramundane wholesome states, only the state of being superior (paṇīta) is mentioned. Indeed, that supramundane development is called 'paṇīta' because of its excellence and because it is unsurpassable (atpaka).

In the first tetrad of development, 'bhāveti' (he develops) means that in a single moment, one develops the Noble Path while penetrating [the truths] in various ways. In the second tetrad of development, 'esanā-bhāvanā' (seeking-development) refers to the development in the preliminary stage of absorption (appanā). It is called 'esanā' because one seeks absorption by means of this development. 'paṭilābha-bhāvanā' (attainment-development) refers to the development of absorption itself. It is called 'paṭilābha' because absorption is obtained by that seeking-development. 'ekarasā-bhāvanā' (single-function development) refers to the development at the time of practice by one who wishes to achieve mastery (vasībhāva) after having obtained absorption. It is called 'ekarasā' because it has a single function through the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa), being liberated from various defilements by various abandonments. 'āsevanā-bhāvanā' (repetition-development) refers to the development at the time of use as desired by one who has achieved mastery after obtaining absorption. It is called 'āsevanā' because it is frequently cultivated. Some teachers, however, explain that 'āsevanā-bhāvanā' is the act of mastery (vasīkamma) and 'ekarasā-bhāvanā' is that which is universally required (sabbatṭhika).

In the Catukka-vibhaṅga, the phrase 'samādhiṃ samāpajjantānaṃ' (for those entering concentration) is a use of the present tense to indicate the near-present. Therein, 'tattha jātā' (born therein) refers to the states born in that preliminary stage. 'ekarasā honti' (they have a single taste) means they have a common function in producing absorption. 'samādhiṃ samāpannānaṃ' (for those who have entered concentration) refers to those who have attained absorption. Therein, 'tattha jātā' refers to the states born in that absorption. 'aññamaññaṃ nātivattanti' (they do not transcend each other) means they do not overstep each other by way of occurring in harmony. In the sense of decision (adhimokkha)...
123:
In the phrases beginning with "Saddhindriyaṃ bhāvayato," even within a single moment, while each faculty performs its own function, by virtue of depending on their respective associated states, the remaining faculties also have a uniform function through the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa). Therefore, it is called development (bhāvanā) in the sense of having a uniform function through the taste of liberation. The same method applies to the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the path factors (maggaṅga). In the word "ekarasa," the masculine gender has been changed to the neuter.

"A monk in this Dispensation" refers to a monk within this Teaching. He is called a monk (bhikkhu) because he perceives danger (bhaya) in the cycle of rebirths (saṃsāra), such as birth and so forth. In phrases such as "in the morning time," although the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga), in meaning it is simply the locative case (bhumma), signifying the early part of the day. "He cultivates" means he intensely cultivates the absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) that has reached mastery. "At midday" means the middle period of the day. "In the evening" means the evening period of the day. "Before the meal" means the time before the day's meal. "After the meal" means the time after the day's meal. "In the first watch" means the first part of the night. It also refers to the "dark fortnight" and the "bright fortnight." "In the first stage of life" means the first division of age. In the three stages of life for a person with a hundred-year lifespan, each stage consists of 33 years and 4 months.

28. In the third tetrad of development, "in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein" means that the yoked states (yuganaddha-dhamma) known as concentration and wisdom, which arise in the specific developments such as renunciation (nekkhamma) and so forth, do not surpass one another. "In the sense of the single taste of the faculties" means that in those very developments, the faculties such as faith (saddhā) and so forth, because of being liberated from various defilements, have the state of a single taste through the taste of liberation. "In the sense of conveying the energy corresponding thereto" means by way of conveying the energy suitable for those states that do not surpass one another and have a single taste. "In the sense of cultivation" means by way of the state of cultivation occurring for that person at that time.

"Perception of form" (rūpasaññā) refers to the perception of form known as the fifteen types of fine-material sphere jhānas by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness. In Pali passages such as "Possessing form, one sees forms" (rūpī rūpāni passati), the fine-material sphere jhāna is also called "form" (rūpa). Its object is also described in terms such as "Externally, one sees forms, beautiful and ugly." Because perception is prominent in the fine-material sphere jhāna, it is called "perception of form," meaning perception in the fine-material sphere. "Perception of resistance" (paṭighasaññā) refers to the ten types of perception of resistance, consisting of five wholesome resultants and five unwholesome resultants. The perceptions associated with the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness are called "perceptions of resistance" because they arise from the impact between the sense bases such as the eye and the objects such as forms. The names perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, and perception of tangible objects are also names for this very perception of resistance. "Perception of diversity" (nānattasaññā) refers to the forty-four types of perception of diversity: 8 wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, 12 unwholesome perceptions, 11 wholesome sense-sphere resultant perceptions (excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness), 2 unwholesome resultant perceptions, and 11 functional sense-sphere perceptions. Because this perception has various natures...
124:
Perception is called "perception of resistance" (paṭighasaññā) because it arises from the impact between the sense bases such as the eye and the objects such as forms. This very perception of resistance is also given the names: perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, and perception of tangible objects. The perception that has forty-four divisions—8 wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, 12 unwholesome perceptions, 11 wholesome sense-sphere resultant perceptions, 2 unwholesome resultant perceptions, and 11 functional sense-sphere perceptions—is called "perception of diversity" (nānattasaññā). It is called perception of diversity because it occurs in objects such as forms, sounds, etc., which have various natures, and because it has natures that are mutually different and distinct through its forty-four divisions. Although there are many perceptions, the singular form is used by taking them as a class (jāti).

The perception that regards things as permanent is called "perception of permanence" (niccasaññā). Similarly, "perception of pleasure" (sukhasaññā) and "perception of self" (attasaññā) should be understood. Craving accompanied by joy is called "delight" (nandi). Craving devoid of joy is called "lust" (rāga). The arising of lust is called "origin" (samudaya). Alternatively, because only dissolution is seen through the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā), the arising of conditioned formations is called "origin." It is called "grasping" (ādāna) either because of the arising of defilements or because of clinging to conditioned objects due to the inability to see their faults. The perception that regards things as a solid mass due to their continuity is called "perception of compactness" (ghanasaññā). The exertion for the sake of conditioned formations is called "accumulation" (āyūhana). The perception that regards things as stable is called "perception of lastingness" (dhuvasaññā). The sign of permanence is called "sign" (nimitta). The longing for pleasure is called "aspiration" (paṇidhi). The false adherence that "there is a self" is called "insistence" (abhinivesa). The false adherence that takes things as having a permanent core or a self-core is called "insistence on taking a core" (sārādānābhinivesa). The false adherence through delusion, such as "Was I in the past?" and so forth, or "The world arises because of a creator God," and so forth, is called "insistence on confusion" (sammohābhinivesa). The false adherence that "this conditioned formation should be attached to," without seeing its faults, is called "insistence on the abode" (ālayābhinivesa). Clinging by an improper means is called "lack of reflection" (appaṭisaṅkhā). The occurrence of defilements such as the yoke of sensual desire is called "insistence on bondage" (saññogābhinivesa).

Defilements that exist in a single individual along with wrong views are called "co-existent with views" (diṭṭhekaṭṭha). They are called defilements (kilesa) because they burn and oppress. Co-existence (ekaṭṭha) is of two kinds: co-existence in abandonment (pahānekaṭṭha) and co-existence in arising (sahajekaṭṭha). "Co-existence in abandonment" refers to existing in a single individual along with the sixty-three types of views headed by the view of self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), as long as they have not been abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). This "co-existence in abandonment" is what is intended here. Among the ten defilements, although only the defilement of view (diṭṭhi) is explicitly mentioned here, the nine defilements—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—which lead to the lower realms, are also "co-existent in abandonment" with views, and by the path of stream-entry...
125:
The nine defilements, such as sloth (thina), restlessness (uddhacca), shamelessness (ahirika), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), being in a state of abandonment together (pahānekaṭṭha) with wrong view (diṭṭhi). Alternatively, among the one thousand five hundred defilements headed by greed, hatred, and delusion, when wrong view is abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, all defilements leading to the lower realms are abandoned by way of being in a state of abandonment together with wrong view. Sahajekaṭṭha means existing together with wrong view in a single consciousness.

For when the two unprompted consciousnesses associated with wrong view (diṭṭhigatasampayutta asaṅkhārika) are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, these defilements—greed, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—which arise together with them, are abandoned by way of sahajekaṭṭha. When the two prompted consciousnesses associated with wrong view (diṭṭhigatasampayutta sasaṅkhārika) are abandoned, these defilements—greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—which arise together with them, are abandoned by way of sahajekaṭṭha. Gross defilements refer to sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill will (byāpāda) that occur in a gross manner. Subtle defilements refer to sensual lust and ill will that occur in a subtle manner. "All defilements" refers to the remaining defilements after those abandoned by the three lower paths.

"He carries effort" means the practitioner (yogāvacara) exerts effort. Below, the words "seeking" (esanā), "attainment" (paṭilābha), "single taste" (ekarasa), and "repetition" (āsevana) were spoken to show the distinction of developments, as in "development of such a nature." Here, the words "in the sense of not overstepping the states arisen therein, in the sense of the single function of the faculties, in the sense of exerting effort suitable for that development, and in the sense of repetition" are spoken to show the cause of development, as in "it is called development because of this and that cause." Below, development by repetition was spoken by way of various moments, but here, development in the sense of repetition is spoken by way of a single moment; this is the distinction. In phrases such as "he develops while seeing form," it should be understood that the person seeing forms, etc., in the manner they should be seen, develops the development that should be developed. "They have a single taste" (ekarasa) means they have a single function either by the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa) or by the taste of function (kiccarasa). The taste of liberation is the taste of attainment (sampatti). For it is said that "taste" (rasa) is so called in the sense of the attainment of function.

## Commentary on the Description of What Should Be Developed is Finished.

## Commentary on the Description of What Should Be Realized

In the Description of What Should Be Realized, ten types of answers, each increasing by one, are spoken by way of realization through attainment (paṭilābha). Among those ten, "unshakeable deliverance of mind" (akuppā cetovimutti) is the deliverance of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). It is called "unshakeable" (akuppā) because it does not shake, does not move, and does not decline. It is called "deliverance of mind" (cetovimutti) because the mind is liberated from all defilements. "Knowledge" (vijjā) refers to the three types of knowledge. "Liberation" (vimutti), according to the teaching of the Dasuttara Sutta, refers to the Fruit of Arahantship. However, according to the teaching of the Saṅgīti Sutta, liberation is of two kinds: the mind's liberation from the hindrances (adhimutti) and Nibbāna. Among these two, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are called liberation because they are purely liberated from the hindrances and so on. Nibbāna is called liberation because it is liberated from all conditioned things (saṅkhata). The three types of knowledge are: the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa), and the knowledge of the destruction of taints (arahattamagga-ñāṇa). It is called "knowledge" (vijjā) because it destroys the darkness of delusion (moha) and because it makes clear what should be known. When the knowledge of recollecting past lives arises, it destroys the darkness (delusion) that covers the sequence of aggregates lived in the past, and it makes clear the sequence of aggregates lived in the past. Therefore, it is called knowledge. The knowledge of passing away and rebirth destroys the darkness that covers death and rebirth, and it makes clear death and rebirth. Therefore, it is called knowledge. The knowledge of the destruction of taints destroys the darkness that covers the Four Noble Truths, and it makes clear the Four Noble Truths...
126:
Because the mind is liberated from defilements, it is called liberation of mind (cetovimutti). The knowledges (vijjā) are the three knowledges. Liberation (vimutti), according to the sequence of the Dasuttara Sutta, refers to the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). However, according to the sequence of the Saṅgīti Sutta, it is said: "Liberation (vimutti) consists of two: the liberation of the mind (adhimutti) and Nibbāna" (Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, 3.304). Here also, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are called liberation because they are well-liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth; Nibbāna is called liberation because it is liberated from all conditioned things (saṅkhata).

The three knowledges (tisso vijjā) are: the knowledge of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa), and the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa). It is called knowledge (vijjā) in the sense of piercing the darkness of ignorance, and also in the sense of making things known. When the knowledge of the recollection of past lives arises, it pierces the darkness that stands covering past lives, and because it makes past lives known, it is called knowledge. The knowledge of passing away and rebirth pierces the darkness that covers death and rebirth, and because it makes death and rebirth known, it is called knowledge. The knowledge of the destruction of taints pierces the darkness that covers the Four Noble Truths, and because it makes the Four Noble Truths known, it is called knowledge.

The four fruits of recluseship (cattāri sāmaññaphalāni) are: the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). One is called a recluse (samaṇa) because he stills or destroys evil states; the state of being a recluse is recluseship (sāmañña). This is a name for the four noble paths. The fruits of recluseship are the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala).

The five aggregates of Dhamma (pañca dhammakkhandhā) are: the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha), and the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha). Aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) mean divisions of Dhamma or portions of Dhamma. The same method applies to the aggregate of virtue and so forth. Only mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom are called the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Only the liberations of eradication (samuccheda), tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi), and escape (nissaraṇa) are called the aggregate of liberation. Only the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) that reflects on the three kinds of liberation is called the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation. That is purely mundane. It is called knowledge (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing, and vision (dassana) in the sense of seeing; thus it is knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana). The knowledge and vision of liberations is called the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana). However, the liberations of suppression (vikkhambhana) and substitution (tadaṅga) are included within the aggregates of concentration and wisdom respectively.

These five aggregates of Dhamma are called trainee (sekkha) if they belong to trainees, and non-trainee (asekkha) if they belong to non-trainees. Among these, mundane states and the liberation of escape (Nibbāna) are neither trainee nor non-trainee. Nevertheless, because they belong to trainees, they are called "these are of the trainees"; and because they belong to non-trainees, they are called "these are of the non-trainees." In the passage, "He is endowed with the aggregate of liberation belonging to a trainee," it should be understood that he is endowed by way of making the liberation of escape (Nibbāna) his object.

The six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā) are the six superior knowledges. What are the six?
127: The knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of the divine ear-element, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the minds of others, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (the knowledge that arises upon the exhaustion of the taints)—these six are the direct knowledges. The seven powers of an Arahant: One whose taints are exhausted is called a khīṇāsava (Arahant); the powers of such an Arahant are called the powers of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavabala). What are the seven? The Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, here in this Dispensation, an Arahant has clearly seen all conditioned things as they really are with correct insight-path wisdom as impermanent. Bhikkhus, since an Arahant has clearly seen all conditioned things as they really are with correct insight-path wisdom as impermanent, this seeing is a power of an Arahant, by means of which power the Arahant acknowledges the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, the destruction of the taints, saying, 'The taints are destroyed in me.' "Furthermore, bhikkhus, as another power, an Arahant has clearly seen sensual pleasures as being like a pit of glowing coals as they really are with correct insight-path wisdom. Bhikkhus, since an Arahant has clearly seen sensual pleasures as being like a pit of glowing coals as they really are with correct insight-path wisdom, this seeing is also a power of an Arahant... (as above). "Furthermore, bhikkhus, as another power, the mind of an Arahant slants toward Nibbāna, leans toward Nibbāna, inclines toward Nibbāna, is established in Nibbāna, delights in the state of a recluse which is the escape from defilements, and is completely rid of those states that are the basis for the taints. Bhikkhus, that the mind of an Arahant thus slants toward Nibbāna and so forth is also a power of an Arahant... (as above). "Furthermore, bhikkhus, as another power, an Arahant has developed the four foundations of mindfulness, well developed them. He has developed the five faculties, well developed them. He has developed the seven factors of enlightenment, well developed them. He has developed the Noble Eightfold Path, well developed it. Bhikkhus, since an Arahant has developed the Noble Eightfold Path, well developed it, this development of the Eightfold Path is also a power of an Arahant, by means of which power the Arahant acknowledges the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, the destruction of the taints, saying, 'The taints are destroyed in me.'"
128:
Among those seven (powers), the first power shows the penetration of the Truth of Suffering. The second power shows the penetration of the Truth of the Origin of Suffering. The third power shows the penetration of the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. The four powers beginning with the fourth power show the penetration of the Truth of the Path.

The Eight Liberations (Aṭṭha Vimokkhā) are called liberations because they incline towards the object (the kasina object) and because they are well-freed from opposing states. "What are the eight? Having form, one sees forms; this is the first liberation. Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally; this is the second liberation. One is resolved only on the 'beautiful'; this is the third liberation. With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and through non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing,' one enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation. With the complete surmounting of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation" (Thus it is taught in Dī. Ni. 2.174, 3.358; A. Ni. 8.66).

The Nine Successive Cessations (Nava Anupubba-nirodhā) are the nine states that are ceased in successive order. "What are the nine? For one who has attained the first jhāna, the perception of sensual desire has ceased. For one who has attained the second jhāna, initial and sustained thought have ceased. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, in-breathing and out-breathing have ceased. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form has ceased. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space has ceased. For one who has attained the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness has ceased. For one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness has ceased. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased" (Thus it is taught in A. Ni. 9.13; Dī. Ni. 3.344, 359).

The Ten Qualities of One Beyond Training (Dasa Asekkhā Dhammā) are called 'Asekkhā' because there is nothing further to be trained in above the Fruit of Arahantship, and thus they no longer train. Alternatively, those who are still training in the three trainings are called 'Sekkhā' (trainees), while those who have reached the summit of growth...
129:
...those who are no longer training are called 'Asekkhā' (adepts), which refers to Arahants. These are called Asekkhā qualities because they are the qualities of Asekkhā persons. "What are the ten? Asekkhā Right View, Asekkhā Right Intention, Asekkhā Right Speech, Asekkhā Right Action, Asekkhā Right Livelihood, Asekkhā Right Effort, Asekkhā Right Mindfulness, Asekkhā Right Concentration, Asekkhā Right Knowledge, and Asekkhā Right Liberation" (Thus it is taught in Dī. Ni. 3.348, 360). Asekkhā Right Knowledge is the mundane wisdom associated with functional consciousness (kiriya), excluding the wisdom of the Fruit of Arahantship. Right Liberation is the Fruit of Arahantship itself. However, in the Commentary to the Saṅgīti Sutta, it is stated: "All these states, such as Asekkhā Right View and so on, are indeed states associated with the Fruit. Here, in the two instances of Right View and Right Knowledge, only wisdom (paññā) is spoken of. By the term 'Right Liberation,' the remaining states of the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti) that were not yet mentioned are included."

In passages such as "Monks, all should be realized," realization by way of the object should be understood. In passages such as "One who sees the aggregate of form realizes it," one who sees the mundane aggregates such as form through the aspect of being seen as impermanent, etc., realizes those very aggregates of form by way of realization through the object. Or, one who sees the aggregates of form through the aspect of how they should be seen, realizes Nibbāna—which is what should be realized—by means of that seeing. Grammarians also accept the word "passanto" (seeing) in the sense of a cause. One who sees the supramundane faculties such as the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) by way of the process of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), realizes those very supramundane faculties by way of realization through the object. The statement, "One realizes Nibbāna, which is immersed in the Deathless, in the sense of being the final end," is a direct teaching because among the states to be fully understood, to be abandoned, to be realized, and to be developed, Nibbāna is the state to be realized (sacchikātabba). "Whatever states are realized, those states are touched" means that states realized by way of the object are touched by contact with the object, and states realized by way of attainment are touched by contact with attainment.

## The Explanation of the Description of What Should Be Realized is finished.

## Explanation of the Description of the Fourfold Division of Decline

Now, because the states such as being part of decline occur through the different stages of each individual jhāna-concentration, the fourfold division of decline is described together. Among those four, for one who has attained the first jhāna...
130:
In the word "lābhino," the accusative case is used in the sense of possession (sāmī). He is called "lābhī" (one who has gained) because he has the realization (attainment) of the first jhāna. In this term "kāmasahagatā," the word "sahagata" is intended in the sense of "object" (ārammaṇa). It means taking the objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) and the defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāma) as objects. "Saññāmanasikārā" refers to perceptions associated with greed-rooted impulsive consciousness (lobhajavana), the adverting (āvajjana) attention that takes those objects of sensual desire and defilements as objects, and the mental factor of attention associated with perception. "Samudācaranti" means they arise or occur. "Dhammo" refers to the state of the first jhāna.

A person who declines from jhāna does so through these three causes: the arising of defilements (kilesasamudācāra), performing unsuitable acts (asappāyakiriyā), or lack of application (ananuyoga). One who declines due to the arising of defilements declines quickly. One who declines due to performing unsuitable acts—by way of delighting in work, delighting in talk, delighting in sleep, and delighting in company—declines slowly. One who declines due to lack of application—being unable to enter jhāna frequently because of impediments such as illness or lack of the four requisites—also declines slowly. In this Pali text, however, only the arising of defilements is mentioned, as the intention is to show the powerful cause. A person who declines from the second jhāna and so on may also decline due to the arising of attachment (nikanti) to lower jhānas.

To what extent is one said to have "declined"? The answer is: when one is no longer able to enter the jhāna, to that extent one is said to have declined. "Tadanudhammatā": a state that arises depending [on something] is called "anudhamma." This name "anudhamma" is a designation for the state of attachment (nikanti) that occurs depending on the jhāna. "Anudhamma" itself is "anudhammatā." Because it is a state depending on that jhāna, it is called "tadanudhammatā." "Satī" refers to attachment (nikanti). "Santiṭṭhati" means it stands or is established. It means that attachment arises and remains depending on that first jhāna.

"Avitakkasahagatā" refers to taking the second jhāna as an object. Because there is no initial application (vitakka) in that second jhāna, it is called "avitakka" (a jhāna without vitakka). "Nibbidāsahagatā" refers to taking insight (vipassanā) as an object. Because that insight is weary of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), it is called "nibbidā" (weariness). Is it not said: "One who is weary becomes dispassionate"? "Virāgူpasaṃhitā" refers to insight connected with the Noble Path. When insight reaches its peak, it leads to the emergence of the Path. Therefore, the perception and attention that take insight as an object are called "virāgူpasaṃhitā." Is it not said: "Through dispassion, one is liberated"?

"Vitakkasahagatā" refers to taking the first jhāna as an object by way of initial application (vitakka). "Upekkhāsukhasahagatā" refers to taking the third jhāna as an object by way of specific equanimity (tatramajjhattūpekkhā) and pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā). "Pītisukhasahagatā" refers to taking the second jhāna as an object by way of rapture (pīti) and pleasant feeling. "Adukkhamasukhasahagatā" refers to taking the fourth jhāna as an object by way of equanimity-feeling (upekkhāvedanā). Because that feeling is neither painful nor pleasant, it is called "adukkhamasukha."
131:
In this context, the letter 'm' is stated by way of euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). "Rūpasahagata" refers to states that have fine-material jhānas as their object. For one established in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), although the states of partaking in decline (hāna), stability (ṭhiti), and penetration (nibbedha) exist, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not mentioned [here] because it lacks the state of partaking in distinction (visesa).

All this mundane concentration (lokiya samādhi) is said to be:
Decline-partaking (hānabhāgiya) for one who dwells in negligence and has weak faculties (mudindriya).
Stability-partaking (ṭhitibhāgiya) for one who dwells in diligence and has weak faculties.
Distinction-partaking (visesabhāgiya) for one of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita) who has sharp faculties (tikkhindriya).
Penetration-partaking (nibbedhabhāgiya) for one of view-temperament (diṭṭhicarita) who has sharp faculties.

## End of the Explanation of the Fourfold Decline-partaking.

## Explanation of the Triad of Characteristics

Now, because every single mundane state is struck by the three characteristics, the triad of characteristics (lakkhaṇattika) is shown together. In that triad, "aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena" (impermanent in the sense of exhaustion) means it is impermanent because of the nature of being exhausted right where it arises. Some teachers say: "It is impermanent because of the nature of exhaustion, the nature of fall, the nature of fading away, and the nature of cessation."

"Dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena" (suffering in the sense of fear) means it is suffering because it is accompanied by fearsome danger. Whatever is impermanent is a source of fear, just as it was for the devas in the Sīhopama Sutta. Some teachers say: "It is suffering because of the sense of the fear of birth, aging, sickness, and death."

"Anattā asārakaṭṭhena" (non-self in the sense of corelessness) means it is non-self because of the absence of a self-core imagined as: "The self dwells within, it acts, it feels, it is self-governing." Since that which is impermanent and suffering cannot even prevent its own impermanence or the oppression of its own arising and falling, how could the state of being an agent (kāraka) and so on exist in it?

And it has been said: "Bhikkhus, if this form were self, this form would not lead to affliction," and so forth. Some teachers say: "It is non-self because it is devoid of a self-core and a permanent core."

## End of the Explanation of the Triad of Characteristics.

## Explanation of the Truth of Suffering

32-33. The four Noble Truths (ariyasacca) are also shown together because the truths are interconnected by way of their actual nature (tatha). In that [text], "tattha" means "among those four Noble Truths." "Katamaṃ" means [the question "Which?"].
132:
This is a question asked from a desire to speak (kathetukamyatāpucchā). The phrase "Dukkhaṃ Ariyasaccaṃ" is an indication of the Dhamma being asked. In the passages beginning with "jātipi dukkhā," many meanings of the word "jāti" are first shown. As it is said: "Existence, clan, group, virtue, designation, characteristic, parturition, and rebirth-linking are declared as the meanings of jāti."

To illustrate this, in the passages such as "ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo," the meaning is existence (bhava). In the phrase "akkhitto anupakkuṭṭho jātivādena," the meaning is clan (kula). In the phrase "atthi, visākhe, nigaṇṭhā nāma samaṇajātī," the meaning is group (nikāya). In the phrase "yatohaṃ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto nābhijānāmi," the meaning is the virtue (sīla) of the Noble Ones. In the phrase "tiriyā nāma tiṇajāti nābhiyā uggantvā nabhaṃ āhacca ဌိtā ahosi," the meaning is designation (paññatti). In the phrase "jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitā," the meaning is the characteristic of the conditioned (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa). In the phrase "sampatijāto, ānanda, bodhisatto," the meaning is parturition (pasūti). In the phrases "bhavapaccayā jāti" and "jātipi dukkhā," the meaning is the rebirth-linking aggregates (paṭisandhi-khandha) in a figurative sense (pariyāyato). In the literal sense (nippariyāyato), however, it is the first manifestation of whichever aggregates appear for beings being born in various states of existence.

If it is asked why this birth (jāti) is called suffering (dukkha), it is because it is the basis (cause) for many sufferings. Sufferings are many. They are: suffering as suffering (dukkha-dukkha), suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkha), suffering due to formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), concealed suffering (paṭicchanna-dukkha), unconcealed suffering (appaṭicchanna-dukkha), indirect suffering (pariyāya-dukkha), and direct suffering (nippariyāya-dukkha).

Among these, bodily and mental painful feeling is called 'suffering as suffering' because it is suffering both by nature and by name. Pleasant feeling is called 'suffering due to change' because it is a cause for the arising of suffering when it changes. Equanimous feeling and the remaining formations of the three planes are called 'suffering due to formations' because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. Bodily and mental ailments such as earache, toothache, the fever of lust, and the fever of hatred are called 'concealed suffering' (paṭicchanna-dukkha) because they can only be known by questioning and because the cause of the affliction is not obvious. Afflictions arising from the thirty-two types of torture and so forth are called 'unconcealed suffering' (appaṭicchanna-dukkha) because they can be known without questioning and because the cause of the affliction is obvious. Excluding suffering as suffering, the remaining...
133:
...all suffering such as birth (jāti) mentioned in the Analysis of the Truth of Suffering (Dukkhasacca-vibhaṅga, Vibhaṅga 190 etc.) is called indirect suffering (pariyāya-dukkha) because it is the basis for those respective sufferings. Intrinsic suffering (dukkha-dukkha), however, is called direct suffering (nippariyāya-dukkha).

Among these, birth (jāti) is suffering because it is the basis for the suffering of the states of woe (apāya) which the Blessed One illustrated by way of similes in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 3.246 etc.), and also for the various sufferings in the happy destination of the human world, such as those rooted in the descent into the womb (gabbhokkanti). Herein, this is the variety of suffering rooted in the descent into the womb: when this being is produced in the mother's womb, he is not produced in a red, white, or blue lotus, etc. On the contrary, he is produced like a worm in rotting fish, rotting dough, or a cesspool, in the region of the belly which is extremely cramped, pitch dark, permeated by the extremely foul stench of various corpses, and intensely loathsome, situated between the stomach (āmāsaya) below and the lower intestine (pakkāsaya) above, and between the abdominal membrane and the backbone. Having been produced there, for ten months he is cooked by the heat generated in the mother's womb like a medicinal poultice steamed in a leaf-wrap, or like a ball of dough being steamed; he undergoes intense suffering, deprived of the ability to stretch or bend his limbs. This is first of all the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb (gabbhokkanti-mūlaka-dukkha).

Furthermore, when the mother suddenly stumbles, walks, sits, stands, tosses, or turns, the being dwelling in the womb undergoes intense suffering through being pulled, dragged, shaken, and tossed, like a lamb in the hands of a drunkard or a young snake in the hands of a snake-charmer. Also, when the mother drinks cold water, he feels as if he were born in a cold hell; when she swallows hot gruel or rice, etc., he feels as if he were showered with a rain of embers; when she eats salty or sour food, etc., he feels as if he were undergoing the torture of being scraped with salt. This is the suffering rooted in the maintenance of the womb (gabbhapariharaṇa-mūlaka-dukkha).

Furthermore, when the mother has a malpresentation of the fetus (mūḷhagabbha), the child undergoes suffering through being cut or torn in a place of suffering so terrible that even friends and companions cannot bear to look. This is the suffering rooted in the failure of the womb (gabbhavipatti-mūlaka-dukkha).

When the mother is giving birth, the child, being turned upside down by the winds born of kamma, undergoes suffering as he is forced into the terrifying birth canal as if falling into a hellish pit; as he is dragged through the extremely narrow birth-opening like a great elephant being pulled through a keyhole, or like a hell-being being crushed by the mountains of the Saṅghāta hell. This is the suffering rooted in parturition (vijāyana-mūlaka-dukkha).
134:
When a newborn, who has a delicate body like a fresh wound, is handled by hands, bathed, washed, or wiped with a rough cloth, suffering arises like being pierced by the point of a needle or being cut by a razor's edge. This is suffering rooted in coming out from the mother's womb (bahinikkhamanamūlaka-dukkha).

Furthermore, in the course of life, the suffering that arises for one who tortures oneself, who exerts oneself in ascetic practices such as being unclothed, who does not eat out of anger, or who attempts suicide by hanging, is suffering rooted in one's own effort (attupakkamamūlaka-dukkha).

The suffering that arises for one who experiences being killed or bound by others is suffering rooted in the effort of others (parūpakkamamūlaka-dukkha). Thus, birth (jāti) is the very basis for all this suffering. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"If a being were not born in the hells,
Where would that unbearable suffering, such as the burning of fire, find a footing?
Therefore, the Sage here said that birth is suffering.

In the animal realm, there are many sufferings
Arising from being struck by whips, goads, sticks, and so forth.
How could that exist there without birth?
Birth is even more suffering than that.

Among the Petas, there are various sufferings
Arising from hunger, thirst, wind, sun, and so forth.
Since these do not exist for one who is not born there,
For that reason too, the Sage said that birth is suffering.

In the Lokantara hell, which is in intense darkness
And unbearable cold, and among the Asuras, the suffering that exists there
Would not occur if there were no birth.
Since this suffering arises because of birth, birth is indeed suffering."
135:
"The being stays for a long time in the mother's womb, which is like a cesspool hell, and then comes out; the being reaches this most dreadful suffering. This too cannot exist without birth; thus, birth is suffering. What is the use of much speaking? Whatever suffering exists anywhere in this world, it can never truly exist apart from birth. Therefore, the Great Sage spoke of birth first among all sufferings."

In the phrase "Aging is also suffering," aging is of two kinds: aging as a characteristic of the conditioned (saṅkhatalakkhaṇa), and aging as the state of decay of the aggregates included in a single existence within the continuity of aggregates, known by such things as broken teeth and so on. Here, the aging that is the decay of the aggregates is intended. That aging is suffering both because it is the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkha) and because it is a basis for suffering. For aging is the basis for the physical and mental suffering that arises due to many causes, such as the loosening of the limbs and organs, the transformation of the sense faculties, the disfigurement of the body, the destruction of youth, the impairment of strength, the loss of memory and intelligence, and being despised by others. Therefore, it is said:

"Because of the loosening of the limbs, because of the transformation of the sense faculties, because of the destruction of youth, and because of the impairment of strength;

Because of the loss of memory and so on, because of not being respected even by one's own children and wife, and because of becoming more like a child again;

Whatever suffering a mortal reaches, physical as well as mental, all this is caused by aging; therefore, aging is suffering."

Although the suffering of sickness (byādhi-dukkha) should be mentioned after the suffering of aging, it should be understood that it is not mentioned separately because it is already included by the mention of physical suffering (kāyikadukkha).

In the phrase "Death is also suffering," death is also of two kinds: death as a characteristic of the conditioned, with reference to which it is said, "Aging and death are included in two aggregates" (Dhātukathā 71); and the interruption of the continuity of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) included in a single existence, with reference to which it is said, "There is always fear of death" (Sutta Nipāta 581). That [latter] is intended here. Death conditioned by birth (jātipaccayamaraṇa), death by violence (upakkamamaraṇa), natural death (sarasamaraṇa), death through the exhaustion of the life-span (āyukkhayamaraṇa), and death through the exhaustion of merit (puññakkhayamaraṇa) are also names for that same interruption of the life-faculty. Furthermore, the distinctions of momentary death (khaṇikamaraṇa), conventional death (sammutimaraṇa), and death as cutting off (samucchedamaraṇa) should also be understood here. Of the material and immaterial states occurring in the course of existence...
136:
The dissolution (of mental and physical phenomena) is called momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa). The death referred to as "Tissa has died, Phussa has died" is called conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa) because, in the ultimate sense, no being exists. The death referred to as "the crop has died, the tree has died" is called conventional death because of the absence of the life faculty (jīvitindriya). The death of an Arahant, which involves no further rebirth, is called death by cutting off (samuccheda-maraṇa).

Excluding the external conventional death (of crops, trees, etc.), the remaining conventional death (of Tissa, Phussa, etc.) and death by cutting off are included within the cessation of the aforementioned continuity of the life faculty. Because it is a basis for suffering, it is called suffering (dukkha). Therefore, it is said:

"There is the mental suffering that arises when a person of evil deeds reaches death and sees signs such as their unwholesome kamma.
There is the mental suffering that arises when a virtuous person reaches death and cannot endure separation from beloved objects.
There is the bodily suffering that arises for all beings without distinction, whether evil or virtuous, when they are pierced by the winds that sever the joints and ligaments.
Because this death is the root cause of such unbearable and incurable suffering, this death is spoken of simply as suffering."

Among sorrow and so forth, sorrow (soka) is the burning of the mind characterized by inner consuming in one affected by the loss of relatives and so forth. That sorrow is called suffering because it is 'suffering as suffering' (dukkha-dukkha) and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

"Sorrow pierces the hearts of beings like a poisoned arrow;
Like a fire-heated iron spike, it burns intensely again and again.
Because that sorrow brings about various sufferings and diseases rooted in aging, death, and destruction, it is called suffering."

Lamentation (parideva) is the verbal wailing of one affected by the loss of relatives and so forth. That lamentation is called suffering because it is 'suffering in formations' (saṅkhāra-dukkha) and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

"Because one who wails, being struck by the spike of sorrow, reaches an unbearable and excessive suffering that causes the drying up of the throat, lips, and palate, the Blessed One has preached that lamentation is suffering."

Pain (dukkha) is bodily suffering characterized by bodily oppression. That pain is called suffering because it is 'suffering as suffering' and because it brings about mental suffering. Therefore, it is said:
137:
"Because this bodily pain oppresses the associated states and further generates mental pain, for that reason, it is specifically called suffering (dukkha)."

Grief (domanassa) is mental suffering characterized by oppression of the mind. That grief is called suffering because it is 'suffering as suffering' and because it brings about bodily suffering. Indeed, beings overwhelmed by mental suffering wail with disheveled hair, beat their breasts, roll about, fall down with feet upturned, stab themselves with weapons, swallow poison, hang themselves with ropes, and enter fires. Thus, they experience various kinds of suffering. Therefore, it is said:

"Because grief oppresses the mind and also brings about the oppression of the body,
Therefore, the virtuous ones such as the Buddha, who are free from grief,
Have declared that grief is suffering."

Despair (upāyāsa) is the very state of anger (dosa) produced by excessive mental suffering in one affected by the loss of relatives and so forth. Some teachers say, "It is a single state included within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)." That despair is called suffering because it is 'suffering in formations', because it causes the mind to burn, and because it causes the body to become exhausted. Therefore, it is said:

"Because of the burning of the mind and the exhaustion of the body,
Despair generates excessive suffering;
Therefore, it is called suffering."

Among these, sorrow should be understood like the cooking of something in a pot over a weak fire. Lamentation should be understood like the boiling over from the pot when cooked over a strong fire. Despair should be understood like what remains after boiling over, which, being unable to come out, continues to cook inside the pot until it dries up.

Association with the unloved (appiya-sampayoga) is meeting and being together with unpleasant beings and formations. That association with the unloved is called suffering because it is a root cause of suffering. Therefore, it is said:

"In this world, merely by seeing those who are unloved, suffering first arises in the mind;
From that, suffering subsequently arises in the body.
Therefore, because it is the root cause of both bodily and mental suffering,
The Great Sage has declared that meeting with the unloved is suffering."

Separation from the loved (piya-vippayoga) is being parted from pleasant beings and formations. That separation from the loved is also called suffering because it is a root cause of suffering. Therefore, it is said:
138:
“Because of separation from relatives, wealth, and so forth, fools who are pierced by the arrow of sorrow are tormented. Therefore, this separation from the loved ones is understood as suffering.”

Regarding the failure to obtain a desired object, the very desire for unattainable things is stated as: “Whatever one desires but does not get, that too is suffering.” It means that when one desires an unattainable object (such as freedom from aging and death) through a certain state but does not obtain it, that desire for the unattainable object is the cause of suffering. Suffering arises because of the object of suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“In this world, for beings who long for various objects, that suffering which consists of mental exhaustion arises because of the failure to obtain those objects.
Since longing for unattainable objects is the cause of that suffering, the Victorious Buddha declared that not getting what one wants is suffering.”

In the statement, “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering,” the phrase “in brief” is said with reference to the teaching (desanā). For it is not possible to summarize suffering itself as being so many hundreds or thousands of types of suffering, but it is possible to summarize the teaching. Therefore, the Buddha, wishing to summarize the teaching, said: “Suffering is nothing else; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.” “Five” is the delimitation of number. “Aggregates of clinging” (upādānakkhandhā) means the aggregates that are the domain of clinging.

“The suffering beginning with birth that is mentioned here by the Such-like One, and all that suffering which is not mentioned, do not exist apart from these [aggregates].
Therefore, the Great Sage (Mahesi), the teacher of the end of suffering, declared these aggregates of clinging to be suffering in brief.”

Indeed, just as fire afflicts fuel, as weapons afflict a target, as gadflies and mosquitoes afflict a herd of cattle, as reapers afflict the crop, and as bandits destroy a village, so do birth and the rest afflict the five aggregates of clinging in various ways. Just as grass and creepers grow on the earth, and as flowers, fruits, and sprouts grow on trees, so do birth and the rest arise only in the aggregates of clinging. Among the aggregates of clinging, the initial suffering is birth (jāti), the middle suffering is aging (jarā), and the final suffering is death (maraṇa); it is the suffering of burning caused by the affliction of the suffering at the time of death.
139:
Lamentation (parideva) is the suffering of wailing due to the inability to bear the suffering known as sorrow (soka). Furthermore, pain (dukkha) is the suffering of bodily affliction due to contact with undesirable tactile objects, which is called the disturbance of the elements. Grief (domanassa) is the suffering of mental affliction or mental pain that arises from aversion toward that bodily pain in worldlings (puthujjana) who are oppressed by it. Despair (upāyāsa) is the suffering of dejection or moaning produced by the increase of sorrow and so forth. Not getting what one wants (icchitālābha) is the suffering of the exhaustion of desire, which occurs in beings who have reached the exhaustion of their heart's desire because they do not obtain what they want. When investigated in these various ways, only the aggregates of clinging are suffering. If that suffering were to be shown and explained one by one, it would not be possible to speak of it exhaustively even in many aeons. Just as the taste of the entire ocean's water is summarized in a single drop of water, the Elder spoke, conveying the words of the Blessed One: “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering,” in order to show all suffering by summarizing it within any of the five aggregates of clinging.

In the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya) beginning with “What is birth?”, the word “therein” (tattha) refers to birth and so forth mentioned in the exposition of the Truth of Suffering. The phrase “of those various beings” (tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ) is a summary description common to many beings. If one were to speak all day long of “the birth of Devadatta, the birth of Somadatta,” beings would never be exhausted, nor would the illustration of birth in other beings be complete. However, by these two words [“of those, of those”], no being is left out, and the illustration of the other meaning is indeed accomplished. The phrase “in this or that [group of beings]” (tamhi tamhi) is a general description common to many groups of beings by way of realm (gati) and birth (jāti). “Group of beings” (sattanikāya) means a collection of beings, a multitude of beings, or a group of beings. “Birth” (jāti) is so called by way of being born. This is the individual essence (sabhāva) here. “San-jāti” is by way of being born well; the word is expanded by the prefix ‘saṃ’. “Descent” (okkanti) is by way of entering [the womb]. Alternatively, it is called jāti in the sense of being born, which is said in terms of a being with incomplete sense bases. It is called sañjāti in the sense of being born well, which is said in terms of a being with complete sense bases. It is called okkanti in the sense of descending, which is said in terms of egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings. For they descend into the egg-shell or the womb-casing; while descending, they take rebirth as if entering. It is called abhinibbatti in the sense of appearing, which is said in terms of moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneous-birth (opapātika) beings. For they are born by appearing clearly. This is first the conventional discourse (sammuti-kathā).

Now, the words “the manifestation of the aggregates, the acquisition of the sense bases” constitute the ultimate discourse (paramattha-kathā). For in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates manifest, not beings. Here, “of the aggregates” (khandhānaṃ) should be understood as taking one aggregate in one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava), four in four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), and all five in five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). “Manifestation” (pātubhāvo) means arising.
140:
"Āyatanānaṃ" (of the bases) should be understood as the inclusion by way of the sense bases arising in various existences. "Paṭilābha" (acquisition) means the manifestation in the continuity. Indeed, when those bases manifest, they are said to be acquired. "Ayaṃ vuccati jāti" (this is called birth) means this aforementioned nature is called birth (jāti).
