In the exposition of aging (jarā-niddesa), the word "Jarā" is a specific term expressing the nature itself. "Jīraṇatā" (decaying) is the description of the mode of aging. The three terms starting with "Khaṇḍicca" (brokenness) are descriptions of the function occurring with the passage of time. The last two terms are descriptions of the natural state of aging. In fact, this aging is expressed by its nature with the word "Jarā"; therefore, this is the specific term for its nature. It is expressed by its mode with the word "Jīraṇatā"; therefore, this is the description of the mode. It is expressed by the function of causing teeth and nails to break over time with the word "Khaṇḍicca". It is expressed by the function of making hair and body hair turn gray with the word "Pālicca". It is expressed by the function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to wrinkle with the word "Valittacatā". Therefore, these three terms are descriptions of the function occurring with the passage of time. Through these terms, by seeing such alterations, "evident aging" (pākaṭa-jarā) is shown.

Indeed, just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire becomes evident through the breaking of grass and trees or by charring—yet that path is not the water, wind, or fire itself—likewise, the path of aging becomes evident in the teeth and so on by way of brokenness, etc., and can be perceived just by opening the eyes; however, that brokenness and so on are not aging itself. In truth, aging is not an object directly cognizable by the eye.

With the two terms "Āyuno saṃhāni" (decline of life) and "Indriyānaṃ paripāko" (ripening of the faculties), aging is shown by its natural state, characterized by the exhaustion of life and the ripening of the eye-faculty and others, which become very evident with the passage of time. Thus, these two should be understood as descriptions of the natural state of aging. In this context, because the life of one who has reached old age declines, aging is called "decline of life" by way of phalūpacāra (metonymy of result for cause). And because the eye-faculty and others, which were very clear in youth and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects, become ripe, turbid, and unclear upon reaching old age—unable to grasp even gross objects—aging is called "ripening of the faculties" by way of phalūpacāra.

All such aging thus described is of two kinds: evident aging (pākaṭa-jarā) and concealed aging (paṭicchanna-jarā). Among them, aging in material phenomena (rūpadhamma) is called evident aging because the state of brokenness in teeth and so on is seen. However, aging in immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) is [concealed] because such alteration...
141:
Because it is not seen, it is called concealed aging (paṭicchannajarā). In these material aging processes, the state of broken teeth and so forth is evident; that state is merely the appearance (rūpāyatana) of such things as teeth. Seeing that appearance with the eye and reflecting upon it through the mind-door, one knows aging, thinking, 'These teeth have been struck by aging.' It is like observing ox horns and such tied in a place where there is water and thereby knowing the presence of water below.

Again, this aging is of two kinds: intermittent aging (savīci-jarā) and continuous aging (avīci-jarā). Among these, in gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, etc., and in beings in stages such as the 'slow decade' (manda-dasaka), and in non-sentient formations such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts, the distinction of color etc. in the intervals is difficult to know; therefore, that aging is called continuous aging (avīci-jarā), meaning aging without interval. In other beings and formations mentioned, the distinction of color etc. in the intervals is easy to know; therefore, that aging is called intermittent aging (savīci-jarā).

Among these two, intermittent aging should be understood through the power of grasped matter (upādiṇṇaka) and ungrasped matter (anupādiṇṇaka). For very young children, milk teeth first arise; they are not firm. When those milk teeth fall out, permanent teeth arise again. They are white at first; when struck by the wind of aging, they become black. Hair is first red, then black, then white. Skin is with a reddish hue. As they grow, the whiteness of the white and the blackness of the black become evident. But when struck by the wind of aging, the skin takes on wrinkles. All crops are white when sown, then green. When struck by the wind of aging, they become pale. This can also be shown by mango sprouts.

In the description of death, it is called 'passing away' (cuti) by way of shifting. This word 'passing away' is a general term connected with one, four, or five aggregates. The word 'state of passing' (cavanatā) shows the characteristic of death. The word 'breaking up' (bheda) shows the destruction of the aggregates at the time of passing. The word 'disappearance' (antaradhāna) shows that the aggregates at passing have no place to stay by any means, just as a broken pot has no place. 'Death as the Lord of Death' (maccu-maraṇa) is the death called 'Maccu' (the cessation of the life faculty), not momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa). 'Time' (kāla) refers to the aggregate that makes an end; the destruction of that aggregate is 'making one's time' (kālakiriyā). By this sequence of words, death is shown by way of conventional usage (sammuti).

Now, to show it by way of ultimate sense (paramattha), He said 'the breaking up of the aggregates' (khandhānaṃ bheda) and so forth. Truly, in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates break up; no 'being' dies. However, when the aggregates are breaking up, there is the usage 'a being dies,' and when they have broken up, 'a being has died.' Here, 'the breaking up of the aggregates' should be understood by way of the four-constituent and five-constituent existence. 'The laying down of the carcass' (kaḷevarassa nikkhepa) should be understood by way of the one-constituent existence. Or, 'the breaking up of the aggregates' by way of the four-constituent existence, and 'the laying down of the carcass' by way of the remaining two (one and five-constituent existence). Why? Because in both five-constituent and one-constituent existence, the carcass called the material body (rūpa-kāya) is evident.
142:
Because the carcass called the material body is evident. Or else, in the realms of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) and so forth, the aggregates indeed break up, but they do not leave any carcass behind. Therefore, by way of those devas, it is 'the breaking up of the aggregates' (khandhānaṃ bheda); in the case of humans and so forth, it is 'the laying down of the carcass' (kaḷevarassa nikkhepa). Because death performs the act of laying down the carcass, it is called 'the laying down of the carcass'.

'The cutting off of the life faculty' (jīvitindriyassupaccheda)—by this phrase, He shows that death occurs only for beings connected with faculties (indriya), and there is no such thing as death for things not connected with faculties (such as crops and trees). To say 'the crop has died' or 'the tree has died' is merely conventional usage. In meaning, such words only indicate the exhaustion and disappearance of crops and so forth.

Furthermore, these states of birth, aging, and death wander about seeking an opportunity like murderous enemies of these beings. For example, among three enemies seeking an opportunity to oppress a man, one enemy might say: 'I will speak of the beauty and virtues of such-and-such a forest and, taking this man, go there; this is not difficult for me.' The second enemy might say: 'When you have taken that man to the forest, I will beat him and make him weak; this is not difficult for me.' The third enemy might say: 'When you have beaten him and made him weak, let it be my task to cut off his head with a sharp sword.' Having consulted thus, they act accordingly. In that simile, the first enemy's speaking of the forest's virtues and taking him there is like the function of birth (jāti), which pulls one away from the circle of beloved relatives and causes one to be born in some existence. The second enemy's beating and making him weak is like the function of aging (jarā), which falls upon the arisen aggregates, oppressing them and making one dependent on others or bedridden. The third enemy's cutting off the head with a sharp sword is like the function of death (maraṇa), which brings about the destruction of life.

Furthermore, here, the suffering of birth (jāti-dukkha) should be seen as entering a great forest full of dangers. The suffering of aging (jarā-dukkha) should be seen as being weak in that forest due to lack of food and drink. The suffering of death (maraṇa-dukkha) should be seen as the infliction of calamity and ruin by wild beasts and so forth upon that person who is weak, unable even to move his postures, and whose effort is destroyed.

In the description of sorrow, it is called 'ruin' (byasana) because it 'destroys' (viyasati). It means it destroys welfare and happiness. The ruin of relatives is 'loss of relatives' (ñāti-byasana). It means the exhaustion and destruction of relatives due to the danger of thieves, the danger of disease, and so forth.
143:
It means the destruction of relatives. 'Touched by that loss of relatives' (phuṭṭhassa) means for a person who is overwhelmed, oppressed, or possessed [by it]. The same method applies to the remaining losses (byasana). However, this is the distinction: the destruction of wealth and possessions is called 'loss of wealth' (bhogabyasana); it means the exhaustion or destruction of wealth through kings, thieves, and so on. Illness itself is a loss, thus 'loss through illness' (rogabyasana). Indeed, illness is called a loss (byasana) because it destroys health (ārogya). The destruction of virtue is 'loss of virtue' (sīlabyasana). This is a name for immorality (dussīlya). The wrong view that arises while destroying right view is 'loss of view' (diṭṭhibyasana). Among these five losses, the first two are not produced [by kamma/causes in a specific sense], while the last three are produced and are struck by the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa). The first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; only the two—loss of virtue and loss of view—are unwholesome.

'Aññataraññatarena' means through any one of the five losses mentioned, or through any of those not included here, such as the loss of friends and ministers. 'Samannāgatassa' means for a person who is followed by or not freed from [them]. 'Aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena' means through any cause for the arising of the suffering known as sorrow. 'Soka' (sorrow) is so called because of the act of grieving. This is a term showing the individual essence of sorrow that arises due to those causes. 'Socanā' is the manner of grieving. 'Socitatta' is the state of having grieved. 'Antosoka' is internal sorrow. The second term is expanded by a prefix. Because that sorrow arises as if drying up the inside, as if parching it from all around, it is called 'internal sorrow, internal parching' (antosoka antoparisoka). 'Cetaso parijjhāyanā' is the manner of the mind's burning. Indeed, when sorrow arises, it burns the mind like fire; it makes one say, 'My mind is burnt, nothing appears to me anymore.' A mind that has reached suffering is called 'distressed' (dummana); the state of that mind is 'displeasure' (domanassa). Sorrow itself is called the 'dart of sorrow' (sokasalla) because of its sense of repeatedly piercing.

In the explanation of lamentation (parideva): it is called 'ādeva' because of crying out by referring again and again to 'my daughter, my son,' and so on. It is called 'parideva' because of wailing by repeatedly praising various qualities. The two pairs of terms following these are stated by way of explaining the manner and nature of the first two terms. 'Vācā' means speech. 'Palāpa' means vain and meaningless talk. It is called 'vippalāpa' (distorted lamentation) because it is a distorted wailing by way of half-spoken words or speaking in various ways. 'Lālappa' means repeated wailing. The manner of repeated wailing is 'lālappanā'. The state of having wailed repeatedly is 'lālappitatta'.
144:
In the explanation of pain (dukkha): It is called 'bodily' (kāyika) because it depends on the body. It is called 'unpleasant' (asāta) because of its disagreeable nature. By the word 'bodily', mental unpleasantness is excluded; by the word 'unpleasant', bodily pleasure is excluded. That very [unpleasantness] is called 'pain' (dukkha) because it causes suffering (dukkhayati); it means it makes the person in whom it arises suffer. Or, it is called dukkha because it is difficult to endure. 'Born of bodily contact' (kāyasamphassaja) means it is produced in bodily contact. 'Unpleasant painful feeling' (asātaṃ dukkhaṃ vedayitaṃ) means: unpleasant feeling is asāta; painful feeling is dukkha. The three terms following are stated in the feminine gender. Unpleasant feeling is asāta, painful feeling is dukkha—this alone is the meaning here. The construction should be understood thus: 'That bodily unpleasant painful feeling, that unpleasant painful feeling born of bodily contact, this is called pain (dukkha).'

In the explanation of displeasure (domanassa): It is called 'dummana' because of having a bad mind; or, it is called 'dummana' as a loathsome mind due to inferior feeling. The state of being 'dummana' is 'domanassa'. It is called 'mental' (cetasika) because it depends on the mind. 'Born of mental contact' (cetosamphassaja) means it is produced in the contact of the mind (cittasamphassa).

In the explanation of despair (upāyāsa): It is called 'āyāsa' in the sense of trouble or exhaustion. This is a name for the mental fatigue that occurs in the manner of despondency and exhaustion. Intense trouble is 'upāyāsa'. The state of having reached trouble is 'āyāsitatta'. The state of having reached intense trouble is 'upāyāsitatta'.

In the explanation of association with the unloved (appiyasampayoga): 'Here' (idha) means in this world. 'Yassa' means to whom there are. 'Aniṭṭha' means undesired objects. Whether they are sought or not, it is just a name for disagreeable objects. They are called 'unlovely' (akanta) because they do not enter (settle in) the mind [pleasantly]. They are called 'disagreeable' (amanāpa) because they are not liked by the mind or they do not increase [the joy of] the mind. 'Forms and so on' is an illustration of the nature of those undesired objects. They are called 'anatthakāma' because they desire harm (suffering). They are called 'ahitakāma' because they desire what is not beneficial. They are called 'aphāsukāma' because they desire uncomfortable living (dukkha-vihāra). They are called 'ayogakkhemakāma' because they do not desire the state free from fear (Nibbāna) which is detached from the four bonds (yoga), but desire only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) which is accompanied by fear. Alternatively, they are 'anatthakāma' because they do not desire the benefit (attha) known as the growth of faith and so on, but desire the harm (anattha) known as the decline of those very things. They are 'ahitakāma' because they do not desire the welfare (hita) which is the means for faith and so on, but desire the non-welfare (ahita) which is the means for the decline of faith and so on.
145:
They are called 'aphāsukāmā' because they do not desire to live comfortably and because they desire to live uncomfortably. They are called 'ayogakkhemakāmā' because they do not desire the state of being free from danger and because they desire the presence of danger; this is how the meaning should be understood in this context.

'Saṅgati' means going and associating. 'Samāgama' means meeting with (unpleasant beings and formations) that have arrived. 'Samodhāna' means being together in standing, sitting, and so forth. 'Missībhāva' means performing all tasks together. This is the connection in terms of beings. In terms of formations (saṅkhāra), whatever (saṅgati, samāgama) is obtained should be taken. That 'association with the unloved' (appiya-sampayoga) does not exist as a single ultimate reality (dhamma) in itself; it is called suffering (dukkha) merely because it is the cause of the two kinds of suffering (physical and mental pain) that arise in those who encounter unloved beings and formations.

The 'explanation of dissociation from the loved' (piya-vippayoga-niddesa) should be understood by the method opposite to what has been stated. In this context, the words 'mātā vā' (or mother) etc., are spoken to specifically show those who desire one's welfare. In that text, she is called 'mātā' (mother) because she cherishes; he is called 'pitā' (father) because he loves. He is called 'bhātā' (brother) because he associates; likewise, she is called 'bhaginī' (sister). They are called 'mittā' (friends) because they love, or they are called 'mittā' because they include one in all secrets. They are called 'amaccā' (ministers/companions) in the sense of being together in duties to be performed. They are called 'ñātī' (relatives) because they know, or are known, as 'this person is our inner person'. They are called 'sālohitā' (blood-relations) because they are connected by blood. Relatives from the father's side are called 'ñātī', and relatives from the mother's side are called 'sālohitā'. Alternatively, relatives from both parents' sides are called 'ñātī', and relatives from the in-laws' side are called 'sālohitā'. This 'dissociation from the loved' also does not exist as a single ultimate reality in itself; it is called suffering merely because it is the cause of the two kinds of suffering that arise in those who are separated from loved beings and formations. This is the statement of all Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) in this regard. However, since the Truths have the characteristic of being as they are, it is appropriate to say that the words 'association' and 'dissociation' specifically distinguish the unloved objects and loved objects themselves.

In the 'explanation of not getting what one wants' (icchitālābha-niddesa), 'jātidhammānaṃ' means for beings who have the nature of birth, who are subject to birth. 'Icchā uppajjati' means craving (taṇhā) arises. 'Aho vata' is a wish. 'Assāma' means 'if only we could be'. 'Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ' means 'Oh, it would be good if we were not subject to birth; it would be good if birth did not come to us'. This state of non-birth, which is evident in the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have abandoned the origin (samudaya), and the non-coming of birth, which is evident in those like the Buddha who have attained Parinibbāna, is what is desired. Even though one desires it, it is not something to be attained by mere wishing because it cannot be attained without the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā), and it can be attained through the development of the Path even without wishing. 'Idampi' also refers to this matter. The word 'api' is used in reference to the remaining 'subject to aging' (jarā-dhamma), 'subject to illness' (byādhi-dhamma), and so forth mentioned above.
146:
In the 'explanation of the aggregates of clinging' (upādānakkhandha-niddesa), the word 'seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable; the meaning of that indeclinable 'seyyathidaṃ' should be understood as 'which are those aggregates of clinging?'. The aggregate of materiality itself is called 'rūpupādānakkhandha' because it is the aggregate that is the object of the four types of clinging. The same method applies to the remaining aggregates, such as 'vedanupādānakkhandha' (the aggregate of feeling as an object of clinging) and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Suffering is Finished.

## Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Origin of Suffering

In the 'explanation of the Truth of the Origin of Suffering', the phrase 'yāyaṃ taṇhā' should be analyzed as 'yā ayaṃ taṇhā' (this craving which...). 'Ponobbhavikā' means that which makes renewed existence (punobbhava); because that craving has the habit of making renewed existence, it is called 'ponobbhavikā'. Alternatively, it is called 'ponobbhavikā' because it gives renewed existence, because it leads to renewed existence, or because it causes existence to arise again and again. Among such cravings, there is craving that gives renewed existence and craving that does not. There is craving that leads to renewed existence and craving that does not. There is also craving that, once rebirth has been given, has the karma to produce results in the substratum (upadhi) known as the resultant mental aggregates. Craving with these three varieties receives the name 'ponobbhavikā'. There is also the reading 'ponabbhavikā', and the meaning is the same.

It is called 'nandirāgasahagatā' because it occurs together with 'nandirāga', which is called 'extreme delight'. It means that it has reached the state of being one with 'nandirāga' in terms of essence. 'Tatra tatrābhinandinī' means that in whatever existence (attabhāva) it arises, it takes extreme delight in that particular existence. Alternatively, among objects such as visible forms, it takes extreme delight in those various objects. The meaning is that it delights in visible forms, and it takes extreme delight in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. There is also the reading 'tatra tatrābhinandī', which means it causes the mental states associated with itself to take extreme delight in those various realms of existence.

'Seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable; the meaning should be understood as 'what is that craving?'. 'Kāma-taṇhā' is craving for sensual objects; it is a designation for the lust (rāga) that is attached to the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Bhava-taṇhā' is craving for existence. It is a designation for the lust that arises through the wish for existence and is accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), as well as for the lust for fine-material existence and immaterial existence, and for the attachment to jhāna. 'Vibhava-taṇhā' is craving for non-existence; it is a designation for the lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

Now, in order to show the basis of that craving in detail, the text says 'sā kho panesā' and so forth. Therein, 'uppajjati' means it arises. 'Nivisati' means it establishes itself by way of occurring again and again. The connection should be understood as: 'When it arises, where does it arise? When it establishes itself, where does it establish itself?'. 'Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ' means 'whatever in the world has a lovable nature and a pleasant nature...'
147:
(That craving) is of a nature to be loved and a nature to be enjoyed. In the phrases "In the world, the eye..." and so on, the meaning should be understood as follows: In the world of beings, those beings who are attached to the eye and so forth with the notion of "mine," and who are established in worldly prosperity, regard their own eye as being extremely clear—like a lion-casement window adorned with jewels opened in a golden mansion—following the observation of reflections in mirrors and such, clear with the five colors. They regard the ear as like a silver tube or like a fine thread of an ornament. They regard the nose, which is called "high-nosed," as like a stick of yellow orpiment that has been rounded and placed. They regard the tongue as like a bright red woolen sheet, soft, smooth, and providing excellent taste. They regard the body as like a young Sal tree or like a golden archway. They regard the mind as noble and expansive, unlike the minds of others. They regard [visual] form as like the color of gold or the color of the Kaṇikāra flower, etc. They regard sound as like the song of the Karavīka bird intoxicated with nectar, the song of the cuckoo, or the sound of a jeweled flute softly blown. Regarding smells and so forth produced by the four causes which they have obtained, they think, "Who else besides me would have such objects?" To those beings who think in this way, those things such as the eye are of a nature to be loved and a nature to be enjoyed. Then, craving that has not yet arisen arises in those beings regarding those eyes and so forth, and craving that has already arisen remains latent by way of repeated occurrence. Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta said: "In the world, the eye is of a nature to be loved and a nature to be enjoyed; here this craving, when arising, arises," and so on. In that Pali, "when arising" means at whatever time it arises, at that time it arises in this (thing which is loved and enjoyed).

## End of the Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Origin.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation

In the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation, regarding the Pali "the cessation of that very craving," it should have been said "the cessation of that very suffering." The reason is that suffering ceases only through the cessation of the origin (samudaya), and not by any other means. As the Buddha said:

"Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again as long as its root is firm and unharmed, so also, as long as the latent tendency of craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again." (Dhp. 338).

Therefore, the Buddha, wishing to show the cessation of suffering, spoke thus to show it by way of the cessation of the origin. For the Tathāgatas have conduct like that of a lion. When those Buddhas cause suffering to cease and show the cessation of suffering, they practice regarding the cause, not the effect. But the outsiders (titthiyas) have conduct like that of a dog. When they wish to cause suffering to cease or show the cessation of suffering, they practice only regarding the effect by exhausting the body, not regarding the cause. Because of this lion-like conduct, the Buddha, wishing to practice only regarding the cause, said "of that very craving," etc. The Venerable Sāriputta also spoke following the order taught by the Buddha.

In that Pali, "of that very craving" means of that very craving which was taught as "leading to rebirth" (ponobhavikā), classified as sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), etc., and shown below in the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering by way of occurrence and establishment. In the phrase "fading away and cessation without remainder" (asesavirāganirodho), the Path is called "fading away" (virāga). This is because it is said, "one is liberated because of the fading away of lust." The cessation of craving through the Path is called "fading away and cessation" (virāga-nirodha). Alternatively, "fading away" means abandoning, so it can be applied in this phrase as "abandoning without remainder" and "cessation without remainder." In terms of meaning, according to their nature, these terms such as "fading away and cessation without remainder" are just synonyms for Nibbāna. In the ultimate sense, Nibbāna is called "the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering." Because craving completely fades away and ceases by taking Nibbāna as an object and reaching it, that Nibbāna is called the cessation of that craving. Alternatively, by taking Nibbāna as an object...
148:
Other sectarians who are outside the Dispensation, even when they bring about the cessation of the truth of suffering or show the cessation of suffering, they practice only in the effect of craving through self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) and by teaching only that self-mortification; they do not practice in the cause, which is craving. Because He has the conduct of a lion, the Teacher, wishing to practice only in the cause of craving, spoke the words beginning with "Yo tassāyeva." The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, also spoke in the same order as taught by the Teacher.

In the phrase "tassāyeva taṇhāya," it refers to that very craving which was described below (in the exposition of the truth of suffering) as "leading to rebirth" (ponobhavikā), analyzed as sensual craving and so on, and shown by way of its arising and establishing. "Asesavirāganirodho": here, "virāga" (dispassion) means the Path. Is it not said, "Through dispassion, one is liberated"? The cessation of craving through the Path is called "virāga-nirodha." The absolute cessation due to the total uprooting of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) is called "asesavirāganirodha." Alternatively, "virāga" means abandoning (pahāna). Therefore, the construction of the meaning in this term should be understood as absolute abandoning and absolute cessation.

In terms of meaning, all these terms beginning with "asesavirāganirodha" are synonymous names for Nibbāna. In the ultimate sense, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering refers to Nibbāna. Since craving is absolutely faded away and ceased upon reaching (taking as object) that Nibbāna, it is called "the absolute fading away and cessation of that craving." By taking Nibbāna as the object, craving is given up, relinquished, released, and no longer clings. In this Nibbāna, there is not even a single abode (ālaya) among the abodes of the cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, Nibbāna is called giving up (cāga), relinquishment (paṭinissagga), release (mutti), and non-attachment (anālaya). Although Nibbāna is one, it has many names by way of being the opposite of the names of all conditioned things. They are: absolute fading away, absolute cessation, giving up, relinquishment, release, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless (animitta), the desireless (appaṇihita), non-exertion (anāyūhana), non-rebirth, non-production, non-destination, the unborn, the unaging, the unailing, the deathless (amata), the sorrowless, the lamentationless, the despairless, the undefiled, and so on.

Now, in order to show the absence of craving in those objects where its arising was shown, even for craving that has reached non-occurrence by being cut off by the Path and taking Nibbāna as the object, He spoke the words beginning with "Sā kho panesā." In this regard, for example, a man might see a bitter gourd vine growing in a field, and searching from the tip to the root, he would cut it. That vine would gradually wither and reach a state of disappearance. Then it would be said that the bitter gourd in that field has ceased and been abandoned. Similarly, craving arises in the eye and so on, which are like the field. When that craving is cut off by the Noble Path, it reaches non-occurrence by taking Nibbāna as the object...
149:
Craving that arises in the eye and so forth is like a bitter creeper. When this craving is cut at the root by the Noble Path, it reaches non-occurrence by taking Nibbāna as its object. When it reaches this state of non-occurrence, it is no longer evident in the bases (vatthu) which are the causes of that craving, just like a bitter creeper in a field. Just as when thieves are caught in a forest and executed at the south gate of a city, it is said, "The thieves in the forest are dead" or "have been killed," even so, craving that arises in the eye and so forth, which is like the thieves in the forest, is said to be ceased in Nibbāna because it has ceased by taking Nibbāna as its object, like the thieves at the south gate. When it has ceased in this way, it is no longer evident in those bases, just like the thieves in the forest. Therefore, desiring to show the cessation of that craving in those very bases, it was said: "In the world, the eye is of a lovable and pleasant nature; here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned," and so forth. Alternatively, because the base for the arising of craving has been fully understood (pariññāta), it is said to cease in the very base where craving arises by way of cessation through non-arising (anuppādanirodha), as it no longer arises in the fully understood base. Here, it is said to be "abandoned" by way of being the opposite of arising, and "ceased" by way of being the opposite of adhering and persisting.

## The Description of the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation is finished.

## Description of the Exposition of the Truth of the Path

In the exposition of the Truth of the Path, the word "ayam-eva" (this very [path]) has the meaning of restriction, for the purpose of excluding any other path. It is called "ariya" (noble) because it is far from the defilements abandoned by each respective path, because it makes one a noble one (ariya), and because it causes the attainment of the noble fruition (ariyaphala). It is called "aṭṭhaṅgika" (eightfold) because it has eight factors. This path is merely a collection of factors, like an army with four divisions or an orchestra with five instruments; there is no path separate from its factors.

Now, desiring to show that the path is merely a collection of factors and does not exist separately from them, he said: "Right View ... Right Concentration," and so forth. Among them, that which has the characteristic of seeing rightly is Right View. That which has the characteristic of right application [of the mind] is Right Intention. That which has the characteristic of right grasping is Right Speech. That which has the characteristic of right origination is Right Action. That which has the characteristic of right purification is Right Livelihood. That which has the characteristic of right exertion is Right Effort. That which has the characteristic of right establishment is Right Mindfulness. That which has the characteristic of right concentration is Right Concentration. Each of these path factors has three functions. They are:
150:
First, Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) abandons wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) along with other defilements (kilesas) that are its opposites. It also takes Nibbāna as its object. By dispelling the delusion (moha) that covers Nibbāna, it perceives the associated states (sampayutta-dhammas) without confusion. Similarly, the path factors starting with Right Intention (Sammāsaṅkappa) also abandon wrong intention (micchāsaṅkappa) and so forth, and take Nibbāna as their object.

Specifically, among these eight path factors, Right Intention (Sammāsaṅkappa) properly directs the co-nascent states (sahajāta-dhammas) [towards the object]. Right Speech (Sammāvācā) properly grasps. Right Action (Sammākammanta) properly initiates. Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva) properly purifies. Right Effort (Sammāvāyāma) properly upholds. Right Mindfulness (Sammāsati) properly establishes. Right Concentration (Sammāsamādhi) properly concentrates.

Furthermore, this Right View, in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga/insight period), occurs at various moments and with various objects. However, at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), it occurs in a single moment with a single object (Nibbāna). In terms of function, it receives four names such as "knowledge of suffering" (dukkhe ñāṇa) and so forth. The path factors starting with Right Intention also occur at various moments and with various objects in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Path, they occur in a single moment with a single object. Among those path factors, Right Intention receives three names in terms of function, such as "intention of renunciation" (nekkhamma-saṅkappa). The three path factors starting with Right Speech are both abstinences (virati) and volitions (cetanā) in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the Path, however, they are only abstinences. These two, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, each receive four names in terms of function by way of the Right Strivings (sammappadhāna) and the Foundations of Mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). As for Right Concentration, it is called Right Concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path.

Thus, among these eight factors, the Blessed One taught Right View first because it is of great benefit to the practitioner (yogī) who is practicing to attain Nibbāna. This Right View is also taught as "the light of wisdom" and "the weapon of wisdom." Therefore, by dispelling the darkness of ignorance (avijjā) with this Right View, known as insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in the preliminary stage, and by slaying the thieves of defilements, the practitioner (yogāvacara) reaches the secure Nibbāna. For this reason, Right View was taught first.

Right Intention is of great benefit to that Right View. Therefore, Right Intention was taught immediately after Right View. How? Just as a money-changer, turning a coin over and over in his hand and looking at it with his eyes, knows, "This coin is counterfeit, this coin is genuine"; in the same way, the practitioner, thinking over and over with thought (vitakka) in the preliminary stage and looking with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), knows, "These states are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), these states are of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)," and so forth. Or, in another way, just as a woodworker, hewing with an adze a large tree that has been turned over and over by a man holding it at the end...
151:
...and brings it to the task; in the same way, the practitioner, having reflected over and over with thought (vitakka) and having distinguished the states presented with wisdom (paññā) as "these states are of the sense-sphere, these states are of the fine-material sphere," and so forth, brings them to the task of insight (vipassanā). Therefore, Right Intention (Sammāsaṅkappa) was taught immediately after Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi).

That Right Intention is beneficial to Right Speech (Sammāvācā) just as it is to Right View. As it was said: "Householder, first one thinks and ponders, and afterwards one breaks into speech." Therefore, Right Speech was taught immediately after Right Intention.

Furthermore, because people in the world first arrange with speech, saying "We will do this and that," and then engage in actions, Right Speech is beneficial to bodily action. Therefore, Right Action (Sammākammanta) was taught immediately after Right Speech.

Only for one who abandons the four types of verbal misconduct (vaci-duccarita) and the three types of bodily misconduct (kāya-duccarita) and fulfills both types of good conduct (sucarita) is the morality with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) perfected; it is not so for others. Therefore, Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva) was taught immediately after those two (Right Speech and Right Action).

A person with such pure livelihood should not be content and remain negligent, thinking, "My livelihood is pure." Rather, to show that this effort (vīriya) should be exerted in all postures (iriyāpatha), Right Effort (Sammāvāyāma) was taught immediately after Right Livelihood.

Then, to show that one who has exerted effort should also well establish mindfulness (sati) in the four objects such as the body, Right Mindfulness (Sammāsati) was taught immediately after Right Effort.

When mindfulness is thus well established, one is able to investigate the tendencies of states that are beneficial and unbeneficial to concentration (samādhi) and well-concentrate the mind on a single object. Therefore, it should be understood that Right Concentration (Sammāsamādhi) was taught immediately after Right Mindfulness.

In the explanation of Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi-niddesa), the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the Four Truths is shown by the words "knowledge of suffering" and so forth. Among those four truths, the first two truths are the round of existence (vaṭṭa), and the last two truths are the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). Among them, the monk has the application of the meditation subject to the truth of the round; he does not have the application to the truth of the cessation of the round. For the first two truths, "the five aggregates are suffering (dukkha-sacca), craving is the origin (samudaya-sacca)," are thus briefly, and...
152:
"What are the five aggregates? They are the aggregate of form," and so forth. Having learned this in detail from a teacher and reciting it repeatedly, the practitioner (yogāvacara) performs the task of meditation. Regarding the other two truths, however, they perform the task of penetration (or inclining towards Nibbāna) merely by hearing: "The truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing." While performing the task of meditation in this way, they penetrate the four truths with a single penetration (ekapaṭivedha) and realize them through a single realization (ekābhisamaya). They penetrate the truth of suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha); they penetrate the truth of origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha); they penetrate the truth of cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha); and they penetrate the truth of the path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). They realize the truth of suffering through the realization of full understanding... [and so on]... the truth of the path through the realization of development.

Thus, for that practitioner, in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), there is knowledge through learning, questioning, hearing, memorizing, and examining regarding the two truths (suffering and origin). Regarding the other two truths (cessation and path), there is only knowledge through hearing. In the later stage (at the moment of the path), there is penetration by way of function (kicca) regarding three truths, and penetration by way of object (ārammaṇa) regarding the truth of cessation. In that later stage, all penetrative knowledge is exclusively supramundane (lokuttara), while the knowledge of hearing, memorizing, and examining is mundane (lokiya) and belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa), however, occurs only for the noble person (ariya) who has reached the truths through the path; this practitioner is only a beginner (ādikammika). Therefore, reviewing knowledge is not mentioned here. For this beginner monk, before grasping the meditation subject, there is no reviewing through attention, focusing, mental application, or reflection such as "I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path." Such attention and so forth occur only from the time of grasping the meditation subject. In the later stage, however, suffering is indeed fully understood... [and so on]... the path is indeed developed.

Among those four truths, two truths (suffering and origin) are deep because they are difficult to see; two truths (cessation and path) are difficult to see because they are deep. Indeed, the truth of suffering is evident through its occurrence; it reaches the point where one must say "Oh, what suffering!" when striking a stump or being pierced by a thorn. The truth of origin is also evident through its occurrence by way of the desire to chew, the desire to eat, and so forth. However, through the penetration of characteristics, both are deep. Thus, those two are deep because they are difficult to see. As for the effort to see the other two truths (cessation and path), it is like stretching out one's hand to grasp the peak of existence (bhavagga), or stretching out one's foot to touch Avīci, or making the tip of a hair that has been split a hundred times meet another tip. Thus, those two are difficult to see because they are deep. With reference to the arising of knowledge in the preliminary stage through learning and so forth regarding these four truths—which are deep because they are difficult to see, and difficult to see because they are deep—this statement "knowledge of suffering" and so forth is made. At the moment of penetration (the path), however, that knowledge is only one.

## 1. Commentary on the Description of Knowledge Consisting in Learning (Sutamaya-ñāṇa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Other teachers say: "Knowledge regarding the four truths is fourfold: knowledge consisting in learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa), knowledge of determination (vavatthāna-ñāṇa), knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), and knowledge of realization (abhisamaya-ñāṇa)." Among these four, what is knowledge consisting in learning? Having heard the four truths either in brief or in detail, one knows: "This is the truth of suffering, this is the truth of origin, this is the truth of cessation, this is the truth of the path." Such knowing is called knowledge consisting in learning. What is knowledge of determination? That person investigates and reflects upon the meaning of the truths they have heard, according to their nature and characteristics. They make a decision: "These phenomena are included in this truth; this is the characteristic of this truth." The knowledge that decides in this way is called knowledge of determination. What is knowledge of comprehension? After defining the four truths in this sequence, that person takes only the truth of suffering and comprehends it through the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self up until the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). The knowledge that comprehends in this way is called knowledge of comprehension. What is knowledge of realization? At the moment of the supramundane path, one penetrates the four truths simultaneously with a single knowledge. How does one penetrate them? One knows suffering through the realization of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya), one knows the origin through the realization of abandoning (pahānābhisamaya), one knows cessation through the realization of making manifest (sacchikiriyābhisamaya), and one knows the path through the realization of development (bhāvanābhisamaya). Such knowing is called knowledge of realization.

In the description of right intention (sammā-saṅkappa), it is called intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) because it is free from sensual desire; it is called [intention of non-ill will] because it is free from ill will...
153:
Other teachers also say that knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths is of four kinds: knowledge based on hearing (sutamaya-ñāṇa), knowledge of determination (vavatthāna-ñāṇa), knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), and knowledge of realization (abhisamaya-ñāṇa). Among these four, what is knowledge based on hearing? It is knowing, after hearing the Four Noble Truths either in brief or in detail, that "This is the truth of suffering, this is the truth of the origin, this is the truth of cessation, this is the truth of the path." Knowing in this way is called knowledge based on hearing.

What is knowledge of determination? That person who has heard and known investigates the meaning of the truths heard, according to their nature and characteristics, and makes a decision: "These dhammas are included in such-and-such truth; this is the characteristic of such-and-such truth." The knowledge that makes such a decision is called knowledge of determination.

What is knowledge of comprehension? That person, having thus defined the Four Noble Truths in sequence, then takes only the truth of suffering and comprehends it as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta) up until the stage of change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). The knowledge that comprehends in this way is called knowledge of comprehension.

What is knowledge of realization? At the moment of the supramundane path, one realizes the Four Noble Truths simultaneously with a single knowledge, neither before nor after. It is said: "One realizes the truth of suffering through the realization of full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya), the truth of origin through the realization of abandoning (pahāna-abhisamaya), the truth of cessation through the realization of witnessing (sacchikiriyā-abhisamaya), and the truth of the path through the realization of development (bhāvanā-abhisamaya)." The knowledge that realizes in this way is called knowledge of realization.

In the explanation of Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa), it is called the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) because it is free from sensual desire (kāma). It is called the intention of non-ill will (abyāpāda-saṅkappa) because it is free from ill will (byāpāda). It is called the intention of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa) because it is free from cruelty (vihiṃsā). Among these three, renunciation-thought (nekkhamma-vitakka) arises while striking at and cutting off the basis of sensual thought (kāma-vitakka). Non-ill will thought arises while striking at and cutting off the basis of ill will thought. Non-harming thought arises while striking at and cutting off the basis of cruel thought. Likewise, renunciation, non-ill will, and non-harming thoughts arise as opposites to sensual, ill will, and cruel thoughts.

In thus striking and cutting off the basis, the practitioner (yogāvacara), in order to strike at the basis of sensual thought, comprehends either sensual thought itself or some other formation (saṅkhāra) by applying the characteristics. Then, at the moment of insight (vipassanā) for that person, the intention associated with insight arises, striking at and cutting off the basis of sensual thought by way of temporary abandonment (tadaṅga-pahāna). Having exerted effort in insight, it leads to the Path. Then, at the moment of the Path for that person, the intention associated with the Path arises, striking at and cutting off the basis of sensual thought by way of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). To strike at the basis of ill will thought, one comprehends either ill will thought or another formation; to strike at the basis of cruel thought, one comprehends either cruel thought or another formation. "Then, at the moment of insight for that person," and so on—all such words should be applied in the same manner as the previous method.
154:
Among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) explained in the Pali text, there is not a single one that is not an opponent to the three kinds of thought such as sensual thought. Specifically, however, for sensual thought, only the first absorption (paṭhama-jhāna) occurring in the meditation on foulness (asubha) is the direct opponent. For ill will thought, the third and fourth absorptions occurring in loving-kindness (mettā) are the opponents. For cruel thought, the third and fourth absorptions occurring in compassion (karuṇā) are the opponents. Therefore, for one who enters absorption after performing the preliminary work on foulness, at the moment of attainment, the thought associated with the absorption arises as the opponent of sensual thought by way of abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). For one who develops insight based on absorption, at the moment of insight, the intention associated with insight arises as the opponent of sensual thought by way of temporary abandonment (tadaṅga-pahāna). For one who strives in insight and reaches the Path, at the moment of the Path, the intention associated with the Path arises as the opponent of sensual thought by way of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). It should be understood that the thought arising in this way is called the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa).

For one who enters absorption after performing the preliminary work on loving-kindness or compassion, everything should be understood by applying it in the same manner as the previous method. It should be understood that the thought arising in this way is called the intention of non-ill will (abyāpāda-saṅkappa) and the intention of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa). Thus, these intentions of renunciation and so on are distinct in the preliminary stage of the Path due to the differences in their arising through insight and absorption. However, at the moment of the Path, by way of cutting off the basis of unwholesome thought arising in these three instances and thereby achieving non-arising, a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the path factor. This is called Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa).

In the explanation of Right Speech (sammā-vācā) as well, one abstains from false speech with one consciousness, and from malicious speech and so on with other distinct consciousnesses. Therefore, those four abstinences (veramaṇī) are distinct in the preliminary stage of the Path. However, at the moment of the Path, by way of cutting off the basis of the fourfold unwholesome volition of immorality known as wrong speech and thereby achieving non-arising, a single wholesome abstinence known as Right Speech arises, fulfilling the path factor. This is called Right Speech (sammā-vācā).

In the explanation of Right Action (sammā-kammanta) as well, one abstains from taking life with one consciousness, from taking what is not given with another, and from sexual misconduct with another. Therefore, those three abstinences are distinct in the preliminary stage of the Path. However, at the moment of the Path, by way of cutting off the basis of the threefold unwholesome volition of immorality known as wrong action and thereby achieving non-arising, a single wholesome abstinence known as Right Action arises, fulfilling the path factor. This is called Right Action (sammā-kammanta).
155:
## Exposition of Right Livelihood
'Idha' (here) means in this Dispensation (sāsana). 'Ariyasāvaka' (noble disciple) means a disciple of the Noble Buddha (a trainee or a noble worldling). 'Micchā-ājīvaṃ pahāya' (having abandoned wrong livelihood) means having given up evil livelihood. 'Sammā-ājīvena' (by right livelihood) means by wholesome livelihood praised by the Buddha. 'Jīvikaṃ kappeti' (earns a living) means he carries on the process of life. In this Exposition of Right Livelihood as well, because one abstains from transgression through the bodily door with one mind and from transgression through the verbal door with another mind, it arises at various different moments in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). However, at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), a single wholesome abstinence (kusalavirati) known as Right Livelihood arises, fulfilling the Path-factor by way of achieving the non-recurrence of the volition of wrong livelihood (immorality) which had arisen by virtue of the seven courses of action (kammapatha) in the two doors (bodily and verbal), by cutting off its cause. This is called Right Livelihood.

## Exposition of Right Effort
'Idha bhikkhu' (here, a monk) means a monk practicing in this Dispensation. 'Anuppannānaṃ' (of the unarisen) means of those not yet produced. 'Pāpakānaṃ' (of evil) means of vile. 'Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ' (of unwholesome states) means of states born of lack of skill. 'Anuppādāya' (for the sake of non-arising) means for the purpose of not producing them. 'Chandaṃ janeti' (he generates desire) means he generates or produces wholesome desire known as the wish to act (kattukamyatā). 'Vāyamati' (he makes an effort) means he generates application and makes an exertion. 'Vīriyaṃ ārabhati' (he arouses energy) means he puts forth bodily and mental energy. 'Cittaṃ paggaṇhāti' (he upholds the mind) means he lifts up the mind with that very co-nascent energy. 'Padahati' (he strives) means he puts forth supreme effort (padhāna-vīriya). In due order, these four terms should be applied in conjunction with cultivation, development, frequent practice, and constant application.

'Uppannānaṃ' (of the arisen) means of those states that have reached the condition where they cannot be said to be "not yet arisen." 'Pahānāya' (for the sake of abandoning) means for the purpose of giving up. 'Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ' (of unarisen wholesome states) means of those states born of skill that have not yet been produced. 'Uppādāya' (for the sake of arising) means for the purpose of producing them. 'Uppannānaṃ' (of the arisen) means of those produced. 'Ṭhitiyā' (for maintenance) means for the purpose of remaining; 'asammosāyā' (for non-disappearance) means for the purpose of not being lost; 'bhiyyobhāvāya' (for repeated occurrence) means for the purpose of occurring again and again; 'vepullāya' (for abundance) means for the state of being vast; 'bhāvanāya' (for development) means for growth; 'pāripūriyā' (for fulfillment) means for the purpose of completion.

These four Right Strivings (sammappadhāna), known as Right Effort, are mundane (lokiya) in the preliminary stage and supramundane (lokuttara) at the moment of the Path. At the moment of the Path, however, a single energy (vīriya) receives four names by virtue of accomplishing four functions. Therein, the mundane ones should be understood according to the method stated in the Kassapa Saṃyutta. For it is said there—
156:
"Friends, there are these four right strivings. Which four? Here, friends, a monk generates effort, thinking: 'If unarisen evil unwholesome states were to arise in me, they would lead to harm.' He generates effort, thinking: 'If arisen evil unwholesome states were not abandoned in me, they would lead to harm.' He generates effort, thinking: 'If unarisen wholesome states were not to arise in me, they would lead to harm.' He generates effort, thinking: 'If arisen wholesome states were to cease in me, they would lead to harm.'" (SN 2.145).

In that discussion on Right Striving, 'unarisen' (anuppanna) means unarisen either by way of not having occurred habitually or by way of not having experienced an object. Otherwise, in the beginningless Saṃsāra, there are no such things as evil unwholesome states that have never arisen. In fact, even unarisen unwholesome states that arise are only those that have arisen before in Saṃsāra; even those that are abandoned are only those that have arisen before.

For some individuals, those unwholesome states do not occur through one of these: performing duties (vatta), studying scriptures (gantha), undertaking ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), developing concentration (samādhi), practicing insight (vipassanā), performing new works (navakamma), or being in the Brahma realm. How? Some individuals are fulfilled in duties. While performing the eighty Khandhaka duties and the fourteen major duties, as well as duties regarding the shrine terrace, the Bodhi tree terrace, the water-pot stand, the Uposatha hall, guests, and travelers, defilements find no opportunity. Later, if he abandons the duties and lives with broken duties, defilements arise due to unwise attention and lapse of mindfulness. Thus, unwholesome states that have not occurred habitually are said to arise.

Some individuals are devoted to scriptural study. They learn one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas. While learning, reciting, contemplating, teaching, preaching, and explaining the Tipitaka—the word of the Buddha—by way of meaning, text, sequence, and context, defilements find no opportunity. Later, if he abandons scriptural work and lives lazily, defilements arise due to unwise attention and lapse of mindfulness. Thus, unwholesome states that have not occurred habitually are said to arise.

Some individuals are dhutaṅga-holders. They undertake and practice the thirteen ascetic qualities. While maintaining those ascetic qualities, defilements find no opportunity.
157:
Later, however, for that person, having abandoned the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and turning back to an abundance of requisites, defilements arise due to unwholesome attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and the loss of mindfulness while living thus. In this way, defilements that have not arisen before are said to arise by way of lack of practice (asamudācāra).

A certain person is proficient in the eight attainments (samāpatti); while he dwells by way of proficiency in reflecting on the first jhāna and so on, defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, for that person, whether the jhāna has declined or been neglected, while he dwells devoted to talk and so on, defilements arise due to unwholesome attention and the loss of mindfulness. In this way, defilements that have not arisen before are said to arise by way of lack of practice.

A certain person is a practitioner of insight (vipassanā), dwelling while performing the work of the seven contemplations (anupassanā) or the eighteen principal insights (mahāvipassanā); while he dwells thus, defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, for that person, having abandoned the work of insight and dwelling devoted to physical robustness, defilements arise due to unwholesome attention and the loss of mindfulness. In this way, defilements that have not arisen before are said to arise by way of lack of practice.

A certain person is a builder (navakammika), constructing Uposatha halls, dining halls, and so on; while he is thinking about the materials and timber for those buildings, defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, for that person, when the new work is finished or neglected, defilements arise due to unwholesome attention and the loss of mindfulness. In this way, defilements that have not arisen before are said to arise by way of lack of practice.

A certain person is a pure being come from the Brahma world (brahmaloka); for him, because of non-indulgence, defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, for that person, when he has found indulgence, defilements arise due to unwholesome attention and the loss of mindfulness. In this way, defilements that have not arisen before are said to arise by way of lack of practice. Thus, first, the state of not having arisen by way of lack of practice should be understood.

How does it occur by way of an unexperienced object (ananubhūtārammaṇa)? Here, a certain person obtains an object such as a pleasant one that has not been experienced before; for him, defilements such as lust (rāga) arise in that object due to unwholesome attention and the loss of mindfulness. In this way, defilements that have not arisen before are said to arise by way of an unexperienced object. Thus, when unwholesome states that have not arisen before arise...
158:
Seeing his own disadvantage, he develops the first Right Effort (Sammappadhāna) by devotion to the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) so that those (unarisen unwholesome states) do not arise. When those (unwholesome states) have arisen, seeing his own disadvantage because of not abandoning them, he develops the second Right Effort in the same way to abandon those (arisen unwholesome states).

Unarisen wholesome states are serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the Path (magga). Seeing his own disadvantage in the non-arising of those states, he develops the third Right Effort in the same way for the sake of their arising. Arisen wholesome states are serenity and insight only. As for the Path, although it arises once and then ceases, it is not something that leads to disadvantage. This is because that Path ceases only after giving the condition for the Fruit (phala). Seeing his own disadvantage due to the cessation of that serenity and insight, he develops the fourth Right Effort in the same way for their stability. At the moment of the supramundane Path, however, energy (vīriya) is only one.

In this way, since those (unwholesome states) that have not arisen might arise, he accomplishes the task of non-arising for those unarisen states and the task of abandoning for those that have arisen. Herein, 'arisen' (uppanna) is of four kinds: presently arisen (vattamanuppanna), arisen and passed (bhūtāpagatuppanna), opportunity-made arisen (okāsakatuppanna), and plane-obtained arisen (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Among these four, all states endowed with arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga) are called 'presently arisen'. Wholesome and unwholesome states that have ceased after experiencing the flavor of the object are called 'experienced and passed' (anubhūtapagata); the remaining conditioned states that have ceased after reaching the three moments such as arising are called 'become and passed' (bhūtapagata); both are called 'arisen and passed'. Kamma spoken of in the manner 'There are those kammas done in the past' and so on, although it is past, stands having blocked other results (vipāka) and having made an opportunity for its own result; therefore, such a result for which an opportunity has been made, although it has not yet arisen, is called 'opportunity-made arisen' because it will certainly arise when the opportunity is thus made. Unwholesome states that have not been uprooted in various planes are called 'plane-obtained arisen'.

Herein, the difference between the plane (bhūmi) and what is obtained in the plane (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. The 'plane' refers to the five aggregates belonging to the three planes which are the objects of insight. 'Obtained in the plane' refers to the collection of defilements that are fit to arise in those aggregates. Because that plane is obtained by those defilements, it is called 'obtained in the plane'. Furthermore, that 'obtaining' is not by way of the object. This is because, if it were by way of the object, defilements could arise even in relation to the aggregates of Arahants—which are past, future, or fully understood—by taking them as objects. If that (which arises by taking an Arahant's aggregates as an object) were called 'obtained in the plane', no one could abandon the root of existence because those defilements could not be abandoned. Therefore, 'obtained in the plane' should be understood by way of the basis (vatthu). Where...
159:
Aggregates that are not fully understood by insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) arise in whatever place; from the moment they arise in those various places, the collection of defilements (kilesa), which is the root of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭamūla), underlies them. Because they have not yet been abandoned, they should be known as 'having attained the ground' (bhūmiladdha).

In that state of having attained the ground, for whichever person the defilements underlie certain aggregates in the sense of not being abandoned, those aggregates alone are the basis (vatthu) for those defilements for that person, not the aggregates belonging to others. Regarding past aggregates, the basis for defilements that underlie them without being abandoned is only the past aggregates, not others (future or present). This same principle applies to future aggregates and so on. Similarly, for defilements that underlie the aggregates of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara) without being abandoned, the basis is only the kāmāvacara aggregates, not others (fine-material or immaterial). This same principle applies to the fine-material (rūpāvacara) and immaterial (arūpāvacara) aggregates.

However, among Noble Persons (ariya-puggala) such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), if the collection of defilements, which is the root of the cycle, has been abandoned in certain aggregates of a particular Noble Person by a particular path (magga), then those aggregates of that person no longer receive the name 'ground' (bhūmi) because they are no longer the basis for those abandoned defilements that were the root of the cycle. For a worldling (puthujjana), because the defilements that are the root of the cycle have not been abandoned in any way, whatever wholesome or unwholesome kamma is performed, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) revolves for that person precisely because of the condition of kamma and defilements. It should not be said that the root of the cycle for that person exists only in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and not in feeling (vedanā) and so on; nor should it be said that it exists only in the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) and not in the aggregate of form and so on. Why? Because it underlies all five aggregates without distinction.

How? It is like the soil nutrients (pathavī-rasa) and so on in a tree. For instance, a great tree, established on the ground and depending on soil nutrients and water nutrients (āpo-rasa), grows by means of roots, trunk, main branches, minor branches, sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits, filling the sky and continuing the lineage of the tree through a succession of seeds until the end of the aeon. It should not be said that those soil nutrients and so on exist only in the roots and not in the trunk and so on; nor that they exist only in the fruit and not in the roots and so on. Why? Because they pervade all parts, such as the roots, without distinction.

Just as a man who is weary of the flowers, fruits, and so on of that tree might strike a poisonous thorn called a 'frog-thorn' (maṇḍūka-kaṇṭaka) into the four directions of the tree; then that tree, touched by the contact of that poison, reaches a state of being unable to thrive because the soil and water nutrients are exhausted, and it can no longer produce a further succession. In the same way, a son of good family (kulaputta) who is weary of the occurrence of the aggregates begins the development of the four paths (catu-magga) in his own continuity, just as that man applied poison to the tree. Then, his continuity of aggregates, being touched by the poisonous contact of those four paths, because the defilements that are the root of the cycle are completely exhausted...
160:
...all varieties of kamma, such as bodily action, reach the state of mere functional nature (kiriya-sabhāva). Because they reach a state where they do not cause a new existence in the future, they are no longer able to produce the continuity of another life. Merely through the cessation of the final consciousness (death consciousness), like a fire without fuel, one attains final Nibbāna (parinibbāyati) without clinging (anupādāna). Thus, the distinction between the 'ground' (bhūmi) and 'that which has attained the ground' (bhūmiladdha) should be understood.

Furthermore, 'arisen' (uppanna) is of four types: arisen through active manifestation (samudācāruppanna), arisen through being seized by an object (ārammaṇādhi-ggahituppanna), arisen through not being suppressed (avikkhambhituppanna), and arisen through not being eradicated (asamūhatuppanna). Among these four, that which is presently arising in the present moment (vattamanuppanna) is indeed called 'arisen through active manifestation'. When an object comes into the range of the eye-door and so on, even if the collection of defilements has not yet arisen in the preceding stage, it is called 'arisen through being seized by an object' because it will certainly arise in the subsequent stage due to the object being seized. The collection of defilements that has not been suppressed by either tranquility (samatha) or insight (vipassanā), even if it has not yet entered the mental continuity, is called 'arisen through not being suppressed' because there is no cause to prevent its arising. That which has been suppressed by tranquility and insight but has not yet been eradicated by the Noble Path is called 'arisen through not being eradicated' because it has not yet transcended the nature of arising. These three types—arisen through being seized by an object, arisen through not being suppressed, and arisen through not being eradicated—should be understood as being included within 'that which has attained the ground' (bhūmiladdha).

Among these various types of 'arisen' mentioned, that which is called 'presently arisen' (vattamanuppanna), 'arisen as a past reality' (bhūtapagatuppanna), 'arisen by having found an opportunity' (okāsakatuppanna), and 'arisen through active manifestation' (samudācāruppanna) cannot be abandoned by any path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) because they are not things to be killed/abandoned by the path. However, that which is called 'arisen by attaining the ground' (bhūmiladdhuppanna), 'arisen through being seized by an object', 'arisen through not being suppressed', and 'arisen through not being eradicated' is said to be abandoned in its entirety because various mundane and supramundane knowledges arise, destroying the state of being liable to arise. Thus, the phrase 'of the arisen [defilements]' (uppannānaṃ) and so on was spoken with reference to those defilements that the path abandons.

If that is so, how is there development (bhāvanā) for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen at the path-moment, and how is there development for the maintenance (ṭhiti) of wholesome states that have arisen? It is through the occurrence of the path itself. For when the path occurs, it is called 'not yet arisen' (anuppanna) because it has never arisen before. People who have reached a place they never reached before, or who experience an object they never experienced before, are known to say, 'We have reached a place not reached before, we experience an object not experienced before.' The very duration of the occurrence of that path-consciousness is called 'maintenance' (ṭhiti); therefore, it is appropriate to say that one develops for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states. Thus, for this monk, at the moment of the supramundane path, this single energy (vīriya) is...
161:
"For the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states," etc.—it receives these four names. This is the discourse on Right Effort (Sammappadhāna) at the moment of the supramundane path. Thus, in this explanation of Right Effort, a mixture of mundane and supramundane Right Effort is shown.

In the explanation of Right Mindfulness (Sammāsati), "in the body" (kāye) refers to the physical body (rūpakāya). Indeed, here "physical body" is intended as "body" (kāya) in the sense of a collection of parts, such as limbs and hair, etc., like a collection of elephants or a collection of chariots. Just as it is intended as "body" in the sense of a collection, it is also intended as "body" in the sense of being the place of arising (āya) of loathsome (kucchita) things like hair, etc. Because it is the place of arising of those things which are extremely loathsome, it is called "kāya." "Āya" means the place of arising. The word-definition (vacanattha) in that term is: loathsome things like hair, etc., arise from it (or in it); therefore, it is called "āya." Thus, because it is the place of arising of loathsome things, it is called "kāya."

"Kāyānupassī" means one who has the habit of repeatedly contemplating the body, or one who is repeatedly contemplating the body. Even after saying "in the body" (kāye), the second mention of the word "body" in "kāyānupassī" should be understood as being done to show the determination without mixing with other states, and the breaking down of the compactness (ghana-vinibbhoga), etc. By doing so, it is shown that one is not a contemplator of feelings, mind, or dhammas in the body, but rather only a contemplator of the body. By showing only the mode of contemplating the body in the object called "body," the determination without mixing is shown.

Similarly, one is not a contemplator of a single state separate from the limbs and parts in the body, nor a contemplator of a woman or a man separate from hair, body hair, etc. Even in this physical body, which is called a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya) such as hair and body hair, one is not a contemplator of a single state separate from those material states. Rather, like one contemplating the parts of a chariot, one contemplates the collection of limbs and parts; like one contemplating the components of a city, one contemplates the collection of hair, body hair, etc.; and like one peeling and contemplating the layers of a banana trunk, or like one opening and contemplating an empty fist, one is only a contemplator of the collection of primary elements and derived matter. 

Thus, by showing the object called "body" in various ways through the power of the collection, the breaking down of the compactness is shown. Indeed, in this body, no body, woman, man, or any other state can be found separate from the aforementioned collections. However, beings wrongly misinterpret and cling to just the aforementioned collection of states in various ways. Therefore, the ancients said:

"What he sees, that is not seen; what is seen, he does not see. Not seeing, the fool is bound; being bound, he is not released."
162:
It is said "for the purpose of showing the breaking down of compactness, etc." Here, by the word "etc." (ādi), this meaning should also be understood: this person contemplates only the body in this body, not other states. What is meant? Just as people contemplate water in a mirage which is not water, one does not contemplate permanence, happiness, self, or beauty in this body which is only impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Rather, it means one is a "contemplator of the body" (kāyānupassī) who contemplates only the collection of modes of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.

Alternatively, in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the body is taught starting from inhalation and exhalation and ending with bones turned to dust, in the manner: "Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest or to the root of a tree... mindful, he breathes in." Later in the Satipaṭṭhāna discourse, it is taught: "Here, someone contemplates the earth-collection, the water-collection, the fire-collection, the air-collection, the hair-collection, the body-hair-collection, the skin-collection, the hide-collection, the flesh-collection, the blood-collection, the tendon-collection, the bone-collection, and the marrow-collection as impermanent." Because of contemplating all those bodies in this very physical frame, it should be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" (kāye kāyānupassī).

Alternatively, it should be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" because one does not contemplate any state that could be grasped as "I" or "mine" in the body, but contemplates only the collection of various states such as hair, body hair, etc. Furthermore, it should be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" because of contemplating the body called the collection of modes such as the mark of impermanence, according to the entire method that follows in sequence: "In this body, he contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent," etc. This meaning is common to all four foundations of mindfulness.

"Contemplating the body in the body" means contemplating one of the bodies among the bodies taught in various ways, such as the breath-body, etc. "Dwells" (viharati) indicates being engaged with one of the four postures. It means he carries or maintains himself so as not to fall, by interrupting the pain of one posture with another posture. "Ardent" (ātāpī) indicates being endowed with energy (vīriya) that guards the body. This is because that energy at that time is called "ardor" (ātāpa) because it burns away the defilements in the three planes of existence; being endowed with that...
163:
Because he is endowed with energy that burns up defilements, he is called 'ardent' (ātāpī). 'Clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) means being endowed with the wisdom known as clear comprehension that grasps the body. 'Mindful' (satimā) means being endowed with the mindfulness that grasps the body. This person is so called because he grasps the object with mindfulness and contemplates it repeatedly with wisdom. Indeed, there is no contemplation for one who is devoid of mindfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, I say that mindfulness is useful in all things.' Thus, in this context, with the words 'dwells contemplating the body in the body,' the meditation subject of the foundation of mindfulness of body-contemplation is stated. Alternatively, for one who is not ardent, laziness is harmful. One who lacks clear comprehension is confused about grasping what is the cause and avoiding what is not the cause. One who is forgetful is unable to abandon what is the cause and grasp what is not the cause. Therefore, the meditation subject does not succeed for him.
