Thus, to show those qualities by whose power the meditation subject succeeds, it should be understood that the words 'ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful' were spoken.

Having shown the foundation of mindfulness of body-contemplation and its associated factors, now, to show the factor to be abandoned, the words 'having removed covetousness and grief in the world' were spoken. In that phrase, 'having removed' (vineyya) means having removed by means of the discipline of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vinaya) or the discipline of suppression (vikkhambhana-vinaya). 'In the world' (loke) means that very body which was previously grasped; here it is called 'world' in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. The meaning is: having abandoned covetousness and grief in that world (the body). However, since covetousness and grief are abandoned not only regarding the body but also regarding feelings and so forth, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'The five aggregates of clinging are the world.' It should be understood that this was said by way of extracting the meaning of those states because they are called the world. The statement 'Therein, what is the world? That very body is the world' also means this. The term 'covetousness and grief' (abhijjhā-domanassa) is spoken in brief. In other versions of the Saṃyutta and Aṅguttara, they are read separately. Covetousness (abhijjhā) is so called because one longs by means of it, or it longs by itself, or it is just the act of longing. However, since in this context sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is included by the term 'covetousness' and ill-will (byāpāda) is included by the term 'grief,' it should be understood that the abandoning of the hindrances is stated by showing the two powerful states included among the hindrances. Furthermore, to state a distinction: by removing covetousness, the abandoning of attraction (anurodha) rooted in the excellence of the body is stated; by removing grief, the abandoning of repulsion (virodha) or displeasure rooted in the failure of the body is stated.
164:
Specifically, in this context, by the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of attraction (anurodha) rooted in the excellence of the body is stated; by the removal of grief, the abandoning of repulsion (virodha) rooted in the failure of the body is stated. By the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of excessive delight in the body is stated; by the removal of grief, the abandoning of lack of delight in the development of body-contemplation is stated. By the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of the unwholesome state of attributing non-existent beauty, happiness, and so forth to the body is stated; by the removal of grief, the abandoning of the unwholesome state of removing the existing foulness, suffering, and so forth from the body is stated. Thereby, the power of the yoga (yogānubhāva) and the capability for yoga (yogasamatthata) of the practitioner are illustrated. For this is the power of yoga: that this practitioner becomes free from attraction and repulsion, endures both delight and lack of delight, and is devoid of attributing what is non-existent and removing what is existent. Being free from attraction and repulsion, enduring delight and lack of delight, not attributing what is non-existent and not removing what is existent, he becomes capable of the practice.

Another method: In the phrase 'contemplating the body in the body,' the meditation subject is stated by the volition associated with contemplation. In the word 'dwells' (viharati), the maintenance of the body of the person practicing the meditation subject by means of the stated postures is mentioned. Among the words beginning with 'ardent' (ātāpī), by the word 'ardor' (ātāpa), right effort (sammappadhāna) is meant. By the words 'mindfulness and clear comprehension,' the all-purpose meditation subject or the means of maintaining the meditation subject is meant. Or, by mindfulness, the tranquility (samatha) obtained by way of body-contemplation is meant, and by clear comprehension, insight (vipassanā) is meant. By the removal of covetousness and grief, the fruit of the development (bhāvanā-phala) should be understood as being stated.

In the passages beginning with 'contemplating feelings in feelings,' the purpose of repeating the words 'feelings,' 'mind,' and 'dhammas' should be understood by applying the method stated in body-contemplation as appropriate. The specific meaning here is: contemplating each feeling one by one as impermanent and so forth among the many varieties of feelings such as pleasant feelings; contemplating each mind one by one as impermanent and so forth among the sixteen varieties of mind such as the mind with lust; contemplating each dhamma one by one as impermanent and so forth among the remaining states of the three planes, excluding the body, feelings, and mind; or contemplating the dhammas such as the hindrances according to the method stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Here, the use of the singular 'in the body' (kāye) is done because of the oneness of the body (or by taking it as a class). The use of the singular 'in the mind' (citte) should be understood as being done because there is no difference in the mind's nature of cognizing the object (or by taking it as a class). Just as feelings and so forth should be contemplated, one who contemplates in that way should be known as 'one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings,' 'mind in mind,' and 'dhammas in dhammas.' First, how should feelings be contemplated?
165:
First, pleasant feeling should be contemplated as suffering (dukkha), painful feeling as a dart (salla), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant (equanimity) feeling as impermanent (anicca). Regarding how it should be contemplated, it is said: "The person who sees pleasant feeling as suffering, sees painful feeling as a dart, and sees the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent—that bhikkhu, seeing rightly, truly and fully understands feelings." (Saṃ. Ni. 4.253). All these feelings should also be contemplated as suffering. For it is said: "Whatever is felt, all that I declare to be included in suffering." (Saṃ. Ni. 4.259). They should also be contemplated in terms of pleasure and pain. As it is said: "Pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists and painful when it changes. Painful feeling is painful when it persists and pleasant when it changes. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant when there is knowledge and painful when there is ignorance." (Ma. Ni. 1.465). Furthermore, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence and so forth.

Among mind and phenomena, the mind should first be contemplated by way of various distinctions such as object, predominance, conascence, plane, kamma, result (vipāka), functional (kiriya), and so forth; by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence; and by way of the sixteen distinctions such as 'with lust' (sarāga) and so forth. Phenomena (dhamma) should be contemplated by way of their individual characteristics, general characteristics such as impermanence, the nature of emptiness (suññatā), the seven contemplations such as impermanence, and presence or absence, etc. Indeed, in this foundation of mindfulness, for a person who has abandoned covetousness and displeasure (abhijjhā and domanassa) in the world of the body, they are already abandoned in the worlds of feelings and so forth. However, it is taught in all aspects by way of different individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness occurring at different moments. Alternatively, when covetousness and displeasure are abandoned in one object, they are abandoned in the remaining objects as well; thus, it should be understood that this is taught to show the abandonment in those remaining objects.

Thus, these four foundations of mindfulness are obtained in different consciousnesses in the preliminary stage of the path. For with one consciousness one grasps the body, with another the feeling, with another the mind, and with another the phenomena. But at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained in a single consciousness. For one who comes having grasped the body from the beginning, the mindfulness associated with insight (vipassanā) is called 'contemplation of the body' (kāyānupassanā); the person endowed with that mindfulness is called 'a contemplator of the body' (kāyānupassī). For one who, having exerted effort in insight, reaches the noble path, the mindfulness associated with the path at the path-moment is called 'contemplation of the body'; the person endowed with that mindfulness is called 'a contemplator of the body'. For one who comes having grasped feeling, having grasped mind, and having grasped phenomena, the mindfulness associated with insight is...
166:
...called 'contemplation of phenomena' (dhammānupassanā); the person endowed with that mindfulness is called 'a contemplator of phenomena' (dhammānupassī). For one who, having exerted effort in insight, reaches the noble path, the mindfulness associated with the path at the path-moment is called 'contemplation of phenomena'; the person endowed with that mindfulness is called 'a contemplator of phenomena'. Thus, first, the teaching stands by way of the person (puggala-dhiṭṭhāna).

I shall speak further by way of the Dhamma (dhamma-dhiṭṭhāna): Mindfulness that abandons the perversion (vipallāsa) of 'beauty' (subha) in the body and grasps the body is called 'contemplation of the body' (kāyānupassanā) because it is accomplished by the path. Mindfulness that abandons the perversion of 'pleasure' (sukha) in feeling and grasps feeling is called 'contemplation of feeling' (vedanānupassanā) because it is accomplished by the path. Mindfulness that abandons the perversion of 'permanence' (nicca) in the mind and grasps the mind is called 'contemplation of the mind' (cittānupassanā) because it is accomplished by the path. Mindfulness that abandons the perversion of 'self' (atta) in phenomena and grasps phenomena is called 'contemplation of phenomena' (dhammānupassanā) because it is accomplished by the path. Thus, a single mindfulness associated with the path receives four names because it accomplishes four tasks. Therefore, it was said: "But at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained in a single consciousness."

In the explanation of Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi), 'vivicceva kāmehi' means being secluded from, without, or departed from sensual pleasures. Here, the word 'eva' should be understood as having the sense of restriction (niyama). Because it has the sense of restriction, it shows that although sensual pleasures are not present at the time of dwelling in the attainment of the first jhāna, they are the opposite of that first jhāna, and that the attainment of that jhāna is only through the abandonment of sensual pleasures. How is this shown? When the restriction is made by the word 'eva' as 'quite secluded from sensual pleasures,' this becomes clear: indeed, sensual pleasures are the opposite of this jhāna; while they exist, this jhāna does not occur, just as the light of a lamp does not occur while there is darkness. Its attainment is only through their abandonment, just as reaching the further shore is only through abandoning this shore. Therefore, the restriction is made with the word 'eva'.

Regarding that phrase (vivicceva kāmehi), a question may arise: Why is this word 'eva' mentioned only in the first phrase and not in the subsequent phrase? Can one dwell in the attainment of jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states? This should not be regarded in that way. This 'eva' is mentioned in the first phrase because it is the escape (nissaraṇa) from those sensual pleasures. Because of the transcending of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) and because of being the opposite of sensual lust (kāmarāga), this jhāna is indeed the escape from sensual pleasures. As it is said: "This renunciation (nekkhamma) is the escape from sensual pleasures." (Itivuttaka 72). In the subsequent phrase also, just as in the teaching "Bhikkhus, only here is there a recluse, here a second recluse," the word 'eva' is brought in and spoken; so too should it be spoken here. For it is not possible to dwell in the attainment of jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states known as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Therefore, "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, quite secluded from..."
167:
The word 'eva' (quite/only) should be noted in both phrases: 'vivicceva kāmehi' and 'vivicceva akusalehi dhammehi'. In both phrases, the general term 'vivicca' (seclusion) encompasses tadaṅga-viveka (seclusion by substitution of opposites), vikkhambhana-viveka (seclusion by suppression), samuccheda-viveka (seclusion by eradication), paṭippassaddhi-viveka (seclusion by tranquilization), and nissaraṇa-viveka (seclusion by escape), as well as citta-viveka (mental seclusion), kāya-viveka (physical seclusion), and upadhi-viveka (seclusion from the substrata of existence). However, in the preliminary stage (of the Path), kāya-viveka, citta-viveka, and vikkhambhana-viveka are to be understood. At the moment of the supramundane Path (lokuttara-magga), kāya-viveka, citta-viveka, samuccheda-viveka, paṭippassaddhi-viveka, and nissaraṇa-viveka are to be understood.

By the word 'kāmehi', one should understand that it includes all objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) as taught in the Mahāniddesa in the manner of 'What are objective sensualities? Pleasant forms, etc.', as well as defilement sensuality (kilesa-kāma) as taught in the same Mahāniddesa and the Vibhaṅga in the manner of 'Desire is sensuality, lust is sensuality, desire and lust are sensuality, thought is sensuality, lust is sensuality, thought and lust are sensuality.' When they are thus included, the meaning 'being secluded even from objective sensuality' in the phrase 'vivicceva kāmehi' is appropriate. By such seclusion from objective sensuality, physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) is said to be taught.

In the phrase 'vivicca akusalehi dhammehi', the meaning 'being secluded from defilement sensuality and from all unwholesome states' is appropriate. By such seclusion from defilement sensuality and unwholesome states, mental seclusion (citta-viveka) is said to be taught. Between these two phrases, because the first phrase teaches seclusion from objective sensuality, the abandoning of sensual happiness (kāmasukha) is shown. Because the second phrase teaches seclusion from defilement sensuality, the acquisition of the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha, i.e., jhanic bliss) is shown. Furthermore, because of teaching seclusion from objective and defilement sensuality, the first phrase shows the abandoning of the objects of defilement, and the second shows the abandoning of the defilements themselves. The first shows the abandoning of the cause of greed (lolabhāva), and the second shows the abandoning of the cause of delusion (bālabhāva). It should be understood that the first shows the purity of effort (payoga-suddhi), and the second shows the purity of intention (āsayaposana). This is the method regarding the aspect of objective sensuality in the word 'kāmehi'.

Regarding the aspect of defilement sensuality, 'kāma' (sensuality) refers specifically to sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which has many varieties such as desire (chanda) and lust (rāga). Although that sensual desire is included among unwholesome states, it is taught separately in the Vibhaṅga above in the manner of 'Therein, what are sensualities? Desire is sensuality,' because it is the direct opposite of the jhana factors. Or, it is taught in the first phrase because it is defilement sensuality, and in the second phrase because it is included among unwholesome states. Because of the many varieties of that sensuality, it is stated as 'kāmehi' (plural) instead of 'kāmato' (singular).
168:
Although other states also have the nature of being unwholesome, only the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are taught in the Vibhaṅga in the manner of 'Therein, what are unwholesome states? They are sensual desire,' etc. This is because of the intention to show the opposition of the hindrances to the jhana factors which will be mentioned later. In fact, the hindrances are the opposites of the jhana factors; it means that only the jhana factors are the opposites that destroy and eliminate those hindrances. Therefore, it is stated in the Peṭakopadesa: 'Concentration (samādhi) is the opposite of sensual desire; rapture (pīti) is the opposite of ill will; applied thought (vitakka) is the opposite of sloth and torpor; happiness (sukha) is the opposite of restlessness and remorse; sustained thought (vicāra) is the opposite of doubt.'

Thus, in this text, by the phrase 'quite secluded from sensual pleasures,' the seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka) of the hindrance of sensual desire is taught. By the phrase 'secluded from unwholesome states,' the seclusion by suppression of all five hindrances is taught. Alternatively, the first phrase refers to sensual desire, and the second to the remaining hindrances. Similarly, by the first phrase, among the three unwholesome roots, greed (lobha) occurring in the five strands of sensual pleasure is taught; by the second phrase, hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) occurring in the objects of malice, etc., are taught. Or, among the floods (ogha), etc., the first phrase teaches the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of sensual lust; the second phrase teaches the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. The first phrase teaches craving (taṇhā) and its associated states; the second teaches ignorance (avijjā) and its associated states. Furthermore, it should be understood that the first phrase teaches the seclusion by suppression of the eight consciousnesses rooted in greed, and the second teaches the seclusion by suppression of the remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses.

Having thus shown the factors of abandoning (pahaṇanga) of the first jhana, the text now states 'with applied thought and sustained thought,' etc., to show the constituent factors (sampayoganga). Therein, the state characterized by directing the mind onto the object is called applied thought (vitakka). The state characterized by the repeated examination of the object is called sustained thought (vicāra). Although vitakka and vicāra are inseparable in certain types of consciousness, vitakka is the first impact of the mind on the object, like the striking of a bell, due to its grossness and its role as a precursor. Vicāra is the continuous engagement of the mind with the object, like the resonance of the bell, due to its subtlety and its nature of examining the object. In this jhana, vitakka has the nature of spreading out by way of vibration at the moment of initial occurrence of the mind, like a bird flapping its wings when wanting to fly into the sky, or like a bee whose mind follows the scent as it dives towards a lotus. Vicāra has the nature of occurring calmly without excessive vibration of the mind, like a bird flying in the sky with its wings spread, or like a bee that has reached the lotus and is hovering over it.
169:
In the Dukanipāta Commentary, however, it is stated: "Just as a large bird flying in the sky takes the wind with both wings and, spreading its wings, proceeds, so vitakka (applied thought) occurs in the sense of directing the mind onto the object. Just as the bird's movement of flapping its wings to take the wind, so vicāra (sustained thought) occurs in the sense of repeatedly examining the object." This explanation is suitable for the time when the mind occurs continuously on the object (at the time of access or absorption). The distinction between vitakka and vicāra is clear in the first and second jhānas.

Alternatively, vitakka should be understood as being like the hand that holds a tarnished bronze bowl firmly, and vicāra should be understood as being like the hand that rubs it with oil-mixed stone powder using a woolen cloth. Similarly, vitakka should be understood as being like the hand of a potter that presses down while turning the wheel with a stick to make a pot, and vicāra should be understood as being like the hand that moves back and forth. Likewise, vitakka is called the directing of the mind onto the object, like the fixed pin (of a compass) planted in the center by one making a circle; vicāra is called the repeated examination of the object, like the pin that revolves around the outside. Thus, because it occurs together with this vitakka and this vicāra, this jhāna is called "jhāna with vitakka and vicāra," like a tree with its flowers and fruits.

In the word "vivekaja" (born of seclusion), seclusion is called viveka; it means the disappearance of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Alternatively, the group of mental states associated with jhāna that is secluded from the hindrances is called viveka. It is called "vivekaja" (born of seclusion) because it is born from that seclusion or because it arises in that seclusion. In the word "pītisukha," it is called pīti (joy/rapture) because it pleases; that pīti has the characteristic of endearment towards the object. That pīti is of five kinds: minor joy (khuddikā pīti), momentary joy (khaṇikā pīti), showering joy (okkantikā pīti), uplifting joy (ubbegā pīti), and pervading joy (pharaṇā pīti).

Among those five, minor joy is only able to make the hair on the body stand on end. Momentary joy is like a flash of lightning at every moment. Showering joy enters the body and breaks like waves striking the seashore. Uplifting joy is powerful and reaches the extent of being able to lift the body up and make it leap into the sky. Pervading joy is extremely powerful. When it arises, it spreads throughout the whole body like a bladder filled with blown air or like a mountain cavern into which a great flood of water has poured. When these five kinds of joy are conceived and reach maturity, they fulfill the two kinds of tranquility: bodily tranquility (kāya-passaddhi) and mental tranquility (citta-passaddhi). When that tranquility is conceived and reaches maturity, it fulfills the two kinds of happiness: bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha) and mental happiness (cetasika-sukha). ...
170:
When happiness (sukha) is conceived and reaches maturity, it fulfills the three kinds of concentration: momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Among those five kinds of joy, that pervading joy (pharaṇā pīti) which, having become the root of absorption concentration and increasing, reaches association with concentration, is the joy intended in this context.

Furthermore, the feeling of happiness (sukha-vedanā) other than joy is called sukha because it causes happiness. It means that it makes the person in whom it arises happy. Alternatively, the state of being happy is called sukha. Or, it is called sukha because it thoroughly consumes or digs out (khādati, khaṇati) the affliction of body and mind. This is a name for pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā). That sukha has the characteristic of being pleasant (sāta). Although pīti and sukha are inseparable in certain states of mind, the delight due to obtaining a desired object is called pīti. The experiencing of the taste of the object already obtained is called sukha. Where there is pīti, there is sukha. Where there is sukha, pīti is not necessarily present. Pīti is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); sukha is included in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Pīti should be understood as being like the joy of a person exhausted in a difficult journey upon seeing or hearing of a forest grove and water. Sukha should be understood as being like the happiness of entering the shade of the forest grove and using the water. It should be understood that this (analogy of the desert traveler, etc.) is stated because of its clarity at those respective times. Thus, this pīti and this sukha belong to this jhāna, or are present in this jhāna; therefore, this jhāna is called "pītisukha." Or, pīti and sukha together are pītisukha (like the compound Dhamma-Vinaya). The pītisukha born of seclusion belongs to this jhāna, or is present in this jhāna; thus it is also called vivekaja-pītisukha. Just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too the pītisukha here is only born of seclusion. Since that pītisukha belongs to this jhāna, it is also appropriate to call it "vivekajampītisukha" as a single term by forming an alopa-samāsa (a compound where the case ending is not dropped).

"First" (pathama) is so called because it is first in numerical order, or because it arises first. "Jhāna" is of two kinds: object-scrutinizing jhāna (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and characteristic-scrutinizing jhāna (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Among them, the eight attainments are called "ārammaṇūpanijjhāna" because they closely scrutinize objects such as the earth kasina. Insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and Fruition (phala) are called "lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna." Among them, insight is lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna because it closely scrutinizes characteristics such as impermanence. The Path is lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna because the work of insight is completed by the Path. Fruition is lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna because it closely scrutinizes the true characteristic of the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). Among those jhānas, in this context, ārammaṇūpanijjhāna is intended in the preliminary stage, and lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna is intended at the moment of the supramundane Path. Therefore, it should be understood as "jhāna" because of scrutinizing the object, because of scrutinizing the characteristics, and because of burning up opposing states. "Upasampajja" means having approached, having reached. Or, it means having fulfilled, having accomplished. "Viharati" (abides) means one lives by means of a posture suitable for that jhāna; being one endowed with the aforementioned jhāna, one carries out the continuity of the individual existence.
171:
"Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā"—in this phrase, it means the subsiding, the surmounting, and the non-appearance of both applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) at the moment of the second jhāna. Although it is true that all factors of the first jhāna are absent in that second jhāna (since the contact etc. in the first jhāna are of one kind, while the contact etc. here in the second jhāna are of another), it should be understood that this is stated as "vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā" to show the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth, which are superior to the first jhāna, by way of surmounting the gross factors of the jhāna. "Ajjhattaṃ" here means one's own internal state; therefore, it means arising within oneself, produced in one's own continuity.

"Sampasādanaṃ" refers to faith (saddhā). Just as a cloth is called "blue cloth" because of its association with the color blue, the jhāna is also called "sampasādana" because of its association with faith. Alternatively, that jhāna is called "sampasādana" because it is endowed with faith and because it clarifies the mind by subsiding the disturbance of applied and sustained thought. In this interpretation, the words should be connected as "sampasādanaṃ cetaso" (tranquillity of mind). In the previous interpretation, however, the word "cetaso" should be connected with "ekodibhāvaṃ".

In that context, the connection of the meaning is as follows: It is "ekodi" because it arises as single (noble). It means it arises as pre-eminent or noble because it is not overwhelmed by applied and sustained thought. In the world, that which is noble is also called "eka" (single). Or, it may be said to be "eka" as being without a companion because it is devoid of applied and sustained thought. Alternatively, it is "udi" because it causes associated states to arise (rouses them). Being both "eka" in the sense of noble and "udi", it is called "ekodi". This is a synonym for concentration (samādhi). Because it develops such an ekodi, this second jhāna is called "ekodibhāvaṃ". That ekodi belongs to the mind (cetaso), not to a being or a soul (jīva). Therefore, it is called "cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ" (singleness of mind).

One might ask: "Does this faith not also exist in the first jhāna? And does this concentration called ekodi not also exist there? If so, why is only this second jhāna called 'sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ'?" The answer is: That first jhāna is not perfectly clear, like water disturbed by waves due to the agitation of applied and sustained thought; therefore, even though faith is present, it is not called "sampasādana". And because it is not perfectly clear, concentration is also not very distinct there; thus, it is not called "ekodibhāva". But in this second jhāna, because there is no obstacle of applied and sustained thought, faith gains its opportunity and becomes strong. Because of obtaining a companion in the form of strong faith, concentration also becomes distinct. Therefore, it should be understood that only this second jhāna is described in this way.
172:
In the phrase 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ', it is called 'avitakka' (without initial thought) because initial thought (vitakka) is absent in this second jhāna, or for this second jhāna, having been abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā). In the same way, it is called 'avicāra' (without sustained thought) because sustained thought (vicāra) is absent. Here, one might ask: 'Since this meaning is already established by the Pāli phrase "vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā" (with the stilling of initial and sustained thought), why is it stated again as "avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ"?' To this, it should be answered: While it is true that the meaning is established, this phrase does not merely indicate that meaning. Was it not stated as 'vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā' to show that the second jhāna and so forth, which are superior to the first jhāna, are attained by transcending the gross factors?

Furthermore, because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought, this second jhāna is 'sampasādana' (internal confidence), as it clarifies the associated states; it does not clarify them through the stilling of the turbidity of defilements. Because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought, it is 'ekodibhāva' (singleness of mind), which increases noble concentration. It is not called 'ekodibhāva' due to the abandoning of hindrances as in access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), nor due to the manifestation of factors as in the first jhāna. Thus, this statement points out the cause of 'sampasādana' and 'ekodibhāva'. Similarly, because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought, this second jhāna is called 'avitakka avicāra'; it is not called 'avitakka avicāra' simply because of the absence of initial and sustained thought, as is the case with the third and fourth jhānas, or as with eye-consciousness and so forth. In this way, it is also a demonstration of the cause for being 'avitakka' and 'avicāra'. It is not a statement merely indicating the absence of initial and sustained thought. Only the phrase 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ' itself is the statement that indicates the mere absence of initial and sustained thought. Therefore, although the former phrase was stated, the latter must be stated again.

'Samādhijaṃ' means born of the concentration of the first jhāna, or born of the associated concentration. In that regard, although the first jhāna is also born of associated concentration, only this concentration of the second jhāna deserves to be called 'concentration' (samādhi) because it is free from the disturbance of initial and sustained thought, and is thus exceedingly unshakable and very pure. Therefore, to praise the quality of this second jhāna, only this second jhāna is described as 'samādhijaṃ'. The phrase 'pītisukhaṃ' is to be understood in the same way as previously explained. 'Dutiyaṃ' (second) means it is second in numerical order; it is also called second because this second jhāna has arisen as the second one.

In the phrase 'pītiyā ca virāgā', 'virāga' (fading away/dispassion) means either the revulsion towards the aforementioned rapture (pīti) or the transcending of it. The word 'ca' (and) between pīti and virāga has the sense of conjunction. That word 'ca' connects either with 'stilling' (vūpasama) or with 'the stilling of initial and sustained thought.' Between these two, when it connects only with 'stilling,' the construction (yojanā) should be understood as: 'due to the revulsion towards rapture and, furthermore, due to the stilling [of rapture].' In this construction, 'virāga' has the meaning of revulsion. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'due to the revulsion towards rapture and due to the transcending [of it].' However, when it connects with 'the stilling of initial and sustained thought,' the construction should be understood as: 'due to the transcending of rapture and, furthermore, due to the stilling of initial and sustained thought.' In this construction, 'virāga' has the meaning of transcending. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'due to the transcending of rapture and due to the stilling of initial and sustained thought.'
173:
Although these vitakka and vicāra have already subsided in the second jhāna, this is stated here to show the cause of this third jhāna and to praise its qualities. Indeed, when it is said, "with the subsiding of vitakka and vicāra," it becomes clear that "the subsiding of vitakka and vicāra is the cause of this jhāna."

Just as in the third Noble Path (the Path of Non-returning), although sakkāya-diṭṭhi and others are not newly abandoned (having been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, etc.), the statement "with the abandoning of the five lower fetters" is made to praise the qualities of that Path and to inspire effort in those striving to attain it; in the same way, in this third jhāna, the mention of the subsiding of vitakka and vicāra—which had already subsided—is for the purpose of praising its qualities. Therefore, this meaning is stated: "with the fading away of pīti and with the subsiding of vitakka and vicāra."

In the phrase "he dwells equanimous (upekkhako)," it is called upekkhā because it observes (ikkhati) appropriately (upapattito). The meaning is that it observes evenly, observing without partiality. Because he is endowed with that upekkhā which is pure, abundant, and has reached its full strength, the person possessed of the third jhāna is called "one who is equanimous."

Equanimity (upekkhā) is of ten kinds: six-limbed equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), equanimity as a divine abiding (brahmavihārupekkhā), equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgupekkhā), equanimity of energy (vīriyūpekkhā), equanimity regarding formations (saṅkhārūpekkhā), equanimity as feeling (bitter-sweet neutrality) (vedanūpekkhā), equanimity of insight (vipassanūpekkhā), equanimity as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā), equanimity of jhāna (jhānūpekkhā), and equanimity of purification (pārisuddhūpekkhā).

Among those ten, that which is mentioned thus: "Here, monks, a monk whose taints are destroyed, on seeing a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending"—this equanimity, which takes the form of not abandoning the pure natural state when the six agreeable or disagreeable objects impinge upon the six doors of an Arahant, is called "six-limbed equanimity."

That which is mentioned thus: "He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity"—this equanimity, which takes the form of neutrality towards sentient beings, is called "equanimity as a divine abiding."

That which is mentioned thus: "He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity based on seclusion"—this equanimity, which takes the form of neutrality towards conascent states, is called "equanimity as a factor of enlightenment."
174:
That equanimity which is mentioned thus: "From time to time he attends to the sign of equanimity (the cause of moderate energy)"—which is described as energy that is neither over-exerted nor over-lax—is called "equanimity of energy."

That equanimity which is mentioned thus: "How many equanimities regarding formations arise by the power of serenity (samatha)? How many equanimities regarding formations arise by the power of insight (vipassanā)? Eight equanimities regarding formations arise by the power of serenity; ten equanimities regarding formations arise by the power of insight"—which takes the form of neutrality in standing firm after reflecting on the abandoning of hindrances (nīvaraṇa), etc., and in the grasping (of arising, existence, occurrence, etc.), is called "equanimity regarding formations."

That equanimity which is mentioned thus: "At whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen accompanied by equanimity"—which is described as the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant (adukkhamasukha)—is called "equanimity as feeling."

That equanimity which is mentioned thus: "Whatever (five aggregates) exists, whatever has come to be, that he abandons (through the knowledge of desire for deliverance), and he acquires equanimity"—which takes the form of neutrality in investigating (the characteristics of formations), is called "equanimity of insight."

That equanimity which is mentioned among the "or-whatever" (yevāpanaka) mental factors starting with desire (chanda), etc., and which exists as the cause for the balanced state of conascent (sahajata) phenomena, is called "equanimity as specific neutrality."

That equanimity which is mentioned thus: "He dwells equanimous"—which produces impartiality even towards that third jhāna which is the highest bliss (in the sense of avoiding excess or deficiency)—is called "equanimity of jhāna."

That equanimity which is mentioned thus: "The fourth jhāna which has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity"—which is pure from all opposing states (hindrances) and takes the form of being unconcerned even in the subsiding of those opposing states—is called "equanimity of purification."

Among those ten kinds of equanimity, six-limbed equanimity, equanimity as a divine abiding, equanimity as a factor of enlightenment, equanimity as specific neutrality, equanimity of jhāna, and equanimity of purification are, in terms of ultimate essence, one and the same, namely, equanimity as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā). However, this distinction exists because of the difference in various states (circumstances). It is like the distinction of a single person being called a child, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king. Therefore, it should be understood that among those equanimities, when there is six-limbed equanimity, there is no enlightenment factor of equanimity, etc.; or when there is the enlightenment factor of equanimity, there is no six-limbed equanimity, etc.
175:
Just as those six types of equanimity are one in essence, so too are equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) and equanimity in insight (vipassanūpekkhā) one in essence. Although this equanimity is simply wisdom (paññā), it is divided into two by way of function. For example, a man searching for a snake that entered his house in the evening with a goat-foot-shaped stick sees the snake lying in a heap of chaff. When he looks at it, wondering, "Is it a snake or not?", he sees the three rings on its neck and, becoming free from doubt, neutrality (majjhattatā) arises in his investigation as to whether it is a snake or not. In the same way, for one who has begun insight, when the three characteristics (lakkhaṇattaya) are seen through insight-knowledge, the neutrality that arises in the investigation of the impermanent nature of formations is called vipassanūpekkhā.

Again, just as that man firmly catches the snake with the goat-foot stick and, while seeking only the means of release, thinking, "How can I release this snake without harming it and without being bitten myself?", neutrality arises in his act of holding it; in the same way, for one who has already seen the three characteristics and views the three worlds like a mass of burning fire, the neutrality that occurs in the grasping of formations is called saṅkhārupekkhā. Thus, when vipassanūpekkhā is accomplished, saṅkhārupekkhā is also accomplished. However, it should be understood that this wisdom is divided into two by way of the functions of neutrality known as investigation and grasping. As for equanimity of energy (vīriyūpekkhā) and equanimity of feeling (vedanūpekkhā), they are distinct in essence from each other and from the remaining types of equanimity.

In this regard, the summary verse is stated:
Equanimity of neutrality, of the divine abodes, of the factors of enlightenment, of the six-fold sense-doors, of jhāna, and of purity;
Equanimity in insight, equanimity towards formations, equanimity of feeling, and equanimity of energy.
Thus, in detail, there are ten types of equanimity. Among these ten, the first six, beginning with equanimity of neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā), are one in essence.
When combined with the two types of wisdom—vipassanūpekkhā and saṅkhārupekkhā—and the two types of feeling and energy, these types of equanimity are only four in essence.

Among these ten types of equanimity, equanimity of jhāna (jhānūpekkhā) is intended here. That jhānūpekkhā has the characteristic of neutrality. Here, a question arises: "Is this equanimity not indeed tatramajjhattūpekkhā in essence? Since that tatramajjhattūpekkhā exists in the first and second jhānas as well, why is it not said there that 'he dwells equanimous'?" The answer is: because its function is not distinct. In the first and second jhānas, its function is not distinct because it is overwhelmed by initial application (vitakka) and so on. But in this third jhāna, because it is not overwhelmed by initial application, sustained application, and rapture, it becomes prominent in its function, like one with an uplifted head; therefore, it is so stated.

Now, regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending" (sato ca sampajāno): he is mindful (sato) because he remembers. He is clearly comprehending (sampajāno) because he knows well in various ways. Thus, mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña) are stated in terms of the person. Among those two, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, and clear comprehension (wisdom) has the characteristic of non-delusion. It is true that this mindfulness and clear comprehension also exist in the preceding first and second jhānas. For one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension, even access concentration (upacāra jhāna) cannot be fulfilled, let alone absorption (appanā jhāna). However, because those first and second jhānas are coarse, the movement of the mind is easy, like a person's movement on level ground; thus, the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not distinct. But in this third jhāna, because it is subtle due to the abandonment of coarse factors, the mind's movement must be maintained by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a person walking on the edge of a razor.
176:
Mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion. Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist in the previous jhānas, for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension, even access concentration cannot be fulfilled, let alone absorption. However, because those jhānas are coarse, the movement of the mind is easy, like a person walking on level ground; thus, the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension in those jhānas is not distinct. Because this third jhāna is subtle due to the abandonment of coarse jhāna factors, the movement of the mind must be desired only as it is grasped by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a person walking on the edge of a razor; therefore, mindfulness and clear comprehension are mentioned only in this third jhāna. Furthermore, just as a calf that follows its mother, if removed from the mother but not guarded, will return to the mother again; in the same way, this third jhāna happiness, although removed from rapture (pīti), if not guarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension, would return to rapture again and would be associated only with rapture. Otherwise, beings are prone to be intensely attached to happiness. And this third jhāna happiness is extremely sweet because there is no happiness superior to it. However, by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, there is no attachment to this happiness, and not for any other reason. It should be understood that mindfulness and clear comprehension are mentioned only in this third jhāna to show this special benefit.

Now, regarding the phrase "he experiences happiness with the body" (sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti): although for the person possessed of the third jhāna there is no advertence of mind to experience happiness, yet he has the happiness associated with the mental body (nāmakāya). Or, whatever happiness is associated with the mental body, the physical body (rūpakāya) is permeated by the extremely sublime materiality produced by that happiness. Because of being so permeated, even after emerging from the jhāna, he would experience happiness. Therefore, to show this meaning, it is said, "he experiences happiness with the body."

Now, regarding the phrase "of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He dwells happily, equanimous and mindful'" (yan taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti): the meaning is that because of which third jhāna, the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas declare, designate, disclose, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and praise that person possessed of the third jhāna as "one who dwells equanimous, mindful, and happily." It should be understood that the connection here is: "having attained that third jhāna, he dwells." 

Why do they praise him in this way? Because he is worthy of praise. For this person is equanimous even in the third jhāna, which has extremely sweet happiness and has reached the perfection of happiness; he is not pulled away by attachment to that happiness. In such a manner that rapture does not arise...
177:
He is called 'mindful' because of the presence of established mindfulness. Because he experiences through the mental body a happiness that is pleasing to the Noble Ones, cultivated only by the Noble Ones, and unsoiled by defilements, he is worthy of praise. Thus, being worthy of praise, the Noble Ones praise him by revealing those qualities that are the cause for praise, saying: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and a dweller in happiness.' This is how it should be understood.

'Third' is so called because it is third in numerical order, or because it has arisen for the third time.

'The abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain' refers to the abandoning of physical pleasure and physical pain. 'Beforehand' means that this abandoning occurs prior to the fourth jhāna, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna itself. 'With the disappearance of joy and grief' means the prior disappearance and abandoning of these two: mental pleasure and mental pain. When are these feelings abandoned? They are abandoned at the moment of access (upacāra) to the four jhānas. Joy (somanassa) is abandoned only at the moment of access to the fourth jhāna. Pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and pleasure (sukha) are abandoned at the moments of access to the first, second, and third jhānas, respectively. Although not taught in this order of abandoning, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief taught here should be understood according to the sequence of the faculties (indriya) as presented in the Indriya-vibhaṅga.

If these feelings are abandoned only at the moment of access to each respective jhāna, then why is it said: 'Monks, where does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Here the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder. Where do the faculties of grief, pleasure, and joy cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Here the arisen faculty of joy ceases without remainder'? It is because of their 'surpassing cessation' (atisayanirodha). Their surpassing cessation occurs in the first jhāna and so on, not just mere cessation. In the moment of access, there is mere cessation, not surpassing cessation. This is true: the faculty of pain, though ceased in the access to the first jhāna with its various advertings (āvajjanas), might still arise due to the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or due to discomfort from an uneven seat; but it cannot arise within absorption (appanā). Alternatively, this faculty of pain, though ceased in access, is not fully ceased because it has not been struck down by its opposite. But within absorption, the entire body is pervaded by bliss (pīti), and for one whose body is pervaded by bliss...
178:
...the faculty of pain is fully ceased because it has been struck down by its opposite. And the faculty of grief, though abandoned in the access to the second jhāna with its various advertings, arises when there is physical fatigue and mental distress caused by initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra). It does not arise when initial and sustained thought are absent. If the faculty of grief arises in a certain mind, it is because initial and sustained thought are present in that mind. Since initial and sustained thought are not yet abandoned in the access to the second jhāna, the faculty of grief may arise there; but it cannot arise in the second jhāna because its cause, initial and sustained thought, has been abandoned. Similarly, the faculty of pleasure, though abandoned in the access to the third jhāna, might arise in one whose body is touched by the sublime material form produced by rapture (pīti); but it cannot arise in the third jhāna. This is because in the third jhāna, rapture, which is the cause of pleasure, has entirely ceased. Similarly, the faculty of joy, though abandoned in the access to the fourth jhāna, might arise because of its proximity and because it has not been fully transcended due to the absence of equanimity (upekkhā) that has reached absorption; but it cannot arise in the fourth jhāna. Therefore, the phrase 'without remainder' (aparisesaṃ) is included in the teaching regarding each respective jhāna: 'Here the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder,' and so on.

Here a question is raised: 'If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access to each respective jhāna, why are they brought together and taught here in the fourth jhāna?' The answer is: to make [equanimity-feeling] easy to grasp. This 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' feeling is subtle and difficult to know, and cannot be easily grasped. Therefore, just as a cowherd, in order to catch a wild bull that is difficult to catch by approaching it directly, gathers all the cattle into a single pen and then, as he lets them out one by one, has the wild bull caught as it comes out in sequence, saying, 'This is the one; catch it!'; even so, all these feelings are brought together here to make the grasping of equanimity easy. By showing them together in this way, it is possible to make this equanimity-feeling known: 'That which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither joy nor grief, this is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.'

Alternatively, it should be understood that these feelings are taught to show the cause for the 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant deliverance of mind' (adukkhamasukha-cetovimutti). The abandoning of pleasure and pain, etc., are the causes for that deliverance of mind. As the Venerable Sāriputta said: 'Friends, there are four causes for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant deliverance of mind. Here, friends, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. These, friends, are the four causes for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant deliverance of mind.' Or else, just as self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) and so on, though already abandoned in other stages, are said to be abandoned in the third path in order to praise the virtues of that path...
179: It should also be understood that these feelings are taught in this fourth jhāna to describe the benefits of this fourth jhāna. Alternatively, it should be understood that these feelings are taught to show the extreme distance of lust and hatred in this fourth jhāna by the destruction of their causes, pleasure and pain. Indeed, among those feelings, pleasure is the cause of joy, joy is the cause of lust, pain is the cause of grief, and grief is the cause of hatred. By the destruction of pleasure and so on, lust and hatred, along with their causes, are destroyed and thus become extremely distant. "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (adukkhamasukha) means "not painful" because of the absence of pain, and "not pleasant" because of the absence of pleasure. By using this expression of opposites to pleasure and pain, the third feeling, which is the opposite of pain and pleasure, is shown in this fourth jhāna; it does not merely show the absence of pain and pleasure. The third feeling is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" and is also called "equanimity" (upekkhā). That equanimity has the characteristic of experiencing a neutral object (iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇa) which is distinct from both desirable and undesirable objects. "Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" (upekkhāsatipārisuddhi) means the jhāna that has the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity (tatramajjhattupekkhā). Indeed, in this fourth jhāna, mindfulness is extremely pure, and that purity of mindfulness is brought about by equanimity, not by anything else. Therefore, this fourth jhāna is called "purity of mindfulness due to equanimity." The equanimity by which the purity of mindfulness occurs in this fourth jhāna should be understood as tatramajjhattata (neutrality) in its ultimate sense. In this jhāna, it is not only the mental factor of mindfulness that is purified by that equanimity; rather, all associated states are also purified. However, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the head. Among those feelings, although this tatramajjhattupekkhā exists in the lower three jhānas as well, just as the moon, though present during the day, is not pure or bright because it is overcome by the sun's radiance and because it does not obtain the night which is compatible with its cool nature and helpful to it; similarly, this moon-like tatramajjhattupekkhā, although present in the divisions of the first jhāna and so on, is not pure because it is overcome by the power of opposing states such as initial application (vitakka) and because it does not obtain the night of the compatible equanimity-feeling. Because that tatramajjhattupekkhā is not pure, the states such as mindfulness that arise together with it are also not pure, like the light of the impure moon during the day. Therefore, none of those lower jhānas is called "purity of mindfulness due to equanimity." But in this fourth jhāna, because there is no overcoming by the radiance of opposing states such as initial application, and because the night of the compatible equanimity-feeling is obtained, this moon-like tatramajjhattupekkhā is extremely pure. Because that tatramajjhattupekkhā is pure, the states such as mindfulness that arise together with it are also pure and bright, like the light of the pure moon. Therefore, it should be understood that only this fourth jhāna is called "purity of mindfulness due to equanimity." "Fourth" means fourth in the numerical order, and it is also called fourth because it arises for the fourth time. These four jhānas are distinct both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. They are distinct in the preliminary stage by way of attainment, and at the moment of the path by way of the path having different jhānas. Indeed, the first path of a person...
180: (The first path of a person) is of the first jhāna; the second path and so on are also either of the first jhāna or of any one of the second jhāna and so on. The first path of a person is of any one of the second jhāna and so on; the second path and so on are also either of any one of the second jhāna and so on or of the first jhāna. Thus, the four paths may be similar, dissimilar, or partially similar by way of jhāna. In fact, this distinction of the path occurs as determined by the basic jhāna (padakajjhāna). In detail, for a person who has attained the first jhāna, when they practice insight after emerging from the first jhāna, the path that arises is of the first jhāna. In this path similar to the first jhāna, the path factors and the factors of enlightenment are indeed complete. For one who practices insight after emerging from the second jhāna, the path that arises is of the second jhāna; in this path similar to the second jhāna, there are seven path factors. For one who practices insight after emerging from the third jhāna, the path that arises is of the third jhāna; in this path similar to the third jhāna, there are seven path factors and six factors of enlightenment. This method applies from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. In the formless realm, jhāna occurs by way of the fourfold and fivefold methods; that jhāna is said to be only supramundane (lokuttara), not mundane (lokiya). How can this be in the formless realm? In this formless realm too, for one who, after emerging from any one of the jhānas such as the first jhāna, attains the path of stream-entry and then develops the formless attainments and is born in the formless realm, the three higher paths arise for them there, having only the jhāna that was the basis for that path of stream-entry. Thus, only the basic jhāna determines it. However, some elders say, "The aggregates which are the objects of insight determine it." Some elders say, "The inclination of the person determines it." Some elders say, "The insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) determines it." Among those views, this is the sequential explanation: By way of determination by insight, the path that arises for a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka), the path that arises for one who has attained meditative absorptions without making a jhāna the basis, and the path produced by making the first jhāna the basis and contemplating various formations—all these are of the first jhāna only. In all these, there are seven factors of enlightenment, eight path factors, and five jhāna factors. The insight occurring in the preliminary stage for those persons, whether it occurs together with joy or together with equanimity, when it reaches the state of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) at the time of emergence, it occurs only together with joy. In the fivefold method, in the paths produced by making the second, third, and fourth jhānas the basis, the jhāna has four factors, three factors, and two factors respectively in due order. In all those paths, there are seven path factors; in the path of the fourth jhāna, there are six factors of enlightenment. This distinction occurs both by determination by the basic jhāna and by determination by insight.
181:
For those dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka), the insight occurring in the preliminary stage of the path may be accompanied by joy (somanassa) or accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā). However, insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) is accompanied only by joy. In the path produced by basing it on the fifth jhana, there are two jhana factors by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind (citt'ekaggatā). The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and the path factors (maggaṅga) are only six or seven. This distinction occurs by way of the dual determination of the basic jhana (pādakajjhāna) and insight. In this method, the insight in the preliminary stage of the path may be accompanied by joy or equanimity, but insight leading to emergence is accompanied only by equanimity. The same method applies to the path produced by basing it on the formless jhanas (arūpajjhāna). In this fourfold method, since there is no second jhana which has only sustained thought (vicāra) without initial thought (vitakka), that second jhana is excluded and the application is made by way of the remaining four jhanas. Thus, the attainment (samāpatti) that arises near the path produced after emerging from the basic jhana and contemplating all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) makes itself similar to it, just as the color of the ground makes the color of a monitor lizard similar to itself.

In the second Theravāda view, from whichever attainment one emerges and whichever states of attainment one contemplates to produce the path, that path is similar only to those respective contemplated attainments. In this second Theravāda view also, the determination of insight should be understood in the manner already stated.

In the third Theravāda view, according to one's own inclination (ajjhāsaya), basing on whichever jhana and contemplating whichever jhana-states the path is produced, that path is similar only to those respective jhanas. Without the basic jhana or the contemplated jhana, it cannot be achieved by mere inclination alone. In this third Theravāda view also, the determination of insight should be understood in the manner already stated.

The one-pointedness (ekaggatā) present in these four jhanas is called Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi). This concentration is called mundane Right Concentration in the preliminary stage and supramundane Right Concentration in the later stage. Thus, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, teaches the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca) by way of the mundane and supramundane. Therein, in the mundane path, all path factors take one of the six objects as appropriate. In the supramundane path, however, for the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) practicing for the penetration of the Four Truths, the eye of wisdom that takes Nibbāna as its object and uproots the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) is called Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi). For one possessed of such view, the state associated with it that uproots the three types of wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa) and directs the mind towards the state of Nibbāna is called Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa). For one thus seeing and thinking, the abstinence from wrong speech associated with those states that uproots the four types of verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita) is called Right Speech (Sammā-vācā). For one thus abstaining, the abstinence from wrong action associated with that Right Speech that cuts off the three types of wrong action (micchā-kammanta) is called Right Action (Sammā-kammanta). For that noble disciple, the abstinence from wrong livelihood associated with those states, which is the purification of Right Speech and Right Action and which cuts off wrong livelihood such as scheming (kuhana) and so forth, is called Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva). For one established on the ground of virtue (sīla) consisting of Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood, the arousing of energy associated with those states and consistent with those three abstinences (virati), which cuts off laziness and accomplishes the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the maintenance of arisen wholesome states, is (Right Effort).
182:
Abstinence from wrong action is called Right Action (Sammā-kammanta). For that noble disciple, the abstinence from wrong livelihood, which is the purification of Right Speech and Right Action, associated with those states, and which absolutely cuts off wrong livelihood such as scheming (kuhana) and so forth, is called Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva). For that noble disciple established on the ground of virtue (sīla) known as Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood, the arousing of energy associated with those states and consistent with those three abstinences (virati), which absolutely cuts off laziness and accomplishes the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the maintenance of arisen wholesome states, is called Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma).

For one thus striving, the non-forgetfulness of the mind associated with that Right Effort, which destroys wrong mindfulness and accomplishes the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) and so forth, is called Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati). For one whose mind is well-guarded by such peerless mindfulness, the one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) associated with that Right Mindfulness, which destroys wrong concentration, is called Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi). This is the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path.

There is that path which, together with the mundane path, is designated as the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering" (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā). Indeed, this path is called both "knowledge" (vijjā) because Right View and Right Intention are subsumed under knowledge, and "conduct" (caraṇa) because the remaining path factors are subsumed under conduct. Similarly, it is called both "serenity" (samatha) and "insight" (vipassanā) because those two (Right View and Right Intention) are subsumed under the vehicle of insight, and the remaining six are subsumed under the vehicle of serenity. It is also called the "three aggregates" (khandha) because those two are subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-kkhandha), the next three under the aggregate of virtue (sīla-kkhandha), and the remaining three under the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-kkhandha). It is also called the "three trainings" (sikkhā) because they are subsumed under the training of higher wisdom (adhipaññā), higher virtue (adhisīla), and higher mind (adhicitta).

The noble disciple endowed with this path, like a traveler endowed with eyes capable of seeing and feet capable of walking, becomes one possessed of knowledge and conduct (vijjā-caraṇa-sampanna). Avoiding the two extremes—devotion to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) through the vehicle of insight and devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) through the vehicle of serenity—he practices the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā). Shattering the mass of delusion with the aggregate of wisdom, the mass of hatred with the aggregate of virtue, and the mass of greed with the aggregate of concentration, he attains the three fulfillments: the fulfillment of wisdom (paññā-sampadā) through the training of higher wisdom, the fulfillment of virtue (sīla-sampadā) through the training of higher virtue, and the fulfillment of concentration (samādhi-sampadā) through the training of higher mind, and thus realizes the deathless Nibbāna. He becomes one who has entered the plane of the Nobles (ariya-bhūmi), which is good in the beginning, middle, and end, adorned with the jewels of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), and known as the certainty of rightness (sammatta-niyāma).

## The Exposition of the Truth of the Path is finished.
183:
## Explanation of Miscellaneous Points on the Truths (Saccapakiṇṇakavaṇṇanā)

Among the Four Truths, the Noble Truth of Suffering (Dukkha-sacca) has the characteristic of oppression. The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Samudaya-sacca) has the characteristic of being the cause. The Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Nirodha-sacca) has the characteristic of peace. The Noble Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca) has the characteristic of deliverance. Furthermore, they also have the characteristics of occurrence (pavatti), causing occurrence (pavattaka), cessation (nivatti), and causing cessation (nivattaka) respectively. Similarly, they have the characteristics of being conditioned (saṅkhata), craving (taṇhā), being unconditioned (asaṅkhata), and the seeing of Nibbāna (dassana).

If it is asked, "Why are only four Noble Truths taught, neither less nor more?" The answer is: because no other truth is possible, and because none of these four can be removed. Indeed, there is no other truth additional to these four, nor can even one of these be discarded. Regarding this meaning, it was taught: 
"Monks, if any ascetic or brahmin should come and say, 'This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering; another is the Noble Truth of Suffering. Setting aside this Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the Ascetic Gotama, I will point out another Noble Truth of Suffering,' such a thing is impossible," and so forth.

And as it was further said:
"Monks, if any ascetic or brahmin should say, 'This is not the first Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the Ascetic Gotama; rejecting this first Noble Truth of Suffering, I will point out another first Noble Truth of Suffering,' such a thing is impossible," and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1086).

Furthermore, when the Blessed One explained the process of occurrence (pavatti), He explained it together with its cause. When He explained cessation (nivatti), He explained it together with its means. Thus, because occurrence, cessation, and their respective causes are limited to these four, only four were taught. Similarly, they are taught as four by way of: things to be fully understood (pariññeyya), things to be abandoned (pahātabba), things to be realized (sacchikātabba), and things to be developed (bhāvetabba); or by way of the object of craving, craving itself, the cessation of craving, and the means to reach the cessation of craving; or by way of attachment (ālaya), delight in attachment, the uprooting of attachment, and the means to uproot attachment.

Among these four truths, the Noble Truth of Suffering is taught first because it is gross (oḷārika), common to all beings (sabbasaṭṭasādhāraṇa), and thus easy to understand. To show the cause of that suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin is taught immediately after it...
184:
The Noble Truth of Cessation is taught after the Truth of Origin to make known the meaning that with the cessation of the cause (Samudaya), the effect (Dukkha) ceases. The Noble Truth of the Path is taught at the end to show the means of attaining that cessation. Alternatively, the Truth of Suffering is taught first to arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in beings who are attached to the pleasures of existence. To make known that this suffering does not come without a cause, nor is it created by a creator such as Brahma or Vishnu, but rather arises because of this craving, the Truth of Origin is taught immediately after the Truth of Suffering. Thereafter, the Truth of Cessation is taught to provide relief by showing the escape (Nibbāna) to those whose minds are terrified by being oppressed by suffering along with its cause, and who are seeking an escape from suffering. After that, the Truth of the Path, which leads to Nibbāna, is taught for the purpose of attaining the Truth of Cessation. This is the order of these four truths.

Among these four truths, the Truth of Suffering should be seen as a burden; the Truth of Origin as the taking up of the burden; the Truth of Cessation as the laying down of the burden; and the Truth of the Path as the means for laying down the burden. Alternatively, the Truth of Suffering is like a disease; the Truth of Origin is like the cause of the disease; the Truth of Cessation is like the cure of the disease; and the Truth of the Path is like the medicine. Alternatively, the Truth of Suffering is like a famine; the Truth of Origin is like a drought; the Truth of Cessation is like abundance; and the Truth of the Path is like good rain. Furthermore, these four truths should be understood through similes by associating them with: an enemy, the root of the enemy, the total destruction of the enemy, and the means to destroy the enemy; a poison tree, the root of the poison tree, the cutting of the root, and the means to cut the root; fear, the cause of fear, fearlessness, and the means to attain fearlessness; and this shore, a great flood, the far shore, and the effort to reach the far shore.

In the ultimate sense, all these truths should be understood as empty, because there is no feeler (vedaka), no doer (kāraka), no one who is extinguished (nibbuta), and no traveler (gamaka). Therefore, it was said by the former teachers:

"Suffering alone exists, but no sufferer is found;
The deed is there, but no doer is found;
Peace (Nibbāna) exists, but no person who is extinguished;
The path exists, but no traveler is found."

Alternatively:
The first two (Dukkha and Samudaya) are empty of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self.
The state of the Deathless (Amata-pada), called Nibbāna, is empty of self.
The Truth of the Path is empty of permanence, happiness, and self.
Thus, emptiness should be understood in these four truths.

Alternatively, the three truths—Suffering, Origin, and Path—are empty of the Truth of Cessation. The Truth of Cessation is also empty of the remaining three truths. Alternatively, among these four truths, the causal truths—Origin and Path—are empty of the resultant truths. This is because the effect, Suffering, does not exist in the cause, Origin; and the effect, Cessation, does not exist in the cause, the Path. Unlike the view of the proponents of Prakṛti (Pakativādī), where the cause (Prakṛti) is pregnant with the effect (Vikṛti), these causal truths are not pregnant with the resultant truths. The resultant truths—Suffering and Cessation—are also empty of the causal truths—Origin and Path. This is because the causal truth and the resultant truth do not coexist. Unlike the view of the proponents of Inherence (Samavāyavādī), where the product such as a dyad (dvi-aṇuka) is inherent in the cause (paramāṇu), this resultant truth is not inherent in the causal truth. Therefore, it was said by the former teachers:
185:
“Among these four truths, the triad [of suffering, origin, and path] is empty of the truth of cessation;
Cessation is also empty of that triad.
The truth of cause is empty of the truth of effect;
The truth of effect is also empty of that truth of cause.”

All truths are similar in terms of being unerringly true, being empty of self, and being difficult to penetrate. As the Blessed One said: “What do you think, Ānanda? Which is more difficult to do or more difficult to achieve: that a man from a distance, with a subtle arrow, should shoot through a narrow keyhole, shot after shot without missing; or that he should pierce the tip of a hair split into seven parts with another tip?” “Venerable sir, it is more difficult and harder to achieve to pierce the tip of a hair split into seven parts with another tip.” “Ānanda, those who penetrate as it really is, ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ penetrate something much more difficult to penetrate [than splitting a hair].”

They are dissimilar in terms of the definition of their individual characteristics. The first two truths [suffering and origin] are similar in being deep due to being difficult to fathom, being worldly, and being with taints. They are dissimilar in terms of the distinction between effect and cause, and between what is to be fully known (pariññeyya) and what is to be abandoned (pahātabba). The last two truths [cessation and path] are also similar in being deep and difficult to fathom, being supramundane, and being without taints. They are dissimilar in terms of the distinction between the object (visaya) and the subject/possessor of the object (visayī), and between what is to be realized (sacchikātabba) and what is to be developed (bhāvetabba). 

The first and third truths [suffering and cessation] are also similar in being designated as effects. They are dissimilar in being conditioned and unconditioned. The second and fourth truths [origin and path] are also similar in being designated as causes. They are dissimilar in being strictly unwholesome and wholesome. The first and fourth truths [suffering and path] are also similar in being conditioned phenomena. They are dissimilar in being worldly and supramundane. The second and third truths [origin and cessation] are also similar in being states that are neither trainee (sekha) nor non-trainee (asekha). They are dissimilar in terms of having an object (sārammaṇa) and having no object (anārammaṇa).

“Thus, in these ways and methods, the wise person
Should know the similarity and dissimilarity of the Noble Truths.”

Among these, all suffering is one-fold in terms of the nature of occurrence (pavatti); two-fold in terms of mind and matter; three-fold in terms of existence in the sense sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere; and four-fold in terms of the four nutriments.
186:
[Suffering] is five-fold in terms of the five aggregates of clinging. The origin is also one-fold in terms of the nature of causing occurrence; two-fold in terms of craving associated with views and unassociated with views; three-fold in terms of craving for sense pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence; four-fold in terms of being abandoned by the four paths; five-fold in terms of delighting in the aggregate of form, etc.; and six-fold in terms of the six classes of craving.

Cessation is also one-fold in terms of being the unconditioned element; but figuratively, it is two-fold as Nibbāna with residue and Nibbāna without residue; three-fold as the stilling of the three types of existence; four-fold as being attainable by the four paths; five-fold as the stilling of delight in the five [aggregates]; and six-fold in terms of the destruction of the six classes of craving.

The path is also one-fold in terms of being what is to be developed; two-fold in terms of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), or in terms of vision (dassana) and development (bhāvanā); and three-fold in terms of the three aggregates. This truth of the path, because it has parts, is like a city within a kingdom, and is included within the three aggregates which have no parts. As the Blessed One said:

“Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not included in the Noble Eightfold Path, but the Noble Eightfold Path is included in the three aggregates. Friend Visākha, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue. Right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration. Right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom.”

It is four-fold by way of the path of stream-entry, and so on.

Furthermore, all truths are one-fold because they are unerring or because they are to be known by higher knowledge (abhiññeyya). They are two-fold as worldly and supramundane, or as conditioned and unconditioned. They are three-fold as what is to be abandoned by the path of vision and the path of development, what is not to be abandoned, and what is neither to be abandoned nor not to be abandoned. They are four-fold as what is to be fully known, abandoned, realized, and developed.

“Thus, for the sake of welfare and happiness, the wise person
Should know the variety of the Noble Truths, which are difficult to understand, in many ways.”

## The Explanation of Miscellaneous Truths is finished.
