In the explanation of knowledge consisting of virtue (sīlamayañāṇaniddesa), the word ‘five’ (pañca) is a delimitation of number. ‘Virtues’ (sīlāni) shows the phenomena thus delimited. The passage beginning with ‘virtue of limited purification’ (pariyantapārisuddhisīla) is the text itself showing the five kinds of virtue. The meaning of terms like ‘limited’ (pariyanta) should be understood thus: just as a cloth is called a ‘red cloth’ because it is associated with the color red, so too this virtue has a limit by way of the numbers five, eight, ten, and so on; therefore, it is called ‘limited’ (pariyanta). Alternatively, unlike the virtue of monks, the virtue of laypeople is limited...
187:
Now, the General of the Dhamma (Dhamma-senāpati), following the sequence taught by the Blessed One, points out the group of the Four Truths at the end, concluding the explanation of knowledge based on learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa) by way of the Four Truths, starting with: "It is knowledge in the sense of knowing that truth." In this way, he concludes everything previously stated: "The wisdom that arises from listening is knowledge based on learning."

## In the Saddhammappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga,
## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge Based on Learning is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge Based on Virtue

In the description of knowledge based on virtue, "five" refers to the delimitation by number. "Virtues" (sīlāni) refers to the indication of the specific dhammas being delimited. "Virtue of limited purification" (pariyantapārisuddhisīla) and so forth, is the demonstration of the five types of virtue according to their individual nature. In the terms "pariyantapārisuddhi" and so forth, the meaning should be understood as follows: Just as a cloth is called "blue" because of its association with the color blue, so too, it is called "pariyanta" (limited) because it has a delimitation (pariyanta) by way of number. Alternatively, it is called "pariyanta" because when one reaches the virtue of the ordained (upasampanna), the virtue of the unordained (anupasampanna) comes to an end (pariyanta). In the word "sapariyanta," it should be understood that the letter "sa" has been elided, just as the letter "u" is elided in the phrase "dakaṃ dakāsayā pavisanti."

Purified state is "pārisuddhi." Since that purification is limited (or has an end), it is "pariyantapārisuddhi." Virtue characterized as limited purification is "pariyantapārisuddhisīla."

It is "apariyanta" (unlimited) because it is the opposite of what was mentioned and has no limit. Or, it is "apariyanta" because there is no limit to this virtue, or because its limit has expanded (transcended). Because it has been unbroken and unperforated since its undertaking, or because it has been rehabilitated even if broken, and because it is free from even the slightest stain of an intention to transgress, it is pure like a genuine natural gem or like well-smelted and well-refined gold. Thus, being the proximate cause for the Noble Path, it is "paripuṇṇa" (fulfilled) in the sense of being non-deficient. It is "aparāmaṭṭha" (unmisapprehended) because wrong view has been abandoned and because it is not grasped by the misapprehension of view (diṭṭhiparāmāsa). Alternatively, it is "aparāmaṭṭha" because no accuser can find fault and grasp it, saying, "This is a flaw in your virtue." It is "paṭippassaddhi" (tranquillization) because of the tranquillization of all distress at the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship. "Anupasampannānaṃ" means those who are not "upasampanna." One who is exceedingly endowed with virtue by way of complete undertaking is called "upasampanna"; those who are not so endowed are "anupasampanna." (It refers to the virtue) of those unordained persons.
188:
In the term "pariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ," it is "sikkhā" (training) in the sense of that which should be trained in, and "pada" (steps/portions) in the sense of constituent parts; thus, it means the portions that should be trained in. Furthermore, for one established in virtue, all wholesome states (kusalā dhammā) are "sikkhā" because they are to be attained higher up (in the path and fruit). Virtues are "pada" for those trainings in the sense of being their foundation. Thus, being the foundation for trainings, they are "sikkhāpada" (training rules). Those who have limited training rules are "pariyantasikkhāpada." (This refers to) those who have such limited training rules. Here, there are two kinds of limits: the limit of training rules and the limit of time.

What is the limit of training rules? For laymen (upāsaka) and laywomen (upāsikā), there are one, two, three, four, five, eight, or ten training rules according to their undertaking. For probationers (sikkhamānā), male novices (sāmaṇera), and female novices (sāmaṇerī), there are ten training rules. This is the limit of training rules.

What is the limit of time? Laymen and laywomen, when giving gifts, undertake virtue with the limit of the distribution (or seeking) of food. When they go to a monastery, they undertake virtue for the duration of their stay in the monastery. They undertake virtue by delimiting it for one, two, three, or more days and nights. This is the limit of time. Among these two kinds of limits, virtue undertaken with a limit on training rules is terminated either by transgression or by death. Virtue undertaken with a limit on time is terminated by the passing of that specific delimited time.

Regarding "apariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ":
"Nine thousand crores, and one hundred and eighty crores,
Fifty hundred-thousands, and thirty-six thousand more.
These disciplines of restraint were proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One;
In the discipline of the Vinaya, the training rules are indicated by the method of abbreviation (peyyāla)."

Although there is a limit by way of such counting, these training rules are "apariyanta" (unlimited) because they are undertaken without remainder, because no limit is seen even for the sake of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, or life, and because there is no delimitation of the virtue to be protected in the future. Those who have such unlimited training rules are called "apariyantasikkhāpada." (This refers to) those who have such unlimited training rules. Alternatively, it means those whose limited training rules have been developed (increased).

In the terms "puthujjanakalyāṇakānaṃ" and so forth:
"He is a worldling (puthujjana) because of reasons such as generating various (puthu) defilements;
Because he is included among the many (puthu) folk, or because he is a person separate (puthu) from the Noble Ones."
Even though they do not transcend the characteristics of a worldling as stated...
189:
The Blessed One, who is the Kinsman of the Sun, said:
'Two types of worldlings (puthujjana) are spoken of: one is the blind worldling (andha-puthujjana), and one is the noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana).'

Among the two types of worldlings mentioned, those noble worldlings who have transcended the state of a blind worldling by associating with the good Dhamma and remain in the state of a noble worldling are meant by the term 'kalyāṇa-puthujjana'. Alternatively, it refers to the good persons among worldlings as 'puthujjana-kalyāṇaka'.

In the phrase 'kusala-dhamme yuttānaṃ', the word 'kusala' is found in the senses of health (ārogya), blamelessness (anavajja), skill (cheka), and happy result (sukhavipāka). This word 'kusala' is evident in the sense of health (ārogya) in passages such as: 'Is the venerable one healthy (kusala)? Is the venerable one free from ailment?' It is evident in the sense of blamelessness (anavajja) in passages such as: 'Venerable sir, what kind of bodily conduct is wholesome (kusala)? Great King, that bodily conduct which is blameless (anavajja) is wholesome,' and 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One teaches this unsurpassed Dhamma regarding wholesome states (kusala-dhamma).' It is evident in the sense of skill (cheka) in passages such as: 'You are skillful (kusala) in the parts of a chariot,' and 'Women who are skillful (kusala) in dancing and singing and are well-trained.' It is evident in the sense of happy result (sukhavipāka) in passages such as: 'Monks, because of the undertaking of wholesome states (kusala-dhamma),' and 'Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome (kusala) kamma.' In this context, the word 'kusala' is appropriate in the senses of health, blamelessness, and happy result.

The etymological meaning (vacanattha) of this word 'kusala' is: they are called 'kusala' because they shake, disturb, or destroy contemptible (kucchita) and evil states. Alternatively, states that occur in a contemptible manner are called 'kusa'; they are called 'kusala' because they cut (luna) those 'kusa'. Or, wisdom is called 'kusa' because it thins out contemptible unwholesome states; they are called 'kusala' because they are to be taken or produced by that wisdom called 'kusa'. Or, just as kusa grass cuts the palms of both hands, these wholesome states cut the two groups of defilements—those that have arisen and those that have not yet arisen—and thus they are called 'kusala' in the sense of cutting like kusa grass. Furthermore, they are called 'kusala' because of the sense of health, blamelessness, or being produced by skill. In this context, since only insight-wholesome (vipassanā-kusala) is intended, it should be understood that the singular form 'kusala-dhamme' is used to show only that insight-wholesome, excluding other states. It means those who are endowed with constant and respectful practice in the states of insight-wholesome.

In the phrase 'sekkhapariyante paripūrakārīnaṃ', the meaning is: they are called 'sekkha' (trainees) because they are born in the three trainings (sikkhā). They are called 'sekkha' because they belong to the seven types of trainees. They are called 'sekkha' because they train themselves. They attain the paths and fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, Non-returning, and the path of Arahantship. They are called 'sekkha-pariyantā' because those states belonging to the seven trainees arise at the end of the practice fulfilled by those worldlings. Or, they are called 'sekkha-pariyanta' because the states of the seven trainees are the limit (end) of the practice fulfilled by those worldlings. In that Dhamma which has the state of a trainee at the end, or which has the state of a trainee as its limit...
190:
Sekkha (trainee) is so called because they are involved in the three trainings such as the higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), because they are the property of the seven types of noble trainees, and because the four paths and the three lower fruits are being practiced by them. It refers to the states of the path of Stream-entry, the fruit of Stream-entry, the path of Once-returning, the fruit of Once-returning, the path of Non-returning, the fruit of Non-returning, and the path of Arahantship. These are called 'sekkha-pariyanta' because they occur at the end of the practice fulfilled by worldlings. Or, they are called 'sekkha-pariyanta' because the trainee-states are the boundary (limit) for the practice fulfilled by those worldlings. There is a connection with the phrase 'in that sekkha-pariyanta Dhamma'.

They are called 'paripūrakārī' because they bring about fulfillment, or they are called 'paripūrakārī' because those noble worldlings practice to reach fulfillment. It refers to those noble worldlings who bring insight (vipassanā) to fulfillment in the practice that precedes the path of Stream-entry and has the trainee-states as its end. In the phrase 'kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhānaṃ', 'kāya' refers to the physical body. Indeed, the body is called 'kāya' because it is a collection of impure things like hair, and because it is the site for hundreds of diseases such as eye diseases. 'Jīvita' refers to the life faculty (jīvitindriya). It is called 'jīvita' because beings live by it. 'Anapekkha' means they have no longing; the meaning is that they are without affection. It refers to those persons who have no longing for that body and life.

Now, to show the reason for their lack of longing for those things, he said 'pariccattajīvitānaṃ' (those who have relinquished life). By relinquishing their own lives for the sake of the Blessed One or the teacher, those persons have no longing even if the body is exhausted or if life is destroyed. 'Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ' refers to the seven noble persons, such as those standing in the path of Stream-entry, who are called 'sekkha' because they are training. 'Tathāgatasāvakānaṃ' refers to the disciples of the Tathāgata. The eight noble persons are called 'sāvaka' (disciples) because they are born of the noble birth at the end of hearing the Dhamma, and because they listen respectfully to the teaching and instruction of the Blessed One with unwavering confidence. 

Among those disciples, to specifically show those standing in the fruit of Arahantship, he said 'khīṇāsavānaṃ', which means the Arahants whose taints (āsava) are entirely destroyed by the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. 'Paccekabuddhānaṃ' refers to a Private Buddha who, depending on various causes, has realized the Four Noble Truths alone without a teacher. It refers to such Private Buddhas. 

In the word 'Tathāgatānaṃ', the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata' for eight reasons: He is 'Tathāgata' because He has come in the same way (as previous Buddhas); He is 'Tathāgata' because He has gone in the same way; He is 'Tathāgata' because He has arrived at the true characteristic; He is 'Tathāgata' because He has fully awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is; He is 'Tathāgata' because of seeing truly; He is 'Tathāgata' because of speaking truly; He is 'Tathāgata' because of acting truly; and He is 'Tathāgata' in the sense of overcoming everything.
191:
In what way is the Blessed One called 'Tathāgata' because he has come (āgata) in that same way (tathā)? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas came, exerting themselves for the benefit of the entire world, so too has our Blessed One come. What does this mean? By whatever aspiration (abhinīhāra) the previous Blessed Ones came, by that same aspiration has our Blessed One also come.

Alternatively, just as the previous Blessed Ones came after fulfilling the thirty perfections—namely, the ten perfections (pāramī), the ten sub-perfections (upapāramī), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī) consisting of generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity; after making the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), namely, the sacrifice of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and sons and wives; and after fulfilling the preliminary efforts (pubbayoga), former conduct (pubbacariya), proclamation of the Dhamma (dhamm-akkhāna), conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), and so forth, reaching the pinnacle of conduct for enlightenment (buddhi-cariyā)—so too has our Blessed One come. 

And just as the previous Blessed Ones came after developing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path, so too has our Blessed One come; thus he is called 'Tathāgata'.

"Just as the sages such as Dīpaṅkara Buddha and others came into this world to attain omniscience,
So too has this Sakyan Sage come; therefore, the One with Vision is called 'Tathāgata'."

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has gone (gata) in that same way (tathā)? He has gone just as the previous Blessed Ones went immediately upon being born. And how did they go? Indeed, immediately upon being born, they stood firmly on the earth with level feet and went with a stride of seven steps, facing the north. As it is said: "Ananda, as soon as the Bodhisatta is born, he stands firmly on the earth with level feet and, facing the north, goes with a stride of seven steps while a white umbrella is held over him; he surveys all directions and speaks a noble (asabha) speech: 'I am the highest in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the foremost in the world. This is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.'"

And that going of his was true (tatha) and not false (avitatha), being a precursor for the attainment of many special qualities. For his standing with level feet as soon as he was born was the precursor for his attainment of the four bases of power. His facing the north was the precursor for his being transcendent over the entire world. His stride of seven steps was the precursor for his attainment of the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment. "The golden-handled yak-tail fans were waved..."
192:
The waving of the yak-tail fans mentioned here in the Nālaka Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta is the precursor for the crushing of all sectarian doctrines. The holding of the white umbrella is the precursor for the attainment of the stainless white umbrella of the noble liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. The surveying of all directions is the precursor for the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. The speaking of the noble speech beginning with "I am the highest" is the precursor for the turning of the noble Wheel of Dhamma, which cannot be turned back by devas or Brahmas. In the same way, this Bodhisatta of ours also went. And that going of his was true and not false, being the precursor for those very attainments of special qualities. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Just as a bull-king, as soon as it is born, touches the earth with level feet,
So did Gotama take seven steps as soon as he was born, while the gods held the white umbrella."

"Having gone seven steps, Gotama surveyed all directions equally on all sides;
He uttered a speech endowed with eight qualities, like a lion standing on a mountain peak."

Thus, he is called 'Tathāgata' because he went in a true manner.

Alternatively, just as the previous Blessed Ones went after abandoning all defilements by the path of Arahantship, so too this Blessed One went after abandoning sensual desire through renunciation... [pe]... the hindrances through the first jhāna... [pe]... the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence... [pe]... and all defilements through the path of Arahantship. In this way also, he is called 'Tathāgata' because he went in a true manner.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at (āgata) true characteristics (tatha-lakkhaṇa)? The characteristic of hardness of the earth element is true and not false. So too are the characteristic of flowing of the water element, the characteristic of heat of the fire element, the characteristic of supporting of the air element, the characteristic of non-contact of the space element, and the characteristic of cognizing of the consciousness element.

The characteristic of deforming of form, the characteristic of experiencing of feeling, the characteristic of perceiving of perception, the characteristic of constructing of mental formations, and the characteristic of cognizing of consciousness are also true.

The characteristic of directing onto an object of initial application (vitakka), the characteristic of examining an object of sustained application (vicāra), the characteristic of pervading of zest (pīti), the characteristic of gratification of happiness (sukha), the characteristic of non-distraction of one-pointedness of mind (citt-ekaggatā), and the characteristic of touching of contact (phassa) are also true.
193:
The characteristic of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is resolution; the characteristic of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) is exertion; the characteristic of the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) is establishing; the characteristic of the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is non-distraction; the characteristic of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is full understanding.

The characteristic of the power of faith (saddhābala) is unshakability in the face of lack of faith; the characteristic of the power of energy (vīriyabala) is [unshakability] in the face of laziness; the characteristic of the power of mindfulness (satibala) is [unshakability] in the face of forgetfulness; the characteristic of the power of concentration (samādhibala) is [unshakability] in the face of distraction; the characteristic of the power of wisdom (paññābala) is unshakability in the face of ignorance.

The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) is establishing; the characteristic of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga) is investigation; the characteristic of the energy enlightenment factor (vīriyasambojjhaṅga) is exertion; the characteristic of the rapture enlightenment factor (pītisambojjhaṅga) is pervasion; the characteristic of the tranquillity enlightenment factor (passaddhisambojjhaṅga) is calming; the characteristic of the concentration enlightenment factor (samādhisambojjhaṅga) is non-distraction; the characteristic of the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga) is reflection.

The characteristic of right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is seeing; the characteristic of right intention (sammāsaṅkappa) is directing [the mind] onto the object; the characteristic of right speech (sammāvācā) is embracing; the characteristic of right action (sammākammanta) is originating well; the characteristic of right livelihood (sammāājīva) is purification; the characteristic of right effort (sammāvāyāma) is exertion; the characteristic of right mindfulness (sammāsati) is establishing; the characteristic of right concentration (sammāsamādhi) is non-distraction.

The characteristic of ignorance (avijjā) is non-knowing; the characteristic of volitional formations (saṅkhāra) is volition; the characteristic of consciousness (viññāṇa) is cognizing; the characteristic of name (nāma) is inclining towards itself or towards the object; the characteristic of form (rūpa) is being deformed; the characteristic of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) is being a base; the characteristic of contact (phassa) is touching; the characteristic of feeling (vedanā) is experiencing; the characteristic of craving (taṇhā) is being a cause; the characteristic of clinging (upādāna) is grasping; the characteristic of becoming (bhava) is striving; the characteristic of birth (jāti) is arising; the characteristic of aging (jarā) is maturing; the characteristic of death (maraṇa) is passing away.

The characteristic of elements (dhātu) is emptiness of a living being or soul; the characteristic of sense bases (āyatana) is being a base; the characteristic of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is establishing; the characteristic of the right efforts (sammappadhāna) is striving; the characteristic of the bases of power (iddhipāda) is fulfillment; the characteristic of the faculties (indriya) is predominance; the characteristic of the powers (bala) is unshakability; the characteristic of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) is leading out; the characteristic of the path (magga) is being a cause.

The characteristic of the truths (sacca) is being real; the characteristic of serenity (samatha) is non-distraction; the characteristic of insight (vipassanā) is repeated contemplation; the characteristic of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) is having a single taste; the characteristic of the yoked pair (yuganaddha) is non-overstepping.

The characteristic of purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) is restraint; the characteristic of purification of mind (cittavisuddhi) is non-distraction; the characteristic of purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) is seeing [the Four Noble Truths].
194:
The knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa) has the characteristic of cutting off the cycle [of rebirth]; the knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇa) has the characteristic of the calming of the suffering of the cycle. Desire (chanda) has the characteristic of being the root; attention (manasikāra) has the characteristic of originating well; contact (phassa) has the characteristic of combining; feeling (vedanā) has the characteristic of meeting; concentration (samādhi) has the characteristic of being the head; mindfulness (sati) has the characteristic of predominance; wisdom (paññā) has the characteristic of being superior to that concentration; liberation (vimutti) has the characteristic of being the essence; the final characteristic that enters into the deathless Nibbāna is real and unerring. Because He has come to such a real characteristic by the way of knowledge, because He has reached it without error, and because He has attained it, He is called 'Tathāgata.' Because He has come to the real characteristic in this way, He is called 'Tathāgata.'

How is He called 'Tathāgata' because He has fully awakened to the real phenomena as they truly are? Real phenomena (tatha-dhamma) are the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: 'Monks, these four are real, unerring, and not otherwise. Which four? "This is suffering," monks, this is real, this is unerring, this is not otherwise...' and so on in detail. Because the Blessed One has fully awakened to these, because He has fully awakened to the real things, He is called 'Tathāgata.' For in this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'fully awakening to.'

Furthermore, the meaning of the arising of aging and death through the condition of birth is real, unerring, and not otherwise... [the meaning of] the arising of volitional formations through the condition of ignorance is real, unerring, and not otherwise. Likewise, the meaning of ignorance being a condition for volitional formations is real, unerring, and not otherwise... the meaning of birth being a condition for aging and death is real, unerring, and not otherwise. The Blessed One has fully awakened to all of that. Therefore, because He has fully awakened to the real natures, He is called 'Tathāgata.' In this way, because He has fully awakened to the real phenomena as they truly are, He is called 'Tathāgata.'

How is He called 'Tathāgata' because of His seeing the real nature? Whatever visible object (rūpārammaṇa) comes into the range of the eye-door of the immeasurable beings in the world with its devas... in the immeasurable world-systems with their devas and humans, the Blessed One knows and sees all of that in every aspect. Knowing and seeing in this way, the Blessed One [analyzes] that visible object by way of its being pleasant or unpleasant, or by way of the terms found among things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: 'What is that form which is the form-base (rūpāyatana)? That form which, depending on the four great elements, has color and brightness, is visible, and is impinging, such as blue, yellow,' and so on. That visible object, which is analyzed by many names, or by thirteen turns, or by fifty-two methods, is only real; it is not false...
195:
There is no deviation. The same applies to sounds and so forth that come into range at the ear-door and other [sense-doors]. The Blessed One also said: "Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... in the world of beings with its devas and humans, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought, and pondered by the mind—that I know, that I have fully realized; that is understood by the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata does not take his stand upon it" (A. Ni. 4.24). Thus, because he sees things as they truly are, he is called 'Tathāgata'. In this sense of seeing truly, the derivation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood.

In what sense is he the Tathāgata because of speaking truly? From the night the Blessed One sat on the Unconquered Seat at the terrace of enlightenment and attained supreme and perfect enlightenment, having crushed the heads of the four Māras, until the night he attained Parinibbāna by the Nibbāna element without residue remaining between the twin Sāla trees—during this interval of forty-five years, whatever the Blessed One spoke as Sutta, Geyya, and so forth of the nine limbs, all of it is flawless and irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing, neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect. It destroys the intoxication of lust, hatred, and delusion. In those nine limbs, there is not even a slip as small as the tip of a hair. All of it is just as it truly is, as if stamped with a single seal, as if measured by a single measure, or as if weighed by a single balance. As it is said: "Cunda, from the night the Tathāgata attains supreme and perfect enlightenment until the night he attains Parinibbāna by the Nibbāna element without residue remaining, whatever he speaks, utters, or explains in this interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'" (Dī. Ni. 3.188). Here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (speaking). Thus, because he speaks truly, he is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, 'āgadana' is 'āgada', meaning speech (vacana). The Blessed One has speech (āgada) that is true (tatha) and not otherwise; thus, by changing the letter 'd' to 't', the formation of the word 'Tathāgata' in this sense should be understood.

In what sense is he the Tathāgata because of acting accordingly? For the Blessed One's actions of body conform to his speech, and his speech conforms to his actions of body. Therefore, as he speaks, so he acts; and as he acts, so he speaks. For the Blessed One who is such, as his speech is, so his body has gone (gata), that is, proceeded. And as his body is, so his speech...
196:
...has gone (gata), that is, proceeded in that manner; thus he is the Tathāgata. Therefore he said: "Bhikkhus, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called 'Tathāgata'." Thus, because he acts accordingly, he is the Tathāgata.

In what sense is he the Tathāgata because of overcoming? From the peak of existence above to the Avīci hell below, and across the infinite world systems in between, he overcomes all beings by means of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. There is no one equal to him or comparable to him. He is peerless, immeasurable, supreme, the King of kings, the God of gods, the Sakka of Sakkas, and the Brahma of Brahmas. Therefore he said: "Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... in the world of beings with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, unconquered, all-seeing, and wielder of power. Therefore he is called 'Tathāgata'" (A. Ni. 4.23).

In this regard, the word formation should be understood as follows: He is called 'Agada' because he is like a divine medicine. What is that? It is the elegance of his teaching and the abundance of his merit. For by this, the Great Physician of great power overcomes all other teachers and the world with its devas, just as one overcomes snakes with divine medicine. Thus, in overcoming the entire world, he has a medicine (agada) consisting of the elegance of teaching and merit that is true (tatha) and not otherwise; by changing the letter 'd' to 't', he should be known as 'Tathāgata'. Thus, because of overcoming, he is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, he is the Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) to the truth (tatha), or because he has understood (gata) the truth (tatha). 'Gata' has the meanings of understood, transcended, reached, and practiced. Among these, he is the Tathāgata because he has understood (gata) the entire world truly (tathāya) through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). He is the Tathāgata because he has transcended (gata) the origin of the world truly (tathāya) through the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). He is the Tathāgata because he has reached (gata) the cessation of the world truly (tathāya) through realization (sacchikiriyā). He is the Tathāgata because he has practiced (gata) the path leading to the cessation of the world truly (tatha). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world. Bhikkhus, the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. The cessation of the world..."
197:
“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has awakened to the cessation of the world (nirodha-sacca); the Tathāgata has realized the cessation of the world. Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has awakened to the practice leading to the cessation of the world (magga-sacca); the Tathāgata has developed the practice leading to the cessation of the world. Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... whatever is pondered by the mind, all that the Tathāgata has awakened to. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata’” (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 4.23). The meaning of the term ‘Tathāgata’ should also be understood in this way. This statement is merely a brief indication of the Tathāgata’s nature as a Tathāgata. In truth, only the Tathāgata himself could fully describe the nature of his being a Tathāgata in every aspect. Since all Buddhas are equal in their quality as a Tathāgata, the Venerable Sāriputta used the plural form ‘Tathāgatānaṃ’ (of the Tathāgatas) to refer to all Buddhas.

‘Arahaန္တာနံ’ (of the Arahats) means: because of being far remote from defilements, because of having destroyed the enemies and the spokes [of the wheel of saṃsāra], because of being worthy of requisites and offerings, and because of the absence of secret wrongdoing, the Tathāgata is called ‘Arahaṃ’. Indeed, he is remote (ārakā) because he stands very far away from all defilements, having abandoned all defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā) by means of the Path; thus he is ‘Arahaṃ’.

He is called remote because he is not associated with those [defilements],
And since the Lord is not associated with faults, he is considered ‘Arahaṃ’.

And because those enemies, the defilements, have been destroyed by him through the Path, he is ‘Arahaṃ’ due to the destruction of enemies (arīnaṃ hatattā).

Since all enemies known as greed and so on have been destroyed,
By the Lord with the weapon of wisdom, he is therefore considered ‘Arahaṃ’.

Furthermore, this wheel of saṃsāra has been revolving from time immemorial, joined to the chariot of the three worlds, with a hub made of ignorance, becoming, and craving, with spokes consisting of meritorious formations and so on, with a rim of aging and death, and pierced by the axle of the taints (āsavas). The Buddha, standing on the ground of virtue (sīla) with the feet of energy (vīriya) at the Great Bodhi Tree, took the axe of knowledge (ñāṇa) which destroys kamma with the hand of faith (saddhā), and destroyed all the spokes. Therefore, he is called ‘Arahaṃ’ because of the destruction of the spokes (arānaṃ hatattā).

Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra were destroyed with the sword of knowledge,
By the Lord of the World, he is therefore called ‘Arahaṃ’.

Because he is the supreme recipient of offerings, he is worthy (arahati) of requisites such as robes and special offerings. For this reason, when the Tathāgata arises, whatever powerful devas and humans there are, they worship him with jewel-garlands as large as Mount Sineru. They do not perform such worship for anyone other than the Tathāgata. Indeed, Sahampati Brahmā worshipped the Tathāgata with a jewel-garland as large as Mount Sineru. Other devas and humans such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala also worshipped him according to their ability. Furthermore, in honor of the Tathāgata who had attained Parinibbāna, King Asoka spent ninety-six crores (960 million) of wealth to establish eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. What need is there to mention other special offerings? Thus, he is called ‘Arahaṃ’ because he is worthy of receiving requisites and so on.

This Lord of the World is worthy of special offerings along with the requisites,
Because he is worthy in the world according to his benefits, the Conqueror (Jina) deserves this name ‘Arahaṃ’.

Just as in the world, those fools who pretend to be wise commit evil in secret for fear of losing their reputation or for fear of blame, the Buddha never does so. Thus, he is called ‘Arahaṃ’ because of the absence of secret (raha) wrongdoing.

Since there is no such thing as a secret in the evil deeds of such a one,
Because of that absence of secret, he is renowned as ‘Arahaṃ’.
198:
Those [deities] do not perform such worship for others. For instance, Sahampati Brahmā worshipped the Tathāgata with a garland of jewels as large as Mount Sineru. Other devas and humans such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala also worshipped him according to their ability. Even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, King Asoka the Great spent ninety-six crores of wealth to establish eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa as an offering. What need is there to mention other special honors? Thus, he is called ‘Arahaṃ’ because he is worthy of special offerings such as the four requisites.

This Lord of the World is worthy of special offerings along with the four requisites.
Because he is worthy in the world according to his benefits, the Conqueror (Jina) deserves this name ‘Arahaṃ’.

In the world, those fools who pretend to be wise commit evil in secret for fear of losing their reputation or for fear of blame. The Blessed One, however, never does so at any time; because there is no secret in his performance of actions, he is called ‘Arahaṃ’.

For the one endowed with the quality of patience, there is no such thing as a secret in evil deeds.
Because of that absence of secret, the Blessed One is renowned as ‘Arahaṃ’.

Thus, in every aspect—
Because he is remote from defilements, and because he has destroyed the enemies of defilements,
Because he has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, and because he is worthy of requisites and so on,
Because he does not commit evil in secret, he is called ‘Arahaṃ’.

Since all Buddhas are equal in their quality of Arahatship, he spoke referring to all of them as ‘Arahaန္တာနံ’.

‘Sammāsambuddhāနံ’ means: because he has awakened to all phenomena (dhamma) rightly (sammā) and by himself (sāmaṃ), he is called ‘Sammāsambuddha’. Indeed, he has rightly awakened to all phenomena: he has awakened to things to be known through higher knowledge (abhiññeyya) as things to be known through higher knowledge; things to be fully understood (pariññeyya) as things to be fully understood; things to be abandoned (pahātabba) as things to be abandoned; things to be realized (sacchikātabba) as things to be realized; and things to be developed (bhāvetabba) as things to be developed. Therefore, he said:

‘O Brahmin, what should be known through higher knowledge has been known by me; what should be developed has been developed;
What should be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, I am a Buddha.’

In another way: the eye (cakkhu) is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The craving from previous lives which is the root cause of that eye is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-arising of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The practice that knows the Truth of Cessation is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). In this way, by extracting them one by one, he has rightly awakened to all phenomena by himself. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. By this method, the 6 external bases such as forms, the 6 types of consciousness such as eye-consciousness, the 6 types of contact such as eye-contact, the 6 feelings, the 6 perceptions, the 6 volitions, the 6 cravings, the 6 thoughts (vitakka), the 6 examinations (vicāra), the 5 aggregates, the 10 kasinas, the 10 recollections (anussati), the 10 perceptions of foulness (asubha-saññā), the 32 parts of the body, the 12 bases (āyatana), the 18 elements (dhātu), the 9 planes of existence (bhava), the 4 jhanas, the 4 immeasurables (appamaññā), the 4 formless attainments, and the factors of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be applied in forward and reverse order. To apply them one by one: aging and death is the Truth of Suffering. Birth is the Truth of the Origin. The escape from both is the Truth of Cessation. The practice that knows the Truth of Cessation is the Truth of the Path.
199:
Alternatively, the eye is the Truth of Suffering; the craving in the previous life, which is the root cause and the generator of that eye, is the Truth of the Origin; the non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation; the practice that penetrates and knows the Truth of Cessation is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by extracting and knowing each part individually, he is called the Buddha because he has rightly known all things by himself. The same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

In this way, one should apply [the truths to] the six bases such as the visible form, the six classes of consciousness such as eye-consciousness, the six classes of contact such as eye-contact, the six classes of feeling born of eye-contact, the six classes of perception such as perception of form, the six classes of volition such as volition regarding form, the six classes of craving such as craving for form, the six classes of initial thought such as initial thought regarding form, the six classes of sustained thought such as sustained thought regarding form, the five aggregates such as the aggregate of form, the ten kasiṇas, the ten recollections, the ten perceptions such as the perception of a bloated corpse, the thirty-two parts of the body such as hair, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the nine types of existence such as sensual existence, the four jhānas such as the first jhāna, the four immeasurables such as the meditation on loving-kindness, the four immaterial attainments, and the factors of Dependent Origination in reverse order such as aging and death, and in forward order such as ignorance.

In such application, this is the application of a single part: aging and death are the Truth of Suffering; birth is the Truth of the Origin; the escape from both is the Truth of Cessation; the practice that knows the Truth of Cessation is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by extracting each part, he is the Buddha, the Awakened One, the Penetrator, who has rightly known all things by himself. Alternatively, he is the Sammāsambuddha because he has rightly and by himself known everything that is to be known (neyya-dhamma), and by the power of the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) occurring at the end of the Fruit of Arahantship. The detailed analysis of that knowledge will be made clear later. Since all Buddhas are equal in the quality of being a Sammāsambuddha, he said "Sammāsambuddhānaṃ" (to the Fully Enlightened Ones) with reference to all of them.

Now, in order to show each of the two virtues—the limited virtue of purification and the unlimited virtue of purification—by dividing them into five types, he said: "Atthi sīlaṃ pariyantaṃ, atthi sīlaṃ apariyantaṃ" (There is virtue that is limited, there is virtue that is unlimited), and so on. In the remaining three types of virtue, there is no such division. In that text, "lābhapariyantaṃ" means virtue that is limited or broken by gain and honor. The same should be understood for the remaining virtues. "Yaso" means retinue. "Idha" means in this world. "Ekacco" means a certain person. "Lābahetu" means because of the cause of obtaining gain. (The ablative case is used in the sense of cause.) "Lābhapaccayā, lābhakāraṇā" are synonyms of that "lābahetu." Because the effect arises depending on the cause, it is called "paccaya" (condition), and because it brings about the production of the effect, it is called "kāraṇa" (reason).
200:
"Yathāsamādinnaṃ" means whatever (virtue) has been undertaken or taken up. "Vītikkamati" means to transgress in practice. "Evarūpāni" means having such a nature, meaning of the aforementioned types. As for virtues, whether they are the virtues of householders or the virtues of monastics, if one virtue (or rule) is broken at the beginning or at the end, those virtues are called "khaṇḍa" (broken virtue), like a cloth torn at the edges. If one virtue is broken in the middle, they are called "chidda" (perforated virtue), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three virtues are broken in succession, they are called "sabala" (spotted virtue), like a cow that has a different color (black, red, etc.) in long or circular shapes appearing on its back or belly. If virtues are broken one by one at intervals, they are called "kammāsa" (mottled virtue), like a cow variegated with spots of different colors at intervals. Alternatively, without distinction, all virtues are called khaṇḍa, chidda, sabala, and kammāsa because they are destroyed by the seven types of sexual bond and by evil states such as anger and malice. 

Those same virtues are "na bhujissa" (not free) because they do not bring about the state of freedom, not being released from the slavery of craving. They are "na viññuppasattha" (not praised by the wise) because they are not praised by the wise such as the Buddha. They are "parāmaṭṭha" (misapprehended) because they are wrongly grasped by craving and views, or because someone is able to criticize them, saying, "This is a flaw in your virtue." They are "asamādhisamvattanika" (not leading to concentration) because they do not lead to access concentration, absorption concentration, or path concentration and fruition concentration. There is also a variant reading "na samādhisamvattanikāni."

Some teachers, however, explain the meaning thus: "khaṇḍa" is because they are not a foundation for wholesome states; "chidda" is also for the same reason; "sabala" is because they cause discoloration; "kammāsa" is also for the same reason; "na bhujissa" is because they have fallen into the slavery of craving; "na viññuppasattha" is because they are blamed by those with merit; "parāmaṭṭha" is because they are seized by craving; "asamādhisamvattanika" is because they are a basis for remorse.

"Na avippaṭisāravatthukāni" means they do not become a basis for non-remorse because they bring about remorse. "Na pāmojjavatthukāni" means they do not become a basis for weak joy (gladness) born of non-remorse, because they do not bring about that gladness. The same application should be made for the remaining terms. "Na pītivatthukāni" means they do not become a basis for strong joy born of weak joy. "Na passaddhivatthukāni" means they do not become a basis for tranquility of body and mind born of strong joy. "Na sukhavatthukāni" means they do not become a basis for bodily and mental happiness born of tranquility. "Na samādhivatthukāni" means [they do not become a basis for concentration] born of happiness...
201:
They are not the basis for concentration. 'They are not the basis for the knowledge and vision of things as they really are' means they are not the basis for insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), which have concentration as their proximate cause. This is because those states cannot lead to such knowledge and vision. In the phrases such as 'not for absolute disenchantment,' the negative particle 'na' (not) should be taken and applied to the remaining terms in the same manner, such as 'not for dispassion,' and so on. In the phrases 'not for dispassion,' etc., there is also a reading with the particle 'na' included. In the phrase 'for absolute disenchantment,' it should be connected as 'they do not lead to the purpose of disenchantment with the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa).' The same method should be applied to the remaining terms.

'For dispassion' means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate towards the round of rebirth. 'For cessation' means for the purpose of the cessation of the round of rebirth. 'For peace' means for the purpose of the stilling of the round of rebirth by way of its non-arising again once it has ceased. 'For direct knowledge' means for the purpose of penetrating the round of rebirth. 'For full enlightenment' means for the purpose of awakening from the round of rebirth by emerging from the sleep of defilements. 'For nibbāna' means for the purpose of the deathless Nibbāna.

'For the transgression of the training rules as they have been undertaken' means for the purpose of violating the training rules that one has accepted. Here, the accusative case (second declension) is used by way of case-substitution (vibhatti-vipallāsa). The phrase 'does not even give rise to a thought' is said to show the extreme purity of virtue through the purity of the arising of thought; however, virtue is not broken merely by the arising of a thought. 'Why would he transgress?' means for what purpose would he commit a transgression? The meaning is that he would not commit a transgression at all. The terms 'unbroken,' etc., should be understood by the method of opposites already mentioned below. There is also a reading 'not broken.' In the phrases 'for absolute disenchantment,' etc., they should be connected by the method: 'for the purpose of absolute disenchantment with the round of rebirth,' and so on. Here, 'disenchantment' (nibbidā) refers to insight (vipassanā). 'Dispassion' (virāga) refers to the Path (magga). 'Cessation' (nirodha) and 'peace' (upasama) refer to Nibbāna. 'Direct knowledge' (abhiññā) and 'full enlightenment' (sambodha) refer to the Path. 'Nibbāna' refers to Nibbāna itself. Thus, the sequential explanation should be understood as: insight in one place, the Path in two places, and Nibbāna in three places. Figuratively (pariyāyena), however, all these terms are synonyms for both the Path and Nibbāna.

Now, having shown the existing distinctions by way of limited and unlimited virtue, he said 'What is virtue?' etc., to show the distinctions of virtue again by way of state (dhamma), nature (jāti), cause (paccaya), and association (sampayutta). Therein, 'that by which something arises' is the origin (samuṭṭhāna). This is a name for the cause. 'What is its origin?' thus it is 'kim-samuṭṭhāna.' 'The combination or coincidence of how many states is it?' thus it is 'kati-dhamma-samodhāna.'

'Volition is virtue' refers to the volition of one who abstains from taking life, etc., or of one who fulfills the duties and practices. 'Mental factor is virtue' refers to the abstinence (virati) of one who abstains from taking life, etc. Furthermore, volition is called virtue in the sense of one who abandons taking life, etc...
202:
The sevenfold volition of the courses of action (kammapatha-cetanā) is called 'virtue as volition.' 'Virtue as mental factor' refers to the states of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, as described in the passage: 'Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness,' and so on. In the phrase 'restraint is virtue,' five types of restraint (saṃvara) should be understood: (1) restraint by the Pātimokkha, (2) restraint by mindfulness, (3) restraint by knowledge, (4) restraint by patience, and (5) restraint by energy. Among these, 'He is endowed, fully endowed with this restraint by the Pātimokkha'—this is restraint by the Pātimokkha. 'He guards the eye-faculty, he practices restraint over the eye-faculty'—this is restraint by mindfulness.

'Whatever streams there are in the world, (O Ajita, said the Blessed One,)
Mindfulness is their dam.
I call it the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut off.'
—This is restraint by knowledge. The use of the four requisites after reflection is also included within this restraint by knowledge. That which is mentioned in the passage, 'He is patient with cold and heat,' etc., is called restraint by patience. That which is mentioned in the passage, 'He does not tolerate (endure) an arisen thought of sensual desire,' etc., is called restraint by energy. The virtue of livelihood purification (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) is also included within this restraint by energy. Thus, these five types of restraint, as well as the abstinence from an encountered object by sons of good family who fear evil—all this should be understood as 'virtue as restraint.' 'Virtue as non-transgression' is the non-transgression by body or speech of one who has undertaken the precepts. This is the answer to the question 'What is virtue?'

In the answer to the question 'How many kinds of virtue are there?', there are wholesome virtue, unwholesome virtue, and indeterminate virtue. Therein, because in the world the nature (pakati) of various beings is called 'virtue' (sīla), people say: 'This person has a pleasant nature, this person has a painful nature, this person has a quarrelsome nature, this person has a decorative nature.' Therefore, by that figurative sense (pariyāya) and by way of extracting the meaning, unwholesome virtue is also called 'virtue.' However, that unwholesome virtue is not the virtue intended here, according to the statement: 'Wisdom in restraint through hearing.'
203:
Because the mind associated with intention (cetanā) and abstinence (virati) is the cause (samuṭṭhāna) of virtue (sīla), which is diverse by way of intention etc., it is said to be 'wholesome virtue having wholesome mind as its cause,' and so forth.

Virtue as a combination of restraint (saṃvara-samodhāna-sīla) refers to the aggregates (khandhas) associated with the five kinds of restraint. Because those aggregates associated with the five kinds of restraint exist in a mixed and combined state with those restraints, they are called 'combination of restraint.' Similarly, virtue as a combination of non-transgression (avītikkama-samodhāna-sīla) should be understood. Likewise, virtue as a combination of intention (cetanā-samodhāna-sīla) refers to the aggregates associated with the intention that arises in the state of restraint and non-transgression. Since the dhammas associated with restraint and non-transgression are intended in all three types of combination, and since mental factor virtue (cetasika-sīla) is already included within the combination of intention, it should be understood that virtue as a combination of mental factors (cetasika-samodhāna-sīla) is not mentioned separately. Below, dhammas such as intention are called 'virtue.' This triad of combinations (samodhāna-tika) is stated to show that not only are intention etc. called virtue, but the dhammas associated with them are also indeed virtue.

Now, since the virtues of intention and mental factors are only restraint and non-transgression and do not exist separately, [the teacher], wishing to connect restraint and non-transgression in a common sequence up to the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga), said: 'Virtue in the sense of guarding against killing (pāṇātipāta), virtue in the sense of not transgressing,' and so forth. Abstinence from killing etc. are called virtue in the sense of guarding because they guard against their opposites, such as killing, and virtue in the sense of non-transgression because they do not transgress those actions. In that text, 'in the sense of guarding against killing' means virtue in the sense of blocking killing. What is that? It is abstinence from killing (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī). And since that abstinence guards against killing and does not transgress it, it is called virtue in the sense of non-transgression. Similarly, abstinence from taking what is not given (adinnādāna), etc., as well as non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill-will (abyāpāda), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi), should be applied and understood.

Among the ten unwholesome paths of action (akusala-kammapatha) such as killing (pāṇātipāta), the rapid falling of a being's life faculty is called pāṇātipāta. It means the slaying of a being, the destruction of a being. Here, 'being' (pāṇa) is a conventional term for a creature, but in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). The intention to kill, occurring through either the door of body or speech, which originates the effort to cut off the life faculty of a being by one who perceives that being as a living being, is called pāṇātipāta. That killing is of less blame in the case of beings without virtue, such as animals, when they are small, and of great blame when they have a large body. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort (payoga). Even when the effort is equal, it is because of the greatness of the object (vatthu). Among virtuous beings such as humans, it is of less blame in the case of a being with few virtues and of great blame in the case of a being with great virtues.
204:
If the body and virtues are equal, it should be understood that the blame is less if the defilements (kilesa) and effort are weak, and the blame is great if they are intense. The five factors (sambhāra) of that killing are: a living being, the perception of a living being, the thought of killing, the effort to kill, and death resulting from that effort.

Taking what is not given is adinnādāna. It means the carrying away of another's property, theft, the act of thieves. In this context, 'not given' (adinna) refers to property possessed by another, where the owner is not liable to punishment or blame when acting according to their will. The intention to steal, occurring through either the door of body or speech, which originates the effort to take that property by one who perceives it as another's property, is called adinnādāna. That theft is of less blame in the case of inferior property belonging to another, and of great blame in the case of excellent property. Why? Because of the excellence of the object (vatthu). When the objects are equal, the blame is great in the case of property belonging to those with superior virtues, and less in the case of property belonging to those with fewer virtues compared to those with superior virtues. The five factors are: property possessed by another, the perception of it being another's property, the thought of stealing, the effort, and the carrying away by that effort.

'In sexual matters' (kāmesu) refers to sexual intercourse. Misconduct (micchācāra) means a low practice that is utterly censured. By way of characteristic, the intention to transgress against prohibited persons (agamanīya-ṭṭhāna), occurring through the body door with the intent of unrighteousness (asaddhamma), is called kāmesu micchācāra.

Therein, 'prohibited persons' for men are first the ten such as: one guarded by mother (mātura-kkhita), one guarded by father, one guarded by both parents, one guarded by brother, one guarded by sister, one guarded by relatives, one guarded by clan, one guarded by fellow practitioners of Dhamma, one who is protected (sārakkhā), and one who is under penalty (saparidaṇḍā). And the ten such as: a wife bought with wealth (dhanakkīta), a wife who lives of her own will, a wife who lives for wealth, a wife who lives for clothes, a wife wedded by dipping hands in water, a wife wedded by removing the head-pad, a wife who is both a slave and a wife, a wife who is both a worker and a wife, a wife captured in war, and a temporary wife—making twenty types of women. For women, other men are prohibited persons for twelve types of women: the two types (protected and under penalty) and the ten types starting with those bought with wealth. This sexual misconduct is of less blame in the case of prohibited persons devoid of virtues such as morality, and of great blame in the case of those endowed with virtues such as morality. The four factors are: a prohibited object (agamanīya-vatthu), the thought of engaging with that object, the effort to engage, and the consenting to the union of the organs.
205:
...men are (prohibited persons). This aforementioned group of women and men is called the prohibited place (agamanīyaṭṭhāna). This base practice of sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra) is of small blame if committed with those prohibited persons who are devoid of virtues such as morality. There are four factors (sambhāra) of that sexual misconduct. They are: being a prohibited object, having the mind desiring to associate with that object, making an effort to associate, and taking delight in the union of the organs.

Musā means the effort of speech (vacīpayoga) or the effort of body (kāyapayoga) that destroys the welfare [of others], preceded by the desire to deceive. The volition (cetanā) that gives rise to the bodily or verbal effort to deceive others with the intent of deception is called musāvāda. Another way: musā is an untrue, false matter, and vāda is making that matter known as if it were true. By characteristic, the volition that gives rise to such a communication by one who wishes to make another understand an untrue matter as true is called musāvāda. That musāvāda is of small blame if the welfare destroyed is small, and of great blame if the welfare is great. Alternatively, for laypeople, saying "I do not have it" because of not wishing to give one's own property is of small blame; speaking as a witness to destroy another's welfare is of great blame. For monks, if they receive a little oil or ghee and say, out of a desire to jest, "Today in the village, oil is flowing like a river," in the manner of pūraṇakathā (exaggerated speech), it is of small blame; speaking by saying one has seen what was not seen, etc., is of great blame. The four factors (sambhāra) of that musāvāda are: an untrue matter, the mind with intent to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the other person's understanding of that meaning.

The speech which, when spoken to a certain person, is done to make oneself dear to that person's heart and to make the other person [the one spoken about] hated and distant, is called pisuṇavācā (slanderous speech). The speech which makes oneself as well as the other person harsh, and which is itself harsh, being neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart, is called pharusavācā (harsh speech). Speaking useless words frivolously is called samphappalāpa (frivolous talk). The volition which is the root of those speeches also receives the names pisuṇavācā, etc. And in this context, it is that volition which is intended.

Among those, the volition of one with a defiled mind that gives rise to bodily or verbal effort, either for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire to be dear to them, is called pisuṇavācā. That speech is of small blame if the virtues of the person to be divided are few, and of great blame if the virtues are great. Its four factors are: another person to be divided, the intent to divide thinking "Thus these people will be divided" or the desire to be dear thinking "Thus I will be dear and trusted," the corresponding effort, and the other person's understanding of that meaning. As long as others are not yet divided, it does not constitute a breach of the course of action (kammapatha); it only becomes a kammapatha when they are divided.

The purely harsh volition that gives rise to bodily or verbal effort which cuts the heart of another is called pharusavācā. However, even if it is an effort that cuts the heart, if the mind is soft, it is not pharusavācā. For parents sometimes say to their children, "May thieves cut you into pieces!" Yet, even if a lotus leaf were to fall upon those children...
206:
(Parents) do not wish even a lotus leaf to fall (upon their children). Teachers and preceptors also sometimes say to their pupils: "These are shameless and fearless of wrongdoing; expel them!" Yet, they desire for those pupils the achievement of learning and realization. Just as harsh speech does not occur when the mind is gentle, so too, speech is not un-harsh merely because the words are gentle. For the words "Let this person sleep comfortably," spoken by one who wishes to have someone killed, are indeed harsh speech because of the harshness of the mind. That harsh speech is of little blame if the person referred to has little virtue, and of great blame if they have great virtue. Its three factors are: a person to be abused, an angry mind, and the act of abusing.

Unwholesome intention that gives rise to bodily and vocal efforts to communicate what is useless is called frivolous speech (samphappalāpa). It is of little blame when the habit is slight, and of great blame when the habit is great. Its two factors are: the prioritizing of useless talk such as the Bhārata war or the abduction of Queen Sītā, and the act of speaking such talk. If others do not listen to that talk, there is no breach of the course of action (kammapatha); it becomes a course of action only when it is taken up by another.

It is called covetousness (abhijjhā) because it contemplates others' wealth; the meaning is that it proceeds by inclining towards others' goods. It has the characteristic of contemplating others' wealth as "O, may this be mine!" Like theft (adinnādāna), it is of little blame or great blame. Its two factors are: another's property and the inclining of it towards oneself. For even if greed arises with another's property as the object, it does not yet become a breach of the course of action as long as one does not incline it towards oneself, thinking, "O, may this be mine!"

It is called ill-will (byāpāda) because it destroys welfare and happiness. It has the characteristic of mental malevolence for the destruction of others. Like harsh speech, it is of little blame or great blame. Its two factors are: another being and the thought of that being's destruction. For even if anger arises with another being as the object, it does not yet become a breach of the course of action as long as one does not think of their destruction, "O, may this person be cut off, may they perish!"
207:
It is called wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) because it sees pervertedly, due to the absence of seeing according to reality. That wrong view has the characteristic of perverted seeing, such as in the manner: "There is no result of giving," and so forth. Like idle chatter (samphappalāpa), it can be of minor blame or of great blame. Furthermore, indefinite wrong view (aniyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is of minor blame, while definite wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is of great blame. There are two factors (constituents) of that wrong view: the perversion of the mode in which the object is taken, and the appearance of that object to him in that perverted way. Among those views, the course of action (kammapatha) is completed only by the nihilistic view (natthika-diṭṭhi), the view of non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi), and the view of the inefficacy of action (akiriya-diṭṭhi), and not by other views.

The analysis of these ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) should be understood by way of five aspects: by way of nature (dhamma), by way of category (koṭṭhāsa), by way of object (ārammaṇa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of root (mūla).

Among those five, 'by way of nature' means: among these unwholesome courses of action, seven in sequence are solely the state of volition (cetanā). The three beginning with covetousness (abhijjhā) are states associated with volition.

'By way of category' means: the seven in sequence and wrong view—these eight are only courses of action (kammapatha) and not roots (mūla). Covetousness and ill-will (byāpāda) are both courses of action and roots. For when covetousness reaches the status of a root, it becomes the unwholesome root of greed (lobha); ill-will becomes the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa).

'By way of object' means: killing (pāṇātipāta) has formations as its object (saṅkhārārammaṇa) because it takes the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) as its object. Stealing (adinnādāna) has either beings as its object (sattārammaṇa) or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct (micchācāra) has formations as its object by way of the tangible (phoṭṭhabba); some teachers say it also has beings as its object. False speech (musāvāda) has either beings or formations as its object. Slanderous speech (pisuṇā vācā) is the same. Harsh speech (pharusā vācā) has only beings as its object. Idle chatter (samphappalāpa) has either beings or formations as its object by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. Covetousness should be understood in the same way. Ill-will has only beings as its object. Wrong view has only formations as its object by way of the phenomena belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma).

'By way of feeling' means: killing is accompanied by painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Indeed, although kings, upon seeing a thief, might say laughingly, "Go, men, kill him," their decisive volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) is associated only with painful feeling. Stealing has three feelings. For when one takes another's property with joy and delight, there is pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā); when one takes it with fear and trembling, there is painful feeling; likewise for one who reflects on the consequences (the result and its overflow). When one takes it while remaining in a neutral state at the time of taking, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). Sexual misconduct has two feelings by way of pleasure and neutrality.
208:
In the decisive mind (sanniṭṭhāpaka-citta), however, neutral feeling (majjhatta-vedanā) does not occur. False speech (musāvāda) has three feelings, just as described for stealing; slanderous speech (pisuṇā vācā) likewise has three feelings. Harsh speech (pharusā vācā) has painful feeling. Idle chatter (samphappalāpa) has three feelings. Indeed, when others are shouting "Sādhu!" and tossing up clothes and so forth, for one who is joyful and delighted while telling stories such as the abduction of Sītā (Sītā-haraṇa) or the Bhārata war, that idle chatter has pleasant feeling. When one who has been previously paid a fee is later approached by someone saying, "Tell it again from the beginning," and he tells it while being displeased, thinking, "Will I be able to tell the miscellaneous talk in its entirety and in proper sequence or not?", there is painful feeling. For one who tells it with neutrality, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). Covetousness (abhijjhā) has two feelings by way of pleasure and neutrality; wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) likewise has two feelings. Ill-will (byāpāda) has painful feeling.

By way of root (mūla): killing (pāṇātipāta) has two roots by way of hatred and delusion. Stealing (adinnādāna) has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion. Sexual misconduct (micchācāra) has two roots by way of greed and delusion. False speech (musāvāda) has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion. Slanderous speech and idle chatter likewise have two roots each. Harsh speech has two roots by way of hatred and delusion. Covetousness has one root by way of delusion; ill-will likewise has one root. Wrong view has two roots by way of greed and delusion.

## The Discussion on the Unwholesome Courses of Action is Finished.

Abstinence (virati) from killing and so forth, along with non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view—these are called the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha). They are called 'abstinence' (virati) because by means of this, they abstain from killing and so forth, or it abstains by itself, or it is merely the act of abstaining. The abstinence associated with a wholesome mind in one who abstains from killing and so forth is of three kinds by way of division: natural abstinence (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati).

Among those three, 'natural abstinence' is the abstinence that arises in those who have not undertaken the precepts, but who, reflecting on their own birth, age, learning, and so forth, do not transgress against an object that has been encountered, thinking, "It is not proper for us to do such an evil deed."

'Abstinence by undertaking' is the abstinence that arises in those who have undertaken the precepts and who, both in the undertaking of the precepts and beyond that, do not transgress against an object even at the cost of their own lives.

'Abstinence by eradication' is the abstinence associated with the Noble Path (ariyamagga); from the moment of its arising, even the thought, "I will kill a living being," and so forth, does not occur to Noble Persons (ariyapuggala).
209:
Now, just as with the unwholesome courses of action, the determination of these wholesome courses of action should be understood by way of five aspects: by way of state (dhamma), by way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), by way of object (ārammaṇa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of root (mūla).

Among those five, "by way of state" means: among these ten wholesome courses of action, in order, the first seven are both volitions (cetanā) and abstinences (virati). The last three are states associated with volition.

"By way of portion" means: in order, the first seven are only courses of action (kammapatha), not roots (mūla). The last three are both courses of action and roots. When non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) reaches the status of a root, it is the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha). Non-ill-will (abyāpāda) is the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa). Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).

"By way of object" means: the very objects of the unwholesome courses of action such as killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth are the objects of these wholesome courses of action. This is because abstinence (veramaṇī) occurs only in relation to the object that would otherwise be transgressed. Just as the Noble Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, having the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and so forth as their objects, abandon immorality (dussīlya) such as killing and so on.

"By way of feeling" means: all wholesome courses of action occur with either pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) or equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā). This is because, in the context of the wholesome, there is no such thing as painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

"By way of root" means: for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge, the first seven in order have three roots by virtue of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, they have two roots by virtue of non-greed and non-hatred. For one who abstains from covetousness with a consciousness associated with knowledge, non-covetousness has two roots by virtue of non-hatred and non-delusion. For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root by virtue of non-hatred. Non-greed itself cannot be its own root. The same method applies to non-ill-will. Right view should be understood as having only two roots by virtue of non-greed and non-hatred.

## The Discussion on the Wholesome Courses of Action is Finished.

Having thus shown virtue by way of the ten wholesome courses of action, he now says, "Virtue is in the sense of restraint of sensual desire through renunciation (nekkhamma), in the sense of non-transgression," and so forth, in order to show it by way of the thirty-seven states beginning with renunciation and ending with the Path of Arahantship. In that text, the meaning is that renunciation (nekkhamma, i.e., jhāna) is called virtue because it restrains and blocks sensual desire, and because it does not transgress. Alternatively, using the instrumental case in the sense of the agent, it means "Renunciation is virtue." The same method applies to the remaining factors such as non-ill-will.

Specifically, in this Paṭisambhidāmagga text, after showing renunciation and non-ill-will, the remaining terms such as the perception of non-greed (alobha-saññā) and so forth are condensed according to the method mentioned below, and only the Path of Arahantship is shown at the end.

Having thus shown virtue by way of restraint (saṃvara) and non-transgression (avītikkama), he now says, "The five virtues are called virtue," and so forth, to show the distinctions of that restraint and non-transgression. Here, it should be read in conjunction as: "The abandoning of killing is virtue, the abstinence from killing is virtue, the volition opposite to killing is virtue, the restraint of killing is virtue, the non-transgression of killing is virtue."

As for "abandoning" (pahāna), apart from the mere non-arising of the aforementioned killing and so forth, there is no other ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma). Nevertheless, the abandoning of each instance of killing and so forth is figuratively called a "foundation" (upadhāraṇa) because it is the basis for wholesome states. Because it does not allow for a state of disorder, it is called "coordination" (samodhāna). Therefore, as stated previously in the Matika, it is called virtue (sīla) because of the meaning of "composing" (sīlana), which consists of founding (upadhāraṇa) and coordinating (samodhāna). As for the remaining four states—abstinence (veramaṇī), volition (cetanā), restraint (saṃvara), and non-transgression (avītikkama)—they are taught as virtue with reference to the nature of the mind's occurrence by way of abstaining from each instance of killing, the volition associated with those two, and the non-transgression of one who does not transgress.

Alternatively, abandoning (pahāna) does indeed exist as a distinct state. How? It is called abandoning because the opposite states, such as killing and so forth, are abandoned by this wholesome aggregate. Or, it is called abandoning because it abandons those opposite states. What is that state which abandons? It is the entire wholesome aggregate.

Other teachers, however, take only the word "virtue of abstinence" (veramaṇī-sīla) in the subsequent terms such as renunciation and so forth, and say that abstinence (virati) exists as a fixed (niyata) "or-whatever-else" (yevāpanaka) mental factor in all wholesome states (even though abstinence is not present in the first jhāna and so on). According to what has been said, it should be understood that there is no abstinence when developing this first jhāna and so forth. By this aforementioned method, having shown the distinction through the five terms such as abandoning and so forth, he teaches only the virtue of limited purification (pariyantapārisuddhisīla). Indeed, it is of this very virtue that it is said, "He practices such virtues."
210:
The same method applies to the remaining factors. In the Pali text, however, after showing renunciation (nekkhamma) and non-ill will (abyāpāda), the remaining factors are summarized according to the method previously mentioned, and finally, only the Path to Arahantship (arahattamagga) is shown.

Thus, after showing virtue (sīla) by way of restraint (saṃvara) and non-transgression (avītikkama), the Buddha now spoke of the five aspects of virtue, such as "abandoning the taking of life is virtue," in order to show the distinctions among those virtues. In this context, it should be understood by connecting them as follows: abandoning the taking of life is virtue; abstinence from the taking of life is virtue; the volition opposite to the taking of life is virtue; restraint regarding the taking of life is virtue; and non-transgression of the taking of life is virtue. Regarding "abandoning" (pahāna), there is no separate state other than the mere non-arising of the aforementioned taking of life and so on.
