In the teaching that aging and death are impermanent, etc., aging and death themselves are not impermanent, but they are called impermanent because they are the aging and death of the aggregates which have the nature of impermanence. The same method applies to terms like 'conditioned'. In the elided portion (peyyāla) in between, the impermanence of birth, etc., should be understood in this same way. In the text 'with birth as condition, aging and death', it is not taught by way of insight (vipassanā), but simply by way of the individual factors of dependent origination...
234:
Alternatively, it should be understood by way of connection: as 'khayadhamma' (the nature of wasting away) by way of the destruction of matter (rūpa) included within a single existence; as 'vayadhamma' (the nature of vanishing) by way of the expiration of matter included within a single continuity; as 'virāgadhamma' (the nature of fading away) by way of the momentary destruction of matter; and as 'nirodhadhamma' (the nature of cessation) by way of the non-recurrence of all three.

In the Pāḷi passages such as "Aging and death are impermanent (anicca)," aging and death are not impermanent in themselves; rather, they are called impermanent only because they are the aging and death of the aggregates (khandhas) which are impermanent by nature. The same method applies to terms such as 'conditioned' (saṅkhata). In the elisions (peyyāla) in between, the same method should be understood regarding the impermanence of birth (jāti) and so on.

The teaching such as "Aging and death occur because of birth" is not stated by way of insight (vipassanā). It is stated figuratively as 'knowledge of comprehension' (sammasana-ñāṇa) because it is a concise determination by way of each individual factor of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). However, this is not 'knowledge of comprehension of groups' (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa), but rather 'knowledge of the stability of phenomena' (dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa). In the phrase "asati jātiyā," a gender reversal (liṅgavipallāsa) has been made, meaning "asatiyā jātiyā" (when birth does not exist). In the phrase "asati saṅkhāresu," a number reversal (vacanavipallāsa) has been made, meaning "asantesu saṅkhāresu" (when formations do not exist). It should be connected in this manner: "Birth occurs because of becoming; when becoming does not exist, birth does not exist," and so on.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Comprehension is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Rise and Fall

Now, regarding the explanation of the 'knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall' (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa), which is taught for the purpose of insight into impermanence and so on, by a yogi who has reached the further shore by strengthening the previously mentioned knowledge of comprehension through various methods of meditation (bhāvanā), and who, having delimited the formations seen as impermanent and so on by way of rise and fall, contemplates them as impermanent and so on: in the words "jātaṃ rūpaṃ" (arisen matter) and so forth, 'matter' refers to the matter produced by its respective causes according to the continuity. For that arisen matter, 'rise' (udaya) refers to the characteristic of production (jāti), arising (uppāda), or the new state of appearance; 'fall' (vaya) refers to the characteristic of change, wasting away, or breaking up; 'contemplation' (anupassanā) refers to repeated observation. This is the meaning of 'knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall'. The same method applies to feeling (vedanā) and the other aggregates. Because the rise and fall must be grasped only for things that possess birth, aging, and death, and because birth, aging, and death do not themselves have rise and fall, the elision is made as "arisen eye... etc... arisen becoming" without touching upon birth, aging, and death.

When that yogi contemplates the rise and fall of the five aggregates in this way, he knows thus: "Before these aggregates arose, there was no heap or accumulation of unarisen aggregates. The aggregates currently arising do not come from any heap or accumulation. The aggregates currently ceasing do not go to any of the directions. The aggregates that have already ceased do not remain in any place as a heap, an accumulation, or a store."

Indeed, to make this meaning clear: when a lute (vīṇā) is played, the sound that arises did not exist as an accumulation before it arose. When the sound arises, it does not come from an accumulation. The sound that is ceasing does not go to any of the directions. The sound that has ceased does not remain accumulated in any place. Instead, just as it arises without having been before, depending on the lute, the bow, and the appropriate effort of the person, and having arisen, it vanishes; in the same way, all mental and physical phenomena arise without having been before, and having arisen, they vanish.
235:
The yogi who contemplates rise and fall knows thus: "Before the arising of these aggregates, there was no heap or accumulation of unarisen aggregates; when they arise, they do not come from any heap or accumulation; when they cease, they do not go to any of the directions or intermediate directions; and after they have ceased, they do not remain in any place as a heap, accumulation, or store." Just as when a lute is played, the sound that arises has no prior accumulation before its arising; when it arises, it does not come from an accumulation; when it ceases, it does not go to any of the directions or intermediate directions; and after it has ceased, it does not remain accumulated anywhere. Instead, it comes into being without having been before, depending on the lute, the strings, and the appropriate effort of the person, and having been, it vanishes. In the same way, all phenomena, whether material or immaterial, come into being without having been before, and having been, they vanish.

Having thus shown the vision of rise and fall in brief, now to show it in detail, the count is asked by way of groups: "How many characteristics does one who sees the arising of the five aggregates see?" and the count is answered by way of groups: "One who sees the arising of the five aggregates sees twenty-five characteristics." Again, the count is asked by way of parts: "How many characteristics does one who sees the arising of the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) see?" and the count is answered by way of parts: "One who sees the arising of the aggregate of matter sees five characteristics." Again, the question is asked by distinguishing the characteristics: "Which five characteristics does one who sees the arising of the aggregate of matter see?" and then the answer is given.

In that answer, "the arising of matter from the arising of ignorance (avijjā)" means that when there is ignorance, which is called delusion (moha) in the previous kamma-becoming (kammabhava), the arising of matter occurs in this existence. "By way of the arising of causes" (paccayasamudayaṭṭhena) means by way of the state of the causes having arisen. Here, ignorance, craving (taṇhā), and kamma are the past causes that serve as the root for rebirth in this life. When these three are taken, formations (saṅkhāra) and clinging (upādāna) are also included. "From the arising of nutriment (āhāra)" means that among the causes for maintenance, physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) alone is taken because it is prominent. When that nutriment is taken, temperature (utu) and mind (citta), which are causes for maintenance, are also included. "The characteristic of production" (nibbattilakkhaṇa) refers to the arising of matter by way of duration (addhā), continuity (santati), and moment (khaṇa). Arising itself is called a "characteristic" (lakkhaṇa) because it is a characteristic of the conditioned (saṅkhata). The "five characteristics" are ignorance, craving, kamma, nutriment, and production.
236:
There are five characteristics. Factors such as ignorance (avijjā) and so on are also called characteristics because, when they exist, the arising of form (rūpa) is marked by them. The characteristic of production (nibbattilakkhaṇa), however, is indeed the characteristic of the conditioned (saṅkhata); it is called a characteristic because conditioned things are marked by this production.

'With the cessation of ignorance, form ceases' means that when ignorance in this present life, which is the cause of future existence, is brought to cessation by the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggañāṇa), the non-arising of future form due to the absence of its cause is called cessation. 'In the sense of the cessation of conditions' (paccayanirodhaṭṭhena) means due to the state of the condition having ceased. Here, cessation refers only to the cessation of ignorance, craving (taṇhā), and kamma in this life, which are the causes of future rebirth (paṭisandhi). 'With the cessation of nutriment, form ceases' means that in the absence of physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra), which is the cause for maintenance, there is an absence of the forms produced by that nutriment. The characteristic of change (vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa) refers to the dissolution (bhaṅga) of form by way of duration (addhā), continuity (santati), and moment (khaṇa). Dissolution itself is called a characteristic because it is a characteristic of the conditioned. In this section on cessation, the five characteristics are: the four characteristics of cessation, namely the absence of ignorance, craving, kamma, and nutriment; and the one characteristic of change. This method also applies to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so on.

There is this distinction: the observation of the arising and passing away of the mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha) occurs only by way of duration and continuity, not by way of the moment. Contact (phassa) is the cause for the maintenance of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations; with the cessation of that contact, those aggregates cease. Mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) is the cause for the maintenance of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); with the cessation of mentality-materiality, that aggregate of consciousness ceases.

Some teachers say: 'When observing arising and passing away by way of the four causes, without analyzing them as past and so on, one takes only the state of being produced—that it arises due to ignorance and so on—by way of general commonality; one does not take the moment of arising (uppāda). When saying it ceases due to the cessation of ignorance and so on, one takes only the state of not being produced; one does not take the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga). However, when observing arising and passing away by way of the moment, one takes the arising and dissolution of present aggregates.'

A meditator practicing insight first attends to arising and passing away by way of causes. Then, at the time of practicing insight, having set aside the four factors such as ignorance, they take only the aggregates that possess arising and passing away and observe their arising and passing away. Thus, for that meditator who observes arising and passing away in detail by way of both cause and moment—thinking, 'In this way the arising of form etc. occurs, in this way their passing away occurs; in this way form etc. arise, in this way they cease'—the knowledge becomes exceptionally clear: 'Indeed, these phenomena come into being without having been before, and having come into being, they disappear.' The distinctions of the characteristics in the method of the Truths and Dependent Origination become manifest.
237:
When that meditator sees the arising of the aggregates due to the arising of causes such as ignorance, and the cessation of the aggregates due to the cessation of causes such as ignorance, this is their 'seeing of arising and passing away by way of cause' (paccayato udayabbayadassana). When they see the arising and passing away of the aggregates while observing the characteristic of production (nibbattilakkhaṇa) and the characteristic of change (vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa), this is their 'seeing of arising and passing away by way of the moment' (khaṇato udayabbayadassana). For the characteristic of production exists only at the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa), and the characteristic of change exists at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa).

Thus, for that meditator who sees arising and passing away in these two ways—by way of cause and by way of the moment—the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) becomes manifest through seeing arising by way of cause, because of the understanding of the producer (janaka). The Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) becomes manifest through seeing arising by way of the moment, because of the understanding of the suffering of birth (jāti-dukkha). The Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca) becomes manifest through seeing passing away by way of cause, because of the understanding of the non-arising of the effects when the causes do not arise. The Truth of Suffering itself becomes manifest through seeing passing away by way of the moment, because of the understanding of the suffering of death (maraṇa-dukkha). That seeing of arising and passing away which they possess is the mundane path (lokiyamagga); thus the Truth of the Path (maggasacca) becomes manifest because of the destruction of delusion (moha) regarding that arising and passing away.

For that meditator, through seeing arising by way of cause, Dependent Origination in forward order (anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda) becomes manifest because of the understanding: 'When this exists, that comes to be.' Through seeing passing away by way of cause, Dependent Origination in reverse order (paṭiloma-paṭiccasamuppāda) becomes manifest because of the understanding: 'With the cessation of this, that ceases.' Through seeing arising and passing away by way of the moment, however, dependently arisen phenomena (paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā) become manifest because of the understanding of the characteristics of the conditioned (saṅkhatalakkhaṇa). For conditioned things possess arising and passing away, and those things are indeed dependently arisen.

For that meditator, through seeing arising by way of cause, the method of unity (ekattanaya) becomes manifest because of the understanding of the non-interruption of the continuity (santāna) through the connection of cause and effect. Then, they abandon the view of annihilation (ucchedadiṭṭhi) more effectively. Through seeing arising by way of the moment, the method of diversity (nānattanaya) becomes manifest because of the understanding of the arising of ever-new phenomena. Then, they abandon the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) more effectively. Through seeing arising and passing away by way of cause, the method of non-agency (abyāpāranaya) becomes manifest because of the understanding of the state of phenomena not being under one's control (avasavattibhāva). Then, they abandon the view of self (attadiṭṭhi) more effectively. Through seeing arising by way of cause, the method of suchness of nature (evaṃdhammatānaya) becomes manifest because of the understanding of the arising of the effect in accordance with the cause. Then, they abandon the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi) more effectively.
238:
By seeing the arising of the aggregates through their causes, the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) becomes manifest to that yogi. This is because he understands the lack of exertion (nirīhakatta) in phenomena and their existence being dependent on causes (paccayapaṭibaddhavuttitā). By seeing the rise and fall in each moment, the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) becomes manifest. This is because he understands their non-existence after having been (hutvā abhāva) and their emptiness of a beginning and an end (pubbāntāparāntaviveka). The characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) also becomes manifest through understanding the constant oppression by rise and fall. The specific characteristic (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) becomes manifest through understanding the limits defined by rise and fall. Within the specific characteristic, the temporary nature (tāvakālikatta) of the conditioned characteristic (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa) also becomes manifest, because he understands the absence of fall at the moment of rise, and the absence of rise at the moment of fall.

To the yogi for whom the truths, dependent origination, the methods, and the various characteristics have thus become manifest, the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) appear as if they are always new, thinking, "Indeed, these phenomena arise without having arisen before, and having arisen, they cease." They appear to have a very short duration, like a drop of dew at sunrise, like a water bubble, like a line drawn on water with a stick, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle, or like a flash of lightning. They also appear as being without core or substance, like a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, a circle of fire, a city of the Gandharvas, foam, or the trunk of a banana tree. By this much, the yogi penetrates the fifty characteristics in the manner of "Only the nature of passing away arises, and that which has arisen reaches destruction," and thus attains the first tender insight knowledge (taruṇa-vipassanā-ñāṇa) called the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa). By attaining this knowledge, he is called "one who has begun insight" (āraddha-vipassaka).

For one established in this knowledge, the ten defilements of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) such as light (obhāsa) arise. When they arise, an unskilled yogi misidentifies them as the knowledge of the path, taking what is not the path to be the "path," and becomes entangled in the thicket of defilements. However, a skilled yogi applies insight to those phenomena and, disentangling the thicket of defilements, distinguishes between the path and what is not the path, thinking, "These phenomena are not the path; only the insight knowledge that is free from defilements and has entered the course of insight is the path." The knowledge established by thus knowing the path and what is not the path is called the purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

By this much, the yogi has defined the Four Noble Truths. How? Since the grasping of causes is possible when there is the grasping of mind and matter, the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) is defined by the defining of mind and matter, which is called the purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi). The truth of origin (samudaya-sacca) is defined by the grasping of causes, which is called the purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi). By seeing the rise and fall in each moment through the contemplation of rise and fall...
239: The definition of the Truth of Suffering has been made. The definition of the Truth of Origin has been made by seeing arising through causes. The definition of the Truth of Cessation has been made by seeing passing away through causes. The yogi's knowledge that sees this arising and passing away is the mundane path (lokiya-magga); because it can dispel confusion regarding that knowledge of arising and passing away, and because the one who practices insight in this purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path (maggāmagga-āᅇadassana-visuddhi) firmly marks the correct path, the definition of the Truth of the Path has been made. Thus, the definition of the Four Noble Truths has been made first by mundane knowledge. ## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away is finished. ## 7. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution. The practitioner (yogāvacara) established in that contemplation of arising and passing away, by defining what is and what is not the path, knows the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away—which is free from defilements and has entered the path of insight—as "the path." To make that path very clear by marking it with the three characteristics, he again undertakes the contemplation of arising and passing away and contemplates formations (saᅃkhāra), which are delimited by arising and passing away, as impermanent (anicca), etc. To him who contemplates thus, that knowledge occurs sharply, and formations appear rapidly. When the knowledge occurs sharply and formations appear rapidly, mindfulness transcends arising (uppāda) and stands only in dissolution (bhaᅃga). Or, because of being inclined toward cessation, he abandons arising and establishes mindfulness only in dissolution. At this point, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaᅃgānupassanāāᅇa) arises. Now, in the description of that knowledge, "the mind having form as object arises and dissolves" (rŦpārammaᅇatā cittaᅃ uppajjitvā bhijjati) means the mind that takes form as an object arises and dissolves. Or it means the mind arises and dissolves in the nature of the form-object. "Having reflected on that object" (taᅃ ārammaᅇaᅃ paᅣisaᅃkhā) means having known that form-object, seeing it as vanishing and passing away. "He contemplates the dissolution of that mind" (tassa cittassa bhaᅃgaᅃ anupassati) means he contemplates the dissolution of the mind by which that form-object was seen as vanishing and passing away, with a subsequent mind. Therefore, the ancient teachers said: "He contemplates both the known object and the knowing knowledge." Here, "mind" (citta) is intended as the mind together with its associated states (sampayutta-dhamma). "Contemplates" (anupassati) means he contemplates repeatedly; he sees again and again in many ways. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), the Elder, said: "How does he contemplate repeatedly? As impermanent..."
240:
## 7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution

Regarding the passage beginning with "Anupassati"—in that context, since what is called dissolution (bhaṅga) is the ultimate limit of impermanence (aniccatā), the practitioner (yogāvacara) possessing the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution repeatedly views all materiality (rūpagata) as impermanent (anicca), not as permanent (nicca). Then, because the impermanent is suffering (dukkha), he views that same materiality as suffering, not as pleasure (sukha). He views it as non-self (anatta), not as self (atta). Since that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self should not be delighted in, and that which should not be delighted in should not be lusted after, he, following the course of the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, becomes weary (nibbindati) of that materiality seen as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and does not delight in it. He becomes dispassionate (virajjati) and does not feel lust.

Being thus dispassionate, he first causes lust (rāga) to cease through mundane insight knowledge (lokiya vipassanā) and does not allow it to arise. This means he does not bring about the arising (or the cause of arising) of lust. Alternatively, being thus dispassionate, just as with the materiality already seen, he causes the materiality not yet seen (past and future) to cease through inductive knowledge (anvayañāṇa) and does not allow it to arise. This means he attends only to cessation (nirodha) and sees only the cessation of that materiality, not its arising.

One who practices in this way relinquishes (paṭinissajjati) and does not cling (ādiyati). What does this mean? This contemplation of impermanence and so on is called "relinquishment as giving up" (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) because it gives up defilements along with the aggregates and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), and it is called "relinquishment as entering into" (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga) because, by seeing the fault in the conditioned (saṅkhata), the mind inclines and enters into Nibbāna, which is the opposite of the conditioned. Therefore, the monk endowed with that contemplation gives up defilements and enters into Nibbāna in the manner described. He does not cling to defilements by way of bringing them into existence, nor does he cling to the conditioned object by way of not seeing its faults. Thus it is said, "He relinquishes and does not cling."

52. Now, to show which states are abandoned by those knowledges, the passage beginning with "One contemplating as impermanent abandons the perception of permanence" was spoken (by the Elder Mahākassapa). In that text, "delight" (nandi) refers to craving accompanied by joy (pīti). "Lust" (rāga) refers to the remaining types of craving. "Arising" (samudaya) refers to the arising of lust or the arising of materiality. "Clinging" (ādāna) refers to the grasping of defilements by way of bringing them into existence. The terms beginning with "the state of having feeling as an object" (vedanārammaṇatā) should be understood in the same manner as already explained here and below.

In the verses, "shifting of the object" (vatthusaṅkamanā) means that after seeing the dissolution of each materiality and so on, one then sees the dissolution of the insight mind that saw that dissolution; thus, it is the shifting from the previous material object to another mental object. "Turning away by wisdom" (paññāya ca vivaṭṭanā) means the wisdom that stands in passing away (vaya) having abandoned arising (udaya). "The power of reflection" (āvajjana balañceva) means the ability to reflect immediately after seeing the dissolution of materiality and so on, in order to see the dissolution of the mind that had that dissolution as its object. "Insight of reflection" (paṭisaṅkhā vipassanā) refers to the contemplation of dissolution that reflects on the object that has such power of reflection. "Defining both as one by the induction of the object" (ārammaṇa-anvayena ubho ekavavatthanā) means that by following the induction of the object seen directly, one defines both past and future with the same nature, thinking, "Just as this present materiality dissolves, so too formations dissolved in the past, and so they will dissolve in the future." This is the meaning stated by the former teachers.

The yogi of pure vision, seeing the moment of dissolution in the five aggregates that are present,
Just as dewdrops perish when the sun rises,
So all formations in the past and future perish,
Following the sequence of the present aggregates...
241:
Insight is this contemplation of dissolution that reflects on the object. "Defining both as one by the induction of the object" (ārammaṇa-anvayena ubho ekavavatthanā) means that by following the induction of the object seen directly, one defines both past and future aggregates with the same nature, thinking, "Just as this present aggregate dissolves, so too the collection of formations dissolved in the past, and so they will dissolve in the future." This was also said by the Ancients:

"One of pure vision regarding the present, applies that induction to the past and future;
All formations are perishable, like dewdrops when the sun has risen."

"Resolution on cessation" (nirodhe adhimuttatā) means that after defining both past and future as one by way of dissolution, one is resolved on that cessation called dissolution; it means being focused on it, inclining toward it, leaning toward it, and slanting toward it. "Insight into the characteristic of passing away" (vayalakkhaṇa-vipassanā) means that this resolution on cessation is called the insight into the characteristic of passing away. "Reflecting on the object" (ārammaṇañca paṭisaṅkhā) means having known the previous object such as materiality. "And contemplates dissolution" (bhaṅgañca anupassati) means that after seeing the dissolution of that object, one also contemplates the dissolution of the mind that knew that object. "Appearance as void" (suññato ca upaṭṭhānaṃ) means that for the yogi who thus contemplates dissolution, the appearance as void is accomplished, thinking, "Only formations break up; their breaking is death; there is no one else." Therefore, the Ancients said:

"Only aggregates cease, there is no other; the breaking of aggregates is called death;
The heedful one sees their exhaustion, as one piercing a gem with a diamond (vajira) according to reality."

"Higher wisdom insight" (adhipaññā vipassanā) means that this collection of states—the reflection on the object, the contemplation of dissolution, and the appearance as void—is called higher wisdom insight. "Skilled in the three contemplations" (kusalo tīsu anupassanāsu) refers to the monk who is expert in the three contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence. "And in the four insights" (catasso ca vipassanāsu) refers to being skilled in the four insights beginning with the contemplation of weariness (nibbidā). "Skill in the three appearances" (tayo upaṭṭhāne kusalatā) refers to skill in these three kinds of appearance: as exhaustion (khaya), as passing away (vaya), and as void (suñña). "Unshaken by various views" (nānādiṭṭhīsu na kampati) means being unmoved by various types of wrong views.
242: He does not waver in various views such as eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). That meditator (yogāvacara), being thus unwavering, has the attention (manasikāra) that arises as 'only that which has not yet ceased, ceases; only that which is not yet broken, breaks.' Relinquishing the signs of arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and occurrence (pavatta) of all formations (saṅkhāra), he sees only their dissolution (bheda), like a weak vessel filled with water breaking, like fine dust being scattered by the wind, or like sesame seeds being roasted. Just as a man with sight standing on the bank of a pond or a river might see large bubbles of water appearing and quickly breaking on the surface of the water when heavy rain falls, even so, he sees that 'all formations are breaking, breaking.' Referring to such a meditator, the Blessed One said: 'One who looks upon the world as one would look upon a bubble, or as one would look upon a mirage, is not seen by the King of Death.' (Dhp. 170). For that meditator who repeatedly sees that 'all formations are breaking, breaking,' the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa), accompanied by eight benefits, reaches a state of strength. These are the eight benefits: abandoning the view of becoming (bhavadiṭṭhi), relinquishing attachment to life (jīvitanikanti), constant application of effort, pure livelihood, abandoning the exertion of kamma that leads to becoming, freedom from fear, attainment of patience and gentleness, and the ability to endure dissatisfaction and delight. Therefore, the ancient teachers said: 'Seeing these eight supreme qualities, the sage, who is like one whose clothes or head are on fire, contemplates repeatedly in that contemplation of dissolution for the sake of attaining the Deathless (Nibbāna).' ## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Dissolution is finished. ## 8. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Danger In the description of the Knowledge of Danger (ādīnavā-ñāṇa), 'arising' (uppāda) means the appearance in this life due to past kamma. 'Occurrence' (pavatta) means the occurrence of the aggregates that have thus arisen. 'Sign' (nimitta) means the sign of all formations. 'Accumulation' (āyūhana) means the kamma that is the cause of future rebirth-linking. 'Rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) means the arising in the future. 'Destination' (gati) means the destination where that rebirth-linking occurs. 'Manifestation' (nibbattī) means the manifestation of the aggregates. 'Attainment' (upapatti) means the occurrence of resultant states for one who has attained meditative absorption or for one born in the Brahma realm. 'Birth' (jāti) means the birth that is caused by becoming (bhava) and is the cause of aging (jarā), etc. In terms of meaning, it is the first manifestation of the aggregates of beings who are produced in various births. 'Aging' (jarā) means the decaying of the continuity of aggregates included in a single life, designated as the breaking of teeth, etc. 'Sorrow' (soka) means the burning of the mind of one who encounters the destruction of relatives, etc. 'Lamentation' (parideva) means the wailing of one who encounters the destruction of relatives, etc. 'Despair' (upāyāsa) means the intense burning of one who encounters the destruction of relatives, etc.; it is indeed anger (dosa) that causes great mental suffering. In this passage beginning with 'uppādo bhayaṃ' (arising is fear), only the five terms such as 'arising' are taught by way of being the basis for the Knowledge of Danger. The remaining terms such as 'destination' and 'manifestation' are taught as synonyms for those five terms like 'arising.' In fact, 'manifestation' and 'birth' are synonyms for both 'arising' and 'rebirth-linking.' 'Destination' and 'attainment' are also...
243:
...the occurrence of the result (vipāka). 'Birth' (jāti) is birth caused by becoming, which is the cause of aging and so on. In sense, whatever aggregates of beings being generated in various types of becoming manifest, the first manifestation of those aggregates is called birth. 'Aging' (jarā) is the state of being old and decayed of the continuity of aggregates included in a single life, designated by broken teeth and so on. 'Sorrow' (soka) is the burning of the mind of one affected by the loss of relatives and so on. 'Lamentation' (parideva) is the verbal wailing of one affected by the loss of relatives and so on. 'Despair' (upāyāsa) is intense distress; it is indeed anger (dosa) that causes great mental suffering for one affected by the loss of relatives and so on. Here, only the five terms such as arising (uppāda) are taught by way of the basis of the Knowledge of Danger; the remaining terms are taught by way of synonyms for those five terms. These two, 'generation' (nibbatti) and 'birth' (jāti), are synonyms for 'arising' (uppāda) and 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi). These two, 'destination' (gati) and 'reappearance' (upapatti), are synonyms for 'occurrence' (pavatta). Aging and so on are synonyms for 'sign' (nimitta). Therefore, [the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta] said: 'He sees arising, occurrence, and the sign as suffering; this is the knowledge of accumulation and rebirth-linking in [the contemplation of] danger,' and 'This knowledge of danger arises in five instances.' In all terms, the word 'bhayanti' should be analyzed as 'bhayaṃ iti.' It is called 'fear' (bhaya) because it is associated with oppression and is fraught with danger. 'Iti' indicates the cause of the appearance as fear.

However, the passage beginning with 'Non-arising is safety (khema), knowledge in the state of peace' is taught to show the knowledge that is the opposite of the Knowledge of Danger. Or else, it is taught for the purpose of giving reassurance to those whose hearts are terrified by seeing the danger through the appearance as fear, [showing that] 'there is also a place without fear, there is the safety of Nibbāna which is free from danger.' Or else, it should be understood that this is taught to show the benefit of the Knowledge of Danger, which is established by way of the appearance as fear, for one to whom arising and so on are well-manifested as fear, the mind inclines towards the opposite (Nibbāna). The passage beginning with 'Non-arising, non-occurrence' refers to Nibbāna itself. 'In the state of peace' (santipade) means in the portion of peace, in Nibbāna. Even the knowledge that arises by taking only the name 'state of peace' as an object through hearsay is called 'knowledge in the state of peace.' The passage beginning with 'Arising is fear, non-arising is safety' is taught by taking the knowledge that arises by summarizing both by way of the opposite and the non-opposite. Here, whatever fear there is, that fear is invariably suffering (dukkha). Whatever suffering there is, that is indeed 'with bait' (sāmisa) because it is not liberated from the bait of the rounds (vaṭṭāmisa), the bait of the world (lokāmisa), and the bait of defilements (kilesāmisa). Whatever is 'with bait' is merely formations (saṅkhāra).
244:
Therefore, to show the benefit of the Knowledge of Danger (Ādīnavajñāṇa) which is accomplished through the power of the Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful (Bhayatupaṭṭhānajñāṇa), it is stated: "Arising is suffering," "Knowledge of Danger," and so forth. Even though there is no difference in meaning, a distinction should be understood here because it occurs through various modes: the mode of fear, the mode of suffering, the mode of being with taints (sāmisa), and the mode of formations (saṅkhāra). In the phrase "Arising is fear, suffering, with taints, and formations," the gender of the terms such as 'arising' (uppāda) is ignored, and it is stated according to the gender of its own term (bhaya), just as in the verses: "This refuge is not secure (khemaṃ), this refuge is not supreme (uttamaṃ)."

Regarding the term "formations" (saṅkhārā), the singular state (of the nature of formations) is ignored, and the plural is used, just as in the Pali passages: "States without conditions (appaccayā dhammā), unconditioned states (asaṅkhatā dhammā)." Alternatively, because arising and so forth are parts of the nature of formations, the plural is used even for a part of many things, just as in worldly usage: "The Pañcālas in the north, the Pañcālas in the south."

By way of the opposite of the aforementioned modes (arising, etc.), Nibbāna itself is described in four ways: "Secure (khemaṃ), happy (sukhaṃ), without taints (nirāmisaṃ), and Nibbāna."

"He knows the ten knowledges" means that one who knows the Knowledge of Danger understands the ten knowledges distinctly, penetrates them, and realizes them through the five knowledges having arising etc. as their object, and the five knowledges having non-arising etc. as their object. "The skillfulness in the two knowledges" refers to the skillfulness in these two knowledges: the Knowledge of Danger and the Knowledge of the State of Peace (Santipadajñāṇa, the knowledge that takes Nibbāna as its object). "Unshakable in various views" means not trembling in views that occur by way of Nibbāna in the present life (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbāna) and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Danger is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations

In the description of the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhājñāṇaniddesa), the terms such as 'arising' have the meanings already stated. The terms "suffering, fear, with taints, and formations" are the causal statements for the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance (Muñcitukamyatājñāṇa) which releases one from arising and so forth. Having thus shown the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations by its characteristics, he now says: "Arising is formations; he looks on those formations with equanimity; therefore it is called Equanimity towards Formations," and so forth, to show it by way of its definition (vacanattha).

In that context, "he looks on those formations with equanimity" means that for that yogi who has begun insight (vipassanā), because the three characteristics have been seen through insight knowledge, the effort in investigating the characteristics has ceased. To one who looks at the three planes of existence like a house in flames, that insight knowledge which is indifferent in grasping formations looks at those formations specially (visesena) and looks at them while being free from grasping. Thus, it is called 'Equanimity towards Formations' (Saṅkhārupekkhā). Just as in the world, one who conquers specially is said to "over-conquer" (adhijayati), and one who dwells apart from food is said to "fast" (upavasati). Again, the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations, which stands in the state of being indifferent in grasping (observing) formations after having contemplated them as impermanent and so forth, contemplates them again as impermanent and so forth...
245:
...contemplating with insight even the Equanimity towards Formations which stands in a state of indifference as impermanent and so forth, because the Equanimity towards Formations standing in a mode of indifference can arise in the perception of that very Equanimity towards Formations, it is stated: "Whatever formations and whatever equanimity," and so forth.

Now, to show the different ways of directing the mind (cittassa abhinīhāro) in the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations, he says: "By how many modes?" and so forth. In that text, the word "saṅkhārupekkhāya" is in the locative case (bummavancana). "Directing of the mind" (cittassa abhinīhāro) means, for one who has attained the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations, the intense carrying of the mind—other than the equanimity that has formations as its object—towards the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations. Here, the prefix "abhi" denotes 'towards' and the prefix "nī" has the sense of 'intense'. Having answered the question "By how many modes?" with "By eight modes," and wishing to show those eight modes only through the answer to the second question, he did not show those answers yet but asked the question: "For a worldling (puthujjana), by how many modes?" and so forth. Regarding the term "for a worldling":

The Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun,
Has spoken of two kinds of worldlings:
One is the blind worldling (andha-puthujjana),
And one is the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana).

Among those two, the one who lacks learning, inquiry, hearing, retention, and reflection regarding the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), and so forth, is called a "blind worldling." The one who possesses that learning and so forth is called a "virtuous worldling." Both types of worldlings are also called "puthujjana" because:

They are worldlings because they generate many defilements and so forth,
Because they are included among the multitude of folk,
And because they are distinct (separate) from the Noble Ones.

Indeed, he is a worldling because of reasons such as generating many various defilements and so forth. As it is said in the Pali: "They are worldlings because they generate many (puthu) defilements; they are worldlings because they have many un-discarded self-identity views (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); they are worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers; they are worldlings because they have not yet emerged from all the many destinations (gati); they are worldlings because they construct many various formations (saṅkhāra); they are worldlings because they are swept away by many various floods (ogha); they are worldlings because they burn with many various torments; they are worldlings because they are scorched by many various fevers; they are worldlings because they are attached, greedy, tied, infatuated, deeply absorbed, fastened, stuck, and obstructed by the many five cords of sensual pleasure; they are worldlings because they are hindered, obstructed, closed off, shut in, covered, and overturned by the many five hindrances (nīvaraṇa)."
246:
A 'worldling' (puthujjana) is so called because they are included among the multitude of people who are turned away from the Noble Dhamma and practice base qualities, or because they are a person who stands apart and is distinct from the Noble Ones who are endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) and learning (suta). Among these worldlings, only the 'noble worldling' (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) is intended here, because other worldlings lack the practice of meditation (bhāvanā).

In the term 'trainee' (sekha), there are seven types of trainees: those standing in the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the fruit of once-returning, the path of non-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the path of arahantship. They are called 'trainees' because they are still training in the three trainings (sikkhā). Among them, only the three types—those standing in the fruition of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning—are intended here, because those standing in the path (maggaṭṭhāna) do not have the directing of the mind towards equanimity regarding formations (sankhārupekkhā).

In the term 'one free from lust' (vītarāga), it refers to one whose lust has been removed by the abandonment of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna); this is a designation for the Arahant. In all three terms, the singular form is used to represent the class or category.

'Delights in equanimity regarding formations' means that, having perceived the state of abiding in that equanimity as a peaceful abiding (phāsuvihāra), one delights in it by looking forward to it with the craving for peaceful abiding, thereby producing craving accompanied by joy (pīti).

Regarding 'practices insight' (vipassati): a worldling practices insight into impermanence and so on to attain the path of stream-entry; a trainee (sekha) practices for the sake of higher paths; and one free from lust (vītarāga/Arahant) practices insight for the sake of pleasant abiding in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra).

'Having reflected' (paṭisankhāya) means having investigated through the lens of impermanence and so on. Since Noble Ones, such as stream-enterers, cannot enter their respective fruition attainments (phalasamāpatti) without practicing insight through the nine insight knowledges, such as the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), it is said that they enter fruition attainment 'having reflected'.

To show the occurrence of fruition attainment, these questions are raised: What is fruition attainment? Who enters it? Who does not enter it? Why do they enter it? How is it entered? How is it maintained? How is it emerged from? What follows the fruit? And what does the fruit follow?

Among those questions, 'What is fruition attainment?' It is the absorption (appanā) of the Noble Fruit in the cessation (nirodha/Nibbāna). 'Who enters it? Who does not enter it?' All worldlings do not enter it. Why? Because they have not attained it. However, all Noble Ones enter it.
247:
Why? Because they have attained it. However, those in higher fruitions do not enter lower fruitions because those lower states have subsided as they have reached a distinct higher stage of personhood; and those in lower fruitions do not enter higher ones because they have not yet attained them. Indeed, the conclusion here is that all Noble Ones enter only their own respective fruition.

Some teachers, however, say: "Stream-enterers and once-returners do not enter fruition attainment; only the two higher types of persons (non-returners and Arahants) enter it." Their reason is: "These persons are those who fulfill the practice of concentration (samādhi)." That argument is invalid because even a worldling can enter the mundane concentration (lokiya-samādhi) that they have attained. What is the use of debating what is or is not a valid reason here? Is it not stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali itself, in the answer to the questions, "Which ten types of equanimity regarding formations arise by the power of insight? Which ten change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) states arise by the power of insight?" that they are "for the sake of the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, for the sake of the attainment of the fruit of once-returning," and so on, mentioned separately? Therefore, it should be concluded here that all Noble Ones enter their own respective fruition.

Why do they enter it? For the sake of pleasant abiding in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra). Just as kings enjoy royal bliss and deities enjoy divine bliss, so too the Noble Ones, thinking "We shall enjoy supramundane bliss," determine a duration and enter fruition attainment at any moment they desire.

How is it entered? How is it maintained? How is it emerged from? Firstly, it is entered in two ways: by non-attention to any object other than Nibbāna, and by attention to Nibbāna. As it is said: "Friend, there are two conditions for the attainment of the signless deliverance of mind (animitta-cetovimutti): non-attention to all signs (objects) and attention to the signless element (Nibbāna)."

The sequence of entry is as follows: a Noble disciple who desires fruition attainment, dwelling alone in seclusion, should practice insight into formations (sankhāra) by way of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) and so on. For one who thus practices progressive insight, immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which has formations as its object, the mind absorbs into cessation by way of fruition attainment. Because the mind is inclined toward fruition attainment, for a trainee (sekha) as well, only the fruit already attained arises, not the path. Those who say, "A stream-enterer, having started insight thinking 'I will enter fruition attainment,' becomes a once-returner, and a once-returner becomes a non-returner," should be told: "If that were so, a non-returner would become an Arahant, an Arahant would become a Paccekabuddha, and a Paccekabuddha would become a Sammāsambuddha."
248:
Therefore, this statement (of the Abhayagirivāsins) is without essence; since it is also rejected by the authority of the Pāli, it should not be accepted. Only the following statement should be accepted: For a trainee (sekha) as well, only the fruition (phala) that has been attained arises, not the path (magga). If that trainee has attained a path corresponding to the first jhāna, then only the fruition corresponding to the first jhāna arises. If they have attained a path corresponding to any of the other jhānas such as the second, then only the fruition corresponding to that particular jhāna arises. Thus, first, is the entry into the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) for that person.

According to the statement (from the Mahāvedalla Sutta): "Friends, there are three conditions for the persistence of the signless deliverance of mind (animitta-cetovimutti): non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element (Nibbāna), and prior preparation (pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro)"—the persistence of that attainment of fruition occurs through these three factors. Among them, "prior preparation" means the delimitation of time before entering the attainment. Because the time is delimited as "I shall emerge from the attainment at such and such a time," the persistence of the attainment of fruition lasts until that delimited time arrives. Thus should the persistence of that attainment of fruition be understood.

According to the statement: "Friends, there are two conditions for the emergence from the signless deliverance of mind: attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element"—the emergence from that attainment of fruition occurs through these two factors. Therein, "all signs" refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Although, in reality, one does not attend to all these signs simultaneously, this is stated in an all-inclusive sense. Therefore, for one who attends to the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), emergence from the attainment of fruition occurs. Thus should the emergence from that attainment of fruition be understood.

As to the question: "What occurs immediately after fruition, and after what does fruition occur?"—Immediately after fruition, either fruition itself or the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs. Fruition, however, occurs immediately after the path (maggānantara), immediately after fruition (phalānantara), immediately after change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-anantara), and immediately after the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatanānantara). Among these four, the fruition occurring immediately after the path in the path-process is called maggānantara. The fruition occurring after a preceding fruition is called phalānantara. The first fruition in the attainments of fruition is called the fruition occurring immediately after change-of-lineage. Here, it should be understood that "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū) refers to "conformity" (anuloma). For it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: "The conformity of an Arahant is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of proximity-condition. The conformity of trainees is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of proximity-condition." The fruition by which there is emergence from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called the fruition occurring immediately after the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Excluding the fruition that arises in the path-process among these four...
249:
...all the rest of the fruition is said to occur by way of the attainment of fruition. Thus, whether it occurs in the path-process or in the attainment of fruition, by way of its arising, it is said:

"It stills all distress, has the Deathless as its object, is beautiful,
Has vomited the baits of the world, is peaceful,
And is the supreme fruition of recluseship (sāmaññaphala)."

## This is the Discussion on the Attainment of Fruition.

"Tadajjhupekkhitvā" means observing (contemplating) that equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) with another similar insight knowledge. In the phrases such as "or by the void abiding" (suññatavihārena vā), an Arahant who wishes to abide by the abiding in insight alone, without entering the attainment of fruition, sees the adherence to a self as a danger. Being inclined towards the void Nibbāna, when they observe the passing away of equanimity towards formations, the collection of the three insight knowledges that arises is called the "void abiding" (suññatavihāra). Seeing the sign of formations as a danger, being inclined towards the signless Nibbāna, when they observe the passing away of equanimity towards formations, the collection of the three insight knowledges that arises is called the "signless abiding" (animittavihāra). Seeing the longing of craving as a danger, being inclined towards the undirected Nibbāna, when they observe the passing away of equanimity towards formations, the collection of the three insight knowledges that arises is called the "undirected abiding" (appaṇihitavihāra). Therefore, it is stated later:

"Seeing adherence as a danger, because of being inclined towards the void, one touches it with knowledge again and again and observes its passing away; this is the void abiding. Seeing the sign as a danger, because of being inclined towards the signless, one touches it with knowledge again and again and observes its passing away; this is the signless abiding. Seeing longing as a danger, because of being inclined towards the undirected, one touches it with knowledge again and again and observes its passing away; this is the undirected abiding" (as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

Because of the presence of six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) and because of the presence of abidings such as the perception of the unrepulsive in the repulsive, the mind of an Arahant alone is under control in every way. Therefore, it is meant that this abiding in insight is accomplished only for an Arahant. In the phrase "one free from lust contemplates equanimity towards formations," it should be understood that this refers to pure insight alone, without entering into the three kinds of danger and the three kinds of inclination (adhimutti). Only in this way will there be a distinction between the preceding and succeeding statements.

Now, wishing to show the division of unity (ekatta) and diversity (nānatta) of equanimity towards formations by way of two or three types of persons, the teacher said: "How for the worldling and the trainee," and so on.
250:
## 
In that (section on worldlings and trainees), 'the application of the mind is one' means it is identical. This should be understood as the abstract suffix (bhāva-sadda) used in its own sense. For example, just as 'idappaccaya' (this-conditionality) is called 'idappaccayatā', so too 'eka' (one) is called 'ekatta' (oneness/unity). The term 'abhinīhāro' (application) is either the nominative case (paccatta) used in the sense of possession (sāmi), or it means 'of the application' (abhinīhārassa). It should be understood that there is an interchange of cases, as in the phrase "having swept that place" (so deso sammajjitvā), etc.

'The mind is defiled' means the mind is defiled by the defilement of greed known as attachment to insight (vipassanā-nikanti); it means it is heated and oppressed. 'It is an obstacle to meditation' means it is a hindrance to the insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā) already attained. 'It is an obstacle to penetration' means it is an obstacle to attaining the penetration of the [Four Noble] Truths (saccappativedha) which should be attained through insight meditation. 'It is a cause for future rebirth' means because the kamma associated with equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) is powerful, when that kamma itself gives rise to a happy rebirth, the defilement of greed known as excessive delight (atinandana) becomes a (supportive) cause for future rebirth in the happy destinations of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-sugati-patisandhi). Since kamma accompanied by defilements produces a resultant (vipāka), kamma is the productive cause (janaka-paccaya) and the defilement is the supportive cause (upatthambhaka-paccaya).

In the section on the trainee (sekha), 'of the penetration higher and higher' means the penetration of the Truths by way of the path of Once-returning, etc. 'It is a cause for future rebirth' means for Stream-enterers and Once-returners among trainees who have not yet attained jhāna, the defilement of delight (abhinandana) is the cause for rebirth in the happy destinations of the sense sphere given by the kamma of equanimity towards formations. However, for those who have attained jhāna and for Non-returners, it is not a cause because they are reborn only in the Brahma world. It should be understood that this very defilement is the cause for the rebirth given by the knowledge of conformity (anuloma) and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).

'As impermanent' means as impermanent because of the sense of non-existence after having been, because of having impermanence as its end, and because of having a beginning and an end. 'As suffering' means as suffering because of the sense of constant oppression, because of being oppressed by arising and passing away, and because of being the basis of suffering. 'As non-self' means as non-self because of the sense of not being under control, because of being dependent on conditions, and because of the absence of an owner, a resident, a doer, or an experiencer. 'In the sense of contemplation' means in the sense of repeatedly seeing as impermanent, etc. 'The application is diverse (nānatta)' means the application is various, or it should be understood as the state of the application being various.

'Wholesome' (kusala) means wholesome because of the sense of being healthy, blameless, and born of wisdom. 'Indeterminate' (abyākata) means those states not declared as wholesome or unwholesome. At some times...
251:
## 
'Well-known' (suvidita) means clearly manifest at the time of practicing insight. 'At some times not well-known' means not clearly manifest at the time of delighting in insight-knowledge. 'Completely well-known' means definitely well-known because the craving that delights in insight has been abandoned. In the phrase 'by the sense of being known and the sense of being unknown', the sense of being well-known for worldlings and trainees, and the sense of being completely well-known for the one free from lust (the Arahant), are both simply 'the sense of being known' (viditattha). The sense of not being well-known for both [worldlings and trainees] is simply 'the sense of being unknown' (aviditattha).

'Due to being unsatisfied' (atittattā) means because the task to be done through insight (the path and fruit) is not yet finished, thus being in an incomplete state. The opposite of that is 'being satisfied' (tittattā). 'For the abandoning of the three fetters' means for the purpose of abandoning self-identity view, doubt, and adherence to rites and rituals. Bodhisattas in their final existence are also included here in the insight that leads to the abandoning of these three fetters. However, Bodhisattas who have not yet reached their final existence bring insight to the level of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) and then stop. The phrase 'for the sake of attaining the path of Stream-entry' is read without compounding; the reading with the compound 'sotāpattimaggappaṭilābhatthāya' is more appropriate. 'The trainee, because of having abandoned the three fetters' is said generally in connection with Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners. Indeed, for Once-returners and Non-returners, those three fetters are already abandoned. 'For the sake of attaining the higher' means for the sake of attaining the higher paths. 'For the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life' means for the sake of dwelling happily in the present visible state of existence. 'In the sense of the attainment of dwelling' means in the sense of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) for the trainee, and in the sense of the dwelling in insight and the attainment of fruition for the one free from lust (the Arahant).

Now, to show the numerical determination of the types of equanimity towards formations, he said 'How many types of equanimity towards formations?' etc. In that text, 'by way of serenity' (samathavasena) means by the power of concentration (samādhi). Or this is the reading itself. 'Reflecting on the hindrances' means having grasped the five hindrances as things to be abandoned. 'Steadying' (santiṭṭhanā) means being directed towards the abandoning of the hindrances, and upon reaching the state of non-exertion even in their abandonment, it is the steadying in the state of neutrality. 'In the types of equanimity towards formations' means in the equanimity towards the formations known as hindrances, without making an effort in abandoning the hindrances. This method applies also to initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), and so on. In the context of serenity (samatha), what is called equanimity towards formations is the wisdom consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa) that has reached strength in the preliminary stage close to the process of absorption (appanā-vīthi). In the four sections on the Path, such as 'for the sake of attaining the path of Stream-entry', one or another of the paths—void, signless, or undirected—is attained. In the four sections on Fruition, such as 'for the sake of the attainment of the fruition of Stream-entry', the undirected attainment of fruition (appaṇihita-phala-samāpatti) should be understood. Why? Because he will later teach the other two—the void attainment of fruition and the signless attainment of fruition—separately, saying 'for the sake of the void attainment of dwelling, for the sake of the signless attainment of dwelling'. Indeed, by the power of the contemplation of impermanence...
252:
"For the sake of attaining the Signless Dwelling Attainment," this is said because the other two fruition attainments are taught separately. Indeed, by the power of emerging from the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), the Signless Path (animitta-magga) arises. Likewise, at the time of fruition attainment, the Signless Fruition Attainment (animitta-phala-samāpatti) occurs. By the power of emerging from the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), the Desireless Path (appaṇihita-magga) and the Desireless Fruition Attainment occur. By the power of emerging from the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), the Void Path (suññata-magga) and the Void Fruition Attainment occur; this should be understood according to the Suttanta method.

In these four Path sections, fifteen terms are taught: five root terms such as arising (uppāda), and ten synonymous terms such as destination (gati). However, in the six Fruition Attainment sections, only the five root terms are taught. Why is this so? When the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) is sharp, the Path capable of abandoning defilements arises. Therefore, to demonstrate the sharpness of that equanimity towards formations, the root terms are taught firmly together with the synonymous terms. As for the Fruition, because it is of a peaceful nature without effort and because it depends on the Path, the root terms alone are taught to show that even a subtle knowledge of equanimity towards formations serves as a condition for the Fruition.

Now, in order to answer according to what is obtainable by way of class (jāti), it is said: "How many types of equanimity towards formations are wholesome (kusala)?" and so forth. Therein, the fifteen types of equanimity towards formations are: eight by way of serenity (samatha), and seven by way of the four Paths and three Fruitions. For an Arahant, the eight types of equanimity towards formations by way of serenity are not called indeterminate (abyākata) because there is no re-reflection on the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and because they are abandoned happily without the effort of abandoning initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) and so forth; thus they are unsuitable for the name 'equanimity towards formations'. However, when an Arahant enters fruition attainment, it is impossible to do so without the knowledge of equanimity towards formations; therefore, three types of equanimity towards formations are called indeterminate. By way of the desireless (appaṇihita), the void (suññata), and the signless (animitta), these three types of equanimity towards formations for an Arahant are indeterminate.

Now, in the three verses taught by way of explaining the types of equanimity towards formations: "Wisdom well-established through reflection is equanimity towards formations." "The eight domains of the mind" refers to the eight types of equanimity towards formations taught by way of serenity, meaning they are the objects and planes of concentration (samādhi). Just as in passages like "Develop the mind and wisdom," concentration is indicated by the head of 'mind'. Just as in passages like "Monks, wander in your own ancestral domain (gocara)," the word 'domain' indicates the object. Whatever is dependent on something is called the object of that thing. "Two for the worldling" means by way of serenity and by way of insight (vipassanā). "Three for the trainee (sekha)" means by way of serenity, insight, and attainment. "Three also for the one free from passion (vītarāga)" means by way of the desireless, void, and signless fruition attainments. Although it should be said as "tisso" (feminine), the masculine form "tayo" is used by changing the gender, referring to the states of equanimity towards formations. "By which the mind turns away" means the mind turns away from initial and sustained thought, etc., or from arising (uppāda), etc., through those states of equanimity towards formations. Since the knowledge of equanimity towards formations is clearly present even for an Arahant, it means the mind turns away from formations and leaps into Nibbāna. "Eight causes of concentration" means the eight types of equanimity taught by way of serenity are the causes for absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) because they lead to absorption. "Causes of the three liberations" means they are the sufficing condition (upanissaya) causes for the void, signless, and desireless liberations. "Unshaken by various views" means that one who contemplates formations as impermanent, etc., without abandoning the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga), is not shaken by various views such as eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi).

The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations is finished.
253:
For the trainee (sekha), the domains are by way of serenity, insight, and attainment. For the one free from passion (vītarāga/Arahant), there are three domains by way of the desireless, void, and signless fruition attainments. Where it should be said as "tisso" (feminine), the gender is changed to "tayo" (masculine). Or it should be construed as "tayo saṅkhārupekkhā dhammā" (three states of equanimity towards formations). "By which the mind turns away" means the mind turns away and retreats from initial and sustained thought, etc., or from arising (uppāda), etc., through those states of equanimity towards formations. Indeed, because the knowledge of equanimity towards formations is present even for an Arahant, it is said that the mind turns away from formations and leaps into Nibbāna. "Eight causes of concentration" means the eight types taught by way of serenity are the causes for absorption concentration because they lead to absorption. "Ten domains of knowledge" means the ten planes (bhūmi) of Path knowledge and Fruition knowledge taught by way of insight. "Causes of the three liberations" means they are the sufficing condition causes for the void, signless, and desireless liberations. "Unshaken by various views" means that one who contemplates formations as impermanent, etc., without abandoning the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), does not tremble at various kinds of views such as eternalism.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations is finished.

## 10. Gotrabhūñāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Description of Change-of-lineage Knowledge)

In the description of Change-of-lineage Knowledge, "abhibhuyyati" means it overcomes or transcends. "Bahiddhā saṅkhāranimittaṃ" refers to the sign of formations which is external to the unwholesome aggregates occurring within one's own continuity. In truth, worldly formations are called "signs" (nimitta) because they are the causes of defilements, or because they appear in the mode of a sign. By the word "abhibhuyyati," the state of being 'change-of-lineage' (gotrabhū) is stated because it overcomes the lineage of worldlings (puthujjana-gotta). By the word "pakkhandati" (leaps into), the state of being 'change-of-lineage' is stated because it causes one to enter the lineage of the Noble Ones (ariya-gotta). By the phrase "abhibhuyyitvā pakkhandati" (having overcome, it leaps into), both meanings are stated in summary. The types of change-of-lineage called "vuṭṭhāti" (emerges) and "vivaṭṭati" (turns away) refer only to the meaning of suppressing the worldling lineage, in accordance with the terms 'emergence' and 'turning away' found in the Matika. Furthermore, the change-of-lineage types taught by way of serenity are called 'change-of-lineage' because they overcome the lineage of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth. In the six fruition attainment sections such as "for the sake of the fruition attainment of stream-entry," it is called 'change-of-lineage' because it overcomes the lineage of arising (uppāda) and so forth. In the three Path sections such as "for the sake of obtaining the path of once-returning," it is called 'change-of-lineage' because it overcomes the lineage of the stream-winner and so forth...
254:
The meaning of 'gotrabhū' should be understood. Here, the meaning of 'gotta' is 'seed'. In the Vattani text, it is said: 'Nibbāna is called gotta because it is secure from all dangers; because one reaches that Nibbāna, it is called gotrabhū. The eight attainments are also called gotta because they are secure from the dangers of gotrabhū; because one reaches those attainments, it is called gotrabhū.' Teachers say: 'Only the gotrabhū of the four paths has Nibbāna as its object; the gotrabhū of the four fruit attainments has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object because it inclines towards fruit attainment.'

In the Visuddhimagga, it is also said: 'For one who has insight (vipassanā) occurring in due order, immediately after the gotrabhū-ñāṇa which has formations as its object, the mind enters into cessation (nirodha/Nibbāna) by the power of fruit attainment (phala-samāpatti).' Therefore, it should be understood that here, the term 'external sign of formations' (bahiddhā-saṅkhāra-nimitta-pada), which is taken as the sixteenth in the Path Cycles (magga-vāra), is not taken as the sixth in the Attainment Cycles (samāpatti-vāra). Otherwise, it would have to be taken by taking the original term.

Other teachers, however, say: 'Whatever is the first attention, the first application of mind towards Nibbāna, this is called gotrabhū.' That statement is not appropriate with reference to the Fruit. In this context where it is said 'the fifteen gotrabhū states are wholesome (kusala)', it should be understood that for an Arahant, because there are no hindrances (nīvaraṇa) to be suppressed and because initial and sustained thoughts (vitakka-vicāra) etc. are easily abandoned, they do not deserve the name gotrabhū in the sense of 'suppressing'; thus, the indeterminateness (abyākata) of gotrabhū is not mentioned. However, when an Arahant enters fruit attainment, because it is impossible to enter without suppressing formations, it is said: 'the three gotrabhū states are indeterminate (abyākata).' Some teachers say: 'Only the eight attainments which are part of penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya) are shown here; therefore, the eight attainment-gotrabhū are wholesome.' The same should be understood regarding the equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā).

In the terms beginning with 'sāmisañca', it is called 'sāmisa' (with bait/carnal) because it occurs together with attachment (nikanti) through the bait of defilements (kilesāmisa) among the bait of the round (vaṭṭāmisa), the bait of the world (lokāmisa), and the bait of defilements. What is that? It is the eightfold calm-gotrabhū-ñāṇa (samatha-gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Here, 'vaṭṭāmisa' is the round of existence in the three planes itself. 'Lokāmisa' refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Kilesāmisa' refers to the defilements themselves. Because of the absence of attachment, the ten types of insight-gotrabhū-ñāṇa (vipassanā-gotrabhū-ñāṇa) are called 'nirāmisa' (without bait/spiritual). Indeed, the Noble Ones (ariyas) do not form attachment to gotrabhū. In some books, they write 'sāmisañce', but that writing is not very good. In this same way, paṇihita and appaṇihita, saññutta and visaññutta, vuṭṭhita and avuṭṭhita should be understood. Because there is attachment and longing (paṇidhi), it has the meaning 'paṇihita' (aimed/desired). Because of the absence of that longing, it is called 'appaṇihita'.
255:
Appaṇihita-gotrabhū is called 'appaṇihita' because of the absence of the longing (paṇidhi) which is craving. It is called 'saññutta' (yoked) only because of being associated with craving, and 'visaññutta' (unyoked) because of the absence of that association. 'Vuṭṭhita' (emerged) refers only to the insight-gotrabhū-ñāṇa which has the function of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). That gotrabhū is called 'vuṭṭhita' because it cuts off the craving of attachment. Other gotrabhū are called 'avuṭṭhita'. Alternatively, it is called 'vuṭṭhita' because it emerges from external formations. The gotrabhū occurring before the Fruit should also be understood as 'vuṭṭhita' because it faces Nibbāna by the power of the inclination towards Nibbāna, and thus emerges from the sign of external formations. In the cycles of lower suppression, emergence, and rolling back (heṭṭhā-abhibhavana-vuṭṭhāna-vivaṭṭana-vāra), the gotrabhū before the Fruit should be understood as suppressing, emerging, and rolling back from formations because it faces Nibbāna by the power of inclination.

'Tiṇṇံ vimokkhānaံ paccayā' means that for the three supramundane liberations—the void (suññata), the signless (animitta), and the undirected (appaṇihita)—the gotrabhū occurring before calm (samatha) serves as a natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya); the gotrabhū having the function of insight leading to emergence serve as conditions by way of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), and decisive support (upanissaya).

'Paññā yassa paricitā' means that the person has practiced the wisdom of discerning formations (saṅkhāra-paritaraṇa-paññā) which occurs in the preliminary stage of the path-process.

'Kusalo vivaṭṭe vuṭṭhāne' means being a person skilled in the gotrabhū-ñāṇa called 'vivaṭṭa' (rolling back) by the power of non-delusion; or being a person skilled in the gotrabhū-ñāṇa called 'vivaṭṭa' through the wisdom consisting in learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa) occurring in the preliminary stage of the path.

'Nānādiṭṭhīsu na kampatī' means not being shaken by various views that have been abandoned by cutting them off completely with the path.

## The explanation of the meaning of Gotrabhū-ñāṇa is finished.

## 11. Magga-ñāṇa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā

In the Magga-ñāṇa-niddesa, 'micchādiṭṭhiyā vuṭṭhāti' means one emerges from the sixty-two types of wrong view by the power of abandoning the underlying tendency of wrong view (diṭṭhānusaya) through complete cutting off. 'Tadanuvattaka-kilesehi' means one emerges from various defilements that follow wrong view, either because of being associated with wrong view or because of arising in dependence on wrong view. By this statement, the abandoning of defilements that have the same basis (tadekaṭṭha) as that wrong view is meant. There are two kinds of ekaṭṭha: co-nascent basis (sahajekaṭṭha) and basis of being abandoned together (pahānekaṭṭha). They are called 'tadekaṭṭha' because they exist together with that wrong view in a single consciousness or in a single person until they are abandoned by the path. When wrong view is abandoned, in the two types of unprompted (asaṅkhārika) consciousness associated with wrong view, these defilements—greed (lobha), delusion (moha), restlessness (uddhacca), shamelessness (ahirika), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa)—which are co-nascent with that wrong view, are abandoned by the power of sahajekaṭṭha. In the two types of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness, these defilements—greed, delusion, sloth (thina), restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—which are co-nascent with that wrong view, are abandoned by the power of sahajekaṭṭha. When only the defilement of wrong view is abandoned, these defilements which lead to the states of deprivation (apāya) and exist in a single person together with that wrong view—greed, hatred (dosa), delusion, conceit (māna), doubt (vicikicchā), sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—these defilements...
256:
These defilements—sloth (thina), restlessness (uddhacca), shamelessness (ahirika), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa)—are abandoned by way of being established in a single state of abandonment (pahānekaṭṭha). 

"With aggregates" means with the aggregates that follow that wrong view, with the four mental aggregates (arūpakkhandha) that are conascent (sahajekaṭṭha) and established in a single state of abandonment (pahānekaṭṭha) following that wrong view, or with the five aggregates including the matter produced by them, and with the resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandha) that are to arise in the future due to defilements such as wrong view. "From all external signs of formations" means from all signs of formations that are external to the aforementioned aggregates of defilements.
