"Emerges from wrong intention" means it emerges from the wrong intentions associated with the five types of consciousness—namely, the four associated with wrong view and the one accompanied by doubt—which are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), as well as from the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses that lead to the lower realms.

"Emerges from wrong speech" means it emerges from false speech (musāvāda) and from slanderous (pisuṇavācā), harsh (pharusavācā), and frivolous speech (samphappalāpa) that lead to the lower realms. "Emerges from wrong action" means it emerges from killing (pāṇātipāta), stealing (adinnādāna), and sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra). "Emerges from wrong livelihood" means it emerges from the modes of livelihood such as scheming (kuhana), talking (lapana), hinting (nemittikatā), belittling (nippesikatā), and pursuing gain with gain (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā), or from the seven types of bodily and verbal actions based on livelihood. The emergence from wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration should be understood in the same manner as described for the emergence from wrong intention. Furthermore, "wrong mindfulness" (micchā-sati) is merely the arising of unwholesome consciousness in a manner that is the opposite of mindfulness. In the three higher paths, the eight path factors, such as "Right View in the sense of seeing," are obtained just as they are in the first path (the Path of Stream-entry) which is like the first jhāna. Among those, in the first path, Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) is so called because it abandons wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). Right Intention and the others should also be understood as such because they abandon wrong intention and so forth. If this is so, since the sixty-two types of wrong views are already abandoned by the first path alone, there is no wrong view to be abandoned by the three higher paths.

How then does the name "Right View" apply to those three higher paths? Just as medicine is called "agada" (antitoxin) whether poison is present or not, so too this state is named Right View whether wrong view exists or not. If it were merely a name, then Right View would have no function in the three higher paths, and the path factors would not be fulfilled. Therefore, Right View must be made to have its own function, and the path factors must be fulfilled. Here, Right View is shown to have its own function according to the rule of attainment. There is a type of conceit (māna) to be destroyed by the three higher paths; that conceit stands in the place of wrong view, and because Right View abandons that conceit, it is called Right View. In the Path of Stream-entry, Right View abandons wrong view. For a Stream-enterer, there is conceit to be abandoned by the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga); because it abandons that conceit, it is called Right View. For that same Stream-enterer, there are intentions associated with the seven unwholesome types of consciousness; because of those very consciousnesses, there exist verbal intimation (vacī-viññatti), bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti), the use of requisites, conascent effort, the state of non-mindfulness (assati), and conascent one-pointedness (ekaggatā). These states, such as intention and verbal intimation, are called wrong intention and so forth. In the Path of Once-returning, Right Intention and the others are known as Right Intention and so forth because they abandon those states of wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, and so on.

In this way, the eight path factors in the Path of Once-returning have their own functions. For a Once-returner, there is conceit to be abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga); that conceit stands in the place of wrong view. For that same Once-returner, there are states such as intention associated with the seven types of consciousness. Because they abandon those states of wrong intention and so forth, the eight path factors in the Path of Non-returning are known to have their own functions. For a Non-returner, there is conceit to be abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga); that conceit stands in the place of wrong view. For that same Non-returner, there are five unwholesome types of consciousness, and there are intentions and so forth associated with those five types of consciousness. Because they abandon those states of wrong intention and so forth, the eight path factors in the Path of Arahantship are known to have their own functions.
257:
In the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) abandons wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). However, for a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), there still remains conceit (māna) to be eradicated by the path of once-return (sakadāgāmi-magga); because of abandoning that conceit, it is called right view in the path of once-return. For that stream-enterer, there is thought (saṅkappa) associated with the seven unwholesome consciousnesses. Due to those seven consciousnesses, there are vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti), bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti), use of requisites, energy (vīriya) associated with unwholesome consciousness, lack of mindfulness (assatiya), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā). These states are called wrong thought (micchā-saṅkappa) and so forth. In the path of once-return, the path factors such as right thought (sammā-saṅkappa) should be understood as right thought and so forth by way of abandoning those [wrong states] such as wrong thought. Thus, in the path of once-return, the eight path factors perform their respective functions. For a once-returner (sakadāgāmī), there still remains conceit to be eradicated by the path of non-return (anāgāmi-magga); that conceit stands in the place of [wrong] view. For that person, there are wrong thought and so forth associated with the seven unwholesome consciousnesses. By abandoning them, the performance of the respective functions of the eight path factors in the path of non-return should be understood. For a non-returner (anāgāmī), there still remains conceit to be eradicated by the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga); that conceit stands in the place of [wrong] view. For that person, there are five unwholesome consciousnesses, and there are wrong thought and so forth associated with those consciousnesses. By abandoning them, the performance of the respective functions of the eight path factors in the path of arahantship should be understood.

'Gross' (oḷārika) refers to states that are coarse because they are the cause of transgression through the doors of body and speech. 'The fetter of sensual lust' (kāmarāga-saṃyojana) is the fetter known as sexual lust (methuna-rāga). It is called a fetter because it binds beings to the sensual realm (kāmabhava). 'The fetter of aversion' (paṭigha-saṃyojana) is the fetter of ill will (byāpāda). It is called aversion (paṭigha) because it strikes against the object. Those very same gross sensual lust and ill will are called 'underlying tendencies' (anusaya) because they lie dormant in the mental continuity upon reaching a state of strength. 'Accompanied by the subtle' (aṇusahagata) means occurring in a subtle way; it has the meaning of being subtle. Here, the word 'sahagata' (accompanied by) is used in the sense of that subtle state (tabbhāva). For a once-returner, sensual lust and ill will become subtle due to two reasons: because of their [infrequent] occurrence in the continuity (adhiccuppatti) and because of the weakness of their obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna-mandatā). For that person, defilements do not arise constantly as they do for foolish worldlings (bāla-puthujjana); they arise only occasionally. Even when they arise, they do not arise by way of crushing, spreading, covering, or causing total blindness as they do for foolish worldlings. Having been abandoned by the two [lower] paths, they arise only in a very weak and thin manner, and they are not capable of leading to transgression. Thus, sensual lust and ill will, which have become attenuated, are abandoned by the path of non-return. 'Lust for fine-material existence' (rūparāga) is the desire and lust (chandarāga) for the fine-material realm. 'Lust for immaterial existence' (arūparāga) is the desire and lust for the immaterial realm. 'Conceit' (māna) is the state characterized by loftiness. 'Restlessness' (uddhacca) is the state characterized by lack of peace. 'Ignorance' (avijjā) is the state characterized by blindness. 'The underlying tendency to lust for existence' (bhavarāgānusaya) is the underlying tendency to lust for existence occurring by way of lust for fine-material and immaterial existence.

Now, wishing to provide the commentary on path knowledge, he said 'ajātaṃ jhāpeti' and so forth. In that text, 'ajātaṃ jhāpeti' means that by means of the supramundane jhāna that has clearly arisen in his continuity, the person endowed with that path completely cuts off (burns up) those various defilements that have not yet arisen in terms of their plane (bhūmi). Therefore, that supramundane jhāna is called 'jhāna'. 'Skillfulness in jhāna and liberation' (jhānavimokkhe kusalatā) refers to the state of being unshakable by various views already abandoned by the path of stream-entry, due to skillfulness by way of non-delusion in the jhāna consisting of thought and so forth associated with that noble path, and in the noble path called liberation (vimokkha). There are two kinds of jhāna: meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Mundane first jhāna and so forth are called jhāna because they closely contemplate objects such as the kasina. Insight (vipassanā) is called jhāna because it closely contemplates the individual and general characteristics of formations (saṅkhāra). The supramundane path is called jhāna because it closely contemplates the true characteristic in Nibbāna. In this term 'jhānavimokkha', the meaning of 'jhāna' is not taken as meditation on characteristics that is connected with change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), but it is called 'jhāna' because of the meaning of burning up defilements that are not connected with change-of-lineage. The meaning of the word 'vimokkha' (liberation) is the full entering (adhimuccana) into the object that is Nibbāna...
258:
By means of that respective supramundane jhāna that has clearly arisen within his own continuity, the person endowed with that Path burns, destroys, and utterly cuts off those respective defilements (kilesa) that have not yet arisen (in terms of their plane). For that reason, that supramundane state is called 'jhāna'. 'Skillfulness in jhāna and liberation (vimokkha)' means that, through the power of non-delusion regarding the jhāna factors such as initial application (vitakka) associated with that Noble Path, and regarding the Noble Path called liberation (vimokkha), one is skillful and thus remains unshaken by various views that have already been abandoned by the first Path (the Path of Stream-entry) alone.

Jhāna is of two kinds: meditation by closely contemplating an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation by closely contemplating characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). The mundane first jhāna and so on are called 'jhāna' in the sense of closely contemplating an object such as a kasiṇa. Insight (vipassanā) is called 'jhāna' in the sense of closely contemplating the individual and common characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra). The supramundane Path is called 'jhāna' in the sense of closely contemplating the true characteristic of Nibbāna. However, in this context, the sense of lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna, which is also common to change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), is not taken; rather, 'jhāna' is spoken of in the sense of burning away defilements, which is not common to gotrabhū. Here, the meaning of liberation (vimokkha) is the sense of being well-inclined toward the object of Nibbāna and the sense of being well-freed from defilements.

'Having concentrated, he sees with insight' means that after first making the mind concentrated with one of the types of concentration—attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi), access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), or momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi)—he subsequently sees with insight. The word 'ce' (if/and) in the sense of conjunction includes insight. 'While seeing with insight, he should likewise concentrate' means that this thing called insight is rough and without relish, while tranquility (samatha) is subtle and accompanied by relish. Therefore, in order to moisten (soften) the mind that has become rough through that insight, the one seeing with insight should likewise make the mind concentrated through concentration. It means that the one seeing with insight should again enter concentration and make the mind concentrated just as he was seeing with insight. Here, the word 'ce' includes concentration. In both places, the syllable 'ce' is used to follow the metrical arrangement of the verse, but its meaning is simply that of 'ca' (and).

'Then there were insight and tranquility' means that since the Noble Path appears when tranquility and insight are yoked together (yuganaddha), and because they are capable of producing the Noble Path, when that union of both occurs, then insight and tranquility arise; it is said that tranquility and insight have clearly appeared. Those two, tranquility and insight, at the time of facing the Noble Path and at the moment of the Path, have equal shares and are yoked together (yuganaddha). They are called 'equal shares' (samānabhāga) because they have an equal portion or part. They are called 'yoked together' (yuganaddha) because they are like a pair yoked to a pole. It means they are equally yoked (samadhurā) and equal in power (samabalā) in the sense of not overstepping one another. The detail of this will be made clear in the 'Discussion on Yoking Together' (Yuganaddhakathā).

'Conditioned phenomena are suffering, cessation is bliss'—such is the vision. Wisdom emerging from both touches the Deathless state. 'Conditioned phenomena are suffering, the cessation that is Nibbāna is bliss'...
259:
For the practitioner, the Noble Path Knowledge (ariya-magga-ñāṇa) that sees Nibbāna from the three moments of that Path-consciousness is called 'wisdom emerging from both'—that is, from the occurrence of formations and from the sign of formations. That very wisdom touches and attains Nibbāna, the Deathless state (amata-pada), by way of touching it as an object. Nibbāna is called 'Deathless' (amata) because it is like ambrosia in the sense of being non-distressing; it is also called 'Deathless' because it has no death, destruction, or decay. It is called 'State' (pada) because it is reached or attained through great effort and a great practice starting from the purification of virtue, which is the preliminary stage of the Path.

'He knows the course of liberation' means he knows the occurrence of liberation through the power of non-delusion and through the power of the reviewing process (paccavekkhaṇā-vīthi). One should understand the courses of liberation as they appear in the 'Discussion on Liberation' (Vimokkhakathā) above: "Liberation emerging from both, the four liberations emerging from both, the four liberations in conformity for those emerging from both, and the four liberations as the subsiding of those emerging from both." Their details should be understood as they appear in that very Vimokkhakathā. 'Skilled in diversity and unity' means being skillful in the diverse nature and the unified nature of those Paths. The unity of those liberations should be understood by way of liberation emerging from both; their diversity by way of the four Noble Paths; or the diversity of each Noble Path by way of the different types of contemplation (anupassanā), and their unity by way of being the Noble Path.

'Skillfulness in the two knowledges' means skillfulness in these two knowledges: the one called 'seeing' (dassana) and the one called 'development' (bhāvanā). 'Seeing' refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). It is called 'seeing' because it sees Nibbāna for the first time. Although change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) sees Nibbāna even before the Path of Stream-entry, it is like a man who comes to the king on some business and sees the king from afar riding an elephant in the street; when asked, "Have you seen the king?", he says, "I have not seen him," because his business has not been completed. Similarly, although gotrabhū sees Nibbāna, it is not called 'seeing' because the task of abandoning defilements has not yet been performed. That knowledge stands in the position of adverting (āvajjana) to the Path. 'Development' (bhāvanā) refers to the remaining three higher Paths. They arise by way of development regarding the very truths already seen by the first Path; they do not see anything not seen before. Therefore, they are called 'development'. In the lower verse, because the path of development was not yet completed, it did not say 'two knowledges' but said 'skillfulness in jhāna and liberation' with reference to those who have attained the Paths of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning. However, for one who has attained the Path of Arahantship, because the path of development is completed, it should be understood that it is called 'skillfulness in the two knowledges'.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Path Knowledge is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Fruit Knowledge

63. In the exposition of Fruit Knowledge (phala-ñāṇa), 'because of the subsiding of that endeavor' (taṃ-payoga-ppaṭippassaddhattā) means because the endeavor of the Path, which is the emergence from internal and external phenomena, has subsided. The Path is said to make the endeavor of emerging from internal and external phenomena by abandoning defilements in its own moment. But in the moment of Fruition, because the defilements have already been abandoned, the Path's...
260:
## 12. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Fruition

In the exposition of the knowledge of fruition, the phrase "tampayogappaṭippassaddhattā" means because the effort of emerging from those internal and external phenomena has subsided. Indeed, the Path (magga), at its own moment, is said to perform the effort of emerging from both internal and external phenomena by abandoning the defilements. At the moment of Fruition (phala), however, because the defilements have already been abandoned, the Path's effort of emerging from both is said to be subsided or calmed.

"Uppajjati" (arises) means it arises once or twice immediately after the Path. During the time of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), however, it arises many times. For one emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), it arises twice. All such fruition arises because the effort has subsided. In the phrase "maggassetaṃ phalaṃ," the neuter form "etaṃ" is used in reference to the word "phala." In the moments of the Path of Once-Returning (sakadāgāmimagga) and so forth, the application of emergence should also be understood by the power of each individual Path-factor.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Fruition is finished.

## 13. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Liberation

In the exposition of the knowledge of liberation, "sakkāyadiṭṭhi" (personality view) is so called because it is a view regarding the body (kāya), which is the collection of the five aggregates, existing in the sense of being real. Alternatively, it is called sakkāyadiṭṭhi because it is a view that exists in that body by itself. "Vicikicchā" (skeptical doubt) is so called because it is devoid of remedy (cikicchā). Alternatively, it is called vicikicchā because a person who investigates the nature of things with this state becomes weary or fatigued. "Sīlabbataparāmāsa" (clinging to rules and observances) is the wrong adherence or grasping that "purity comes through habits, purity comes through vows, purity comes through habits and vows." Indeed, it is called sīlabbataparāmāsa because it misinterprets by overstepping the true nature of purity and grasping it in another way.

Although both sakkāyadiṭṭhi and sīlabbataparāmāsa are identical in being views (diṭṭhi), sakkāyadiṭṭhi is mentioned to show the abandonment of all views by the abandonment of the twenty-based personality view, which is the natural view taken by itself without depending on reasoning or the instruction of others. Sīlabbataparāmāsa, however, should be understood as being mentioned separately to show the falsity of the practice of those sectarians who practice with the thought, "We shall practice the path to purity."

To show the abandonment of the three fetters by the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) alone, it is said "the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) and the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)," not because they are separate defilements. "Upakkilesa" (corruptions) are called defilements (kilesa) because they defile, burn, and distress. Intense defilements are called upakkilesa in the sense of having reached strength. "Sammā samucchinnā honti" means they are well and completely cut off by the abandonment of uprooting (samucchedappahāna), which is the cessation of non-arising. "Sapariyuṭṭhānehi" means the mind...
261:
...they are called active manifestations (pariyuṭṭhāna) because they arise and overwhelm the mind from all sides. This is a synonym for defilements that have reached the stage of active manifestation (samudācāra). "Sapariyuṭṭhāna" means together with active manifestations. The mind is liberated from those secondary defilements (upakkilesa) along with underlying tendencies (anusaya) and active manifestations (pariyuṭṭhāna). Since those defilements are incapable of arising again, the mind occurring in the continuity is said to be liberated from them. Because it is well liberated, it is called "suvimutta." In the sense of knowing that liberation, it is called "vimuttiñātaṭṭha."

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Liberation is finished.

## 14. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Reviewing

In the exposition of the knowledge of reviewing, at the moment of the Path itself, the Path-factors (magganga) are first explained individually in the sense of cause. Then, factors that are Path-factors and factors that are not Path-factors are shown individually as Enlightenment-factors (bojjhanga) because they are parts (anga) of the Noble Disciple (ariya) who has gained the name 'Bodhi' in the sense of awakening. Indeed, the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, and concentration are Path-factors themselves. The enlightenment factors of joy, tranquility, and equanimity are not Path-factors. Again, among those factors pointed out individually by the power of the powers (bala) and by the power of the faculties (indriya), faith (saddhā) alone is not a Path-factor. Again, wishing to show the states arising at the moment of the Path by way of groups, he said "āဓိပတေယျဋ္ဌေန" (in the sense of predominance) and so forth. Among them, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) in the sense of establishing (upaṭṭhāna) means that a single mindfulness taking Nibbāna as its object is called the four foundations of mindfulness by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self in the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects. A single energy taking Nibbāna as its object is called the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning arisen unwholesome states, preventing unarisen unwholesome states, arising unarisen wholesome states, and maintaining arisen wholesome states.

Truths (sacca) in the sense of being real means the four Noble Truths in the sense of being unerring in the nature of suffering and so forth. At the moment of the Path, these very four truths are well-attained then in the sense of penetration (paṭivedha). Nibbāna, which is preached separately as "Nibbāna, the plunge into the deathless," and the remaining states are well-attained then in the sense of acquisition (paṭilābha). Because of the statement "Truths in the sense of being real are well-attained then," it should be concluded here that one definitely reviews the four truths at the conclusion of the Path and Fruition. Also, because of the word, "He understands: 'Done is what was to be done, there is no more for this state'" (Dīgha Nikāya 1.248), he reviews: "Suffering has been fully understood by me, the origin has been abandoned by me, cessation has been realized by me,"
262: "I have developed the Path"—this is indeed the teaching on the contemplation of the four truths. Such contemplation is also appropriate. In this context, "Origin" (Samudaya) should be understood only as the defilements to be abandoned by each respective Path. By the power of contemplating the Origin mentioned here, the Commentary states that the two kinds of contemplation of defilements, as well as the contemplation of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna, are explicitly included here. Only the contemplation of Suffering (Dukkha) is not specifically mentioned. Even if it is not mentioned, it should be taken as included due to the existence of the Pali text and logical consistency. For one practicing to penetrate the Truths, it is appropriate to contemplate one's own task performed once the penetration of the Truths is completed. ## "Tranquility in the sense of non-distraction" (avikkhepaṭṭhena samatho), etc., is said to show the states of tranquility and insight associated with the Path as having a single function and as not overstepping each other. "Purification of virtue in the sense of restraint" (saṃvaraṭṭhena sīlavisuddhi) refers to Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood. "Purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction" (avikkhepaṭṭhena cittavisuddhi) refers to Right Concentration. "Purification of view in the sense of seeing" (dassanaṭṭhena diṭṭhivisuddhi) refers to Right View. "In the sense of being liberated" (vimuttaṭṭhena) means liberation from the defilements to be abandoned by the Path through the power of eradication (samuccheda), or the sense of being intent upon Nibbāna as the object. "Deliverance" (vimokkha) is the Noble Path itself, which is deliverance through eradication. "Knowledge in the sense of penetration" (paṭivedhaṭṭhena vijjā) is Right View, which is knowledge in the sense of penetrating the Truths. "Liberation in the sense of relinquishment" (pariccāgaṭṭhena vimutti) is the Noble Path itself, which is liberation because of being freed from the defilements to be abandoned by the Path through relinquishing them. "Knowledge of destruction in the sense of eradication" (samucchedaṭṭhena khaye ñāṇaṃ) is Right View, which is the knowledge in the Noble Path that effects the destruction of defilements in the sense of eradicating them. ## Zeal (chanda) and so forth should be understood according to the method already mentioned below. However, here they are shown only at the moment of the Path in terms of the beginning, middle, and end of the Path. Here, "liberation" (vimutti) is the liberation of the Path itself. It should be understood that Nibbāna, though already taken in the phrase "Truth in the sense of reality" (tathaṭṭhena saccā), is mentioned again as "Nibbāna as the plunging into the Deathless" (amatogadhaṃ nibbānaṃ) to show it as the final goal. The same method applies to the moment of the Fruit. However, here "Path in the sense of cause" (hetuṭṭhena maggo) refers only to the state of the Path associated with the Fruit. "Right Efforts" (sammappadhāna) should be understood as being mentioned because the function of energy, which accomplishes the four tasks at the moment of the Path, is completed at the moment of the arising of the Fruit. Otherwise, Right Efforts cannot be obtained at the moment of the Fruit. Indeed, the Elder Mahāsāriputta, while extracting the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment at the moment of the Path, stated: "Excluding the four Right Efforts at the moment of the Fruit, the remaining thirty-three factors are obtained." Thus, the Truths and so forth should also be understood accordingly through the power of completing the task of penetration. "Deliverance" (vimokkha) is the deliverance of the Fruit. "Liberation" (vimutti) is the liberation of the Fruit. "Knowledge of non-arising in the sense of tranquilization" (paṭippassaddhaṭṭhena anuppāde ñāṇaṃ) has the meaning already stated. "Having emerged" (vuṭṭhahitvā) is said thus at the end of the Fruit because there is no emergence between the Path and the Fruit. (He contemplates:) "These states were well-produced at that time." This...
263: It should be understood that the connection is made by treating the word 'iti' as a remainder of the text, meaning: 'He reviews that these states of various kinds, such as the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), have arisen well at the moment of the Path and at the moment of Fruition.' ## The Exposition of the Description of the Knowledge of Reviewing is finished. ## 15. Exposition of the Description of the Knowledge of Diversity of Bases In the description of the knowledge of diversity of bases, 'he defines the eye as internal' (cakkhuṃ ajjhattaṃ vavattheti) means he defines the eye that is of an internal nature or that occurs within the internal continuity. The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, wishing to teach the manner in which that meditator defines the eye, asks, 'How does he define the eye as internal?' and then shows the manner of definition with the words starting with, 'He defines that the eye arises because of ignorance (avijjā).' Therein, ignorance and craving (taṇhā) are past and are supporting causes (upatthambhaka-hetu). Kamma is past and is the generative cause (janaka-hetu). Nutriment (āhāra) is the supporting cause in the present. By the statement that it arises because of nutriment, the temperature (utu) and consciousness (citta) that support the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) are also included. In the Pali 'catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya', the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. It means 'occurring depending on the four great elements'. By this, the state of the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) is shown, and the state of the composite eye (sasambhāra-cakkhu) is rejected. 'Uppannaṃ' (arisen) refers to the present eye in terms of a period (addhā), a continuity (santati), or a moment (khaṇa). 'Samudāgataṃ' means arisen from a cause. By this much, the definition of the eye in the preliminary stage of insight (vipassanā) is shown. Insight into impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is shown by the words starting with 'arisen without having been' (ahutvā sambhūtaṃ). It is called 'arisen without having been' because it did not exist before its arising (uppāda). It is called 'having been, it will not be' (hutvā na bhavissati) because it does not exist after its falling away (bhaṅga). 'Antavantato' means 'antavā' because it has an end (the moment of falling away). 'Antavā' is the same as 'antavanta'. As in the verse: 'The sage who is mindful, who has a destination, and who has steady energy...' Therefore, it means 'because it has an end' or 'because its falling away (bhaṅga) is evident'. 'Adhuvaṃ' (unstable) means not firm because it perishes at every moment and because of the absence of a permanent state. 'Asassataṃ' means not eternal. 'Vipariṇāmadhammaṃ' means having the nature of change in two ways: through aging (jarā) and through death (maraṇa). The passages starting with 'the eye is impermanent' (cakkhu aniccaṃ) and 'the eye as impermanent' (cakkhuṃ aniccato) have the meanings already stated. By the word 'mano' (mind), the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta) is intended here; therefore, the connection with 'arisen from ignorance' (avijjā-sambhūta), etc., is indeed appropriate. In the phrase 'arisen from nutriment' (āhāra-sambhūta), it should be understood in terms of associated contact-nutriment (phassāhāra) and mental-volition-nutriment (manosañcetanāhāra). 'Uppanno' (arisen) should also be understood in terms of period and continuity. ## The Exposition of the Description of the Knowledge of Diversity of Bases is finished.
264:
## 16. Gocaranānattañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the Description of the Knowledge of Diversity of Range (Gocaranānattañāṇaniddesa), the phrase "vavattheti bahiddhā rūpe" means that it delimits the phenomena of the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) which exist outside the internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana). The phrase beginning with "born of ignorance" (avijjāsambhūta) is spoken because it refers to kamma-born matter (kammajarūpa) included within the individual existence (attabhāva) of the visible-form base. In fact, edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) also assists kamma-born matter as a supporting condition (upatthambhaka-paccaya). Specifically, because the sound-base (saddāyatana) is produced only by temperature (utu) and consciousness (citta), the fourfold group starting with "born of ignorance" is not mentioned. Since tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba) are themselves great elements (mahābhūta), the term "dependent on the four great elements" (upādāya) is not used.

In this context of diversity of range, "dhammā" refers to the three immaterial aggregates—the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—which are associated with the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta); it also refers to subtle matter (sukhumatūpa) included in the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), and all kamma-produced visible forms and so forth. Alternatively, whatever visible forms and so forth arise from whatever causes such as kamma and consciousness, those respective mental and material phenomena produced by those respective causes should be understood. The reason is that if the meaning is taken in any other way, all phenomena such as visible forms included within one's own continuity would not be encompassed by the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) as being produced by the four causes.

Since phenomena such as visible forms not bound to the faculties (anindriyabaddha) are also suitable for insight meditation, they should be understood as being included by the term "kamma-produced" (kammasambhūta). Indeed, those material phenomena are also produced by temperature (utu) which has kamma common to all beings as its root. Other teachers, however, say that "visible forms and so forth not bound to the faculties are not suitable for insight meditation." The words of those teachers contradict the Pali such as:

"When one sees with the wisdom of insight that all formations are impermanent,
then one becomes weary of suffering;
this is the path to purity."

It is also stated in the Visuddhimagga Commentary: "In this Dispensation, a certain person adverts to and contemplates internal formations (ajjhatta-saṅkhāra) with insight from the beginning. However, since the emergence of the Path (maggavuṭṭhāna) cannot occur by the mere seeing of purely internal formations, and external formations must also be seen, one therefore contemplates with insight the aggregates of others and also non-clung-to formations (anupādinnasaṅkhāra) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self." Therefore, the delimiting of others' eyes and so forth, and the delimiting of visible forms and so forth not bound to the faculties, is certainly desired. Thus, there are no formations of the three planes (tebhūmaka-saṅkhāra) that are unsuitable for insight meditation.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Diversity of Range is finished.

## 17. Cariyānānattañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the Description of the Knowledge of Diversity of Behavior (Cariyānānattañāṇaniddesa), among the Pali terms such as "viññāṇacariyā," it is called "cariyā" (behavior/conduct) because it occurs in an object. Consciousness (viññāṇa) itself, specifically the eighteen rootless consciousnesses, is called "viññāṇacariyā" because it occurs in an object. Because of delusion...
265:
...occurring because of delusion, or occurring through delusion, or occurring in an unknown object, or the occurrence of ignorance is called "aññāṇacariyā" (behavior of ignorance). Wisdom itself being the occurrence, or occurrence because of wisdom, or occurring by means of wisdom, or occurring in a known object, or the occurrence of knowledge is called "ñāṇacariyā" (behavior of knowledge). "Dassanatthāya" means occurring for the purpose of seeing visible forms (referring to the adverting consciousness). "Āvajjana-kiriyā-byākatā" is called "āvajjana" (adverting) because it turns the mental continuum toward the visible object after departing from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) flow; it is called "kiriyā" (functional) because it is a mere action without resultant (vipāka) effect; it is called "abyākata" (indeterminate) because it is not declared as wholesome or unwholesome. "Dassanaṭṭho" is called "dassana" (seeing) because one sees with that eye-consciousness, or it sees by itself, or it is the mere act of seeing; since that nature of seeing is itself the sense, it is called "dassanaṭṭho."

Eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) is either wholesome-resultant or unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness. "Diṭṭhattā" means because the visible object has been seen by eye-consciousness, for receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) cannot exist for an object not yet seen. "Abhiniropanā vipāka-manodhātu" is called "abhiniropanā" because it ascends to (accepts) only the seen object; it is the receiving mind-element (sampaṭicchana-manodhātu) which is the resultant of both (wholesome and unwholesome). "Abhiniropitattā" means because of the state of having ascended to the visible object. "Vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu" is the investigating mind-consciousness element (santīraṇa-manoviññāṇadhātu) which is the resultant of both. This same method should be understood for the ear-door and so forth.

Although the determining consciousness (votthabbana) which occurs immediately after investigation (santīraṇa) is not mentioned in the Pali, it should be taken as obtainable because the teachers of the Commentaries have mentioned it. "Vijānanatthāya" means for the purpose of cognizing mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) as well as objects such as visible forms. "Āvajjana-kiriyā-byākatā" refers to the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana). "Vijānanaṭṭho" means the sense is the mere cognizing of the object by way of the impulsion (javana) that occurs immediately after that adverting; it is nothing else. Since unwholesome impulsions, and the impulsions of insight, the Path, and Fruition are mentioned separately above, the remaining impulsions should be taken here. However, according to the statement "viññāṇacariyā behaves dissociated from wholesome kamma," only the smile-producing impulsion (hasituppāda-javana) should be taken. Since only rootless consciousnesses (ahetuka-citta) are mentioned in the six doors, the eighteen rootless consciousnesses—namely, 2 advertings, 10 fivefold-sense-consciousnesses, 2 receivings, 3 investigatings, and 1 smile-producing consciousness—should be understood as "viññāṇacariyā."

Now, to show how it is called "viññāṇacariyā" in the sense of mere cognizing of the object, the text says "nīrāgā carati" (it behaves free from lust) and so forth. In truth, consciousness reaches a different state when associated with lust and so forth, or when associated with faith and so forth. In the absence of those lust, faith, etc., it remains in its own original state. Therefore, by the words "nīrāgā" and so forth, the text shows only the mere function of consciousness of those aforementioned consciousnesses. It is called "nīrāgā" because there is no lust in this consciousness-behavior. Some also read it as "nirāgā" by shortening the vowel.
266:
That state is called lust (rāga) by virtue of attachment. In other states, it is called hatred (dosa) by virtue of corruption. It is called delusion (moha) by virtue of bewilderment. It is called conceit (māna) by virtue of the assumption 'I am superior.' It is called wrong view (diṭṭhi) by virtue of distorted seeing. Restlessness (uddhacca) is the state of being distracted or unpeaceful. Doubt (vicikicchā) has the meaning already stated. They are called latent tendencies (anusaya) because they tend to arise when suitable conditions are met. Although it should be said as 'niranusaya,' it is stated as 'nānusaya'; the meaning is the same. In this conduct of consciousness (viññāṇacariyā), only the absence of defilements that have reached the state of non-destruction should be understood. It is not that only the viññāṇacariyā of the Arahants, who have abandoned latent tendencies, is taught. Because that viññāṇacariyā which is named 'lust-free' (nīrāga) and so on is indeed dissociated from lust and so forth, the phrase 'dissociated from lust' (rāgavippayutta) and so on is spoken to show another method of exposition. Again, to show dissociation from other states, the phrase 'with wholesome actions' (kusalehi kammehi) and so on is spoken. Only wholesome states are called 'faultless' (anavajja) because of the absence of faults such as lust. They are called 'bright' (sukka) because they are associated with shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), which produce purity. They are called 'resulting in happiness' (sukkhudraya) because they are pleasant in their occurrence or because they have happy results. Unwholesome states should be applied by the opposite of the stated meaning.

An object known by consciousness is called 'the known' (viññāta); it occurs in that known object. What does this mean? Just as a cloth is called 'blue cloth' due to its association with the color blue, the known object is called 'consciousness' (viññāṇa) due to its association with consciousness; because it occurs in that consciousness, it is called 'conduct of consciousness' (viññāṇacariyā). It means that the occurrence of consciousness in such a manner is called viññāṇacariyā. Although it is spoken of as 'the conduct of consciousness' by way of conventional usage, there is no conduct separate from consciousness. This mind is pure by nature because of the absence of defilements such as lust. Therefore, because the mere act of cognizing is the conduct, it is called viññāṇacariyā. There is also a variant reading 'nikklesaṭṭhena'.

In the conduct of ignorance (aññāṇacariyā), 'manāpiyesu' means they enter the mind or please the mind, or they increase and gladden the mind, thus they are 'manāpa'; 'manāpa' itself is 'manāpiya.' In those pleasant objects. Whether those objects are desirable (iṭṭha) or undesirable (aniṭṭha), they are called pleasant (manāpiya) by way of the manner in which they are taken. Lust does not arise only in desirable objects, nor does hatred arise only in undesirable objects. It occurs for the sake of the impulsion (javana) of lust in a continuous sequence. It is the functional indeterminate mind-element (āvajjanakiriyābyākata manodhātu) which is the unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) at the eye-door. The impulsion of lust means generally...
267:
The occurrence of lust (rāga) generally happens seven times. It is indeed lust (or the consciousness-arising dominated by lust) occurring repeatedly. 'Conduct of ignorance' (aññāṇacariyā) means the conduct of lust through ignorance, because lust arises due to ignorance. The same method applies to the remaining terms such as the conduct of ignorance in painful feeling. 'In an object not looked upon with equanimity by both' (tadubhayena asamapekkhanasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ) means in an object known as a visible form that is devoid of looking with equanimity due to lust and hatred. 'For the sake of the impulsion of delusion' (mohassa javanatthāya) means for the sake of the impulsion (occurrence) of delusion by way of doubt and restlessness. 'Conduct of ignorance' (aññāṇacariyā) is the conduct of ignorance itself, not of anything else.

The terms 'vinibandha' and so on are words describing the nature of conceit and so forth. Among them, 'vinibandha' refers to the state of conceit that stands bound by way of haughtiness (unnati). 'Parāmaṭṭha' refers to the state of wrong view that, having bypassed the impermanent nature of form and so on, wrongly touches upon and clings to it as permanent and so on. 'Vikkhepagata' refers to the state of restlessness (uddhacca) that has reached a state of distraction regarding the visible object. 'Aniṭṭhaṅgata' refers to the state of doubt (vicikicchā) that has reached a state of indecision. 'Thāmagata' refers to the state of latent tendencies (anusaya) that have reached strength. 'In states' (dhammesu) means in objects such as visible forms or in states that have become mental objects.

Since lust and so forth occur because of ignorance, the Buddha said 'one conducts oneself with lust' (sarāgā carati) and so on, wishing to specify ignorance through its association with lust and so forth. In that text, 'one conducts oneself with lust' (sarāgā carati) should be understood as the conduct by way of the impulsions of delusion, conceit, wrong view, the latent tendency of conceit, the latent tendency of wrong view, and the latent tendency of ignorance. 'One conducts oneself with hatred' (sadosā carati) is understood by way of the impulsions of delusion and the latent tendency of ignorance. 'One conducts oneself with delusion' (samohā carati) is understood by way of the impulsions of lust, hatred, conceit, wrong view, restlessness, doubt, and latent tendencies. 'One conducts oneself with conceit' (samānā carati) is understood by way of the impulsions of lust, delusion, the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of lust for existence, and the latent tendency of ignorance. 'One conducts oneself with wrong view' (sadiṭṭhi carati) is understood by way of the impulsions of lust, delusion, the latent tendency of sensual lust, and the latent tendency of ignorance. 'One conducts oneself with restlessness' (sa-uddhaccā carati) and 'one conducts oneself with doubt' (savicikicchā carati) are understood by way of the impulsions of delusion and the latent tendency of ignorance. In the phrase 'one conducts oneself with latent tendencies' (sānusayā carati), following the method already stated, one should apply the state of being with latent tendencies by making each latent tendency the root and considering the remaining latent tendencies found in that consciousness.

Terms like 'associated with lust' (rāgasampayuttā) are merely synonyms (vevacana) for 'with lust' (sarāgā) and so on. That very conduct receives names like 'with lust' (sarāgā) because it occurs together with lust and so forth by way of association. It receives names like 'associated with lust' (rāgasampayuttāni) because it is associated with lust and so forth in ways such as arising together (ekuppāda), ceasing together (ekanirodha), having the same physical base (ekavatthu), and having the same object (ekārammaṇa). Furthermore, to show that this very conduct of ignorance is called 'conduct of ignorance' because it is dissociated from wholesome actions and associated with unwholesome actions, the Buddha said 'with wholesome actions' (kusalehi kammehi) and so on. In that text, 'in the unknown' (aññāte) means in an object not known according to its true nature, because ignorance has the characteristic of not knowing. The remaining meanings are just as already stated.
268:
In the conduct of knowledge (ñāṇacariya), because there is no functional indeterminate (kiriya-abyākata) state known as mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjanā) which is the immediately preceding condition for insight into turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā) and so forth, the functional indeterminate advertence is not mentioned for the sake of that insight into turning away, but only insight into turning away and so forth are mentioned. Advertence (āvajjanā) occurs only for the sake of conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) [preliminary, access, conformity]; from that conformity, the path and fruition of insight into turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā-magga-phala) [change-of-lineage, path, fruition] arise. Here, regarding the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), both the fruition arising immediately after the path and the fruition arising at a different time of attainment are intended.

In the phrases such as "he wanders free from lust" (nīrāgā carati), the state of being free from lust should be understood by way of opposition to lust and so forth. In the conduct of consciousness (viññāṇacariya), the state of being free from lust is understood in the sense of the mere absence of lust and so forth. "In the known" (ñāte) means occurring in an object known according to its true nature. By the words "consciousness-conduct is another" (aññā viññāṇacariya) and so forth, the non-mixture of the three types of conduct with one another is shown.

The arising of rootless consciousness (ahetuka-citta) by way of the mere function of consciousness is called consciousness-conduct (viññāṇacariya). Only by way of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses which have the function of ignorance is it called ignorance-conduct (aññāṇacariya). Especially by way of insight, path, and fruition, which perform the function of knowledge, it is called knowledge-conduct (ñāṇacariya). Thus, these three types of conduct are not mixed with one another. It should be understood that, setting aside insight, the functional, wholesome, and resultant states of the sense sphere with roots (sahetuka-kāmāvacara-kiriya-kusala-vipāka), and the wholesome and indeterminate states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpāvacara-arūpāvacara-kusala-abyākata), are liberated from these three types of conduct. Since insight into turning away having Nibbāna as its object is shown in knowledge-conduct, the reviewing knowledges (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) of trainees (sekha) and non-trainees (asekha) which review Nibbāna, the path, and fruition should also be understood as being included in knowledge-conduct. This is because those reviewing knowledges also especially perform the function of knowledge.

## The Explanation of the Niddesa on the Diversity of Conduct Knowledge is finished.

## 18. Explanation of the Niddesa on the Diversity of Planes

In the Niddesa on the Diversity of Planes, "planes" (bhūmi) means parts or divisions. In the term "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara), sense-desire (kāma) is twofold: sensuality as defilement (kilesakāma) and sensuality as objective base (vatthukāma). Lustful desire (chandarāga) is called sensuality as defilement; the round of existence (vaṭṭa) revolving in the three planes is called sensuality as objective base. Sensuality as defilement is called kāma because it desires; sensuality as objective base is called kāma because it is desired. That twofold sense-desire, by way of occurrence, frequents a certain place; because the two types of sense-desire frequent that place, it is called "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara). That place, by way of the four states of deprivation, the human world, and the six deva worlds...
269:
...is of eleven kinds. Just as a place where hunters with weapons frequent is called "the sphere of those with weapons" (sasatthāvacara), even though other two-footed and four-footed creatures also frequent there, because it is characterized by those hunters; in the same way, even though other states such as those of the fine-material sphere frequent those eleven places, this place is called only "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) because it is characterized by those sense-sphere states. That term "sense-sphere", just as the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) is called "fine-material" (rūpa), is also called "sense-desire" (kāma) by dropping the latter word (avacara). Each state connected with that sense-desire is called "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) because it frequents this sense-desire known as the elevenfold place.

Indeed, although some of these sense-sphere states also frequent the fine-material and immaterial existences, just as a noble elephant that has gained the name "war-sphere elephant" (saṅgāmāvacara) because of frequenting the battlefield is called "war-sphere" even when wandering in the city; and just as land and water creatures are called "land-frequenting" and "water-frequenting" even when staying in places that are not land or water; so too, it should be understood that those states are "sense-sphere" even when frequenting other planes. Alternatively, they are "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacarā) because sense-desire (kilesakāma) frequents these aforementioned states by way of making them an object. Although this sense-desire also frequents fine-material and immaterial states, just as when it is said, "it is called a calf (vaccha) because it lows, it is called a buffalo (mahiṃsa) because it lies on the earth", those names do not apply to every creature that lows or every creature that lies on the earth; thus the fulfillment of this analogy should be understood. Here, having grouped all those sense-sphere states together, the feminine gender "kāmāvacarā" is used in consideration of the word "plane" (bhūmi) which will be mentioned. In terms like "fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacara), fine-material existence is called "fine-material" (rūpa); they are called "fine-material sphere" because they frequent that fine-material realm. Immaterial existence is called "immaterial" (arūpa); they are called "immaterial sphere" because they frequent that immaterial realm. They are called "included" (pariyāpanna) because they are contained within the round of the three planes; they are called "unincluded" (apariyāpanna) because they are not contained within that round.

In the Niddesas of the planes such as the sense-sphere, "from below" (heṭṭhato) means by way of the lower part. "Avīci hell" (avīcinirayaṃ)—here, it is called "Avīci" because there is no gap or interval (vīci) between the flames, or the beings, or the feelings. It is called "Niraya" because there is no happiness (aya); it is also called "Niraya" in the sense of being devoid of delight. "Making it the limit" (pariyantaṃ karitvā) means making that hell known as Avīci the end. "From above" (uparito) means by way of the upper part. "The devas who wield power over the creations of others" (paranimmitavasavattī deve) refers to the devas who have gained this name because they exercise control over the sense-pleasures created by others. "Making it the interior" (anto karitvā) means including it within. "Whatever is in this interval" (yaṃ etasmiṃ antare) means whatever states exist in this space. In the word "yaṃ", the gender and number have been changed. By this Pali "frequenting here" (etthāvacarā), since other (fine-material/immaterial) states may also occasionally arise in that interval, the word "frequenting" (avacarā) is used to exclude those states. Therefore, those states that arise by being immersed in this interval are counted because they should occur at all times in the entire sense-sphere, and because of the arising of primary and derived matter (bhūtarūpa-upādārūpa) even below the Avīci hell. Because those states arise by being immersed, they are called "frequenting" (avacarā). Because those states also arise below the Avīci hell, they are called "frequenting" (avacarā). Again, by this Pali "included here" (ettha pariyāpanna)...
270:
Because they can occur at all times, and because they exist below the Avīci hell starting from the arising of the primary elements and derived matter (bhūta-upādāya), these states are included in the count. They are called 'avacara' (sphere) because they enter and frequent [these realms], and because they frequent the lower parts. In this context, by the term 'included' (pariyāpanna)—since these sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states also frequent other planes but are not included in them, they are included [here] even when frequenting other planes.

Now, wishing to show these states included in the sense-sphere in terms of aggregates (khandha) as a group, elements (dhātu) as void, and bases (āyatana) as causes, etc., he said 'khandha-dhātu-āyatanā', etc. 'Brahmaloka' refers to the abode of Brahmas, known as the plane of the first jhāna. 'Akaniṭṭha' refers to those Brahmas who are not 'junior' (kaniṭṭha) because of their supreme status. By the word 'samāpannassa', he refers to the wholesome jhāna (kusala-jhāna) of one who has attained meditative attainment. By the word 'upapannassa', he refers to the resultant jhāna (vipāka-jhāna) of one who is reborn in the Brahma world by the power of resultants. 'Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa' means dwelling happily in the present visible state of existence is 'diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra'; one who has such a habit is an Arahant; [it refers to] that Arahant. By this word, the functional jhāna (kiriya-jhāna) is mentioned. 'Cetasikā' means states arising in the mind, meaning they are associated with the mind (cittasampayutta). 'Ākāsānañcāyatanūpage' refers to one who has reached the state of existence known as the sphere of infinite space. The same method applies to the second term. 'Maggā' refers to the four noble paths. 'Maggaphalāni' refers to the four noble fruits. 'Asaṅkhatā ca dhātu' is the element of Nibbāna, which is not conditioned by causes.

The other four planes should also be understood by way of each set of four (catukka). 'Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā' are the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of mental objects. Its meaning: it is called 'paṭṭhāna' because it stands firm; it is called 'upaṭṭhāna' because it occurs by entering and appearing clearly in the object. Mindfulness itself is the foundation, thus 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Alternatively, 'sati' in the sense of remembering, and 'paṭṭhāna' in the sense of appearing; it is 'satipaṭṭhāna' because it is both mindfulness and appearance. They are called 'satipaṭṭhānā' (plural) because those mindfulnesses are many by way of objects. 'Cattāro sammappadhānā' are the efforts to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to arouse unarisen wholesome states, and to maintain arisen wholesome states. It is called 'padhāna' because one strives or exerts by means of this; it is a name for energy (vīriya).
271:
(Padhāna is) a name for energy (vīriya). 'Sammappadhāna' means right exertion, causal exertion, exertion by means of skillful means, and wise exertion. A single energy (vīriya) is divided into four by way of function and called 'sammappadhānā'.

The four bases of power (iddhipāda) are the base of power of desire (chandiddhipāda), the base of power of consciousness (cittiddhipāda), the base of power of energy (vīriyiddhipāda), and the base of power of investigation (vīmaṃsiddhipāda). Their meaning has already been stated.

The four jhānas are: the first jhāna with five factors by way of initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā); the second jhāna with three factors by way of zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; the third jhāna with two factors by way of happiness and one-pointedness of mind; and the fourth jhāna with two factors by way of equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind. These factors are called 'jhāna' in the sense of closely contemplating the object.

The four illimitables (appamaññā) are loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā). They are called 'appamaññā' because of the limitlessness of the object to be pervaded. These states pervade limitless beings by way of the object, or they pervade even a single being by way of pervading without remainder; thus they are called 'appamaññā' by way of the limitless nature of pervasion.

The four formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti) are the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) have the meanings already stated.

The four modes of progress (paṭipadā) are those taught as: 'painful progress with slow intuition, painful progress with swift intuition, pleasant progress with slow intuition, and pleasant progress with swift intuition'.

The four objects (ārammaṇa) are those taught as: a limited state with a limited object, a limited state with a limitless object, a limitless state with a limited object, and a limitless state with a limitless object. It should be understood that jhānas possessing objects are mentioned (as objects) because objects such as kasinas are not to be delimited.

The four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa): Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Tathāgata are called 'ariyas'; the lineages, traditions, and heritages of those ariyas are 'ariyavaṃsa'. What are they? These four: contentment with robes, contentment with alms-food, contentment with lodgings, and delight in meditation (bhāvanā). Contentment with medicinal requisites is already included when contentment with alms-food is mentioned. For how could one who is content with alms-food be discontent with medicinal requisites?

The four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) are the four causes for winning over people: giving (dāna), endearing speech (peyyavajja), beneficial conduct (atthacariyā), and impartiality (samānattatā). 'Dāna' means giving as is appropriate. 'Peyyavajja' means endearing speech as is appropriate. 'Atthacariyā' means performing what should be done in various matters, and acting for growth by way of instructing on what should and should not be done.
272:
Samānattatā (commonality) refers to the meaning of having a common measure or calculation along with pride (māna). It is called samānatta because by this quality, one treats the self of another as equal to one's own. The state of being samānatta is samānattatā. It means behaving appropriately toward others after distinguishing, "This person is inferior to me, this person is equal to me, this person is superior to me." They also say, "Experiencing happiness and suffering together is samānattatā."

In the phrase cattāri cakkāni (four wheels), there are five kinds of wheels (cakka): the wooden wheel, the gem wheel, the wheel of Dhamma, the wheel of postures, and the wheel of prosperity. Among these, "O Great King, the wheel that was finished in six months minus six nights" refers to the wooden wheel. "The one turning the gem wheel, having surveyed (the land)" refers to the gem wheel. "I have set the wheel of Dhamma in motion" refers to the wheel of Dhamma. "Having four wheels and nine doors" refers to the wheel of postures. "Monks, these are the four wheels; for the devas and humans who are endowed with these four wheels, the four wheels turn. What are the four? Living in a suitable region, relying on good people, right self-direction, and having performed merit in the past" refers to the wheel of prosperity. In this context, it is this wheel of prosperity that is intended.

Among those four, living in a suitable region (patirūpadesavāsa) means living in a place where the four assemblies are clearly present and which is appropriate. Relying on good people (sappurisāvassaya) means relying on, serving, and associating with good people such as the Buddha. Right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) means establishing oneself rightly. If one was previously endowed with lack of faith and so on, it means abandoning those and establishing oneself in faith and so on. Having performed merit in the past (pubbe ca katapuññatā) means having wholesome merit accumulated in previous lives. Among these four, only this merit performed in the past is the primary factor (pamāṇa). This is because when a wholesome deed is performed with a mind associated with knowledge, that very merit leads that person to a suitable region, causes them to associate with good people, and that person can also establish themselves rightly.

Cattāri dhammapadāni refers to the four groups of Dhamma. What are the four? They are the factor of Dhamma of non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), the factor of Dhamma of non-ill will (abyāpāda), the factor of Dhamma of right mindfulness (sammāsati), and the factor of Dhamma of right concentration (sammāsamādhi). The factor of Dhamma of non-covetousness refers to non-greed, or the jhānas, insight, paths, fruits, and Nibbāna attained through the power of non-covetousness. The factor of Dhamma of non-ill will refers to non-anger, or the jhānas and so on attained based on loving-kindness (mettā). The factor of Dhamma of right mindfulness refers to well-established mindfulness, or the jhānas and so on attained based on mindfulness. The factor of Dhamma of right concentration refers to the eight attainments, or the jhānas and so on attained based on the eight attainments. Alternatively, the jhānas and so on attained through the power of the ten foul objects (asubha) are the factor of Dhamma of non-covetousness; those through the power of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra)...
273:
...attained through the power of the four divine abodes are the factor of Dhamma of non-ill will. The states attained through the power of the ten recollections (anussati) and the perception of the repulsiveness of food (āhārepaṭikūlasaññā) are the factor of Dhamma of right mindfulness. The states attained through the power of the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) are the factor of Dhamma of right concentration. The phrase "these four planes" (imā catasso bhūmiyo) should be applied according to each set of four.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Diversity of Planes is finished.

## 19. Explanation of the Knowledge of Diversity of Phenomena (Dhammanānattañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā)

In the explanation of the knowledge of diversity of phenomena, "kammapatha" (courses of action) means they are both actions and the paths for going to the lower realms; thus they are called kammapatha. Among those courses of action, the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) are: the three bodily good conducts, namely, abstinence from killing, abstinence from stealing, and abstinence from sexual misconduct; the four verbal good conducts, namely, abstinence from lying, abstinence from divisive speech, abstinence from harsh speech, and abstinence from idle chatter; and the three mental good conducts, namely, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view. The ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha) are: the three bodily misconducts, namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the four verbal misconducts, namely, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter; and the three mental misconducts, namely, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. Only the wholesome and unwholesome volitions (cetanā) that produce rebirth are called "kammapatha." Other actions such as drinking intoxicants, which remain after the aforementioned courses of action, and the volitions that are the abstinence from those actions, are not called "kammapatha" because they do not definitely produce rebirth. It should be understood that by taking the gross wholesome and unwholesome actions, the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states are also included.

"Rūpa" (matter) refers to the twenty-eight kinds of matter categorized as primary elements and derived matter. "Vipāka" (resultant) refers to the twenty-three kinds of resultant consciousness by way of the sixteen wholesome resultants of the sense sphere and the seven unwholesome resultants. "Kiriya" (functional) refers to the eleven kinds of functional consciousness of the sense sphere by way of the three rootless functional states and the eight functional states with roots. They are called "kiriya" because they are merely active and do not have the capacity to produce results. By this sequence of words, only the sense-sphere phenomena are spoken of by way of indeterminate matter, indeterminate resultants, and indeterminate functional states.

"Idhaṭṭhassa" refers to a person staying in this human world. It is spoken in terms of the human world because jhāna meditation mostly arises in the human world. In truth, however, jhānas can sometimes be found in the deva worlds as well. In the fine-material Brahma worlds, they can be found by way of jhānas that produce rebirth in one's own plane, lower planes, or higher planes. However, in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) and the immaterial planes (Arūpāvacara), there are no jhānas that produce rebirth in lower planes.
274:
There is no jhāna that leads to rebirth in a lower realm. Those who have not developed jhāna in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), if they are to be reborn in a lower realm, are reborn only in the happy destinations of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara sugati), not in the states of deprivation (duggati). The term 'tatrūpappannassa' refers to the four resultant jhānas occurring by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti) for one who is reborn in the Brahma-world through the power of resultants (vipāka). Although the functional indeterminates (kiriya-abyākata) in the fine-material and immaterial jhāna attainments are not explicitly mentioned, it should be understood that because their mode of occurrence is the same as the wholesome (kusala), when the wholesome is mentioned, the functional is also mentioned. Just as in the Paṭṭhāna, by taking wholesome impulsion (kusala-javana) in the statement 'When the wholesome and unwholesome cease, the resultant registration (tadārammaṇa) arises,' functional impulsion (kiriya-javana) is also included; so should it be understood here as well. 'Sāmaññaphala' refers to the four fruits of recluseship. By this, the supramundane resultant indeterminate (lokuttara-vipāka-abyākata) is spoken of. 'Nibbāna' refers to the indeterminate Nibbāna.

'Pāmojjamūlakā' means those states that have gladness (pāmojja) as their root or beginning; thus they are called 'pāmojjamūlakā,' meaning the states beginning with gladness. In fact, they only occur together with gladness. In the context of 'gladness arises for one who attends to impermanence,' gladness arises only for one who attends wisely (yoniso), not for one who attends unwisely (ayoniso). For one who attends unwisely, even the arising of the wholesome does not exist, let alone insight (vipassanā). Why is it mentioned by its own form? It is to show the strength of gladness. Indeed, when gladness is absent, dissatisfaction (arati) or boredom arises in secluded dwellings and in the higher wholesome states. When this happens, one withdraws from meditation (bhāvanā). But when gladness is present, because of the absence of dissatisfaction, one reaches the fulfillment of meditation. To show how wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is of great help to meditation as a root, the group of nine (navaka) will be mentioned later.

'Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, one attains rapture and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know it.' (Dhammapada 374) —
According to these words, gladness having insight as its cause arises for the practitioner of insight. Here, however, gladness having comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana) as its cause should be taken. The state of one who is joyful is gladness (pāmojja); it is weak rapture (pīti). The prefix 'pa-' should be understood in the sense of beginning. 'Pamuditassa' means for one who is joyful or satisfied with that gladness. There is also a reading 'pamoditassa,' which has the same meaning. 'Pīti' refers to strong rapture. 'Pītimanassa' means for one whose mind is associated with rapture. The word 'yutta' (associated) should be understood as elided, as in the word 'assaratha' (a horse-drawn chariot). 'Kāya' refers to the mental body (nāmakāya), or the mental body together with the physical body (rūpakāya). 'Passambhati' means the distress is calmed.
275:
'Passaddhakāya' refers to one who has a tranquil body because of being endowed with both kinds of tranquility (tranquility of the mental body and tranquility of consciousness). 'Sukhaṃ vedeti' means experiencing mental happiness, or experiencing mental happiness along with physical happiness. 'Sukhino' refers to a person endowed with happiness. 'Cittaṃ samādhiyati' means the mind is placed evenly on the object; it becomes one-pointed. The phrase 'samāhite citte' is a locative case (bhumma-vacana) in the sense of a characteristic action (bhāvena bhāva-lakkhaṇa). This is because knowing things as they really are is characterized by the state of the mind being concentrated. 'Yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti' means knowing formations (saṅkhāra) truly according to their nature through the power of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) and so forth. 'Passati' means seeing with the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu), making it as clear as if seeing with the physical eye. 'Nibbindati' means becoming weary of formations because of being endowed with the nine types of insight knowledge. 'Nibbindaṃ virajjati' means the practitioner, bringing that insight to its peak, becomes dispassionate toward formations because of being endowed with the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa). 'Virāgā vimuccati' means being liberated through the liberation of the fruit (phala-vimutti) caused by the path called dispassion (virāga), by way of decision (adhimokkha) in Nibbāna.

In some versions of the text, the method of the Truths is written in this section as: 'With a concentrated mind, one truly knows: This is suffering,' and so on. Furthermore, in some texts, it is written in the manner: 'One wisely attends: This is suffering,' and so on. In both versions, there is a difference only in phrasing (byañjana), not in meaning (attha). Since 'nibbindaṃ virajjati' is spoken of as the knowledge of the path, when the knowledge of the path is accomplished, the task of realizing the Four Noble Truths is also accomplished. Therefore, the section taught by way of the Four Noble Truths is not different in meaning from this section.

Now, because it was previously stated as 'impermanent' (anicca) etc., without specifying the object, he says 'rūpaṃ aniccato manasi karoti' (one attends to form as impermanent) etc., wishing to specify the object. 'Yonisomanasikāramūlakā' means those states have wise attention as their root and foundation. Indeed, without wise attention, the nine states beginning with gladness (pāmojja) do not occur. 'Samāhitena cittena' means by means of the mind which is the cause. 'Yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti' means knowing with wisdom. In the statement 'One wisely attends: This is suffering,' the realization of the Truths in the preliminary stage through hearing from the virtuous (anussava) is also included. 'Yoniso manasikāra' means attending by way of the right means.

'Dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānattaṃ' means that depending on the diversity of elements such as the eye-element, the diversity of contact such as eye-contact arises. 'Phassanānattaṃ paṭicca' means depending on the diversity of contact such as eye-contact. 'Vedanānānattaṃ' refers to the diversity of feelings born of eye-contact and so forth. 'Saññānānattaṃ' refers to the diversity of perceptions such as the perception of sense-desire. 'Saṅkappanānattaṃ' refers to the diversity of thoughts such as the thought of sense-desire. 'Chandanānattaṃ' means that because of the diversity of thoughts, there is desire for forms, desire for sounds, and so forth.
276:
In this way, various kinds of desire arise. 'Various kinds of fever' means that due to the diversity of desire, various kinds of fever such as fever for forms and fever for sounds arise. 'Various kinds of seeking' means that due to the diversity of fever, various kinds of seeking such as seeking for forms arise. 'Various kinds of gain' means that due to the diversity of seeking, various kinds of gain such as the acquisition of forms arise.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Diversity of Phenomena is finished.

## 20-24. Explanation of the Fivefold Knowledge

In the explanation of the fivefold knowledge, because those five knowledges are connected in sequence, the questions and answers are presented together. 'They are fully known (abhiññātā)' means they are well-known by way of knowing the individual characteristics of the nature of phenomena. 'They are known (ñātā)' means they are called 'known' because they are known according to their nature by way of the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). The knowledge by which those phenomena are known is connected as 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing, and as 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of knowing in various ways. In this same way, the remaining knowledges should also be applied. 'They are comprehended (pariññātā)' means they are known all around by way of general characteristics. 'They are judged (tīritā)' means they are investigated and completed as impermanent, etc., by way of the full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā). 'They are abandoned (pahīnā)' means that by knowledge such as the contemplation of impermanence, the perception of permanence, etc., are abandoned starting from the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā). 'They are relinquished (pariccattā)' means they are discarded by the power of abandonment itself. 'They are developed (bhāvitā)' means they are increased and cultivated all around. 'They are of a single flavor (ekarasa)' means they have a single function by abandoning the opposition to the accomplishment of their own task; or, they are of a single flavor by the flavor of liberation (vimuttirasa) through the power of liberation from opposing factors. 'They are realized (sacchikatā)' means the fruit (phala) is realized by way of acquisition, and the state of Nibbāna is realized by way of penetration. 'They are touched (phassitā)' means they are touched and experienced through the touch of acquisition and the touch of penetration. These five knowledges were previously taught by way of knowledge consisting in what is heard (sutamayañāṇa); here, however, they are taught by way of accomplishing their own task.

## The Explanation of the Fivefold Knowledge is finished.

## 25-28. Explanation of the Knowledge of Analytical Insight

In the explanation of the knowledge of analytical insight, since it is not possible to speak of the function of phenomena without having taught the phenomena themselves, the phenomena are first described without following the order of the summary.
277:
The meaning of 'phenomena' (dhamma) and so forth has already been stated. Having taught the phenomena included under the term 'dhamma' with such words as 'the faculty of faith is a phenomenon,' the Teacher said, 'The other faculty of faith is a phenomenon,' and so on, wishing to show the meaning of the word 'diversity' (nānatta). When it is said 'another phenomenon,' the diversity (nānatta) of phenomena is shown. 'Penetrated' (paṭividita) means things that are known and evident by being present. By this, the meaning of the term 'analytical insight' (paṭisambhidā) is stated. With the words 'the meaning is the sense of decision (adhimokkhaṭṭha),' etc., it is shown that the function of faith and so forth, such as decision (adhimuccana), is called 'meaning' (attha). 'To demonstrate' (sandassetuṃ) means for one who wishes to make another know, to show it to another. However, it is also obtained for one who is listening to the words of another. Phrasing (vyañjana), language (nirutti), and description (abhilāpa) are name-phrasing, name-language, and name-description.
