Because a name makes the meaning evident (vyañjayati), it is called 'phrasing' (vyañjana). 'Monks, they are called formations (saṅkhāra) because they form what is formed'; because it is stated thus with its cause after making a definition (niddhāraṇa), it is called 'language' (nirutti). Because the meaning is described by this word, it is called 'description' (abhilāpa).

That name is of four kinds: general name (sāmaññanāma), qualitative name (guṇanāma), given name (kittimanāma), and primordial name (opapātikanāma). Among these four, the name of the king 'Mahāsammata' is a general name because it was established by the agreement of the people at the beginning of the aeon. Referring to that general name, it was said: 'Vāseṭṭha, because he is agreed upon by the great multitude of people, the first designation "Mahāsammata, Mahāsammata" arose.' Names derived from qualities such as 'Dhamma-teacher (dhammakathika), rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), bearer of the Vinaya (vinayadhara), bearer of the Tipitaka (tipiṭakadhara), faithful (saddha), mindful (sata)' are qualitative names. The many hundreds of names of the Tathāgata, such as 'Blessed One (bhagavā), Worthy One (arahaṃ), Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddho),' are also qualitative names. Therefore, it is said:

'The names of the Great Sage, together with His qualities, are innumerable;
If one were to extract the names arising from His qualities, they would exceed thousands and tens of thousands.'

The name that relatives, having made offerings to those worthy of gifts on the naming day of a newborn boy, think of and assign, saying 'This person has such a name,' is a given name (kittimanāma). A primordial name (opapātikanāma) is when a previous designation falls into a later designation, or a previous usage falls into a later usage. For example, in the previous aeon, the moon was called 'Canda,' and now it is still called 'Canda.' In the past, the sun, the ocean, the earth, and the mountains were called 'Suriya, Samudda, Pathavī, Pabbata,' and now they are called exactly the same; this is a primordial name. These four kinds of names are just one 'name' (nāma).
278:
That name is established merely by the convention of the world of beings; in the ultimate sense, it does not exist. Other teachers, however, say, "What is called 'name' is a vocal expression (sound) that clarifies the meaning." The meaning of the powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and path factors (maggaṅga) should be understood according to the method already stated.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Discrimination is finished.

## 29-31. Explanation of the Description of the Three Knowledges

In the description of the three knowledges, "nimitta" refers to the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta). "Animitta" (signless) occurs in Nibbāna, which is the opposite of the sign of formations. "Adhimuttattā" (being resolved) is due to the state of liberation of the mental continuum, together with insight, by way of being inclined towards that Nibbāna. "Phussa phussa vayaṃ passati" (touching and touching, one sees the passing away) means touching the sign of formations with insight knowledge and seeing the dissolution of those formations only with insight knowledge. By seeing in this way, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa) is accomplished. That contemplation of dissolution brings to fulfillment the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); because what is impermanent is suffering, that same contemplation of dissolution brings to fulfillment the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā); because what is suffering is non-self, that same contemplation of dissolution brings to fulfillment the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). Thus, the three contemplations are taught here. "Animittavihāra" (signless dwelling) means that dwelling by means of these three insights is called the signless dwelling because the sign of formations is seen as fearful. "Paṇidhi" refers to craving (taṇhā). "Appaṇihita" (desireless) occurs in Nibbāna, which is the opposite of craving. "Abhinivesa" refers to the adherence to self (attā). "Suññata" (void) occurs in Nibbāna, which is devoid of self. "Suññata" is simply the voidness of self. "Pavattaṃ ajjhupekkhiitvā" (having looked on with equanimity at the occurrence) means looking on with equanimity at the occurrence of the result (vipāka-pavatta) by means of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa). Beings are very fond of the occurrence of results called the happy destinations (sugati). However, this person who wishes to enter the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) looks on with equanimity, seeing that occurrence and all groups of formations as impermanent and so forth. Only by seeing in this way can one enter the attainment of fruition, not by any other way. "Āvajjitvā" (having adverted) means having reflected with the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana). "Samāpajjati" (attains) means entering the attainment of fruition. "Animittā samāpatti" (signless attainment) is so called because one enters it after seeing the sign of formations as fearful. "Animittavihārasamāpatti" is the name for both, by virtue of the dwelling of insight and by virtue of the attainment of fruition.

Now, wishing to analyze the sign of formations itself, the words beginning with "rūpanimittaṃ" (the sign of form) are spoken. What should be said regarding the grasping of aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) has already been stated previously. The meanings already taught by the Pali passages beginning with "añño animittavihāro" (another signless dwelling) are shown in conclusion. In brief, "knowledge in the sense of dwelling" (vihāraṭṭhe ñāṇa) is the knowledge in the diversity of insight dwelling of one who stands in the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, which occurs prior to the attainment of fruition. "Knowledge in the sense of attainment" (samāpattaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is the knowledge in the diversity of the attainment of fruition. "Knowledge in the sense of dwelling and attainment" (vihārasamāpattaṭṭhe ñāṇa) is the knowledge in the diversity of both insight dwelling and the attainment of fruition. A person who wishes to spend time only with insight dwelling brings about only insight dwelling. A person who wishes to spend time only with the dwelling of the attainment of fruition progresses through the sequence of insight and brings about only the dwelling of the attainment of fruition. A person who wishes to spend time with both brings about both. Thus, by the power of the person's wish, the knowledge of diversity of dwelling (vihārānānatta-ñāṇa) is of three kinds. The remaining explanation regarding these three knowledges has already been stated in the explanation of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Three Knowledges is finished.
279:
A person who wishes to spend time only with insight dwelling brings about only insight dwelling. A person who wishes to spend time only with the dwelling called the attainment of fruition progresses through the sequence of insight and brings about only the dwelling called the attainment of fruition. A person who wishes to spend time with both insight dwelling and the attainment of fruition brings about both. Thus, by the power of the person's wish, the knowledge of diversity of dwelling (vihārānānatta-ñāṇa) is of three kinds. The remaining explanation regarding the collection of these three knowledges has already been stated in the explanation of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Three Knowledges is finished.

## 32. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Concentration of Immediate Result

In the description of the knowledge of concentration of immediate result, among the words beginning with "nekkhammavasena" (by way of renunciation), the seven factors called renunciation (nekkhamma), non-ill will (abyāpāda), perception of light (ālokasaññā), non-distraction (avikkhepa), definition of phenomena (dhammavavatthāna), knowledge (ñāṇa), and joy (pāmojja), which are associated with the access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) of a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and are the opposites of various defilements, are associated with a single mind. Non-distraction, which is the stability of the mind, is the state of the mind having a single object. By that concentration, the mind is not distracted among various objects; therefore, it is called non-distraction (avikkhepa). It means non-distraction, which is called one-pointedness of mind (cittassa ekaggatā). Concentration (samādhi) means that by that non-distraction, the mind is placed evenly on a single object; therefore, it is called concentration. "By the power of that concentration" means by the power of the concentration of the kind already described, because of the penetration of the true nature by one whose mind is concentrated even by access concentration. Path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) arises in due order. They are exhausted by way of the abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna). The word "iti" is the conclusion of the meaning already stated. In the prior stage, there is concentration. In the subsequent stage, at the moment of the path, there is knowledge.

'Kāmāsava' (taint of sensual desire) is the lust (rāga) that is attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Bhavāsava' (taint of existence) is the desire and lust (chandarāga) for the fine-material and immaterial realms of existence, attachment to jhāna, lust associated with the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), and the longing by way of existence. 'Diṭṭhāsava' (taint of views) refers to the sixty-two kinds of views. 'Avijjāsava' (taint of ignorance) is the lack of knowledge regarding the eight bases, such as suffering. Having asked about the place where the taints are exhausted using the locative case, and having shown the destruction of the taints by the path that causes the destruction of the taints with the words beginning with "sotāpattimaggena" (by the path of stream-entry), the answer regarding the location is given as "ettha" (here), meaning at the moment of the path. "Anavasesa" (without remainder) means that there is no remainder of those taints. "Apāyagamanīya" (leading to states of deprivation) means the four states of deprivation: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras; they are called "apāya" because they are devoid of the happiness called "aya" (success/happiness). For a person who...
280:
(The taint) exists; because it leads that person (who possesses the taint) to the four states of woe, it is called āpāyagamanīya (leading to states of woe). The explanation of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayakathā) has been explained in the Ubhatovuṭṭhānakathā.

'Avikkhepavasena' means by way of concentration that stands as a strong dependence (upaniṣsaya) for the concentration that is currently occurring. In the passages beginning with 'pathavīkasiṇavasena', the ten kasiṇas are spoken of by way of attainment concentration (appanāsamādhi) having those kasiṇas as objects. The (six) recollections beginning with buddhānussati, as well as maraṇassati and upasamanussati, are spoken of by way of access concentration (upacārajjhāna). Ānāpānassati and kāyagatāsati are spoken of by way of attainment concentration (appanāsamādhi). The ten foulnesses (asubha) are spoken of by way of the first jhāna.

Recollection that occurs repeatedly by taking the Buddha as the object is called buddhānussati. It is a name for the mental factor of mindfulness (sati) that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object, such as 'Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ...', etc.; it means by way of that buddhānussati. Similarly, recollection that occurs by taking the Dhamma as the object is called dhammānussati. It is a name for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Dhamma as its object, such as 'Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo...', etc. Recollection that occurs by taking the Saṅgha as the object is called saṅghānussati. It is a name for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Saṅgha as its object, such as 'Suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho...', etc. Recollection that occurs by taking one's own virtue as the object is called sīlānussati. It is a name for mindfulness that has the qualities of one's own virtue as its object, such as its being unbroken (akhaṇḍatā), etc. Recollection that occurs by taking one's own generosity as the object is called cāgānussati. It is a name for mindfulness that has the qualities of one's own generosity as its object, such as being freely generous (muttacāgatā), etc. Recollection that occurs by taking deities as the object is called devatānussati. It is a name for mindfulness that, placing deities in the position of witnesses, has one's own qualities such as faith (saddhā), etc., as its object. Mindfulness that occurs by taking the in-breath and out-breath as the object is called ānāpānassati. It is a name for mindfulness that has the sign of the in-breath and out-breath as its object. Mindfulness that occurs by taking death as the object is called maraṇassati. It is a name for mindfulness that has death, defined as the cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) included within a single existence, as its object. Mindfulness occurring in the body, which is called 'body' (kāya) because it is connected with loathsome parts such as hair, etc., or because it is their accumulation, is called kāyagatāsati. Or, mindfulness that is fixed by way of taking such a body as its object is kāyagatāsati. Although it should be said as 'kāyagatasati', it is said as 'kāyagatāsati' without shortening the vowel. Here too, it is said in the same way as 'kāyagatāsati-vasena'. It is a name for mindfulness that has the sign of loathsomeness in the parts of the body (kāyakoṭṭhāsa) such as hair, etc., as its object. Recollection that occurs by taking Nibbāna as the object is called upasamanussati. It is a name for mindfulness that has Nibbāna, the pacification of all suffering, as its object. The meaning of the ten foulnesses (asubha) has been stated below.
281:
The passages beginning with 'by way of a long breath' are spoken only to show the different types of attainment concentration (appanāsamādhi) and access concentration (upacārasamādhi). 'By way of a long breath' means by way of the breath that is called 'long'. For it is said: 'Breathing in long, he knows, "I breathe in long."' The same method applies to the remaining terms.

'Experiencing the whole body' means experiencing the entire group of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Calming the bodily formation' means calming the bodily formation called the gross in-breaths and out-breaths. By this tetrad—'long, short, experiencing the whole body, calming the bodily formation'—only attainment concentration (appanāsamādhi) is spoken of.

'Making rapture clear' means making rapture evident. 'Making the mental formation clear' means making the mental formation called perception (saññā) and feeling (vedanā) evident. 'Greatly gladdening the mind' means making the mind joyful. 'Concentrating the mind' means placing the mind evenly on the object. 'Liberating the mind' means liberating the mind from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), etc.

The tetrad 'making rapture clear, making happiness clear, making the mental formation clear, calming the mental formation,' and the tetrad 'making the mind clear, greatly gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind, liberating the mind,' are spoken of by way of attainment concentration (appanāsamādhi) and by way of concentration associated with insight (vipassanā).

'Contemplating repeatedly as impermanent' means by way of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). 'Contemplating repeatedly as fading away' means by way of the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā). 'Contemplating repeatedly as cessation' means by way of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā). 'Contemplating repeatedly as relinquishment' means by way of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). That insight leading to emergence abandons the defilements along with the aggregates (khandha) and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga). And by seeing the fault in conditioned things (saṅkhāra), it enters into Nibbāna, which is the opposite of those conditioned things, by way of inclining towards it.

This tetrad is spoken of only by way of concentration associated with insight (vipassanā). Here, in saying 'by way of the in-breath, by way of the out-breath,' it is spoken of by taking only the occurrence of the in-breath and out-breath. It is not spoken of by way of taking those as objects of impermanence, etc. The detail of this will be made clear in the Ānāpānakathā.

## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Immediate Concentration is finished.

## 33. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Dwelling in Non-conflict

In the description of the knowledge of dwelling in non-conflict (araṇavihārañāṇa), the terms such as contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), etc., have the meanings already stated. 'Dwelling in voidness' (suññatavihāra) is the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpatti) that occurs by way of the mode of voidness for one who has emerged from the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). 'Dwelling in the signless' (animittavihāra) is the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship that occurs by way of the signless mode for a person who has emerged from the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā).
282:
"Appaṇihito vihāro" refers to the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpatti) occurring by way of the desireless (appaṇihita) mode for one who has emerged from the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). "Suññate adhimuttatā" refers to the inclination towards the void (suññata) by the power of wisdom occurring in the preliminary stage of the attainment of the fruit of voidness (suññataphalasamāpatti). The same applies to the remaining two (inclination towards the signless and the desireless). By the words "Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ" and so forth, the meditative attainments (jhānasamāpatti) which are the objects of insight (vipassanā) for one wishing to enter the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship are shown. In fact, the insight, the fruit attainment, the inclination towards the sublime Dhamma, and the meditative attainments of an Arahant deserve to be called "Araṇavihāra" (dwelling in non-conflict) because all defilements have been abandoned.

"Paṭhamena jhānena nīvaraṇe haratīti araṇavihāro" means that a person endowed with the first jhāna removes the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by means of the first jhāna; therefore, that first jhāna is called "Araṇavihāra." The same applies to the remaining jhānas. It should be understood that although an Arahant has no hindrances, it is said that the first jhāna removes them because it is the opposite of the hindrances. After the knowledge of dwelling in non-conflict (araṇavihārañāṇa) has been shown in three ways by the power of insight, fruit attainment, and inclination towards the sublime Dhamma, why are only the meditative attainments detailed as "Araṇavihāra"? It is because those three are already established as Araṇavihāra by way of the brief exposition (uddesa). However, the Araṇavihāra nature of the meditative attainments, which are the basis for fruit attainment and insight, would not be established if not spoken; therefore, it should be understood that "Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ araṇavihāro" and so forth are taught to establish what was not yet established. Although the Araṇavihāra nature of those jhānas is not established in the brief exposition, it is established because it is taught in the detailed exposition (niddesa).

Alternatively, it should be understood by connecting them according to the appropriate method: "Contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the perception of permanence (niccasaññā); contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the perception of pleasure (sukhasaññā); contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the perception of self (attasaññā); the dwelling in voidness (suññatavihāra) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes non-voidness (asuññata); the dwelling in the signless (animittavihāra) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the sign (nimitta); the dwelling in the desireless (appaṇihitavihāra) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes desire (paṇidhi); the inclination towards voidness (suññatādhimuttatā) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the inclination towards non-voidness (asuññatādhimutti); the inclination towards the signless (animittādhimuttatā) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the inclination towards the sign (nimittādhimutti); the inclination towards the desireless (appaṇihitādhimuttatā) is called Araṇavihāra because it removes the inclination towards desire (paṇihitādhimutti)."

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Dwelling in Non-conflict is finished.

## 34. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Attainment of Cessation
In the exposition of the knowledge of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpattiñāṇaniddesa), "Samathabala" (the power of serenity) is called serenity (samatha) because it calms opposing states such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda); that same serenity is called power (bala) in the sense of being unshakable. Only for Non-returners and Arahants, because they have abandoned sensual desire, which is the opponent of concentration, and have reached the state of being perfect in concentration, is their concentration said to have reached power (balappatta), and not that of others. There is also a variant reading "Samādhibala" (the power of concentration). "Vipassanābala" (the power of insight) is called insight (vipassanā) because it sees things in various modes such as impermanence; that same insight is called power in the sense of being unshakable. Only the insight-knowledge of those two types of persons (Non-returners and Arahants) has reached power. Among those two, the power of serenity is for gradually calming the mental continuum and for leading to cessation (nirodha); the power of insight is for seeing the danger in the occurring conditioned things (saṅkhāra) and for seeing the benefit in cessation.

The word "Nīvaraṇe" is a locative case used in the sense of cause (nimittattha); it means because of the cause of hindrances, or because of the condition of hindrances. Or, it is a locative case in the sense of instrument (karaṇattha), meaning by means of hindrances. "Na kampati" means the person endowed with jhāna does not shake. Alternatively, because the word "jhāna" is intended to mean the jhāna-factors, the concentration associated with that first jhāna does not shake because of the hindrances. In this context, only this interpretation (yojanā) should be taken. "Uddhacce ca" means because of restlessness (uddhacca) occurring in the consciousness associated with restlessness; restlessness is the state of being distracted and has the characteristic of not being calm. "Uddhaccasahagatakilese ca" means because of the defilements associated with restlessness, such as delusion (moha), lack of shame (ahirika), and lack of dread (anottappa), which have reached the state of co-arising and so forth with restlessness. "Khandhe ca" means because of the four mental aggregates associated with restlessness (one does not shake).

The words "Na kampati, na calati, na vedhati" (does not shake, does not move, does not waver) are synonyms of each other. It should be understood by connecting them: one does not shake because of restlessness, one does not move because of the defilements associated with restlessness, and one does not waver because of the aggregates associated with restlessness. Since the power of insight is taught only by way of the seven contemplations (anupassanā), it should be understood that the power of insight is perfected by the power of those seven contemplations. "Avijjāya ca" means because of ignorance (avijjā) occurring in the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. "Avijjāsahagatakilese ca" means because of the defilements associated with ignorance, such as greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), conceit (māna), wrong view (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), sloth (thina), restlessness (uddhacca), lack of shame (ahirika), and lack of dread (anottappa), as appropriate (one does not shake). "Vacīsaṅkhāra" (verbal formations) are thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra). "Friend Visākha, having first thought and examined, one afterwards breaks into speech; therefore, thought and examination are called verbal formations" (as taught in the Majjhima Nikāya).
284:
They are called verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra) because they produce speech. Bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) are the in-breaths and out-breaths. According to the teaching (M. i. 463), "Friend Visākha, these in-breaths and out-breaths are bodily things, they are bound up with the body; therefore, in-breaths and out-breaths are bodily formations," they are called bodily formations because they are conditioned by the body. The cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha) is the cessation of both perception and feeling. Mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra) are perception and feeling. According to the teaching (M. i. 463), "These things are mental factors (cetasika), they are bound up with the mind; therefore, perception and feeling are mental formations," they are called mental formations because they are conditioned by the mind.

Among the knowledges of conduct (ñāṇacariyā), it should be understood that by including the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā) at the end of the seven contemplations, the other contemplations mentioned in the Cariyākathā, which is the beginning of that contemplation, are also included as ñāṇacariyā. The limit of "sixteen knowledges of conduct" is the highest limit. For a Non-returner (anāgāmī), however, it also occurs with fourteen knowledges of conduct, excluding the path and fruit of Arahantship, because of the fulfillment of the powers (bala).

Regarding "with nine concentration-conducts" (samādhicariyā), there are nine concentration-conducts: eight by way of the first jhāna and so on, and one by way of access concentration (upacārajjhāna) in all instances for the sake of attaining the first jhāna and so on. What is the difference between the powers (bala) and the conducts (cariyā)? Indeed, in the power of serenity (samathabala), access concentration is taught by way of seven modes such as "by way of renunciation" (nekkhamma-vasena). By expanding the elision (peyyāla), both absorption (appanā) and access concentration are taught as appropriate through seventy turns such as "by way of the first jhāna." In concentration-conduct (samādhicariyā) as well, absorption concentration is taught by way of eight modes such as "the first jhāna." Access concentration is taught by way of eight modes such as "for the sake of attaining the first jhāna." Thus, in both cases, only absorption and access concentration are meant. This being so, they should be understood as 'powers' in the sense of being unshakable (akampiyaṭṭhena) and as 'conducts' in the sense of mastery (vasībhāvaṭṭhena). In the power of insight (vipassanābala), however, only the seven contemplations are called "power of insight." In the knowledge of conduct (ñāṇacariyā), the seven contemplations are also taught, and the nine beginning with the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā) are also specifically taught. This is the difference between them. The seven contemplations should be understood as 'powers' in the sense of being unshakable and as 'conducts' in the sense of mastery.

In the phrase "Wisdom is the state of mastery" (vasībhāvatā paññā), to explain the masteries (vasī) mentioned there, it is stated using the feminine term as "the five masteries" (pañca vasiyo). It means that the control (vaso) itself is called mastery (vasī).
285:
Both absorption concentration and access concentration are meant. In the description of concentration-conduct (samādhicariyā-niddesa) as well, absorption concentration is mentioned by way of the eight modes such as 'the first jhāna.' Access concentration is mentioned by way of the eight modes such as 'for the sake of attaining the first jhāna.' Therefore, in both serenity-power and concentration-conduct, both absorption and access concentration are indeed intended. This being so, they are called 'powers' (bala) in the sense that the opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) cannot shake them. They are called 'conducts' (cariyā) in the sense of being practiced with mastery. 

I shall further state the difference between insight-power (vipassanābala) and knowledge-conduct (ñāṇacariyā). In the description of insight-power, only the seven contemplations are called insight-power. In the description of knowledge-conduct, however, the seven contemplations together with the nine beginning with the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā) (i.e., change-of-lineage, the four paths, and the four fruits) are specifically mentioned. This is their difference. The seven contemplations should be understood as 'powers' in the sense of being unshakable, and as 'conducts' in the sense of being practiced with mastery.

Furthermore, wishing to explain those five masteries (vasī) through a teaching focused on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), he said "mastery in adverting" (āvajjanavasī) and so on. Control over adverting is mastery in adverting. Because that person has mastery in adverting, he is called one with mastery in adverting. The same method applies to the remaining masteries. Being able to advert to the first jhāna in whatever place one desires, whether in a village or a forest, is called 'wherever desired' (yatthicchaka). Being able to advert at whatever time one desires, whether in the cold season or the hot season, is called 'whenever desired' (yadicchaka). Or else, it means being able to advert to whatever object one desires, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so on. Since masteries are mentioned for jhānas having each individual kasiṇa object, the former explanation is better. Being able to advert for as long a duration as one desires, whether for just a finger-snap or for seven days, is called 'for as long as desired' (yāvaticchaka).

'In adverting' (āvajjanāya) refers to adverting by way of the mind-door (manodvārāvajjana). 'Sluggishness' (dandhāyitattaṃ) means the state of not being under one's control, or a state of laziness. 'Attains' (samāpajjati) means enters upon, the meaning is that one reaches absorption. 'Resolves' (adhiṭṭhāti) means staying firmly within the attainment. In the mastery of emergence (vuṭṭhānavasī), the term 'the first jhāna' (paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ) expresses the meaning of the ablative case (from the first jhāna). 'Reviews' (paccavekkhati) means looking back and contemplating with the reviewing impulsions (paccavekkhaṇajavana). This is the word-commentary on the Pali text here.

This is the explanation of the meaning: For one who adverts to applied thought (vitakka) after emerging from the first jhāna, immediately after the adverting that occurs having cut the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), four or five impulsions (javana) having applied thought as their object arise. Then two life-continuums occur. Then again, adverting to sustained thought (vicāra) and impulsions occur in the same manner as previously mentioned. In this way, when one is able to direct the mind without interruption to the five jhāna factors, then mastery in adverting is accomplished for him. This mastery, having reached its peak, is obtained only by the Blessed One in the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriya). There is no mastery in adverting faster than this. For others, the occurrences of the life-continuum in between are beyond counting. The ability to attain an attainment quickly, as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna did when subduing the dragon Nandopananda, is called mastery in attaining (samāpajjanavasī). The ability to maintain the attainment for a moment, such as for a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps, is called mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhānavasī). Likewise, the ability to emerge quickly from it is called mastery in emergence (vuṭṭhānavasī). Mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇavasī) is mentioned within mastery in adverting itself. For there, the reviewing impulsions occur immediately after adverting. Thus, when mastery in adverting is accomplished, mastery in reviewing is also accomplished; and when mastery in resolving is accomplished, mastery in emergence is also accomplished. This being so, because it is said, "This mastery, having reached its peak, is obtained only by the Blessed One in the Twin Miracle," at the time of performing the miracle, there is no longer reviewing of the jhāna factors, but rather the creation of various forms is accomplished by the power of various kasiṇas. Therefore, the ability to produce adverting in that kasiṇa as desired and as quickly as mentioned, for one who wishes to enter the jhāna having that particular kasiṇa as its object, is called mastery in adverting. In that very adverting process (āvajjanavīthi)...
286:
The ability to advert to a specific kasina quickly as desired, by the method already described, for one who wishes to enter a meditative absorption (jhāna) having that kasina as its object—whether because of the absence of creating various colors and so forth, or because of the accomplishment through various kasinas—is called mastery in adverting (āvajjana-vasī). The ability to attain absorption (appanā) or the ability to enter that jhāna within the very same cognitive process (vīthi) of adverting is called mastery in attaining (samāpajjana-vasī). When explained in this way, the logic is not contradicted, and the sequence of masteries follows the proper order. However, regarding the mastery in reviewing the factors of jhāna, since it is said that 'at the peak, only five impulsion (javana) moments occur,' even if seven impulsion moments occur according to the method described, it is still mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-vasī).

If it is argued that the statement 'he adverts to the first jhāna' is inappropriate in this context: just as the jhāna occurring with a kasina as its object is called 'kasina' by way of causal metaphor (kāraṇūpacāra), so too the kasina, which is the cause of jhāna, is called 'jhāna' by way of resultant metaphor (phalūpacāra), as in the passage 'Happy is the arising of the Buddhas' (sukho buddhānamuppādo). Even if there is a re-entry into jhāna, like a person who wakes up from sleep at a predetermined time and then falls back to sleep, it is called mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī). However, if there is a resolution only for emerging at the predetermined time, it is called mastery in emerging (vuṭṭhāna-vasī). This is the distinction between those masteries.

## These questions are asked to clarify the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

What is the attainment of cessation? Who attains it? Who does not attain it? In which realm is it attained? Why is it attained? How is it attained? How is the duration? How is the emergence? Toward what does the mind of one who has emerged incline? What is the difference between a dead person and one who has entered this attainment? Is the attainment of cessation conditioned (saṅkhata) or unconditioned (asaṅkhata), mundane (lokiya) or supramundane (lokuttara), produced (nipphanna) or unproduced (anipphanna)?

Among those questions, what is the attainment of cessation? It is the non-occurrence of mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) through the power of successive cessation.

Who attains it? Who does not attain it? All worldlings (puthujjana), Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), Once-returners (sakadāgāmī), and those Non-returners (anāgāmī) and Arahats who are dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka) do not attain it. Only Non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava, i.e., Arahats) who have attained the eight meditative attainments can attain it.
287:
In which realm is it attained? It is attained in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava). Why? Because the successive attainments are clearly present only in the five-constituent realm. In the four-constituent realm (formless realm), the arising of the first jhāna and so forth does not exist; therefore, it is not possible to enter it there. Why is it attained? Becoming weary of the specific occurrence and dissolution of formations (saṅkhāra), and wishing to 'dwell in bliss, having reached Nibbāna which is cessation' by being without mind even in the present life, they enter it. How is it attained? For a person who has performed the preliminary duties and ascends through the power of both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), the attainment occurs when he causes the cessation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. For one who ascends by serenity alone, he stops at the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. For one who ascends by insight alone, he stops at the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). But for one who ascends by both and causes the cessation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation. This is the summary here. 

The detailed explanation is as follows: In this Dispensation, a monk who wishes to enter the attainment of cessation, having finished his meal and washed his hands and feet well, sits down in a secluded place on a well-prepared seat, folding his legs cross-legged, keeping his body erect, and establishing mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject. That monk enters the first jhāna, and after emerging, contemplates the formations within that first jhāna as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta) through insight. That insight is of three kinds: insight that grasps formations, insight preceding the attainment of fruition, and insight preceding the attainment of cessation. Among these three, whether the insight that grasps formations is slow or sharp, it is certainly a proximate cause for the Path (magga). Insight for the attainment of fruition should be sharp, as it is similar to the development of the Path. However, insight for the attainment of cessation should be neither too slow nor too sharp. Therefore, he contemplates those formations with insight that is neither too slow nor too sharp. Then, having entered the second jhāna and emerged, he contemplates the formations therein in the same way. Then the third jhāna... (and so on). Then, having entered the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and emerged, he contemplates the formations therein in the same way. Then, having entered the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and emerged, he performs the four preliminary duties: (1) protecting separate belongings from destruction (nānābaddha-avikopana), (2) waiting for the Saṅgha (saṅgha-paṭimānana), (3) waiting for the Teacher's call (satthu-pakkosana), and (4) determining the duration of life (addhāna-pariccheda). Among these four, 'protecting separate belongings from destruction' (nānābaddha-avikopana) refers to those requisites such as the bowl, robes, bed, stool, or the dwelling place, which are not physically attached to the monk but exist separately.
288:
One should also make a resolution for any other various requisites so that they are not destroyed by fire, water, wind, thieves, rats, and so on. The procedure for this resolution is: "May this and that requisite not be burnt by fire, not be swept away by water, not be scattered by wind, not be stolen by thieves, and not be gnawed by rats and so on within these seven days." If one makes such a resolution, there will be no danger to those items for the entire seven days. If one does not make the resolution, they may be destroyed by fire and so on. This is called "protecting various separate requisites" (nānābaddha-avikopana). For items that are connected to the body, such as the inner robe, the outer robe, or the seat one is sitting on, there is no need for a separate resolution; the attainment of cessation itself protects them.

Saṅgha-paṭimānana means awaiting the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. It refers to waiting without performing a Saṅgha act until that monk arrives. Here, the act of waiting itself is not the preliminary duty, but rather the reflection on the Saṅgha's expectation is the preliminary duty. Therefore, one should reflect thus: "If, while I am sitting in the attainment of cessation for seven days, the Saṅgha wishes to perform any Vinaya act such as an apalokana-kamma, I shall emerge even before any monk comes to call me." One who enters the attainment after reflecting in this way will surely emerge at that time. If one does not do so, and the Saṅgha, having assembled and not seeing that monk, asks, "Where is such-and-such a monk?" and is told, "He has entered cessation," they will send a monk, saying, "Go and call him by the command of the Saṅgha." Then, when the sent monk stands within hearing distance and says, "Friend, the Saṅgha is awaiting you," the emergence occurs immediately upon those words being spoken. Such is the weight of the Saṅgha's command. Therefore, one should enter the attainment after reflecting on the Saṅgha's expectation so that one emerges by oneself.

In the case of Satthu-pakkosana (summons by the Teacher) as well, the reflection on the Teacher's summons is the preliminary duty for this monk. Therefore, one should reflect thus: "If, while I am sitting in the attainment of cessation for seven days, the Teacher lays down a training rule regarding a certain matter that has arisen, or teaches the Dhamma due to a similar occurrence, I shall emerge even before anyone comes to call me." One who sits after reflecting in this way will surely emerge at that time. If one does not do so, and the Teacher, not seeing that monk in the assembled Saṅgha, asks, "Where is such-and-such a monk?" and is told, "He has entered cessation," He will send a monk, saying, "Go and call him in my name."

Addhāna-pariccheda refers to the limitation of the duration of the life faculty (jīvitindriya). A monk who enters this attainment of cessation must be skilled in the limitation of the duration. One should enter only after reflecting, "Will my life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) last for seven days or not?"
289:
Then, when the sent monk stands within hearing distance of the monk in cessation and says, "The Teacher summons the venerable one," the emergence occurs immediately upon those words being spoken. Such is the weight of the Teacher's summons. Therefore, one should enter the attainment after reflecting on the Teacher's summons so that one emerges by oneself.

Addhāna-pariccheda is the limitation of the duration of life. The monk who enters this attainment of cessation must be skilled in the limitation of the duration of life. One should enter only after reflecting, "Will my life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) last for seven days or not?" If one enters without reflecting on the life-force that might cease within the seven days, his attainment of cessation cannot prevent death. Since there is no death within the attainment of cessation, he will emerge from the attainment in the interval. Therefore, one should enter only after reflecting on this life-force. It is said in the Commentary that while it is acceptable not to reflect on other things, this life-force must certainly be reflected upon. Having thus entered the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and emerged from it, and having performed these four preliminary duties, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). Then, after one or two thought-moments have passed, he becomes mindless and attains cessation (nirodha). Why do thought-moments not proceed beyond two thoughts? Because of the preparation for cessation. For this monk, the ascending through the eight attainments by coupling the two states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is the preparation for the sequential cessation, not for the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thus, because it is the preparation for cessation, thoughts do not proceed beyond two thought-moments.

How is it maintained? The attainment thus entered is maintained by the power of the time limit and by the absence of the exhaustion of life, the awaiting of the Saṅgha, or the summons of the Teacher in the interval.

How is the emergence? There are two ways of emergence: by the attainment of the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) for a Non-returner, and by the attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala) for an Arahat.

What is the state of mind of one who has emerged? It is a mind inclined towards Nibbāna. For it is said: "Friend Visākha, the mind of a monk who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is inclined towards Nibbāna, leans towards Nibbāna, and tends towards Nibbāna."

What is the difference between a dead person and one who has entered the attainment? This meaning is also stated in the Sutta. As it is said: "Friend Mahākoṭṭhika, in the case of one who is dead and has passed away, the bodily formations have ceased, the verbal formations have ceased, the mental formations have ceased, the life is exhausted, the heat is extinguished, and the faculties are broken. In the case of a monk who has entered the attainment of cessation, the bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations have also ceased, but the life is not exhausted, the heat is not extinguished, and the faculties are not broken."
290:
In that dead person, the bodily formations (in-breathing and out-breathing) have ceased and subsided. The verbal formations (applied and sustained thought) and the mental formations (perception and feeling) have also ceased and subsided. Vitality is exhausted, the heat [born of kamma] is extinguished, and the faculties such as the eye are broken. In a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, the bodily formations have also ceased and subsided. The verbal formations and the mental formations have also ceased and subsided. However, vitality is not exhausted, the heat is not extinguished, and the faculties are not broken. Thus it is stated (in the Majjhima Nikāya).

Regarding the question of whether the attainment of cessation is conditioned and so forth, it should not be said to be 'conditioned' or 'unconditioned,' 'mundane' or 'supramundane.' Why? Because it lacks intrinsic nature (sabhāva). However, because it is called 'attained' by virtue of the person who enters the attainment, it is proper to call it a produced state (nipphanna), and not an unproduced state (anipphanna).

"Thus, this peaceful attainment, frequented by the Noble Ones,
Reaches the designation of Nibbāna in this very life."

## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of the Attainment of Cessation is finished.

## 35. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Parinibbāna

In the description of knowledge of Parinibbāna, 'here' means 'in this Dispensation.' 'Sampajāna' (clearly comprehending) refers to one who knows well through the four kinds of clear comprehension: clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka), of suitability (sappāya), of the resort (gocara), and of non-delusion (asammoha). 'Pavattaṃ' (occurrence) refers to the occurrence of obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) as appropriate in all places. 'Pariyādiyati' (exhausts) means he brings to an end or makes non-occurrent: by way of abandonment through suppression (vikkhambhana) in places taught by way of access and absorption concentration; by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) in places taught by way of insight; and by way of abandonment through eradication (samuccheda) in places taught by way of the Path. Indeed, the attainments of the second jhāna and so forth, the great insights, and the paths are summarized by way of ellipsis (peyyāla). The knowledge that arises in one who reviews this exhaustion is called 'knowledge of Parinibbāna.' Therefore, it is also called Parinibbāna through suppression, Parinibbāna through substitution of opposites, and Parinibbāna through eradication. In this way, the knowledge of reviewing the Parinibbāna of defilements is stated. Alternatively, by the words 'or else' (atha vā pana) and so forth, the knowledge of reviewing the Parinibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna) is shown. The element of Nibbāna is of two kinds: with residue (sa-upādisesa) and without residue (anupādisesa). Therein, it is called 'upādi' because it is strongly grasped as 'I' and 'mine'.
291:
This name 'upādi' is a designation for the five aggregates. The five aggregates themselves are called 'upādisesa' because they are the residue (remaining). It is called 'sa-upādisesa' because it exists together with the residue of the aggregates. It is called 'anupādisesa' because there is no residue of the aggregates in this Nibbāna. The Nibbāna with residue was taught first. But this Nibbāna taught by the words 'or else' (atha vā pana) is the Nibbāna without residue. In that element of Nibbāna without residue, 'cakkhupavattaṃ' means the occurrence of the eye, the activity of the eye. 'Pariyādiyati' means it is exhausted or crushed. In the remaining terms, the method should be understood in this same way.

## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Parinibbāna is finished.

## 36. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of the State of Calm Leadership (Samasīsaṭṭha)

In the description of knowledge of the state of calm leadership, the inclusion of all phenomena (dhamma) should be understood through the ten groups (rāsi) such as the five aggregates. This is because, excluding the group of bases (āyatana) and the group of elements (dhātu), all phenomena cannot be separately included by the remaining eight groups. However, although supramundane phenomena are included by the term 'all phenomena,' they should not be taken here as being possible by way of eradication (samuccheda), because supramundane phenomena are not to be eradicated by the eradication of causes. Only the phenomena of the three planes (tebhūmaka), which are to be eradicated by the eradication of causes, should be taken. 'Sammā samucchindati' (rightly eradicates) means he rightly cuts off, causing the cessation of the obsessions and underlying tendencies that strike [the mind], by way of the abandonment through suppression, substitution of opposites, and eradication as appropriate. Thus, the right eradication is shown by the teaching based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). 'Nirodheti' (causes to cease) means he causes cessation through the cessation of non-arising (anuppādanirodha). By this, the meaning of eradication (samuccheda) is stated. 'Na upaṭṭhāti' (does not appear) means that when cessation has been thus effected, that particular phenomenon no longer stands or arises. By this, the meaning of cessation (nirodha) is stated. Thus, the state of non-appearance is shown by way of the nature of non-arising. 'Sama' (calm) is so called because of the stilling of sensual desire and so forth. Those calm states are thirty-seven: seven states such as renunciation (nekkhamma), eight fine-material and immaterial jhānas, eighteen great insights, and the four noble paths.

The thirteen 'heads' (sīsa) are stated by way of including all phenomena that are 'heads.' However, in this context, only the eight heads such as faith (saddhā) and so forth are appropriate. This is because for an Arahant, the five heads such as craving (taṇhā) and so forth do not exist. 'Palibodhasīsa' (obstacle-head): 'palibodha' means entanglement from all sides; it means an obstruction to the path to Nibbāna. 'Sīsa' means the head, the chief, or specifically the predominant one. Because the obstacle itself is the head...
292:
It is called the 'head of obstacles' (palibodha-sīsa) because it is predominant or like a head among all obstacles, such as those associated with craving. The same method should be understood for the remaining terms. Specifically, 'binding' (vinibandhana) means fettering in saṃsāra through the power of elevation (conceit). 'Misapprehension' (parāmāsa) means wrong reflection (clinging). 'Distraction' (vikkhepa) means the state of being scattered. 'Defilement' (kilesa) means affliction. 'Resolution' (adhimokkha) means entering into the object. 'Exertion' (paggaha) means effort. 'Establishment' (upaṭṭhāna) means the appearance of the object (non-forgetfulness). 'Non-distraction' (avikkhepa) means the state of not being scattered. 'Seeing' (dassana) means penetration according to the nature of things. 'Occurrence' (pavatta) means the occurrence of the clung-to aggregates (upādinnak-khandha). 'Range' (gocara) means the object. In these twelve sections, the sense of predominance is the sense of 'head' (sīsa). 'Liberation' (vimokkha) refers to Nirvana, which is liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti) among the five types of liberation: suppression (vikkhambhana), substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), destruction (samuccheda), tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi), and escape (nissaraṇa). 'Head of formations' (saṅkhāra-sīsa) means being like the head, the peak, or the end of all conditioned formations. By these terms 'range-head' (gocara-sīsa) and 'liberation', the Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna) is meant. Or, it refers to the Parinibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna) by way of the mere absence of formations. One is called 'equal-headed' (samatasīsī) because of having the 'equal' (sama) states such as renunciation (nekkhamma) and the 'head' (sīsa) states such as faith (saddhā).

Alternatively, among the thirteen 'head' states, the five starting with craving are the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (samudaya-sacca); the five starting with faith are the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca); the 'head of occurrence' (pavatta-sīsa), which is the life-faculty, is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); and the 'head of range' (gocara-sīsa) and 'head of formations' (saṅkhāra-sīsa) are the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). Thus, for a person in whom the penetration of these Four Noble Truths and the Parinibbāna without remainder occur in a single illness, or in a single posture, or in a single similar life-faculty, that person is called 'equal-headed' (samatasīsī) due to the presence of the previously mentioned 'equal' states and these 'head' states.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Knowledge of Equal-Headedness is Finished.

## 37. Explanation of the Section on the Knowledge of Effacement

In the section on the knowledge of effacement, 'lust is manifold' (rāgo puthū) means that lust is distinct and not mixed with supramundane states. The same method applies to the rest. It is called 'lust' (rāga) in the sense of staining. 'Hatred' (dosa) in the sense of corrupting. 'Delusion' (moha) in the sense of blinding. Having spoken of these three primary defilements—lust characterized by staining, hatred characterized by corrupting, and delusion characterized by blinding—the text now says 'anger' (kodha), etc., to show them by way of division.

Therein, 'anger' (kodha) is characterized by being incensed; here, it refers to hatred directed towards living beings. 'Enmity' (upanāha) is characterized by tying a grudge; it is simply anger that has reached a state of firmness. 'Contempt' (makkha) is characterized by smearing the virtues of others; it means erasing others' virtues. 'Rivalry' (paḷāsa) is characterized by taking a pair (competing); it means looking at others' virtues with the intent of competing. 'Envy' (issā) is characterized by disparaging (jealousy of) others' success.
293:
The meaning is: 'Avarice' (macchariya) is characterized by hiding one's own success. It means, 'May my wonderful success not belong to another.' 'Deceit' (māyā) is characterized by concealing the evil one has done. It means it is like a magic trick in the sense of concealing. 'Hypocrisy' (sāṭheyya) is characterized by displaying virtues that one does not possess. It means the state of being a rogue. 'Obstinacy' (thambha) is characterized by the state of the mind being inflated. It means the state of being stiff. 'Presumption' (sārambha) is characterized by excessive action (or excessive speech). 'Conceit' (māna) is characterized by elevation. 'Arrogance' (atimāna) is characterized by excessive elevation. 'Intoxication' (mada) is characterized by the state of being drunk (with pride). 'Heedlessness' (pamāda) is characterized by letting the mind loose among the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Having thus shown them separately by way of defilements, the text says 'all defilements' (sabbe kilesā), etc., to show both the mentioned defilements and other unmentioned defilements by way of all-inclusive grouping. In that text, they are called 'defilements' (kilesā) because they defile, burn, and oppress beings in the present life and the future life. They are called 'misconduct' (duccarita) because they are badly practiced (or are bad practices), whether included in the courses of unwholesome action (akusala-kammapatha) or not. Those misconducts are of three types: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. They are called 'volitional formations' (abhisaṅkhāra) because they construct and prepare the result (vipāka). Those formations are also of three types: meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations. They are called 'leading to existence' (bhavagāmi) because they go to a state of existence through the power of the result. Actions leading to existence are called 'existence-leading kammas' (bhavagāmi-kamma). By this term 'existence-leading kamma', it should be understood that even though they are formations, 'lapsed kamma' (ahosi-kamma) which has no opportunity to produce a result is excluded. In the words 'duccaritā' and 'kammā', a change of gender (making neuter into masculine) is made. In the heading 'diversity and unity' (nānattekattaṃ), although the word 'unity' (ekatta) is not present in the initial summary, the heading is made as 'diversity and unity' because diversity and unity are mutually dependent, and there is a desire to point out unity as well. When unity, which causes the thinning of diversity, is shown, the knowledge of effacement (sallikha-ñāṇa) can be easily demonstrated. 'Diversity' (nānatta) means having various natures because of being unstable and vibrating. 'Unity' (ekatta) means having a single nature because of being stable and non-vibrating.

'Splendor of conduct' (caraṇa-teja) means: it is called 'conduct' (caraṇa) because by it, one goes to the unreached direction, Nirvana. What is that? It is virtue (sīla). That itself is called 'splendor' (teja) in the sense of burning up the opposite (immorality). 'Splendor of quality' (guṇa-teja) is the splendor of concentration (samādhi) which has gained a footing in virtue. 'Splendor of wisdom' (paññā-teja) is the splendor of insight (vipassanā) which has gained a footing in concentration. 'Splendor of merit' (puñña-teja) is the splendor of the wholesome Noble Path which has gained a footing in insight. 'Splendor of Dhamma' (dhamma-teja) is the splendor of the Buddha's word (buddha-vacana), which is the foundation of the four splendors. 'Sharpened by the splendor of conduct' (caraṇa-tejeņa tejitattā) means being made sharp by the splendor of virtue. 'Splendor of immorality' (dussīlya-teja) is the splendor consisting of the state of being immoral. That immorality is also called 'splendor' (teja) because it burns the mental continuity. 'Exhausts' (pariyādiyati) means it finishes or consumes. 'Splendor of non-virtue' (aguṇa-teja) means...
294:
The potency of distraction (vikkhepa), which is the opposite of concentration (samādhi); the potency of delusion (moha), which is the opposite of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), is called the potency of bad wisdom (duppañña-teja). The potency of unwholesome kamma, which is the companion of the defilements to be abandoned by the respective paths, is called the potency of demerit (apuñña-teja). This path does not only exhaust demerit (apuñña); according to the words, 'Bhikkhus, there is kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma,' it also exhausts wholesome kamma. The potency of demerit is primarily taught as the opposite of the potency of merit (puñña-teja). The potency of unrighteousness (adhamma-teja) refers to the potency of the doctrines and words of various sectarians. In the second explanation of the meaning presented in the opening of the summary (mātikā) of this knowledge, the nineteen states beginning with lust (rāga) are the respective potencies of immorality (dussīlya-teja). In the context of 'volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) and kamma leading to rebirth (bhavagāmikamma),' the volitional formations of demerit and unwholesome kamma are the potency of demerit. The volitional formations of the imperturbable (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) and mundane wholesome kamma are included in the side of the potency of demerit because they are to be exhausted only by the potency of merit (i.e., the Noble Path). The fifteen diverse states (nānatta) beginning with sensual desire (kāmacchanda) are the potency of non-virtue (aguṇa-teja). The eighteen diverse states beginning with the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) are the potency of bad wisdom (duppañña-teja). The four diverse states abandoned by the four paths are the potency of demerit (apuñña-teja). The potency of unrighteousness (adhamma-teja) is to be included within the diverse states abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga).

In the section of the description (niddesa), wishing to show effacement (sallēkha) by means of its opposite, non-effacement (asallēkha), the description is given by placing non-effacement first. The thirty-seven states of unity (ekatta) beginning with renunciation (nekkhamma) are called 'effacement' (sallēkha) because they scrape away (efface) the opposing states. Knowledge concerning those thirty-seven types of effacement beginning with renunciation is called 'knowledge in the sense of effacement' (sallēkhaṭṭha-ñāṇa).

## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge in the Sense of Effacement is finished.

## 38. Vīriyārambha-ñāṇa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā

In the description of the knowledge of the arousal of energy (vīriyārambha-ñāṇa), 'anuppannānaṃ' (of the unrisen) refers to states that have not yet arisen in a single individual existence (attabhāva) or in a single object. In the saṃsāra without a perceivable beginning, there are no unwholesome states that have never arisen, but there are wholesome states. 'Pāpakānaṃ' (of the evil) refers to base states. 'Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ' (of unwholesome states) refers to states born of lack of skill (akosalla). 'Anuppādāya' (for non-arising) means for the purpose of not bringing them into existence. 'Uppannānaṃ' (of the risen) refers to states that have arisen in this individual existence. 'Pahānāya' (for abandoning) means for the purpose of giving them up. 'Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ' (of unrisen wholesome states) refers to states in this individual existence...
295:
...for the sake of wholesome states born of skillfulness (kosalla) that have not previously arisen in this individual existence. 'Uppādāya' (for arising) means for the purpose of bringing into existence. 'Uppannānaṃ' (of the risen) refers to those states that have arisen in this individual existence. 'Ṭhitiyā' (for persistence) means for the purpose of remaining. 'Asammosāya' (for non-disappearance) means for the purpose of non-destruction. 'Bhiyyobhāvāya' (for increase) means for the purpose of repeated occurrence. 'Vepullāya' (for fullness) means for the purpose of abundance. 'Bhāvanāya' (for development) means for the purpose of growth. 'Pāripūriyā' (for fulfillment) means for the purpose of completion.

Now, in order to show specifically sensual desire (kāmacchanda) among the unwholesome and renunciation (nekkhamma) among the wholesome, the phrase beginning with 'anuppannassa kāmacchandassa' is stated. In that text, 'kāmacchanda' is sensual lust (kāmarāga), which is the opposite of concentration (samādhi). 'Nekkhamma' is either the concentration associated with the first jhāna, the first jhāna itself, or indeed all wholesome states are called renunciation.

Now, in order to show them in connection with all defilements and the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga), which is the opposite of all defilements, the phrase beginning with 'anuppannānaṃ sabba-kilesānaṃ' is stated. In that text, in the phrases such as 'uppannassa arahattamaggassa ṭhitiyā,' the connection with 'ṭhitiyā' etc. should be understood by way of the moments of presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa) and dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the path of Arahantship that has arisen at the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa). In the Vibhaṅga Commentary (Sammohavinodanī) also, it is said: 'Whatever is its occurrence (pavatti), this itself is called persistence (ṭhiti).' Some teachers, however, say: 'The path (of Non-returning) occurring in the preceding stage of the path of Arahantship should be understood.'

## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of the Arousal of Energy is finished.

## 39. Atthasandassana-ñāṇa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā

In the description of the knowledge of demonstrating the meaning (atthasandassana-ñāṇa), terms such as 'pañcakkhandhā' (five aggregates) have the meanings already stated. 'Pakāseti' (explains) means he makes it clear; the meaning is that he accomplishes the seeing with the eye of wisdom for the listeners. 'Nānādhammā' (various states) refers to all states, both mundane and supramundane. If it is asked: 'Why are only mundane states mentioned in the description of explanation (pakāsanā-niddesa)?' It is because the explanation is undertaken by way of impermanence (anicca) etc., and because supramundane states do not come under such comprehension (sammasana), supramundane states are not mentioned there. However, since they are included by the description of various states (nānādhammā) and the description of demonstrating the meaning (atthasandassana), in whatever way they should be explained, such explanation is indeed 'pakāsanā'. 'Pajahanto' (abandoning) means making the listener abandon (hindrances etc.). 'Sandasseti' (demonstrates) means he shows correctly to the listeners. Some teachers, however, recite in this way: 'Because of the abandoning of sensual desire, he correctly demonstrates the meaning of renunciation,' and so forth.
296:
They recite in the manner beginning with, "It shows the meaning of renunciation appropriately." The meaning in the words of those teachers is indeed straightforward. It should be understood that this method was taught to show that if it can effect the abandoning of faults and the acquisition of virtues in the listeners, it is the knowledge of teaching that has reached the pinnacle.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Knowledge of Showing the Meaning is finished.

## 40. The Explanation of the Exposition of Knowledge of Purification of View

In the Exposition of Knowledge of Purification of View, "all dhammas are included in one way" means all conditioned and unconditioned dhammas are included and delimited by one way (such as tathaṭṭha, etc.). "By way of tathaṭṭha (the nature of being real)" means by way of the evident nature, by way of the nature existing through its own individual essence. "By way of anattaṭṭha (the nature of non-self)" means by way of the nature being devoid of a self characterized as a doer or an experiencer. "By way of saccaṭṭha (the nature of truth)" means by way of the nature of non-deceptiveness, by way of the absence of change from its own individual essence. "By way of paṭivedhaṭṭha (the nature of being penetrated)" means by way of the nature that should be penetrated by knowledge according to its individual essence. Here, penetration should be understood as being through non-delusion and through the object by means of supramundane knowledge.

"By way of abhijānanaṭṭha (the nature of knowing directly)" means by way of the nature of those various dhammas that should be known directly according to their individual essence, through the object by means of mundane knowledge, and through non-delusion and the object by means of supramundane knowledge. For it was said: "Bhikkhus, all should be directly known" (S. iv, 46). "By way of parijānanaṭṭha (the nature of knowing fully)" means, in the same manner as mentioned, by way of the nature of those dhammas already directly known according to their individual essence through mundane and supramundane knowledges, which should be known by delimiting them as impermanent, etc., and as leading out, etc. For it was said: "Bhikkhus, all should be fully known."

"By way of dhammaṭṭha (the nature of bearing)" means by way of the nature of bearing its own individual essence, etc. "By way of dhātuṭṭha (the nature of element)" means by way of the nature of being soulless, etc. "By way of ñātaṭṭha (the nature of being known)" means by way of the nature that is capable of being known by mundane and supramundane knowledges. Just as it was said, "the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized form" because of the meaning of being capable of being seen, etc., so too here, the meaning of being capable of being known should be understood as ñātaṭṭha. "By way of sacchikiriyaṭṭha (the nature of realization)" means by way of the nature that should be realized through the object. "By way of phusanaṭṭha (the nature of touching)" means by way of the nature that should be touched repeatedly through the object once it has been realized. "By way of abhisamayaṭṭha (the nature of clear realization)" means by way of the nature that should be clearly realized by mundane knowledge.

In truth, it was said that each knowledge is single, such as "Wisdom in the sense of being real is the knowledge of the opening of truth; direct-knowledge wisdom is the knowledge in the sense of being known; realization wisdom is the knowledge in the sense of touching." And in the Commentary—
297:
“It is seen in [the senses of] meeting, occasion, time, group, cause and view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration.”

In the explanation of the verse, the meaning of the word abhisamaya is said to be the meaning of penetration (paṭivedha); however, here, the distinction between those dhammas should be understood by the aforementioned meaning. For in the Commentary itself, that dhammābhisamaya (clear realization of the Dhamma) is spoken of by way of mundane knowledge.

Sensual desire (kāmacchanda) has the nature of diversity (nānatta) because of the presence of distraction and because of having various objects. All defilements should be understood in this way. Renunciation (nekkhamma) has the nature of unity (ekatta) because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind and because of the absence of distraction among various objects. All wholesome states should be understood in this way. Here, the diversity (nānatta) of unwholesome states like ill-will (byāpāda), which are abbreviated by the ellipsis (peyyāla), should be understood according to the aforementioned meaning. The diversity (nānatta) of lower factors of jhāna such as initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) should be understood in the sense of being grosser than the higher factors. Since the penetration of diversity and unity included in one way is accomplished by the penetration of the truths at the moment of the path, therefore, having extracted the word “penetration” (paṭivedha), he showed the clear realization of the truths (saccābhisamaya).

“Full understanding penetrates penetration” means one clearly realizes through the clear realization of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya). This is the method for the remaining terms. For at the time of the clear realization of the truths, four functions occur in a single moment of path-knowledge: full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriya), and development (bhāvanā). For example, just as a boat, in a single moment without before or after, performs four functions: it leaves the near shore, cuts the current, carries the cargo, and reaches the far shore; even so, path-knowledge clearly realizes the four truths in a single moment without before or after. It clearly realizes suffering through the clear realization of full understanding; it clearly realizes the origin through the clear realization of abandoning; it clearly realizes the path through the clear realization of development; and it clearly realizes cessation through the clear realization of realization. What is meant? Having made cessation the object, by way of function, it reaches, sees, and penetrates all four truths. Just as it leaves the near shore, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering. Just as it cuts the current, so it abandons the origin. Just as it carries the cargo, so it develops the path by way of being a conascent condition, etc. Just as it reaches the far shore, so it realizes cessation, which is the far shore. Thus the comparison with the simile should be understood.

“Vision is purified” means that through the abandoning of the darkness of defilements to be abandoned by the respective paths, the knowledge and vision reach the state of purification. “Vision is purified” means that at the moment of the arising of the respective fruits, because of the completion of the function of the respective path-knowledge, the knowledge and vision reach the state of purification. Because of the wisdom that penetrates the diversity and unity of all dhammas such as the aggregates included in one way, the path and fruit knowledges are spoken of at the end.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Knowledge of Purification of View is finished.
298:
At the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) of each fruition, because of the attainment of the accomplishment of the function of each path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), knowledge and vision (ñāṇa-dassana) reaches the state of purity. Because the wisdom that penetrates diversity (nānatta) and unity (ekatta), which encompasses all phenomena such as the aggregates in a single way, is accomplished by the path and fruition knowledges, the path and fruition knowledges are stated at the end.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Purification of Vision is finished.

## 41-42. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Acceptance and the Knowledge of Penetration

92-93. In the expositions of the knowledge of acceptance (khanti-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of penetration (pariyogāhaṇa-ñāṇa), "Form is known as impermanent" (rūpaṃ aniccato viditaṃ) means it is known as impermanent through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). "Form is known as suffering" means it is known as suffering through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). "Form is known as non-self" means it is known as non-self through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). "Whatever is known, that he accepts" (yaṃ yaṃ viditaṃ, taṃ taṃ khamati) means whatever form is known through the aspect of impermanence, etc., he accepts (accepts/approves) that form through the aspect of impermanence, etc. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, it is written separately as "Form is known as impermanent; whatever is known, that he accepts." The gender and number should be changed and applied as "Feelings, perceptions, and mental formations are known as impermanent," etc. "He touches" (phusati) means he touches or pervades due to the touching of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). "He penetrates" (pariyogahati) means he enters through insight knowledge. There is also a variant reading pariyogāhati.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Acceptance and the Knowledge of Penetration is finished.

## 43. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Abiding in a Part

In the exposition of the knowledge of abiding in a part (padesavihāra-ñāṇa), desiring to show the manner in which the part (padesa) briefly indicated in the table of contents (mātikā) should be reflected upon, he said "Feeling experienced due to the condition of wrong view," etc. Therein, "due to the condition of wrong view" (micchā-diṭṭhi-paccayā) refers to feelings associated with [wrong] view, as well as wholesome feelings, unwholesome feelings, and resultant feelings that arise by making wrong view a strong decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). Among those three types of feelings, the feeling associated with wrong view is only unwholesome. However, depending on [wrong] view, wholesome feelings also arise, and unwholesome feelings also arise. Indeed, those with wrong view, depending on [wrong] view, give gifts of gruel, rice, etc., on the days of the waxing and waning moon; they establish regular service for the blind, the disabled, etc.; they build rest houses at crossroads; they have ponds dug; they plant flower gardens and fruit orchards; they lay bridges over rivers and streams; they make uneven ground level. Thus, for them, wholesome...
299:
...feeling arises. However, depending on wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), they abuse and threaten those with right view; they perform acts such as killing and binding; they kill living beings and offer them to deities (as sacrificial offerings). Thus, for them, unwholesome feeling arises. Resultant feeling (vipāka-vedanā), however, occurs for those who have gone to another birth. That wrong view conditions the feeling co-nascent with itself through the conditions of sahajāta (co-nascence), aññamañña (mutuality), nissaya (support), sampayutta (association), atthi (presence), and avigata (non-disappearance). Wrong view that has just ceased in the immediately preceding moment conditions the feeling associated with the present wrong view through the conditions of anantara (proximity), samanantara (contiguity), upanissaya (decisive support), āsevana (repetition), natthi (absence), and vigata (disappearance). For one who values and delights in wrong view, it conditions the feeling accompanied by greed through the conditions of ārammaṇa (object), ārammaṇādhipati (object-predominance), and ārammaṇူpanissaya (object-decisive support). For one who makes wrong view a mere object with all unwholesome states, it conditions all unwholesome feelings; and for one who reflects on or contemplates wrong view with insight, it conditions wholesome and indeterminate (abyākata) feelings through the ārammaṇa condition. It conditions wholesome and unwholesome feelings arising due to the cause of wrong view, and resultant feelings in another birth, through the upanissaya condition.

"Due to the condition of the subsiding of wrong view" (micchā-diṭṭhi-vūpasama-paccayā) refers to right view (insight knowledge, the path knowledge of stream-entry) which is the cause for the subsiding of wrong view. Therefore, whatever feeling is taught as being due to the condition of right view, that very feeling should be understood as being "due to the condition of the subsiding of wrong view." Some teachers, however, say that the subsiding of wrong view occurs at the moment of insight and at the moment of the path of stream-entry.
