"Feeling experienced also due to the condition of right view" (sammā-diṭṭhi-paccayāpi vedayitaṃ) — in this context too, feeling associated with right view, wholesome and unwholesome feelings arising depending on right view, and resultant feeling are all appropriate. Among those feelings, the feeling associated with right view is only wholesome. Depending on right view, however, they perform meritorious deeds such as worshiping the Blessed One, lighting oil lamps, listening to the sublime Dhamma, and establishing pagodas in regions where none had been established before. Thus, for them, wholesome feeling arises. Depending on that very right view, they abuse and threaten those with wrong view, exalt themselves, and disparage others. Thus, for them, unwholesome feeling arises. Resultant feeling, however, occurs only for those who have gone to another birth. That right view conditions the feeling co-nascent with itself, and the right view that has just ceased in the immediately preceding moment conditions the present feeling, through the very same conditions stated for wrong view. Mundane right view conditions feelings associated with reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), feelings associated with insight (vipassanā), and feelings associated with attachment (nikanti) through the ārammaṇa condition. It conditions through the upanissaya condition in the same manner as stated for wrong view. Supramundane (magga-phala) right view [conditions] reviewing...
300:
It is a condition for the associated feeling by way of object, object-predominance, and object-decisive support conditions. Regarding "feeling also due to the condition of the subsiding of right view" (sammādiṭṭhi-vūpasama-paccayāpi vedayitaṃ), the so-called subsiding of right view is indeed wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). Therefore, the feeling that arises due to wrong view as a condition should be understood as "due to the condition of the subsiding of right view." The same method applies to "due to the condition of wrong intention," "due to the condition of the subsiding of wrong intention," and so on. For whenever it is said "due to the condition of the subsiding" of a certain state, it refers to that specific feeling arising due to the condition of the state's opposite.

In the case of wrong knowledge and so on, wrong knowledge (micchā-ñāṇa) means the planning of means in performing evil deeds. Alternatively, wrong knowledge is wrong reflective knowledge (micchā-paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Right knowledge (sammā-ñāṇa) is the remaining wholesome and indeterminate knowledge, excluding insight right view and supramundane right view. Wrong liberation (micchā-vimutti) is the inclination toward evil. Alternatively, it is incorrect liberation, liberation that does not lead out of saṃsāra, or the perception of being liberated while not yet liberated. Right liberation (sammā-vimutti) is good inclination and the liberation of fruition. Right view and the others have the same meanings as stated below.

In the terms such as "due to the condition of desire" (chanda-paccayā), desire means greed (lobha). Due to the condition of desire, the feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood. Due to the condition of the subsiding of desire, there is the feeling of the first jhana. Due to the condition of initial application (vitakka), there is the feeling of the first jhana. Due to the condition of the subsiding of initial application, there is the feeling of the second jhana. Due to the condition of perception (saññā), there are the feelings of the remaining six attainments, excluding the first jhana. Due to the condition of the subsiding of perception, there is the feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In the phrases "desire is not subsided" (chando ca avūpasanto hoti), and so on, it means if desire, initial application, and perception have not subsided. Due to that condition—meaning the non-subsiding of desire, initial application, and perception is the condition—therefore, "due to that condition." It means the feeling arises due to the condition of the non-subsiding of desire, initial application, and perception. That is the feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. If desire has subsided but initial application and perception have not subsided, due to that condition, there is the feeling of the first jhana. If desire and initial application have subsided but perception has not subsided, due to that condition, there is the feeling of the second jhana. If desire, initial application, and perception have subsided, due to that condition, there is the feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Some teachers, however, say: "Desire means [thinking] 'I shall reach absorption...'"
301:
Some teachers explain: "Thinking 'I shall strive to reach absorption,' the desire occurring in the preliminary stage is the desire for Dhamma (dhamma-chanda) associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness; for one who has reached absorption, that desire is subsided." In the first jhana, there is initial application (vitakka), but for one who has reached the second jhana, initial application is subsided. In the seven attainments up to the base of nothingness, there is perception (saññā), but for one who has entered the jhana of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and for one who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), perception is subsided. Thus they explain. However, in this context, the attainment of cessation is not appropriate.

"For the attainment of the unreached" (appattassa pattiyā) means for the sake of reaching the fruition of Arahatship. "There is effort" (atthi āyavaṃ) means there is the energy of exertion. There is also a variant reading "āyāvaṃ." "When that state is not yet reached" (tasmimpi ṭhāne anuppatte) means when the noble path, which is the cause of the fruition of Arahatship, is reached in due order by the power of that exertion of energy. "Feeling also due to that condition" (tappaccayāpi vedayitaṃ) means the feeling that arises due to the condition of the noble path, which is the cause of Arahatship. By this, the supramundane feeling born together with the four paths is taken. Some teachers, however, explain: "Effort" (āyavaṃ) is the practice (paṭipatti) occurring in the preliminary stage of the path, and "when that state is reached" means when one has reached the state of that practice.

## The Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Living in One Part is finished.

## 44-49. Explanation of the Description of the Sixfold Knowledge of Turning Away

In the description of the sixfold knowledge of turning away, "wisdom through the predominance of renunciation" (nekkhamma-adhipatattā paññā) means wisdom that proceeds by making renunciation (jhana) predominant. "Turning away from sensual desire through perception" (kāmacchandato saññāya vivaṭṭati) means that with perception associated with wisdom that has renunciation as its predominant factor acting as the cause or instrument, one turns away from sensual desire, turns back, or turns one's face away from it. This is the method for the remaining terms.

"Sensual desire is diversity" (kāmacchando nānattaṃ) means that because sensual desire lacks a peaceful state, it does not have a single nature. "Renunciation is unity" (nekkhammaṃ ekattaṃ) means that because renunciation (jhana) has a peaceful state, it has a single nature. "For one who intends the unity of renunciation" (nekkhamma-ekattaṃ cetayato) means for one who brings about renunciation by seeing the danger in sensual desire. "The mind turns away from sensual desire" (kāmacchandato cittaṃ vivaṭṭati) means that because of seeing the danger, the mind turns away from sensual desire at the moment of renunciation (jhana). This is the method for the remaining terms.

"Abandoning sensual desire" (kāmacchandaṃ pajahanto) means one who abandons sensual desire by the abandonment through suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) at the moment renunciation (jhana) occurs. "One resolves the mind by way of renunciation" (nekkhamma-vasena cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti) means of the attained...
302:
By the power of renunciation (jhāna), one causes the mind associated with it to be established and to proceed as the predominant factor. This is the method for the remaining terms.

'The eye is empty of self' means that because there is no self—conceived by the foolish as an agent or an experiencer—the eye is empty of self. Whatever is not present in a place, that place is said to be empty of it. 'It is also empty of what belongs to self' means that since the self itself does not exist, that which belongs to the self also does not exist; thus, the eye is empty of what belongs to the self. Because in the world, grasping can occur in both ways—as 'self' and as 'what belongs to self'—the absence of self and the absence of what belongs to self are taught to prohibit both types of grasping. 'It is also empty of a permanent nature' means that because there is nothing that remains after passing beyond destruction (bhaṅga), it is empty of a permanent nature. 'It is also empty of a stable nature' means that because there is nothing stable even at the moment of occurrence, it is empty of a stable nature. 'It is also empty of an eternal nature' means that because there is nothing that exists for all time, it is empty of an eternal nature. 'It is also empty of a non-changing nature' means that because there is nothing whose nature does not change in two ways through aging and destruction, it is empty of a non-changing nature. Alternatively, it means it is empty of the state of being permanent, stable, eternal, and non-changing. The word 'vā' (or) has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya).

'For one who knows and sees according to reality' means for one who knows according to the true nature through the knowledge of the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā-ñāṇa), seeing clearly as if with the eyes. 'Knowledge turns away from adherence to the eye' means that knowledge turns away (is liberated) from the adherence of wrong view that arises as 'the eye is self' or 'the eye belongs to self' through the power of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna). This is the method for the remaining terms.

'One relinquishes sensual desire through renunciation' means that a person who has attained renunciation (jhāna) abandons sensual desire, which is its opposite, through renunciation. 'Wisdom in relinquishment' means the wisdom associated with renunciation, which is the relinquishment of sensual desire. This is the method for the remaining terms. The meanings of 'oppression' (pīḷanaṭṭha), etc., are just as stated above. 'One who fully understands turns away' is a teaching based on the person; a person endowed with the path, while fully understanding the four meanings of the truth of suffering through the function of the path, turns away (is liberated) by the power of emerging from both (defilements and the sign of formations). Even in the turning away of knowledge, it is said that the one endowed with knowledge 'turns away'.
303:
Wisdom in the sense of truth means the wisdom of that very person endowed with the path, which turns away regarding the two truths: the truth of suffering and the truth of origin. This should be understood in the same way for the remaining terms. Now, in order to show the six types of turning-away knowledge (vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa) through the distinction of modes by the power of the function of the path-moment (maggakkhaṇa) alone, having set forth the matrix (mātikā) starting with 'saññā-vivaṭṭo' (turning away of perception), the text says 'sañjānanto vivaṭṭati' (perceiving, one turns away), etc., wishing to analyze that matrix by way of meaning.

In that 'saññā-vivaṭṭa' (turning away of perception) expressed as 'perceiving, one turns away,' it means that because a yogi, having perceived renunciation, etc., as predominant in the preliminary stage, later turns away from sensual desire, etc., by the knowledge associated with renunciation at the time of the path, that path-knowledge is called 'saññā-vivaṭṭa.' In 'ceto-vivaṭṭa' (turning away of volition) expressed as 'volitionally directing, one turns away,' it means that because a yogi, volitionally directing towards the oneness of renunciation, etc., turns away from sensual desire, etc., by the associated knowledge, that path-knowledge is called 'ceto-vivaṭṭa.' In 'citta-vivaṭṭa' (turning away of consciousness) expressed as 'cognizing, one turns away,' it means that because a yogi, cognizing by establishing the mind through renunciation, etc., turns away from sensual desire, etc., by the knowledge associated with that path, that path-knowledge is called 'citta-vivaṭṭa.' In 'ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa' (turning away of knowledge) expressed as 'making knowledge, one turns away,' it means that because a yogi, making the six internal bases known as empty through the knowledge of the contemplation of non-self, turns away from the adherence of wrong view by that very knowledge, that path-knowledge is called 'ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa.' In 'vimokkha-vivaṭṭa' (turning away of liberation) expressed as 'relinquishing, one turns away,' it means that because a yogi, relinquishing sensual desire, etc., through renunciation, etc., turns away from sensual desire, etc., by the knowledge associated with that path, that path-knowledge is called 'vimokkha-vivaṭṭa.' In 'sacca-vivaṭṭa' (turning away of truth) expressed as 'one turns away in the sense of truth,' it means that because a yogi turns away from both (the defilements and the sign of formations) by the power of emerging regarding the four noble truths, the path-knowledge is called 'sacca-vivaṭṭa.' Or, because the path-knowledge itself turns away from both (the defilements and the sign of formations) regarding the four truths, it is called 'sacca-vivaṭṭa.'

Since the words 'saññā-vivaṭṭo,' etc., are stated in the explanation of the knowledge of turning away regarding truth (sacca-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa-niddesa), it should be understood that they are spoken with reference only to the moment of the path, which is the knowledge of truth. Indeed, all these knowledges are combined only at the moment of the path. How are they combined at the moment of the path? Excluding the knowledge of the contemplation of non-self in 'ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa,' the noble path itself appears in its own form in the remaining five knowledges. However, since the function of insight (vipassanā) is accomplished only by the path, 'ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa' is also combined at the moment of the path by the power of the accomplishment of the function of insight. Alternatively, because it is only by the path-knowledge that 'the eye is empty,' etc., is penetrated by way of function, it is appropriate to speak of that 'ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa' at the moment of the path. The connection of meaning here is: 'At whichever path-moment there is saññā-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa, at that path-moment there is ceto-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa. At whichever path-moment...'
304:
“In whichever moment of the Path there is the knowledge of turning away from perception (saññā-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa), in that same moment of the Path there is the knowledge of turning away of the mind (ceto-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa),” and so forth; in this manner, the application should be made in all correlations. Alternatively, since the four Noble Paths are explicitly included within the turning away from perception, turning away of the mind, turning away of consciousness (citta-vivaṭṭa), and turning away of liberation (vimokkha-vivaṭṭa), the knowledge of turning away from truth (sacca-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa) is already included. The knowledge of turning away of knowledge (ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa) is also accomplished through the function of the Path knowledge itself, which is called sacca-vivaṭṭa.

Even when the ellipsis (peyyāla) is expanded only for the turning away from perception, mind, consciousness, and liberation, the following texts are possible: “Because it occurs by making the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) the predominant factor, wisdom turns away from perception due to adherence (abhinivesa); therefore, wisdom that is predominant is the knowledge in the turning away from perception”; and “Adherence is diversity (nānatta), the contemplation of non-self is unity (ekatta). The mind of one who directs it towards the unity of the contemplation of non-self turns away from adherence; therefore, wisdom in diversity is the knowledge in the turning away of the mind”; and “One who abandons adherence establishes the mind by the power of the contemplation of non-self; therefore, wisdom in establishment (adhiṭṭhāne) is the knowledge in the turning away of consciousness”; and “One relinquishes adherence through the contemplation of non-self; therefore, wisdom in relinquishment (vossagge) is the knowledge in the turning away of liberation.” Because of the possibility of such texts, the contemplation called the knowledge of turning away of knowledge (ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa) is also included in those four types of turning away.

Furthermore, in the turning away of knowledge, for a person who has emerged from the signs of defilements and formations through the contemplation of non-self and attained the Noble Path, the knowledge of turning away from truth (sacca-vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa) is obtained through the suitability of knowing, by the power of the Path’s function, that “the eye is empty of self or what belongs to self,” and so forth. Therefore, in each single knowledge of turning away, the remaining five types of turning away are obtained. Thus, it should be understood that the correlated words such as “wherever there is turning away from perception, there is turning away of the mind,” and so forth, were taught.

## The Explanation of the Sixfold Description of the Knowledge of Turning Away is finished.

## 50. Commentary on the Description of the Knowledge of the Modes of Psychic Power

In the description of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-ñāṇa), “a monk in this dispensation” refers to a monk within this teaching (sāsana). In the phrase “possessed of concentration of intention and volitional formations of effort (chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgata),” concentration that has intention as its cause, or concentration that has intention as its predominant factor, is called concentration of intention (chanda-samādhi). This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the intention to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) the predominant factor. Formations that have become primary are volitional formations of effort (padhāna-saṅkhāra). This is a designation for the energy of Right Effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya) which accomplishes the fourfold task. The plural form is used by way of accomplishing the fourfold task. “Possessed of” (samannāgata) means being endowed with both concentration of intention and volitional formations of effort. “Base of power” (iddhipāda) is so called either because of the reason of attainment (nipphatti), meaning the sense of succeeding, or because by this factor, beings succeed, prosper, and reach excellence...
305:
The remaining group of consciousness and mental factors, which serve as the base (pāda) in the sense of being the foundation for the concentration of intention and volitional formations of effort—which are associated with wholesome consciousness such as access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) and have reached the designation of 'power' (iddhi)—is called the base of power (iddhipāda). Indeed, it is stated in the Suttanta classification (Suttanta-bhājanīya) of the Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga: “The base of power is the aggregate of feeling... the aggregate of consciousness of one who has become so.” And in the Abhidhamma classification (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya), it is stated: “The base of power is the contact, feeling... exertion (paggāha), and non-distraction (avikkhepa) of one who has become so.” Therefore, in the phrase “the remaining group of consciousness and mental factors,” it should be understood that by making any one of intention (chanda), concentration (samādhi), or volitional formations of effort (padhāna-saṅkhāra) the 'power' (iddhi), the other two along with the remaining factors are called “remaining” (sesa).

In this way, the four mental aggregates and all factors such as contact are included. By this method, the meaning should also be understood for the remaining factors of energy (vīriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā). Just as concentration obtained by making intention the predominant factor is called concentration of intention (chanda-samādhi), so too concentration obtained by making energy, consciousness, or investigation the predominant factor is called concentration of investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi), and so on. Thus, in each single base of power, the three factors such as intention, energy, consciousness, and investigation are both 'power' (iddhi) and 'base of power' (iddhipāda). However, the remaining four associated mental aggregates are only the 'base of power' (iddhipāda). Alternatively, since these three factors succeed only together with the four associated aggregates and not without them, for that reason, all four aggregates are called 'power' (iddhi) in the sense of succeeding, and 'base' (pāda) in the sense of being the foundation.

In the phrase “possessed of concentration of energy and volitional formations of effort (vīriya-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgata),” both 'energy' (vīriya) and 'volitional formations of effort' (padhāna-saṅkhāra) refer to the single mental factor of energy. If it is asked why it is stated in two ways, it is because energy is first mentioned to show its state as a predominant factor (adhipati), and then the term 'volitional formations of effort' is used to show its accomplishment of the fourfold task. It is precisely because it is stated in two ways that it is said there are three factors here in this base of power of energy as well.

Some teachers, however, say that because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga, “Power (iddhi) is the success, fulfillment, succeeding, and fulfilling of those various factors,” power is unproduced (anipphanna), and only the base of power (iddhipāda) is produced (nipphanna). But in this text, the conclusion is made that both power and the base of power are produced (nipphanna) realities and are affected by the three characteristics. It should be understood that by terms such as 'power' (iddhi) and 'success' (samiddhi), only the factors themselves are spoken of by way of the mode of succeeding.

“Develops” (bhāveti) means repeatedly practicing and cultivating. As in the Suttanta-bhājanīya, the development of the bases of power here is also purely mundane (lokiya). Therefore, one who wishes to first accomplish the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-abhiññā)...
306:
A person developing mundane psychic powers (lokiya iddhipāda), having attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) and mastery over the eight kasiṇas such as the earth kasiṇa, disciplines the mind through these fourteen modes: (1) kasiṇānuloma (forward through kasiṇas), (2) kasiṇapaṭiloma (backward through kasiṇas), (3) kasiṇānulomapaṭiloma (forward and backward through kasiṇas), (4) jhānānuloma (forward through jhānas), (5) jhānapaṭiloma (backward through jhānas), (6) jhānānulomapaṭiloma (forward and backward through jhānas), (7) jhānukkantika (skipping jhānas), (8) kasiṇukkantika (skipping kasiṇas), (9) jhānakasiṇukkantika (skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas), (10) aṅgasaṅkantika (shifting factors), (11) ārammaṇasaṅkantika (shifting objects), (12) aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantika (shifting both factors and objects), (13) aṅgavavatthāna (defining factors), and (14) ārammaṇavavatthāna (defining objects). Having thus disciplined the mind, one repeatedly enters jhāna by way of making desire (chanda), energy (vīriya), mind (citta), or investigation (vīmaṃsā) the predominant factor. Some teachers also desire the defining of both factors and objects (aṅgārammaṇavavatthāna). For a person endowed with past supporting conditions (upanissaya), it is also appropriate to perform this by merely having mastery over the four jhānas of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) in the kasiṇas. Thus, the person developing concentration associated with each respective iddhipāda exerts the fourfold energy, starting with "for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states," and knowing the decline and increase of that energy, exerts for the state of balanced energy. That person, having thus saturated and developed the mind in the four iddhipādas, accomplishes the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-abhiññā).

In the passage beginning with "So imesu catūsu iddhipādesu," the word "So" (He) refers to that monk who possesses the four developed iddhipādas. "Saturates and develops the mind in the four iddhipādas" means that by repeatedly entering jhāna and making one of the factors such as desire (chanda) predominant, one saturates and develops the mind in them; the meaning is that one causes the mental continuum to be saturated with mental factors like desire. "Disciplines" (paridameti) means making the mind free from the poisons of lust (rāga) and so on. The preceding statement is the cause for the subsequent one. Indeed, a mind that is saturated and developed is said to be disciplined. "Makes it malleable" means making the mind that is already tamed reach mastery (vasībhāva). A mind that follows one's will is called "malleable" (mudu). "Wieldy" (kammañña) means making it fit for work. A malleable mind is wieldy for work like well-refined gold; here, however, it means wieldy for the work of performing psychic powers. "So" (He) refers to that monk whose mind is thus saturated and developed. The passage "He merges the body into the mind" and so on is spoken to show the procedure for the successful movement of the mind as desired at the time of performing psychic powers. In that passage, "He merges the body into the mind" means he merges, places, or mounts his own physical body (karajakāya) into the foundation jhāna mind (pādakajjhāna-citta); the meaning is that he makes the body follow the will of the mind. Doing so is helpful for traveling with an invisible body. "He merges the mind into the body" means he merges or mounts the foundation jhāna mind into his own physical body...
307:
...places [it], and makes the mind follow the body (making it similar to the body). Doing so is helpful for traveling with a visible body. There is also a variant reading 'samādahati', which means 'establishes'. 'He transforms the mind by way of the body' means taking the foundation jhāna mind and mounting it upon the physical body (karajakāya), making it follow the body; this is a synonym (vevacana) for merging the mind into the body (samodahana). 'He transforms the body by way of the mind' means taking the physical body and mounting it upon the foundation jhāna mind, making it follow the mind; this is a synonym for merging the body into the mind. 'Adhiṭṭhāti' (He determines) means he determines, "Let it be thus." The term 'pariṇāma' (transformation) is mentioned to explain the meaning of 'samodahana', and 'adhiṭṭhāna' (determination) is mentioned to explain the meaning of 'pariṇāma'. Since 'samodahati' is the root term, and 'pariṇāmeti' and 'adhiṭṭhāti' are terms defining its meaning, it is said "having transformed" (pariṇāmetvā) and "having determined" (adhiṭṭhahitvā) by way of those two terms; it is not said "having merged" (samodahitvā).

'He abides having entered the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness into the body' means that by way of attaining the perception of bliss (sukhasaññā) and the perception of lightness (lahusaññā) which arise together with the fourth jhāna, he abides having entered (inserted) them into the physical body. For him whose body is entered by that perception, the physical body becomes light like a tuft of cotton. 'So' (He) refers to that monk who has performed the said procedure. In the phrase 'with the mind thus developed', the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) indicates either a characteristic or a cause; the meaning is 'due to the mind being the cause, having been thus developed'. 'Pure' (parisuddha) means pure because of the state of purity of mindfulness through equanimity (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi). Because it is pure, it is 'bright' (pariyodāta), meaning radiant (pabhassara). 'For the sake of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power' (iddhividha-ñāṇāya) means for the sake of knowledge in the categories of psychic power or the varieties of psychic power. 'He directs the mind' means that when the mind which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā-pādaka) has arisen in the manner described, that monk directs the preparatory mind (parikamma-citta) for the attainment of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power; he removes it from the kasiṇa object and sends it towards the iddhividha-abhiññā. 'Abhininnāmeti' means he makes it incline towards the psychic power to be attained. 'So' (He) refers to that monk who has thus directed the mind. 'Anekavihitaṃ' means of many kinds, of various sorts. 'Iddhividhaṃ' means a category of psychic power or a variety of psychic power. 'Paccanubhoti' means he experiences, touches, realizes, or attains.

Now, to show the many kinds of that category of psychic power, it is said, 'Being one, he becomes many,' and so on. Therein, 'Being one' means being one naturally as before performing the psychic power. 'He becomes many' means he desires to walk back and forth in the presence of many people, or desires to recite, or [desires to answer] a question...
308:
Whether one wishes to engage in recitation or wishes to ask questions, one can become a hundred or a thousand. How does this happen? Having perfected the states that are the ground, the basis, the step, and the root of psychic power (iddhi), and having entered and emerged from the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), if one desires a hundred forms, one performs the preliminary work (parikamma) by thinking, "May I become a hundred, may I become a hundred." Then, having entered and emerged from the basis jhāna once more, one makes a determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Simultaneously with the mind of determination, one becomes a hundred. The same method applies to a thousand and so on. If it is not successful in this way, one should perform the preliminary work again, enter [the jhāna] for a second time, emerge, and then make the determination. Indeed, in the Saṃyutta Commentary, it is said: "It is proper to enter [the jhāna] once or twice."

In that process, the basis-jhāna mind has the sign (nimitta) as its object. The preliminary minds have the hundred or the thousand as their object. Furthermore, these occur only by way of appearance (color and form), not by way of concept (paññatti). The mind of determination likewise has the hundred or the thousand as its object. That mind, like the first attainment (appanā) mind, arises only once immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) as a fourth fine-material jhāna (rūpāvacara catuttha jhāna) mind. In that creation, because the many created forms are emanated without specific distinction, they are exactly like the possessor of psychic power. Whatever the possessor of psychic power does—whether standing, sitting, speaking, or remaining silent—those created forms do exactly the same.

However, if one wishes to create various appearances—some in the first stage of life (youth), some in the middle stage, some in the last stage; likewise, those with long hair, those with half-shaved heads, those with fully shaved heads, those with mixed hair; those wearing bright red robes, those wearing pale robes; those reciting Pali, preaching the Dhamma, chanting with a melodious voice, asking questions, answering questions, preparing dye, sewing robes, washing robes, and so on—or if one wishes to perform other various activities, that monk, having emerged from the basis jhāna, should perform the preliminary work in the manner beginning with "Let this many monks be in the first stage of life," and then enter [the jhāna] again, emerge, and make the determination. Simultaneously with the mind of determination, they become exactly as desired. This same method applies to such passages as "Having been many, he becomes one."

This is the distinction: After this monk has created such a state of being many, if he thinks again, "Being one alone, I will walk back and forth, I will recite, I will ask a question," or if, out of fewness of wishes (appicchatā), he thinks, "This monastery has few monks; if visitors come, where could so many identical monks have come from? They will surely know me, thinking, 'This is the elder's psychic power'," and thus desires in the midst of it to be one, he enters and emerges from the basis jhāna, performs the preliminary work by thinking, "May I be one," enters and emerges again, and then [determines], "May I be one"...
309:
...one should make the determination. Simultaneously with the mind of determination, one becomes one alone. However, for one who does not do so, one becomes one alone naturally by the power of the predetermined time.

'Āvibhāva' means making manifest or clear. 'Tirobhāva' means making concealed or hidden. The phrases 'Āvibhāvaṃ paccanubhoti' (He experiences manifestation) and 'Tirobhāvaṃ paccanubhoti' (He experiences concealment) are connected with the preceding word 'paccanubhoti'. Regarding these two, when this possessor of psychic power wishes to effect manifestation, he makes darkness into light, or makes the concealed open, or makes the unmanifest manifest. How does he do it? Just as one might be seen even if concealed or standing far away, when he wishes to make himself or another so, he emerges from the basis jhāna and adverts, "May this darkness become light," or "May this concealed thing become open," or "May this unmanifest thing become manifest." Having thus performed the preliminary work, he makes the determination in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the determination, it becomes exactly as determined. Others standing far away can see, and if he himself wishes to see, he sees. When he wishes to effect concealment (tirobhāva), however, he makes light into darkness, or the unconcealed concealed, or the manifest unmanifest. How does he do it? Just as one is not seen even if unconcealed or standing nearby, when he wishes to make himself or another so, he emerges from the basis jhāna and adverts, "May this place of light become darkness," or "May this unconcealed thing become concealed," or "May this manifest thing become unmanifest." Having thus performed the preliminary work, he makes the determination in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the determination, it becomes exactly as determined. Others standing nearby do not see, and if he himself does not wish to see, he does not see. Furthermore, all manifest miracles are called 'āvibhāva', and unmanifest miracles are called 'tirobhāva'. Among these two, in a manifest miracle, both the psychic power and the possessor of psychic power are evident. This should be illustrated by the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya). In an unmanifest miracle, only the psychic power is evident, not the possessor of psychic power. This should be illustrated by the Mahaka Sutta and the Brahmanimantanika Sutta.

'Tirokuṭṭa' means the other side of a wall, or the part beyond the wall. This same method applies to 'tiropākāra' (beyond an enclosure) and 'tiropabbata' (beyond a mountain). 'Kuṭṭa' means the wall of a house. 'Pākāra' means the surrounding wall of a house, a monastery, a village, and so on. 'Pabbata' means an earth mountain or a stone mountain. 'Asajjamāno' means without sticking or being obstructed. For example...
310:
"Ākāse" means as if in the sky. One who wishes to travel in this manner should attain the space-kasiṇa (ākāsa-kasiṇa), emerge from it, and after adverting to a wall, an enclosure, or a mountain and performing the preliminary work (parikamma), should resolve: "Let there be space." It then becomes space. For one who wishes to descend, it becomes a hollow; for one who wishes to ascend, it becomes a hollow; for one who wishes to go through, it becomes a hole. That person of psychic power goes through that place without sticking. If, while that monk is traveling after making a resolution, a mountain or a tree should appear in between, one might ask: "Should he attain [the jhāna] and resolve again?" There is no fault in attaining and resolving again. Indeed, attaining and resolving again is like taking the support (nissaya) from a preceptor. However, in reality, because this monk has already resolved "Let there be space," it remains space. By the power of the previous resolution, it is impossible for another mountain or tree produced by the seasons (utu-mayo) to arise in between. But if it is created by another person of psychic power, the first creation is stronger. In that case, the latter monk must go either above or below that creation.

In the phrase "diving and emerging in the earth," "emerging" (ummujjana) means rising up, and "diving" (nimujjana) means sinking down. The combination is called "diving and emerging" (ummujjana-nimujjana). One who wishes to do this should attain the water-kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa), emerge from it, and after delimiting a certain area and performing the preliminary work, resolve in the manner already described: "Let the earth in this area be water." Simultaneously with the resolution, the earth in the delimited area becomes water. He performs diving and emerging there as if in natural water. Not only diving and emerging, but he can also perform whatever he wishes, such as bathing, drinking, washing the face, or washing utensils. Not only can he make it water, but if he wishes for ghee, oil, honey, molasses, etc., he adverts to it, performs the preliminary work, and resolves: "Let this and that much of this substance be here," and it becomes exactly as resolved. When he takes it out and puts it in a vessel, the ghee is ghee, the oil is oil, and the water is water. If he wishes to get wet, he gets wet; if he does not wish to get wet, he does not. That earth becomes water only for that monk; for others, it remains earth. People there still walk on foot, travel by vehicles, and perform farming. If this monk wishes, "Let it be water for them too," then it becomes so. When the delimited time has passed, except for the original water in jars or ponds, the rest of the delimited area becomes earth again.

In the phrase "he goes on water without breaking [the surface]," water that one sinks into when stepping on it is called "broken water"; the opposite is "unbroken water." One who wishes to go in this way...
311:
...should attain the *pathavī-kasiṇa* (earth kasiṇa), emerge from it, define the area saying "Let the water in this much space be earth," perform the preliminary work, and resolve in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, the water in the defined area becomes earth. There, he walks as if on the ground. Not only does he walk, but he can also adopt whatever posture he wishes. He can create not only earth; for objects like gems, golden mountains, or trees, he contemplates whatever he wishes and resolves in the manner already described, and it becomes exactly as resolved. That water becomes earth only for that monk; for other people, it remains water. Fish, turtles, water-crows, and so on, move about as they please. If this monk wishes to make that water earth for other people as well, he can certainly do so. However, with the passing of the defined time, it becomes water again.

"In the sky also he travels cross-legged" means that in the open sky, he can travel in a posture with his thighs bound all around. "A winged bird" means a bird endowed with wings, not a bird with incomplete wings or one whose wings have been plucked. Only such a bird can travel in the sky. A monk who wishes to travel in the sky in this way should attain the *pathavī-kasiṇa*, emerge from it, and if he wishes to go sitting, he should define an area the size of a cross-legged seat, perform the preliminary work, and resolve in the manner already described. If he wishes to go lying down, he should define an area the size of a couch; if he wishes to go on foot, an area the size of a path. Thus, having defined a suitable area, he should resolve "Let there be earth" in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, it becomes earth. A monk who wishes to travel in the sky should also be one who has attained the Divine Eye (*dibba-cakkhu*). Why? Because in the middle of the journey, there may be mountains, trees, and so on, produced by the elements (*utu*), or Nagas, Garudas, and so on, might create mountains, trees, etc., out of jealousy; [the Divine Eye is needed] in order to see them. What should be done upon seeing those mountains, trees, and so on? He should attain the basic *jhāna* (*pādaka-jhāna*), emerge from it, perform the preliminary work, and resolve "Let there be space." Furthermore, this monk should be one who has attained the Divine Eye for the purpose of descending in a suitable place. For if he descends in an unsuitable place, such as a bathing ghat or a village gate, he will become visible to the public. Therefore, seeing with the Divine Eye, he avoids unsuitable places and descends in a suitable place.

In the phrase "these moons and suns of such great power, of such great majesty," the "great power" (*mahiddhika*) of the moon and sun is to be understood by their traveling above at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas; their "great majesty" (*mahānubhāva*) is to be understood by their providing light to three continents simultaneously. Or, they are of great power due to such traveling above and the spreading of light; and because of that very great power...
312:
He possesses great power. 'Paramasati' means touching all around or touching a part. 'Parimajjati' means stroking extensively, like rubbing the surface of a mirror. This supernormal power of the monk is accomplished only through the power of the jhana that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññāpādaka-jhāna); there is no restriction of kasina-attainments here. If that monk wishes to go and touch [the moon and sun], he goes and touches them. If, however, he wishes to touch them while sitting or lying right here, he resolves, 'Let them be within arm's reach.' By the power of the resolution, when the moon and sun come within his reach like palm fruits fallen from their stalks, he touches them, or he touches them by stretching out his hand. If it is asked whether it is the kamma-born matter (upādinnaka) or the non-kamma-born matter (anupādinnaka) that increases when stretching the hand, it is the non-kamma-born matter (utuja-rūpa) that increases based on the kamma-born matter. In doing so, he does not only touch the moon and sun; if he wishes, he can make them a footstool and place his feet on them, make them a chair and sit, make them a bed and lie down, or make them a leaning board and lean against them. Just as one monk does this, another can do the same. Even if hundreds of thousands of monks do this, it is accomplished for each one in the same way. The movement and illumination of the moon and sun remain just as they were. Just as the moon's disc appears in a thousand pots filled with water, yet the natural movement and illumination of the moon remain normal, so too is this miraculous display. 'He wields power with his body even as far as the Brahma world' means that, having delimited the Brahma world, he performs various types of direct knowledge within that range, wielding mastery with his own body. The details of this will be made clear in the 'Discussion on Supernormal Powers' (Iddhikathā). 

## The Description of the Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Powers is concluded. 

## 51. Description of the Knowledge of the Purification of the Divine Ear-element 

In explaining the knowledge of the purification of the divine ear-element, the passage beginning with 'even sounds that are far' is spoken to show the method for a beginner monk who wishes to arouse the direct knowledge of the divine ear. Therein, 'the sound-sign of sounds that are far' means the sound in the midst of sounds occurring at a distance. Sound itself is called the 'sound-sign' (sadda-nimitta) because it acts as the cause for focusing. Although it says 'at a distance,' it refers only to the range within which the natural ear can hear. 'Oḷārikānaṃ' means of gross sounds; 'sukhumānaṃ' means of subtle sounds; 'saṇhasaṇhānaṃ' means of sounds more subtle than subtle, meaning extremely subtle sounds. By this, extremely subtle sounds are meant. A meditator who is a beginner wishing to arouse this knowledge should attain the jhana that is the basis for direct knowledge, and after emerging, with the mind of preliminary-work concentration (parikamma-samādhi), he should first contemplate gross sounds within the natural range of hearing. He should contemplate the sounds of lions and so on in the forest; the sound of a bell, a drum, or a conch in the monastery; the sound of novices and young monks reciting with all their strength; the natural sounds of speech such as 'What, venerable sir?' or 'What, friend?'; the sounds of birds, the wind, footsteps, the 'ci-ci' sound of boiling water, the sound of palm leaves drying in the sun, and the sounds of red ants, black ants, and so on. In this way, starting from very gross sounds, he should contemplate sounds that are progressively more and more subtle.
313:
A meditator who is a beginner wishing to arouse this knowledge should emerge from the base jhana and, with the mind of preliminary-work concentration, first contemplate gross sounds within the natural range of hearing, such as the sounds of lions and so on in the forest. He should contemplate the sound of a bell, a drum, or a conch in the monastery; the sound of novices and young monks reciting with all their strength; the natural sounds of speech such as 'What, venerable sir?' or 'What, friend?'; the sounds of birds, the wind, footsteps, the 'ci-ci' sound of boiling water, the sound of palm leaves drying in the sun, and the sounds of red ants, black ants, and so on. In this way, starting from very gross sounds, he should contemplate sounds that are progressively more and more subtle. 

One who does this should, in the ten directions such as the East, progressively attend to the sound-sign in each direction according to the method mentioned. While attending, among the sounds heard with the natural ear, he should give up hearing with the natural ear and attend with the mind-door consciousness. To him, those sounds are clear even to the natural mind, but they are exceedingly clear to the mind of preliminary-work concentration. As he attends to the sound-sign in this way, thinking 'Now the divine ear-element will arise,' the mind-door adverting consciousness arises making one of those sounds its object. When that mind has ceased, four or five impulsions (javana) occur. Among those impulsions, the first three or four are sense-sphere impulsions named preliminary-work (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhu). The fourth or fifth impulsion is the absorption mind (appanā-citta) associated with the fourth jhana of the fine-material sphere. Therein, the knowledge that arises together with that absorption mind is called the divine ear-element. 

One who wishes to make that divine ear-element knowledge powerful should delimit a space of about one finger-breadth, thinking 'I shall hear sounds within this range,' and then expand it. From there, he should expand it by degrees—two finger-breadths, four, eight, a span, a cubit, the interior of a room, the front of a building, a palace, a precinct, a monastery, a service village, a district, and so on, up to the world-system, or even beyond the world-system, delimiting it further and further. A person who has attained direct knowledge in this way can hear sounds within the space pervaded by the object of the base jhana through the power of direct knowledge, even without re-entering the base jhana. One who hears in this way, even if there is a single uproar of sounds from conchs, drums, and tabors reaching as far as the Brahma world, is able to distinguish them if he wishes to do so, thinking 'This is the sound of a conch, this is the sound of a drum.' After hearing a sound that has meaning through the knowledge of direct knowledge, he later understands the meaning with sense-sphere consciousness.
314:
The divine ear-element (dibba-sota-abhiññā) arises only for those with natural hearing, not for the deaf. It is said that even if the natural hearing is destroyed after the higher knowledge has been attained, the divine ear-element does not perish.

In the phrase "so dibbāya sotadhātuyā," it is called "dibba" (divine) because it is similar to that of the devas. To explain in detail, the divine ear-element of the devas, which is produced by well-practiced wholesome kamma, is not obstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and being free from defilements, is capable of receiving objects even at a distance; thus it is called "dibba." This ear-element of knowledge (ñāṇa-sotadhātu) of this monk, which is produced by the power of energy and meditation, is also called "dibba" because it is similar to that of those devas. Alternatively, it is called "dibba" because it is obtained by means of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra/jhāna) and because it itself relies on the divine abiding. It is called "sotadhātu" (ear-element) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of being non-soul (nijjiwa). It is also called "sotadhātu" because it performs the function of the natural ear-element and is similar to the ear-element. With that divine ear-element (he hears). "Visuddhāya" means purified and free from defilements. "Atikkantamānusikāya" means surpassing the range of human hearing and standing beyond the human fleshly ear-element by hearing sounds.

"Ubho sadde suṇāti" means he hears two kinds of sounds. Which two? Divine and human; it means he hears the sounds of devas and humans. By this, the inclusion of sounds by part is to be understood. "Ye dūre santike ca" means he hears sounds that are far away, even in other world-systems (cakka-vāḷa), and those that are near, even the sounds of insects residing in his own body. By this, the inclusion of all sounds without exception is to be understood.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of the Purification of the Ear-element is finished.

## 52. Explanation of the Knowledge of Penetrating Others' Minds (Cetopariya-ñāṇa)

In the explanation of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, the phrase "so evaṃ pajānāti" (he knows thus) indicates the procedure to be described now. The words "this matter is produced by the faculty of joy (somanassindriya)," etc., refer to the procedure to be practiced by a beginner meditator (jhāyī). How? A meditator who wishes to produce this knowledge of penetrating others' minds should first produce the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). This knowledge of penetrating others' minds is accomplished by the power of the divine eye; that divine eye is the preliminary work (parikamma) for this knowledge. Therefore, that monk should expand the light (āloka-kasiṇa) and, with the divine eye, search for the mind by repeatedly observing the color of the blood that exists depending on the heart-base (hadaya-rūpa) of another person. For that blood, when wholesome joy (kusala-somanassa) is present, is red like the color of a ripe banyan fruit. When unwholesome joy (akusala-somanassa) is present, that same blood is turbid. When grief (domanassa) is present...
315:
...when grief (domanassa) is present, the blood dependent on the heart-base is dark-black like the color of a ripe jambu fruit and turbid. When equanimity associated with the wholesome (kusala-upekkhā) is present, it is clear like the color of sesame oil. When equanimity associated with the unwholesome (akusala-upekkhā) is present, that same clear blood is turbid. Therefore, that monk, by repeatedly observing the color of another's heart-blood and searching for the mind, thinking, "This matter is produced by the faculty of joy, this matter is produced by the faculty of grief, this matter is produced by the faculty of equanimity," should make the knowledge of penetrating others' minds strong. When that knowledge has become strong, he gradually knows all minds classified as sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), etc., by passing from mind to mind without needing to see the heart-matter. This matter is also stated in the Commentary:

"When one wishes to know another's mind in the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi), whose heart-matter does he see, or whose change in faculties does he observe? He observes no one's. This is the domain of one with psychic power (iddhimant), such that by reflecting on the mind anywhere, he knows the sixteen types of mind. However, this discussion is stated in terms of one who has not yet practiced the direct observation without the heart-blood." (Visuddhimagga 2.401).

"Para-sattānaṃ" means other beings, excluding oneself. "Para-puggalānaṃ" has the same meaning as this, but the distinction in terms is made according to the nature of those to be taught (veneyya) and the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa). "Cetasā ceto paricca pajānāti" means that having delimited their minds with his own mind, he knows them in various ways by way of lust (sarāga), etc.

In the phrases such as "sarāgaṃ vā," the word "vā" (or) has the sense of inclusion (samuccaya). Therein, the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed are called "sarāga-citta" (mind with lust). The remaining wholesome and indeterminate (abyākata) consciousness of the four planes are called "vītarāga-citta" (mind without lust). The two types of consciousness accompanied by grief (domanassa) and the two types accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca)—these four types of consciousness are not included in this dyad. However, some Elders include them under the term "vītarāga." The two types of consciousness accompanied by grief are called "sadosa-citta" (mind with hate). All wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes are called "vītadosa-citta" (mind without hate). The remaining ten types of unwholesome consciousness are not included in this dyad. However, some Elders include them under the term "vītadosa."

In the dyad "samohaṃ vītamohaṃ," only the two types accompanied by doubt and restlessness are called "samoha" (mind with delusion) by way of having delusion as the sole root. However, since delusion (moha) occurs in all unwholesome consciousness, all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness should be understood as "samoha." The remaining wholesome and indeterminate consciousness are "vītamoha." Consciousness accompanied by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) is "saṅkhitta" (shrunken). Consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca) is "vikkhitta" (distracted). Fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) consciousness are "mahaggata" (exalted). The remaining consciousness are "amahaggata." All consciousness of the three planes are "sauttara" (surpassable).
316:
Supramundane consciousness is called unsurpassed (anuttara) consciousness. Consciousness that has reached access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) is called concentrated (samāhita). Consciousness that has not reached either of these is called unconcentrated (asamāhita). Consciousness that has reached the five kinds of liberation—namely, liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti)—is called liberated (vimutta). Consciousness that has not reached any of these five kinds of liberation should be known as unliberated (avimutta). Thus, a monk who has attained the knowledge of encompassing others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) knows consciousness in its sixteenfold variety. However, worldlings (puthujjanas) do not know the path and fruition consciousness of Noble Ones (ariyas). Even lower Noble Ones do not know the path and fruition consciousness of higher Noble Ones. But higher Noble Ones know the consciousness of lower Noble Ones.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Encompassing Others' Minds is finished.

## 53. The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives

In the description of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the words "thus he knows" and so forth are spoken to show the method of producing that knowledge for one who desires to produce the knowledge of recollection of past lives, whose mind has been developed by the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Indeed, by seeing dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in due order, one sees the present result-cluster (phala-saṅkhepa) known as consciousness, mind-and-matter, the sixfold sense base, contact, and feeling. One sees the cause-cluster (hetu-saṅkhepa) known as kamma and defilements (kamma-kilesa) in the previous life, which is the cause of that result. One sees the result-cluster in that same previous life, which is the cause of that cause. One sees the cause-cluster in the third life, which is the cause of that result. Thus, by seeing dependent origination, one sees the succession of births. In this way, the reflection on dependent origination is of great benefit to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

In that text, "When this is, that is; with the arising of this, that arises" is the summary statement (uddesa) of the description of dependent origination. Why is it taught in two ways when the meaning is accomplished by either one of these statements? It is because there is a distinction in meaning. How so? "When this is" means when this condition exists. This is a general statement referring to all conditions. "That is" means this conditionally arisen state (paccayasuppanna) occurs. This is a general statement referring to all conditionally arisen states. By this entire statement, the doctrine of non-causality (ahetuka-vāda) is refuted. For states that arise from conditions do not arise without conditions, and thus they are not "causeless."

"With the arising of this" means the arising of this condition is the root cause. This is a statement showing that all conditions have the nature of arising. "That arises" means this conditionally arisen state arises because of that. This is a statement showing how all conditionally arisen states arise from that [condition]. By this entire statement, the doctrine of eternalist non-causality (sassata-ahetuka-vāda) is refuted. Indeed, states that have the nature of arising are impermanent (anicca). Therefore, even though they have a cause, these states have only impermanent causes; it means they do not have causes such as "Primordial Nature" (Pakati) or "the Self" (Purisa), which are considered eternal in the world.
317:
The word "yadidaṃ" (that is to say) is for pointing out the meaning to be described. In the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), that which a result depends upon to arise is the condition (paccaya). "Paṭicca" (depending on) means not without, not having set aside. "Eti" (comes/goes) means it both arises and persists. Alternatively, the meaning of "paccaya" is the state of being a helper (upakāraka). Ignorance is [the state], and that ignorance is also a helping condition; thus it is "ignorance-condition" (avijjāpaccaya). Therefore, the construction is: "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come into being." The word "come into being" (sambhavanti) should be applied to the remaining terms in the same way.

In the terms sorrow and so forth: sorrowing is sorrow (soka). Lamenting is lamentation (parideva). It is called pain (dukkha) because it causes suffering. Or, it is called "dukkha" because it destroys in two ways through the power of arising (uppāda) and presence (ṭhī). The state of an unhappy person is grief (domanassa). Intense exhaustion is despair (upāyāsa). "Sambhavanti" means they are produced. The word "evaṃ" (thus) is an illustration of the method already described. By that word, he shows that [this mass of suffering] arises only through causes such as ignorance, and not through [causes like] a creator god (issara-nimmāna) and so forth. "Etassa" (of this) means of what has been mentioned. "Kevalassa" (whole/only) means unmixed [with happiness] or entire. "Dukkhandhassa" (of the mass of suffering) means of the collection of suffering; it is not the arising of a being, nor the arising of pleasure, beauty, and so forth. "Samudaya" means arising. "Hoti" means it occurs.

In that [dependent origination], what is ignorance (avijjā)? It is non-knowledge of the truth of suffering, non-knowledge of the truth of the origin of suffering, non-knowledge of the truth of the cessation of suffering, non-knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (the truth of the path), non-knowledge of the past (the prior end), non-knowledge of the future (the posterior end), non-knowledge of both the past and the future, and non-knowledge of states that are dependently arisen through specific conditionality (idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppanna). What are volitional formations (saṅkhārā)? They are meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra), verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra), and mental formations (citta-saṅkhāra). The eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere and the five wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere are meritorious volitional formations. The twelve unwholesome volitions are demeritorious volitional formations. The four wholesome volitions of the immaterial sphere are imperturbable volitional formations. Volition occurring in the body-door is bodily formation; volition occurring in the speech-door is verbal formation; volition occurring in the mind-door is mental formation.

Here, it might be asked: "How is it to be known that these formations arise because of ignorance?" It is known because they exist when ignorance exists. To explain: for someone in whom the non-knowledge called ignorance regarding suffering and so forth has not been abandoned, first, through non-knowledge regarding the truth of suffering and the past etc., he takes the suffering of saṃsāra to be happiness and undertakes the three kinds of formations which are the causes of that very suffering. Through non-knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering], he takes formations accompanied by craving—which are the causes of suffering—to be the causes of happiness and undertakes them. Through non-knowledge regarding cessation and the path, he perceives specific destinations (gati) as the cessation of suffering, even though they are not the cessation of suffering; and in things like sacrifices and ascetic vows to gods, which are not the path to cessation...
318:
Perceiving the path to cessation and longing for the cessation of suffering, one undertakes the three types of formations, beginning with sacrifices and practices that lead to celestial rebirth. Furthermore, because ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths has not been abandoned, that person does not recognize as suffering the result of merit—which is called suffering because it is interspersed with many dangers such as birth, aging, sickness, and death. To attain that [result], they undertake meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) consisting of bodily, verbal, and mental formations. This is like a man desiring a celestial nymph jumping from a mountain peak. Not seeing the suffering due to change (vipariṇāmadukkha) which causes great distress at the end of that meritorious result—though it is called happiness—and not seeing its lack of gratification, they undertake that same meritorious volitional formation which is the cause of that suffering due to change. This is like a moth falling into a lamp flame, or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking a honey-smeared sword blade. And not seeing the danger in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, etc., which bring bad results, they undertake demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) occurring through the three doors, due to the perception of happiness and being overcome by defilements. This is like a fool playing with excrement, or like one wishing to die eating poison. Also in the case of formless resultants, not understanding the suffering due to the change of formations, and through the perversion (vipallāsa) of 'permanence,' etc., they undertake imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) which are mental formations. This is like a lost person heading towards a city of demons. Thus, it is because of the existence of ignorance that formations arise, not because of its absence. Therefore, it should be understood: 'These formations have ignorance as their condition.'

Here, an objector says: 'We accept that ignorance is a condition for formations. But is ignorance the only condition for formations, or are there other conditions?' If it is only one, then the doctrine of a single cause (ekakāraṇavāda) follows. If there are others, then the description of a single cause as 'With ignorance as condition, formations' is inappropriate. [The answer is:] It is not inappropriate; it is appropriate. Why? Because—

'In this [Dependent Origination], one [effect] does not arise from one [cause], nor many [effects] from many [causes], nor one [effect] from many [causes]. However, there is a purpose in showing one cause and one effect.'

For the Blessed One shows only one cause and one effect because of predominance in some places, clarity in some places, uniqueness (asādhāraṇa) in some places, and according to the elegance of the teaching and the suitability for those to be led (veneyya). Therefore, although other causes for formations such as physical base, object, and co-nascent phenomena exist, for one who habitually contemplates gratification—
319:
Because of the words, "Craving increases" (S.ii.52) and "With the arising of ignorance, taints arise" (M.i.104), although there are other causes for formations such as craving, ignorance (avijjā) should be understood as the cause of formations because it is principal, because it is evident in the words, "Bhikkhus, the ignorant man, gone to ignorance, fashions even a meritorious formation," and because it is unique (asādhāraṇa). By this statement explaining each cause and fruit, the benefit of explaining each cause and fruit throughout the entire Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) should be understood.

Here, an objector says: Even if this is so, how can ignorance, which is definitely of undesirable fruit and is faulty, be a condition for meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra)? Surely, sugarcane does not grow from a neem seed. [Response:] Why should it not be suitable? In the world:

"A condition for states is established as contrary or non-contrary, and likewise as similar or dissimilar; and those [fruits] are not only resultants."

Thus, although this ignorance has a definitely undesirable fruit by way of result (vipāka) and is faulty by way of its nature, it should be understood as a condition for all these meritorious formations, etc., as appropriate, by way of contrary or non-contrary conditions in terms of place, function, and nature, and by way of similar or dissimilar conditions.

Furthermore:
"He who is confused about death and rebirth, about the round of rebirths, about the characteristic of formations, and about states that are dependently arisen;
He fashions these three types of formations. Therefore, ignorance is the condition for those three types.
Just as a man born blind, who has no guide, sometimes walks on the right path and sometimes on the wrong path;
So the fool, wandering in the round of rebirths without a guide, sometimes performs merit and sometimes even demerit.
But when he knows the Dhamma and penetrates the Truths, then, with the subsiding of ignorance, he will proceed in peace."

"With formations as condition, consciousness" (saṅkhāra-paccayā viññāṇaṃ): There are six groups of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Among these six, eye-consciousness is of two types: wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant. Ear, nose, tongue, and body-consciousness are also of two types each. Mind-consciousness is of twenty-two types: two resultant mind-elements, three rootless mind-consciousness-elements, eight beautiful resultant consciousnesses, five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses, and four immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses. Thus, with these six types of consciousness, there are thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness in all.

In this phrase "With formations as condition, consciousness," an objection might arise: "How is it known that these mundane resultant consciousnesses occur because of causes such as meritorious formations?" [Response:] Because of the kamma that has been accumulated...
320:
Regarding the statement 'With formations as condition, consciousness [arises],' there are six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Among these six, eye-consciousness is of two types: wholesome resultant eye-consciousness and unwholesome resultant eye-consciousness. Similarly, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness are also of two types each. Mind-consciousness consists of 22 types: 2 resultant mind-elements, 3 rootless mind-consciousness elements, 8 resultant consciousnesses with roots, 5 fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses, and 4 immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses. Thus, all mundane resultant consciousnesses total 32.

In this regard, a question may arise: 'How is it to be known that this aforementioned consciousness arises with formations as condition?' It is known because in the absence of accumulated kamma, there is no result (vipāka). Indeed, this consciousness is a result, and a result cannot arise in the absence of accumulated kamma. If it could, then all results would arise for everyone, but they do not. Therefore, it should be known that 'this consciousness arises with formations as condition.' In fact, all these mundane resultant consciousnesses occur in two ways: during the course of existence (pavatti) and at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Among these, 13 types of consciousness—namely, the two sets of fivefold consciousness, the two mind-elements, and the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy—occur only during the course of existence in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). The remaining 19 types occur both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking in the three spheres of existence, as appropriate.

'Only this mere phenomenon, having obtained its conditions, passes into another existence;
There is no transmigration of it from the past existence, nor does it arise from there without a cause.'

Thus, it is said that only the mere phenomenon of mind and matter, having obtained its conditions, arises and passes into another existence; it is not a 'being,' nor a 'soul.' There is no transmigration of that mind and matter from the past existence to this one, nor does it manifest here without a cause (kamma) from that past existence. In this regard, the preceding consciousness is called 'death' (cuti) because it passes away, and the succeeding consciousness is called 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) because it connects with the new existence.

Here, an objector says: 'If there is no transmigration and yet manifestation occurs, then since the aggregates in this human existence have ceased, and since the kamma which is the cause of the fruit does not go to that next life, the fruit would belong to one person while the kamma was performed by another. If there is no enjoyer, for whom would that fruit be? Therefore, this explanation is not good.' To this objection, it is said:

'The fruit that arises in a continuum does not belong to another, nor is it from another;
The cultivation of seeds is the proof of this meaning.
By the very arising of the fruit, the conventional designation of "enjoyer" is established,
Just as when a tree bears fruit, it is conventionally said that "the tree fruits".'
321:
If someone should say: 'Even if this is so (that there is no self but results occur), these formations might be the conditions for the fruit either while they exist or while they no longer exist. If they are conditions while existing, their result should occur at the very moment of their occurrence. If they are conditions while no longer existing, they would always bring fruit both before and after the moment of their occurrence.' To him, it should be said: 'These are conditions because they have been performed (in one's own continuum), but they do not always bring fruit. In this matter, evidence such as a loan or a guarantee should be understood.'

In this teaching of 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises],' the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations are called 'name' (nāma). The four great elements and the derived matter dependent on the four great elements are called 'form' (rūpa). At the moment of rebirth-linking for womb-born and egg-born beings who do not obtain sex-matter, there are twenty types of matter—the heart-decad and the body-decad—and the three mental aggregates. These twenty-three phenomena should be understood as 'name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.' For those who obtain sex-matter, the sex-decad is added, making thirty-three. Among spontaneously born beings, at the moment of rebirth-linking for Brahmās such as those of the Brahma-group, there are thirty-nine types of matter—the eye, ear, and heart decads, and the life-nonad—and the three mental aggregates. These forty-two phenomena are 'name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.' In the sense-sphere existence, for other spontaneously born beings or moisture-born beings with complete sense-bases, there are seventy types of matter—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, heart, and sex decads—and the three mental aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking. These seventy-three phenomena are 'name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.' This is the maximum (ukkaṃsa) method. By the minimum (avakaṃsa) method, for those individuals who lack certain decads, name-and-form conditioned by consciousness at rebirth-linking should be understood by reducing them according to their respective deficiencies. For immaterial beings, only the three mental aggregates arise. For non-percipient beings, only the life-nonad from the group of matter arises. This is the method at the time of rebirth-linking.

In this regard, a question may arise: 'How is it to be known that rebirth-linking name-and-form arises with consciousness as condition?' It is known through scripture (Sutta) and through logic (Yukti). In the Suttas, the fact that feeling and so on have consciousness as their condition is established in many ways through such methods as 'phenomena that follow in the wake of consciousness' (Dhs. 62). Through logic: by the mind-produced matter seen here in the course of existence, it is established that consciousness is the condition for unseen (rebirth-linking) matter.
322: In the phrase "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," the 'name' which is the cause has already been explained under the 'name' which is the result. Specifically, in the name-and-form that is the cause of these six sense bases, 'form' consists of eleven types: the four great elements, the six base-forms, and the life-faculty. The six sense bases are the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base. Regarding this, one might ask: "How is it to be known that 'name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases'?" It is known because they exist when name-and-form exist. Indeed, only when those respective names and forms exist do those respective bases arise, and not otherwise. "With the six sense bases as condition, contact": briefly, there are only six types of contact, such as eye-contact. In detail, however, they are thirty-two, just like consciousness. "With contact as condition, feeling": feelings such as those born of eye-contact are taught as six by way of doors. In this context, they are thirty-two by way of classification. "With feeling as condition, craving": here, six types of craving are shown, such as craving for forms. Among them, each one is understood to be of three kinds according to the mode of occurrence. One who has suffering longs for happiness; one who has happiness desires even more. Equanimity, however, because of its peaceful nature, is spoken of simply as happiness. Therefore, all three feelings are conditions for craving. Thus, the Great Sage taught, "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]." "With craving as condition, clinging": there are four types of clinging—clinging to sense-pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and rituals, and clinging to a doctrine of self. "With clinging as condition, existence": here, kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) is intended. Rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava), however, is stated by way of extracting the term. "With existence as condition, birth": this is the manifestation of the rebirth mental aggregates and kamma-born matter due to the condition of kamma-existence. Regarding this, one might ask: "How is it to be known that 'existence is the condition for birth'?" It is known because differences such as inferiority and superiority are seen even when external conditions are equal. Indeed, even when external conditions such as parents, semen, blood, and nutriment are equal, a difference such as inferiority or superiority is seen even among twin beings. And that difference is not without a cause...
323:
...because of the absence [of other causes] at all times and for all beings. Since there is no other cause in the internal continuity of beings produced by that kamma-becoming, other than kamma-becoming itself, it has only kamma-becoming as its cause. Indeed, kamma alone is the cause of the differences among beings, such as low and high status. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Kamma divides beings, that is, into low and high status." (M. Ni. 3.289)

In the phrases "With birth as condition, aging and death," etc., since aging and death or states such as sorrow do not exist if there is no birth, but when there is birth, aging and death occur, and for the fool touched by the suffering known as aging and death, sorrow and so on occur—whether in connection with aging and death or not in connection with it when touched by various states of suffering—therefore, this birth should be understood as the condition for aging and death as well as for sorrow and so on.

In the phrases "With the mind thus developed," etc., "for the knowledge of recollecting past lives" (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya) means for the acquisition or attainment of this knowledge.
