"Manifold" (anekavihitaṃ) means of many kinds, of various sorts, or produced and described in many ways. "Past lives" (pubbenivāsaṃ) means the continuity of aggregates that dwelt in various lives, starting from the life immediately preceding. "Recollects" (anussarati) means to remember by following along by way of the sequence of aggregates or by way of death and rebirth. 

Six types of persons recollect these past lives: heretics (titthiyas), ordinary disciples (pakati-sāvakas), great disciples (mahā-sāvakas), chief disciples (agga-sāvakas), Paccekabuddhas, and Buddhas. 

Among them, heretics recollect only forty aeons, not beyond that. Why? Because of weak wisdom. Their wisdom is weak because they lack the discernment of mentality and materiality. Ordinary disciples, being of strong wisdom, recollect even a hundred or a thousand aeons. The eighty great disciples recollect a hundred thousand aeons. The two chief disciples recollect one incalculable (asankheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas recollect two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. This is the extent of their initial aspiration (abhinīhāra). For the Buddhas, however, there is no limit.

Heretics recollect only by the sequence of aggregates; they are unable to recollect by way of death and rebirth by leaving the sequence. Just as blind persons walk without letting go of their staff, so these heretics recollect without letting go of the sequence of aggregates. Ordinary disciples recollect by the sequence of aggregates and also transition to recollect by way of death and rebirth. The eighty great disciples are the same. For the two chief disciples, however, there is no need to follow the sequence of aggregates. For a single existence...
324:
Chief disciples see their passing away (cuti) and then perceive their rebirth (paṭisandhi); again, they see their passing away in another existence and perceive their rebirth. Thus, they proceed by moving only by way of passing away and rebirth. The Paccekabuddhas are the same as those chief disciples. For the Buddhas, however, there is no task of following the succession of aggregates, nor is there the task of moving by way of passing away and rebirth. For those Buddhas, whatever place they desire, whether below or above across many millions of aeons, that very place becomes manifest. Therefore, even contracting many millions of aeons, they descend into whatever place they desire, proceeding by way of the 'lion's descent' (sīhokkanta). As they proceed in this way, their knowledge, being unattached to the intervening births, takes hold of exactly the desired place.

Among these six types of persons who recollect past lives, the vision of past lives by heretics appears like the light of a firefly. The vision of ordinary disciples appears like the light of a lamp. The vision of great disciples appears like the light of a torch. The vision of chief disciples appears like the light of the morning star (Osadhī). The vision of Paccekabuddhas appears like the light of the moon. The vision of the Buddhas appears like the autumn sun adorned with thousands of rays. The recollection of past lives by heretics is like the walking of the blind by holding the tip of a stick. The recollection of ordinary disciples is like walking across a bridge made of a single plank. The recollection of great disciples is like walking across a footbridge. The recollection of chief disciples is like walking across a cart bridge. The recollection of Paccekabuddhas is like traveling on a footpath. The recollection of the Buddhas is like traveling on a great highway. In this context, the recollection of past lives by disciples is intended.

Therefore, a monk who is a beginner and wishes to recollect in this way, having returned from his alms round after the meal, should go into seclusion and sit in solitude. Having attained the four jhānas in succession and emerged from the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā-pādaka-jhāna), he should reflect on dependent origination in the manner described, and then reflect on his most recent sitting. From there, he should reflect in reverse order on the activities of the entire day and night: the spreading of the seat, entering the lodging, putting away the bowl and robes, the time of eating, the time of returning from the village, the time of wandering for alms in the village, the time of entering the village for alms, the time of leaving the monastery, the time of worshipping the shrine and the Bodhi tree, the time of washing the bowl, the tasks performed from receiving the bowl until washing the face, the tasks performed at dawn, and the tasks performed in the middle watch and the first watch. This much is clear even to an ordinary mind, but it is extremely clear to a mind in preliminary concentration (parikamma-samādhi). If anything is not clear here, he should again attain the basic jhāna, emerge, and reflect. By doing so, it becomes clear as if a lamp had been lit.
325:
In this way, in reverse order, one should reflect on the tasks performed on the second day, the third, fourth, and fifth days, ten days, half a month, a month, and even a year. By this same method, reflecting back ten years, twenty years, and so on, up to one's own rebirth in this life, one should then reflect on the mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) occurring at the moment of passing away in the previous life. A wise monk is able to break through the rebirth and take the mind-and-matter at the moment of passing away as an object even at the first attempt. However, because the mind-and-matter in the previous life has completely ceased and another has arisen here, that point is like a mass of darkness, very difficult to see for one with little wisdom. Even so, one should not give up, thinking, 'I am unable to break through the rebirth and take the mind-and-matter at the moment of passing away as an object.' One should repeatedly attain that same basic jhāna and, upon emerging, reflect on that point.

A monk who does this is like a strong man who, while cutting a large tree for the peak of a gabled house, finds his axe-edge spoiled just by cutting the branches and foliage. Although unable to continue cutting the large tree, he does not give up but goes to the smithy, has the axe sharpened, and returns to cut again. If it becomes blunt again, he does the same and continues cutting. As he cuts in this way, because there is no need to cut again what is already cut, and because he cuts what is not yet cut, he will fell the large tree before long. In the same way, a monk who emerges from the basic jhāna and, without reflecting again on what was previously reflected upon, reflects only on the rebirth, will before long break through that rebirth and take the mind-and-matter at the moment of passing away as an object. In this process, the knowledge that occurs by taking objects from the last sitting up to the rebirth is not yet called 'knowledge of recollection of past lives'; it is called 'preliminary concentration knowledge' (parikamma-samādhi-ñāṇa). Some teachers call this 'knowledge of the past' (atītāṃsa-ñāṇa). Since that 'knowledge of the past' belongs to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), that statement is not appropriate in reference to the fine-material sphere. But when that monk, having transcended the rebirth and taken as an object the mind-and-matter occurring at the moment of passing away, experiences the arising of mind-door advertence followed by absorption (appanā) in the manner previously described, then the knowledge associated with that absorption is called 'knowledge of recollection of past lives' (pubbenivāsa-anussati-ñāṇa). With the mindfulness associated with that knowledge, he recollects the succession of aggregates lived in the past.

In that Pali text, the word 'seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable used to show the manner of what has been undertaken. Therefore, wishing to show the different varieties of that recollection of past lives which has been undertaken, he said 'ekampi jātiṃ' and so on. There, 'ekampi jātiṃ' means (the succession of aggregates) having a single rebirth as its root.
326:
It refers to the continuity of aggregates comprised within a single existence, ending in death (cuti). The same method applies to terms such as "two types of birth" and so on.

In the words "many aeons of contraction" and so forth, the aeon that is in the process of declining and being destroyed is called the Saṃvaṭṭakappa (aeon of contraction). At that time, all beings gather in the Brahma world. The aeon that is in the process of re-evolving is called the Vivaṭṭakappa (aeon of expansion). At that time, beings descend from the Brahma world. Among these aeons, the term Saṃvaṭṭakappa also includes the Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī (the period when the world remains contracted), because the contraction is its root. Likewise, the term Vivaṭṭakappa includes the Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī (the period when the world remains expanded). In this way, the four incalculable aeons taught by the Blessed One are encompassed: "Monks, there are these four incalculable aeons. Which four? Monks, when the aeon contracts (Saṃvaṭṭakappa), it is not easy to calculate that destruction. Monks, when the aeon remains contracted (Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī)... Monks, when the aeon expands (Vivaṭṭakappa)... Monks, when the aeon remains expanded (Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī), it is not easy to calculate that duration" (A.N. 4.156).

Among these, there are three types of contraction (destruction): contraction by fire (tejo-saṃvaṭṭa), contraction by water (āpo-saṃvaṭṭa), and contraction by air (vāyo-saṃvaṭṭa). There are three boundaries of contraction: the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. When the world is destroyed by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is burnt by fire. When it is destroyed by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it is destroyed by air, everything below the Vehapphala realm is dispersed and destroyed by wind. In detail, however, the entire Buddha-field (Buddhakhetta) is always destroyed. There are three kinds of Buddha-fields: the birth-field (jātikhetta), the authority-field (āṇākhetta), and the range-field (visayakhetta). Among these, the birth-field extends over ten thousand world systems (cakkavāḷa), which tremble at the Tathāgata’s conception and so on. The authority-field extends over a hundred billion world systems, where the power of protections (paritta) such as the Ratana Paritta, Khandha Paritta, Dhajagga Paritta, Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and Mora Paritta prevails. The range-field is infinite and immeasurable, as it is said: "As far as he may desire" (A.N. 3.81), where the Tathāgata knows whatever he wishes to know. Among these three Buddha-fields, the entire authority-field is destroyed. When the authority-field is destroyed, the birth-field is also necessarily destroyed. They are destroyed together and they are re-established together.

The destruction and re-establishment of these fields should be understood as follows: When the world is to be destroyed by fire, first, a great world-destroying cloud arises and rains heavily throughout the hundred billion world systems. People, being delighted, take out all seeds and sow them. When the crops have grown to the height of a cow’s bite, the rain thunders like a donkey’s bray and then not a single drop falls again. From that time on, the rain ceases completely. Beings who depend on rain for their livelihood are reborn in the Brahma world in due course. Devas who depend on the essence of flowers and fruits are also reborn in the Brahma world. After a long time has passed, the water in lakes and oceans dries up. Then, fish and turtles die and are reborn in the Brahma world. Beings in hell are also reborn in the Brahma world. Some say that hell-beings are destroyed only when the seventh sun appears. In truth, rebirth in the Brahma world is impossible without attaining jhāna. A question may arise: "Among those beings, some are afflicted by famine and some are unworthy of attaining jhāna; how then can they be reborn in the Brahma world?" Those who die of hunger and those unworthy of jhāna are reborn in the deva realms, and from there, through the power of jhāna attained there, they are reborn in the Brahma world. To speak in more detail: When a hundred thousand years remain before the world is destroyed, the Kāmāvacara devas called Lokabyūha wander through the human paths in the sky with disheveled hair, sad faces, weeping, wiping tears with their hands, wearing red garments, and assuming a very strange and altered appearance. Thus...
327:
After braying like a donkey, not even a single drop of rain falls; from that time on, the rain is completely cut off. Beings who depend on rain for their livelihood are reborn in the Brahma world in due course; the deities who depend on the essence of flowers and fruits are also reborn in the Brahma world. When such a long period has passed, the waters in various places reach exhaustion. Then, in succession, even the fish and turtles die and are reborn in the Brahma world, as are the beings in hell. Regarding those beings, some say: "Hell-beings perish only when the seventh sun appears."

There is no rebirth in the Brahma world without attaining Jhana. Among those beings, some are afflicted by famine and some are unworthy of attaining Jhana; how then can they be reborn in that Brahma world? They are reborn through the power of Jhana attained in the celestial realm. For at that time, the sense-sphere deities called Lokabyūha, with bare heads, disheveled hair, and weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, wearing red garments and assuming a very distorted appearance, wander through the paths of men and announce: "Friends, friends! After a hundred thousand years from now, the end of the aeon (kappa) will occur. This world will perish. Even the great ocean will dry up. This great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be burnt up and destroyed. The destruction of the world will reach as far as the Brahma world. Friends, develop loving-kindness (mettā). Friends, develop compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā). Attend to your mothers, attend to your fathers, and respect the elders in the family."

Upon hearing the words of those deities, most humans and terrestrial deities become stirred with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Having become soft-hearted toward one another, they perform meritorious deeds such as mettā and are reborn in the celestial realm. In that celestial realm, they consume divine ambrosia (sudhā), perform preliminary exercises on the wind-kasina (vāyo-kasiṇa), and attain Jhana. Other beings are reborn in the celestial realm through kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya kamma). Indeed, there is no being wandering in saṃsāra who is without aparāpariyavedanīya kamma. They too attain Jhana in that celestial realm in the same way. Thus, through the power of Jhana attained in the celestial realm, all beings are reborn in the Brahma world.

After the cessation of rain, when a long period has passed, a second sun appears. When that sun appears, there is no longer a distinction between night and day. One sun rises as another sets; the world remains under the continuous heat of the sun. Unlike the ordinary sun, which has a sun-deity (Suriya-devaputta), the sun that destroys the world has no deity. While the ordinary sun exists, clouds and vapors move in the sky; however, when the sun that destroys the world appears, the sky becomes clear like the surface of a mirror, free from vapors and clouds. Except for the five great rivers, the water in other small rivers and such dries up. Then, after a long period has passed, a third sun appears. Due to the heat of that sun, even the five great rivers dry up. Then, after a long period has passed, a fourth sun appears. Due to the heat of that sun, the seven great lakes in the Himalayas, which are the sources of the great rivers—namely, Lake Sīhapapātana, Lake Haṃsapātana (or Mandākinī), Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Anotatta, Lake Chaddanta, and Lake Kuṇāla—dry up. Then, after a long period has passed, a fifth sun appears. Due to the heat of that sun, in due course, not even enough water to wet a finger-joint remains in the great ocean; it dries up completely.
328:
In the ordinary sun, there is a sun-deity; however, in the sun that destroys the world, there is no deity. In this universe (cakkavāḷa), while the ordinary sun exists, clouds and vapors move in the sky. When the sun that destroys the world exists, the sky is free from smoke and clouds, becoming pure like the surface of a mirror. Except for the five great rivers, the water in the remaining small rivers and such dries up.

After that, when a long period has passed, a third sun appears; because of the appearance of that third sun, even the five great rivers dry up.

After that, when a long period has passed, a fourth sun appears; because of the appearance of that fourth sun, these seven great lakes in the Himalayas, which are the sources of the great rivers—namely, Lake Sīhapapātana, Lake Haṃsapātana, Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Anotatta, Lake Chaddanta, and Lake Kuṇāla—dry up.

After that, when a long period has passed, a fifth sun appears; because of the appearance of that fifth sun, in due course, not even enough water to wet a finger-joint remains in the great ocean.

After that, when a long period has passed, a sixth sun appears; because of the appearance of that sixth sun, the entire universe becomes filled with a single mass of smoke, its moisture exhausted by the smoke. Just like this universe, a hundred thousand crores of universes also become the same.

After that, when a long period has passed, a seventh sun appears; because of the appearance of that seventh sun, the entire universe, together with a hundred thousand crores of universes, becomes a single mass of flame. The peaks of Mount Sineru, which are a hundred yojanas and more in extent, crumble and vanish into the open sky. That flame rises and consumes the Cātumahārājika realm. In that realm, after burning the golden mansions, the jewel mansions, and the ruby mansions, it consumes the Tāvatiṃsa celestial abode. In this manner, it consumes up to the first Jhana realm. In that first Jhana realm, it burns all three Brahma realms and stands having reached the Ābhassara realm. As long as there is even a minute amount of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra) remaining, that flame does not go out. But when all formations are exhausted, it goes out like a flame of ghee or oil that has finished burning, leaving not even ashes behind. The upper sky becomes one with the lower sky, resulting in a great mass of darkness.

Then, after a long period has passed, a great cloud appears and first rains very, very gently. Then, in succession, with torrents of rain the size of lotus stalks, staffs, pestles, and palm trunks...
329:
Falling in streams of rain, it fills all the burnt places in the hundred thousand times ten million world systems and then disappears. The wind, arising from below and from the sides, causes that water to swirl and makes it compact, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. How does it make such a vast mass of water compact? It is by providing openings. For the wind provides openings here and there. Thus, being compressed and made compact by the wind, and being diminished, that mass of water gradually recedes downwards.

As the water recedes, the Brahma realms appear in the places where the Brahma realms are situated, and the four lower sensual-sphere celestial realms appear in the places where the deva realms are situated. When the water recedes to the place where the earth was formerly situated, powerful winds arise. These winds obstruct and block the water, making it breathless, like water held in a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa) with its opening closed. When the sweet water dries up, the savory earth (rasapathavī) arises on the surface. That savory earth is endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, like the film on the surface of milk-porridge that has no water. At that time, beings who were first reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma realm, having passed away from there due to the exhaustion of their life-span or merit, are reborn here. They are self-luminous and travel through the air. As described in the Aggañña Sutta, they taste that savory earth and, overcome by craving, begin to eat it by making it into morsels.

Then, their self-luminance disappears, and darkness ensues. Seeing the darkness, they become afraid. Then, the sun's orb (suriyamaṇḍala), fifty yojanas in size, appears, destroying their fear and producing courage. Seeing it, they are delighted and joyful, saying, "We have obtained light!" and they name it 'Suriya' (Sun), thinking, "It has arisen, destroying the fear of us who were afraid and producing courage (sūra-bhāva)." Then, after the sun has provided light throughout the day and set, they become afraid again, thinking, "The light we obtained has vanished again." They think, "It would be truly good if we could obtain another light." As if knowing their desire, the moon's orb (candamaṇḍala), forty-nine yojanas in size, appears. Seeing it, they are even more delighted and joyful, and they name it 'Canda' (Moon), thinking, "It has arisen as if knowing our desire (chanda)."

When the moon and sun have thus appeared, the constellations and stars also appear. From then on, night and day are known, and gradually the months, half-months, seasons, and years. On the very day the moon and sun appear, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavanta mountains also appear. These moons, suns, and so forth appear simultaneously on the full moon day of Phagguna (Tabaung), neither earlier nor later. How do they appear? Just as when millet-rice is being cooked, bubbles arise all at once, and some places are high, some are low, and some are level; even so, mountains arose in the high places, oceans in the low places, and islands in the level places. This is how it should be understood. At that time, among those beings who consumed the savory earth, some gradually became beautiful and some became ugly. Among them, those who were beautiful looked down upon those who were ugly. Because of their pride, the savory earth disappeared, and a soil-crust (bhūmipappaṭaka) appeared. After that...
330:
They appear. These moons, suns, and so forth appear simultaneously on the full moon day of Phagguna, neither earlier nor later. How do they appear? For example, just as when millet-rice is being cooked, bubbles arise all at once, and some places are high, some are low, and some are level; even so, mountains arose in the high places, oceans in the low places, and islands in the level places. This is how it should be understood.

At that time, among those beings of the first eon who consumed the savory earth, some gradually became beautiful and some became ugly. Among them, those who were beautiful looked down upon those who were ugly. Because of their excessive pride, that savory earth disappeared, and a soil-crust (bhūmipappaṭaka), resembling a mushroom, appeared. Then, in the same manner as before due to their pride, that soil-crust also disappeared, and creeping plants (padālatā) appeared. In the same manner, those plants also disappeared, and self-ripening rice (sāli) appeared, which was without powder, without husk, pure, fragrant, and bore grains like rice, without needing to be tilled. Then, vessels appeared for those beings. They put the rice in the vessels and placed them on the surface of stone slabs. Flames arose spontaneously and cooked that rice. That rice became cooked food resembling the jasmine flower. For that food, there was no need for soup or curry; whatever flavor they desired to eat, that very flavor arose. For those who consumed that coarse food, from that time on, excrement and urine were produced. Then, for the purpose of discharging that excrement and urine, openings like wounds appeared in them. The male organ appeared in the man, and the female organ appeared in the woman. Then, the woman gazed at the man, and the man at the woman, excessively. Because of their excessive gazing, sensual fever arose in them. Then, they indulged in sexual intercourse (methuna-dhamma). Because of their indulgence in that unrighteous practice, when they were censured and harassed by the wise, they built houses to conceal that unrighteous practice. Those beings living in houses gradually followed the example of a certain lazy being and began to hoard food. From the time they began to hoard, both powder and husk enveloped the rice, and it did not grow back in the places where it had been harvested. They gathered together and lamented repeatedly, saying, "Friends, evil states have indeed appeared among beings; for formerly we were mind-made..." This should be expanded as stated in the Aggañña Sutta. Then, they established boundaries.

Then, a certain frivolous being took another's portion that was not given. They rebuked him twice, and on the third time, they struck him with their hands, clods of earth, and sticks. They thus...
331: When theft, censure, lying, and the taking up of weapons arose, beings gathered to deliberate. They thought, "It would be good if we were to appoint one being who should rightly rebuke those who deserve rebuke, censure those who deserve censure, and banish those who deserve banishment. We, in turn, shall give him a portion of our rice." When the beings made this decision, in this aeon, the Blessed One himself, as a Bodhisatta, was the most handsome, most pleasing, most majestic, endowed with wisdom, and capable of exercising restraint and encouragement among those beings. They approached and requested him, electing him as king. He became known by three names: "Mahā Sammata" because he was elected by the great multitude; "Khattiya" because he was the lord of the fields; and "Rājā" because he gladdens others through righteousness (Dhamma). In whatever wonderful phenomena exist in the world, the Bodhisatta is the first person. Thus, with the Bodhisatta at the head, the circle of Khattiyas was established, and subsequently, the other four castes such as Brahmins were also established. In that [destruction], the period from the falling of the world-destroying great cloud until the cessation of the flames is called the "Saṃvaṭṭa" (Dissolution) Incalculable Aeon. From the cessation of the world-destroying flames until the falling of the world-evolving great cloud that fills a hundred thousand crores of world-systems is called the second incalculable, "Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" (Duration of Dissolution). From the falling of the world-evolving great cloud until the appearance of the moon and sun is called the third incalculable, "Vivaṭṭa" (Evolution). From the appearance of the moon and sun until the falling of the world-destroying great cloud again is called the fourth incalculable, "Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" (Duration of Evolution). These four incalculables constitute one Great Aeon (Mahākappa). Thus should destruction and re-establishment by fire be understood. When the aeon is destroyed by water, the process of the world-destroying great cloud arising should be understood in detail as previously described. However, there is this distinction: just as a second sun appeared in the destruction by fire, here in the destruction by water, a world-destroying great saline rain (khārūdaka-mahāmegha) arises. It first falls as a fine drizzle and gradually falls in great torrents the size of logs or palm trees, filling a hundred thousand crores of world-systems. The earth, mountains, and so on, wherever touched by the saline water, melt and crumble away. The water is held on all sides by winds. The water covers from below the earth up to the second jhāna realm; it melts the three Brahma realms there and stands touching the Subhakiṇha realm. As long as even a minute amount of formations (saṅkhāra) remains, that water does not subside.
332: Having overcome the entirety of formations that followed the force of the water, it suddenly subsides and disappears. The lower space and upper space become one, forming a great mass of darkness; all this is the same as what was said before. However, in this destruction by water, the world-system appears starting from the Ābhassara Brahma realm. Beings passing away from the Subhakiṇha realm are reborn in places like the Ābhassara realm. In that aeon destroyed by water, the period from the falling of the world-destroying great cloud until the cessation of the world-destroying saline water is one Incalculable Aeon. From the cessation of the saline water until the falling of the world-evolving great cloud is the second Incalculable Aeon. From the falling of the world-evolving great cloud... [and so on]. These four Incalculable Aeons constitute one Great Aeon. Thus should destruction and re-establishment by water be understood. When the aeon is destroyed by wind, the process of the world-destroying great cloud arising should be understood in detail as previously described. The following is the distinction: just as a second sun arose in the destruction by fire, similarly, in this destruction by wind, a wind arises to destroy the world. That wind first raises coarse dust not connected to the ground. Then it raises fine dust connected to the ground, fine sand, coarse sand, gravel, stones, and so on, up to rocks the size of gabled houses and large trees growing in uneven places. Those rocks and large trees, having risen from the earth into the sky, do not fall back but are pulverized to dust right there in the sky and vanish. Then, gradually, wind arises from beneath the great earth, turns the earth over, turning it upside down, and hurls it into the sky. Regions of earth measuring a hundred yojanas, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred yojanas break apart and, being hurled by the force of the wind, are pulverized to dust in the sky and vanish. The wind also lifts the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Sineru and hurls them into the sky. They strike against each other, are pulverized to dust, and are destroyed. In this same manner, destroying the mansions on the ground and the mansions in the sky, it destroys the six sensual-sphere deva realms and a hundred thousand crores of world-systems. In that destruction by wind, world-systems collide with world-systems, Himavantas with Himavantas, and Sinerus with Sinerus, and they are pulverized to dust and destroyed. The wind blows and destroys from the earth up to the third jhāna realm. In doing so, it destroys the three Brahma realms and stops upon reaching the Vehapphala realm. Thus, having destroyed the entirety of formations, the wind itself also vanishes. The lower space and upper space become one, forming a great mass of darkness; all this is the same as what was said before. In this destruction by wind...
333:
Furthermore, starting from the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm, the world becomes manifest. Passing away from the Vehapphala realm, beings are reborn in the places where the Subhakiṇha realm is established, and so on. In that [world destroyed by wind], the period from the falling of the great world-destroying rain until the cessation of the world-destroying wind is called one incalculable eon (asaṅkheyya-kappa). From the cessation of the wind until the falling of the great rain that settles [the world] is the second incalculable eon... [Pe]... These four incalculable eons constitute one great eon (mahākappa). Thus, destruction and establishment by wind should be understood.

For what reason does the world perish in this way? It is because of the unwholesome roots (akusalamūla). When the unwholesome roots are abundant, the world perishes in this manner. That world perishes by fire when greed (rāga) is excessive; it perishes by water when hatred (dosa) is excessive. However, some teachers say, 'When hatred is excessive, it perishes by fire; when greed is excessive, it perishes by water.' When delusion (moha) is excessive, it perishes by wind. In perishing thus, it perishes by fire for seven consecutive times without interruption, and on the eighth time, it perishes by water. Again, seven times by fire, and on the eighth time, by water. In this way, perishing every eighth time, after it has perished seven times by water, it perishes again seven times by fire. By this point, sixty-three eons have passed. Within these sixty-three eons, even when the time for destruction by water arrives, the wind, having gained the opportunity by averting that time, destroys the world, including the Subhakiṇha Brahmas whose lifespan is a full sixty-four eons.

A monk who recollects his past existence and who can recollect eons, can recollect many eons of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭakappa), many eons of evolution (vivaṭṭakappa), and many eons of dissolution and evolution (saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappa). The terms 'eon of dissolution' and 'eon of evolution' are spoken by taking half of a great eon. The term 'eon of dissolution and evolution' is spoken by taking the entire great eon. How does he recollect? He recollects in the manner beginning with 'I was there.' Therein, 'I was there' means: in that eon of dissolution, I was in such a birth (bhava), or mode of birth (yoni), or destination (gati), or station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), or abode of beings (sattāvāsa), or group of beings (sattanikāya). 'Such was my name' means he had the name Tissa or Phussa. 'Such was my clan' means he was of the Kaccāna or Kassapa clan. This is said in terms of the person with direct knowledge (abhiññā) recollecting his own name and clan in a past life. If, at that time, he wishes to recollect the perfection of his appearance, or his meager or excellent livelihood, or the abundance of pleasure and pain, or the shortness or length of his lifespan, he can indeed recollect all of that. Therefore, it is said: 'Such was my appearance... [Pe]... such was the limit of my lifespan.' Therein, 'such was my appearance' means he had a fair or dark complexion. 'Such was my food' means he had food consisting of rice and meat, or he ate fruits that fell naturally. 'Such was my experience of pleasure and pain' means...
334:
...he experienced various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, classified as carnal (sāmisa), spiritual (nirāmisa), and so on. 'Such was the limit of my lifespan' means having a lifespan of a hundred years, or a lifespan of eighty-four thousand eons.

'Passing away from there, he was reborn there' means: I, having passed away from that birth, mode of birth, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings, was reborn again in such a birth, mode of birth, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings. 'There too I was' means: then, in that birth, mode of birth, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings, I existed again. 'Such was my name' and so on are in the same manner as already described. Furthermore, since 'I was there' is the recollection as much as desired by one ascending in order, and 'passing away from there' is the reflection while turning back, it should be understood that 'he was reborn there' is said in reference to the place of rebirth immediately following this rebirth [indicated by] 'he was reborn here.' 'There too I was' and so on are said to show the recollection of the name, clan, etc., in that place of rebirth immediately following this rebirth. 'Passing away from there, he was reborn here' means: I, having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, was reborn here in such a khattiya family or brahmin family. 'Thus' means in this way. 'With its aspects and with its details' means: with details (sa-uddesaṃ) by way of name and clan, and with aspects (sākāraṃ) by way of appearance and so on. For a being is described (uddisīyati) by name and clan as Tissa, Phussa, or Kassapa; and is known in his distinctiveness by appearance and so on as dark or fair. Therefore, name and clan are 'details' (uddesa), and the others are 'aspects' (ākāra).

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Existences is finished.

## 54. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

In the description of the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa), 'he attends to the perception of light' means he attends to the light of the sun, the light of fire, the light of the moon, or the light of gems, whether by day or by night. In so attending, because he brings about the perception of 'light' in his mind, it is said, 'he attends to the perception of light.' 'He determines the perception of day' means having thus attended to the perception of light, he establishes the perception of 'day'.
335:
"As by day, so by night" means that one attends to light at night just as light is seen during the day. "As by night, so by day" means that one attends to light during the day just as light is seen at night. "With a mind that is open" means with a mind that is uncovered. "With a mind that is unhindered" means with a mind free from the hindrance of the mental obstructions (nīvaraṇas). "Develops a mind accompanied by light" means that one increases a mind that possesses radiance. By this statement, it refers to the access mind (upacāra-citta) having the light kasina (āloka-kasiṇa) as its object, which is the preparation (parikamma) for the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Alternatively, it is said with reference to the fourth jhāna itself having the light kasina as its object.

For the practitioner who develops it in this way, a radiant mind arises that is free from the obstruction of the mass of darkness. Indeed, a noble son (kulaputta) who is a beginner and wishes to produce the divine eye should, according to the sequence of this Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, make the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna)—which has a kasina as its object and serves as the basis for direct knowledge—capable of directing towards direct knowledge in fourteen ways. Then, he should bring one of these three kasinas—the fire kasina (tejo-kasiṇa), the white kasina (odāta-kasiṇa), or the light kasina (āloka-kasiṇa)—near to the access mind. Having made it the object of access jhāna (upacāra-jhāna) and developed it, he should maintain it; the meaning is that he should not produce absorption (appanā) in that object. If he were to produce absorption, it would only be the basis for the basic jhāna, and not the basis for the preparation.

Among these three kasinas, the light kasina is the most excellent. However, because they are compatible with the light kasina, the other two kasinas are also mentioned. Therefore, having produced the four jhānas of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-jhāna) by taking either the light kasina or one of the other two as the object, he should again stay at the level of access (upacāra) and develop the kasina. He should see the collection of material forms (rūpā-gata) only within the area he has expanded. For the one who has the effort to see material forms, if he does not make the light pervade with that preparatory access mind, the turn of the preparatory mind passes. Then the light disappears. When the light disappears, the material forms are no longer visible. Then, that practitioner should repeatedly enter the basic jhāna, emerge from it, and pervade the light with the access mind. In this way, by following the sequence, the light becomes powerful.

'Let there be light in this place'—whatever area he delimits in this way, the light remains in that place. For the bhikkhu who sits and watches all day, the seeing of material forms occurs. In that process, when the collection of material forms that cannot be seen by the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu)—such as forms inside the belly, forms dependent on the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), forms below the ground, forms on the other side of walls, mountains, or enclosures, and forms in other world systems (cakka-vāḷa)—comes into the range of the eye of knowledge (ñāṇa-cakkhu) and becomes as if seen by the fleshly eye, then it is said that the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) has arisen. Among the minds that take these material forms as objects, only that divine eye direct-knowledge mind is capable of seeing the material forms; the preceding minds such as preparation and access are not capable of seeing the material forms.
336: The sequence of the arising of this divine-eye higher power is as follows: having made that visible form of the described nature the object, when the mind-door adverting consciousness has arisen and ceased, four or five javanas arise making that same visible form the object; this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated (regarding the divine-ear higher power). This knowledge is called both "knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" and "divine-eye knowledge." However, this divine-eye knowledge can be a danger to a worldling. For when that person resolves, "Let there be light in such and such a place," a single spread of light appears, even penetrating through the earth, oceans, and mountains in those places. Then, seeing the terrifying forms of yakkhas, rakkhasas, and so on in that place, fear arises in him. Due to that fear, his mind becomes distracted and he either falls away from jhāna or becomes maddened by jhāna. Therefore, one must be heedful and mindful when viewing visible forms. "For the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" means for the sake of the knowledge of the passing away and the rebirth of beings. It means for the sake of that knowledge (divine-eye knowledge) by which the passing away and rebirth of beings are known. "With the divine eye" has the same meaning as already stated. "Purified" means purified because it is the cause for the purification of view through the seeing of passing away and rebirth. For he who sees only the passing away and not the rebirth, he holds the annihilationist view. He who sees only the rebirth and not the passing away, he holds the view that new beings appear. But he who sees both, because he transcends both types of wrong views, his seeing is the cause for the purification of view. Only the sons of the Buddha see both. Therefore, it is said, "Purified because it is the cause for the purification of view through the seeing of passing away and rebirth." "Surpassing the human" means surpassing the human range because of seeing visible forms beyond the human sphere, or it is called "surpassing the human" because it excels the human fleshly eye. With that purified divine eye which surpasses the human. "He sees beings" means he looks at beings just as people look with the fleshly eye. In the phrase "passing away and being reborn," it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the exact moment of death or the exact moment of rebirth. Rather, those who are close to passing away and will die right now are intended as "passing away." Those who have just taken rebirth or are just now being born are intended as "being reborn." He shows that he sees such beings who are passing away and being reborn. "Inferior" means beings who are despised, greatly humbled, known as low, or disdained by way of inferior birth, family, wealth, etc., because of being associated with the result of delusion. "Superior" means those opposite to the inferior because of being associated with the result of non-delusion. "Beautiful" means those endowed with desirable, lovely, and pleasing color because of being associated with the result of non-hatred. "Ugly" means those endowed with undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasing color because of being associated with the result of hatred.
337:
"Anabhirūpe" also means "virūpe" (of ugly form). "Sugate" refers to beings who have reached a happy destination (sugati), or it means those who are wealthy and possess great riches because they are endowed with the result of non-greed (alobha). "Duggate" refers to beings who have reached a miserable destination (duggati), or it means those who are poor and destitute with little food and drink because they are endowed with the result of greed (lobha). "Yathākammūpage" refers to beings who have arrived [at their destination] according to their various accumulated kammas. Among these terms, the preceding words such as "cavamāne" (passing away) describe the function of the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), whereas this term "yathākammūpage" describes the function of the Knowledge of [beings] Passing According to Kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa).

The sequence of the arising of that knowledge is as follows: In this Dispensation, a monk extends light (āloka-kasiṇa) towards the hell realms below and sees the beings in hell experiencing great suffering; that seeing is solely the function of the Divine Eye. That monk then reflects: "By performing what kamma do these beings experience this suffering?" Then, the knowledge that takes that kamma as its object arises in him: "By performing such-and-such kamma, they experience this suffering." Similarly, he extends light towards the heavenly realms above and sees beings experiencing great prosperity and bliss in the Nandana Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and so on; that seeing is also solely the function of the Divine Eye. That monk then reflects: "By performing what kamma do these beings experience this prosperity?" Then, the knowledge that takes that kamma as its object arises in him: "By performing such-and-such kamma, they experience this prosperity." This is called the Knowledge of [beings] Passing According to Kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa). There is no separate preliminary preparation (parikamma) for this knowledge. Just as for this knowledge, there is also no separate preliminary preparation for the Knowledge of the Future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa). For these knowledges are based on the Divine Eye and are perfected together with the Divine Eye itself.

In the sentences beginning with "Ime vata bhonto," the word "ime" is a demonstrative term pointing to the objects seen with the Divine Eye. "Vata" is a particle used in the sense of an appropriate exclamation. "Bhonto" means "sirs" or "beings." It is called "duccaritaṃ" (misconduct) because it is badly practiced, or because it is foul with defilements. Misconduct practiced by the body or arising from the body is called "kāya-duccaritaṃ" (bodily misconduct). The same method applies to the remaining verbal misconduct and mental misconduct. "Samannāgatā" means being endowed with. "Ariyānaṃ upavādakā" (revilers of Noble Ones) refers to those who, desiring harm, revile, abuse, or disparage the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples, even down to lay stream-enterers—either by accusing them of an ultimate matter (antima-vatthu, i.e., a Pārājika offense) or by disparaging their virtues. Between those two, one who says, "These monks have no recluse-dharma; they are not recluses," reviles them by accusing them of an ultimate matter. One who says, "These monks have no jhāna, liberation (vimokkha), path (magga), or fruit (phala)," should be understood as reviling them by disparaging their virtues. Whether that person reviles them knowingly or unknowingly, in both cases, it is "reviling Noble Ones" (ariyūpavāda). That kamma is a heavy kamma, similar to the "immediate" (ānantariya) kammas, and it obstructs the attainment of heaven and the path; however, it is a remediable (satekiccha) kamma. Therefore, if a person has reviled a Noble One, he should go to them, and if he himself is the elder, he should sit in a crouching position and say, "Ahaṃ (I...)"
338:
"I have said such and such to the venerable one; please forgive me for that fault," thus he should ask for forgiveness. If he is junior, he should pay homage, sit in a squatting position, and with hands raised in salutation (añjali), say: "Venerable sir, I have said such and such to you; please forgive me for that fault," thus he should ask for forgiveness. If that venerable one has gone to another place, he should go himself or send a pupil (saddhivihārika) or others to ask for forgiveness. If it is not possible to go or send someone, he should go to the monks living in that monastery. If they are junior to him, he should sit in a squatting position; if they are senior, he should act according to the method mentioned for seniors and say: "Venerable sirs, I have said such and such to the venerable one named so-and-so; may that venerable one forgive me," thus he should ask for forgiveness. Even if the person does not forgive in his presence, he should act in this same way.

If the monk is a solitary wanderer and his dwelling place or destination is unknown, he should go to a wise monk and consult: "Venerable sir, I have said such and such to the venerable one named so-and-so; remembering those words, I feel remorse. What should I do?" That wise monk will say: "Good man, do not worry; that elder forgives you. Calm your mind." Then, the monk who committed the offense should face the direction where that Noble One (ariya) has gone, raise his hands in salutation, and say: "Please forgive me." If that venerable one has attained Parinibbāna, he should go to the place of the Parinibbāna couch or even as far as the cemetery to ask for forgiveness. When this is done, there is no obstruction to heaven nor obstruction to the Path; it becomes normal as before.

Micchādiṭṭhikā means those with distorted vision. Micchādiṭṭhikမ္မသမာဒါနာ (Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā) means those who have various actions undertaken through the power of wrong view, and those who cause others to undertake bodily actions, etc., rooted in wrong view. Here, although insulting Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) is included by taking verbal misconduct, and wrong view is included by taking mental misconduct, it should be understood that these two are mentioned separately to show their great blamefulness. Indeed, insulting Noble Ones is very blameful because it is similar to an action with immediate result (ānantariya). It has also been said: "Sāriputta, just as a monk endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain Arahantship in this very life; Sāriputta, I say that if one does not abandon those words, does not abandon that mind, and does not relinquish that view, he is cast into hell as if carried and dropped there" (Majjhima Nikāya). There is no other thing more blameful than wrong view. As it is said: "Monks, I do not see any other single thing so blameful as this, namely, wrong view. Monks, wrong view is the ultimate limit of faults" (Aṅguttara Nikāya).
339: 'With the breakup of the body' (kāyassa bhedā) means the relinquishing of the clung-to aggregates (upādinnak-khandha). 'After death' (paraṃ maraṇā) means at the taking up of the newly arisen aggregates immediately after that relinquishing. Alternatively, 'with the breakup of the body' means the cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). 'After death' means after the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). All these terms such as 'state of loss' (apāya) are just synonyms for hell (niraya). Indeed, it is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of the path (aya) known as merit, which is the cause for heaven and liberation, or because of the absence of the arrival (āya) of happiness. It is called 'duggati' (unhappy destination) because it is a destination that is the resort of suffering. Or, it is called 'duggati' because it is a destination produced by kamma corrupted by an abundance of faults (dosa). It is called 'vinipāta' (perdition) because those who do evil fall there against their will. Or, it is called 'vinipāta' because they fall there with their limbs and organs being broken. It is called 'niraya' (hell) because there is no 'aya' (pleasure) known as enjoyment there. Alternatively, by the term 'apāya', the animal realm (tiracchāna-yoni) is indicated. For the animal realm is an 'apāya' because it is away from the happy destination (sugati), but it is not a 'duggati' because great powerful dragon kings (nāga-rāja), etc., can be born there. By the term 'duggati', the realm of hungry ghosts (petti-visaya) is indicated. For that realm is both an 'apāya' and a 'duggati' because it is away from the happy destination and is a destination of suffering, but it is not a 'vinipāta' because they do not fall with broken limbs like the asuras. By the term 'vinipāta', the host of asuras (asura-kāya) is indicated. For that host is called 'apāya' and 'duggati' for the reasons already mentioned, and it is called 'vinipāta' because they fall with all their bodies being broken. By the term 'niraya', only the various kinds of hells such as Avīci are indicated. 'Upapannā' means gone to, or reborn there. The white side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite of the meanings already stated. This is the distinction: therein, by the term 'sugati', the human destination is also included; by the term 'sagga' (heaven), only the celestial destination is included. Between those two, it is called 'sugati' because it is a good destination. It is called 'sagga' because it is exceedingly excellent (agga) due to objects such as forms (rūpa). All that, including the happy destination, is called 'loka' (world) in the sense of crumbling and dissolving. Thus, all the words starting with 'with the divine eye' (dibbeṇa cakkhunā) are concluding words. Thus, 'he sees with the divine eye' is the summary meaning here. ## The Exposition of the Description of the Divine Eye Knowledge is finished. ## Miscellaneous Notes on the Five Superknowledges Among these five kinds of superknowledge, the knowledge of the kinds of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to seven kinds of objects: limited (paritta), exalted (mahaggata), past, future, present, internal (ajjhatta), and external (bahiddha). The knowledge of the purification of the ear-element (sotadhātu-visuddhi-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to four kinds of objects: limited, present, internal, and external. The knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects: limited, exalted, immeasurable (appamāṇa), the path (magga), past, future, present, and external.
340:
The knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to eight objects: limited, exalted, immeasurable (path and fruit), the path only, past, internal, external, and the non-describable (anavattabba). The knowledge of the divine eye occurs with respect to four objects: limited, present, internal, and external. The knowledge of faring according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to five objects: limited, exalted, past, internal, and external. The knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to eight objects: limited, exalted, immeasurable (path and fruit), the path only, future, internal, external, and the non-describable.

## The Miscellaneous Discussion on the Five Superknowledges is Finished.

## 55. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints

In the description of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, terms like the faculty "I shall know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) have the meanings already stated. The question "To how many stations does it go?" is asked for the purpose of defining the place of arising for each faculty. "It goes to one station" means it arises in one station (a single moment of consciousness). Indeed, the place where the faculty "I shall know the unknown" arises is established in this moment of the path of stream-entry; therefore, it is called a "station" (ṭhāna). "Six stations" refers to the moments of the three higher paths and the three lower fruits. To show that among the faculties, only one is predominant in each of the three faculties starting with "I shall know the unknown," it is said: "the faculty of faith has decision (adhimokkha) as its retinue," and so on.

Just as in passages like "the sense of decision of the faculty of faith," decision and others are stated by way of the function of the faculty of faith and others, so here too, in saying "it has decision as its retinue," it means the faculty of faith is the retinue of the faculty "I shall know the unknown" in the sense of plunging into the object. The same method applies to the remaining faculties of energy, mindfulness, etc. In the word "parivāraṃ" (retinue), there is a change of gender. "The faculty of wisdom" (paññindriya) is mentioned separately to show the nature of knowing the faculty "I shall know the unknown" in its various aspects. In the Abhidhamma (Indriya-vibhaṅga) as well, to show the specific function of wisdom, the single wisdom is divided into eight ways in the moments of the path and the fruit.

"The retinue of overflowing" (abhisandana-parivāra) means that just as water surrounds bathing powder by the function of cohesion, so the "overflowing" (pīti) surrounds the mind and mental factors by the function of cohesion. This is stated only by way of the path associated with joy (somanassa). In the path associated with equanimity, however, the faculty of equanimity should be understood in the place of the faculty of joy. That faculty of equanimity should be taken as a retinue by the function of not overly intensifying (calming) the associated states. "The retinue of the predominance of the occurring continuity" means the continuity that is currently occurring (the present mental process). Predominance is ādhipateyya; predominance in the currently occurring continuity is pavattasantatādhipateyya. Indeed, it is the retinue of the faculty "I shall know the unknown" by way of being a condition for the further occurrence of the currently occurring life-faculty from the moment of the path onwards, and by way of predominance in the mental continuity that has occurred, is occurring, and will occur in sequence.
341: The phrase 'states arisen at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry' and so forth is spoken to praise the virtues of all states associated with the Path. In that text, 'arisen at the moment of the Path' means only those states produced by the Path, and no others. However, since matter produced by the Path cannot be called 'wholesome' (kusala) and so forth, the text says 'excluding mind-produced matter' to set aside that material form. Indeed, all those states are called wholesome (kusala) because of their meanings such as destroying contemptible things. They are called taintless (anāsava) because the taints (āsava) that occur by making those states their object do not exist for them. They are called 'leading to deliverance' (niyyānika) because they lead out from the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) by taking Nibbāna as their object and cutting the root of the round. They are called 'leading to the undoing of accumulation' (apacayagāmi) because they proceed by taking Nibbāna as their object, which is called 'undoing' (apacaya) because it is free from the accumulation (caya) known as wholesome and unwholesome kamma; or they are called apacayagāmi because they go along while undoing and destroying the currently proceeding states of the three planes. They are called supramundane (lokuttara) because they have transcended and risen above the world by being unincluded in the world. They are called 'having Nibbāna as object' (nibbānārammaṇa) because Nibbāna is their object.The phrase 'these eight faculties' and so forth is spoken to show the nature of being a retinue as mentioned before, to show the nature of being conascent (sahagata) and so forth with that faculty of 'I shall know the unknown', and to show the aspects mentioned at the beginning. In that text, 'eight faculties' means eight including the faculty of wisdom according to the method mentioned before. 'Conascent retinue' (sahajātaparivāra) means that among the eight faculties, each one together with the other seven becomes conascent, thus being its conascent retinue. In the same way, they are 'mutually associated retinues' (aññamaññaparivāra), one to another. Likewise, they are 'dependence retinues' (nissayaparivāra) and 'associated retinues' (sampayuttaparivāra). 'Conascent' (sahagata) means they have reached the state of having a single arising and so forth together with that faculty of 'I shall know the unknown'. 'Co-born' (sahajāta) means they are born together with that very faculty. 'Mixed' (saṃsaṭṭha) means they are mixed together with that faculty. 'Associated' (sampayutta) means they are associated with that faculty by way of having a single arising and so forth. 'Te va' means only those eight faculties. 'Tassa' refers to the portion or group of the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown'. 'Ākārā' means the portions of the retinue.In the statement 'all states arisen at the moment of the Fruit are indeterminate (abyākata)', they are spoken of together with mind-produced matter because matter is also indeterminate. Because only the Path is wholesome, leading to deliverance, and leading to the undoing of accumulation, the terms 'wholesome' (kusala), 'leading to deliverance' (niyyānika), and 'leading to the undoing of accumulation' (apacayagāmi) are not used for the moment of the Fruit. The word 'iti' and so forth is the conclusion of the described manner. In that text, 'eight groups of eight' (aṭṭhaṭṭhakāni) means eight groups of eight faculties by way of each of the eight paths and fruits. 'There are sixty-four' means there are sixty-four aspects. The terms 'āsavā' and so forth have the same meaning as stated below. In this context...
342:
It should be understood that the mention of the taints (āsava) destroyed by the three lower paths, and not only those destroyed by the Path of Arahantship, is stated merely by way of the commonality of the term 'destruction of taints' (āsavakkhaya). Some teachers say that only the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship is called 'knowledge of destruction' (khaye ñāṇa) because it exhausts the taints without remainder. For that very reason, only an Arahant is called 'one whose taints are destroyed' (khīṇāsava).

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints is Finished.

## 56-63. Explanation of the Description of the Two Tetrads of Knowledge of the Truths

108-109. In the description of the two tetrads of knowledge of the truths, the words beginning with 'the sense of oppression of suffering' (dukkhaassa pīḷanaṭṭho) have the meanings already stated. The knowledge of one possessed of the path is stated by way of simultaneous penetration (ekābhisamaya), as in the tetrad mentioned immediately after, such as 'this knowledge in suffering'. Knowledge of the truths is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Mundane knowledge is also twofold: conformable knowledge (anubodha-ñāṇa) and reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). For a beginner, conformable knowledge occurs in the truth of cessation and the truth of the path by way of successive hearing and so forth; however, it occurs in the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin by way of taking them as objects. Reviewing knowledge occurs for a noble disciple (ariya) who has penetrated the truths, by way of taking all four truths as objects. Supramundane penetrative knowledge (the knowledge of the path) takes the truth of cessation (Nibbāna) as its object and penetrates the four truths by way of function. With reference to such penetration, it is said in its entirety: 'Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the way leading to the cessation of suffering (the path).' Here too, in this section, this very knowledge of the truths is intended. It is stated to show that even though that knowledge of the truths is supramundane, it receives names such as 'knowledge in suffering' (dukkhe ñāṇa). Nevertheless, in this context, only mundane knowledge is intended. For that very reason, He said, 'In that case, what is the knowledge in suffering?' and so forth.

In that Pali, 'concerning suffering' (dukkhaṃ ārabbha) means having taken the truth of suffering as an object. In the terms such as 'wisdom' (paññā), it is called wisdom because of the sense of making known (paññāpanaṭṭha) by making each respective meaning clear; or it is called wisdom because it knows states in various ways such as impermanence. This term 'wisdom' is the fundamental term (sabhāvapada) for this knowledge of suffering. The mode of understanding is 'understanding' (pajananā). It is 'investigation' (vicaya) because it investigates impermanence and so forth. 'Thorough investigation' (pavicaya) is a term expanded by the prefix 'pa', meaning investigation in various ways. It is 'investigation of states' (dhammavicaya) because it investigates the states of the four truths. The proper marking by way of characteristics of impermanence and so forth is 'marking' (sallakkhaṇā). That same marking, by the distinction of prefixes, is called 'discrimination' (upalakkhaṇā) and 'close discrimination' (paccupalakkhaṇā). The state of being wise is 'erudition' (paṇḍicca). The state of being skillful is 'skill' (kosalla). The state of being subtle is 'subtlety' (nepuñña). It is 'clarity' (pabbā) by way of the power to make impermanence and so forth clear. It is 'thought' (cintā) by way of the power to reflect on impermanence and so forth. It is 'scrutiny' (upaparikkha) because it scrutinizes impermanence and so forth closely from all sides. 'Bhūrī' is the earth. This wisdom is also called 'bhūrī' because it is like the earth in the sense of being subtle and in the sense of being broad. Or, wisdom itself is called 'bhūrī' because it delights in the true...
343:
...meaning. It is called 'sagacity' (medhā) because it destroys defilements as a thunderbolt destroys a rock mountain, or because of the sense of grasping and retaining quickly. It is called 'guidance' (pariṇāyikā) because when wisdom arises in a person, it leads that person toward the practice of their own welfare and toward the penetration of the true characteristics of associated states. It is called 'insight' (vipassanā) because it sees formations in various and diverse ways by way of impermanence and so forth. It is called 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāna) because it knows impermanence and so forth well and in various ways; the state of such a person is 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña). It is called 'the goad' (patodo) because it is like a goad used to set Sindh horses that have gone astray back onto the right path; it pricks the deceitful mind that runs on the wrong path to bring it to the right path.

It is called a 'faculty' (indriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing; the faculty consisting of wisdom is the 'wisdom faculty' (paññindriya). What is meant? This 'wisdom faculty' is not like 'the faculty of a man is the male faculty' (purisindriya), where the faculty belongs to the man; rather, it is meant that wisdom itself is the faculty, thus it is called the wisdom faculty. It is the 'power of wisdom' (paññābala) because it is unshakable by ignorance. Wisdom itself is the 'sword of wisdom' (paññāsatta) in the sense of cutting through defilements. Wisdom itself is the 'palace of wisdom' (paññāpāsāda) in the sense of being exceedingly high (noble). Wisdom itself is the 'light of wisdom' (paññā-āloka) in the sense of making light. Wisdom itself is the 'radiance of wisdom' (paññā-obhāsa) in the sense of illuminating. Wisdom itself is the 'lamp of wisdom' (paññā-pajjota) in the sense of being brilliant. For when a wise person is seated on a single seat, the ten-thousandfold world system becomes a single light, a single radiance, a single brilliance. Therefore, it is so stated. Although the meaning is accomplished by even one of these three terms, the Elder stated them here in accordance with the Suttas taught by the Blessed One according to the inclinations of beings, such as: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four lights. Which four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the four lights. Among these four lights, the light of wisdom is the best.' Likewise...
344:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four lights. Bhikkhus, there are these four radiances” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.144-145). These discourses were taught according to the inclinations of beings. In accordance with those very discourses, the Elder also gave this teaching here in this Paṭisambhidāmagga. For when the meaning is analyzed in many ways, it is said to be well-analyzed; one person understands it in one way, and another person understands it in another way. Wisdom alone is called a jewel because it creates delight, gives delight, generates delight, is highly esteemed, is a rare occurrence, is incomparable, and is the use of noble beings; therefore, it is called the jewel of wisdom (paññāratana).

It is called non-delusion (amoha) because beings are not deluded by it, or because it is not deluded in the object itself. The term 'investigation of states' (dhamma-vicaya) has the same meaning as previously stated. Why is this term mentioned again? It is mentioned to show that non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. Therefore, it shows: “This non-delusion is not merely a state different from delusion, but non-delusion known as investigation of states, which is the opposite of delusion, is intended here.” Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is the wholesome view (wisdom) that leads to liberation from the round of rebirth as it really is. The questions “In that, what is the knowledge of the origin of suffering? In that, what is the knowledge of the cessation of suffering? In that, what is the knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?” are stated in brief.

## The Explanation of the Two Sets of Four Knowledges of the Truths is finished.

## 64-67. Explanation of the Knowledge of Pure Analytical Insight

In the description of the knowledge of pure analytical insight (suddhika-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), because there is no division of these knowledges, it is stated as “knowledge of meanings is the analytical insight into meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)” and so on, without showing divisions as done below. Even though there is no division of wisdom, because of the existence of diversity by way of the four noble truths personally penetrated, it is stated as “wisdom in the diversity of meanings is the analytical insight into meaning” and so on. There, 'diversity' (nānatta) refers to the state of being manifold of meanings and so on. 'Determination' (vavatthāna) refers to the deciding of meanings and so on. 'Observation' (sallakkhaṇa) refers to the proper seeing of meanings and so on. 'Close observation' (upalakkhaṇa) refers to the intense seeing of meanings and so on. 'Differentiation' (pabheda) refers to the various divisions of meanings and so on. 'Manifestation' (pabhāvana) refers to the producing by making manifest meanings and so on. 'Illumination' (jotana) refers to the showing of meanings and so on. 'Shining forth' (virocana) refers to the various ways of showing meanings and so on. 'Making known' (pakāsana) refers to...
345:
...the shining forth of meanings and so on. Taking the word “diversity” (nānatta) as the root term, it is taught as being common to all [four noble paths]. The term “determination” (vavatthāna) is taught by way of the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). The terms “observation” (sallakkhaṇa) and “close observation” (upalakkhaṇa) are taught by way of the Once-returner (sakadāgāmi). The terms “differentiation” (pabheda) and “manifestation” (pabhāvana) are taught by way of the Non-returner (anāgāmi). The terms “illumination” (jotana), “shining forth” (virocana), and “making known” (pakāsana) are taught by way of the Arahant. Thus should the connection be made in this knowledge of pure analytical insight.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Pure Analytical Insight is finished.

## Thus, the First Part of the Saddhammappakāsinī,

## the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga, is finished.
